en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Vinaya Piṭaka:
The Commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, which is the refuge for all living beings,
[this work is composed] for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya for monks who are practitioners of yoga.
Having gathered together in one place the various scattered explanations that lie outside the canonical texts, I shall present them here clearly and without confusion.
Herein, this is the table of contents (mātikā):
“Reclining during the day, requisites, and the preparation of medicine;
A protective charm, hospitality, making a request, and gathering families.
Fish and meat are not to be consumed; formal determination and assignment.”
Dwelling without a robe, putting away one’s belongings;
engaging in buying and selling, receiving gold and silver;
diverting gains through gifts, trusts, and deposits.
“Earth and the class of living beings—these two kinds of ‘sleeping together’;
having spread out a bed in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, one departs.
There are also four [types of] time-bound [medicines], and four grounds that are allowable.”
Receiving solid food and so forth, the prohibition, and the invitation ceremony;
Going forth, dependence, the boundary, the Uposatha, and the Invitation ceremony;
The entry for the rains, the duties, and the distribution of the four requisites.
“The Kathina, heavy articles, the determination of formal accusations and so forth, the rehabilitation from grave offenses, legal and illegal acts, and miscellaneous matters.

1. Herein, "lying down during the day" means reclining during the day. Regarding this, the following is the analysis:
from the statement, "Monks, I allow one who is seeking seclusion during the day to seek seclusion after securing the door," one who lies down during the day must do so after securing the door.
And here, although it is not stated in the Pāḷi that "this is such-and-such an offense,"...

It has been stated that, although lying down after uncovering oneself is mentioned [as a fault], since it is permitted to lie down having closed the door when a situation arises, the *Aṭṭhakathā* states there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who lies down without closing the door.
Indeed, the *Aṭṭhakathās* were composed by Theras such as Upāli after they understood the intention of the Blessed One. "There is an offense incurred during the day, but not..."
This is also established by the word “night.

But what kind of door should be secured, and what kind should not? Having made a door-panel out of anything such as wood, bamboo, reeds, grass mats, or leaves, and having inserted it below into a mortar and above into a lintel, [that is the kind that should be secured].
Only the revolving door should be secured. Others include: a door with wooden spikes and thorns like the pens for cattle;
a door with wheels at the village entrance; a revolving-panelled door made by joining two or three wheels together on wooden planks or in small booths;
and a sliding-panelled door made like those found in marketplaces. In two [types...]
A door made of leaf-huts with a hand-held tally-stick—where three bamboo slips are inserted at three points—or a cloth-screened door:
such a door must not be kept closed. However, when one has a bowl in hand, opening the door-panel, only a single cloth-screened door is non-offensive;
for all others, there is an offense for one who opens them. But for one who is meditating in seclusion during the day, only a revolving door is permitted.
Regarding that which causes an offense: for one who lies down while restraining the remaining [limbs], whether by restraining them or not, there is no offense;
however, one should lie down having restrained them—this is the proper conduct (vatta).
3. To what extent is the door secured? It is indeed secured once the pins and bolts have been applied.
Furthermore, it is permissible even if given by the measure of a needle; it is permissible even if given by the measure of a water-pot;
it is permissible even when placed so as to merely touch the doorpost; it is permissible even if not touched slightly;
and by the most minimal method, it is permissible even if not touched to the extent that the head does not enter. If it is a place used by many, [he should appoint] a monk...
It is permissible to lie down even after saying to a novice, "Friend, watch the door.
Furthermore, if monks are sitting engaged in robe-making or some other task, it is permissible to lie down after forming the intention, "They will watch the door.
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Even after asking permission from a lay follower..."

It is said: "Or it is permissible to lie down after forming the intention, 'He will watch over me,' but it is not permissible to simply [lie down] without asking permission of a bhikkhunī or a woman. This is correct.
Thus, in all instances, whichever position of the Elders (Theravāda) or the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) is stated later should be accepted as the authoritative standard.
4. Now, if the door’s mortar or upper bolt is broken or not fixed so that it cannot be secured;
or if, for the sake of construction work, a pile of bricks or a heap of clay and such materials has been placed inside the doorway;
or if they have erected a scaffolding (aṭṭa) so that it cannot be secured—when such obstacles exist:
It is permissible to lie down even without having secured the door. However, if there is no door, it is only allowable if one has obtained permission.
One who lies down above must lie down after having brought up a ladder. If there is a device for bolting the top of the ladder, one may lie down even after bolting it.
For one lying down in a room, [the door of] the inner room or the outer door—whichever...
It is permissible to lie down after having restrained oneself in some way. If there are two doors opening onto two sides of a house with a single wall, both doors must be swept;
likewise, even in a three-storied palace, the door must certainly be swept.
If, upon returning from alms-round, many bhikkhus enter a palace such as the Lohapāsāda for the purpose of their midday rest...

They enter; having been told by the senior of the Saṅgha, "Guard the door," or having made the mental resolve, "Guarding the door is indeed his duty," they should enter and lie down. This same procedure should be followed by the junior of the Saṅgha.
For those entering first, [the thought] should be: "Guarding the door is the duty of those who come later. Thus...

It is permissible to make an effort [to guard the door]. However, for those who lie down inside a chamber, or outside at an unsecured door, without having asked permission or made such an effort, there is an offense.
Even at the time of lying down, whether inside or outside, it is indeed permissible to lie down after making the effort, thinking:
"Guarding the door is the responsibility of the gatekeeper at the main gate. This applies likewise in the case of the Lohapāsāda and other such buildings.
Even when lying down on the surface of the sky, the door must certainly be secured.
This is the summary here: this daytime seclusion is spoken of in reference to a place enclosed by anything whatsoever and provided with a secure door;
therefore, whether in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion—wherever it may be—it must have a secure door.
When going to lie down, one should lie down only after securing the door.

If it is a large compound—such as the courtyard of the Mahābodhi, the courtyard of the Lohapāsāda, or a place of assembly for many people—where the door remains unsecured even when locked because those who do not find the door even climb over the wall to wander about, then there is no need to secure it. At night, the door...
If one lies down after opening [the door] and rises when the dawn has appeared, there is no offense. However, if one wakes up and then sleeps again, there is an offense.

But for one who, having determined, "I shall rise when the dawn appears," lies down at night without closing the door and rises exactly according to that determination, there is indeed an offense. (From the *Mahāpaccarī*)
However, it is said: "One who lies down in this manner is not exempt from the dukkaṭa offense of disrespect.

But for one who, having stayed awake for most of the night or having traveled a long distance, lies down during the day while appearing exhausted—sitting on a couch and falling asleep through the power of drowsiness without having even removed his feet from the ground—there is no offense, provided he has fallen into sleep.
Even if one does not know it, if one places a bed upon the foot [of a tree], there is indeed an offense.
There is no offense for one who, having sat down, falls asleep without leaning back. Furthermore, there is no offense for one who, while walking to dispel drowsiness, falls and suddenly wakes up.
However, for one who falls and lies down right there without rising, there is an offense.
Who is released, and who is not released? First, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Only one who lies down with a single break [in the posture] is released.
But even one who lies down having freed his feet from the ground, or one seized by a *yakkha*, or one who has lost consciousness, is not released.
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Only one who is made to lie down after being bound is released. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*...
However, [Mahāpaduma Thera] stated: "Even for one who, while walking, faints and falls down, and then sleeps right there, no offense is seen because that is not within his domain.
Yet the teachers do not speak thus; therefore, it is indeed an offense.
However, two persons are indeed released from the offense: he who is possessed by a *yakkha*, and he who has been made to lie down after being bound."
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of sleeping during the day in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 2.
Discourse on the Determination of Requisites.
6. "Requisites" means the requisites of a recluse. Regarding this, the following is the determination of what is allowable and what is unallowable among the requisites:
some sew a palm-leaf umbrella with thread of five colors, inside or out, and make it glossy;
that is not permitted. However, [it is permitted] if it is sewn with thread of a single color—whether blue, yellow, or any other—either inside...
It is permissible either to sew on the outside or to attach a lattice-work frame for holding the handle of the umbrella;
however, this is permitted only for the sake of making it sturdy, not for the sake of ornamentation or smoothness.
It is not permissible to cut shark-tooth or half-moon patterns into the umbrella leaves. A knob may be attached to the umbrella handle, as one would to a house pillar.
Or a beast-shaped ornament is not permitted. Even if a line has been applied with a needle all over it, that too is not permitted.
One should either break off the knob or the beast-shaped ornament and wear it, or scrape away the line, or wrap the handle with thread.
However, a mushroom-shaped handle is permitted at the base of the handle. By the force of the wind...
For the purpose of preventing movement, they attach a circular umbrella with cords and tie it to the handle;
at that point of attachment, they carve out a ring-like shape and apply a decorative mark—this is permissible.
7. For the purpose of adorning the robe, they sew it with various threads in a pattern like a hundred-petalled flower and attach a border for visitors.

They may also perform any other kind of needlework modification; however, it is not permitted to make patterns at the edge or border such as braids, chains, clubs, and so forth—all of this is forbidden. Only ordinary needlework is permitted.
They also make knotted cloth strips and hanging cloth strips, either eight-cornered or sixteen-cornered; therein they [depict] tridents, elephants, clubs, and the like.
If they show [the patterns] or carve out eyes like those of a crab, none of it is permissible; only a four-cornered pattern is allowed.

Furthermore, when the robe is dyed, corner-thread marks and pressure-marks are permissible if they are not easily discernible. It is not permissible to place the robe in sour gruel, flour-dough, oil-cakes, and so forth;
however, at the time of working on the robe, it is permissible for the purpose of washing hand-dirt, fine dust, and the like when it has become soiled.
It is permissible for the purpose of washing, but it is not permissible to add perfume, lac, or oil to the dye.
Among dyes, everything except turmeric is permissible as a root-dye;
and everything except madder and *tuṅgahāra* is permissible as a stem-dye. *Tuṅgahāra* is the name of a certain thorny tree; of that—
Yellow turmeric is a dye for stalks. With the exception of *lodda* and *kaṇḍula*, all dyes made from bark are permissible.
With the exception of the *allī* leaf and the *nīlī* leaf, all dyes made from leaves are permissible.
However, it is permissible to dye once with a leaf that has been used by a householder, provided it is an *allī* leaf. With the exception of the *kiṃsuka* flower and the *kusumbha* flower...
All flower-dyes are permissible. However, regarding fruit-dyes, there is nothing that is not permissible.
8. After dyeing the robe, one must not rub it against a conch shell, a gem, or anything else whatsoever.
One must not even scrub it in a wooden tub while kneeling on the ground and holding it with the hands. Nor should one place it in a tub or on a plank [and rub it].

However, it is permissible to strike [the cloth] with the hand after having dipped it [in dye]; even that must not be done with a clenched fist. The ancient Elders, moreover, did not even place it in a wooden trough.
One person stands holding the robe, while another, having taken it in his hands, strikes it with his hand.
It is not permissible for there to be a cord at the corner of the robe; it should be cut when the time for dyeing arrives. As for what was said: "I authorize..."
"Monks, [this is] the 'ear-string,'" thus it was permitted; that should be made into a loop and tied when dyeing, for the purpose of hanging [the robe].
Even on the cord, lines or knots for the sake of ornamentation are not allowed;
having removed them, it may be used.
9. It is not permitted to draw lines on an alms bowl or a dish with a sharp instrument, whether on the inside or the outside.
It is not permitted to place a bowl on a lathe, polish it, and fire it, thinking, "We shall make it jewel-colored"; however, an oil-colored finish is permitted.
It is not permitted to apply mural painting (wall-decoration) on the surface of a bowl; however, the "crocodile-tooth" pattern is permitted.
A line is not permitted on the upper, lower, or inner surface of the handle of a sunshade; however, a line is permitted on the rim of the sunshade’s opening.
10. For the sake of beautifying a waistband, it is not permitted to twist the thread double in various places or to produce "crab-eyes" (knotted protrusions);
however, one may twist the thread double at both ends for the sake of securing the fringe.
It is permissible. However, at the mouth of the fringe, it is not permissible to make any decorative form such as a pitcher, a makara’s mouth, or the head of a water-monster;
nor is it permissible to depict eyes here and there, or to make floral designs and the like, or even a polished waistband.
It must be simply straight, like a fish-bone, a date-palm leaf, or a smooth strip of leather.
or having made [it so], it is permissible to beat it. For a waistband (*kāyabandhana*), one fringe is permissible; two, three, or even four are permissible, but beyond that they are not permissible.
A waistband made of a single cord is permissible, but even one in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a type of net or fringed ornament) is not permissible;
however, fringes in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* are permissible. When many cords are joined together as one, by means of one...
It should not be said that what is made by wrapping [the cloth] continuously is "many-stringed"; that is permissible.

Regarding the method of the waistband (*kāyabandhana*), any decorative form such as the eight auspicious symbols (*aṭṭhamangala*) and so forth is not permitted; however, a mere boundary line is permitted. They also make a loop at both ends of the woven cloth for the sake of securing it firmly; this too is permitted. 11.

In the ointment box (*añjanī*), forms of women, men, quadrupeds, or birds, or various designs such as floral patterns, vine-work, makara-dentals, cow-urine patterns, or half-moons and the like—[are not permitted].
Alternatively, it is not permissible for it to have a modified shape;

rather, having rubbed it or broken it down so that its original form is no longer recognizable, it should be used by wrapping it with thread. However, a straight eye-salve stick (añjanī) that is four-sided, eight-sided, or sixteen-sided is permissible.
Furthermore, two or three circular lines are permissible on its lower part, and also on its neck.
A single circular line is permitted for the purpose of securing the lid.
It is not permitted to apply decorative coloring (vaṇṇamaṭṭhakamma) even to the applicator stick for the ointment;

nor is it permitted to apply decorative coloring with any kind of multicolored thread to the ointment box. The same rule applies to the key-case. As for the key itself, decorative coloring is not permitted.
It is not permissible [to sew] with a needle; likewise, it is not permissible with a thimble. However, it is permissible to sew anything with any single-colored thread. 12.
On the neck [of a bowl], it is not permissible to have a round jewel or anything else that is polished and colored; however, a demarcation line on the neck is permissible.
On the handle, it is not permissible to cause a jewel, a knob, or anything at all to protrude; [this applies] to the handle.
However, a boundary line is permissible. They fashion the fingernail-cutter as a curved shape; therefore, that is permissible.
Whether on the upper fire-drill, the lower fire-drill, or the upper pressing-stick, no kind of decorative polish or ornamentation is permitted.
However, there is a circle in the middle of the pressing-stick; there, a mere boundary line is allowed.
It is permissible. They make a needle-pincers by which they hold the needle while sharpening it;

in that regard, any kind of polished ornamentation, such as a makara-mouth design and so forth, is not permissible. However, a mere mouth [for the handle] for the purpose of holding the needle is permissible.
Regarding the axe for cutting tooth-sticks as well, any kind of polished ornamentation is not permissible; it must be made straight from allowable metal.
It is permissible to tie [the handle] on both sides, or in a four-cornered or eight-cornered shape. Regarding the walking staff (*kattaradaṇḍa*) as well, any kind of polished color is not permitted;
however, one or two circular lines at the bottom and a knob the size of an *ahicchattaka* mushroom at the top are permitted.
13. Regarding oil vessels: except for those made of horn, bamboo, gourd, or coconut shell, [those shaped like] a female form are not permitted.
The human form and all other decorative work involving color and polish are permissible.
[This applies to] beds and chairs, mattresses and pillows, floor coverings, foot-wipers, meditation-cushions for the walking path,
brooms, dustbins, dye-vats, water-jugs, water-pots, foot-stools, wooden benches, bracelets, and staffs.
Regarding the bowl-cover and the palm-leaf fan used for fanning—in these cases, all forms of floral decoration and work in variegated polish are permitted.
14. Furthermore, in the case of a dwelling, even if made of all kinds of gems, work in variegated polish is permitted on the door panels, window shutters, and so forth.
In a dwelling, there is nothing whatsoever that is prohibited, except for a discordant dwelling. A discordant dwelling...
This refers to lodgings built by royal favorites within the boundary (*sīmā*) of others.
Therefore, those who build such lodgings should be told: "Do not build lodgings within our boundary.
If they nevertheless proceed to build them, they should be told again: "Do not do this; do not create an obstacle for our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies."
"Do not break the harmony; otherwise, even the lodgings you have prepared will no longer remain in their place.
If they continue to act by force, then when their assembly of modest monks has grown large and it is possible to obtain a righteous adjudication, one should send word to them:
"Take back your residence. If [they do so] up to the third time...
If they take it away, that is good. If they do not take it away, then—with the exception of the Bodhi tree and the shrine—the remaining dwellings should be dismantled;
however, this must not be done by those who would leave them unusable. Rather, one should remove the roofing, rafters, bricks, and so forth in due order and send word to them:
"Take these building materials for yourselves. If they take them, that is good.
If they do not carry it away, then when those building materials have become rotten due to frost, rain, wind, heat, and so forth; or have been stolen by thieves;
or have been burnt by fire—the monks who are the owners of the boundary are free from blame.

It is not permissible to accuse them, saying, "Our building materials have been lost by you," or "The responsibility for this falls upon you. However, regarding that which [was lost] by the monks who are the owners of the boundary...

Whatever has been done is indeed well done. Even a bhikkhu who is learned and knowledgeable in the Vinaya, having seen another bhikkhu wandering about carrying an improper requisite, may have it cut or broken; he is without fault.
He should neither be accused nor reminded [of the offense], nor can it be said of him: "This is my requisite which you have destroyed; give it back to me."
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of requisites in the Compendium of Determinations on the Vinaya Excluding the Pāḷi. 3.
The Discourse on the Determination of the Making of Medicines and Other Items.

15. Regarding the preparation of medicine and the provision of protection: first, concerning the preparation of medicine, this is the determination—it must not be prepared for any outsider who happens to arrive;
one who does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, it may be prepared for five who share the same Dhamma:
for a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (*sikkhamānā*), a male novice (*sāmaṇera*), and a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*).
For it is not permitted for one who is devoted to these three trainings—possessing equal virtue, faith, and wisdom—to fail to provide medicine.
And when providing it, if they have some, one should take what belongs to them, compound it, and give it;

if they have none, one should do so with what belongs to oneself. If one has nothing even of one's own, one may obtain it through the practice of alms-round or from a place where one has been invited by relatives.
Or it should be sought; if it cannot be obtained, even if it has not been requested for the sake of the sick, one may bring it and prepare it.
It is also permissible to make [robes] for five other persons: for one’s mother, for one’s father, for those who attend on them, for one’s own attendant, and for a *paṇḍupalāsa*.
A *paṇḍupalāsa* is one who is seeking the going-forth and is preparing his bowl and robes.
He dwells in the monastery for that long. Among them, if his parents are wealthy and do not expect anything in return, it is permissible not to provide [assistance].
However, if they are even established in royalty and do expect something, it is not permissible not to provide it. To those who expect medicine, medicine must be given;
to those who do not know how to compound it, it must be compounded and given. For the sake of all, among fellow practitioners of the Dhamma...
It should be sought in the same manner as previously described. However, if he brings his mother to the monastery and attends to her, he must perform all the services without touching them;

he should give her hard and soft food with his own hands. As for his father, he should attend to him just as he would a novice, performing tasks such as bathing and massaging with his own hands. And those who attend to their mother and father—

They look after [the sick]; for them also, it should be done in exactly the same way. One called a *veyyāvaccakara* (servant) is one who, having received wages, cuts wood in the forest or performs some other work;
when illness arises in him, medicine must be administered until his relatives see him. But as for one who, while remaining entirely dependent on the bhikkhus, performs all the tasks...
If he does so, medicine must indeed be administered to him; one should behave toward even a novice monk as toward a withered leaf.

17. It is also permissible to do so for ten others: an elder brother, a younger brother, an elder sister, a younger sister, a junior mother, a senior mother, a junior father, a senior father, a paternal aunt, and a maternal uncle. For all of them, however—
While preparing it, one should take medicine belonging to those very people, compound it, and give it back.
However, if they do not have enough and request, saying, "Venerable sir, please give us [some]; we shall repay you," it should be given on loan.
Even if they do not request it, one may say, "We have medicine; take some on loan," or, "When..."
One should give [the requisites] after forming the intention, "They will have need of them; then they shall take them. If they acknowledge [the debt], it may be accepted.
If they do not pay, they should not be pressed for payment. Apart from these ten types of relatives, this should not be done for others.
However, for the descendants of these relatives, as long as they belong to the seventh generation of the family line, one may cause them to bring the four requisites.
There is no offense for one who prepares medicine without a formal request, nor is there an offense of "corrupting a family" for performing medical treatment.
If the brother’s wife or the sister’s husband is ill, it is permissible if they are relatives.
If they are not relatives, [the medicine] should be prepared by the brother and sister and given with the instruction: “Give this where you are looking after them. Or else:
Having prepared it for those sons, it should be given with the instruction: "Give this to your mother and father.
By this method, the legal decision should be understood in all cases.
And when novices are having medicinal requisites brought from the forest for their sake, they should have them brought by novices who are relatives.
If strangers bring [medicines] for one's own sake, they should be given. They too, under the pretext of performing their duties, should bring them, thinking, "We are bringing them for our preceptor.
If the preceptor’s parents, being ill, come to the monastery while the preceptor has gone abroad, the student (saddhivihārika) must give the medicine belonging to the preceptor.
If there is nothing, one should give one’s own medicine after having relinquished it to the preceptor.

Even if one has nothing oneself, one should seek it in the manner already described, make it the property of the preceptor, and then give it. The preceptor should also act in exactly the same way toward the mother and father of the resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*).
This same method applies to the teacher and the student (*ācariya-antevāsika*) as well. This also applies to any other visitor.

Whether it be a thief, one defeated in battle, a lord abandoned by his kinsmen, a pauper, or a traveler who has fallen ill, if he enters a monastery, medicine should be prepared for all of them without expectation of anything in return. 18.
There may be a faithful family that supports the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the four requisites, acting as parents to them.
In that case, if someone is ill and they say out of trust, "Venerable sir, please prepare medicine for him and give it," one should neither give it nor prepare it.

However, if they ask after understanding what is allowable (kappiya), saying, "Venerable sir, what medicine do you prepare for such-and-such a disease? one may say, "Having taken this and that, one prepares it."
It is permissible. However, when asked, "Venerable sir, my mother is ill; please tell me what medicine she should take," one must not give a direct prescription.
Instead, one should engage in conversation with them, saying, "Friend, for such-and-such a monk suffering from this same illness, what medicine did they use?
or "Venerable sir, such-and-such and such-and-such are the medicines. Having heard that, [the patient]...
If another person prepares medicine for one’s mother, it is permissible.

It is said that when Queen Vasabha was afflicted by illness, the Elder Mahāpaduma was approached by a certain woman who came and asked him about her; instead of saying, "I do not know," he conversed with the bhikkhus in exactly that manner.
Hearing this, they prepared medicine for her. When the illness had subsided, [he gave her] his three robes.
Having filled a medicine basket with three hundred kahāpaṇas and brought it, they placed it at the feet of the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, perform an offering of flowers.
The Elder, thinking, "This is called the teacher’s portion," had it accepted as a permissible gift and performed the flower offering.
This, then, is how one should proceed regarding medicine.
19. However, regarding a protective chant (*paritta*): when it is said, "Venerable sirs, please perform a protective chant for the sick person," one should not do so;
but when it is said, "Please recite a protective chant," then it should be recited. Even if one thinks, "People are ignorant by nature;
if this is not done, they will feel regret," then it should be performed. [Having made] protective water and protective thread...
When they say, "Do so," he should stir the water with his hand, rub the thread [in it], and give it back to them.
If he gives water from the monastery or thread belonging to himself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When people take the water and the thread, sit down, and say, "Recite the protective chant (paritta)," he should do so. If they do not know how, he should explain it to them.
When people pour water on the feet of monks who are sitting and place a thread [around their necks] before departing, saying, "Perform a protective recitation (paritta);
chant the paritta," the feet must not be removed. For people become remorseful [if they do so].
Even if they send someone from within the village to the monastery for the sake of a sick person, saying, "Let them chant the paritta," it should be chanted.

When a disease or a calamity arises within the village, such as in the royal palace or similar places, they are summoned and asked to recite; the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta and other discourses should be recited.
Even when sent with the message, "Come and give the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) to the sick person, preach the Dhamma;
come to the royal inner quarters or to the minister’s house and give the training rules, preach the Dhamma," they go there.
The training rules (sikkhāpada) should be given, and the Dhamma should be taught. If they call out, "Come for the sake of attending the dead," one should not go.

However, it is permissible to go under the pretext of a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), thinking, "We shall obtain mindfulness of death through the sight of the charnel ground and the sight of the foul.

As for the statement, "It is said there is no offense for one who has no intention of dying even when the funeral pyre has been set alight," it is not on that account alone [that one may disregard the precepts].
A blow should be administered to one possessed by a non-human spirit; alternatively, a palm leaf or a protective thread (*parittasutta*) should be tied to the hand or foot.
Protective discourses (*paritta*) such as the *Ratana-sutta* should be recited, a Dhamma talk should be given saying, "Do not harass a virtuous monk," or the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta* should be recited.
Now, the preliminary practice for the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta should be understood as follows: first of all, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should not be recited;
rather, these three—the Metta Sutta, the Dhajagga Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta—should be recited for seven days.
If [the patient] is released, that is well. If they are not released, then the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be recited. By one reciting it:
Furthermore, a bhikkhu must not eat flour or meat, nor should he dwell in a cemetery. Why? Because non-human beings (amanussa) find an opportunity to enter.
Having had the place for performing the protective rite (paritta) smeared with green grass, one should sit there after arranging a pure seat.
The bhikkhu performing the protective rite [must be accompanied] by those carrying wooden shields and weapons as they lead him from the monastery to the house.
He should be led away surrounded [by guards]. One should not speak while sitting in the open air;

rather, one should sit with the doors and windows closed, surrounded by those with weapons in hand, preceded by a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), and having first caused him to take up the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), one should establish him in virtue (*sīla*) and then perform the protective recitation (*paritta*). In this way, too, he may be liberated.
If he is unable [to walk], he should be brought to the monastery, laid down on the terrace of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*), and made to perform an offering of seats;
lamps should be lit, the shrine terrace should be swept, and auspicious words (*maṅgalakathā*) should be recited.

A proclamation should be made for the entire assembly to gather. In the grove surrounding the monastery, there is what is called the "eldest tree"; there one should say, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus awaits your arrival."
It must be sent. It is not permitted for anyone not to come to every place where an assembly is held. Therefore, one possessed by a non-human spirit should be asked, "What is your name?
Once the name has been stated, he should be addressed by that very name: "So-and-so, you have a share in the garlands, perfumes, and so forth;
you have a share in the offering of seats; you have a share in the alms-food; [you have a share] from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for you..."
"The Discourse on the Great Auspiciousness was spoken for the sake of a gift; release this out of respect for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. Thus he should be made to release it.
If he does not release it, one should inform the deities: "You know that this non-human being does not carry out our word;
we shall carry out the Buddha’s command. Then the protective chant (paritta) should be recited. This, first of all, is the preliminary procedure for laypeople.

But if a bhikkhu has been seized by a non-human being, one should wash the seats, have the entire assembly announced, give a portion of alms-food (pattidāna) for scents, garlands, and so forth, and recite the protective chant (paritta); this is the service to be performed for the bhikkhus.
Thus should one proceed regarding the protective chant.
20. Regarding the distribution of alms-food, this is the analysis: to whom should unclaimed alms-food be given, and to whom should it not be given?
First of all, it should be given to one’s mother and father; even if it is worth a kahāpaṇa coin, there is no misappropriation of what was offered in faith.
It should also be given to those who attend upon one’s mother and father, to a servant, and to a fallen leaf.

In that regard, it is permissible to give even a withered leaf after placing it in a bowl; however, apart from that, it is not permissible for others, including one’s own parents who are householders.
For the requisites used by those gone forth are like a shrine (cetiyatthāniya) to householders.
Furthermore, this so-called "unclaimed alms-food" (anāmaṭṭha-piṇḍapāta) may be given even to a robber or a thief who has arrived, as well as to a ruler. Why is that?
For even when alms are not being given, they become angry, thinking, "They will not give," and even when they are being given, they become angry, thinking, "They are giving what is leftover.
Being thus enraged, they even deprive others of life and create obstacles for the Dispensation.
In this regard, the story of the thief-nāga who wandered about longing for sovereignty should be told. This is how one should conduct oneself regarding alms that have not been touched.

To whom should this hospitality be extended, and to whom should it not? Hospitality must indeed be shown to anyone who arrives at the monastery, whether they be a newcomer, a pauper, a thief, or a lord. How so?
First, seeing a newcomer who has arrived at the monastery with his provisions exhausted, one should give him water to drink, saying, "Drink some water."
Foot-oil for massaging should be given; to one who arrives at the proper time, rice gruel and a meal should be given;
to one who arrives at an improper time, if there is rice, the rice should be given. Even if someone arrives at an untimely hour, one should not say, "Go away";
rather, a place to sleep should be provided. All of this must be done without expecting anything in return. "People, indeed, are givers of the four requisites; thus..."
One should not give rise to the thought: "When we repeatedly perform acts of conciliation, they will become confident and thus provide assistance.
However, even property belonging to the Saṅgha may be given to thieves.

For the purpose of illustrating the benefits of such hospitality, there are the story of the thief Nāga, the story of King Mahānāga who went to Jambudīpa with his brother, and [the story] of the four [brothers] during the reign of their father king.
Many such stories, including "The Story of the Ministers" and "The Story of the Fearless Robbers," are recounted in detail in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

Herein is the illustration of one such story: It is said that in the island of Siṃhala, a robber named Abhaya, with a retinue of five hundred men, established his camp at a certain place and lived there, terrorizing the surrounding region for three leagues. The inhabitants of Anurādhapura...
They did not cross the Kadamba River, and the movement of people on the road to Cetiyagiri was cut off.
Then one day, a bandit went there thinking, "I will plunder Cetiyagiri. When the monastery attendants saw him, they informed the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya.
The Elder asked, "Is there ghee, molasses, and so forth? "There is, venerable sir," they replied. "Give it to the bandits," he said.
“There is rice. “There is, venerable sir; there is rice brought for the Saṅgha, as well as cooked vegetables and milk products.
“Prepare a meal and give it to the bandits. The monastery attendants did so.
After the bandits had eaten the meal, they asked, “By whom was this hospitality extended? “By our noble Elder Abhaya.”
The thieves went to the elder, paid homage, and said: "We came intending to seize whatever belongs to the Saṅgha and the cetiya by way of theft;
however, we have become inspired with confidence by this hospitality of yours.
From today onward, let the righteous protection of the monastery be under our charge; let the citizens come and offer gifts."
"Let them pay homage to the Cetiya. From that time forth, whenever the city-dwellers came to give alms, [the monks] would go out to meet them right at the riverbank and escort them to the monastery;
they also remained there providing protection for those giving alms within the monastery.
When it was time for the monks to depart, those thieves would deliver the remnants of the food to the monks and then turn back.
Then one day, a disparaging discussion arose among the community of monks:
"The Elder, out of a sense of lordship, gave what belonged to the Saṅgha to the robbers. The Elder had an assembly convened and said:
"The robbers came thinking, 'We shall seize both the Saṅgha’s ordinary property and the property belonging to the Cetiya. Then I [acted] so that they would not take it away."
“Whatever hospitality has been rendered, let all of it be gathered together and valued; for that reason, let the goods not stolen be gathered together and valued.
Then, even all that had been given by the Elder was not worth a single fine cloth painting-covering in the shrine hall. Thereupon they said, “What has been done by the Elder...”
"Since hospitality has been well-performed, one cannot be reproved or reminded [of a fault], nor is there any liability for a fine or forfeiture.
Thus, having observed that hospitality brings such great benefit, it should be performed by a wise bhikkhu.
Thus ends the summary of the Vinaya analysis not found in the canonical texts (*Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe*).
The discussion on the determination of the preparation of medicines and so forth is finished.
4. The Discussion on the Determination of Intimation (Viññatti).
21. "Intimation" means requesting. Regarding this, the following is the determination: it is not permissible to request a person for the purpose of cutting off their roots [of life].
It is permissible to request, "Give me a man for assistance and for labor.
It is likewise permissible to request the performance of manual labor—termed *hatthakamma*—which constitutes the duties of a male. For manual labor is not a specific object;
therefore, setting that aside, [it is permissible to ask for] whatever remains of one's own work, such as hunting deer, fishing, and so forth.
All is permissible. Whether asked or not asked, "Venerable sir, why have you come? What service may we do for you? it is allowable to request [assistance];

there is no fault in making such a request. However, hunters and the like should not be requested for their own specific work, nor should they be requested by saying, "Give us manual labor," without specifying the task. For if they are requested in this way, they might say, "Very well..."
Having dismissed the monks with the words, "Venerable sirs," they might even kill a deer and bring it back.
However, one should request them specifically, saying, "There is something that must be done in the monastery; please provide manual labor there.
Or, [one may take] a farmer who, having taken implements such as plows and harrows, is going to plow, sow, or reap, and is thus occupied with his own work.
It is indeed permissible to ask for some other kind of manual labor. However, if there is one who eats scraps,
or anyone else who is inactive, idle in speech, or remains sleeping, it is permissible— even without asking him—
to have him do whatever one wishes by saying, "Come here, my good man, do this or that."
However, they explain this method in order to demonstrate that manual labor is entirely permissible:
if a bhikkhu wishes to have a palace built, he should go to the house of stone-cutters for the sake of pillars and say, "It is necessary to obtain manual labor, lay followers.
[They will ask], "What should be done, venerable sir? [He replies], "The stone pillars must be extracted..."
“...should be given. If they give it after having it removed, or if they give it from their own pillar that has been removed, it is permissible.
Furthermore, if they say, “Venerable sir, we have no time to do manual labor;
please have another removed, and we will pay for its cost,” then after having it removed, [one may take] from those people who have had the stone pillars removed.
It is permissible to say, "Give me the timber. By this same method, for the sake of palace timber, one may go to carpenters;
for the sake of bricks, to bricklayers; for the sake of roofing, to roofers;
and for the sake of painting, to painters—in short, for whatever purpose is required, one may go to those respective craftsmen for that specific purpose.

It is permissible to go into his presence and ask for manual labor; and by means of such a request for manual labor, it is also permissible to take all that is obtained, whether by cutting down the very roots [of the trees] or by providing food and wages.
Furthermore, one who causes [wood] to be brought from the forest must have everything brought that has not been inhabited.

22. Not only by one desiring to have a palace built, but also by one desiring to have beds, chairs, bowls, water-strainers, Dhamma-caskets, robes, and so forth made, having obtained wood, metal, thread, and the like, one should approach the various craftsmen and request manual labor in the manner already described.
And by means of requesting manual labor, either through the cutting down of the price [of the goods] or through the provision of food and wages—

Or rather, even if it has been obtained, all of it should be accepted. However, if they do not wish to do the work themselves but expect payment for their food, one should not give them unallowable coins or the like;
it is permissible to give rice and so forth after having sought them out according to the practice of alms-gathering.
Having had a bowl made by manual labor and likewise having had it fired, [one may use] oil for wiping the newly fired bowl.
When one has entered the village, having observed that [the donor] has come for alms, the bowl should be covered with the hand when rice gruel or a meal is being brought.
If a female lay follower asks, "What is it, venerable sir?", one should say, "The bowl is newly washed;
there is a need for wiping-oil. If she says, "Give it, venerable sir," and takes the bowl, one should wipe it with oil and [pour] the rice gruel into it.
Or if one gives after filling [the bowl] with food, it is not called a formal request (*viññatti*); it is permissible to accept.

23. If monks, having already gone for alms and arrived at the assembly hall, stand there because they do not see a seat, and if lay followers, seeing the monks standing there, themselves have seats brought, then those who sit down and depart—[there is no offense].
One must depart after having asked for permission; for those who have departed without asking, there is no liability for what is lost, yet departing after asking is the proper duty (*vatta*).
If seats have been brought by monks who were told, "Bring the seats," one must still depart only after asking for permission;
for those who depart without asking, there is both a breach of duty and liability for what is lost. This same principle applies to rugs, coverlets, and so forth.
If there are many flies, one should say, "Bring a fly-whisk.
If they bring branches of the *pucimanda* tree or other such items, these should be accepted after having them made allowable (*kappiya*).
If the water vessel in the dining hall is empty, one should not say, "Take the water-pot. For one who is placing the water-pot into an empty vessel...
If one were to break [the rule], it is permissible to say, "Go to a river or a pond and bring water," but it is not permissible to say,
"Bring it from the house," nor is it permissible to consume what has been brought. When those performing their meal duties in a dining hall or in the forest,
whatever leaf or fruit grown there that is fit for use as a supplement to the meal and has not been previously inhabited— [is permissible].
Or, if he has someone bring something while performing some work, it is permissible to use it after having it brought by means of manual labor;
however, manual labor must not be made to be performed by shameless monks or novices.
This, first of all, is the method regarding those who perform manly tasks.
24. However, it is not permissible to have a bull brought from a place where one is neither known nor invited; for one who has him brought, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even from a place where one is known and invited, it is not permissible to ask for it so as to cut off the source [of future supply];
it is permissible everywhere by way of temporary use. And having protected and tended the bull thus brought, the owner should be made to accept it. If his...
If a leg or a horn breaks or is lost, it is well if the owners accept [the responsibility]; if they do not accept it, there is a fine.
If they say, "We shall give it back to you yourselves," one must not accept it.
But when they say, "We shall give it to the monastery," one should say, "Tell the monastery attendants so that they may look after it."
25. It is not permissible to say, “Give us a cart,” even to those who are unrelated and have not invited one;
this constitutes a formal request (*viññatti*), and one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, it is permissible in the case of relatives or where one has been invited;

it is also permissible for a temporary period, but after the work has been done, it must be returned. If the wheels or other parts break, they must be repaired before being returned; if they are lost, [they must be replaced].
It becomes a neck. When it is said, “We give it to you yourselves,” it is permissible to accept what is called a wooden vessel.

This same principle applies to axes, adzes, hatchets, mallets, and spades, as well as to creepers and so forth that belong to others. Solicitation is permitted only for creepers and such items that are sufficient to constitute a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*), and not for anything less than that.
26. However, it is permissible to have whatever has not been dwelled upon brought [to one].
For it is precisely in a place that is guarded and protected that what is called "requesting" (*viññatti*) occurs. This is entirely and in every way impermissible regarding two requisites.

Regarding the requisite of lodging (*senāsana-paccaya*), however, the mere act of requesting by saying, "Bring it! Give it! is not permitted; but indirect speech (*parikathā*), hinting (*obhāsa*), and making signs (*nimitta-kamma*) are permitted.

In this context, when someone desires a Uposatha hall, a dining hall, or some other lodging, and says by way of such expressions as, "It would be fitting to build such a lodging in this spot," or "It is suitable," or "It is appropriate," and so forth—this is called *parikathā* (indirect talk). For example:
"Lay followers, where do you live? "In a mansion, venerable sir. "What..."
However, for monks, it is not permissible for lay followers to build a mansion; such statements as these are called "hinting" (*obhāsa*).

Seeing people, stretching out a rope, having a stake driven in, or when asked, "What is this, Venerable Sir?", replying, "We shall build a dwelling here"—such actions are called "sign-making" (*nimittakamma*).
Furthermore, even requesting requisites for the sick is permissible, let alone indirect speech and the like.
Thus ends the Discussion on the Determination of Intimation in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 5.
Discussion on the Determination of the Support of Families.
27. *Kulasaṅgaha* (Inclusion of Families): The inclusion of families by means of flowers, fruits, and so forth, is called *kulasaṅgaha*. Herein is the detailed analysis:
for the purpose of including families, it is not permissible to plant or cause to be planted flowering shrubs and the like;
to water or cause to be watered them; to pluck or cause to be plucked their flowers; or to string or cause to be strung them together. In this regard:
These five should be known: improper speech, proper speech, indirect expression, hinting, and making signs. 28.
Therein, "improper speech" means the pounding or having pounded of fresh greens; the digging or having dug of a pit;
the planting or having planted of a flowering shrub; the tying or having tied of a fence; and [the taking] of water...
Sprinkling means causing to sprinkle; it includes making the channel visible, sprinkling with allowable water, and sprinkling with water for washing the hands, feet, face, or bathing.
"Allowable terminology" refers to such statements as, "Know this tree," "Know this pit," "Know this flower garden," or "Know the water here," as well as straightening a dry channel.
"A method" refers to [the planting of] flower gardens and so forth by a wise person...

“[Trees] should be planted; before long they will lead to great benefit,” and so forth. What is called “illumination” (obhāsa) is standing while holding a hoe, a pickaxe, and so on, as well as a garland and a spade.
For when novices and others see one standing thus, they think, “The elder wishes to have [something] done,” and they go and do it.
What is called “sign-making” (nimittakamma) is bringing a hoe, a pickaxe, an axe, a hatchet, a water vessel, and so forth, and placing them nearby.
29. These five are not permitted for the purpose of gathering a family, such as in planting, causing to plant, and so forth.

For the purpose of consuming the fruit, only the two modes of expression—*kappiya-vohāra* (permissible terminology) and *akappiya-vohāra* (impermissible terminology)—are not permitted; the other three are permitted. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated:
"Even *kappiya-vohāra* is permitted, and that which is permitted for one's own consumption is [also permitted] for another person."
It is stated: "It is permissible even for the sake of the Saṅgha or for the sake of a cetiya.
However, for the sake of a grove, a forest, or shade, it is not permissible to use even a mere improper expression; the rest is permissible.
And not only the rest, but whatever [is needed]—such as making a path straight, sprinkling water that is allowable (kappiya-udaka), or making a bathing place and bathing—is also permissible.
It is also permissible to discard water used for washing hands, feet, and the face there.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*, it is stated: "It is also permissible to plant [trees] oneself upon allowable ground (*kappiyabhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is permissible to consume the fruit of that which has been planted or caused to be planted for the sake of a monastery or similar purpose.
30. Now, this detailed determination of offenses from the beginning:

for one who plants a flowering shrub on unsuitable ground for the purpose of defiling a family, there is both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa*; likewise for one who causes it to be planted by means of an improper transaction.

Even when planting on suitable ground, there is a *dukkaṭa* for both the planter and the one who causes it to be planted. In both cases, even if there are many [plants], it is [an offense] for a single command.
In the case of planting, there is only one offense: either a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa*, or a simple *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense in having [trees] planted in a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area made allowable) or an *akappiya-bhūmi* (an area not made allowable) for the purpose of consumption, provided it is done using allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*).

However, for one who plants in an *akappiya-pathavī* (unallowable ground) even for the sake of a monastery or similar purpose, or who has them planted by means of an *akappiya-vacana* (unallowable speech), there is a *pācittiya*. This method, moreover, is found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
It has not been well analyzed; however, it is analyzed in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Regarding sprinkling and causing to sprinkle with unallowable water, there is a *pācittiya* offense in all cases;

there is also a *dukkaṭa* for the purpose of corrupting families or for the purpose of consumption. With allowable water, there is a *dukkaṭa* for those same two purposes, and here, for the purpose of consumption...

There is no offense in having [a tree] sprinkled by means of allowable speech. However, regarding the points where an offense occurs, one should understand that there is a multiplicity of offenses due to the multiplicity of applications, such as the cutting off of streams.
When plucking [flowers] for the purpose of supporting a family, there are *dukkaṭa* and *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of flowers; in other cases, there are only *pācittiya* offenses.
However, one who plucks many flowers with a single effort must be dealt with according to that specific effort.
If one is commanded once for the purpose of defiling a family and plucks many flowers, there is only one offense of *pācittiya* and one of *dukkaṭa*; otherwise, it is simply *pācittiya*. 31.
Regarding the making and having made of garlands, all six varieties of flower-work are to be understood: the knotted (*ganthima*), the woven (*gopphima*), and so forth.

[Flowers] are knotted, woven, filled, or blown. Among these, "knotted" (ganthima) should be understood as referring to flowers such as blue lotuses, red lotuses, and so forth, which have long stalks; it is precisely that which is made by tying stalk to stalk or stem to stem.
Even for a monk or a nun to make such [a flower] is not permissible by word.

It is not permissible to have it made [by command], but it is permissible to have it made using appropriate speech such as, "Know this; it will look beautiful when done in this way; act so that these flowers are not scattered," and so forth.

A "gopphima" (garland for the ankles) is a garland of *vassika* flowers and the like, made either with a single stem or with stems on both sides, using thread or materials such as bark-fiber (*vāka*).
Having doubled a piece of bark, a thread, or a cord, they insert stalked flowers such as *nīpa* blossoms into it and bind them in a row;
this too is merely "anklet-style" (*gopphima*). All of these are likewise not permitted, for the same reasons as previously stated.

That which is called "pierced-style" (*vedhima*) consists of stalked flowers such as *vassika* blossoms [inserted] into their stalks, while stalkless flowers such as *vakula* blossoms are [inserted] into themselves...
They pierce through the holes with needles, awls, chisels, and so forth, and thread them; this is called "pierced" (*vedhima*). That is not permissible for the same reasons as before.
However, some insert thorns or awls and the like into the trunk of a plantain tree and place flowers there, piercing them through;
others do so on thorny branches; and still others do so for the purpose of making flower-canopies or flower-pavilions.
Regarding thorns placed by inserting them into the umbrella and the wall: some [hold that] it is permissible to tie thorns to the canopy of the Dhamma-seat;
others [hold that] one may pierce flowers such as the *kaṇikāra* with pins, making them like a "parasol upon a parasol" (*chatādhichatta*), but that is indeed too coarse.
However, for the purpose of piercing flowers, even tying a single thorn to the canopy of the Dhamma-seat, or piercing even a single flower with thorns and the like, is permissible.
It is not permissible to pierce [the wall] or to insert flowers into the flowers themselves.

However, there is no fault in inserting flowers into the gaps of lattice-work, canopies, railings, pegs, flower-receptacles, palm-leaf fans, balls, and so forth, or into the spaces between *asoka* clusters; for this does not constitute "piercing.
The same principle applies to the "Dhamma-rope" (dhammarajju) as well.
"Veṭhimaṃ" (wound or wrapped) should be understood as referring to flower garlands and flower bouquets.
For some, when making a head-garland, wrap flowers around it to give it the shape of a vase at the bottom;
others bind eight or ten blue lotuses (*utpala*) and so forth onto sticks with thread or bark-cord, creating either a bouquet of blue lotuses or a bouquet of red lotuses (*paduma*).

Or if they do so, all that is not permissible according to the previous method. It is not permissible for novices to pluck lotuses and the like from the water, place them on dry land, and tie them into a bundle with a yellow robe (*kāṣāya*).
However, it is permissible for them to tie them together with their own thread or cord and make a shoulder-bag (*aṃsabhaṇḍika*). A "shoulder-bag" refers to a yellow robe placed upon the shoulder.
Having brought both ends together and made a bundle, they place the flowers inside it as if in a sack;

this is called a shoulder-bundle (*aṃsabhaṇḍikā*), and it is permissible to make one. Having pierced a lotus leaf with sticks and wrapped the blue lotuses (*uppala*) and so forth with the leaf, they carry them;
in that case as well, it is permissible to tie a lotus leaf over the flowers.
However, it is not permitted to tie the lower part of the staff.
What is called "filling" (pūrima) should be understood as occurring with a string of garlands and a flower-cloth.
For when one who is encircling a cetiya, a Bodhi tree, or a railing with a string of garlands brings it back again and passes it beyond its previous position, at that point the "filling" is complete.
This is called "filling" (*pūrima*); how much more so for one who encircles it many times?
Having inserted [the flowers] through the gaps between the pegs (*nāgadantaka*), one draws them out and makes them hang down, then encircles the peg again; this too is called "filling.
However, it is permissible to insert a flower-garland (*pupphavalaya*) into the pegs. They make a flower-cloth (*pupphapaṭa*) with strings of garlands; in that case as well, there is only one [type].
It is permissible to remove the flower garland. When bringing it back again, it remains as it was before; however, doing all that in the same manner as previously is not permitted.
But having received a flower wreath made even from many strands of garlands, it is permissible to tie it to the top of the seat or similar places.
However, once a very long strand of garland has been removed and wrapped around [the object], then for another...
It is permissible for a monk to give [the flowers], and it is likewise permissible for him to do so himself.
"Woven" (*vāyima*) should be understood as referring to flower-networks (*pupphajāla*), flower-cloths (*pupphapaṭa*), and flower-figures (*puppharūpa*).

For one making a flower-network on a cetiya, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each individual opening of the network. The same principle applies to walls, canopies, Bodhi-tree pillars, and so forth. Regarding a flower-cloth...
However, even if it has been filled by others, it is not permitted to weave it. They make figures of elephants, horses, and so forth using *gopphima* flowers;
these too must remain in the place where weaving occurs. In all cases, it is not allowed according to the previous method.
But it is permissible to make figures of elephants, horses, and so forth by one who places flowers within a boundary already established by others. (From the *Mahāpaccarī*)
Furthermore, eight floral arrangements are mentioned together with the *kaḷambaka* and the *aḍḍhacandaka*.
32. Therein, the *kaḷambaka* is said to be a hanging garland of small bells suspended between two *aḍḍhacandakas*.
The *aḍḍhacandaka* is a circular arrangement of garlands in the shape of a half-moon. Both of these are included within the previous [category]. This is stated in the *Kurundi*.
However, it is stated that "even making a flower garland by joining two or three strings of flowers together is indeed woven.
That too is included here under the same heading as before. And not only a flower garland, but a flour-made garland and a ball-shaped flower garland are also mentioned in the *Kurundi*.
Because the training rule is common to both, a garland of coarse leaves applies to both monks and nuns.
It is not permissible to do it oneself or to cause it to be done; however, it is permissible everywhere to speak words that are allowable for the purpose of making an offering.
Methods involving indirect speech or signs are also permissible.
Whether one has carried [the items] away, caused them to be carried away, summoned [someone], caused them to be summoned, or [received them from] those who have come of their own accord—whatever...

If one gives any flower belonging to oneself for the purpose of winning over a family, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one gives what belongs to another, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
If one gives with the intention of theft, one is to be dealt with according to the value of the object. This same principle applies to property belonging to the Saṅgha as well.
However, this is the distinction: for one who gives out of a sense of ownership that which has been specifically set aside for the purpose of lodgings, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).

33. Regarding flowers: for whom is it appropriate to give them, and for whom is it not appropriate? First, in the case of one’s mother and father, it is appropriate to give them even by taking them oneself, having someone else take them, inviting them, or having someone else invite them. In the case of other relatives, it is appropriate only after having invited them.

Furthermore, this is for the purpose of honoring the person; however, for the purpose of decoration or for the purpose of worshipping objects such as the *śivaliṅga*, it is not appropriate to give them to anyone at all.
It is not permissible to give [the flowers] away. When having [flowers] brought by one's mother or father, they should be had brought by their own *sāmaṇeras*.
However, if others wish for them themselves, it is permissible.

At the time of distributing the flowers, it is permissible for the appointed distributor of flowers to give half a share to the *sāmaṇeras* who have arrived. But in the *Kurundi*, it says: "To the householders who have arrived..."
The *Mahāpaccarī* states that it is permissible to give "half a portion" or "a small amount. It should be given after seeking permission from one who has not been formally authorized.
Novices who have respect for their teachers and preceptors may bring many flowers and set them out in a heap;
then, when elders arrive at dawn, they may say to their own students, such as *saddhivihārikas*, or to lay devotees (*upāsakas*), and so forth: "You [should take] this..."
If they give it saying, "Take this, you take this," it is not called a gift of flowers.

Even if people take flowers with the thought, "We shall worship the Cetiya," and while going or while worshipping, they give them here and there for the purpose of worshipping the Cetiya for whoever happens to arrive, this too is not called a gift of flowers.
Seeing lay followers worshipping with *akkapuppha* and other flowers, [if one thinks], "In the monastery..."
It is also appropriate to say, "There are *kaṇikāra* flowers and others; lay followers, take them and offer worship.
When the monks have performed the flower-worship and enter the village early in the day, people ask, "Venerable sirs, why have you entered so early?
They reply, "There were many flowers in the monastery; we performed worship. People then say, "Indeed, there are many..."
It is permissible for people to take a large quantity of hard and soft food to a monastery on the following day,
perform flower offerings, and give alms, thinking,
"We shall honor [the Sangha] on such-and-such a day. Having requested a turn for flowers, they may do so on the day it has been authorized.
When they arrived, the novice monks had already gathered the flowers and set them aside;
not seeing the flowers on the trees, they asked, "Venerable sir, where are the flowers? [The elder replied], "They were gathered and set aside by the novices.
You should perform the worship and depart; the Saṅgha will perform the worship on another day. Having performed the worship and given alms, they departed.
They go; it is permissible. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*, it is stated:
"The elders may not have the novices give [the flowers]; if the elders themselves give those flowers to them, it is permissible.
But the elders should only say, 'These were gathered and set aside by the novices. If, however, one has requested a turn for flowers...

When strangers come bringing rice gruel, cooked rice, and so forth, having gathered flowers that have not yet been plucked, and say, "Pluck some and give us," it is permissible to pluck and give them only to those who are known as *sāmaṇeras*.
If they throw them up and place them on a tree branch, one must not climb down and run away;
it is permissible to pluck them and give them. However, if someone who is a Dhamma-preacher says, "Many..."
If he says, "Lay followers, go to the monastery taking flowers, rice gruel, food, and so forth, and perform a flower offering," it is not allowable for him alone;
thus it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated without distinction: "This is unallowable and not permitted."
35. It is also permissible, according to the method already stated, to give one’s own fruit to one’s mother and father, as well as to other relatives.

However, for one who gives for the sake of maintaining the family, the offenses such as *dukkaṭa* should be understood according to the method already stated, whether the fruit belongs to oneself, belongs to another, belongs to the Saṅgha, or has been set aside for the purpose of lodging. [It is likewise permissible] to give what belongs to oneself to sick persons.
It is permissible to give [fruit] to those who have arrived or to those whose provisions are exhausted; however, it does not constitute a formal gift of fruit (*phaladāna*).
When the fruit is being distributed by one appointed as the distributor of fruit for the Saṅgha, it is permissible to give half a share to people who have arrived at that time;
if one is not so appointed, one should give after seeking permission. Within the monastery grounds as well, [the distribution may be made] either by delimiting the fruit or by delimiting the trees.

Or a formal agreement (*katikā*) should be made: "When people who are ill or others come requesting fruit, four or five fruits should be given according to the established limit; or the trees should be pointed out [saying], 'It is permitted to take from here.
However, one must not say, "The fruits here are excellent; take them from here. [This applies only to] what belongs to oneself.
If one gives *sirisacuṇṇa* (mimosa powder) or any other astringent for the purpose of winning over a family, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The determination regarding things belonging to others and so forth should be understood by the same method already stated. However, this is the distinction:

even the bark of trees that has been protected and guarded by the Saṅgha is indeed a "heavy article" (*garubhaṇḍa*). One should also recognize that among clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, and leaves, those that fall under the category of heavy articles are likewise [treated as such].
The analysis [of this] should be understood in the same manner as that stated for *cuṇṇa* (powder).
36. *Jaṅghapesaniya*: This refers to acting as a messenger or carrying messages for householders;
such work must not be done. For one who goes taking a message from householders, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step. Food obtained on account of that work—
Even while eating, for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Even for one who has not first accepted the message but later descends from the road thinking, "Now that I have reached this village, I shall announce the message," there is an offense of wrong-doing for every step taken.
For one who eats the food obtained after announcing the message, there is an offense of wrong-doing according to the same method as before. [This applies] even if one has not accepted the message...

However, when one has arrived and is asked, "Venerable sir, what is the news regarding such-and-such a person in that village?", it is permissible to speak; there is no fault in answering a question thus asked.

It is also permissible to carry a message for five types of fellow practitioners, for one's parents, for a withered leaf, or for one’s own personal attendant, as well as a message concerning what is allowable (kappiya) for laypeople. Therefore:

“Have you any qualms regarding such instructions as: ‘Worship the feet of the Blessed One in my name,’ or ‘Worship the shrine, the image, the Bodhi tree, or the senior monk of the Saṅgha,’ or ‘Offer fragrant worship at the shrine,’ or ‘Offer floral worship,’ or ‘Assemble the monks;
we shall give a gift and have the Dhamma preached’?”
It should not be done. For these are permissible communications (*kappiya-sāsana*), not matters concerning householders' domestic affairs.
However, requisites obtained through these eight acts that corrupt families are not permissible even for those who share the same Dhamma;
they are exactly like requisites obtained through false representation or trading in money.
Furthermore, one who has been subjected to the formal act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma) is neither permitted to wander in the village or town where the act of corrupting families was committed,
nor is he permitted to dwell in the monastery where he resided at that time.
Even when the formal act has subsided, he must not accept any requisites arising from those families where he previously committed the act of corrupting families.
They must not be accepted; even by one who has attained the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), they must not be accepted, for they are indeed unallowable (*akappiya*).
If, when asked, "Why do you not accept them?", one says, "Because it was done so previously," and they reply, "We do not give for that reason;

we give now because of your virtuous character (*sīlavantatā*)," then they may be accepted. This refers to a case where, at the very place of giving, there was an act of defiling a family (*kuladūsaka-kamma*) committed as a matter of course.
When it has been said, it is permissible to accept only the natural gift (*pakatidāna*). That which they give after having increased [the amount] is not permissible.

And because there is no fault in answering a question when asked, therefore, if someone should ask another bhikkhu who has entered among the houses in the morning or in the evening, "Venerable sir, for what purpose do you wander?"—whatever purpose he wanders for, [he may explain that].
Having described it, if he says, "Was it obtained or not? and if it was not obtained, one may accept what he gives after saying, "It was not obtained. 37.
"Monks, you must not dwell in the forest with a specific purpose in mind; whoever should so dwell, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
"Monks, one should not go for alms with a specific intention... monks, one should not walk back and forth with a specific intention...
monks, one should not stand with a specific intention... monks, one should not sit down with a specific intention...
monks, one should not prepare a bed with a specific intention; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," because it has been said thus.
"One should not dwell in the forest having made such a wish as: 'People will regard me, dwelling thus in the forest, as one who has attained Arahatship or the stage of a trainee;
consequently, I shall be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the world.
For one who goes into the forest with the aspiration, 'I shall dwell in the forest,' at every step..."

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); likewise, for all activities in the forest—such as building a hut, walking meditation, sitting, dressing, and putting on robes—there is an offense of wrong-doing for every single instance of such action.
Therefore, one should not dwell in the forest in this manner.

For if one dwells thus, whether or not one gains respect, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing. However, he who has undertaken the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) and thinks, "I will guard the ascetic practice," [should act otherwise].
Or, having thought, "While living near a village my mind is distracted;
the forest is suitable," or "Surely in the forest I shall attain one of the three kinds of seclusion," or "Having entered the forest,
I will not come out until I have attained Arahantship," or "Forest-dwelling is praised by the Blessed One, and while I am dwelling in the forest..."
Or, thinking, "Many fellow celibates will leave the vicinity of villages and become forest-dwellers," he desires to dwell in blameless residence;

for that reason, he should dwell [in the forest]. Even while wandering for alms, having composed himself with regard to the "excellent" and so forth, from the time of the duties concerning the undergarment and upper robe up until the conclusion of the meal, throughout that entire procedure—
If one acts with negligence, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), whether or not one gains a reputation; it is simply *dukkaṭa*.

However, when entering for alms with graceful movements such as advancing and retreating—either for the sake of fulfilling the duties of the Khandhakas and the training rules (*sekhiyavatta*) or for the sake of following the example of one's fellow celibates—one is beyond reproach in the eyes of the wise.
The same principle applies to walking meditation (*caṅkama*) and other such activities.
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of the inclusion of families within the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 6.
Discussion on the Determination of Fish and Meat.
38. Regarding fish-meat, by the mention of "fish," all that is born in water is included; therein, there is nothing that is impermissible (*akappiya*).
Among meats, however, ten types of meat are impermissible by way of human, elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena.
In that regard, for human flesh there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), and for the others, a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus, for these ten—humans and the rest—neither the flesh, nor the bone, nor the blood, nor the skin, nor the hair is permitted.
Among the fats, however, only human fat is not permitted. Regarding milk and the other [liquids], there is nothing called "unallowable" (akappiya).
But for one who eats any of these unallowable meats, or any of the bones and so forth, whether knowing [their nature] or not knowing it, [there is an offense].

It is indeed an offense. When one becomes aware of it, it must then be confessed. For one who takes [the food] thinking, "I will eat it without asking," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even at the moment of receiving it;
for one who takes it thinking, "I will eat it after asking," there is no offense. However, an offense applies only to one who eats knowing that it was prepared specifically for them;
one who learns of this afterwards is not to be charged with an offense.
In this context, "prepared specifically" refers to fish or meat that has been slaughtered and prepared for the sake of monks.
Indeed, both types of "prepared specifically" are not permitted. However, even that is permissible if it is unseen, unheard, and unsuspected.
For the Blessed One has authorized fish and meat that is pure in three respects: unseen, unheard, and unsuspected. In this regard, "unseen" means:

What is "unseen" is that which is being taken after killing deer or fish for the sake of the bhikkhus. What is "unheard" means not having heard that deer or fish were killed for the sake of the bhikkhus and then taken.
Furthermore, regarding what is "not suspected," one should understand it by way of its opposite, having first understood the four types of suspicion:
