suspicion based on what was seen, suspicion based on what was heard, suspicion based on both, and suspicion free from both.
How so? Here, monks see people with nets, snares, and other such implements, either leaving a village or wandering in the forest.
Then, on the following day, when those monks have entered that village for alms, they bring them alms-food containing fish and meat.
Having seen this, they become suspicious, thinking: "Is this for the sake of the monks?"
"Made" means this is suspected to have been made for those present; it is not permissible to accept this. That which is not suspected in this way is permissible.
However, if those people ask, "Venerable sir, why do you not accept it?
and after hearing the reason, say, "Venerable sir, this was not made for the sake of the monks; it was made by us for our own sake, or for the sake of the king's officials and so forth..."
If they say, "It was made for our sake," it is allowable.
Furthermore, the monks do not see them, but they hear:
"It seems people are going out from the village or wandering in the forest with nets, snares, and other such tools in their hands. And on the following day, they go to that village for alms.
They bring alms-food containing even equal portions of fish and meat. Because of that hearing, they suspect: "Has this been prepared for the sake of the monks?
This is called "suspected because of what was heard," and it is not permitted to accept it.
That which is not suspected in this way is permitted. But if those people should say, "Venerable sir, why do you not take it?"
Having asked about the matter and heard it, if they say, "Venerable sir, this was not made for the sake of the monks;
it was made by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and the like," it is allowable.
However, if the monks neither see nor hear [this], but rather [hear it] when they have entered that village for alms—
Having taken a bowl and prepared almsfood consisting of equal portions of fish and meat, they offer it.
They suspect, "Was this prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus? This is called "suspected as being free from both [the donor and the recipient)," and it is not permitted to accept it.
That which is not suspected in this way is permitted. But if those people say, "Why..."
Having asked, "Venerable sir, do you not accept it? and having heard that matter, if they say, "Venerable sir, this was not done for the sake of the bhikkhus;

it was done for our own sake or for the sake of those connected to the king and so forth, or it was prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus after obtaining meat that was already available and permissible," then it is allowable. [Also allowable is meat] for the sake of performing funeral rites for the deceased.
The same principle applies even when [a building] is constructed for the purpose of auspicious ceremonies and the like.
Indeed, whatever has not been built specifically for the sake of monks, and regarding which one is free from doubt, all that is permissible. 39.
However, if in a certain monastery there is something built specifically for the monks, and they [the builders] have made it known that it was built for their own sake...
They do not know, while others know. For those who know, it is not permitted; for others, however, it is permitted.
Others do not know, while they themselves know; for them alone it is not permitted, while for others it is permitted.
They know, "It was made for our sake," and others also know, "It was made for their sake"; for all of them, it is not permitted.

It is permissible. It is permissible for all, even if not everyone knows [of it]. For among five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, food prepared specifically for any one of them is not allowable for all.
However, if someone kills an animal for a single bhikkhu and gives it to him, filling his bowl, he—
If one, knowing full well that [the food] was prepared for one's own sake, takes it and gives it to another bhikkhu, and he consumes it out of faith in that person, for whom is there an offense?
There is no offense for either. For there is no offense for the one for whose sake it was prepared because he did not eat it;
and there is no offense for the other because he was unaware [of its origin]. Indeed, there is an offense in the acceptance of allowable meat (*kappiyamaṃsa*).
There is no such thing as a duty to confess an offense after one has eaten without knowing that the food was "prepared specifically for him" (uddissakata), and only realizes it afterwards.
However, even if one eats without knowing it is unallowable meat (akappiyamaṃsa) and realizes it afterwards, the offense must still be confessed.

For an offense occurs at the very moment of eating once one knows it was prepared specifically for oneself; likewise, there is indeed an offense for one who eats without knowing it is unallowable meat. Therefore:
One who is fearful of transgressions, even when observing the form [of the meat], should receive the meat only after having asked.
At the time of consumption, one should either take it with the thought, "I will consume it after asking," or consume it only after having asked. Why?
Because it is difficult to discern. For even the flesh of a fish can resemble the flesh of a pig, and the flesh of a leopard and so forth can resemble the flesh of a deer and so forth; therefore—
They say that after asking, one should indeed proceed with the taking [of the food].
Thus ends the discourse on the determination regarding fish and meat in the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
7. Discussion on the Determination of the Untouchable (Anāmāsa-vinicchaya-kathā) 40.
"Untouchable" (anāmāsa) means that which should not be touched. Herein is the determination:
because whether she be a mother, a daughter, or a sister, every woman indeed constitutes an obstacle to the holy life and is untouchable; therefore—
It is stated that even touching [a woman] out of domestic affection, thinking, “This is my mother,” “This is my daughter,” or “This is my sister,” constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, recollecting this command of the Blessed One, even if one sees one’s own mother being carried away by the current of a river, she must not be touched with the hand;
rather, a wise bhikkhu should [use] a boat or a plank.
Or a plantain trunk or a piece of wood should be brought. If these are not available, even a yellow robe may be brought and placed in front [of the patient], but one must not say, "Take it from here.
Once it has been taken, one should walk along while pulling it, thinking, "I am dragging the requisites.
If, however, she is afraid, one should go ahead of her and comfort her, saying, "Do not be afraid."
If, out of fear, she suddenly climbs onto her son’s shoulder or takes hold of his hand, he should not shake her off, saying, "Go away, old woman!
Rather, he should bring her to dry ground. The same rule applies even if she is stuck in the mud or has fallen into a well;
for there too, having thrown in a rope or a cloth and knowing that she has been grasped by the hand, she should be pulled out.
But they must certainly not be touched.

Not only is the body of a woman untouchable, but even her undergarments, upper garments, and ornaments—even down to a blade of grass used as a seat or a palm-leaf ring—are likewise untouchable. And this applies to those undergarments and upper garments as well.

It was set aside specifically for the purpose of being worn as an ornament. However, if one exchanges an undergarment or an upper robe and places it at the base of the feet for the purpose of [obtaining] a robe, it is permissible.
Regarding articles of jewelry, however, if a permissible article such as a head-ornament, a toothpick, or a needle is being offered with the words, "Venerable sir, we give this to you;
please accept it," for the purpose of [obtaining] a small box, a needle, or other such requisites—
It should be taken up. However, that which consists of gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, is strictly *anāmāsa* (untouchable);

even when being given, it must not be accepted. Not only is their physical form *anāmāsa*, but even a wooden figure, a tooth-figure, an iron figure, a copper figure, a tin figure, a paper figure, or a figure made of all kinds of gems fashioned in the shape of a woman is likewise *anāmāsa*.
Even an image made of dough is not to be eaten. However, having received it for the purpose of use with the words,
"May this be yours," one may break it apart— except for that which is made of all-jewels— and place what is suitable as an accessory among accessories,
and what is suitable for use among things for use.
41. And just as with the form of a woman, so too the seven kinds of grain must not be touched.
Therefore, one walking through the middle of a field should proceed without touching even the grain that has grown there.
If grain is spread out at a house door or along the path, and there is a side-path available, one should not walk by trampling it.
If there is no path on the way, one should proceed by resolving upon a path. If, inside a house, they offer a seat placed over grain, it is permissible to sit.
If some people are scattering grain in the sitting hall, if it is possible to have it removed, it should be removed;
if not, one should arrange a bench in such a way that the grain is not crushed at one side.
One should sit down. If there is no space, people may offer it after arranging it right in the midst of the grain; one should sit down.
One must not touch with a playful mind any non-cereal crops grown there, such as mung beans or peas, nor fruits such as palmyra or jackfruit.
The same rule applies even when they have been made into heaps by people. However, in the forest, fruits that have fallen from trees—
“It is permissible to take [it] with the intention: ‘I will give it to those who are not fully ordained.

42. Regarding these ten gems—pearl, mani-jewel, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat’s-eye—it is permissible to touch a pearl that is unwashed, unpierced, and still in its natural state; the others are not to be touched.”
What they say should not be accepted. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* it is stated: "Pearls, whether washed or unwashed, are untouchable;
it is not permitted to accept them for the purpose of their market value, but it is permitted for the purpose of medicine for leprosy.
This is correct. From the *jātiphalika* (cinnamon) fruit downwards, all varieties of colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth—
A gem that has been polished, pierced, and rounded is not subject to the [five-year] rule;

however, it is stated that one which is as it was produced from the mine, unworked, may be accepted for the purpose of providing materials such as bowls and other requisites. This too is rejected in the Mahāpaccarī.
It is stated that only a glass gem (kācamaṇi) made by melting is permitted. The same legal determination applies to beryl (veḷuriya) as it does to gems.
The conch that is perforated, polished, and mixed with gems is not to be handled (anāmāsa); however, the water-conch, whether polished or unpolished, is indeed to be handled (āmāsa).
Furthermore, it is permissible to accept other [shells] for the purpose of medicinal substances such as collyrium or for the purpose of merchandise.
As for stones, those that are polished, perforated, and joined with gems and are the color of mung beans are not to be handled; the rest are for purposes such as a knife-sharpening stone.
It is permissible to accept it. Regarding this, they say that "connected with gems" means those made by joining and smelting together gold.
They further say that coral, whether polished and pierced or unpierced, and the rest, whether pierced or unpierced, may be accepted for the purpose of merchandise;
however, that should not be accepted. But in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "Whether polished or unpolished, all..."
It is said, "And it is not permissible to touch [it] nor to accept [it]," and that is correct.
Both silver and gold—whether fashioned into objects or unfashioned—are entirely untouchable and unacceptable from the very moment they exist as seeds.
It is said that the Prince Uttara, having had a golden cetiya constructed, [gave it] to the Elder Mahāpaduma...
He sent it. The Elder refused, saying, "It is not allowable. In a cetiya-shrine there may be golden lotuses, golden bubbles, and so forth;

these too are untouchable. However, it is stated that since the guardians of the cetiya-shrine stand in the place where silver is discarded, it is permissible to play with them for their sake. In the *Kurundi*, even that is prohibited; regarding a golden cetiya—

It is permitted only to this extent: that it is proper to remove mere refuse. It is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that even brass is of the same category as gold and is untouchable (*anāmāsa*).
However, in the context of using lodgings (*senāsana*), everything is allowable;
therefore, all furnishings for a lodging made of gold or silver are touchable (*āmāsa*) in the exposition of the Dhamma and Vinaya for monks.

In a jeweled pavilion with crystal pillars adorned with jeweled garlands, it is permissible for monks to look after all the requisites there. It is stated that red coral and masāragalla gems, when washed and polished, are untouchable (*anāmāsa*);
others are touchable (*āmāsa*), and it is permissible to accept them for the purpose of providing capital for merchandise. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is said: "Even when washed..."
"Even if they have not been washed, they are entirely untouchable, and it is not permitted to accept them"—thus it was prohibited.
43. All weaponry is untouchable; even if it is being given for the purpose of obtaining the raw materials for such items, it must not be accepted.
Trade in weapons is not permitted. This includes a simple wooden staff, a bow, a crossbow, a goad, a spear, and a hook.
Even items such as axes and hatchets, when categorized as weapons, are not to be touched.
If a spear or a javelin has been placed in a monastery by someone, the one maintaining the monastery should send word to the owners, saying, "Please take it away.
If they do not take it, the monastery must be maintained without moving that object. However, regarding what has fallen on a battlefield...
Upon seeing a sword, a spear, or a javelin, it is permissible to break the blade with a stone or some other object and take it for the purpose of making a knife.
Other parts may also be separated and taken, some for the purpose of making a knife and some for the purpose of making a walking stick or similar items.
However, if something is being given with the words, "Take this," one must not destroy it with the thought, "I will turn it into a permissible article."
It is permissible to accept all of these as well.
Fishing nets, bird-cages, and so forth, as well as shields, lattices, and protective armor against arrows—all these are not forbidden (anāmāsa).
However, among those things obtained for the purpose of use, regarding a net first of all: "I shall tie it over a seat or a cetiya..."
It is permissible to take [an umbrella] thinking, "I shall wrap it as a cover. All protective charms against arrows (sara-paritta) may be accepted for the purpose of their material value.
For these serve to ward off the obstruction caused by others; they do not themselves cause obstruction.
It is permissible to take a wooden board thinking, "I shall make it a container for tooth-sticks."
Lutes, drums, and other instruments covered with leather are not to be touched. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
"Even the frame of a drum, the frame of a lute, an empty gourd, the leather fastened to the rim, and even the neck of a lute—all of these are not to be touched.
One is simply not permitted to cover them, have them covered, play them, or have them played. [This applies] in the courtyard of a cetiya.
Even if one sees that it has been discarded by people after being offered in worship, one should not move it, but should sweep around it from time to time.
However, at the time of discarding rubbish, it is permissible to carry it away as part of the rubbish and deposit it to one side; this is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.
It is also permissible to accept it for the purpose of obtaining materials for requisites; however, among those things available for use, such as a lute or a winnowing basket—

"One shall make a drum, a lotus-bowl, and a tooth-stick box; one shall make a leather case for knives"—it is permissible to take such items for the purpose of providing equipment for those respective requisites and to have them made accordingly.
Thus ends the compendium of legal decisions on the Vinaya not found in the canonical texts (*pāḷimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha*).
The Discussion on the Determination of the Anāmāsa [Rule] is finished.
8. The Discussion on the Determination of Formal Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna) and Entrustment (Vikappana). 44.
Regarding formal resolutions and entrustments, however: "Monks, I allow you to resolve upon the three robes, but not to entrust them."
One may determine the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) for four months of the rains, but beyond that, one must assign it; one may determine the *nisīdana* (sitting mat), but not assign it;

one may determine the *paccattharaṇa* (bedspread), but not assign it; one may determine the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) for as long as there is illness, but beyond that, one must assign it;
and one may determine the *mukhapuñchanacoḷa* (face-wiping cloth), but not assign it.

Because of the statement, "One should neither determine nor assign a requisite robe," one who wishes to use [the robe] after determining it according to the specific rules for the three robes and so forth must determine it by stating its name, such as, "I determine this outer cloak (saṅghāṭi)," and so on.
However, one who assigns [a robe] must assign it without stating its name, saying, "I assign this robe to you."

In that regard, one who is determining the three robes (ticīvara) must determine them only after they have been dyed and marked with the *kappa-bindu* (the authorized mark), and provided they are of the correct measure.
Regarding their measure: at the maximum limit, it is permissible for them to be slightly smaller than the robe of the Sugata;
at the minimum limit, the measure for both the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is five fist-breadths in length and three fist-breadths in width.
It is allowable. An inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) five fist-lengths in length and even two cubits in width is also allowable;

for it is possible to cover the navel even with such a garment. However, anything exceeding or falling short of the stated measurements should be determined as "an accessory cloth" (*parikkhāracola*).
In this regard, since it is said: "There are two ways of determining a robe: one determines it by body or one determines it by speech."

It has been said; therefore, having relinquished the old outer robe by saying, "I relinquish this outer robe," and having taken the new outer robe in hand, one should resolve it with the body—performing a physical gesture while applying mental attention by thinking, "I resolve upon this outer robe.
This is resolution by means of the body, which may be done by any part of the body.
It is not permissible for one who does not touch it. However, when making a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by means of speech, it must be determined by uttering words.
In that regard, there are two kinds of determination: if it is within arm’s reach, the words “I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)” must be spoken.
But if it is inside a room, on an upper story, or in a neighboring monastery, the place where it was laid down—

Having observed it, one should break the silence by saying, "I resolve upon this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). This same method applies to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).
For there is only a difference in name; therefore, all of them must be resolved upon by their own respective names as "outer robe," "upper robe," and "inner robe.
If, after having resolved upon them, [one uses] robes such as the outer robe made from the fabrics set aside...
When it has been dyed and finished, one should relinquish it by saying, "I relinquish this," and then it must be determined again.
However, when sewing on a second patch that is larger than the determined portion, whether it be a strip or a fragment, it must be determined again.
If the patch is equal in size or smaller, there is no need for a formal determination.
"Is it permissible or not permissible to resolve that the three robes (*tricīvara*) are requisites-cloths (*parikkhāracola*)?
Regarding this, it is said that the Elder Mahāpaduma stated: "The three robes must be resolved upon as the three robes themselves;
if they were permitted to be resolved upon as requisites-cloths, then the exemption in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada* would become meaningless. When this was said, the remaining bhikkhus...
They said, "The Blessed One himself stated that even the requisite cloth must be formally resolved upon; therefore, it is permissible.
It is also stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "What is called 'requisite cloth' (parikkhāracoḷa) is a separate category of storage.
It is permissible to use the three robes after resolving them as 'requisite cloth'; however, in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada*, the three robes..."
"For one who maintains [the robe] after having made a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), maintenance is permitted.
It is said that the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavālika and a reciter of both the Vibhaṅgas, also stated: "In the past, we heard from the great elders:
'Forest-dwelling bhikkhus, having placed their robes in hollows of trees and similar places, go forth to exert themselves in meditation; in the neighboring monastery..."
"When those who have gone for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma depart at sunrise, novices or young bhikkhus take their bowls and robes and go away;
therefore, for the sake of comfortable use, it is permissible to determine the three robes as requisites-cloth.
It is also stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "In the past, forest-dwelling bhikkhus found it difficult to maintain [the robes] within an unbound boundary..."
"Having determined that the three robes are indeed requisites for clothing, they used them. 45.
A rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) that is not exceeding the proper measure should be determined for use during the four months of the rains according to the method already stated;
after that period, it must be relinquished and then formally assigned (*vikappetabbā*). Even if it is dyed only slightly or by a mere difference in color, it is [still subject to this rule].
Two, however, are not permitted. The sitting mat must indeed be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) according to the method already stated;
moreover, it must be of the proper measure and only one; two are not permitted. The sheet for spreading over the bed (paccattharaṇa) must also be determined;
that, however, may be large, it may be one, or many may be permitted; it may be blue, yellow, or variegated.
A flower-offering cloth is permitted in every way. A skin-eruption coverlet should be determined as being of the proper measure for as long as there is an illness;
once the illness has subsided, it should be relinquished and then formally assigned [to another], and only one such is permitted. A face-wiping cloth must be determined;
however, as long as one is being washed, another may be desired for the purpose of use.
Even two are permissible. However, other elders say, "This is a heading; many are also permissible.
There is no limit to the number of requisites-cloths (*parikkhāracoḷa*); one should simply resolve upon as many as one desires.
Even a bag, a water-strainer, or anything reaching the minimum size for a robe that is subject to formal assignment (*vikappanūpaga*) must be resolved upon as a "requisite-cloth."
Its measurement is two spans long and one span wide; however, that length is the measure of a carpenter’s cubit, and its width is half that measure.

Regarding this, the canonical text says: “I allow you, monks, to designate the lower robe as being eight finger-breadths in length by four finger-breadths in width according to the Sugata’s finger. Even many [such robes...]
Having set them aside together, it is indeed permissible to resolve upon them by saying, “I resolve that these robes are requisites for clothing.
For one who sets them aside for the purpose of medicine, or for the sake of parents and so forth, there is no offense even if they have not been resolved upon.
However, regarding the bed-cushion, the chair-cushion, the bolster, the woolen rug, and the fur rug—these, for the purpose of bedding and furniture...
Furthermore, there is no need for a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding a rug that has already been given.

However, if one obtains thread from a place where one has been invited by relatives and has a robe woven—either by a weaver who was invited by those same relatives or by another, having provided the materials—there is no offense on account of the weaving itself. There is, however, an offense on account of the transgression of the ten-day limit.
However, one who wishes to guard against an offense must determine [the robe] while it remains exactly at the size that has reached the stage of being fit for distribution (*vikappanupagga*).
For if it were finished after ten days have elapsed, it would become an article subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
This same principle applies even when the robe has been offered by relatives and others who have had the weaving performed, saying: "Venerable sir, please accept this robe-cloth."
If the weaver, being thus engaged or desiring to give it himself, says, "Venerable sir, having woven this robe-cloth for you,

I shall set it aside on such-and-such a day," and the bhikkhu lets ten days pass from that specified date, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). But if the weaver says, "I [shall weave] for you..."
Having said, "I will have a robe woven and send it to you," he does exactly so;
however, the monk sent by him does not inform that bhikkhu. But another person, having seen or heard of it, informs him, saying, "Venerable sir, your robe is finished.
This report is not authoritative. However, when the one actually sent by him reports it, his word [is authoritative].
If one lets ten days pass from the day the robe-cloth was received, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If a weaver says, "I will weave your robe-cloth and send it into the hands of someone," and does exactly so,
yet the monk who took the robe-cloth places it in his own dwelling and does not [send it], [it is an offense].
He reports it, and someone else says, "Venerable sir, is the robe-cloth that has just been brought beautiful?
"Friend, where is the robe-cloth? "It was sent into the hand of such-and-such a person. Even this statement is not authoritative.
However, when that monk gives away the robe-cloth, from the day it is received, if he lets ten days pass, it becomes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, if the price for having it woven has not been paid, one retains [the robe] as long as even a single *kākaṇika* remains unpaid.
46. But for one who uses a robe that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), how is the determination lost?
It is lost by giving it to another, by taking it back after having given it away, by accepting it on trust, by returning to the lower state, by renouncing the training, or by death.
It is relinquished through these nine causes: by change of gender, by giving up [the robe], and by becoming torn.
Among these, by the first eight causes all robes relinquish their formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*);

however, regarding the state of being torn, it is stated in all the commentaries that only the triple robe (*ticīvara*) relinquishes its determination, and that only when there is a hole the size of a fingernail’s surface.
In that context, the measure [of a tear] should be understood by way of the fingernail of the little finger, as large as the back of a fingernail;
and "hole" refers specifically to a pierced hole. For if even a single thread remains uncut within a hole, it protects [the robe].
In that regard, from the long edge of both the *saṅghāṭī* and the *uttarāsaṅga*, [a tear] measuring one span (*vidatthi*) in length and eight finger-breadths (*aṭṭhaṅgula*) in width [is permissible].

A hole within the area [of the robe] breaks the determination; however, for the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), it is only from the long edge measuring one span (*vidatthi*) and from the horizontal edge measuring four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) inward that a hole breaks the determination, not beyond that.
Therefore, when a hole has arisen, the three robes remain in the status of "extra robes" (*atirekacīvara*), and needlework [is permitted].
Having done so, it must be resolved upon once again. However, if one first applies a patch to a weak spot and subsequently removes that weak spot after cutting it out, the resolution is not broken.
The same principle applies to the turning over of a circular patch (*maṇḍala*).
In the case of a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭa*), if a hole or a tear occurs in one layer, the resolution is not broken, provided it remains a minor robe (*khuddaka-cīvara*).
If one makes something large small, or makes something small large, the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not broken.
When making both ends meet in the middle, if one cuts first and then joins them, the resolution is broken;
but if one joins them first and then cuts, it is not broken. Even when having dyers wash [the cloth] and have it made white, the resolution remains intact.
"Only by means of a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). This, first of all, is the analysis regarding resolution. 47.
Regarding assignment (*vikappanā*), there are two types of assignment: face-to-face assignment (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and behind-the-back assignment (*parammukhā-vikappanā*).
How does face-to-face assignment take place? Having ascertained whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or absent—
Having said, “This robe,” or “These robes,” or “That robe,” or “Those robes,” one must say, “I designate this for you.
This is one kind of designation in the presence [of the recipient]. Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside;
however, it is not permissible to use it, to relinquish it, or to resolve upon it as one’s own. “It belongs to me...”

"Use these things belonging to me, or dispose of them, or do with them as you see fit"—when this is said, it is called "renunciation" (*paccuddhāra*); from that point on, even using them and so forth is permissible.
Another method: having likewise understood whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are stored or not stored, [one renounces] to that very person...

In the presence of a bhikkhu, having said, "this robe-cloth," or "these robe-cloths," or "that robe-cloth," or "those robe-cloths," and having taken the name of whichever one among the five types of fellow-followers of the Dhamma he prefers— saying,
"I dedicate this to the bhikkhu Tissa," or "to the bhikkhunī Tissa," or...
One should say: "I assign it to a trainee nun," or "to the novice monk Tissa," or "to the novice nun Tissa.

This is another form of assignment in the presence [of the owner]. Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside; however, for any purpose other than personal use and so forth, not even one of these is permissible.
That monk [should consider it] as "the property of the monk Tissa... [or] the property of the novice nun Tissa."
When it is said, “Use it, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit,” this is called a formal relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*);
from that point on, its use and so forth are permitted.
How does relinquishment in the absence of the recipient (*parammukhā-vikappanā*) occur? It is the same regarding robes, whether they are one or many, and whether they are present or absent.

Having understood this, one should say, "This robe," or "These robes," or "That robe," or "Those robes," and then say, "I give them for the purpose of assigning [the ownership] to you. He should then ask, "Who is your friend or acquaintance?
Thereupon, the other should reply in the same manner as before: "The three monks," or... pe ... "the three female novices."
Or it may be said: "I give [it] to the bhikkhu Tissa," or... pe... "I give [it] to the novice nun Tissā.
This is an assignment in the absence of the recipient (*parammukhā-vikappanā*). Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside;

however, for any of the uses such as consumption and so forth, it is not permissible. But by that bhikkhu, in the case of a second assignment in the presence of the recipient (*dutiyasammukhā-vikappanā*)—

In the same manner as previously stated, when it is said, "Use this belonging to so-and-so, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," this is called "renunciation" (*paccuddhāra*). From that point on, its use and other such actions are permissible.

What is the difference between these two types of assignment (*vikappanā*)? In the case of "assignment in the presence" (*sammukhā-vikappanā*), one performs the assignment oneself and then [hands it] to another.

He causes it to be relinquished; in the case of relinquishment in the absence [of the owner], having had another cause it to be assigned, he then has that same other cause it to be relinquished—this is the distinction here.
But if the one to whom he assigns it is not skilled in the formal rules and does not know how to relinquish it, he should take that robe, go to another who is competent, and assign it again.

It must be relinquished by another. This so-called "reassignment of what has already been assigned" is permissible. Thus, first of all, the method for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappanā*) of a robe should be understood.
48. As for the bowl, this is the method: one who determines a bowl must determine one that is of the appropriate size—either large, medium, or small.
Its measurement is as follows, according to the method beginning with: "It holds half an *āḷhaka* of boiled rice," and so forth.
This is stated in the Pāḷi. Herein, this is the analysis:

having taken two Magadhan nāḷis of unhusked, old rice grains that have been well-husked and purified, one cooks a meal of boiled rice—free from broken grains, not soggy, not clumped together, very clear, resembling a heap of jasmine buds—and having poured it all without remainder into the bowl, of that...

One should add green-gram soup prepared with all its ingredients—neither too thick nor too thin, but in a quantity sufficient to be taken up by the hand—which constitutes one-fourth the measure of the rice;
then, one should add condiments such as fish, meat, and so forth, in portions corresponding to each mouthful of food, until enough remains for the very last mouthful;
however, ghee, oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, and the like are not counted [as separate mouthfuls].
They do not [increase]. For they follow the nature of the boiled rice; they can neither be diminished nor increased.

Thus, all this that has been placed [in the bowl] is "excessive" (ukkaṭṭha) if it stands level with the lower rim of the bowl's mouth, or if, when cutting with a thread or a knife, it touches the lower edge of the thread or the knife.
This is called the "small" bowl. If it stands with its rim protruding beyond that line, this is called the "excellent small" bowl.
If it does not even reach that line and remains entirely within it, this is called the "excellent-excellent" bowl.
A bowl measuring half the size of the excellent one is called the "medium. A bowl measuring half the size of the medium one is the "small. Therefore...

If, when all the food, such as a *nāḷika* measure of boiled rice, has been placed in it according to the aforementioned method, it remains level with the lower rim, this is called a medium bowl (*majjhima-patta*).
If it remains above that rim, piled up like a stupa, this is called a medium-small bowl (*majjhimomaka-patta*). If it does not reach that rim but remains contained within it, this is—
The "moderately large" bowl is as follows: if all the food, such as boiled rice, measured by half a Magadha *nāḷi* when placed inside, remains level with the lower rim, this is called a "small" bowl.
If it stands rising above that rim like a heap, this is called a "very small" bowl. If it does not reach that rim but remains contained within it, [it is a medium bowl].
This is called the inferior-superior bowl. Thus there are these nine bowls. Among them, two are not bowls: the superior-superior and the inferior-inferior.
Therefore, these two should be used as ordinary vessels, but they are not fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor for assignment (*vikappana*).
The other seven, however, may be used after having been formally determined or assigned.
It should be understood that even for those [bowls] of the correct measure, they are suitable for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappaṇā*) only in this way:
an iron bowl is fit for determination when it has been fired five times; a clay bowl is fit for determination when it has been fired twice. Both are fit only when the price due has been paid.
If even a single firing is lacking, or if the price is unpaid by even as much as a *kākaṇika*, it is not [fit].
It does not come under the rule of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). If the owner of the bowl says, "When you have the means [to buy it], then give it back;
for now, determine it and use it," it still does not come under the rule of formal determination. Because the bowl is deficient, it does not count as a bowl;
because the price—whether in full or in part—has not been paid, it does not attain its own status, but remains that of another.
It becomes his own property; therefore, it becomes subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) only when both the cooking and the root-price have been fully completed.
That which is subject to determination is also subject to assignment (*vikappana*). Whether it has come into one’s hand or not, it may be determined or assigned.
For if the bowl-maker, having obtained the root-price, should himself wish to give it, saying: "Venerable sir, I [give this] to you..."
If the bowl-maker says, "Having made the bowl, I will cook it and set it aside on such-and-such a day," and the monk lets ten days pass from that specified date,
it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
However, if the bowl-maker says, "I will make a bowl for you, cook it, and send word by messenger," and does exactly so, and the monk [who receives it]...
However, if he does not inform that bhikkhu, but another person— having seen or heard it— informs him, saying, "Venerable sir,
your bowl is finished," this report is not authoritative. But when the one sent by him himself reports it,
if he lets ten days pass from the day he hears that statement, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

But if the bowl-maker says, "I will make a bowl for you, cook it, and send it in someone's hand," and does exactly so, yet the monk who comes bringing the bowl places it in his own cell and does not inform him, and someone else asks, "Venerable sir, is that beautiful bowl which was recently brought here where? [he replies: "Where?..."
"Friend, has the bowl been received? "It was sent into the hand of such-and-such a person. Even his word is not authoritative.
However, when that monk gives away the bowl, from the day it is obtained, if ten days elapse, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture;
therefore, one must either determine or assign it before the ten days have elapsed.
In this regard, there are two ways of determining the bowl: one determines it by means of the body, or one determines it by means of speech.
By means of these, one who is determining [the bowl] should say, "I relinquish this bowl," or "I relinquish that bowl.
Having thus relinquished the old bowl—whether it be standing before him or out of his sight—one [should then receive] another.

Or, having given away a new bowl, wherever it may be located, one should resolve upon it by making a mental application with the thought, "I resolve upon this bowl," either by means of the body while performing a bodily gesture, or by means of speech after uttering the words.
In that regard, there are two kinds of resolution: if it is within reach of the hand, [one resolves] "this..."

The words "I resolve upon this bowl" must be spoken. Then, whether one is in an inner chamber, on an upper terrace, or in a nearby monastery, having observed the place where it is being set down, the words "I resolve upon this bowl" must be spoken.
Furthermore, when resolving, it is permissible to resolve alone, or it is also permissible to resolve in the presence of another.
It is allowable. This is the advantage of being in the presence of another:
if a doubt should arise as to whether or not his bowl has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), the other person will remind him and cut through that doubt.
If someone obtains ten bowls and wishes to use them all for himself alone, he should not determine all of them; rather, having determined one bowl, on the following day...
Having relinquished that [alms-bowl], another must be determined upon. By this very means, it is possible to maintain it even for a hundred years.
Could there be a loss of determination for one who is thus diligent? There could be.
For if he gives his own bowl to another, or if he disrobes, or renounces the training, or passes away, or if his gender changes—then [the determination is lost].
Or he relinquishes it, or a hole appears in the bowl, or the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is lost. And this has been said:
"By giving it away, by going away, by renouncing it, by death, by the change of gender, by relinquishing it, and by a hole appearing—these are the seven [causes for losing the bowl]."
One may even abandon it by means of taking it into one's own possession or through trust. By how much a breach must the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) be broken?
By that [breach] through which a grain of millet (*kaṅgusittha*) can both exit and enter.
For this is the smallest grain among the seven types of grain. If that breach is repaired with iron filings or a pin, it must be formally determined again within ten days.
This, then, is the analysis regarding formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) here. 49.
Regarding assignment (*vikappana*), however, there are two kinds of assignment: assignment in the presence (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and assignment in the absence (*parammukhā-vikappanā*).
How does assignment in the presence come about? Having ascertained whether the bowls are one or many, and whether they are present or absent, [one says]: "This..."
Having said either “this bowl,” or “these bowls,” or “that bowl,” or “these bowls,” one must say, “I dedicate this to you.

This is one kind of dedication in the presence [of the recipient]. Up to this point, it is permissible to store [the bowl], but it is not permissible to consume it, to dispose of it, or to formally resolve upon its use. [One may say: “Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it.”
"Or do as you see fit according to the circumstances. When this has been said, it is called "renunciation" (paccuddhāra);
from that point on, even using [the bowl] and so forth is permitted.
Another method: having likewise understood whether the bowls are one or many, and whether they are kept nearby or not, of that very [bowl]...

In the presence of a bhikkhu, having said, "This bowl," or "These bowls," or "That bowl," or "Those bowls," and having taken the name of whichever among the five types of fellow practitioners one prefers— saying,
"I assign this to the bhikkhu Tissa," or "To the bhikkhunī Tissa, the sikkhamānā, the sāmaṇera..."
Or one should say, "I assign it to the novice nun Tissā. This is another form of assignment in the presence [of the recipient]. Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside;
however, it is not permissible for any of the uses such as personal consumption and so forth.
That monk may, according to circumstances, either use or dispose of what belongs to the monk Tissa... or what belongs to the novice nun Tissā.
When it is said, "Or do so," there is what is called a formal relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*);
from that point on, even using [the bowl] and other such acts are permissible. How does a formal assignment (*vikappanā*) take place in the absence of the person?
Having ascertained whether the bowls are one or many, and whether they are present or absent, one says, "This bowl," or "These bowls," or "That bowl," or "Those bowls."
He should say, “I give this for your use. He [the recipient] should then ask, “Who is your friend or acquaintance?
Thereupon, the other should reply in the same manner as before: “Three monks,” or …pe… “A novice nun named Tissā.
Then that monk should say, “I give it to the monk named Tissa,” or …pe… “To the novice nun named Tissā.”
Or one should say, "I give it. This is the assignment in the absence of the recipient (*parammukhā-vikappanā*). Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside;

however, for purposes such as personal use, not even one of these is permitted. When that monk has been told by a second person, in the manner already described for an assignment in the presence of the recipient (*sammukhā-vikappanā*):
"Use the property of so-and-so, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," [then it becomes permissible].

There is what is called "renunciation" (*paccuddhāra*); from that point on, even using [the bowl] for consumption and other purposes is permitted. This is the method regarding the assignment [of a bowl].
50. Having thus determined and assigned [the bowl], what should be done by one who uses it when the bowl is broken?
For one whose bowl lacks a rim or mouth-circle measuring two finger-breadths below [the top], nothing need be done.
But for one who has even a single such streak, he should pierce the lower edge of that streak with a leaf-needle,
cook it, and then bind it with a cord of thread, a cord of bark-fiber, and so forth, or with a lead thread;
and that binding should be concealed with a lead-paste or some kind of adhesive resin so that food does not stick to it.
Once it has been obtained, it should be used after making a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, a small hole may be made and it should be tied [with a cord].
However, it is not permitted to tie it with pure substances such as *madhuka* flour, lac, sugar-cane juice, or honey;
it is permitted to tie it with stone powder after the molasses has been burnt. Furthermore, when being pierced near the rim by a bowl-piercer...
Because the skull is thick, it breaks; therefore, it should be pierced from below. For one that has two lines, or even one line measuring four finger-breadths, two bindings should be applied.
For one that has three, or even one measuring six finger-breadths, three [bindings] should be applied.
For one that has four, or even one measuring eight finger-breadths, four [bindings] should be applied. For one that has five, or even one...
Or ten finger-breadths; even if it is bound or unbound, as long as it has not yet reached [the ground], another bowl must be requested.

This, then, is the determination regarding bowls made of clay. As for bowls made of iron, even if there are five or more holes, if those holes are bound with iron filings, a pin, or a copper ring and are polished smooth, that very bowl may be used.

Another [bowl] must not be requested. However, if even one crack is large, or if it is not smooth despite being bound with a copper ring, or if food sticks to the bowl, it is unallowable; this is a non-bowl, and another must be requested.
And when requesting, in a place where the Saṅgha has offered an invitation, one should request another bowl only if one already possesses a bowl with five bindings.
It is permissible to request [a bowl]; however, in a place where one has been invited [to accept a bowl], it is also permissible even if it has fewer than five repairs.
Once a bowl has been obtained and is being used, it must not be used for anything other than its intended purpose, such as for cooking gruel, fuel, or dye.
But if a disease arises while on the road and no other vessel is available, one may smear it with clay and use it for gruel.
It is permissible [to use it] for cooking or heating water. It must not be placed even on an improper location such as a bed, a stool, a canopy, or a peg.
For the proper place for setting down the bowl has indeed been stated in the Khandhaka by way of the passage beginning, "I allow you, monks, a bowl-stand."
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of formal acts and designations in the Compendium of Vinaya Determinations Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 9.
Discourse on the Determination of Separation from Robes.

51. *Cīvarena vinā vāso* (living apart from one’s robe): this refers to being separated from any one of the three robes that have been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) by means of the determination of the triple-robe set.
For when the three robes have been determined in this manner, it is not permitted to live even without one of them;

for one who lives so, at the rising of the dawn, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Therefore, at the time of the rising of the dawn, [one must remain within] a distance of two and a half *ratana*s from the robe.

One must dwell within arm’s reach [of another]. However, there is this distinction regarding villages, inhabited areas, fortified towns, watchtowers, palaces, upper chambers, ships, chariots, fields, threshing floors, monasteries, hermitages, the foot of trees, and open spaces:
if there is a village belonging to a single king or a village headman, and it is surrounded by any kind of wall, fence, or moat—one may deposit one's robe in such a village.
It is permissible to cause the dawn to rise anywhere within the village, in whatever place one prefers.
However, if the village is unenclosed, one must reside in the house where the robe has been deposited;
or else, one must dwell within a radius of two and a half ratanas (cubits) around the vicinity of that house. That is the measure.
Even if a bhikkhu possessing supernormal powers causes the dawn to rise while in the air after having crossed over [the boundary], the robe remains subject to forfeiture.

If there is a village belonging to various kings or local lords, such as Vesālī or Kusinārā, which is enclosed by a boundary, in such a village one must reside in whichever house the robe was deposited; or, by means of audible contact with that place...
Or, if one is unable to dwell [in the monastery] due to a crowding of people, one should dwell in the assembly hall or at the city gate.

If one is still unable to dwell there, one may stay in any comfortable place and, having returned before dawn, dwell within arm’s reach of those very same assembly halls or city gates. As for the house, however, [the rule regarding] the robe—
Or, within arm’s reach, there is simply nothing that can be said [against it].
If, having left it at home with the thought, “I will place it in the assembly hall,” one goes to the assembly hall and,
extending one's hand, says, “Now, please set down this robe,” and thus, while the robe is within arm’s reach for the purpose of depositing it, [leaves it] in some shop—
Having set it down, he should, according to the same method as before, reside either in the assembly hall (*sabhā*) or at the base of the door, within arm’s reach of them.
Even if the city has many gates and many assembly halls, it is not permitted to reside in all of them.
However, regarding the street where the robe was placed, that which is directly in front of it—the assembly hall and the gate—[is where he should stay].
One must remain within arm’s reach of both that assembly hall and the door. For when this is the case, it is possible to know the whereabouts of the robe.

However, if one goes into the assembly hall and the merchant in whose hand the robe was placed takes it away and deposits it in his house, then the arm’s reach of the street does not protect it; [the protection belongs to] the house.
One must remain within arm’s reach. If it is a large house that extends across two streets, one must cause the dawn to rise while still within arm’s reach, either in front or behind.

However, having deposited the items in the assembly hall, one must cause the dawn to rise within arm’s reach of those very persons—either in the assembly hall, in their presence, at the city gate, or nearby.
If, however, the village is unenclosed, one must stay within arm’s reach of the house where the robe was deposited,
or within arm’s reach of that house itself.
If it is a residence belonging to a single family that is enclosed and contains various rooms and various inner chambers, [one must stay within arm’s reach of the house].
Having deposited the robe within the residence, one must dwell within the residence.
If it is unenclosed, one must dwell in the room where the robe was deposited, or within arm’s reach of that room.
If it is the residence of various families and is enclosed, consisting of various rooms and various inner chambers, [one must dwell] in whichever room...
If the robe has been deposited [in a dwelling], one must reside in that same chamber, or within arm’s reach of the house door if it is common to all,
or within arm’s reach of the chamber if it is not common to all. This applies also to open halls, half-halls, palaces, and upper chambers.
The detailed explanation should be understood in the same manner as stated regarding a dwelling.
If the boat belongs to a single family, one should deposit the robe within the boat and reside within the boat.
If the boat belongs to various families, consisting of various cabins and various compartments, [one should reside] in whichever compartment the robe has been deposited.
If there is a dwelling, one must stay in that dwelling or within arm’s reach of it.
If there is a caravan belonging to a single family, having deposited the robe in that caravan, one must not go beyond seven *abbhantaras* either in front or behind;
one must not go beyond the inner range of sight. One *abbhantara*—
It is twenty-eight cubits long. If there is a caravan belonging to various families, one should deposit the robe in the caravan and remain within arm’s reach of the robe.

If the caravan, while traveling, stops by encircling a village or a river, and stands connected as a single unit, covering both this side and the far side, then [one may stay] together with those who have entered inside.
The exemption from the caravan is obtained. Furthermore, if one is included within a village or a river, both the exemption from the village and the exemption from the river are obtained.
If one stands having crossed the monastery boundary while the robe is still within the boundary, one must go to the monastery and stay there.
If the robe is outside the boundary, one must stay right near the caravan.
If, while traveling, the caravan is interrupted— either because a cart has broken down or an ox has been lost—
one must stay in whichever section the robe was deposited.
If it is the field of a single family and is enclosed by a fence, one may deposit the robe within the field and [stay] within the field.
One must dwell there. If it is unenclosed, one must dwell within arm’s reach of the robe.
If it is the field of various families and is enclosed, one must dwell at the foot of the gate or within arm’s reach of the foot of the gate, having placed the robe inside the field.
If it is unenclosed, one must dwell within arm’s reach of the robe.

If there is a threshing floor belonging to a single family and it is enclosed, one may deposit the robe within the threshing floor and must dwell within the threshing floor. If it is unenclosed, one must remain within arm’s reach of the robe.
If there is a threshing floor belonging to various families and it is enclosed, one may deposit the robe within the threshing floor...
One should dwell at the base of the door, or within arm’s reach of the base of the door. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell within arm’s reach of the robe.
In the case of flower gardens or fruit orchards as well, the determination should be understood according to the method explained for fields.
If there is a monastery belonging to a single family that is enclosed, having deposited the robe inside the monastery, [one may stay] inside the monastery.
One must dwell [there]. If it is unenclosed, one must dwell in that monastery where the robe was deposited, or within arm’s reach of that monastery.
If it is the foot of a tree belonging to a single family, one must dwell within the shade that extends all around at midday.

Having laid aside the robe, one must dwell within the shade. However, if it is placed in a spot touched by the sun’s heat under a tree with sparse branches, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); therefore, it should be placed in the shade of such a tree’s branches or its trunk.
If one places it on a branch or a bough, [it is permissible] provided there is the shade of another branch above it.
It should be placed only within the area where one has stood. The shadow of a crooked tree extends far; it is indeed permissible to place it in the place where the shadow has reached.
If the foot of the tree belongs to various families, one must remain within arm’s reach of the robe.
However, in an uninhabited forest in the open air, having placed the robe there, one may stay within a distance of seven *abbhantara*s all around it.
What is called "a forest devoid of a road" (agāmaka-arañña) is found in places such as the Vindhya jungle or on islands in the middle of the ocean that lie outside the paths frequented by fishermen.
For one standing in the middle of such a forest, the area defined by seven *abbhantara* units in every direction—amounting to fourteen in total—is the extent.
Sitting in the center, [the monk should observe] the boundary in either the eastern or western direction.

He guards the robe that has been set aside. However, if at the time of sunrise he goes even as much as the breadth of a hair's tip toward the eastern direction, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture in the western direction. This same principle applies to the other directions as well.
Furthermore, by using a robe that has become subject to forfeiture without having forfeited it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

52. If a monk who is striving, having applied himself to striving throughout the entire night, enters a river at dawn thinking, "I shall bathe," and having placed his three robes on the bank, the dawn breaks while he is still bathing—what should be done?
For if he, having emerged from the water, puts on a robe, it is a robe that must be relinquished; if he does not relinquish it...
One incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by using [the robes]. Now, if one goes about naked, does one also incur an offense of wrong-doing in this way?

One does not. For as long as he has not seen another monk and performed the formal act of the Discipline (*vinayakamma*), he stands in the position of one whose robes have been lost, because those robes are unfit for use;
and for one whose robes have been lost, that which is improper (*akappiya*) is indeed [not to be used].
It does not exist; therefore, having put on one [robe] and holding two [others] with both hands, one should go to the monastery and perform the formal act of the Vinaya.
If the monastery is far away and people are traveling along the path, one should go having put on one [robe], covered with another, and placed one over the shoulder.
If one does not see a fellow monk in the monastery, [one should enter] for alms...

When they have arrived, having placed the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) outside the village and entered the assembly hall wearing only the inner robe and upper garment (*santaruttara*), the formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) should be performed.
If there is fear of thieves outside the village, they should go there while fully robed.
If the assembly hall is crowded and congested, such that it is impossible to perform the formal act of the Vinaya by removing the robes to one side, [one should appoint] a single monk...
Having taken them and gone outside the village, one should perform the formal act of the Vinaya and then use the robes.

If the elder bhikkhus, having placed their bowls and robes in the hands of the junior bhikkhus, wish to sleep during the last watch of the night while traveling on the road, they should sleep keeping each of their own robes within arm’s reach. If, while still traveling...
If dawn breaks while they have not yet reached the young monks, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), yet the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not thereby terminated.
The same rule applies when those walking ahead of the young monks have not yet reached the elders.
This same rule also applies even if they lose their way in the forest and cannot see one another. However, if the young monks [think], "We..."
“Venerable sir, having slept for a short while, we shall reach you at such-and-such a place,” he says;
yet they sleep until sunrise, whereby the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the formal support (*nissaya*) is dissolved.
The same rule applies even when the elders sleep while sending away the juniors. Upon seeing a forked path, the elders [say], “This is the way,”...
The junior monks, saying, "This is the path," departed without heeding one another's words;
with the rising of the dawn, their robes become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and their formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended.
If the junior monks, having left the road, enter a village for the sake of medicine thinking, "We shall turn back before sunrise," and then return, [the rules do not apply].
If the dawn breaks while they have not yet arrived, their robes become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*),
yet the formal support (*nissaya*) is not dissolved. However, if— due to fear of cows or fear of dogs— they stay for a short while and then proceed, whether standing or sitting,
with the intention "we shall go," then even if the dawn breaks in the interim, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture.
[the robes] become [subject to forfeiture] and the formal support (nissaya) is suspended.

However, if they enter a village within the boundary thinking, "We will return before dawn," and the dawn breaks while they are still inside the boundary, then the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, nor is the formal support suspended. But if [they think], "Let it grow light..."

If they sit down [thinking], "We will return within the dawn," and the dawn has already risen, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), but the formal support (*nissaya*) is suspended. However,
if those who have set out for a neighboring monastery with the intention of hearing the Dharma, thinking,
"We will return within the dawn itself," find that the dawn rises while they are still on the road, their robes do become subject to forfeiture.

However, the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not suspended. If, out of reverence for the Dhamma, they sit thinking, "We shall depart only after hearing the teaching to its conclusion," then at the rising of the sun, their robes become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the formal dependence is suspended.
When an elder sends a junior monk to a village to wash his robe, he must first relinquish his own robe.
It must be given; even for a junior monk, the robe should be set aside only after having it formally relinquished.
If he departs without mindfulness, he should relinquish his own robe and, taking the junior’s robe on trust, set it aside.
If the elder does not remember, but the junior does, the junior should relinquish his own robe and [give] that of the elder.
Having taken the robe with confidence and having gone, one should say: "Venerable sir, please determine this robe as yours and make use of it.
One’s own robe should also be determined. In this way, even for a single person, there is release from the offense.
Thus ends the compendium of legal decisions on the Vinaya not found in the canonical texts.
The discussion on the determination of being separated from one’s robes is finished.
10. The Discussion on the Determination of Returning Property. 53.
“Returning property” means the guarding of another’s property. For [it refers to] the allowable goods of others, or—

Whether it be an improper object, or even as little as a mother’s earring or a black leaf belonging to a householder, for one who has it stored away under the pretext that it belongs to the storekeeper, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
However, if it is a suitable article belonging to parents that must necessarily be stored away, it may be taken for one's own use and then stored. "This..."
But when it is said, "Having put it away, give it back," one should refuse, saying, "It is not permitted.
However, if they leave after having dropped it with the words, "Put it away," then it is called an impediment (*palibodha*), and it is permitted to put it away.
Or, when carpenters and others, or royal favorites, are working in the monastery, [if they say], "Having put away our own implements or bedding..."
If they say, "Give it back," one must certainly not do so out of desire or fear;
however, it is permissible to show them a secure place, or to restore items that have been forcibly brought in by those who entered by force.
If goods placed in one's own hand for the purpose of being restored are requested by the owner, saying, "Give me my goods," [one should return them].

If one who does not wish to give, when asked, says, "I will not take it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because even a conscious lie constitutes an application toward taking what is not given.
There is likewise an offense of wrong-doing for one who says things such as, "What are you saying? This is neither suitable for me, nor for you.
[And so on. "I placed it in his hand in private; no one else knows. Will he perhaps give it? [and so forth.]
If the owner, thinking "it is not mine," conceives doubt, there is a *thullaccaya* offense for the bhikkhu.

If, having seen its harsh condition and so forth, the owner gives up the burden, thinking "he will not give it to me," then if this bhikkhu is still intent on giving, thinking "I will give it after making him weary," he is still protected [from the full offense]. Even if he is no longer intent on giving, the owner of the goods—
However, if he has the intention to take it and continues to guard it, [there is no offense].

But if, regarding that gift, the owner of the goods lacks the intention and gives up his responsibility, thinking, "He will not give it to me," then through the relinquishment of responsibility by both parties, the monk incurs a *pārājika*.
Even if he says with his mouth, "I will give it," but in his mind does not wish to give, it is likewise for the owner.

There is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) in the relinquishing of responsibility. However, there is no offense for one who, for the sake of protection, moves goods placed in his own hands by others from an unprotected place to a protected place. Even for one who moves them from that place with a thieving mind, there is no theft. Why?
Because they were placed in his own hands; [in such a case] it is merely a debt of goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
The same principle applies even when one uses [an item] with a thieving mind.
54. However, it is permissible to put away any kind of requisite belonging to five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
If a visiting bhikkhu, having placed his bowl and robe near resident bhikkhus who are engaged in making robes, [leaves them there...]
If, thinking, “These will look after them,” he goes to bathe or elsewhere, and if the residents do look after them, that is well.

If they do not, there is no liability for loss. Even if he says, “Venerable sirs, please keep this,” and departs, and the others do not know because they are occupied with their duties, the same rule applies. Furthermore—

If they are told, "Venerable sirs, please set this aside," and they decline, saying, "We are busy," and the other person departs without taking it up, thinking, "They will certainly set it aside," the same principle applies.
However, if they—whether requested or unrequested by him—say, "We shall set it aside; you may go," then it must be guarded. If they do not guard it, [one should take it back].
If it is lost, it must be made good. Why?

Because it was accepted. If a monk who serves as the storekeeper, at the time of dawn, lowers the bowls and robes of the monks to the lower terrace, closes the door, and goes on alms-round far away without even informing them, those [items]—
If thieves carry them off, the blame falls upon that very person. However, when a bhikkhu is told by other bhikkhus, "Venerable sir, please set aside your bowl and robes;
it is time for the distribution of voting tickets," and having asked, "Are you all assembled?
and being told, "Yes, we are assembled," he takes out his bowl and robes, sets them aside, locks the door of the storehouse, and [says], "You may take your bowls and robes..."
"Having taken [the bowls] and attended to the door of the lower palace, you may go," he said, and then departed.
Now, there was a certain lazy monk who, after the other monks had left, rose up while rubbing his eyes and went to the water source to wash his face.
Seeing that moment, the thieves carried off his bowl and robes; they were well-plundered.
The treasurer is not liable for it. Even if someone, without informing the treasurer, places their own requisites in the storehouse, the treasurer is not liable for them if they are lost.
However, if the treasurer sees that [item] and thinks, "It has been placed in the wrong spot,"...
Having taken it, he sets it aside; if it is lost, the responsibility for it falls upon him. Even if the monk who set it down says, "Venerable sir, such an article has been deposited by me;
please look after it," and the other accepts with "Very well," yet—either suspecting it was poorly placed or thinking it should be kept elsewhere—he moves it to another spot;

if it is then lost, the responsibility for it falls upon the one who originally set it down. As for the one who refuses, saying, "I do not know [where it is]," the responsibility does not fall upon him.
However, there is no liability for loss. Even if someone places it down while he is looking on, and does not have the storekeeper accept it, if it is lost, it is indeed lost [to the owner].
But if the storekeeper places it elsewhere, then in the event of loss, there is liability for the cost.
If the storehouse is well-guarded and all the requisites of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya are kept right there, [there is no liability].
If the storekeeper is foolish and incompetent, and having opened the door, goes elsewhere to listen to a Dhamma talk or to do something else,
whatever thieves steal at that moment is his liability.
This applies whether he has left the storeroom and is walking outside, or has opened the door to let the body [of the goods] take the air.
Or while sitting right there engaged in the practice of the ascetic’s duty; or while sitting right there occupied with some task;
or even when oppressed by the need for excrement or urine, if the precincts are available, he goes outside;
or while being negligent in some other way, he opens the door or enters it while it is already open.
Or, if thieves break into a house and carry off whatever they take due to his negligence, all that is his liability.
However, they say: "It is permissible to lie down with the window open during the heat.

But for one who is oppressed by the urge to defecate, if there is no space nearby and he goes elsewhere, it is not within his domain because he is situated on the side of one who is ill; therefore, there is no liability.
55. However, if one who is oppressed by heat inside goes out while having secured the door well, and thieves seize him and say, "Open the door," it should not be opened even up to the third time.
But if those thieves [say], "If you do not open it, we shall kill you and, having broken down the door, carry off the requisites," and they brandish axes and other weapons—
They throw it out, thinking, "When I am dead and the Sangha’s lodgings have been ruined, there will be no benefit [in keeping it]";
thus, it is permissible to open it. Here too, they say, "Because it is not his domain, there is no liability.
If some visitor gives the key or opens the door, whatever the thieves steal, he is liable for all of it. [If] the Sangha [entrusts] the storehouse...
If, for the sake of security, he has fastened the latch-pin and the key-seal and left them, and the storekeeper, having given only a small turn to the bolt, goes to sleep,
and thieves open the door and carry off the requisites, the responsibility falls on that very person. However,
if he has fastened both the latch-pin and the key-seal and gone to sleep, and thieves come and say, "Open the door!"...
Regarding that which they say, one should proceed there according to the previous method.
However, if, after he has lain down having thus made himself well-guarded, they break through a wall or the roof, or enter by a tunnel and carry it off, he is not liable for the debt.
If other elders also reside in the storehouse, and the door is open, he may take his own requisites [and leave].
They go away; when they have gone, the storekeeper does not guard the door.
If anything is stolen there, because of the storekeeper’s authority, the liability falls upon the storekeeper alone. However, one must be like an elder friend.
This is indeed the proper conduct (*sāmīci*). If the storekeeper says, "Stand outside and take your requisites," [then it is appropriate].

"Do not enter," he says; yet one of them, a greedy *mahāthera*, enters the storehouse together with the novices and attendants, sits down, and even lies down there. Whatever goods are lost, all of it is his liability.
However, the storekeeper and the remaining elders must act as companions [to one another]. Then—
Just as a storekeeper, taking with him restless novices and attendants, sits and lies down in the storehouse,
and whatever is lost is entirely his responsibility; therefore, only the storekeeper should dwell there,
while the rest should dwell even at the foot of a tree, and not in the storehouse.

56. Furthermore, if one places requisites in the dwelling-cells of one's own fellow monks, then if those requisites are lost, the liability for them falls upon those by whom they were placed; the others, however, must act as companions.
But if the Saṅgha causes the storekeeper to have gruel and rice provided right there in the monastery, and he [the storekeeper] goes out for the purpose of alms-round...

If he goes to the village, the loss is his responsibility. When one who has been appointed as the *vihāravārika* (duty-monk) for the purpose of guarding extra robes goes on almsround—provided that he receives either rice gruel or food as his share—the entire amount lost there is his responsibility.
And it is not only this much; like that of a storekeeper, whatever...
If it is lost through his negligence, he must pay for the whole amount.

If the monastery is large, however, when he goes to guard another area and someone steals what has been placed in another area, there is no liability because it was outside his jurisdiction. But in such a monastery, in the middle, at a place where everyone gathers—
One should sit down after setting aside the requisites, or two or three *vihāravārika* (duty-holders) should be stationed there.
Even if something is lost while they are being careful and guarding [the items] here and there, there is no liability for compensation.
This applies even to goods carried away by thieves after the *vihāravārika*s have been bound, or goods carried away by another route when the thieves have gone along a different path.

It is not their responsibility. If there is no rice gruel or meal to be given in the monastery for the monastery attendants (*vihāravārika*), it is permissible for them to set aside two or three extra gruel-sticks and enough meal-sticks for their own portion from what they would otherwise receive;
however, these should not be set aside as a fixed regularity. For people might become resentful, thinking, "These are just the monastery attendants..."
“[They] are eating our meal,” therefore it should be set aside after being turned over again and again.

If they bring and give them similar items such as *salākabhatta* (ticket-meals) and so forth, that is well; if they do not give them, one should have them brought out by having a turn (*vāra*) assigned.
If the monastery steward [has] two or three *yāgu-salākas* (saucepans/tickets for rice-gruel) and four or five *salākabhattas*, [he should act accordingly].
Even when he goes out for alms, it is as if everything were lost and must be made good by a storekeeper;
if there is no food or fodder to be given to the Saṅgha or to the monastery guards,
the monks take turns according to their assigned duty (*vihāravāra*) to look after their respective dwellings, and one who has not received his turn is not permitted to do so.

One should act exactly as other bhikkhus do. However, for one who is without companions or without a second person, or for one who has no fellow bhikkhu to bring and give him food, such a turn should not be assigned.
Furthermore, regarding that which they set aside in the monastery for the sake of the rice-milling cycle—one who lives by taking that [income] must remain [in the monastery]. He who...
He does not subsist [on them]; he should not be made to take his turn. They also appoint a monk in the monastery for the sake of fruits;

having tended and guarded them, they divide and eat the fruit-portion. Whoever eats those [fruits] must remain [in that post], and one who does not subsist [on them] should not be made to take his turn.
They also appoint [a monk] for the sake of guarding the lodgings, beds, chairs, and coverlets.
One who dwells in a residence must remain there; however, one who lives in the open air or at the foot of a tree should not be made to take up residence.

Suppose there is a single junior monk who is learned, recites the Dhamma for many others, provides answers to questions, explains the Canon, delivers Dhamma discourses, and carries out the burdens of the Saṅgha—even while enjoying gains and dwelling in a residence, he [is exempt].
He must not be allowed to enter [the monastery] on other days. They say, "The distinction of the person must be known.
However, for one who maintains the Uposatha hall and the image house, double the amount of rice-gruel and food should be given; a nāḷi of rice daily;
