and at the end of the year, the three robes and articles of allowable property worth ten or twenty [pieces of money] should be provided. But if, while he is receiving those things, through negligence something [is lost or damaged] there...
If it is lost, the entire value must be repaid. If it was forcibly snatched away after being bound [and recovered], there is no obligation to repay.

In that regard, it is permissible for property belonging to the Cetiya to be used to protect property belonging to the Cetiya, or for property belonging to the Saṅgha to be used to protect property belonging to the Cetiya;

however, it is not permissible for property belonging to the Cetiya to be used to protect property belonging to the Saṅgha. Furthermore, as for that which belongs to the Saṅgha together with what belongs to the Cetiya...
If something has been set aside as belonging to the Saṅgha, it is indeed protected if it is placed under the protection of what belongs to the Cetiya; thus this is permissible.

Even for one who guards the Uposatha hall and other such places by turn of the fortnight, if anything is lost through negligence, the responsibility falls upon that person alone. Thus ends the compendium of Vinaya decisions not found in the canonical texts (Pāḷimuttaka-vinaya-vinicchaya-saṅgaha).
The discussion on the determination of bartering with wares is finished.
11. The Discussion on the Determination of Barter and Sale. 57.
"Barter and sale" (*kayavikkayasamāpatti*) means the act of entering into barter and sale. For it is by way of such methods as "Give this for that," and so forth...
One who takes another’s allowable goods enters into buying; one who gives away one’s own allowable goods enters into selling.

This buying and selling, however, is not permitted with anyone except for the five who share the same Dhamma, including all householders and renunciants, and even including one’s own mother and father.
In this regard, the analysis is as follows: whether it be cloth for cloth, or food for food—whatever is allowable—if one says, "Give this with that," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having spoken thus, even if one gives one's own goods to one's mother, it is an offense of wrong-doing;
or if, being told, "Give this with that," one says, "Give this, and I will give you that," even to one's mother, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
If one takes the goods for oneself, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

When one's own goods reach another's hand, or when another's goods reach one's own hand, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). However, for one who says to a mother or a father, "Give this," there is no formal request (*viññatti*);
and for one who gives by saying, "Take this," there is no misappropriation of what has been given in faith (*saddhādeyya-vinipātana*).

When one says to a stranger, "Give this," it is an act of requesting (*viññatti*). When one gives while saying, "Take this," it is the misappropriation of what was given in faith (*saddhādeyyavinipātana*).
When one enters into buying and selling by saying, "Give this for that," it is an offense involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

Therefore, when exchanging allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*), one should exchange them even with one's mother or father; however, when exchanging with strangers, one must avoid the three offenses by ensuring the transaction is free from fault.
In this regard, the procedure for exchange is as follows: A monk has rice for his provisions on a journey.
On the way, he sees a man with food in his hand and says, "We have rice, but we have no need for it; however, we do need food.
The man takes the rice and gives him food. This is permissible, and there are no three kinds of offenses.

There is not even the slightest act of signaling. Why? Because the root [of the offense] is present. However, if one does not do it this way, but instead exchanges goods by saying, "Give this to that person," it remains exactly as it was in its original state.
If, upon seeing a scavenger, one says, "After eating this rice, bring dye or firewood," then there is an offense according to the count of the dye-skins or the count of the firewood.

And these are also offenses involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). If one has a particular requisite made for water-pots and the like by craftsmen such as ivory-workers, saying, "Having eaten this rice, do this [work]," or if one has clothes washed by laundrymen, it is an offense according to the original basis (*yathāvatthuka*).
If one has a barber cut one's hair, or if one has new construction work done by laborers, it is an offense according to the original basis.
However, if he does not say, "Having eaten this meal, do this," but rather says, "Eat this meal; you have eaten, you will eat;

do such-and-such a thing," it is permissible. And here, although in the case of washing clothes, cutting hair, or performing new work such as clearing the ground, another's property that has come into one's own hands must be returned.
There is no [contradiction], for since it is stated emphatically in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, this cannot be rejected;
therefore, just as one confesses a *pācittiya* when a *nissaggiya* object has been used or lost, so too here one must confess.
It is permissible to ask the price out of a desire to acquire any kind of allowable article; therefore, [if one says], "This is yours..."
When asked, "What is this bowl worth?", he replies, "It is worth this much. If his own allowable goods are of great value, he should respond thus:
"Lay follower, this article of mine is of great value; give your bowl to someone else.
Upon hearing this, if the other person says, "I will give you another dish as well," it is permissible to accept it. If...

If the bowl is of great value while the monk’s requisites are of little value, and the owner of the bowl does not know their low value, the bowl must not be accepted; one should explain, "My requisites are of little value.
For even one who accepts it by deceiving him after learning of its high value incurs liability for having the goods appraised. If the owner of the bowl...
If one gives [the gift] saying, "Venerable sir, let the remainder be my merit," it is permissible.
However, it is permissible to instruct a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) by saying, "With this, take that and give it.
Therefore, setting aside the person from whose hand one receives the goods, one may designate anyone else—even his son or brother—as a *kappiyakāraka* and say, "With this..."
If he points it out by saying, "Take this one," and the person is clever, he may take it after repeatedly setting it aside and disputing;
otherwise, one should remain silent. If the person is not clever and does not know how to take it, and the merchant deceives him, one should say, "Do not take it."

But when it is said, “We have this oil or ghee that has been accepted; we need something else that has not been accepted,” if he takes that [accepted portion] and gives him another, one’s own oil must not be measured first. Why?
Because there might be a *nāḷi* of oil remaining; if one were to measure later, that unaccepted portion would spoil it.
And this so-called "buying and selling" is spoken of by way of allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*).
For it is stated that for one who exchanges an allowable thing for an allowable thing, there is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) under the training rule on buying and selling;

however, for one who exchanges an unallowable thing for an unallowable thing, or an allowable thing for an unallowable thing, or an unallowable thing for an allowable thing, [the offense is defined] under the training rule on trading with money (*rūpiyasaṃvohāra*).
It is an offense involving forfeiture; therefore, when either both or one of these two [factors] is unallowable, it is called "trade in money.
58. To illustrate the gravity of trade in money, this fourfold classification of bowls should be understood.
For if someone, having acquired money, uses it to produce iron seed, has that [seed] crushed, and [makes] a bowl from that metal—
If one has it made, this bowl is called "greatly unallowable" (*mahā-akappiya*); it cannot be made allowable by any means whatsoever.
Even if one destroys that [bowl] and has a platter made, that too is unallowable. If one has a knife made, even a tooth-stick cut with it is unallowable.
If one has a fishhook made, even the fish killed with it are unallowable. Or, having heated a knife [and used it for water...]* *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.)*
Or if one heats milk, that too is indeed not allowable.
Furthermore, if someone acquires money and buys an alms bowl with it, this bowl is also not allowable.
"It is not allowable for even those five who share the same Dhamma," so it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī. However, it is possible to make it allowable. That...
Indeed, when it is given to the owners of the raw materials at the root [of the tree] and to the owners of the bowl at the leaf [stage], it becomes allowable;
having given an allowable article and received it, it is permissible to use it.
Even one who, having caused money to be accepted, goes with a kappiyakāra (an agent for allowable goods) to a smithy and sees a bowl—

If he says, “This one pleases me,” and the attendant, having given that money, instructs a smith, this bowl—even though it was obtained through a permissible transaction—is just like the second bowl; because the price was accepted, it is not permissible.
Why is it not permissible for the others? Because the price has not been relinquished.

However, if one does not personally accept the silver, but goes with a messenger who has been sent saying, "Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it to him," and upon reaching the smith's workshop and seeing a bowl,
causes the messenger to hand over the coins by saying, "Take these coins and give this [bowl] to him," and the bowl is thus received,
this bowl is not permissible for that very monk because of his improper conduct; but for others, it is permissible.
However, it is permissible because the root [offense] was not accepted. It is said that the preceptor of the Elder Mahāsumma was the Elder Anuruddha.

He filled his own bowl of this kind with ghee and relinquished it to the Saṅgha. Such a bowl also belonged to the co-residents of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga; the Elder, having filled it with ghee, likewise caused it to be relinquished to the Saṅgha.
This is the set of four improper bowls.

However, if one has not accepted money [in advance], but goes with a steward sent by saying, "Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it to him," and upon reaching the smith's house sees a bowl and says, "This one pleases me," or "I shall take this one"—
Or he speaks thus, and the attendant, having given that money, instructs the smith; this bowl is entirely allowable and fit even for the Buddhas to use.
However, by one who is engaging in such transactions with money, it is not permitted to direct even the attendant, saying, "Take this and give me that."
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of the acquisition of goods through purchase and sale within the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 12.
Discourse on the Determination of Accepting Gold, Silver, and Other Valuables.

59. Receiving gold and so forth means the acceptance of gold and the like. In this context, there are four kinds of objects subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*): gold, silver, a gold coin (*jātarūpa-māsaka*), and a silver coin (*rajata-māsaka*). A copper coin is one made from copper, bronze, or similar materials.
A wooden coin (*dārumāsaka*) is one made by carving an image out of hard wood, bamboo, or even a palm leaf. [Likewise, there are coins] made with lac...
A "gum-seal" (jatumāsa) is one made by producing a form with resin or sap. Whatever [seal] goes into circulation in whichever region at whatever time—
be it made of bone, made of hide, made from the seeds of tree fruits, produced by artificial means,
or not produced by artificial means— all of this is included under the category of the silver seal (rajatamāsa).
Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, rock crystals, coral, red diamonds, and masāragalla stones; the seven kinds of grain; female and male slaves; fields and lands;

flower gardens, fruit gardens, and so forth—this is the object of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding that, it is not permitted to accept an object involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for one's own sake, or for the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a shrine.
For one who accepts it for one's own sake, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

[If one accepts it] for the sake of the rest, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even when accepting for the sake of all [the Sangha], regarding an object that is an occasion for wrong-doing, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.
In this regard, the analysis is as follows: if someone brings gold or silver and says, "I give this to the Sangha;
please build a monastery, or a shrine, or one of the dining halls and so forth," to accept this—

It is not permissible. However, if he refuses, saying, "This is not permissible for monks to accept," and then departs after placing it in the hands of carpenters or laborers, saying, "You yourselves must simply know what is well-made or poorly made," then it is permissible. Or even if he says, "It will be in the hands of my men..."
"It shall remain in my own hands; you need only send whatever is to be given for the sake of each respective purpose"—if he says this, it is likewise permissible.

However, if they do not mention the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, or an individual, but say, "We give this gold and silver to the Cetiya, we give it to the Vihāra, we give it for new construction," it is not permissible to refuse it.
It is not permissible to inform the lay attendants (kappiyakāraka) that "these people are saying this.
However, when it is said, "We have set aside these [goods] for the sake of the cetiya and so forth," one should refuse, saying, "It is not permissible for us to accept them.
But if someone brings much gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha for the four requisites..."
“Enjoy it,” and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the act of acceptance and in the act of consumption.

In that case, if one monk refuses it, saying, “This is not allowable,” and the lay follower, thinking, “If it is not allowable, it shall be mine alone,” takes it away; that monk [commits an offense] by obstructing the gain of the Saṅgha.
"Who made it?"—no one should say anything at all. For whoever accuses him becomes guilty of an offense themselves.
Yet, by that one man alone, many have been rendered free from offense. However, if the monks reject it, saying, "It is not allowable," he might say:
"It will be in the hands of those who make things allowable, or in the hands of my men, or in my own hands; you simply..."
If he says, "Make use of the requisites," it is permissible.
And that which is given for the sake of the four requisites should be applied to whichever requisite is needed.
That which is given for the sake of robes should be applied to robes themselves. If there is no such need for robes, [it may be used] for almsfood and so forth.
If the Saṅgha is weary, it should be brought for that purpose after seeking permission for the well-being of the Saṅgha.

This same method applies when [the gift] is given for the sake of the requisites of almsfood or medicine. However, what is given for the sake of lodgings must be applied to the lodgings themselves because lodgings are considered heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).
But if the lodgings are destroyed when the monks have departed after abandoning them, then at such a time, the lodging—

Even after giving it away, its use by the monks is permitted; therefore, for the purpose of maintaining the lodgings, one should use it as much as necessary for subsistence, without cutting off the very root [of the gift]. 60.
If someone should say, "I have a great lake that produces three harvests of crops; I give it to the Saṅgha," [it may be accepted].
If he speaks thus and the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the consumption.
However, whoever rejects it should not be addressed by anyone in the manner previously described. For whoever accuses him becomes the one who commits the offense.
By that single person, many have been rendered free from offense. But as for whoever [accuses] such a pond...
Having said, "I give it," he is refused by the monks, who say, "It is not permissible. He then asks, "The Saṅgha has such-and-such and such-and-such a pond;
how can that be permissible? He should be told, "It will become permissible once it has been made allowable (kappiya).
How does it become permissible when given? It becomes permissible when it is given after saying, "Use it for the four requisites."
Thus, if he gives it saying, "Venerable sir, please accept and use these four requisites," it is permissible.
But even if, after saying, "Take this pond," he is refused on the grounds that it is not permissible, and he then asks, "Is there a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable)?
and is told, "There is none," [and the donor says], "This person named so-and-so will manage it; it shall be in his hand or in my hand."
If he says, "Let the Saṅgha use the allowable goods," it is permissible.
Even if he has refused, saying, "It is not permissible," if he then says, "He will use the water; he will wash the goods; wild animals and birds will drink [from it]," it is likewise permissible.
Or, even if he has refused, saying, "It is not permissible," he may say, "Take them under the heading of 'allowable.'"
Having said, “Excellent, lay follower! The Saṅgha will drink the water, wash its requisites, and wild animals and birds will drink,” it is permissible to use it.

Furthermore, even if one says, “I give my pond or lotus-pool to the Saṅgha,” it is likewise permissible to use it after saying, “Excellent, lay follower! The Saṅgha will drink the water,” and so forth.
If, however, monks have requested manual labor and, having personally dug the earth with their own hands,
have had a pond constructed for the purpose of using water, and if people, having produced a crop by depending on that [pond],
give allowable goods to the monastery, it is permissible. Furthermore, if people themselves, for the sake of benefiting the Saṅgha, dig into land belonging to the Saṅgha...
If, depending on that [field], they give allowable goods from the crop produced there, this is also permissible.
Furthermore, if it is said, "Appoint one of us as a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable)," it is also permitted to appoint such a person.
Then, those people, oppressed by the king's tax-exaction, depart; others take over, yet they do not give anything to the bhikkhus, nor do they allow water [to be used].
It may be obtained, but only at the time of plowing, not during the harvest season.

If they say, "Venerable sir, did people not also cultivate their crops by depending on this [land] in the past?", then one should reply, "They rendered such-and-such assistance to the Saṅgha and gave such-and-such allowable goods. If they say, "We too..."
“We shall give it,” even this is permissible.
However, if anyone who is incompetent accepts a pond by means of an improper expression or causes one to be built, that must not be used by the monks;
even a suitable article obtained in dependence upon it is indeed unsuitable. If [it is] by the monks...
If, having learned that [the property] has been relinquished, the owner, or his sons and daughters, or anyone else born in the lineage,

gives it back again using a permissible formula (*kappiya-vohāra*), it is allowable. If the family lineage has become extinct, the owner of that district may take it back and give it again using a permissible formula—
as in the case of the water-channel brought out by a monk at Cittalapabbata.
It is also permissible in this way, like the chief queen of King Aḷanāgara.

Even regarding allowable transactions (*kappiya-vohāra*), it is permissible for those with pure minds to perform tasks such as digging up clay or binding embankments in a pond that has been formally accepted [as a gift] by means of water.
However, upon seeing someone cultivating a crop dependent on that [pond], it is not permissible to appoint a steward (*kappiyakāraka*). If they themselves [provide] allowable goods...

If they give [the materials], it should be accepted; if they do not give, one should not urge them. It is permissible to appoint a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) for a pond that has been accepted as a requisite;
however, it is not permissible to have them construct embankments for drawing up clay or similar works. If the *kappiyakārakas* perform the work themselves, it is permissible.
But even if the work is caused to be done by a modest monk who is incompetent, although there is no formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*), [it is still not permissible].

However, because it is mixed with what has arisen through a bhikkhu’s own initiative, it is difficult to separate—like food mixed with poison or like food mixed with the juice of forbidden meat—and thus it is indeed forbidden for everyone. 61.
But if there is room for water, and the embankment of the pond is firm, [one may act] so that it takes up much water.
"Act thus; prepare water near the bank"—if one directs them toward the water in this way, it is permissible.
They do not place fire on the hearth; it is permissible to say, "Let the lay followers perform the water-work," but it is not permissible to say, "Go and bring back grain after you have harvested it.
However, if, seeing that there is too much water in the pond, [he says]:
Or if he has the boundary markers removed from behind; or if, having had a forest cleared, he causes fields to be made;

or if, in ancient fields, he does not accept the customary share but takes an excess; or if, regarding a new crop whose shares have not yet been demarcated, he demands money by saying, "Give so many kahāpaṇas"—all these are improper for everyone.

Furthermore, if instead of saying, "Plow! Sow! one establishes the land by saying, "This much portion belongs to this much ground," or if, while the plowmen are saying, "We have cultivated the crop on this much portion of ground;
take this much portion," one measures it with a rope or a staff for the purpose of determining the extent of the land, or at the threshing floor—
If he stands [over it] and guards it, or has it removed from where it was placed, or stores it away in a storehouse, that is not allowable for him alone.

If farmers bring coins and say, "These have been brought for the Saṅgha," and a certain bhikkhu, with the perception that "the Saṅgha does not consume coins," says, "Bring cloth for this many coins; for this many..."
If he says, "Prepare rice gruel and so forth," whatever they bring is unallowable for all. Why? Because the coins have been handled.

If, however, they bring grain and say, "This has been brought for the Saṅgha," and a certain monk speaks according to the previous method, saying, "Bring such-and-such from this much rice," whatever they bring—
That is not allowable for him alone. Why? Because the grain has already been processed.

If they bring rice or other food and say, "This has been brought for the Saṅgha," and a certain monk speaks as before, saying, "Bring this and that with so much rice," then whatever they bring is allowable for everyone.

Why? Because allowable items such as rice and so forth have already been prepared. There is also no offense regarding buying and selling because the presence of a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) has been indicated. 62.

Previously, however, at Cittalapabbata, a certain monk drew a circle on the ground at the door of the four-hall building for the purpose of making the monastery attendants aware, thinking: "Oh, may they bake this much quantity of cakes for the Saṅgha tomorrow! Seeing that, a clever [person]...
The monastery attendant did exactly as instructed; on the following day, when the drum was beaten and the Saṅgha had assembled, he took some cakes and said to the senior elder of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sir, neither our fathers nor our grandfathers have ever heard of such a thing before.
A certain noble one has given a signal at the door of the four-hall building for the sake of the cakes; from this day forward, may the noble ones [accept them]."
"Let each speak according to his own inclination; it will be a comfortable dwelling for us as well.
The Great Elder turned back from that very spot, and not even a single monk took any of the cakes. Thus, in the past, they did not consume what was produced on the spot. Therefore:
By a bhikkhu who is diligent, Transcending the practice of effacement...
"Even in the case of allowable things, one should not act out of greed for the sake of material gain.
And this same principle applies to ponds, lotus pools, water channels, and irrigation ditches that have been mentioned.
63. Any field or plot of land where grains, vegetables, sugar cane, fruits, or other such produce grow.

Or, even when it is said, "I give," if [the donor] first refuses, saying, "It is not permitted," and then speaks using an allowable expression (*kappiya-vohāra*) in the same manner as described for the pond—saying, "I give for the purpose of using the four requisites"—then it should be accepted.
However, if he says, "I give a grove" or "I give a forest," it is permissible. If people, without being instructed by the monks, [cut] trees there...
If, after cutting [the crops] and preparing other foodstuffs, they give a portion to the monks, it is permissible; those who do not give should not be reproached.
If, due to some obstacle, they have departed and others take over the work but do not give anything to the monks, they should be stopped.
If they say, "Venerable sir, did people not previously cultivate crops here? then—
They should be told, "They gave such-and-such allowable goods to the Saṅgha. If they say, "We too shall give," it is permissible.
If, referring to some plot of land suitable for cultivation, they say, "We give the boundary," it is permissible for the purpose of delimiting the boundary.
However, pillars or stones must not be set up by oneself; for "land" is of incalculable value, and one might incur a *pārājika* offense even for a small amount.
But one may tell the monastery attendants, "The boundary of our [monastery] extends to this place.
Even if they take more than that, there is no offense because it was spoken as a figurative expression. However, if kings, royal ministers, and so forth...
If one has pillars erected oneself and gives them [to the Saṅgha], saying, "Enjoy these four requisites," it is indeed permissible.

If someone digs a pond within the boundary, or leads a watercourse through the middle of the monastery, or causes the courtyard of the shrine (cetiyāṅgaṇa) or the courtyard of the Bodhi tree to be damaged, he must be stopped.
If the Saṅgha, having received something, does not stop him out of a sense of attachment to material things, a single bhikkhu [should intervene].
If a single monk prevents it, saying, "Take them away," that monk alone is the authority.
If the Saṅgha prevents it, the Saṅgha alone is the authority; for in matters belonging to the Saṅgha, whoever performs an act in accordance with the Dhamma is the one who holds authority.
If, even when being prevented, he nevertheless proceeds, he must take the sand already taken from below and put it back down again.
Having thrown the soil taken from above back on top, it should be filled.

If someone wishing to give sugarcane, other crops, or climbing fruits such as bottle gourds and pumpkins says, "I give all of this: the sugarcane field, the site for other crops, and the enclosure for climbing fruits," [one may accept it].
The Elder Mahāsumma said, "It is not permissible because it is offered together with the site. But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "This is merely a matter of phrasing;
for that plot of land belongs to the owners themselves, therefore it is permissible. [If one says], "I give a slave," it is not permissible.
[But if one says], "I give a monastery attendant (ārāmika), I give a service-provider (veyyāvaccakara), I give a preparer of allowable things (kappiyakāraka)..."
If it is said, "I give," it is permissible. If an attendant performs work for the Saṅgha both before and after the meal, then like a novice, all medicine and maintenance must be provided for him.
If he performs work for the Saṅgha only before the meal, but performs his own work after the meal, then his evening fodder should not be given. As for those who...
If, having performed the Saṅgha’s business on every five-day cycle or every fortnight, they perform their own work at other times,
food and fodder must be given to them only at the time they are performing that work. If there is no business for the Saṅgha and they live by performing only their own work,
if they bring what is earned from manual labor and give it [to the monastery], it may be accepted.

If they do not give anything, nothing at all should be said. Whatever they offer—even a gift for a washerman or a weaver—it is permissible to accept it under the name of a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).
If they say, "We are giving cows," one should refuse them, saying, "It is not permissible. [They may ask: "From where did these cows come? [The wise should answer: "By the wise..."
“Given for the purpose of consuming the five products of the cow. If it is said, “We too give for the purpose of consuming the five products of the cow,” it is permissible.
The same principle applies to goats and so forth.
If they say, “We give an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a chicken, or a pig,” it is not permissible to accept them. If some people say, “Be at ease, venerable sir...”
If they say, "You were [the owners]; we shall take these and give them as your allowable goods (kappiyabhaṇḍa)," it is permissible to accept them.
It is permissible to release chickens and pigs into the forest with the thought, "May they live happily.
When it is said, "We give this pond, this field, or this site to the monastery," one is not permitted to refuse.

64. If someone should send a messenger with money, gold, or other requisites for robes to a bhikkhu, saying, “Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with a robe,” and if that messenger, having approached that bhikkhu, should speak thus: “Venerable sir, this—”

“‘Friend, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of [this] venerable one; may the venerable one accept the robe-fund. That monk should say to that messenger: ‘Friends, we do not accept robe-funds;
however, we accept robes at the proper time, provided they are allowable. If that messenger should say to that monk: ‘There is...’”
“If there is no one to perform services for the venerable one,” a monk who needs robes should point out a service-provider,
whether a monastery attendant or a lay follower, saying, “This person, friend, is a service-provider for the monks. He must not say,
“Give it to him,” or “He will store it away,” or “He will exchange it,” or “He will purchase [robes] with it.”
If the messenger, having informed that attendant, should approach the monk and say:
"Venerable sir, the person whom the venerable one pointed out as an attendant has been instructed by me;
let the venerable one approach him at the proper time, and he will clothe you with a robe. Then the monk who needs a robe, having approached the attendant—
He should be urged and reminded two or three times, saying: "Friend, I have need of a robe. He must not say:
"Give me a robe," "Bring me a robe," "Exchange a robe for me," or "Procure a robe for me.
If, while being urged and reminded two or three times, he succeeds in obtaining that robe, that is good.
If he does not succeed in obtaining it, he should go there and stand silently for four, five, or at most six times, designating that person.
He must not sit on a seat, nor accept food, nor preach the Dhamma.
If asked, "For what reason have you come?", he should say only this: "Know, friend."
If he sits on a seat, or receives almsfood, or speaks the Dhamma, he breaks his standing posture.
If he reproves him four times, he must stand four times. If he reproves him five times, he must stand twice.
If he reproves him six times, he need not stand. For with a single reproof, he breaks two instances of standing.
Just as one should not remain after having exhorted six times, so too one should not exhort after having remained twelve times.
Therefore, if one only exhorts and does not remain, six exhortations are obtained.
If one only remains and does not exhort, twelve instances of remaining are obtained. If one both exhorts and remains, two instances of remaining must be deducted for each single exhortation.
In that regard, he who goes back again and again on a single day and urges [the donor] six times,
or who goes only once and says "I have need of a robe, friend" six times; or he who, having gone on a single day,
stands there repeatedly twelve times, or having gone only once, stands in various places— such a person also [is subject to the offense].
He ruins all his requests and all his undertakings, let alone those made on various days.

If, by striving further than that, he succeeds in obtaining that robe-cloth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort, and it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya) upon acquisition.
If he is unable to obtain it, then from a king or a royal minister, for that bhikkhu...
When that robe-fund has been brought, one must either go to that person in person or send a messenger with these words:
"Venerable sirs, the robe-fund you have sent for the sake of this monk does not serve any purpose for that monk;
apply it to your own [needs], lest your property be lost."
This is the proper course of action in that regard. However, if one neither goes there oneself nor sends a messenger, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for the breach of the rule.
65. But should one act in this same manner toward all who provide what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*)?

One should not. For this so-called "provider of what is allowable" is briefly explained as being of two kinds: the designated (*niddiṭṭha*) and the non-designated (*aniddiṭṭha*). Among these, the designated is of two kinds.
"Designated by a monk" means designated by a messenger. "Undesignated" is also twofold:

one who makes [the food] allowable in the presence [of the monk], and one who makes it allowable in his absence. Among these, that which is "designated by a monk" is fourfold according to whether it is done in the presence or in the absence [of the recipient];
likewise for that which is "designated by a messenger. How so? Here, someone [acts] for a monk’s sake regarding a robe by means of a messenger...
If one sends an improper object, and the messenger approaches that bhikkhu and says, "Venerable sir, this has been sent for you by such-and-such a person for the sake of robe-cloth;

please accept it," and the bhikkhu refuses, saying, "This is not allowable," and the messenger asks, "But, venerable sir, do you have anyone who acts as your steward? [the bhikkhu may say], "Yes, those who seek merit..."
Or, if he has been instructed by lay followers (upāsaka) saying,
"Perform services for the bhikkhus," or if there are certain service-providers who are personal friends or associates of the bhikkhus, and at that moment one of them is sitting near the bhikkhu,
and the bhikkhu points him out, saying, "This person is a service-provider for the bhikkhus," [and the message is delivered] into his hand as a messenger—
Having given an improper object [of trade] and saying, "Go and buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him," this person is one designated in the presence of the monk.
If he is not sitting near the monk, yet the monk designates him, saying, "In such-and-such a village,
a certain person is a servant to the monks," then [the messenger], having gone there, [gives] the improper object into his hand.
Having given [the money] and saying, "You should buy a robe-cloth for the elder and give it to him," the messenger returns, informs the bhikkhu, and departs;
this is one case where the messenger has not been designated by the bhikkhu in his presence.
Furthermore, that messenger does not come himself to inform [the bhikkhu], but rather sends another, saying, "It has been given by me."
“Venerable sir, [a person] has in his hand the purchase-price for a robe; you should accept the robe from him.
This is the second case of a monk being designated in absentia.
Furthermore, he does not send another, but rather, while going himself, he says to the monk: “I [have given it] into his hand...”
“I will give you the funds for robes; you may take the robe [with them]”—this is the third case of one who is designated by a monk without being present.
Thus, there are four types of service-providers designated by a monk: one designated in their presence and three designated in their absence.
Regarding these, one should proceed exactly according to the method stated here.

Another monk, having been questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, says—either because the robe-cloth is not available or because he does not wish to investigate—"We have no one who acts as a kappiyakāraka.

At that moment, a certain person arrives; the messenger gives the unallowable article into that person's hand and departs, saying, "You may take the robe-cloth from this person's hand. This is what is called "pointed out in the presence by a messenger."
Thus, one [type of messenger] is designated by being present in person.

Another, having entered a village, gives an improper article into the hand of someone he chooses, and either returns and reports it in the same manner as before, or sends another [messenger], saying: "I have [given] the purchase-price for a robe into the hand of such-and-such a person."
If he departs after saying, “I will give it; you may take the robe,” this is the third case of one designated by messenger who is not designated in person.
Thus, there are four types of those acting as messengers who are designated: one designated in person and three designated not in person.
Regarding these, one should proceed according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka-sikkhāpada. For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, there are people who have faith and confidence;
they place gold in the hands of those who prepare what is allowable, saying, ‘With this, give whatever is allowable for the noble one.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept from them whatever is allowable, but by no means, bhikkhus, should gold and silver be accepted by any means whatsoever.”
"I say it must be sought," he said.
Herein, there is no limit to the number of times one may be urged;

even if the owner does not give it, it is permissible for one who has not accepted the goods to accept a suitable article (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) by being urged or by means of a formal act (ṭhāna), even up to a thousand times. If he still does not give it, one may appoint another steward (kappiyakāraka).
It should be caused to be brought. If he wishes, it should be told even to the original owners. If he does not wish, it should not be told.
Another monk, questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, says, "We have no one who prepares what is allowable.
Then another person standing nearby hears this and says, "Bring it, sir; I will purchase a robe for the venerable one and give it to him."
He speaks. The messenger, having placed [the item] in the other's hand with the words, "Come now, sir, you should give this," departs without informing the bhikkhu;

this is one who makes [something] allowable by means of a mouth-declaration (*mukhavevaṭika-kappiyakāraka*). Another person, having placed an unallowable thing in the hand of a bhikkhu’s attendant or someone else, simply departs after saying, "You should give this robe to the Elder"; this is one who makes [something] allowable in the absence [of the recipient] (*parammukhākappiyakāraka*).
These two are called "unspecified makers of what is allowable. One should behave toward them as one would toward unknown persons who have not been invited.
If they bring a robe themselves and offer it, it may be accepted; if they do not, nothing should be said to them.
And just as the decision was stated regarding a messenger sent with an unallowable object for the sake of a robe, so too is it for alms-food and the rest.
The legal determination regarding what is given when sent for a purpose and then delivered in person should be understood.
66. However, this is the legal determination concerning the acceptance of what has been set down nearby:

if someone places some unallowable object at the feet [of a monk] and says, "Let this be for the noble one," even if he accepts it mentally—that is, if he desires to take it—or by means of the body...
If one rejects it by speech, saying, "This is not allowable," there is no offense.
Or, even if one has not rejected it by body or speech, if one remains pure in mind and does not consent, thinking, "This is not allowable for us," there is likewise no offense.
For among the three doors, what is rejected by any one of them is indeed rejected. However, if one has not rejected it by body or speech...

One consents with the mind; because one does not perform the refusal that ought to be performed by body and speech, one incurs an offense originating from non-action at both the door of the body and the door of speech.
However, there is no such thing as an "offense" at the door of the mind.
Suppose someone places a hundred or a thousand [coins] at the feet [of a monk], saying, "Let this be yours"; the bhikkhu [says], "This is not allowable."
He refuses it, and the lay follower, saying, "I have relinquished this to you," departs. Another person comes there and asks, "Venerable sir, what is this?
He should explain both what that person said and what he himself said.
If the other says, "Venerable sir, I will guard it; show me a secure place," he may even ascend a seven-storied palace.
One should point out, "This is a secure place," but one should not say, "Place it here.
Up to this point, the item stands supported by both what is allowable and what is unallowable; therefore, having closed the door, one should dwell guarding it.
If someone comes carrying some merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or a robe, [one should say], "Venerable sir, you may take this."
When this has been said, one should say: "Lay follower, we have need of this;
such an article is available, but there is no attendant (kappiyakāraka). If he says, "I shall be the attendant;
open the door and give it to me," then having opened the door, one should say, "It is placed in this spot," but not, "Take this."
It must be said: even in this way, it remains dependent upon both what is allowable and what is unallowable.

If he takes that [unallowable item] and gives his own allowable article in exchange, it is permissible. If he takes more than is required, he should be told: "We are not taking your goods; please depart."
67. But what is to be done by that monk who has accepted the fourfold object of forfeiture, such as gold and so forth?

It must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha. How? That monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, and having sat down in the kneeling posture with palms joined—
Having taken hold of it, he should be addressed thus: “Venerable sir, I accepted silver; this is my relinquishment, I relinquish it.
Having relinquished it, the offense should be confessed. A competent and capable monk should accept the confession of the offense.
If a monastery attendant or a lay follower comes there, he should be told: “Friend, ...”
“Know this! If he says, “What shall I bring with this? one must not say, “Bring this or that,” but rather point out what is allowable (*kappiya*), such as ghee, oil, honey, or molasses.
And when pointing it out, one must not say, “Bring ghee, oil, honey, or molasses with this,” but rather, “This and this.”
Only this much should be said: "It is allowable for the Saṅgha.

If he exchanges it with that [money] and brings back what is allowable, then—setting aside the receiver of the money—it should be divided and consumed by everyone; the receiver of the money must not take a share.
Even having obtained a share intended for other monks or monastery attendants, it is not permitted to consume it.

Even if it has been carried away from there by monkeys or other animals and placed in the forest, or has fallen from their hands—even if received from an animal—it is not permissible even for rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*).
Furthermore, using molasses brought from there to fumigate a dwelling is not permissible.
Nor is it permissible to lie down in the light of a lamp made with ghee or oil, to perform the preliminary meditation on the *kasiṇa*, or [to read] a book.
It is not permitted to recite [the scriptures]. Furthermore, it is likewise not permitted to smear a wound on the body with oil, honey, or molasses.
If, by means of that object, they take beds, chairs, and so forth, or construct an Uposatha hall or a dining hall, it is not permitted to use them.
Even the shadow is not permitted as long as it remains within the boundary of the dwelling; once it has passed beyond that boundary, it is permitted.
Because it is adventitious, it is permissible. However, it is not permissible to go by way of a path, a bridge, a boat, or a raft that has been constructed after relinquishing that property.
It is not permissible to drink or consume the water that has overflowed from a lotus pond excavated with that same property.
But if there is no water inside [the pond], and other adventitious water or rainwater has entered, [it is permissible].
It is not permissible. For one who has purchased [the land], even if it is a visitor who came together with the purchaser, it is not permissible.
If the Saṅgha uses the requisites after that property has been set aside as a deposit, those requisites are also not permissible for him.
If the monastery has been acquired, that too is not permissible to use. If both the ground and the seed are unallowable, neither the ground—
It is not permissible to consume the fruit. If one buys the land itself and plants other seeds there, the fruit is permissible.
However, if one buys the seeds and plants them on a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an authorized plot), the fruit is not permissible;
yet it is permissible to sit or lie down upon that ground.

But if a money-changer has come there and does not know how to exchange that [money] for bringing suitable items such as ghee, oil, and so forth for the Saṅgha, he should be told, "Friend, throw this away. If he throws it away, that is well.
If he does not throw it away, a monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the discarder of money.

One who would not go astray through favoritism, nor go astray through hatred, nor go astray through delusion, nor go astray through fear, and who can distinguish between what has been discarded and what has not been discarded—such a person should be appointed in this manner: first, a monk should be requested;
having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money.
This is the motion. Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money.
To whichever venerable one it is pleasing to appoint the monk named so-and-so—”
The appointment of a monk as the discarder of silver: he who approves should remain silent. He to whom it is not pleasing should speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of silver; this is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this. 68.
That appointed monk, without making a sign and with eyes closed, [should throw the silver] into a river or over a precipice.
It should be discarded in a forest thicket like excrement, without regard for it and without looking back at the place where it fell.
If one drops it after making a deliberate sign, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus, although money is to be loathed, the Blessed One taught by way of a method that monks may use it; however, there is no way whatsoever for one who accepts money [to be exempt from blame].
Therefore, the use of requisites obtained through such means is not permissible.

Just as it is not permissible for him, so too requisites obtained through false reputation, by corrupting families, or through hypocrisy and the like, are permissible neither for him nor for anyone else.
Even if obtained righteously and fairly, they are not permissible to use without reflecting upon them. For there are four kinds of use:

—“Enjoyment by theft, enjoyment as a debt, enjoyment as an inheritance, and enjoyment as an owner. Therein, for one who is immoral, even if he sits in the midst of the Saṅgha and enjoys [the requisites], that enjoyment is called “enjoyment by theft.
For one who is virtuous, enjoyment without reflection is called “enjoyment as a debt. Therefore, with each act of enjoying a robe, it should be reflected upon; so too with almsfood.
With every morsel of food, if he is unable to do so, he should reflect during the morning, afternoon, first watch, middle watch, and last watch of the night.
If dawn rises while he is not reflecting, he stands in the position of one who consumes what is borrowed.
The lodging, too, should be reflected upon with each act of use. Regarding medicine, there must be mindfulness both in its acceptance and in its consumption.

It is permissible; yet even so, while there is an offense for one who exercises mindfulness during acceptance but fails to do so during consumption, there is no offense for one who fails to exercise mindfulness during acceptance but does so during consumption. For purity is fourfold:
purity of confession, purity of restraint, purity of search, and purity of reflection.
In this context, "purity of confession" refers to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha. For that is called "purity of confession" because it is purified by means of confession.

"Purity of restraint" refers to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties. For that is called "purity of restraint" because it is purified precisely by the restraint consisting in the mental resolve, "I shall not do so again.
"Purity of search" refers to the virtue of complete purity of livelihood.

For that is called "purity of search" because it is pure in its quest, having abandoned improper means of livelihood and procuring requisites through the Dhamma and in a righteous manner. "Purity of reflection" refers to virtue dependent on the use of requisites;
for it consists in the reflection described by the method beginning with, "I use the robe after careful consideration."
Because it is purified through reflection, it is called "purity through review"; therefore it was said:
"But for one who fails to exercise mindfulness at the time of receiving [the requisites] but exercises it at the time of using them, there is no offense.
For the seven types of trainees (sekkhā), the use of requisites is called "use as an inheritance," for they are indeed the sons of the Blessed One.
Therefore, being heirs to the requisites belonging to their father, they make use of those requisites.
But do they make use of the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they make use of the requisites of householders?
Even though given by householders, because they have been authorized by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One; therefore, they make use of the requisites of the Blessed One.

This should be understood. Here, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma) is the supporting proof. For those whose taints are destroyed, the act of using [the requisites] is called "use as an owner.
Indeed, because they have transcended the servitude of craving, they use them having become masters.
Thus, among these types of use, both "use as an owner" and "use as an heir" are permissible for everyone; however, "use as a debtor" is not permissible.
There is no discussion whatsoever regarding the enjoyment of what has been stolen.
There are four other types of enjoyment: the enjoyment of the conscientious, the enjoyment of the unconscientious, the righteous enjoyment, and the unrighteous enjoyment.
In this regard, the enjoyment of the unconscientious together with the conscientious is permissible; he should not be made to incur an offense. As for the conscientious...
It is permissible [to speak] with one who is shameless only as long as one does not know [of his state]. For from the very beginning, there is no such thing as a "shameless" person;
therefore, when one knows his shamelessness, he should be told: "You are committing transgressions through the door of the body and the door of speech;
that is improper. Do not act in this way. If he continues to act despite being told, and if by him—
If one shares in the enjoyment [of requisites] with another who is shameless, that person too becomes shameless.
Furthermore, whoever shares in the enjoyment with one who is shameless and has become a burden to oneself must also be restrained. If he does not desist, he too becomes shameless.
Thus, one shameless person makes even a hundred shameless ones. However, when shameless people share in enjoyment only with those who are shameless—
There is no such thing as an offense. For one who possesses a sense of shame, sharing with another who possesses a sense of shame is like two princes eating from the same golden bowl.
Whether the use of requisites is lawful or unlawful should be understood according to the circumstances.
In that regard, if both the person is shameless and the alms-food is unrighteous, both are loathsome. If the person is shameless but the alms-food is righteous...
Even if one feels disgust for the person, almsfood should not be accepted. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated:

"If an immoral person, having received designated meals and so forth from the Saṅgha, gives them back to the Saṅgha itself, these are permissible because they were received exactly as they were given.
If the person is modest but the almsfood is unrighteous, the disgusting almsfood should not be accepted. [If] the person...
It is permissible for one who is conscientious to receive even almsfood that is in accordance with the Dhamma.
There are two other kinds of support and two kinds of enjoyment: support for the conscientious and support for the unconscientious; enjoyment of the Dhamma and enjoyment of material things.
In this regard, it is permissible for one who is unconscientious to support one who is conscientious, and he should not be made to undergo disciplinary action for an offense.
But if one who is conscientious supports one who is unconscientious, requests him to offer words of thanksgiving, requests him to give a discourse on the Dhamma, or assists him among families,

and the other likewise speaks in praise of him in his own assembly, saying, "Our teacher is such and such," this should be understood as causing the Dispensation to decline and disappear. This applies to both the enjoyment of the Dhamma and the enjoyment of material goods.
However, where the enjoyment of material goods is permitted, there the enjoyment of the Dhamma is also permitted.
It is said that if a text is situated at the very limit [of survival] and would perish upon the passing of that individual, it is permissible to learn it for the sake of supporting the Dhamma.
Here is an example: it is said that during a great danger, the *Mahāniddesa* belonged to only a single bhikkhu.
He became proficient. Then the Elder Mahātipiṭaka, who was the preceptor of the Elder Catunikāyika Tissa, said to the Elder Mahārakkhita:
"Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the *Mahāniddesa* from him. "Venerable sir, this man is wicked; I will not learn from him.
"Learn it, friend; I shall sit beside you. "Very well, venerable sir. [In the presence] of you...
Thinking, "I will learn [the Dhamma] while they are seated," he set himself to it and mastered it continuously day and night.
On the final day, seeing a woman on the lower couch, he said, "Venerable sir, I have heard this before;
had I known it would be like this, I would not have learned the Dhamma in the presence of one such as you. However, many great elders had mastered it in his presence.
They established the *Mahāniddesa*.
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of the acceptance of money and so forth, within the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
13. Discourse on the Determination of the Characteristics of Giving and Other Factors 69.
Regarding the phrase "the dedication of gain through giving, trust, and acceptance":

here, first, "giving" (*dāna*) refers to the giving of one’s own possessions, such as robes and other requisites, to anyone among one’s co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and others. This is the characteristic of giving (*dānalakkhaṇa*).

If one says, “I give this to you; I bestow it, I grant it, I offer it, I relinquish it, I release it,” or “I give it to [name], …pe… I release it,” whether in the presence of the person or behind their back, it is indeed given.
When told, “Take it from me,” if one says, “I take it for myself,” it is well given and well received. [Regarding] “That which belongs to you…”
When it is said, “Do so; let it be yours; let it be yours,” if one says, “I am making it mine; let it be mine;
I shall make it mine,” it is wrongly given and wrongly received. Neither the giver knows how to give, nor does the other know how to receive.
However, if, when it is said, “Make it yours,” one says, “Very well,”...
“Venerable sir, I am taking it for myself,” and he takes it—it is well taken.
But if one says, “Take this robe-cloth,” and the other says, “I will not take it,” and then the former says, “It has been given by me to you;
take it,” and the other says, “I have no need of this,” yet the former, thinking “it was given by me,” lets ten days pass—[he incurs an offense].
The one at the end also thinks, "It has been refused by me. Whose offense is it? It is no one's.

However, he for whom it is agreeable may use it after making a formal determination (adhiṭṭhahitvā). As for that which is given with the words, "Give this to so-and-so," until it reaches the hand of another, it belongs to the one who sent it; but once it is given with the words, "I give this to so-and-so," [it belongs to the recipient].

Whatever is relinquished belongs to the one to whom it is relinquished. Therefore, if a monk sends a robe to another monk’s hand, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so," and the one who sent it receives it out of trust while on the way, it is well-received.
If the one to whom it was relinquished receives it out of trust, it is poorly received.
A bhikkhu sends a robe to another bhikkhu, saying, "Give this robe to [so-and-so].
On the way, he hears that the sender has died; he then resolves upon it as the deceased's robe. It is properly resolved.
He takes it on trust from the one to whom it was sent. It is wrongly taken. A bhikkhu [sends a robe] to another bhikkhu...
He sends a robe by hand, saying, "Give this robe to such-and-such a person. On the way, he hears that the one to whom it was sent has died;
he then resolves it as the robe of the deceased for that person, and it is resolved twice.
He accepts it on trust from the one who sent it; it is well accepted. A monk sends a robe by hand to another monk.
“Give this robe to so-and-so. On the way, he hears that both have died.
He resolves it as a death-robe for the one who sent it; it is well-resolved. He resolves it as a death-robe for the one to whom it was sent;
it is doubly resolved. A monk sends a robe in the hand of another monk, saying: “This robe…”
“I give this robe to so-and-so. If, on the way, he receives it from the one who sent it out of trust, it is wrongly received.

If he receives it from the one to whom it was sent out of trust, it is rightly received. A monk sends a robe in the hand of another monk, saying, “Give this robe to so-and-so. On the way, he hears: “The one who sent it...”

If [the messenger] hears, "He has passed away," he resolves upon that deceased person’s robe; it is resolved. If [the messenger] hears, "The one to whom it was sent has passed away," he takes it out of trust in the one to whom it was sent;
it is well taken. A monk sends a robe in another monk’s hand, saying, "Give this robe to such-and-such a person.
On the way, he hears, "The one to whom it was sent has passed away. Regarding him...
He resolves upon the robe as the property of the deceased; it is properly resolved. He takes it out of trust for the one who sent it; it is wrongly taken.
A monk sends a robe in the hand of another monk, saying, "Give this robe to so-and-so.
On the way, he hears that both have died. He resolves upon the robe as the property of the deceased of the one who sent it.
It is determined by two factors. When something is relinquished, one determines that it is a "dead person’s robe" (mataka-cīvara); thus it is well-determined.
Once something has been given away after being renounced, one may not, for any reason, become angry and demand its return.

For even a robe given by oneself, if one seizes it back with the perception that it is one's own, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya); this applies to other requisites as well, down to even a needle.
If one seizes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if he gives it of his own accord, saying, "Venerable sir, this is suitable for you," it is permissible to accept it.

But if [the donor] says, "Friend, we gave you this robe thinking, 'He will perform his duties and services, he will take formal affiliation (*upajjhā*) under us, and he will master the Dhamma,' yet now you..."

If, when told such things as, "You do not perform your duties, you do not take a preceptor, nor do you master the Dhamma," he says, "Venerable sir, I suppose you are speaking for the sake of a robe; here is a robe for you," and gives it—this is also permissible.
Or, if a young monk who is departing for another region says, "Do not turn back," and he does not turn back, [the teacher] says, "Seize him by his robe and hold him back. This is also permissible.
If he turns back in this way, it is well. If, however, he gives [the bowl and robes] while saying, "I suppose you are speaking for the sake of the bowl and robes;

take them," this is also permissible. Or, seeing him about to disrobe, [a monk] says, "We gave you the bowl and robes thinking, 'He will perform the duties,' yet now you are wandering having disrobed"; the other replies, "Take back your bowl and robes."
He gives; even in this way it is permissible. [One might say: "I give only to one who receives the *upajjhāya*-ship in my presence, not to one who receives it elsewhere;
I give only to one who performs the duties (*vatta*), not to one who does not;
I give only to one who masters the Dhamma, not to one who does not; I give only to one who does not disrobe, not to one who disrobes."
However, it is not permissible to give in this manner; for one who gives, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). But it is permissible to have it brought back.
One who takes back what was given after it had been relinquished should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. This, then, is the determination regarding giving. 70.
Furthermore, the characteristic of taking on trust is to be understood from this sutta:

“Monks, I allow you to accept a loan from one endowed with five qualities: he is a friend seen [before], a friend long associated with, one who has been spoken to [with kindness], one who is living, and one who is pleased when the loan is taken.
In this context, “seen” means a mere acquaintance. “Long associated with” means a firm friend. “Spoken to” means one who has been told:
“Whatever belongs to me that you desire, you may take it; there is no need to ask for permission before taking it. “Is living” means...
Even while lying on a bed without rising, one does not reach the severance of the life-faculty. And "having taken with a pleased mind" means that one becomes satisfied in heart after taking.
It is permissible for one who knows, "He will be pleased when I take what belongs to such a person," to take it.
Furthermore, these five factors are stated by way of taking everything without remainder; this refers to taking on trust.
However, it is established by three factors: one who is seen [as a friend] lives and is pleased when the property is taken;
one who is trusted lives and is pleased when the property is taken; and one who has been addressed [with affection] lives and is pleased when the property is taken.

But for one who does not live and is not pleased when the property is taken, even if what belonged to him was taken on the basis of trust, it must be given back again. And when giving away the wealth of the deceased, [one should act with mindfulness].
First, it should be given to those who have authority over his wealth, whether they be householders or renunciants.
However, if he is displeased, the property should be given to him alone;
but if someone has already expressed approval—either by verbal expression or even by a mere thought—saying, "You have done well in taking what belongs to me," and subsequently, for some reason...
If one is angry, one is not permitted to demand it back; nor is one permitted to demand it back from one who, though unwilling to give, has mentally consented and said nothing at all.
However, when one says, "I have taken or used what belongs to you," and the other replies, "Whether it was taken or used, I [do not mind] because of some reason..."
If one says, "It was set aside for a specific purpose; it is proper to restore it to its original state," this person is permitted to have it brought back.
This is the legal decision regarding the taking of property through trust. 71.
Regarding the "dedication of gains": this refers to a gain that has been dedicated for the benefit of others, [being redirected] to oneself or another.
Or it was said with reference to dedication. Herein, this is the analysis:

for one who, knowing that something has been dedicated to the Saṅgha—or to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, or to lay followers, or even to one’s own mother—takes it for oneself by dedicating it to oneself, saying, “Give this to me,” there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). [Likewise] if one says, “Give this to such-and-such a bhikkhu.”
Thus, for one who diverts [an offering] to another, there is a *pācittiya* offense of the pure type (*suddhika-pācittiya*).

Therefore, even at the time of the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*), if one knows that a rainy-season robe has been dedicated to the Saṅgha and yet diverts it to oneself, there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense;
if one diverts it to another person, there is a *pācittiya* offense of the pure type. When people, thinking, "We shall provide a meal for the Saṅgha," [prepare] ghee, oil, and so forth...
They bring it; even if the sick monk, knowing that the Sangha of monks has already determined [the gift] for them, asks for something, it is indeed a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense.
However, if he asks, "Do you have ghee and such things brought for yourselves?
and when told, "Yes, we do," he says, "Give some to me too," it is permissible. Furthermore, if the lay followers [act] toward him while he is feeling anxious...
They say, “The Saṅgha also receives only what has been given by us; please take it, venerable sirs,” and even this is permissible.

If, regarding something dedicated to the Saṅgha in one monastery, one redirects it toward another monastery, saying, “Give it to the Saṅgha in such-and-such a monastery,” and [someone objects], “What is the use of giving to the Saṅgha?
Make an offering to the Cetiya,” thus [regarding] the Cetiya—

If one redirects [the offering] elsewhere, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one redirects what was intended for a cetiya to another cetiya, or to the Saṅgha, a Gaṇa, or an individual, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.

Having made a restriction, it is not permitted to place even a flower upon another cetiya from a garland or sapling planted for the sake of a different cetiya; however, for a single cetiya, a sunshade or a banner...
Or, having seen it placed [on the stupa], it is permissible to have the remainder given as an offering to another cetiya.
Even if one redirects what has been intended for a dog, saying, "Do not give this to that dog;
give it to this one," it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. However, if the donors say, "We wish to provide a meal for the Saṅgha, we wish to perform a worship of the cetiya; to one... [and so on].

If they say, "We wish to give requisites to the bhikkhu; we will give them according to your preference, so tell us where we should give them," then that bhikkhu should say, "Give them wherever you wish.
But if they simply ask, "Where should we give them? he should say, "Wherever your gift may be used..."
"It is permissible to say: 'May you receive it,' or 'May you receive the repairs for it,' or 'May it last long,' or 'Give it to wherever your mind feels confident.
Thus ends the compendium of legal decisions on the Vinaya not found in the canonical texts.
The discussion on the determination of the characteristics of giving is finished.
14. The Discussion on the Determination of Digging the Earth.
72. "Earth": there are two kinds of earth—earth that has been produced and earth that has not been produced. Therein, "produced earth" means...
Pure soil—whether it consists of pure earth with few stones, few pebbles, few potsherds, little gravel, and little sand;
whether it is predominantly soil or predominantly earth—even if it has not been burnt, it is called "earth that has arisen.
Furthermore, a heap of soil or a heap of earth that has been covered for more than four months is also called "earth that has arisen. That which has not [arisen] is "unborn" (ajātā).
There is a land consisting of pure stones, pure gravel, pure pebbles, pure sand,
and pure grit— having little dust and little clay, being mostly stones, mostly gravel, mostly pebbles, mostly sand,
and mostly grit— which, even when burnt, is called "unborn earth. This also applies to a heap of dust or a heap of clay.
Or, even one who has resided for less than four months is called "one for whom the earth is not yet born.
In that regard, for one who digs the earth that is already born, or causes it to be dug, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Herein is the analysis:
if he digs it himself, there is an offense of expiation for every stroke. If he commands another, once he has been commanded...
Even if he digs for the entire day, there is only one *pācittiya* offense for the one who gave the command. However, if he is lazy, he must be commanded again and again;
for each time he commands him to dig, there is a *pācittiya* offense for every word of that command.
If he says, "Dig a lotus pond," it is permissible, for only when it has been dug does it truly become a "lotus pond. Therefore...
This is allowable speech (*kappiyavohāra*). This same method applies to such expressions as “Dig a pond, a lake, or a pit.
However, it is not permissible to say, “Dig this spot,” or “Dig a lotus pond in this spot.
It is permissible to speak without specifying, saying, “Dig a bulbous root (*kanda*), dig a root (*mūla*”), but it is not permissible to say, “Dig this creeper,” or “Dig a bulbous root in this spot.”
It is not permissible to say, "Dig up the root.
73. When cleaning a lotus pond, it is permissible to remove the thin mud that can be scooped out with buckets, but thick mud is not permissible.
When the mud dries in the sun, it cracks; in that case, whatever [is on] the earth below...
If it is unrelated [to the boundary], it is permissible to remove that very thing. In a place where water has flowed, there is what is called a "water-film" (udakapappaṭaka);

it moves with the force of the wind, and it is permissible to remove it. If the bank of a lotus pond or similar body of water has broken and fallen into the vicinity of the water, if it has been submerged for less than four months, it is permissible to cut or break it; from [the completion of] the four months...

It is not permitted [to throw it] upwards. However, if it falls into water itself—even if it has been rained upon for more than four months—since it has fallen into water while already in water, it is permitted.
They dig a trench on a stone surface; if fine dust falls there first, that...
If it is covered by rain from the sky, after the lapse of four months it comes to be reckoned as unallowable earth.
When the water has dried up, it is not permissible for those cleaning out the drain to disturb it.

If it was first filled with water and only afterwards did dust fall upon it, it is permissible to disturb it; for even while it is raining there, the water falls only into the water [already present].
On a stone slab there is fine dust; when it rains, it becomes damp and adheres to it, and even that must not be disturbed for the duration of the four months.
On a natural mountain slope where no work has been done, an anthill may have arisen; it is permissible to disturb it as one pleases.
If it arises in an open space, it is permissible only after the minimum period of four months has passed. This also applies to the clay of termite nests grown on trees and such.
The same principle applies here. This same principle applies to anthills, excrement, mouseholes, dogholes, cow-hoof pits, and so forth.

A "cow-hoof pit" (*gokaṇṭaka*) is said to be a patch of mud where a cow’s hoof has been cut into the earth. However, if it is connected to the ground by its lower surface, it is not permitted even for a single day.
The same principle applies to one who takes a clod of earth from a ploughed field that has been cut by a ploughshare.
An old dwelling site— whether it be a roof-covering or a ruined roof-covering—
that has been stored for more than four months becomes reckoned as earth. Whatever remains there, such as bricks, rafters,
or other building materials, one may take them thinking, "I am taking bricks," or "I am taking rafters, wall-footings, floor-mats, or palace pillars."
It is permissible to take [clay] with the intention of perceiving it as such; if the clay falls along with that [intention], there is no offense.
However, for one who takes clay intended for the wall, there is an offense. If he takes whatever portions remain unmoistened, there is no offense.
If there is a heap of clay within the house, and on a certain day they cover the house while it is still moist, if it has all become dry after the lapse of four months—
It is just like earth that has been produced [by rain]. Only its upper surface is moistened, while the interior remains unmoistened;

as much of it as is moistened may be set aside by the preparers using formal terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*), and it is permissible to use the remainder as one pleases because it has been soaked with water.
For earth that has been produced is indeed a single continuous mass, whereas the other [earth] is not. [This refers to] a clay wall in the open air.
If it has been covered for more than four months, it is reckoned as "earth that has arisen," and in such a case, it is permissible to touch and take away the dust clinging to it with a wet hand.
If it is a brick wall standing mostly on a bed of gravel, it is permissible to disturb it as one pleases.
[Likewise] a pillar of a pavilion standing in the open air... from here and there.
It is not permissible to grasp [the tree] by shaking the earth and disturbing it; it is permissible only to pull it up straight.
This same principle applies to anyone grasping another dry tree or a dry stump. 74.
When, for the sake of construction work, they lift up a pillar, a stone, or a tree with levers and roll them along—
They go there, and the earth where they were born breaks open; if they proceed with a pure mind, there is no offense.
But if, under that pretext, they actually desire to break the earth, there is an offense.
The same principle applies to those dragging branches and such, or splitting wood in the earth. Regarding bones, needles, thorns, and so forth in the earth, whatever...
It is not permissible to strike anything or to insert anything [into the earth].
It is also not permissible to urinate with the thought, "I will split the earth by the force of the stream of urine. For one who does so, it breaks, and there is an offense.
It is also not permissible to strike the ground with a broom with the thought, "I will level the uneven ground. One should sweep only in accordance with the proper procedure (*vatta*).

Some dig the ground with a wooden staff, scratch it with their big toes, and walk back and forth repeatedly breaking the ground, thinking, "We will show the walking-place"; all of this is not permitted.
However, for one who practices the ascetic's duty with a pure mind for the sake of exerting energy, it is permitted to walk back and forth. [Thinking], "We will scratch our hands..."
Rubbing against the ground is not permitted; however, it is permissible for one who does not rub to place the hand, while still wet, on the ground and take up the dust.
Some who are afflicted by diseases such as scabies or itch rub their limbs and members against riverbanks and the like; this is not permitted.
If one burns or causes to burn natural earth, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Even when cooking a bowl, for as many places where one applies or causes fire to be applied, there are that many offenses of expiation;

therefore, even when cooking a bowl, it must be cooked only in a place where it has been previously fired. It is not permitted to place fire on earth that has not been burnt; [this applies] to the bowl-cooking pan.
However, it is permissible to place fire on top [of these materials]. If one places it on top of wood, that fire, while burning through them, goes on to burn the earth;
this is not permissible. The same principle applies to bricks, potsherds, and so forth. For there too, it is permissible to place it only on top of the bricks and such.
Why? Because they do not constitute fuel (*anupādāna*). Indeed, those things do not count as fuel for the fire.

They go; it is not permitted to give fire even to dry stumps, dry trees, and so forth. However, if one gives it with the thought, "I will extinguish it before it reaches the ground and then depart," it is permitted.
If he is unable to extinguish it later, there is no offense because it was outside his jurisdiction.
While walking while holding a torch, if his hand is burning and he drops it on the ground...
There is no offense. It is permissible to kindle a fire after placing fuel precisely on the spot where it has fallen.
