Furthermore, it is permissible to disturb as much of the scorched ground as has been permeated by heat.
However, if a monk who is unaware [of the rule] produces a fire using fire-sticks, lifts it up with his hand, and [thinks], "What..."

If he says, "I am doing it," he should be told, "Stop! If he says, "My hand is burning," he should be told, "Act in such a way that it does not burn. However, he must not be told, "Throw it on the ground.
If he throws it while his hand is burning, there is no offense because he did not throw it with the intention, "I will burn the earth"; however, he may make a fire at the spot where it has fallen.
It is allowable. [One may say: “Know the pit for this pillar; know the large clay; know the husk-clay;
give the large clay; give the husk-clay; bring clay; bring earth; there is need of clay; there is need of earth;
make the pit for this pillar allowable; make this clay allowable; make this...”
"Make the dust allowable"— in this way, it is permissible to have anything done by using such "allowable" terminology. If one is distracted and,
while conversing with someone else, stands scratching the earth with one's big toe or a walking stick,
there is no offense for one who scratches or digs in this manner due to lack of mindfulness.
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of digging the earth, in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 15.
Discourse on the Determination of Plant Life.
75. "The class of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) is a designation for trees, creepers, and so forth, which have grown from five kinds of seeds.
In this context, these are the five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seed-seeds.
Therein, "root-seeds" refers to turmeric, ginger, *vacā*, *vacatta*, *ativisa*, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *usīra*, and *bhaddamuttaka*.
Furthermore, whatever other things there are that grow from roots and are produced from roots—this is called "root-seed.

As for "stem-seed," it refers to the *assattha*, *nigrodha*, *pilakkha*, *udumbara*, *kacchaka*, and *kapitthana* trees, or whatever other things there are that grow from stems and are produced from stems—this is called "stem-seed. As for "joint-seed" (*phaḷu-bīja*)...
Sugar cane, bamboo, reeds, or whatever else there is that grows from joints and is produced from joints—this is called "propagated by joint" (*phaḷubīja*).

That which is called "propagated by tip" (*aggabīja*) includes *ajjuka*, *phaṇijjaka*, and *hirivera*, or whatever else there is that grows from the tip and is produced from the tip—this is called "propagated by tip.
That which is called "propagated by seed" (*bījabīja*) includes grain for the first harvest and grain for the subsequent harvest.
Or whatever other things there are that grow from seeds and are produced from seeds—this is called "seed-seed.
In this regard, if one who perceives it as a living plant community cuts or has it cut, breaks or has it broken, cooks or has it cooked, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
For one who destroys a living plant community, there is an offense of expiation; [but there is no offense] for one who [destroys] what has been freed from a living plant community.
For one who destroys even the fivefold class of seeds, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 76.
This so-called "class of seeds" and "class of living beings" exists both as water-dwelling and land-dwelling.

Therein, that which dwells in water—such as varieties of mustard, clay, sesame seeds, and so forth, including those with leaves and those without leaves, and every kind of moss, down to the mere film on the surface of the water—is called the "class of living beings."
It should be understood as follows: what is called a "water-crust" is hard and rough-colored on top, while soft and blue-colored at the bottom.
In that regard, for the moss whose root has gone down and is established in the earth, the earth is its location;
for that which moves about in the water, the water is its location. For one who disturbs it anywhere, even though it is established in the earth—

If one moves [an animal] from its place after lifting it up, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); likewise, there is an offense of expiation for one who disturbs it while it is moving about in the water.
However, it is permissible to bathe by moving the hands here and there through the water.
For the entire body of water is its place; therefore, by that much alone, it has not been moved from its place. But from the water, by means of water...
It is not permissible to uproot [them] intentionally; however, it is permissible to uproot them along with water and then replant them back in the water.
For one who pulls up water-born creepers and grasses such as *uppalinī* and *paduminī* from the water, or who destroys them right there, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
For one who destroys those that have been uprooted by others, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For these belong to the category of seeds (*bījagāma*).

They are included [in the category of seeds]. Even a sesame seed, a mustard seed, a bit of clay, or moss, when pulled up from the water and not yet withered, is included in the category of "seed at the tip.

In the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries, it is stated that "endless sesame seeds, water-moss, and so forth are grounds for a *dukkaṭa* offense," but no reason for this is seen there. In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "It is not a complete living organism (*bhūtagāma*)."

Therefore, it is stated, “it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” but even that does not fit. For while an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) is prescribed for a grove of living plants (bhūtagāma), an offense of wrong-doing is prescribed for a grove of seeds (bījagāma).
A third category called an “incomplete grove of living plants” has appeared neither in the Canon (pāḷi) nor in the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathā);

thus, if one were to say that this [third category] will be included within the category of a grove of seeds, that too is not logical, because such a thing would have its root in what is not a grove of living plants.
"Of a seed-village": furthermore, "in matters of grave offenses, one must stand firm"—this is a characteristic of the Vinaya.

When trees are cut down on dry land, what remains is called a green stump; there, the stumps of *kakudha*, *karañja*, *piyaṅgu*, *panasa*, and so forth, grow upward and are included within the category of living vegetation (*bhūtagāma*).
However, the stumps of *tāla* and *nāḷikera* (coconut) trees do not grow upward...

It grows; thus, it is included within the category of seeds (*bījagāma*). However, in the case of an unfruiting plantain tree, the stump is included within the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*), whereas when it bears fruit, it is included within the category of seeds.
Furthermore, as long as the fruiting plantain tree still possesses green leaves, it is included only within the category of living beings;
the same applies to a bamboo that has borne fruit. But when it begins to wither from the top down, it then comes to be included within the category of seeds.
By what kind of seed-group? By the seed-group of fruit-stones. What is produced from that? Nothing at all.

For if anything were produced, it would be included within the seed-group of living beings. When they cut down trees such as the *indasāla* and make a heap of them, even though branches the size of a jewel emerge from the bundled sticks, they are nevertheless included within the seed-group of non-living things.
They may be planted in the ground for the purpose of a pavilion, a fence, or to grow climbing vines;

once their roots and leaves have emerged, they again come under the category of "grove of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*). However, even when only the roots or only the leaves have emerged, they are still included within the category of "seed-grove" (*bījagāma*).
Whatever seeds have been placed on the earth after being moistened with water,
or have been deposited in skull-bowls and the like after moist soil has been put inside them— all these are still merely "seeds" even when only a root or a mere leaf has emerged.
Even if both roots and a shoot emerge above, they remain merely "seeds" as long as the shoot has not yet turned green.

When the leaves of radishes and the like have emerged, or when the green sprouts of rice and the like have grown blue-colored, they are included within the category of "grove of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*).
In the case of palmyra palms, first the root emerges like a pig’s tusk;
even after it has emerged, as long as the leaf-sheath above has not yet come out, it is still called a "seed-grove" (*bījagāma*). In the case of coconuts, once the husk is broken open—
A sprout emerges like a toothpick; as long as it has not become a coil of blue leaves resembling a deer’s antler, it is still merely the seed-plant (*bījagāma*).
Even when the root has not yet emerged, once such a coil of leaves has grown, it is included within the category of the "unrooted living plant" (*amūlaka-bhūtagāma*).
The *ambaṭṭhi* and other such plants are to be distinguished from rice and the like. Whether they are *vandākā* or any other kind that grows upon trees—
It covers a tree; the tree itself is its location. For one who damages it or uproots it from there, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
There is a single rootless creeper that winds around the stems of forest thickets like a finger-ring;
for this too, the legal determination is exactly the same. Regarding the blue-green algae on house-fronts, walls, railings, shrines, and so forth:

As long as two or three leaf-sprouts have not yet appeared, it is considered a "seed at the tip" (*aggabīja*). Once the leaves have grown, it becomes a matter for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
therefore, in such cases, it is not permitted to apply even a coating of lime.

However, it is permitted to apply a greasy coating over what has been plastered by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). If, during the hot season, dried moss remains, [it must be removed].

It is appropriate to remove that by rubbing it with a broom or similar tools. Algae on the outside of water jars and the like is an object for which there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), but inside they are not to be considered a transgression;
even the mold on tooth-sticks, cakes, and so forth is likewise not to be considered a transgression. For this has been said:
"If a wall treated with red ocher becomes moldy, it should be wiped clean after moistening a cloth and wringing it out."
77. Species of stone, such as *pāsāṇadaddu*, *sevala*, *seleyyaka*, and so forth, which are greenish in color and have not yet become leaves, are matters for a *dukkaṭa* offense.
As for the *ahicchattaka* (mushroom), it is a matter for a *dukkaṭa* offense up until it forms a cap; from the time it has blossomed onwards, it is not an offense (*abbohārika*).
However, one who takes an *ahicchattaka* from a living tree destroys the bark of the tree; therefore, in that case, there is a *pācittiya* offense.

The same principle applies to tree-shoots (*rukkhapapaṭikā*). However, there is no offense for one who takes a shoot of *indasāla*, *kakudha*, or similar trees that has detached from the tree and remains [there].
It is permissible to take sap (*niyyāsa*) that has detached from the tree and stands [on the ground] or clings to a dry tree, but it is not permissible to take that which clings to a moist tree.
The same principle applies to lac (*lākhā*). [Regarding] the tree...
If one shakes down a withered leaf or causes flowers such as the *kaṇikāra* that have already ripened to fall, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone.

The same principle applies even to one who carves letters upon soft surfaces such as the trunks of *indasāla* or *nīpī* trees, or upon palm leaves grown there, by scratching them with the fingers or fingernails.
It is permissible to bend down a branch to give flowers to novices (*sāmaṇera*) who are gathering them; however, by them...
One should not let water infuse with the scent of flowers; one who desires to infuse water with the scent of flowers should have a novice monk pick them up and gather them.
Even when wishing to eat fruit oneself, one should not bend down a fruit-bearing branch; rather, having picked up a novice monk, one should have him pluck the fruit.
It is not permissible to pull out any grass or hair while holding onto it together with novice monks.
However, for the sake of generating enthusiasm in them, it is permissible to take hold of the tip [of the branch] as if showing the manner of pulling without actually pulling.

If one takes the branch of trees that produce shoots for the purpose of fanning away flies and so forth, without having it made allowable (*kappiya*), then there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for anyone who scratches it with their fingernail, even if only on the bark or the leaf. This applies to fresh ginger, long pepper, and so forth as well.
The same principle applies here. However, if a root develops in a cool place where something permissible has been placed, it is allowable to cut off the upper part.
If a sprout develops, it is allowable to cut off the lower part.
But when both the root and the sprout have developed, it is not allowable.
Thinking, "I will cut grass even with a broom or a tally-stick," if one sweeps on the ground and either cuts it oneself or has another cut it, it is not permitted.
Even while walking up and down (*caṅkama*), if one intentionally steps on grass, creepers, and so forth with the feet, thinking, "Let what is to be cut be cut;
let what is to be broken be broken; I shall show the place for walking," [it is likewise not permitted].
If one cuts it oneself or causes another to cut it, it is not permitted. Even if grass or a creeper breaks while one is tying a knot, it is not permitted to tie the knot.
Furthermore, in the case of palm trees and the like, people strike wooden monkeys or bind thorns upon them so that thieves will not climb; it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to do such things. If...
A wooden monkey is merely clinging to a tree; it does not harm the tree, so it is permissible.
It is permissible to say, "Cut the tree, cut the creeper, uproot the bulb, or the root," because there is no specific restriction.
However, it is not permissible to specify by saying, "Cut this tree," and so forth. Even when mentioning a name, one may say, "The mango tree, the four-cornered creeper... [and so on].
Even such statements as "cut, break, and uproot the yam, the muñja-grass, and the bark of the asuka-tree" are likewise indefinite.
Only a statement such as "this mango tree" is called definite, and that [indefinite one] is not permitted.
Even one desiring to cook a leaf who intentionally makes a fire upon grass and so forth either cooks it himself or [causes another to do so].
Or if one causes [them] to be cooked, it is not permitted. However, it is permitted to say without specifying, "Cook the mung beans," or "Cook the black gram," and so forth;
but it is not permitted to say, "Cook these mung beans. One may say, "Know this as a root medicine;
give me this root or leaf," or "Bring this tree or creeper," or "There is need for this flower or fruit."
"Make this tree, or creeper, or fruit allowable," it is thus permissible to say.
At this point, the release from the danger to living beings (*bhūtagāma*) is accomplished.

However, when consuming [the fruit], one must have it made allowable once again for the sake of releasing it from the danger to the seed-plant (*bījagāma*). And here, the manner of making it allowable should be understood according to this sutta:

“I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to five kinds of monastic preparation: that prepared by fire, that prepared by a knife, that prepared by the fingernail, seedless, and fifthly, that from which the seed has been removed.
In this context, “prepared by fire” means prepared by fire—that is, overcome, burnt, or touched by it.
“Prepared by a knife” means prepared by a knife—that is, overcome, cut, or pierced by it. The same method applies to “prepared by the fingernail.”
Seeds that have not been extracted from their husks are themselves allowable (*kappiya*).
One who makes them allowable by means of fire must do so using any kind of fire—whether a fire of wood, cow-dung, and so forth—even down to a piece of glowing iron;
however, it must be done by touching only one part [of the seed] while saying, "It is allowable. One who does it with a knife may use any kind of metal knife.
Even for the cutting of a needle or a fingernail, it must be done by one who has declared it "allowable" (kappiya) while showing the cutting or piercing with the beak or the edge.
When making something allowable with a fingernail, it must not be done with a decayed nail;
however, the nails of humans, lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds are sharp, and [one may use] those.
It should be made. The hooves of deer, wild boars, wild pigs, antelopes, oxen, and so forth are too sharp;
one must not use them, for even if something is made with them, it is as if it were not made. Elephant claws, however, are not considered "hooves," and they are permitted.

Furthermore, whatever materials are permitted for making [the razor], even if they are grown locally or have been extracted [from the ground], one must first have them cut or pierced by someone else, and only after saying, "This is allowable" (*kappiya*), may it be used.

In this regard, even if there were a heap of seeds as large as a mountain, or a thousand trees cut down and tied together, or a great bundle of sugarcane set aside, once one seed, or one tree branch, or one stalk of sugarcane is made allowable (*kappiya*), everything becomes allowable.
If the sugarcane and the firewood are tied together, [one may say]: "The sugarcane..."

If one pierces a piece of wood with the thought, “I shall make it allowable,” it is indeed permissible. However, if one pierces the rope or creeper by which they are tied together, it is not permissible.

When they bring a basket filled with pieces of sugarcane, once one piece has been made allowable, all of them are indeed made allowable. And when they bring rice mixed with pepper, pakkā, and so forth—
When it is said, “Make it allowable,” even if a grain of rice remains stuck [to the spoon], it is indeed permissible.
The same rule applies to sesame seeds, rice grains, and so forth. However, those placed in gruel do not remain stationary because they become joined together;
in that case, one must certainly make each individual grain allowable by piercing it. In the case of fruits such as the wood-apple (*kapittha*), the inner pulp moves about, leaving the shell behind.
Having had it broken, one should have it made allowable; if it remains in a single piece, it is permissible even to do so in a cauldron.
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of the "living plant" rule in the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
16. Discussion on the Determination of Sleeping Together (Sahaseyyavinicchayakathā) 79.

There are two kinds of sleeping together (*sahaseyyaka*): "Whichever bhikkhu should lie down in the same bed with one who is not fully ordained for more than two or three nights, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Whichever bhikkhu should lie down in the same bed with a woman..."
This was said with reference to the two training rules concerning sleeping together (*sahaseyya-sikkhāpada*), which were stated as "an offense entailing expiation" (*pācittiya*).

Herein is the analysis: on the fourth day, beyond the three nights, when the sun has set, in a lodging that is entirely covered and entirely enclosed, or one that is mostly covered and mostly enclosed, [if one sleeps] in front-to-back succession with one who is not fully ordained...
Or for one who lies down at a single moment, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
In this context, even if it is enclosed by anything such as a wall to a height of one and a half cubits without touching the roof-covering, it should be understood as "entirely enclosed.
That lodging which is entirely covered on top by five types of coverings or by any other means whatsoever is called "completely covered" (*sabbacchanna*).
This is the name for a lodging (*senāsana*). However, in the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*), adopting common parlance and following what is familiar to the tongue, it is stated:
"A 'completely roofed' [lodging] is one roofed with five types of roofing materials.

Even though this is stated, nevertheless, it is not possible to avoid an offense even for one sleeping in a tent made of cloth; therefore, here "roofing" and "enclosed" refer to anything capable of providing concealment.
This should be understood. For if only the five kinds of roofing were taken, then even a thatched-roofed dwelling would not constitute "sharing a sleeping place";
therefore, that lodging which is enclosed by a wall or by anything else, down to a mere cloth, starting from the ground up to the roof, is called a "completely roofed" lodging. Roofing—
Even if it is not enclosed by walls or the like on all sides, but is surrounded by such enclosures at least one and a half cubits high in every respect,
it is considered "completely enclosed. However, that which has a greater portion of its upper area covered and only a small portion uncovered,
or which is surrounded on most sides and only a small portion is unenclosed, is "mostly covered."
"Substantially enclosed" means:

if a dwelling possesses this characteristic, even if it is a seven-storied palace with a single precinct, or a four-sided hall with a hundred rooms, it is reckoned as a single lodging (*senāsana*). In such a lodging, by one who is not yet fully ordained...
It is stated that for one who lies down together with them on the fourth day after the sun has set, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
However, if there are several novices and one monk, there are offenses of expiation according to the number of novices.
If they lie down repeatedly, there is an offense for the monk for each such instance; likewise when the monk lies down repeatedly.
However, it is only through the action of a bhikkhu that a bhikkhu incurs an offense. If there are several bhikkhus and one novice, even if only one of them commits the offense, all of them incur it.
Even by his repeated rising up and lying down, it is indeed an offense for the bhikkhus.
This same principle applies when both groups consist of several individuals.
80. Furthermore, here too a tetrad beginning with "living in one residence" (ekāvāsa) should be understood.
For whoever, in a single residence, shares a sleeping place for three nights with even a single person not fully ordained (anupasampanna), from the fourth day onwards, he incurs a daily offense.
This is also the case for whoever, in that very same residence, shares a sleeping place for three nights with various persons not fully ordained.
It applies also to one who, in various dwellings, shares a sleeping place for three nights with even a single person not fully ordained;
and it applies also to one who, having traveled even a hundred leagues in various dwellings, shares a sleeping place with various persons not fully ordained—
from the fourth day onward, there is a daily offense.

And this so-called offense of sharing a sleeping place occurs even with an animal that has become a basis for a *pārājika* offense, because of the statement: "With the exception of a bhikkhu, everyone else is called 'one who is not fully ordained'.

Therefore, even if some creature such as a monitor lizard, a cat, or a mongoose enters and lies down in the same area of the dwelling where the bhikkhu is staying, it constitutes a shared sleeping place.
But if, however, one enters through the hollow of the beam-head situated above the wall of a palace built upon pillars—
where the upper floor is not connected to the wall— lies within the beam, exits by that same hollow, and goes away,
there is no offense for the bhikkhu who was lying in the lower palace. If...
If there is a hole in the roof, one may enter through it, stay within the roof-covering, and depart by that same way;
for one who lies on the upper floor inside the roof-covering in a different vicinity, there is an offense, but for one lying on the lower floor, there is no offense.
If they ascend by means of the interior of the palace itself and make use of all the floors, those floors constitute a single vicinity; among them, where...

There is an offense for one who lies down anywhere [within a structure]. Even when a dwelling is constructed as a half-wall using a collection of rooms, if pigeons and the like lie down on the rafters, beams, and so forth, there is indeed an offense. If they lie down outside the enclosure but within the reach of the eaves, there is no offense.
Whether it be circular or square, even if it is a hundred rooms in a series of chambers under a single roof, [the same applies].

Regarding the lodging: if they enter through a common entrance and, in a case where the interior precincts are not separated by individual walls, they enter all the rooms—even if one person who is not fully ordained is lying down in a single room—there is an offense for those lying down in all the rooms.
If the rooms have vestibules and the vestibule is not covered above, then [an offense applies] to one who lies down in the vestibule while [others lie] in the rooms.
One who lies down does not incur an offense [for those lying with him].
However, if the roof is connected to the roof of the inner chamber itself, then one who lies there incurs an offense for all of them. Why? Because it is entirely covered and entirely enclosed.
For its enclosure is indeed the very enclosure of the inner chamber.

81. Even in the case of great palaces consisting of one hall, two halls, three halls, or four halls arranged together, where it is possible for one who has washed his feet upon entering at one spot to walk all the way around, one is not exempt from the offense of sleeping in the same place [with a woman].
However, if a boundary (*upacāra*) has been demarcated in each respective location, then [the offense applies] only within the area of a single boundary.

There is an offense. When a plastered pavilion with two doors has a wall built in its center, if one enters by one door and an unordained person sleeps in one section while a monk sleeps in another, there is no offense.
However, if there is a gap in the wall large enough for a lizard or similar creature to enter, and lizards are sleeping in one section, [there is an offense].
It is indeed not an offense. For a house with a breach does not become what is called "a single enclosure.

If they construct a door by cutting through the middle of a wall, there is an offense because of its status as a single enclosure. If they sleep after closing that door with a door-panel, it is indeed an offense.
For by closing the door, the house does not become what is called "multiple enclosures," nor does the door become a non-door; for the door-panel [functions] by means of being closed and opened.
It was made for the purpose of being used at one's pleasure, not for the purpose of interrupting its use. If they close that door again with bricks, it becomes a non-door;
it remains within the very same previous non-proximity zone (*anūpacāra*).
If there is a long-faced shrine room with one door inside and one outside, a person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) [stands] between the two doors.
For one sleeping inside a shrine-house, an offense is incurred because it constitutes a single contiguous space.
This is the summary here: whether the dwelling is small or large, connected with another or disconnected, long, circular, square, or consisting of one story or many stories.
Or, in whatever single enclosure there may be, in all such cases there is an offense of sleeping together.

And herein, by means of any covering whatsoever, if it is entirely covered and entirely enclosed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if it is mostly covered and mostly enclosed, there is an offense of expiation;
if it is entirely covered and mostly enclosed, there is an offense of expiation; if it is entirely covered and half-enclosed...
There are eight *pācittiya* offenses: a *pācittiya* for [sitting] where it is mostly covered and half-enclosed; a *pācittiya* for where it is entirely enclosed and mostly covered;
a *pācittiya* for where it is entirely enclosed and half-covered; and a *pācittiya* for where it is mostly enclosed and half-covered.
There is a *dukkaṭa* offense for where it is half-covered and half-enclosed, and a *dukkaṭa* for where it is entirely covered.
Five offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are to be understood: wrong-doing for that which is covered by a small opening; wrong-doing for that which is mostly covered and has a small opening;
wrong-doing for that which is entirely covered and has a small opening; and wrong-doing for that which is mostly covered and has a small opening. [The other two cases are:
entirely covered and not entirely open, and entirely covered and not at all open. [And: mostly not covered.
There is no offense in cases where it is mostly uncovered, half-covered, covered with a small canopy, half-covered, covered with a small canopy, or both covered and half-covered with a small canopy.
This same analysis applies even for one who lies down together with a woman.
However, this is the distinction here: for one who lies down together with one who is not fully ordained, the offense occurs on the fourth day.

"Along with a woman on the first day. However, regarding yakkhinīs, petīs, and female animals who possess a visible form, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense only when the act constitutes the basis for sexual intercourse; with others, there is no offense.
Thus ends the summary of the Vinaya analysis not found in the canonical texts (*Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe*).
The Discussion on the Determination of Sleeping Together is finished.
17. The Discussion on the Determination of How to Proceed Regarding Beds, Chairs, and Other Belongings of the Saṅgha in Monasteries 82.

"Having spread out bedding in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, he departs": this refers to departing from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha after having spread out bedding there, with the intention of dwelling elsewhere. In this regard, the determination is as follows:

“Whosoever, however, a bhikkhu, having spread out a bed or having caused one to be spread out in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, when departing, neither puts it away nor causes it to be put away, or departs without asking permission, incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Because of this statement, for one who,
having personally spread out a bed or having caused another to spread it out in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha,
crosses the enclosure of an enclosed monastery or the vicinity of an unenclosed one without having performed the putting away and so forth, there is an offense of expiation.

In this context, "bedding" (*seyyā*) is tenfold: a mattress (*bhisī*), a quilt (*cimilikā*), an upper coverlet (*uttarattaraṇaṃ*), a floor-covering (*bhūmattharaṇaṃ*), a wooden plank (*taṭṭikā*), a piece of hide (*cammakhaṇḍo*), a sitting mat (*nisīdanaṃ*), a rug (*paccattharaṇaṃ*), a grass-strewing (*tiṇasanthāro*), and a leaf-strewing (*paṇṇasanthāro*). Therein, a "mattress" (*bhisī*) is either a bed-mattress or a chair-mattress.
A "quilt" (*cimilikā*) is for the purpose of preserving the color of the ground that has been prepared with plaster and so forth.
Having spread that [grass] underneath, they spread a straw mat (*kaṭasāraka*) on top.
An "upper covering" (*uttarattharaṇa*) is a bedspread to be spread over beds and chairs. A "ground-covering" (*bhūmattharaṇa*) is a variety of items such as straw mats to be spread upon the ground.
A "mattress" (*taṭṭikā*) is a mattress made of palm leaves or woven grass (*vākā*). A "hide" (*cammakhaṇḍa*)...
"Skin" (*camma*) refers to any kind of hide, such as those of lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and so forth.

For in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, no hide is seen that is prohibited for the use of lodgings; therefore, the prohibition should be understood to apply specifically to the wearing of lion, tiger, and other such skins.
"Rug" (*nisīdana*) should be understood as one with fringes. "Spread" (*paccattharaṇa*) refers only to what is called a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) or a woolen coverlet (*kojava*).
It has been said: "A grass mat" means a mat made of any kind of grass. This same method applies to a leaf mat as well.
Now, when one is departing after having spread or had spread this tenfold bedding in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, one must depart after having asked for permission.
And when asking for permission, if there is a bhikkhu present, that bhikkhu must be asked for permission.
In his absence, a novice; in his absence, a monastery attendant; in his absence, the owner of the monastery who had it built;

or someone from his family may be asked for permission. In his absence as well, having placed a bed upon four stones, having stacked the remaining beds and stools upon that bed, and [having arranged] the ten kinds of bedding such as cotton mattresses and so forth on top—
Having made a bed, having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, having closed the doors and windows,
and having fulfilled the duties for departing,
one should go. However, if the lodging is leaking, and if grass or bricks have been brought for the purpose of roofing it— provided that...
If one is able, it should be covered. If one is not able, one should go and leave the beds, chairs, and so forth in a place that is sheltered from the rain.
If everything is being rained upon, one who is able should deposit them in the house of lay followers within the village.
If they say, "Venerable sir, that which belongs to the Saṅgha is a heavy responsibility; we are afraid of fire, theft, and so forth," [one should take them elsewhere].
If they do not accept it, it is permissible to place a bed upon stones even in the open air, set down the remainder according to the method previously described,
cover it with grass and leaves, and depart— thinking, "Whatever remains there, even if it be but a mere limb,
will be of benefit to other monks who may arrive there. Having removed [the bedding],...
Furthermore, when departing, one must remove all the beds, stools, and door-panels, pack them away, and hang them on the robe-rack before leaving.
When returning later, the monk who is to stay there must likewise act: having set out the bed and stool again, he should do exactly as before.
When staying with the bedding arranged from inside the wall-space to the outside of the wall-space, at the time of departure, once again—

It should be put away in the very place where it was taken up. This same rule applies even to one who, having brought [the bedding] down from the upper story of a palace, is dwelling on the lower story.
When a bed and chair have been prepared in the night-quarters or day-quarters, they must be placed back in the very place where they were taken from when departing.
83. Regarding dwellings, however, this is the determination of what requires permission and what does not: first, as for those long halls on the ground...
Whether it be a leaf-hut or a house built against tree trunks that serves as a dwelling place for termites, one must first take leave before departing from such a site.
For if it is left unattended for a few days, it will simply turn back into an anthill.
However, in the case of a stone slab or houses built against stone pillars...

Whether it be a dwelling made of grass, a rock cave, or a plastered dwelling—wherever there is no danger of termites—one may depart from such a place either after asking for permission or without asking;
however, asking for permission is the proper duty (*vatta*). Even in such a dwelling, if termites are ascending from one side, one must indeed ask for permission before departing.

One must go. However, if an incoming monk, having taken a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, lives there following an existing monk without taking a dwelling for himself, then as long as he does not take one, that dwelling remains an obstacle for the previous monk alone.
But once he takes a dwelling and lives there by his own authority, from that point onward—
It is an impediment only for the newcomer. If both take [the robe] after dividing it, it is an impediment for both.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "If two or three together designate [a robe], all must ask permission at the time of departure.
If, among them, one who is going first goes while making the mental resolve, 'The one behind will look after it'..."

It is permissible; there is no exemption for the last person by means of his own mental attention (*ābhoga*). If many people send one person to have [the bedding] spread out, then at the time of departure, either all must take leave, or one may be sent to take leave.

Having brought beds, chairs, and so forth from elsewhere and having stayed elsewhere, they must be brought back to that very place at the time of departure. If another [person] comes from elsewhere and stays with one who has already brought [the items] from elsewhere...
If one who is senior arrives, he must not be turned away; rather, one should say: "Venerable sir, this has been brought by me from another residence;
please restore it to its original state. When the senior has consented, saying, "I shall do so," it is permissible for the other to depart.
For even if one has moved it elsewhere and then uses it as communal property belonging to the Saṅgha, if it is lost or worn out...
If it is stolen by thieves, there is no liability for the debt; however, for one who uses it as personal property, there is liability for the debt.

But if another person uses a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha—whether using it as communal property or as personal property—and it is lost, the liability for the debt remains with that very person.
Having spread out a bed within the monastery, thinking, "I will return this very day and take care of it,"...
Likewise, if one who has such expectations goes to the other side of a river or to another village, and while still standing at the very place where the intention to go arose,
he sends someone to ask for permission; or if he is hindered or afflicted by some obstacle such as a river in flood,
a king, or thieves, and is unable to return— there is no offense for one in such a situation.
Furthermore, if one has spread out a bed, or had it spread out, in the vicinity of a monastery— whether in an assembly hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—
and when departing neither lifts it up nor has it lifted up, or goes away without asking permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For having arranged the ten kinds of beds described above in a protected place such as an inner chamber, etc., [if one leaves without attending to them, there is an offense].
Because for one who departs, even the bedding and the lodging are destroyed by termites and become nothing but a mound of earth, a *pācittiya* is stated.

However, for one who departs after having arranged [the furniture] outside in the assembly hall or similar places, only the bedding itself might perish due to the lack of protection for the site, but not the lodging;
therefore, in this case, a *dukkaṭa* is stated. [This applies to] the bed and chair.
However, because it is not possible for them to be bitten by ants immediately, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who spreads it out even within the monastery and then departs.
There is likewise an offense of wrong-doing for one who departs after spreading it out in the vicinity of the monastery, in the assembly hall, in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree. 84.
"Whosoever monk, in an open space, [spreads out] a bed belonging to the Saṅgha, or a bench, or a mattress, or a pillow..."

However, according to the statement: "Having spread it out oneself or having had it spread out by another, when departing, one should neither lift it up nor have it lifted up, nor should one go without asking permission;

[if one does so], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," this applies even to one who departs with the thought, "I will return this very day," after having spread out or had spread out four items belonging to the Saṅgha—such as beds and chairs—in the open air, without performing the lifting or other necessary duties.
If it exceeds the distance of a throw of a clod by a man of medium strength, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Here, "stool" (koccha) means that which is made of reeds, or of *usīra* grass, or of *muñja* grass, or of *pabbaja* grass;

it is bound together, being wide at the bottom and top and narrow in the middle, shaped like a drum (*paṇava*). It is said that even if such a stool is wrapped in the skin of a lion or a tiger in the middle...
They do so, for there is no such thing as an improper hide here. Indeed, even a lodging made of gold is permitted; therefore, it is of great value.

However, because of the statement: “I allow you, monks, for eight months during the non-rainy season, to deposit bedding in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree where crows or hawks do not vomit,” [the rule applies] during the eight months of the rainy season.

Thus, when it is not well-known [where the boundary is], it is permissible to leave them for eight months—four in the winter and four in the summer—in a bower of branches, a bower of mats, or at the foot of a tree.
However, one must not leave them at the foot of a tree where crows, hawks, or other birds dwell habitually, having built their nests there. “Eight...
Because of the statement "for four months," it is not permissible to leave [the bowl] outside for four months in those regions where it does not rain during the rainy season.

Because of the statement "in the designation of the non-rainy season," even during the winter, it is not permissible to leave it outside in places where it rains in winter. However, in summer, it is clear of clouds everywhere.
It is pure and inclined [toward the sky]; at such a time, it is permissible to place a bed or chair in the open air for some necessary purpose.
85. One who stays in the open air must also know the proper conduct. For if he has a private bed, he should sleep right there.
If he takes one belonging to the Saṅgha, he should take a bed stripped of its coverlet made of hemp or linen; in that [bed],...
If there is no old bed, one may take a new woven or stuffed one.

Having taken it, however, it is not permitted for one who claims to be a strict tree-root dweller or a strict open-air dweller to lie down after arranging it in an open space or at the foot of a tree at an improper time, without having even constructed a robe-tent (cīvarakuṭi). But if [it is] even fourfold...
A hut made of robes is unable to protect one from the cold; there may be seven-day rains and so forth, yet it is permissible because it follows the body of the bhikkhu.

For those living in leaf huts in the forest, people with hearts inspired by their perfection of virtue give new beds and chairs, saying, "Use these as the property of the Saṅgha for personal enjoyment. When they depart after having stayed there...

One should go after sending for monks who are like-minded in a neighboring monastery; in the absence of such like-minded monks, one should go after depositing [the robes] in a place sheltered from rain;
if there is no such sheltered place, one should go after hanging them on a tree.

Having taken a broom, one should sweep the courtyard of the cetiya, or the courtyard of the dining hall, or the courtyard of the Uposatha hall, or the surrounding cells, the day-quarters, the fire-hall, and so forth.
Or, having swept one [of them] and washed it, it should be placed back in the sweepings-basket itself.
This same method applies even when one takes [the broom] from one of the places such as the Uposatha hall and sweeps the remainder.
However, if a monk who is sweeping the path to the alms-round wishes to go, he should sweep it; if, while on the way, there is—
If there is a hall, it should be placed there. If there is none, one should observe whether the clouds have ceased;
then, knowing that "it will not rain until I return from the village," one may place it anywhere, and upon returning, it should be put back in its original place.
If, however, one knows that it will rain, [one should leave it] in the open air.
"If one sets it down [elsewhere], it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
However, if a broom has been placed in various locations for the purpose of sweeping, it is permissible to sweep each of those places and then place the broom back in those very same locations.
One who sweeps the sitting hall must know the proper procedure (vatta). Herein, this is the procedure: starting from the center, [one should sweep] toward the foot-rests.
Sand must be removed, and rubbish, having been grasped by hand, must be thrown outside.

86. If one causes the fourfold type of lodging belonging to the Saṅgha—whether in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion—to be spread out by one who is not fully ordained, it constitutes an impediment for the person by whom it was caused to be spread.
But if one who is fully ordained (upasampanna) has it spread out, the obstacle belongs to the one by whom it was spread. Herein is the analysis:
An elder, having finished his meal duties in the dining hall, instructs a junior monk, "Go and prepare a bed and chair in the daytime quarters.
Having done so, the junior monk sits down; the elder, having wandered about as he pleased, goes there and [takes] his bag...
If he places either a bag or an upper robe [there], from that point on it becomes an impediment for the elder.

If, having sat down, he himself goes away and neither removes [the items] nor causes them to be removed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) once the distance of a stone’s throw has been exceeded.
However, if the elder, without placing a bag or an upper robe there, says to the junior monk while walking, “Go yourself,” [then there is no offense].
He should point it out, saying, "Venerable sir, this is the bed and chair. If the elder knows the proper conduct (*vatta*), he should say, "You go;
I shall restore it to its original state. If he is ignorant and untrained in the proper conduct, he should simply rebuke the junior, saying, "Go!
Do not stay here; I give you no permission to sit or lie down. By the junior...
“Venerable sir, may you sleep well,” having obtained leave in this way, he should pay homage and depart. Once he has gone, it is an impediment for the elder alone;
and his offense should be understood according to the previous method.
However, if at the very moment of being commanded, the junior monk thinks, “I have some business regarding my belongings, such as washing them,” etc., [the situation is as follows].

If he says, "It exists," but the Elder, having told him, "Go after you have made it known," leaves the dining hall and goes elsewhere, he must be dealt with according to the rule for lifting the feet [from the seat].
If he goes and sits down right there, his offense occurs in the same manner as before once he has crossed the distance of a stone's throw.
However, if the Elder commands the novice, and the novice is there—
Even if one has sat down after arranging a bed and chair, if one goes elsewhere from the dining hall, one is to be dealt with according to the rule regarding the lifting of the foot.
Having gone there and sat down, if one departs again, one is to be dealt with for an offense once the distance of a clod-throw has been exceeded.
However, if while giving orders one commands, "Having arranged a bed and chair, sit right here," then one may go wherever one wishes and return.
He obtains [the offense]. However, for one who departs without putting things back to their normal state, there is a *pācittiya* offense upon exceeding the range of a clod-throw.
When monks have sat down after arranging beds, chairs, and so forth in a gathering in between [monasteries], they must say to the monastery attendants at the time of departure, "Please put this away.
For those who depart without saying this, there is an offense upon exceeding the range of a clod-throw.
87. There is what is called a "Great Dharma-listening" (mahādhammassavana). In that case, they bring out beds and chairs from both the Uposatha hall and the dining hall and arrange them;

this is an impediment for the resident monks alone. If incoming monks take them, saying, "This is for our preceptor," or "This is for our teacher," then from that point on it becomes an impediment for them.
When it is time to depart, [the arrangement] returns to its normal state.
There is an offense for those who cross over without having thrown a clod of earth [to mark the boundary]. However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*:

"As long as others have not sat down, the responsibility lies with those by whom [the seats] were prepared; once others have arrived and are seated, the responsibility lies with those who are now sitting.
If they depart without having removed [the seats] themselves or having caused them to be removed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Why? Because there was no formal instruction."
"Because it has been prepared. As long as no announcer or Dhamma-preacher has arrived when the Dhamma-seat has been prepared, there is an obstacle for those who prepared it.
Once he has arrived and is seated, that becomes his obstacle.
If the hearing of the Dhamma continues for the entire day and night, one announcer or Dhamma-preacher stands up and another sits down. Whoever...
The responsibility belongs only to whoever comes and sits down. However, when rising, one should say, "This seat is your responsibility," and then depart.

Even if the person who sat down first rises and leaves before the other has arrived, provided that the newcomer arrives and sits down while still within the precincts (upacāra), the one who departed should not be charged with an offense.
But if, while the other has not yet arrived, he who sat down first rises from his seat and crosses the distance of a clod’s throw,
he is to be dealt with according to the offense. "In all cases, when crossing the distance of a clod’s throw, there is an *dukkaṭa* for the first foot and a *pācittiya* for the second foot"—
this method is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.
88. But if, having spread out in the open air— whether it be a rug belonging to the Saṅgha other than the aforementioned types of lodgings, or a woolen blanket, or an upper coverlet,
or a floor-covering, or a wooden board, or a piece of hide, or a foot-wiping cloth, or a wooden bench— and then departs,
he neither puts it away himself nor has it put away by another.
If one goes without asking permission, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Even for one who goes after having placed in the open air any wooden article—whether a stand, a bowl-cover, a foot-washer, a fan, a palm-leaf fan, or even a water-pot or a water-conch—it is an offense of wrong-doing.
[Likewise] for one who, having boiled dye in the open air, leaves behind a dye-vessel or a dye-pot...
The oil-jars and all such items must be stored within the fire-hall. If there is no fire-hall, they should be placed in a sheltered mountain cleft.
If even that is unavailable, it is permissible to leave them in a place where monks can see them while looking out, and then depart.
However, regarding bedding such as beds and chairs belonging to another person, the offense is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding this, it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī and other texts: "If the entrustment of confidence does not take root in someone, then there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding what belongs to that person.
However, if the entrustment of confidence does take root in someone, then what belongs to that person becomes one's own personal property.
There is no offense at all regarding one's own personal property. If a monk, a novice, or a monastery attendant is conscientious, [and] his own...
One regards it as an obstacle; thus, there is no offense even for one who goes without having asked permission in such a case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who, while drying [the goods] in the sun, goes away thinking, "I will come back and take them up.
Thus ends the compendium of legal decisions on the Vinaya not found in the canonical texts (*Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*).
The discussion on the determination of how to proceed regarding communal lodgings such as beds and chairs is finished. 18.
Discussion on the Determination of the Timely.
89. Regarding the phrase "the four *kālika* [medicines] as well": here, these four *kālika* [medicines] are to be understood as *yāvakālika*, *yāmakālika*, *sattāhakālika*, and *yāvajīvika*.
Among these, whatever solid or soft food may be received before midday is to be consumed until the time designated as midday, because it must be used within that period.
*Yāvakālikaṃ*: Together with the *anuloma-pāna* (concordant drinks), the eight kinds of drink may be consumed until the watch of the night known as the last watch;
because it has that watch (*yāma*) as its time, it is called *yāmakālika*. The five kinds of medicine, such as ghee and so forth, having been received, may be stored for seven days;
because it has seven days (*sattāha*) as its time, it is called *sattāhakālika*. With the exception of water...
The remainder of all that has been accepted is called "yāvajīvika" (to-be-used-for-life) because it is to be used for as long as life lasts, provided there is a suitable occasion. 90.
Among those things allowable for as long as one lives, "soft food" (*bhojanīya*) consists of rice, boiled millet, flour, fish, and meat—these five.
Excluding foods that are for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for life, the remainder is called "hard food" (*khādanīya*).
Regarding this, first, as for hard food made from primary grains or secondary grains, such as cakes and sweetmeats, there is nothing further to be said.
Furthermore, whatever consists of edible matter, whether it be forest roots and so forth, is included; namely, hard food consisting of roots.
Roots for eating, bulbs for eating, heads for eating, trunks for eating, bark for eating,
leaves for eating, flowers for eating, fruits for eating, bones for eating, flour for eating,
and resin for eating— these also are reckoned as edible food (khādanīya).
In this context, however, this is merely an illustration for the purpose of identifying what belongs to the category of food (*āmisa*):

first, regarding roots used as raw vegetables, the root of the radish, the root of the *khāraka*, the root of the *caccu*, the root of the *tambaka*, the root of the *taṇḍuleyyaka*, the root of the *vatthuleyyaka*, the root of the *vajakali*, and the root of the *jajjhari*—such roots of edible greens belong to the category of food. And herein:
At the root of the *vajjakali* plant, they cut off the old stalks and discard them; that [part] lasts for a lifetime.

Other things of this kind should be understood by this same method. However, it is stated that even the old stalks of the root of the *mūlaka*, *khāraka*, and *jajjharī* plants fall into the category of edible food (*āmisagatika*).
As for those [plants] mentioned in the Pāḷi—
“I allow, monks, medicinal roots: turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, *vacatta*, ativiṣa, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *uśīra*, and *bhaddamuttaka*;
or whatever other medicinal roots there may be that do not serve as food for the purpose of food, nor serve as a meal for the purpose of a meal.”

These are called "lifelong" (yāvajīvika). When counted according to the method beginning with the "small five roots" (cūḷapañcamūla) and the "great five roots" (mahāpañcamūla), there is no end to their enumeration.
Furthermore, their defining characteristic is precisely their non-digestibility for the purpose of either chewing (khādanīya) or eating (bhojanīya).
Therefore, whatever root among those [plants] is a natural food for people in various regions—

It should be understood that what serves for the purpose of solid food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*) is "to be used within the proper time" (*yāvakālika*), while the other is "to be used as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*).
For even after saying much, one must remain firm in this very definition.

However, when names and designations (*nāmasaññā*) are mentioned, there is only confusion for those who do not know those respective names; therefore, without placing undue emphasis on names and designations, one should attend only to the definition (*lakkhaṇa*).
It has been shown. Just as in the case of the root, we shall likewise show the characteristic in the case of the bulb and so forth;

the analysis should be understood by means of that very same principle. Furthermore, regarding those eight kinds mentioned in the Canon—turmeric and the rest—it is stated that all of them, including stalks, bark, flowers, fruits, and so on, are "for as long as life lasts."

Regarding edible tubers (*kandakhādanīya*), there are two kinds of tubers: long ones, such as the tubers of *bhisaka* and *kiṃsuka*; and round ones, such as the tubers of *uppala* and *kaseruka*, which some also call "knots" (*gaṇṭhī*).
Among all these tubers, the parts that are withered and decayed, the outer skin, and the fine root-fibers are [forbidden] for life-long storage;
however, a fresh tuber that is pleasant to eat, such as the tuber of a young *sāla-kalyāṇī* sapling, is permissible.
The *kiṃsuka* tuber, the *ambāṭaka* tuber, the *ketaka* tuber, the *māluva* tuber, what is called the *bhisā* (lotus root), the tubers of the *paduma*, *puṇḍarīka*, *piṇḍāluka*, and *sālu*;
the tubers of milk-creeper (*khīravallikā*), *āluva*, *sigguka*, and *tāla*; the tubers of the blue lotus (*nīluppala*), red lotus (*rattuppala*), *kumuda*, and *sogandhika*;
the *kadalī* tuber, the *veḷu* (bamboo) tuber, and the *kaseruka* tuber—these and others are [eaten] according to the local custom of staple food in their respective regions.
Bulbous roots that serve as food for humans—both as hard foods (*khādanīya*) and as soft foods (*bhojanīya*)—are *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day).

The milk-creeper bulb (*khīravallikanda*) is *yāvajīvika* (usable for life) if it is unwashed, but *yāvakālika* if it is washed. However, bulbs such as the milk-gourd (*khīrakākoli*), the *jīvika*, the *usabha*, the *kalasuṇa*, and so forth, are *yāvajīvika*.
These are included in the Pāḷi under the category of medicinal roots (*mūlabhesajja*) by the phrase: "or whatever other roots there are that are medicines."
Regarding edible stalks (*muḷālakhādanīya*): the stalks of the *paduma* (lotus) and the *puṇḍarīka* (white lotus) are just like [other] roots.

The stalks of *eraka* grass, *kandula*, and so forth—stalks that spread throughout various regions for the purpose of being chewed or eaten as the natural food of people—are *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day).

As for the stalks of turmeric, ginger, *makaci*, the four-sided creeper (*caturassavalli*), *ketaka*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, *kuntāla*, coconut, betel-nut trees, and so on: [The text continues with the classification of these items.]
However, that which lasts for as long as life—all of that is included within the category of root medicines in the Canon by the phrase: "or whatever other medicinal roots there may be.
Regarding the edible fruits at the top [of trees]:
those of the palmyra, hintāla, kuntāla, ketaka, coconut, betel-nut, date-palm, sugar-cane, eraka, and plantain trees.

The "heads" (matthaka) designated as *kaḷīra*— namely, bamboo shoots (*veṇukaḷīra*), reed shoots (*naḷakaḷīra*), sugarcane shoots (*ucchukaḷīra*), radish shoots (*mūlakakaḷīra*), mustard shoots (*sāsapakaḷīra*), and *satāvarikaḷīra*,
as well as the shoots of the seven grains (*sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ kaḷīrā*)— and so forth, which are the tops of trees, creepers,

and the like that spread throughout various regions for the purpose of being chewed or eaten by people according to their local dietary habits, are all "to be consumed at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*).

The stalks of turmeric, ginger, bamboo, *makaca*, garlic, and plantain; and the stalks of palm, *hintāla*, *kuntāla*, and coconut—having been cut and cast down, the withered core (*jaraṭṭhabunda*) is for life.

Among the trunks used as fresh food (*khandhakhādanīya*), the trunk of the *sālakalyāṇī* tree that has grown underground, the sugarcane trunk, and the stalks of blue lotus, red lotus, white water lily, and fragrant water lily [are likewise].

Regarding "stems of the *daṇḍaka* [plant]" and so forth: in various regions, the spreading stem that serves as food for people according to their local dietary habits—whether for chewing (*khādanīya*) or for eating (*bhojanīya*)—is of the "temporary" (*yāvakālika*) category.
However, the leaf-stalks of the *utpala* species, all stalks of the *paduma* species, the *karavinda* stalks and others, and all remaining stems are "life-long" (*yāvajīvika*).

Regarding the bark for eating: the *ucchu-taca* (sugarcane bark) is one that may be used only during the proper time (*yāvakālika*), and even that is flavorful; all the rest are for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*).

Furthermore, the inclusion of the three types of bark—the topmost, the trunk, and the bark—within the category of medicinal decoctions (*kasāva-bhesajja*) should be understood from the Canon. For it is said: "I allow you, monks, medicinal decoctions:
neem decoction, *kuṭaja* decoction, *paṭola* decoction, *phaggava* decoction, *nattamālaka* decoction, or whatever other medicinal decoctions there may be..."
“They serve as food for the purpose of food, not as a meal for the purpose of a meal.
Herein, their inclusion is established. It should be understood that the aforementioned *sāvaka* (vinegar) is entirely allowable.
Among the solid foods (*khādanīya*) for the bowl: radish, *khāraka*, *caccu*, *tambaka*, *taṇḍuleyyaka*, *papunnāga*, and *vatthuleyyaka*.
The leaves of the *vajjakaḷi*, *jajjhari*, *sellu*, *siggu*, *kāsamaddaka*, *ummā*, *cīna-mugga*, *māsa*, *rājamāsa*— excluding *mahānipphāva*—
and the remaining *nipphāva*, as well as *aggimantho*, *sunisannaka*, *setavaraṇo*, *nāḷikā*, and the *loṇī* grown on the ground; these, and other such things,
are for the purpose of being eaten by people as ordinary food in various regions.
Bowl-bases intended for food that are used for spreading [over the alms-food] are exclusively *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day).
However, as for other leaves—such as those the size of a large fingernail that climb upon salt-trees and shrubs—the bowl made from them is *yāvajīvika* (to be kept for life).

The inhabitants of the Island (Dīpavāsino) say that the *brahmi*-bowl is *yāvakālika*. The mango sprout is *yāvakālika*, but the *asoka* sprout is *yāvajīvika*. And as for those others mentioned in the *Pāḷi*—
“I allow, monks, leaf medicines: neem leaves, kuṭaja leaves, bitter gourd leaves, sulasī leaves, cotton-tree leaves,
and whatever other leaf medicines there may be that do not serve as edible food for the purpose of eating,
nor serve as soft food for the purpose of eating.”
These are declared to be lifelong. And it is not only their leaves;

their flowers and fruits as well. Among the leaves that are lifelong, there is no end to their enumeration, such as the *phaggava* leaf, the *ajjuka* leaf, the *phaṇijjaka* leaf, the *tambūla* leaf, and the lotus leaf.
Regarding edible flowers: radish flowers, *khāraka* flowers, *caccu* flowers, *tambaka* flowers,

*vajakali* flowers, *jajjhari* flowers, *cūḷanipphāva* flowers, *mahānipphāva* flowers, *kaseruka* flowers, the young blossoms of coconut, palm, and *ketaka*, white *varaṇa* flowers, *siggu* flowers, and even a mere stamen from the flowers of blue lotuses, red lotuses, and water lilies.

The *karīra* flower, the *jīvantī* flower, and so forth—these are spreading flowers that serve as food for chewing or eating for people in various regions according to their natural diet, and they are "to be taken at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*).

However, the flowers of the *asoka*, *bakula*, *kuyyaka*, *puṇṇāga*, *campaka*, *jāti*, *karavīraka*, *kaṇikāra*, *kunda*, *navamālika*, *mallikā*, and others are "to be taken for life" (*yāvajīvika*), for there is no end to their enumeration.
In the Canon, however, these should be understood as included within the category of medicinal decoctions (*kasāvabhesajja*).

As for fruits— such as those of the breadfruit, the *labuja*, the palmyra, the coconut, the mango, the rose-apple, the *ambāṭaka*, the tamarind, the citron, the wood-apple, the bottle-gourd, the pumpkin, the *pussaphala*, the *timbarūsaka*, the *tipusa*, the *vātiṅgaṇa*, the *cocamoca*, the *madhuka*, and so forth—
which in various regions of the world serve as the natural staple food for people,
intended both as solid food (*khādanīya*) and as soft food (*bhojanīya*)— all of these are "to be taken at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*). It is impossible to enumerate them by name.
...to show the limit. As for those medicines that are mentioned in the Pāḷi:

“I allow you, monks, fruits as medicine: *bilanga*, long pepper (*pippali*), black pepper (*marīca*), yellow myrobalan (*harītaka*), beleric myrobalan (*vibhītaka*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), *goṭṭhaphala*, or whatever other medicinal fruits there may be that are not among the [raw] foods to be chewed...”
“They serve as chewables, but they do not serve as food for the purpose of eating”—thus these are called “lifetime-usable” (yāvajīvika).

Even among those, it is impossible to show their limit by way of name, such as the unripe fruits of the *acchiva*, *bimba*, *varaṇa*, *ketaka*, *kāsmarī*, and so forth; likewise, the *jātīphala*, *kaṭukaphala*, cardamom (*eḷā*), and *takkola*.

Regarding bone-chewables (*aṭṭhikhādanīya*): the seeds of the *labuja*, the seeds of the *panasa*, the seeds of the *ambāṭaka*, the seeds of the *sāla*, and the seeds of the *khajjūrī*, *ketaka*, and *timbarūsaka*.

The seeds of the *taruṇaphala*, the seeds of the *tintiṇika*, the seeds of the *bimbaphala*, the seeds of the various kinds of lotuses such as the *utpala* and *paduma*, and so forth—these are bones that pervade various regions for the purpose of being chewed or eaten according to the natural diet of the people in those respective places; they are "to-be-eaten-at-the-proper-time" (*yāvakālika*).
Furthermore, there are the seeds of the *madhuka*, the seeds of the *punnāga*, the seeds of the *harītakī* and others, and the seeds of the *siddhatthaka*.

Bone such as that of the *rājika* (black mustard) and so forth are "for life" (*yāvajīvika*). Their inclusion within the category of medicinal fruits (*phalabhesajja*) should be understood from the text itself.
Regarding the flour for hard food (*piṭṭhakhādanīya*), there is first the flour of the seven grains, the flour of those things conforming to grain, and the flour of other vegetables:

namely, jackfruit flour (*panasapiṭṭha*), breadfruit flour (*labujapiṭṭha*), hog-plum flour (*ambāṭakapiṭṭha*), *sāla* tree flour (*sālapiṭṭha*), *dhotaka* palm flour (*dhotakatālapiṭṭha*), and milk-creeper flour (*khīravallipiṭṭha*).
Such flours as these, which are found in various regions, serve as food for people according to their natural dietary habits;

those used for chewing or eating are "within the time-limits" (*yāvakālika*), while unrefined palm-flour, milk-creeper flour, and flours such as *assagandha* are "for the duration of life" (*yāvajīvika*).
Their inclusion in the Canon should be understood under the categories of "bitter decoctions" (*kasāva*) and "roots and fruits."
Regarding resinous edible medicines (*niyyāsakhādanīya*): only sugar-cane resin (*ucchuniyyāsa*) is for a seven-day period;

the rest—namely, those resins mentioned in the Canon as follows: “I allow you, monks, resinous medicines: asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), asafoetida powder (*hiṅgujatu*), asafoetida stalks (*hiṅgusipāṭika*), buttermilk (*taka*), buttermilk-pot (*takapatti*), buttermilk-leaves (*takapaṇṇi*), *sajjulasa*, and whatever other resinous medicines there may be”—these resins are for life (*yāvajīvika*).
Among these, mango resin is included by way of the "miscellaneous" category (*yevāpanaka*).
The "exudation of the *kaṇikāra* tree"—it is not possible to show its limits by way of such names.

Thus, among these edible roots and so forth, whatever is "to be taken at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*), all of it is included in this context under the term "edible food" (*khādanīya*) as the remainder. 91.
Among those "to be taken during the watch of the day" (*yāmakālika*), there are eight drinks: mango drink, rose-apple drink, jackfruit drink, breadfruit drink, [and so on].
The drink of madhuka, the drink of muddika, the drink of sālūka, and the drink of phārusaka—these are the eight drinks.
Therein, "ambapāna" (mango drink) is a drink made from mangoes, whether raw or ripe.
Therein, one making it from raw [fruit] should break open young mangoes, put them into water, cook them by the heat of the sun in the open air, strain them, and [use those] received on that very day.
It should be prepared by mixing honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth; thus prepared, it is permissible only before the meal.
However, having received what has been prepared by those who are not fully ordained, if it is accepted before the meal, it is permissible to consume it with solid food (sāmiṣa) before the meal;
after the meal, it is permissible to consume it without solid food (nirāmiṣa) until dawn. This same principle applies to all drinks.
*Jambupāna* is a drink made from *jambu* fruits. *Cocapāna* is a drink made from *kadalī* fruits that have seeds.
*Mocapāna* is a drink made from seedless *kadalī* fruits. *Madhukapāna* is a drink made from the natural juice of *madhuka* flowers;
however, it is permissible when mixed with water, but not when pure. *Muddikapāna* is [a drink made from] *muddika* [grapes].
*Ambapāna* is a drink made by crushing [the fruit] in water. *Sālūkapāna* is a drink made by crushing the roots (*sālūka*) of red lotuses, blue lotuses, and so forth.
*Phārusakapāna* is a drink made from *phārusaka* fruits, prepared in the same manner as *ambapāna*.
These eight drinks are permissible whether they are cold or cooked by the sun; however, those cooked by fire are not permissible.
The remaining small fruit drinks—such as those made from *vetta*, *tintiriṇika*, *mātuluṅga*, *kapittha*, *kosamba*, *karamanda*, and so forth—are included within the eight permitted drinks.
Although these are not mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), they nevertheless conform to what is allowable; therefore, they are permissible.
Because it was said, "Monks, I allow all fruit juices, except for the juice of grain-fruits," one should exclude the juice of grain-fruits that are in conformity with the rule (*sānuloma*).
There is no other fruit juice that is not allowable; all such are strictly for the duration of a watch (yāmakālika).

In this regard, what is called "fruit juice compatible with grain" (sānulomadhaññaphalarasa) refers to the juice of the seven grains, as well as the nine great fruits—namely, the palm, coconut, plantain, breadfruit, bottle gourd, pumpkin, *pussaphala*, *tipusa*, and *eḷāluka*—and the juice of all grains compatible with the morning and evening meals; these are for the duration of the day (yāvakālika).

Therefore, it is not permitted after the meal. Because it was said, “I allow you, monks, all the juices from the bowl except for the juice of raw vegetables,” it is permitted to take the juice of cooked vegetables—excluding those that are raw—after crushing them with cold water, whether the juice is prepared by soaking or by cooking in the sun.
“I allow you, monks, all the juices from flowers except for…” [the juice of raw flowers].
Because it is stated as "the juice of *madhuka* flowers," any flower juice is permissible except for the juice of *madhuka* flowers. 92.
That which is for seven days consists of these five medicines: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.
Therein, "ghee" means the ghee of cows, or the ghee of goats, or the ghee of buffaloes—of those whose meat is allowable.
For them, there is ghee. "Fresh butter" means fresh butter for those very same people. "Oil" means sesame oil, mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil.
"Honey" means honey from bees. "Treacle" means that which is produced from sugarcane.
As for "life-long [medicines]," they should be understood in the same manner as was explained below regarding the "timely" (yāvakālika) items such as roots and edible foods.
93. In this regard, what has been received at dawn as *yāvakālika* (to be used during the day) may be stored even a hundred times and consumed as long as the time does not expire.
What is *yāmakaḷika* (to be used within one watch of the night) may be used for one day and night; what is *sattāhakaḷika* (to be used for seven days) may be used for seven nights;
and the other [the *yāvajīvika*] may be used for as long as life lasts, provided there is a suitable reason. Having received it...

However, when one takes anything—whether *yāvakālika* (food for the day) or *yāmakālika* (food for the watch of the night)—with the desire to swallow it after having let a single night pass, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* at the very moment of receiving it;
but for one who swallows it, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for each individual swallow due to the condition of storing it overnight (*sannidhi*).
Even if the bowl has not been washed well, such that a streak is visible when rubbed with a finger, [the same applies].
If oil has entered between the rim of the bowl's handle, it drips when the bowl is held over heat, or it becomes visible when hot rice-gruel is taken;
even with such a bowl, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who eats from it on the following day.
Therefore, having washed the bowl, one should pour clear water into it again or rub it with a finger to ensure that the oiliness is gone.
This must be understood. For if an oily residue is seen in the water, or if a finger-mark is visible in the bowl, it is not properly washed;
however, if a finger-mark is visible in a bowl that has the color of oil, that is not a matter for censure.
Furthermore, if monks give things to novices without regard for themselves, and the novices, having stored them away, then give them back, all of this is permissible. Having received it oneself...
Indeed, it is not permissible on the second day if it has not been relinquished; for one who swallows even a single grain of rice from that [food], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Regarding unallowable meats, in the case of human flesh, there is an offense of expiation together with a grave offense (thullaccaya); in the remaining cases, it is together with an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

For one who swallows food that is to be consumed within a watch of the night when a requisite condition exists, there is an offense of expiation; for one who swallows it for the purpose of nutriment, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Together with [the offense of] eating at the wrong time, there is a *pācittiya*. If, having been invited, one consumes food that has not been made into *atiritta* (leftover), there are two *pācittiya*s for ordinary meat;
for human flesh, there are two together with a *thullaccaya*; for other unallowable meats, [there are two] together with a *dukkaṭa*.

When consuming *yāmakālika* (medicine to be taken until the end of the watch) with the mouth while containing meat, provided there is a valid reason, there are two [offenses]; when it is without meat, there is only one.
For one who swallows for the purpose of food, a *dukkaṭa* offense increases in both cases of misrepresentation.

If one swallows at an improper time (*vikāla*), two *pācittiya* offenses increase—one on account of storing up ordinary food and one on account of eating at an improper time—and in the case of unallowable meat, a *thullaccaya* and a *dukkaṭa* increase.
There is no offense on account of the improper time regarding what is to be consumed within the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*). On account of [eating] what is not left over (*anatiritta*)...
However, at the improper time, there is no offense in any of the alternative cases.
But for one who accepts *sattāhakālika* (seven-day medicine) or *yāvajīvika* (lifetime medicine) for the purpose of food, there is first a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) due to the act of accepting;
however, for one who consumes it, if it is not mixed with non-food (solid food), there is a *dukkaṭa* for each mouthful. If, on the other hand, it is mixed with non-food...
Once it has been accepted and set aside, it remains a *pācittiya* offense for its original base.

94. Regarding the seven-day medicines, such as ghee and so forth, this is the analysis: first, ghee that was accepted before the meal may be consumed on that same day before the meal, whether mixed with food or not mixed with food; from after the meal onwards, however—
It may be consumed without meat for seven days. If the seven-day period has elapsed, if it was placed in a single vessel, there is one *nissaggiya* offense;
if it was in many vessels, there are *nissaggiya* offenses according to the number of items. What was received after the meal may be consumed even without meat;
however, what was set aside by making it an "accepted-for-storage" (*uggahitaka*)—whether before the meal or after the meal—is not permitted.

It is not permitted to swallow it; however, it may be used for anointing and so forth. Even if seven days have elapsed, there is no offense because it has reached a state where it cannot be swallowed.
If one who is not fully ordained makes ghee out of butter received before midday and gives it, even if it contains food, it is permissible before midday;
if he prepares it himself, it is permissible for seven days provided it contains no food at all.
Clarified butter made from fresh butter received after the meal, prepared by anyone, is permitted for seven days even if it contains meat.
Regarding that which is prepared with fresh butter received before the meal, the determination should be understood according to the same method as the previously explained pure clarified butter.
Clarified butter made from milk or curd received before the meal, even if prepared by one who is not fully ordained, is permitted on that very day before the meal, even if it contains meat.
It is permissible; only that which is prepared by oneself and is strictly non-material (nirāmisa) is permissible.
For one who is heating butter, there is no "self-cooking" (sāmaṃpāka);

however, it is not permissible to have material food (āmisa) together with that which has been self-prepared, nor is it permissible from after midday onwards. Even if seven days have elapsed, there is no offense.
Because it was accepted with a physical basis (*savatthuka*). However, what is prepared after the meal by those who have accepted [the ingredients] should be applied to ointments and the like.
