And even if it is prepared before the meal by those who have taken [the ingredients], there is no offense for either case once seven days have passed. This same principle applies to unallowable meat-ghee (*akappiyamaṃsasappi*).
But this is the distinction: where in the Canon (*pāḷi*) there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) for ghee that has come down in the text, [there is no offense here].
In this regard, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, having stated a semblance of a reason, human ghee and fresh butter are prohibited;
that is an improper prohibition, because they are permitted in all the *aṭṭhakathās*. Furthermore, its detailed explanation will follow later.
Even the fresh butter mentioned in the Canon, if received before the meal, [is permitted].
Therefore, before the meal, it is permissible even if it contains meat; from after the meal onwards, it must be entirely without meat.

If seven days have passed, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) for each vessel if the items were placed in separate vessels, and for each morsel if they were placed in a single vessel without being mixed together.
What is received after the meal should be understood as being like ghee. In this regard:
However, since there are still lumps of curd and even drops of buttermilk [in the butter], the Elder Upaḍḍhatthera said that it is permissible to wash it.
But the Elder Mahāsivatthera said, "From the time the Blessed One permitted it, they ate it as soon as it had been extracted from the buttermilk.
Therefore, one who consumes fresh butter should wash it and remove the curd, buttermilk, flies, ants, and so forth.
It may be consumed. If one wishes to consume it after boiling it and making ghee from it, it is permissible even if it has not been washed;
for whatever portion there is that has become curd or buttermilk will simply go to waste. For to this extent, it is not considered "received with a physical basis" (*savatthuka-paṭiggahita*);
this is the intended meaning here. Because it was cooked together with the foodstuffs (*āmisa*).

However, those who feel remorse even regarding that are called "scrupulous" (*kukkuccakā*). Now, the entire method concerning what is an offense and what is not an offense, and what may or may not be consumed, applies to:
ghee stored after having been received before the meal; ghee made from milk or curd received before the meal; ghee made from those [substances] received after the meal;
ghee made from what was received [before the meal]; ghee made from what was received [after the meal]; and unallowable meat-ghee.

Ghee should be taken in the same manner as described for oil. However, when monks enter for alms of oil, they scatter there not only ghee, fresh butter, cooked oil, and uncooked oil, but also drops of buttermilk and curd, grains of rice, husks of rice, flies, and so forth.
Having been heated by the sun and strained, [it is used].
It becomes seven-day medicine once it has been accepted. Having accepted it, it is permissible to cook it together with stored medicines and even use it as nasal drops.

If, at the time of the alms-round, a modest novice melts it in the fire so that the rice grains and other bits that have fallen there do not burn, strains it, and then cooks it again before giving it, it remains permissible for seven days according to the same method as before.
96. Regarding oils: sesame oil received before the meal is permissible even if it contains food;
from after the meal onwards, it is permissible only if it is free of food. If seven days elapse, its status as an *nissaggiya* offense should be understood according to the number of containers.
Oil received after the meal is permissible for seven days only if it is free of food.
Having made it into a formal acceptance (*uggahitaka*), it is not permitted to swallow what has been set aside;

however, it may be applied to the head and so forth, and there is no offense even if seven days elapse. Having accepted sesame seeds before midday, oil produced from them is permitted even if mixed with food before midday;
from after midday onwards, it becomes unfit for consumption, though it may be applied to the head and so forth.

There is no offense even if seven days have elapsed. Having accepted sesame seeds after the meal, the oil produced from them is indeed not fit for consumption because it was accepted with its base (the seeds) still present;
there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed, as it may be applied to the head and so forth.
The same principle applies to oil made from sesame seeds accepted either before or after the meal. Before the meal...

If oil has been prepared by one who is not fully ordained—either by roasting the accepted sesame seeds, or by grinding them into a paste, or by moistening them with warm water—it is permissible to consume it even with solid food before the midday meal if it was prepared by another;

however, if it was prepared by oneself, it is permissible to consume it without solid food before the midday meal because it has been extracted, but it is not permissible to consume it with solid food because it was cooked by oneself. This is because it was accepted while still possessing its physical basis (the seeds).
However, from the time after the meal onwards, both [types of oil] are inedible; they may be applied to the head and so forth, and there is no offense even if seven days elapse.
If, however, the hot water is only a small amount, sufficient merely for sprinkling, it is not considered a formal case;

it does not count as "cooking by oneself. This applies also to mustard-seed oil and the like when accepted without a proper receptacle, as well as to sesame oil when accepted without a proper receptacle.
The analysis is exactly as stated before.
However, if it is possible to make oil from the powder of mustard seeds and so forth received before midday by means of cooking in the sun, that is permitted even with food before midday;
from after midday onwards, it is permitted only when free from food.

After seven days have passed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). However, since they prepare oil by first steaming mustard seeds and *madhuka* powder and then roasting castor seeds, the oil made from these by those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) is permissible even with food before the midday meal;
furthermore, because these substances are for life-long use, there is no fault in accepting them along with their base materials.
What has been prepared by oneself must be consumed for seven days using only non-material (nirāmisa) requisites.
What has been prepared by those who have received [the food] is not fit to be swallowed; it is permissible for external use, and there is no offense even if the seven-day limit is exceeded.

Oil prepared from mustard seeds, madhuka, or castor seeds after they have been accepted for the purpose of making oil is "seven-day medicine" (sattāhakālika); however, that which is prepared on the second day [of the seven-day period]...

If it is made on the first day, it is permissible for five days; if made on the third day, it is permissible for five days; if made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, it is permissible for that very day.
If it remains until sunrise, it is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). What is made on the eighth day is not fit for consumption;
however, because it is not subject to forfeiture, it is permissible for external use.
Even if one does not use it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for exceeding seven days with mustard seeds or the like taken for the purpose of oil.
Furthermore, although not mentioned in the text, there are other oils such as those from coconut, neem, kosamba, and karamanda;

for one who accepts these and lets seven days pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is the distinction between them—the category of things to be used within the day (yāvakālika) and the category of things to be used for life (yāvajīvika).

Having observed this, everything regarding the rules for self-cooked food, food obtained before the meal, food obtained after the meal, and the handling of accepted items should be understood according to the method already stated.
As for "fat-oil," it is said: "Monks, I allow five kinds of fat: bear-fat, fish-fat, porpoise-fat, [cow-fat, and pig-fat]."
“Pig’s fat,” “donkey’s fat”—thus is the oil of those fats permitted.
And here, by the mention of “bear’s fat,” the fat of all unallowable meats is permitted, with the exception of human fat. By the inclusion of “fish,” the *susukā* (shark) is also included;
however, it is mentioned separately because it is a predatory fish. And by the inclusion of “fish and so forth” here, [the rest is understood].
The fat of all permissible meats is permitted. Among meats, ten types are impermissible: those of humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas;
among fats, only human fat is impermissible. Regarding milk and other liquids, there is nothing that is impermissible.
Fat-oil prepared and extracted by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna), if received before midday—even if containing food—is allowable before midday.
From after the meal onwards, it is permissible for seven days provided it is entirely without meat.
However, whatever therein resembles fine dust—whether it be meat, sinew, bone, or blood—that is not considered a transgression.
But if, having received fat, one prepares it oneself, or having received it before the meal, cooks it and strains it, it may be used for seven days as a non-meat preparation.

It may be consumed. For this was said with reference to non-material consumption: "What was received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time may be consumed as an oil-consumption. Even in that case, what is not allowable is indeed not allowable;
however, it is certainly not permitted to receive or prepare [food] after the meal has been concluded. For this has been stated:
“Monks, if one should consume what was accepted at an improper time, processed at an improper time, and mixed together at an improper time, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*.

Monks, if one should consume what was accepted at a proper time, processed at an improper time, and mixed together at an improper time, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*. Monks, if [what was] accepted at a proper time...”
“If one should consume what was received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, but mixed [with other things] at an improper time, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
But if, monks, it was received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, and one should consume it, there is no offense.
Then the resident pupils asked the Elder Upatissa: “Venerable sir, having cooked ghee, fresh butter, and fat together...”
“Are those that have been extracted allowable, or not?”—“They are not allowable, friend. It is said that the Elder felt scruples here as if over a piece of meat fried in oil.

Then they asked him further: “Venerable sir, if there is a lump of curd or a drop of buttermilk in the butter, is that allowable?”—“That too, friend, is not allowable. Then they said to him: “Venerable sir, …”
“Having cooked them on one side, when they are mixed together on the other side, they become potent and suppress disease.
“Very well, friend,” the Elder accepted. But the Elder Mahāsumma said, “Only the meat and fat that are *kappiya* (permissible) are allowed for use with solid food;
the others are allowed for use with non-solid food. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma, having rejected it by asking, “What is this? [refused].

“Is it not the case that monks afflicted by wind-disorders drink gruel made from the five roots and sour gruel after adding clear pig oil and such, and because that is rich in heat (*tejo*), it suppresses the disease? Having said this, he replied, “It is permissible.
97. “Honey” (*madhu*) means [the product] of honey-bees, small bees, and bumblebees.
Regarding honey: if it was received before midday, it is permissible to consume it with solid food (sāmiṣa) before midday;

from after midday onwards, it is permissible only for seven days as a non-solid food (nirāmiṣa). If, after the seven days have passed, it is not relinquished, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya).
If large quantities of honey resembling molasses have been cut into pieces and set aside, or if it is kept in various separate containers, the count is according to the number of items (vatthu).
These are offenses entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). If there is only one piece, or if the other is in the same vessel, there is only one offense entailing relinquishment.
The method for what has been stored should be understood according to the manner already stated; it may be applied to ointments for wounds and the like.

As for honey-cakes or honey-lumps, if they are not smeared with honey and are pure, they are "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvika*); however, if they are smeared with honey, they fall under the category of honey itself.
The *cīrikā*—a winged long fly called *tumbaḷa*—and the *aṭṭhipakkhikā* black large bees:
in their dwellings there is honey resembling resin (*niyyāsa*). This is permissible for as long as life lasts. 98.
*Phāṇita* (molasses) means the juice of sugarcane, whether uncooked, or cooked without having formed into a solid mass; all such [preparations] that have not yet formed a solid mass are included.
A preparation of sugarcane. That molasses, if received before midday, is permitted even with solid food;
from after midday onwards, it is permitted only as long as it is free of solid food for seven days. If seven days elapse, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) according to the number of items.
Even if many lumps have been ground into powder and placed in a single vessel so that they form a solid mass, it is still considered a single item.
This is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). What has been received should be understood according to the method already stated; it may be applied for purposes such as fumigating houses.

If molasses is made from unstrained sugarcane juice that was received before midday, it is permissible even if it contains food-remnants (*sāmiṣa*) provided it was prepared by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*);
if it was prepared by oneself, it is permissible only if it is free from food-remnants (*nirāmiṣa*). From after midday onwards...
However, because it was received with a physical base [of food], it is not fit for consumption; there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed.
Even if it is prepared after midday using what was received without having been strained, it is still not fit for consumption; there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed.
This same principle applies to molasses made from sugarcane that was received [after midday]. However, if it is prepared before midday using what was received after having been strained...
If it was prepared by one who is not fully ordained, it is permissible even with food before the midday meal;

from after the midday meal onwards, for seven days, it must be without food. If it was prepared by oneself, it must be without food even before the midday meal. However, if it was prepared after the midday meal using what was received through a water-strainer, it is permissible for seven days provided it is without food.
Prepared by one who has learned [the method] is according to the same rule. "Baked sugarcane molasses..."
"Or crushed sugarcane treacle is permissible even before the meal," so it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, after posing the question, "Is this cooked with a substrate (savatthuka) permissible or not? it is said: "There is no such thing as sugarcane treacle that is not permissible after the meal.
That [latter view] is correct. [This refers to] honey-flower treacle made with cold water.
Before the meal, it is permissible even if mixed with meat; from after the meal onwards, for seven days, it is permissible only if unmixed with meat.

If the seven-day period is exceeded, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of instances. Honey-syrup made by adding milk is "to-be-taken-at-the-proper-time" (*yāvakālika*).
However, they purify candied sugar and rock sugar by removing the milk-scum; therefore, it is permissible.
99. As for the *madhuka* flower, it is permissible even before the meal if it is fresh. It is also permissible if it is roasted;

or, having been roasted, it is permissible whether it is mixed with sesame seeds and the like or not, provided it is ground. However, if one takes it and prepares it for the purpose of making liquor, once it has been prepared, it is not permissible from the moment of its being sown as a seed.
[The same applies to] plantains, dates, mangoes, *labuja*, jackfruit, *ciñcā*, and so forth.
For all fruit-juices that are to be consumed during the day (*yāvakālika*), the molasses (*phāṇita*) is likewise to be consumed during the day.

When they prepare molasses with pepper and other ingredients, it is to be used for life (*yāvajīvika*). Thus, the five substances beginning with ghee, which were mentioned as being for seven days (*sattāhakālika*), because they have been authorized by the name of "medicine" in the statement, "Monks, I authorize these five medicines," may or may not perform the function of medicine; however, they are intended for the purpose of food.
Having accepted even those medicines that are capable of lasting long, they may be used at one's pleasure before the midday meal on that same day;
from after the meal onwards, provided there is a requisite need, they may be used for seven days according to the method already stated.

However, if seven days are exceeded, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense under the rule concerning medicines, even if the amount is only the size of a mustard seed or even if taken once with a finger.
Having taken it with the tongue in a quantity sufficient for a taste, one must relinquish it and confess the *pācittiya* offense.
Having received back what was relinquished, it must not be swallowed, nor should it be used through physical consumption;
nor should the body or a wound on the body be smeared with it. Even robes, staffs, sandals, foot-rests, beds, chairs, and so forth, that have been smeared with those [substances]...
[These are] not for use. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Even on the door-panels, window-shutters, and casements, the place where one grasps with the hand must not be smeared.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "But having mixed [the dye] with dregs, the doors, windows, and shutters may be smeared.
It is permissible to apply [the dye] to lamps or to black-colored objects. But by another monk...
It should be used as physical enjoyment, not as food to be swallowed. However, because of the statement,

"There is no offense if one resolves [to keep it] within seven days," there is no offense if, within the seven-day period, one resolves that the ghee, oil, fat, head-oil, or ointment, honey, wound-ointment, molasses, or house-incense [is for such purposes].
It does not become subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

If one wishes to pour oil that has already been determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) into a vessel for oil that has not yet been determined, and if there is a fine hole in the vessel such that each drop of oil entering is submerged by the old oil, it must be determined again. But if the opening is large, and much oil enters all at once and submerges the old oil—
It completely covers [the oil], and there is no further need for an act of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); for it remains simply as that which has been determined.
By this same method, one should understand the case of pouring undetermined oil into a vessel of determined oil.
However, if, after seven days have passed, one gives [the oil] to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) after relinquishing it, then it becomes once again his own property.
It is permissible to consume what has been given after it has been prepared.
For if he, having either prepared it or not prepared it, should give it to that bhikkhu for the purpose of nasal medication, it may be taken and used as nasal medication.
If he is ignorant and does not know how to give it, another bhikkhu should ask him: "Novice, do you have oil?"
“Yes, venerable sir, there is. [The other says: “Bring it; we will prepare medicine for the elder. This is also permissible.
If what belongs to two people has been accepted by one and not yet divided, there is no offense for either of them after the seven-day period has elapsed;
however, it is not permissible to consume it. If the one who accepted it says to the other: “Friend, …”
"This oil may be used for only seven days," yet he does not use it;
who incurs an offense? No one. Why? Because it was relinquished by the one who received it, and it was not received by the other. 100.

Among these four types of "time-bound" (kālika) substances, only this pair—namely, that which is for as long as life lasts (yāvakālika) and that which is for the duration of a watch (yāmakālika)—is both "within the day" (antovutthaka) and...

It is permissible to store both that which is produced by hoarding (*sannidhikāraka*) and that which is for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) as well as that which is for life (*yāvajīvika*) in an improper storeroom (*akappiyakuṭi*), and it does not generate the offense of hoarding.

However, that which is for the time of the day (*yāvakālika*), when its flavor is mixed with those three types—namely, that which is for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) and so forth—brings them back to its own nature.
That which is for the watch of the night brings even the two types—namely, that which is for seven days and so forth—to its own [nature].
It brings [the other] into its own nature; even a seven-day medicine that has been mixed with something that lasts for life brings that which lasts for life into its own nature.

Therefore, the remaining three types of medicine—when mixed and blended in flavor with what is "for as long as life lasts" (yāvajīvika) that was received on that very day—are permissible only before the meal on that same day.
However, the other two [types of medicine], when mixed with what is "for a watch of the night" (yāmakālika), [are permissible only within that watch].

That which was received on that same day is permitted until sunrise. However, when what was received on that same day is mixed with what was received seven days ago, then what was received on that same day—whether it was received on that same day or previously received, or even lifelong medicine—is permissible for seven days.
When mixed with what was received two days ago, it is permissible for six days; with what was received three days ago, for five days... [and so on] ...with what was received seven days ago.

It should be understood that on that very day it is permissible. Furthermore, regarding the transgressions of exceeding the proper time, the watch of the night, or the seven-day limit, they are to be understood by way of the training rules concerning eating at improper times, storing food, and medicine.
However, if even those four types of food accepted together do not have mixed flavors, for him—
It is permissible to consume them according to the specific time [of their preparation].

For if a drink such as mango juice has been received together with an entire coconut fruit, and the husk has not even been removed, then after removing the coconut, that [juice] is allowable even at an improper time.
If they give cold milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top, that which is not mixed with the milk-rice [is allowable].
Having removed the ghee, it is permissible to consume it for seven days. The same principle applies to solid honey, molasses, and so forth.
If they give almsfood adorned with cardamom, nutmeg, and the like, these should be removed and washed;
they may then be consumed for as long as one lives. This also applies to ginger and other such items given by adding them to rice gruel, or those added to oils and the like.

The same principle applies to *dinnalaṭṭhi*, *madhuka*, and so forth. Thus, whatever is of unmixed flavor, even if received together, it is permissible to consume according to its respective time after washing or cutting it so that it becomes pure.
If it is of mixed flavor or combined with other substances, it is not permissible.
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of what is timely (*kālika-vinicchaya-kathā*) in the Compendium of Determinations of the Vinaya Excluding the Pāḷi Text. 19.
Discourse on the Determination of the Proper Ground (*kappiya-bhūmi-vinicchaya-kathā*).
101. Regarding the phrase "the four kinds of allowable sites" (*kappiyā-caturbhūmiyo*): here, based on the statement, "Monks, I allow four kinds of allowable sites:

one established by proclamation (*ussāvanantika*), one shaped like a cow's footprint (*gonisādika*), one belonging to a householder (*gahapati*), and one by formal authorization (*sammuti*)," these four allowable sites are to be understood as: the site established by proclamation, the site shaped like a cow's footprint, the site belonging to a householder, and the site by formal authorization.
Among these, first, the site established by proclamation is to be made in this way: whoever...
A monastery (vihāra) is constructed by either driving pillars into the ground or fixing them into the base of a wall;
the stones used as supports for those pillars beneath it remain fixed in the earth.

However, when many people are setting up the first pillar or the first base of a wall, they must surround it on all sides and utter the words: "We are making a kitchen (kappiyakuṭi), we are making a kitchen!"
When people are lifting [the object] up and setting it down, one should have it set down by touching it, or by lifting it oneself, upon a pillar or the base of a wall.
However, in the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Having said, 'This is a kitchen for allowable things (kappiyakuṭi), this is a kitchen for allowable things,' it should be set down.
In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "I resolve [this] as the Saṅgha’s kitchen for allowable things"; however, that...
Even if one does not enter [the hut], there is no fault in what has been stated according to the method explained in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, the common characteristic here is that "the fixing of the pillar and the conclusion of the speech must occur simultaneously.
For if the pillar is fixed while the speech is not yet finished, or if the speech is finished while it is not yet fixed, the *kappiya-kuṭi* (permissible hut) is not properly made.
For this very reason it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "It should be spoken of as being surrounded by many;
for here, the completion of the speech of even one person and the fixing of the pillar must necessarily coincide.

However, in the case of huts made of bricks, stone, clay, or wattle-and-daub, they may build them either with or without a foundation (cayam) below, starting from the point where the wall [is raised].

Those who wish to build it up should first take a brick, a stone, or a lump of clay and construct the *kappiyakuṭi* (the fire-preparation hut) according to the method already described. Bricks and the like are not permitted below the first bricks and so forth on the wall;
however, pillars that project upwards are permitted, as stated in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*.
It is stated: “When pillars are being erected, four pillars should be determined at the four corners;

on the brick-paved floor, two or three bricks should be determined at the four corners. However, there is no fault even if it is not done so, for the authority is precisely what is stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
There are two kinds of cow-pen boundaries: the cow-pen boundary of a monastery (*ārāma*) and the cow-pen boundary of a dwelling (*vihāra*).
Among these, where there is neither a monastery nor are the lodgings enclosed, this is called the cow-pen boundary of a monastery.
Where all or some of the lodgings are enclosed, but the monastery itself is unenclosed, this is called the cow-pen boundary of a dwelling. Thus...
In both cases, the fact that the monastery (*ārāma*) is unenclosed is the sole criterion.
However, it is stated in the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī* commentaries: "But a monastery, even if half-enclosed or mostly enclosed, is indeed called 'enclosed'";
in such a case, it is permissible to obtain a kitchen (*kappiyakuṭi*).
"A householder" (*gahapati*) refers to those people who, having built a dwelling, say, "We give this as a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a storehouse for allowable goods); please use it.
This is what is called a "householder. It is also permissible when they say, "We give this to build a *kappiya-kuṭi*.
However, in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that [it is not permissible] from the hands of anyone other than a monk—namely, all fellow practitioners of the Dhamma and all gods and humans.
It has been stated: "Receiving, storing, and what was kept overnight—these are permissible for a monk only if they belong to those [laypeople];
therefore, their houses or a suitable hut given by them are called 'the householder's'. Furthermore, it has been stated:
"Excluding a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha of monks, [it refers to] a nunnery, or a dwelling for monastery attendants, or that of other sectarians, or of deities, or of nāgas..."
"Or even a Brahmā’s celestial mansion becomes a *kappiya*-hut"—this has been well said.
For indeed, a house belonging to the Saṅgha or belonging to individual monks does not constitute a *gahapatikuṭikā*.

"Formal authorization" (*sammuti*) means that which is authorized after having announced it through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*). And thus, monks, it should be authorized: a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: [text of the formal act follows].
“Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, the Sangha should authorize such-and-such a monastery as a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area where allowable goods may be kept).
This is the motion (*ñatti*). “Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. The Sangha authorizes such-and-such a monastery as a *kappiya-bhūmi*.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the authorization of such-and-such a monastery as a *kappiya-bhūmi*, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
"Whoever does not approve should speak.
This dwelling named so-and-so, designated by the Saṅgha as a *kappiyabhūmi* (an area where what is allowable may be stored), is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, we hold this to be so.
Even if the formal act (*kammavācā*) is not recited, but it is announced by means of a motion (*apalokanakamma*), it is indeed validly authorized.
102. Whatever food is prepared within these four types of *kappiya-bhūmi* (permissible grounds) does not count as being "cooked inside" (*antovuttha*).
Indeed, *kappiya-kuṭīs* (permissible huts) were authorized for the purpose of releasing the offense of "cooking inside" for both monks and nuns.

However, whatever is prepared on an impermissible ground (*akappiya-bhūmi*) in a house large enough for two people to lie down together—whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual—[is subject to the rules regarding food cooked inside].
If anything belonging to a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī has been kept for even a single night, it is called "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*);

if cooked there, it is called "cooked overnight" (*antopakka*), and this is not permitted. However, things that may be used for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) or for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*) are allowable.
Regarding this, the following is the detailed analysis: Suppose a novice brings food such as rice and so forth to a bhikkhu at the *kappiya-kuṭī* (the kitchen).
If one sets it aside and then cooks and gives it on the following day, it is not considered "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*).
In that regard, if one puts something into ghee or other substances already placed in an improper storeroom (*akappiyakuṭi*) and gives it, it is called "mouth-stored" (*mukhasannidhi*).
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* it is stated: "It is stored overnight. In this case, the only difference is merely in name; for the monk [is acting] in an improper storeroom.

If one cooks clarified butter that has been set aside and leaf-vegetables intended for life-long use together in one pot and consumes them, it is permissible for seven days as long as it is unmixed with non-medicinal food (*nirāmisa*).
If, however, one consumes it after mixing it with non-medicinal food, it becomes both "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*) and "cooked by oneself" (*sāmaṃpakka*).
By this same principle, all types of admixture (*saṃsagga*) are to be understood. Whatever non-medicinal food it may be, it is not permitted for a monk to cook it himself.
If they add *sulasi* leaves, ginger, or salt to his hot rice gruel, it is not permitted to stir it even for that purpose;
however, it is permitted to stir it thinking, "I shall cool the gruel. Having received rice with the grains still distinct, it is not permitted to cover it.
But if people give it after having covered it, it is permitted. [One may think], "Let the rice not go cold."
It is permissible to cover [the fire], but it is also permissible to apply fire to milk, buttermilk, and so forth, once they have been boiled, because re-cooking is permitted.
When, however, do these "permissible huts" (kappiyakuṭi) lose their legal status? First, regarding those established by formal proclamation (ussāvanantikā):
if one was constructed by burying the base of the walls upon the pillars, it loses its status when all the pillars and the bases of the walls are removed.
It has abandoned its foundation. However, if they turn a pillar or a wall-foot, it settles wherever each one stands;
even when all have been turned, it has not abandoned its foundation.
A heap made of bricks and so forth is the beginning of a brick, stone, or lump of clay placed upon it for the purpose of a wall.

Once it has been dismantled and destroyed, it becomes one whose physical basis has been abandoned (*jahitavatthukā*). However, if it was established with bricks or other materials, even when those are removed, it remains established upon others;

thus, it becomes one whose physical basis has not been abandoned (*ajahitavatthukā*). When a *gonisādikā* (a place for cattle) is enclosed by walls and such, it becomes one whose physical basis has been abandoned.
It is then permissible to establish a *kappiyakuṭi* (an allowable storehouse) again in that same monastery.
If, however, the walls and other structures there are broken in various places so that cattle enter from here and there, it becomes a *kappiyakuṭi* (a building for lawful food) once again.
But as for the other two types [of sheds], if everything except the rafters has perished in the roof-covering, they have indeed lost their status as a dwelling.
If there is even a single *pakkhapāsaka* (gable-end support) or *maṇḍala* (circular ridge-piece) above the rafters, it remains protected [as a valid structure].
103. Where these four types of allowable grounds (*kappiyabhūmi*) do not exist, what should be done there?
Having given [the food] to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) and having made it his property, it may be consumed. Here is the story regarding this:
It is said that the Elder Karavikatissa, a preeminent master of the Vinaya, went into the presence of the Elder Mahāsīva. By the light of a lamp, he [saw] a jar of ghee...
Having seen it, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is this? The elder replied, "Friend, a jar of ghee has been brought from the village for the purpose of eating with ghee on the day of coarse food.
Then the Elder Tissa said to him, "It is not permissible, venerable sir.
On the following day, the elder had it placed at the entrance. When the Elder Tissa returned one day and saw it, he did exactly as before.
Having asked him, he said, "Venerable sir, it is not permissible to place [the jar] in a space sufficient for two people to lie down.

On the following day, the Elder had it taken outside and set down; thieves stole it. One day later, when the Elder Tissa arrived, he said to him, "Friend, although you said 'it is not permissible,' that jar was placed outside and carried off by thieves. Then he [said to him]:
The Elder Tissa said: "Venerable sir, should it not be given to one who is not fully ordained?
For having given it to one who is not fully ordained and made it his property, it is permissible to use it.
Thus ends the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
The Discussion on the Determination of the Proper Ground is finished. 20. The Discussion on the Determination of Acceptance. 104.
“Acceptance of fresh food, etc. refers to any kind of fresh food or soft food that is to be swallowed.
...or the acceptance. Herein, this is the analysis: Acceptance is valid when five factors are present:
it is the mere utterance of a man of medium strength; the reach of the hand is discernible; the offering is discernible;
and a deva, a human, or an animal gives it either with the body, with what is connected to the body, or with what is relinquishable. If that...
The monk receives it either with his own body or with something connected to his body. In this way, the receiving is valid through five factors.
Therein, the range of the hand should be understood as follows, according to whether [the person] is standing, sitting, or lying down: if the monk is sitting, it is from the rear edge of the seat;
if he is standing, it is from the tip of the heels; if he is lying down, [it is from the edge of the bed].
Starting from the far end of whichever side one is lying on, the "hand-reach" (*hatthapāsa*) is defined as two and a half cubits,
measured from the near end of that limb which is closer to the donor— whether the donor is sitting, standing, or lying down— excluding the outstretched hand itself.
If, however, among the donor and the recipient, one is in the air and the other on the ground, then for the one standing on the ground, the space within the reach of the hand—
measured by the distance from the edge of the hand— to that nearest limb of the one standing in the air (excluding the hand actually extended for giving or receiving) must be demarcated as the limit.
Even if one is in a well and the other is on the rim of the well, [the same rule applies].
Or else, one may stand alone by a tree or alone on the ground; in either case, the space of a hand’s reach must be demarcated according to the method already described.
Standing within such a hand’s reach, even if a bird picks up a flower or fruit with its beak, or an elephant takes it with its trunk and gives it, the acceptance is valid.
However, if [the donor is] even half-a-cubit less than eight *ratana*...
If one sitting on the back of an elephant takes what is being given by its trunk, it is indeed permissible.
In the case of elephants and other animals, whatever part of the body—even down to a toe—is used to give constitutes what is called "given by the body.
The same principle applies to receiving as well; for whatever is taken by any part of the body is indeed considered "taken by the body."
It is so. Even if, when nasal medicine is being given, one who is unwell receives it through the nostrils or with the mouth, the intentional intent (*ābhoga*) alone is the criterion here.
However, in the case of spoons and other such utensils, whatever is given by means of any implement is said to be "given by what is attached to the body."

It is so. The same principle applies to receiving [the gift]. For whatever is taken by means of anything connected to the body—such as a bowl, a water-pot, or the like—it is considered as if it were taken by what is directly attached to the body.

However, having released it from the body or from what is attached to the body, even if it is dropped onto the body or onto something attached to the body of one standing within arm's reach, it constitutes an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) through that act.
It is called "given. Suppose one person places many food bowls and condiment containers upon their head, approaches a bhikkhu, and stands there saying, "Take them";
as long as they remain standing, it does not yet constitute an "offering," and therefore it should not be accepted.
However, if they lean down even slightly, the bhikkhu may extend his hand and take even a portion from the lowermost container.
It should be accepted. Up to this point, all the vessels have been formally received.

From that point on, it is permissible to take whatever one wishes after having set them down or uncovered them. However, regarding a single vessel such as a rice-tray, there is no need for such a formal declaration.
Even when carrying food with a carrying-pole, it is permissible if he gives it by bending down the pole.
If there is a thirty-cubit bamboo pole with a jar of molasses tied to one end and a jar of ghee to the other, and he accepts it, then everything has been accepted.
If he says, "Take the juice," while it is still dripping from a sugar-mill vat, no formal act of offering (*abhihāra*) is discerned.
It must not be accepted. However, if one discards the dregs, pours out [the liquid] with the hand, and gives it, it is permissible.
If many bowls have been placed on a bed, a chair, a straw mat, a trough, or a plank, one should stand where the giver is within arm’s reach;
standing there, with the perception of receiving, one may even touch the bed or other objects with a finger.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever is given into those bowls is all considered accepted.
Even if one climbs onto a bed or similar furniture and sits there thinking, "I shall accept it," it is still permissible.
However, on the ground, even if they are standing with their bellies touching belly, whatever [is given] by means of a finger or a needle—
Or, having touched it, he sits down; in each such case, what is being given is indeed accepted.

As for the statement that acceptance is not valid when the bowl is placed on a large mat, a woolen rug, a felt rug, or similar items, it should be understood that this was said with reference to the bowl exceeding the reach of the hand;
however, as long as it is within the reach of the hand, it is acceptable on any such surface.

It is permissible [to use] anything other than that which grows there. However, it is not permissible to use lotus leaves or *kiṃsuka* leaves and the like that grow there; for such things do not count as being "connected to the body.
And just as with what grows there, it is likewise not permissible to use a bedstead or similar item fastened to a stump, nor on a non-portable wooden plank or a stone.

For those growing there are considered to be "born on that spot. Receiving [alms] in very fine leaves such as *tintiṇika* spread upon the ground is not permissible, for they are not capable of supporting it.
However, it is permissible in large leaves such as lotus leaves.
If [the donor] stands beyond arm's reach and gives with a ladle using a long handle, [the recipient should say]: "Come and give!"
He should be told [not to do so]. If, having not heard or not heeded the instruction, he simply pours it into the bowl, it must be received again.
The same rule applies even if someone standing at a distance throws a morsel of food [into the bowl].
106. If there is dye-powder in the bowl while it is being taken out from its bag, it should be washed if water is available.
If there is no dust, one may go for alms after wiping it away or receiving it [in a bowl].

If dust falls into the bowl while one is walking for alms, the alms-food must be received [into the bowl] before being taken; for one who takes it without having received it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*vinayadukkaṭa*).
However, there is no offense for one who receives that [dust] again before eating. But if [the donor] says, "Give it after having received it," [one may do so].

If they continue to give alms even after one has not heard or accepted the instruction, there is no offense of wrong conduct (*vinayadukkaṭa*); however, having received [the first] alms, another alms-offering must be accepted.

If a great wind blows dust from all directions such that it is impossible to receive alms, it is permissible to accept them after forming the mental resolve with a pure mind: "I shall give this to one who is not fully ordained."
Having thus wandered for alms and gone to a monastery or a rest-house, it is permissible to give that [alms-food] to one who is not fully ordained;
then, having received what was given back by him or received through his trust, it is allowable to eat it.
If, while on the alms-round, he gives a dusty bowl to a bhikkhu, the latter should be told: "Having accepted this, you may take alms."
"or should you consume it?"—he should act accordingly. If dust floats on top, he should pour off the sour gruel and eat the remainder.

If it has entered inside [the bowl], it should be accepted. If there is no one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) present, he should, without letting go of the hand, lead it to where an anupasampanna is and have it accepted there.
It is permissible to eat dry rice after removing any dust that has fallen upon it.
If the dust is extremely fine, it should be removed along with the rice above it, or the food should be eaten after receiving it [into the bowl].
When those who have placed their rice gruel or soup in front of them stir it, droplets rising from the vessel fall into the bowl; in such a case, the bowl may be accepted.
107. When giving after having brought [food] in a ladle, if some drops fall from the ladle into the bowl before [the food is fully served], they have fallen well;

because they were brought [as part of the offering], there is no fault. Even if, while rice-porridge is being poured from a cooking pot, ashes or soot fall from the pot, because they were brought [along with it], there is no fault at all.
[Likewise, regarding food] that has leaped out from the bowl of the preceding monk as it is being given to the next monk...
If it falls into another's bowl, it is "well-fallen" (*supatita*); for that [food] is indeed already accepted.
If, while people are splitting branches of a *jajjhari* tree or the like and giving them to one monk, drops fall from the branch into the bowl of another, that bowl must be accepted;
for when they are splitting over one bowl, there is the intention to give to whichever bowl the drops have fallen.
There is no fault in [the food] being brought over. When they give a bowl filled with milk-rice (*pāyāsa*), because it is hot, one cannot hold it from below;
however, it is permissible to hold it by the rim. If one still cannot hold it even in that way, it should be held with a support.
If a monk, having taken his bowl in the dining hall, has fallen asleep while sitting, [he should not eat] what is being brought to him.
If he does not perceive that it is being given, it is not accepted. However, if he is sitting with his attention directed toward it, it is permissible.
Even if he falls asleep after letting go of the stand with his hand and nudging it with his foot, it is still permissible.
But for one who accepts while pressing down on the stand with his foot—even if he is awake—it constitutes an acceptance done without respect.

Therefore, it should not be done. Some say, "In this way, receiving [food] by means of a stand constitutes receiving by means of what is connected to the body; therefore, it is not permitted. That is merely a matter of words;
for in substance, all of this is indeed connected to the body. This same principle is also shown regarding physical contact. As for that which...
If something being given to a bhikkhu falls [to the ground], it is permissible for him to pick it up himself and consume it.
Regarding this, there is this Sutta:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to pick up yourself that which falls while being given and consume it; for that, bhikkhus, has been relinquished by the donors.”
Furthermore, this sutta is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*); therefore, its intended sense (*adhippāya*) should be understood as follows:

it is permissible to take and consume that which, when being given, slips from the donor’s hand and falls upon clean ground, or upon a lotus leaf, or upon cloth, a mat, a rug, or similar items. However, that which falls upon dusty ground—
Having wiped, washed, or received that dust, it may be consumed.
If it rolls away and goes into the presence of another monk, it is permissible for him to have it brought back.
If he says to that monk, "You eat it yourself," it is also permissible for him to eat it; however, he must not take it without being so instructed.
“It is permissible to take [the robe] with the thought, ‘I will give it to the other one,’ even though there is no formal act of giving,” so it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
But why is it not permissible to take it for the other monk? Because it was not authorized by the Blessed One.
For when the Blessed One said, “having taken it oneself, one may use it,” he meant that it belongs to whichever person it falls upon when being given, even if it has not been formally accepted.
Having taken it, its use is permitted. However, by the statement, "That has been relinquished, monks, by the donors," the fact that it belongs to another is indicated here;
therefore, it is not permissible to take it oneself and use it, but it is permissible with his authorization—this, it seems, is the intended meaning here.
And because this [medicine] is not received through formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*),...
It has been permitted; therefore, it is allowable to consume on the second day that which was placed down by someone else without touching it while it remained exactly as it was.
There is no offense regarding the condition of storage (*sannidhi*), yet it must be consumed after being formally received (*paṭiggahetvā*).
For indeed, its consumption is permitted only when one has personally taken it up on that very same day, and not beyond that—this, it is said, is the intended meaning here.
108. Now the method concerning what is not an offense (*abbōhārikanaya*) is stated.
For when those eating [food], their teeth wear away, their fingernails wear away, or the color of the bowl wears away—all this is not an offense.
When sugarcane and so forth are split with a knife and the core is revealed, this is called "arisen anew" (*navasamutthita*); having received it, it may be consumed. Having washed the knife...
When [the soil] has been ploughed, no impurity is seen; there is merely the smell of iron, and that is not subject to the formal rule (abbohārika).
The same principle applies even when it has been ploughed by means of a sickle that they carry about. For they do not carry it for the purpose of consumption.
This also applies to the sitting mats, small stools, mortars, pestles, and so forth, belonging to those who are grinding or pounding root medicines and the like.
They spoil; having heated the vessel for keeping [the food], they add it to buttermilk or milk for medicinal purposes, and a bluish tint appears there.
The legal determination is exactly as stated regarding the knife. However, one must not put it in raw buttermilk and the like oneself;
if one does so, one is not exempt from the offense of cooking for oneself (*sāmaṃpāka*). When it is raining while one is walking for alms...
If water soiled from the body or from the robe falls into the bowl, it may be accepted.

The same rule applies even if it falls while one is eating at the foot of a tree or in similar locations. However, if it rains for seven days and the water becomes pure, or if it falls from an open space, it is permissible.
109. When giving rice to a novice, it should be given without touching what is already in his bowl, or else his bowl should be received.
If one touches the rice and then takes rice for oneself from one's own bowl while the other’s bowl has not been received, it constitutes an offense of taking what is not given (*uggahitaka*).
However, if one wishes to give and says, "Bring your bowl, novice; take the rice," [there is no offense].

One says, "I give this to you," and the other refuses, saying, "Enough for me. When he says again, "This has been relinquished by me to you," and the other replies, "I have no need for this," even if he should relinquish it a hundred times, as long as it remains in his own hand, it is still considered accepted [by him].
However, if he says, "Take it," while it is resting on a stand and he is indifferent to it, [then it is indeed accepted].
It must be received again. If, while looking on, he places the bowl on its stand and says to the novice,
"Take some cake or rice from here," and the novice, having washed his hands,
takes it even a hundred times and puts it into his own bowl without touching what is already in his own bowl, there is no further need for formal receiving.
If, however, he touches what is already in his own bowl and then takes from it, it becomes mixed with what belongs to the novice;
it must be received again. Some, however, say: "Even if, while being taken, it breaks off and falls back into that [bowl], it must be received again.
Regarding this, [the instruction is]: "Take one morsel of food; take one cake..."
It should be understood that this applies when it is said, "Take this much portion of the lump of sugar," after which a specific limit has been set;
however, in this case, there is no such limit. Therefore, whatever falls into the novice's bowl constitutes the relinquishment of the formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).
But as for what remains in his hand, it is relinquished only so long as the novice does not stop with the words "Enough," or the monk does not prevent him.
It belongs to the bhikkhus themselves; therefore, the act of receiving does not cease.

If one places food into a vessel for boiling rice-gruel for oneself or for the bhikkhus for the sake of anyone, one should say, "Novice, place your hand over the vessel," and then place it into his hand. From his hand, [it is placed] into the vessel.
For once it has been dropped, on the following day it does not constitute an improper vessel because it has been relinquished.
If one does not do so and places food in it, the vessel should be used after making it free from meat, just like a bowl.
110. The donors left after setting aside the rice-porridge; the young novice was unable to have it received.
If a monk holds out his bowl, and a novice places the neck of the pot onto the rim of the bowl and pours it, the rice gruel contained in the bowl is considered accepted.
Alternatively, if the monk places his hand on the ground and the novice rolls [the vessel] forward and lifts the hand [to receive it], it is permissible.
This also applies to cases such as a basket of cakes, a basket of cooked rice, or a load of firewood.
The same principle applies here. If two or three novices carry a load that is suitable for receiving, or if one strong person lifts it and two or three monks take it up, it is permissible.
Or, if they attach an oil jar or a jar of molasses to the leg of a bed or a chair, it is permissible for a monk to sit on that bed or chair; it does not constitute "taking possession" (uggahitaka).
On a peg or a hook, two oil jars are suspended: one above is received [as a gift], while the one below is not yet received.

It is permissible to take the upper one. If the lower one is the one received and the upper one is not yet received, then by taking the upper one first and subsequently taking the other, the upper one becomes "received. Regarding the lower bed: that which is not yet received...
It has three tiers. If, while sweeping it, one strikes it with the broom, it does not constitute "taken up" (uggahitaka).
If, thinking, "I will take what has been received," one takes what has not been received and then, having realized this, puts it back down, it does not constitute "taken up.
If one perceives it after having carried it outside, it must be placed back in that very spot without having been set down outside.
There is no fault. However, if it was previously left open, it should not be closed; it should be left exactly as it was before.
If one places it outside, it should not be touched again.
111. If a film forms on the oil or other substances received, or a thick powder forms on the ginger and so forth, that arises from those very [substances].

That is its name; furthermore, there is no requirement for receiving it. If one has climbed a palm tree or a coconut tree and, having lowered a cluster of fruit by means of a rope, stands above and says, "Take [it]," it must not be accepted.
If another person standing on the ground takes hold of the rope-loop, hoists it up, and gives it, it is permissible. Having had a large branch with fruit made *kappiya* (rendered allowable),...
If he receives them, the fruits are considered already accepted; it is permissible for him to consume them as he pleases.
If they stand outside the enclosure and, having cut through the fence, give sugarcane or *timbarūsaka* fruit, it is permissible provided they remain within arm’s reach.
For one who takes what has emerged after being struck with sticks, it is permissible; however, regarding what has emerged after being struck, in the commentaries...
The fault has not been shown. However, we reason that it is as if [the goods] have fallen of their own accord from the very spot where they were struck;
this also applies when one goes standing there, like goods that have rolled out after being pushed from a customs station.
Or, they give them after making them leap over a fence or a wall; but if the wall is not thick, whether inside the wall or outside the wall—
And it is permissible for one who is standing within arm’s reach to take hold of something that has come from a distance of even a hundred cubits upward.

A monk carries a sick novice on his shoulder; seeing various fruits, the novice takes them and gives them while still seated on the shoulder—this is permissible. Another person, carrying a monk, gives [something] to the monk seated on his shoulder.

It is indeed permissible. If a bhikkhu takes a fruit-bearing branch for the sake of shade and goes along, when the thought arises to eat the fruits, it is permissible to eat them after having them formally accepted.

If he accepts them after having them made allowable (kappiya) for the purpose of warding off flies, and if he wishes to eat them, only the original acceptance is required; for one who eats them, there is no offense.

An offense. If a bhikkhu places goods suitable for acceptance on people’s vehicles and proceeds along the road, and the vehicle gets stuck in mud, it is permissible for a junior monk to take hold of the wheel and lift it; this does not constitute "taking what has been entrusted.
If he places goods on a boat and propels the boat with a rudder or pulls it by hand, it is permissible.

The same method applies even when there is a raft (*uḷumpa*). Even if one has placed [the robe] on a boat (*cāṭi*) or a basket (*kuṇḍaka*), it is permissible to cross by having a non-ordained person take hold of it and then grasping that non-ordained person by the arm.
If even that is unavailable, it is permissible to cross by having a non-ordained person take hold of [the robe] and then grasping that person by the arm.
The lay followers gave provisions of rice for the traveling monks;
the novices, having taken rice from the monks, were unable to take any rice for themselves.
The monks took their rice, and when the novices' own allotted rice was exhausted, they cooked a gruel with the remaining rice and served the bowls of everyone in succession.
When they pour out the rice-gruel, excluding the one already set aside, the wise novice monk takes his own bowl and gives it to the elder;
the elder gives his bowl to the second elder, and so on, rotating them all until everyone has eaten from the novice’s portion—this is permissible.
Even if the novice is not wise, he may himself [take the gruel] into his own bowl.
If he begins to drink, even if he has requested it from the elders in turn, saying, "Friend, give me your rice-gruel," it is permissible for him to drink;
everything has been consumed by the novice himself, and thus they do not incur an offense on account of storing or on account of hoarding.
However, in this regard, [there is no fault] regarding oil and such things belonging to one's mother and father, or those intended for shade and so forth.
Furthermore, no distinction is seen between those who carry away branches and leaves and these [other monks]; therefore, the underlying reason must be investigated.
112. A novice (sāmaṇera), wishing to cook a meal, washes the rice but is unable to rinse it thoroughly.
The monk, having received both the rice and the vessel, washes the rice, rinses it thoroughly, and places the vessel on the stove.
It should be placed [on the fire], but no flame should be made; when it is cooked, the state of being cooked must be ascertained by opening [the lid].
If it is undercooked, it is not permitted to close [the lid] for the sake of cooking it further, though it is permitted to do so to prevent dust or ashes from falling in.
When it is cooked, it is permitted to remove it and eat it; there is no further need for the act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*). A novice (*sāmaṇera*) who is capable...

If he wishes to go elsewhere and has no time to cook, the monk should receive a vessel of rice-water, place it on the stove, and say, "Light the fire and go. Thereafter, it is permissible for him to do everything according to the previous method.
If the monk places a clean vessel on the stove to heat water for the sake of rice-gruel, [he may depart].
It is permissible. When the water is heated, the novice places the rice grains [into the pot]; from that point on, the monk must not apply fire himself.
Once he has received the cooked gruel, it is permissible for him to drink it.
While the novice is cooking the gruel, a monk who is anxious about touching things with his hands may playfully touch the vessel, touch the lid, or strike away the rising froth.
It is not permitted for him alone to drink it; this is called "badly prepared" (*durupaciṇṇa*).
However, if he stirs it by taking a ladle or a spoon and stirring without tossing it up, it is not permitted for anyone; it is both "self-cooked" (*sāmaṃpāka*) and "badly prepared.
If he tosses it up, it becomes "taken up" (*uggahitaka*) as well.

113. When a bhikkhu, having wandered for alms, has placed his bowl on a stand, if another greedy bhikkhu, playing about, touches the bowl or touches the lid of the bowl, the food obtained from that [act] is not allowable for him alone.
If he does not lift up the bowl and set it aside, it is not allowable for anyone. This applies even to a branch bearing fruit grown there.
If one takes hold of it by means of a branch or a creeper and shakes it, it is not permissible for him to take the fruit obtained from that;

he incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* due to improper conduct (*durupaciṇṇa*). However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: “It is permissible to lean against a fruit tree or to tie a thorn there [to shake it];
this does not constitute improper conduct. But having seen mangoes or other fruits fallen in the forest, [one may take them].
It is permissible to bring back and give [food] after having thought, "I will give this to the novice.
Even upon seeing the remains of a lion's meal or similar food, it is permissible to bring it back and give it to the novice, whether one has formally accepted it or not.
However, if one is able to purify one's thoughts, then it is also permissible to eat what was obtained from there; it is not, however, on account of accepting raw meat that [the offense occurs].
One does not incur an offense on account of what has been formally accepted (*uggahitaka*).

If, while one is traveling after having taken oil or other requisites for the sake of one’s mother or father, an illness arises along the way, it is permissible to accept whatever one desires and consume it.
However, if it has already been accepted even at the source, there is no further need for formal acceptance. [The same applies to] rice for one’s mother or father.
If one brings it and gives it, and they prepare the rice-gruel and other items right there and give them to him, it is permissible;
there is no fault on account of storage (*sannidhi*) or on account of taking what has been stored (*uggahita*). 114.
A bhikkhu heats water by covering it; it is permissible to use it until it is completely exhausted. If...

If ashes fall here [into the oil], it may be accepted. When one is frying oil while holding a pan with long tongs, if ashes fall, it may be accepted after having finished frying and removed from the heat, provided one has not let go of the handle with the hand.
If both the embers and the wood have been accepted and set aside, only the original acceptance is valid. A bhikkhu eats sugarcane.
The novice says, "Give some to me too," and when told, "Take it by cutting from this [pile]," he takes it;
there is no further need for an act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) regarding what remains. The same rule applies even when eating a lump of sugar.

For that which is taken after being cut from the specified portion remains as something whose formal acceptance has not been relinquished. When a monk distributes sugar, having formally accepted it...
He divides it into portions; monks and novices come and each take one portion at a single taking, and what remains after being taken is indeed considered accepted.
If a greedy novice, having taken [a portion] again and again, puts it back down, the remainder of what he took is not accepted.
When a bhikkhu receives the smoke-wick and inhales the smoke, his mouth and throat become as if smeared with realgar (manosilā).

It is permissible to consume [food] that is to be used within the proper time (yāvakālika); there is no fault in mixing what is to be used within the proper time with what is to be used for life (yāvajīvika).
When one is cooking a bowl or dye, smoke enters through the openings of the ears and nose; this is due to the condition of illness.
If one smells a flower or fruit, it is permissible because it does not constitute an offense.

If a morsel of food strikes the palate and enters only inside [the mouth], it is permissible because it is not within the scope of the rule; however, once it has entered the mouth, there is an offense for swallowing it at an improper time.
If the taste of food clinging between the teeth enters [the mouth], there is indeed an offense. If the food is very fine, [it is permissible].
The taste is no longer discernible; it belongs to the category of what is beyond conventional description (*abbohārika*).

When the time has nearly come, having eaten the meal in a place devoid of water and having rinsed the mouth, one should drop two or three lumps of saliva and then go to a place with water to rinse the mouth.
If sprouts emerge from ginger and other such items that were accepted and set aside, there is no further need for the act of formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*).
If salt is not available, it is permissible to use seawater for the purpose of salting.
Salt that has been accepted and set aside becomes salt; or salt becomes water; or the juice becomes molasses; or molasses becomes juice. Only the initial acceptance is permissible.
Ice crystals belong to the category of water. When they clarify water using a cleaning nut (*kataka-kaṭṭha*) carried for that purpose, that is not considered a formal act.
It is permissible together with food. That which is offered by those seeking material gain, such as wood-apple fruits and the like, is permissible only before the meal.
Water from lotus ponds and similar sources is thick; it is permissible. However, if it clings to the mouth or the hands, it is not permissible;
having received it [in a vessel], it should be consumed. In fields, where the soil is tilled, it is thick...
If there is water, it should be accepted. If, after raining, it enters gullies and such places and fills a river, that is permissible.
There are natural pools like the Kakudha spring where the water is covered with flowers fallen from trees; if the scent of the flower-juice is not perceptible, there is no need for formal acceptance.
If the water is scanty but the scent of the juice is perceptible, it should be formally accepted.
The same principle applies even to water in mountain clefts and similar places that is covered by black-colored leaves.
If *saṇṭhuka* flowers or *vaṇṭakhīra* flowers have been placed in a water jar, they may be accepted;
or, having accepted the flowers, they should be thrown away. If *pāṭali* or *mallikā* flowers have been placed [in it], a mere scent...
If it remains [in that state], it is not subject to formal designation (*abbhohārika*). On the following day as well, it is permissible [to drink] together with solid food.
If a novice takes water from a vessel scented with flowers set out by a monk and pours back into that same place the remainder of what he has drunk, it should be accepted.
It is permissible to take water from lotus ponds and the like after removing the pollen of flowers settled therein by suppressing it with a jar.
If it is a tooth-stick that has been made allowable (*kappiya*), accepted, and set aside, and one wishes to drink its juice, only the original act of acceptance (*mūla-paṭiggahaṇa*) is permissible;
however, if it was set aside without being accepted, it must be accepted [at that time]. Even if the juice enters the mouth without one's knowledge, there is still an offense.
For this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is one where no mental state (*acittaka*) is required for the offense to be established.
115. Among the great elements (mahābhūta), what is permissible and what is not permissible? First, milk is permissible;
whether it be the milk of allowable meat or the milk of unallowable meat, there is no offense for one who drinks it.
Tears, saliva, snot, urine, feces, phlegm, tooth-tartar, eye-secretion, ear-wax, and the salt produced within the body—all of this [is not permissible].
It is permissible. However, whatever falls here from its place onto the bowl or into the hand must be accepted;
what adheres to the fingers is already considered accepted. When one eats hot rice porridge, the sweat that follows along the fingers remains connected as it settles into the porridge;
or, when walking for alms, [the sweat] from the hand or from the rim of the bowl...
When descending onto the surface of a leaf, there is no need for formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*);

however, regarding the great elements that have been burnt, there is nothing improper about them, yet what is poorly burnt is not permitted. But what is well-burnt—even human bone—is permitted to be ground into powder and applied to a wound.
Regarding the four great repulsive foods (*mahāvikaṭa*), if no one is available to make them permissible, one may take them oneself and consume them.
These are permissible. In this context, even one who is difficult to speak with or incapable [of performing the task] remains on the side of those who are not present [to act as a *kappiyakāraka*].
If ash is unavailable, one should burn dry wood and take the ash.
If dry wood is unavailable, it is permissible to cut green wood from a tree and use it. This fourfold "great carrion" (*mahāvikaṭa*), however, is from Kālodīsa.
It is permissible only at the very moment of being bitten by a snake.
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of receiving [alms],
in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text.
21. Discussion on the Determination of the Invitation (Pavāraṇā) 116.

*Paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā* (Invitation by Refusal): This is the invitation consisting of the refusal of any food brought forward by anyone, while one is eating any one of the five kinds of cooked food. And this [invitation] is not accomplished by mere refusal alone.
It exists, however, by way of five factors. Herein, these five factors are:

(1) the seat, (2) the food, (3) standing within arm’s reach of the giver, (4) the bringing forward [of the food], and (5) the refusal of what has been brought forward. Therein, "the seat" means a meal that has not yet begun;
the meaning is that this person is one who is currently eating. "The food" means food sufficient for an invitation to eat, such as boiled rice and so forth.

The meaning is that a certain kind of food must be refused. "Standing within the reach of the donor's hand" means standing in a space measuring two and a half cubits from the donor after having received food sufficient for an invitation.

"Bringing forward" (*abhihāra*) means bringing it forward by body while the donor stands within the reach of one's hand. "Refusing what has been brought forward" refers to refusing that which has been brought forward in this manner.
Or it is a refusal by means of body or speech. Thus, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by way of these five factors.

And this has been said: "Upāli, the invitation is recognized in five ways: eating is recognized, food is recognized, [the bowl] is held within arm's reach, [food] is offered, and a refusal is recognized.
117. Herein, this is the analysis: first, regarding "eating" and so forth—whatever one eats, and whatever food is within arm's reach...
He refuses what has been brought by one standing; that must be understood as being one or another of these: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, or meat.
Therein, "boiled rice" (odana) means that which is produced from the grains of seven kinds of crops: *sāli*, *vīhi*, barley, wheat, millet, *varaka*, and *kudrūsaka*.
Among these, "*sāli*" refers to the entire genus of *sāli*, including even wild paddy (*nīvāra*).
"Rice" (*vīhi*) refers to every species of rice. There is no distinction between barley (*yava*) and wheat (*godhuma*).

"Kangu" refers to every species of *kangu*, including the white, red, and black varieties. "Varaka" refers to every species of the white-colored *varaka* grain, including even the small *varaka-coraka*.
"Kodrava" refers to every species of grass-grain (*tiṇadhanna*), including both black *kodrava* and varieties such as *sāmāka*. [The same applies to] *nīvāra*, *varaka*, and *coraka*.
And here they say "conducive to grain" (*dhaññānuloma*);

whether it be actual grains or things conducive to grain, having taken the husked rice from these seven kinds of grain mentioned above, let them cook it for whatever purpose—thinking, "We shall cook a meal," or "We shall cook rice-gruel," or "We shall cook some sour milk-rice (*ambilapāyāsa*) and so forth. If it is hot...
When those eating cold food, at the time of eating, the solid portion (odhi) is visible in each place where it is taken;
it becomes mixed with the rice and produces a sense of fullness (pavāraṇa). If the solid portion is not visible, it becomes mixed with the broth (yāgu) and does not produce a sense of fullness.
Even when rice-gruel, or sour gruel mixed with leaves, fruits, and coconut kernels, has just been removed from the stove and is still hot—
Once it has been brought to mind, it is possible to drink; even when held in the hand, it shows no sediment and does not produce froth.
However, if, after the heat has subsided and it has become cool, it becomes thick, it then shows sediment and again produces froth;
its previous thin state is no longer preserved. Even if one adds curd, buttermilk, and so forth—

If many leaf-plates and sprouts have been placed [in the bowl] and even a mere handful of rice has been added, and at the time of eating the solid food (*odhi*) is still visible, it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*).

In an invitation where there is no gruel (*ayāgu*), thinking "we shall give gruel," they pour water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth into the cooked rice and say, "Take the gruel. Even though it is thin, it certainly generates an invitation. If...
However, if they place [the fish or meat] into boiling water or other liquids and cook it before giving it, it is included within the category of *yāgu* (rice gruel).

Even when it is included within that category of *yāgu*, or in any other case where they throw fish or meat into it—if even a piece of fish or meat the size of a mustard seed, or even a sinew, is discernible, it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). But if it is merely a pure broth, it is simply *rasaka-yāgu*.

Or it does not produce [the offense]. Apart from the grains of rice mentioned, even a meal made with other things such as bamboo-grain rice, or with bulbs, roots, or fruits—whatever they may be—does not produce the *pavāraṇā* (invitation), let alone thick gruel.
However, if fish or meat is added to it, it does produce it. In the *Mahāpaccarī*: "Even a meal prepared for the sake of flowers produces the *pavāraṇā*..."

It is said: “janetī. Regarding “food for the sake of flowers”: this refers to rice grains that have been steamed by adding them to boiling water for the purpose of making flower-shaped snacks (*pupphikhajjaka*).
However, if they dry those rice grains and eat them, it is permissible;
they do not fall under the category of *sattu* (flour/grains) nor the category of *bhatta* (cooked food). One may still offer the food prepared by them during the *pavāraṇā*. They...
They cook rice with ghee, oil, and so forth, or they make cakes, yet they do not offer it as an invitation (*pavāraṇa*).
Or, they do not offer parched grain or the like, such as barley-meal (*sattu*) prepared by them.
As for what is called *kummāsa*, it is *kummāsa* made from barley; however, *kummāsa* made from other things such as mung beans does not produce an invitation.

"Sattu" refers to flour made from *sāli* rice, *vīhi* rice, or barley. Even *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, and *kudrūsaka* grains are roasted, slightly crushed, winnowed to remove the husks, and then ground again until they become powder.
Even if that [powder] remains somewhat cohesive due to being moist, it is still included within the category of "sattu.
As for the rice grains of paddy that have been roasted in a dry frying pan (*kharapāka*), [one takes] the kernels...
If they give [the grain] after pounding it, even that powder constitutes an act of inclusion for the enemy.
However, the rice grains of paddy that has been roasted to an even degree, or the husks of such paddy, or even roasted rice grains themselves, do not constitute an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

But the powder of those rice grains does constitute an invitation. Furthermore, the broken bits (*kuṇḍaka*) of paddy roasted to a coarse degree also constitute an invitation. [This applies likewise to] paddy roasted to an even degree...
However, one does not offer parched grain that has been dried in the sun.
Nor do they offer fried grains, or rice-powder and other such items prepared with them, or roasted flour, or any kind of plain snack (*suddhakhajjaka*).
But one may offer a snack filled with fish and meat, or a *sattumodaka* (a sweetmeat made of rice-flour). Fish and meat are well known.
