But this is the distinction: if, while he is drinking rice gruel, they give him two pieces of fish or two pieces of meat—either in the same vessel or in separate vessels—the size of a single grain of rice, and if he does not eat them but refuses some other food sufficient for an invitation, he has not invited himself to more.
Then, if one has been eaten and one remains in his hand...
Whether it be in the bowl or in the hand, if he rejects another [offering] while doing so, he invites [the guest to eat).
Even if two [mouthfuls] have been eaten and not even a mustard-seed’s worth remains in the mouth, if he rejects another, he does not invite.
When eating allowable meat, if he rejects allowable meat, he invites. When eating allowable meat, [if he rejects] unallowable meat...
He rejects it; he does not invite [the other to eat]. Why? Because of its lack of foundation. For an invitation occurs when one rejects only that which is permissible for a monk to eat.
But knowing this [to be impermissible], he rejects it because it is unallowable (*akappiya*);
even if he does not know, he is indeed said to "reject" it when it stands in a position where it ought to be rejected. Therefore, he does not invite. However, if it is unallowable meat...
While eating allowable meat, he refuses it and then invites [the host] to eat. Why? Because of its nature as a substance (*vatthutā*).

For that which he has refused is the substance for the invitation; however, although what he is eating stands in the place of what ought to be refused, while being eaten it does not lose its status as meat. Therefore, he invites [the host]. Or, while eating unallowable meat...
He rejects unallowable meat; as in the previous method, he does not invite [others] to partake.
Whether it be allowable meat or unallowable meat, while eating, he rejects any allowable food among the five kinds of cooked food and thus invites [others].
That which is produced from corrupting families, medical practice, superhuman states, or the acquisition of money and so forth, is condemned by the Buddha.
He refuses and does not accept unallowable food that has arisen for the purpose of seeking alms;
he does not invite [others to eat]. Or, he refuses and does not accept allowable food or unallowable food.
Even while eating either allowable food or unallowable food, he refuses allowable food but invites [others to eat]. He refuses unallowable food...
The reason for the phrase "he does not invite" should be understood according to the method stated in all previous instances.

118. Thus, having explained what is eaten and how one incurs an offense regarding the invitation by refusing food brought within arm's reach, [the text] now proceeds to explain how one incurs it, for the purpose of making that known.

This is the analysis: regarding the phrase "food is eating," first, if one has swallowed even a single grain of rice, and if—whether from the bowl, the mouth, or the hand—anyone of the five kinds of food is present, yet he rejects another of the five kinds of food, even if it be only a single [particle], he has finished his meal (*pavāreti*).
Even if no food is present anywhere, but there is merely the scent of food...
It is discerned that he does not invite [others to eat]. There is no food in his mouth or in his hand, but there is food in his bowl;

however, if—desiring not to eat on that seat, or desiring to enter the monastery to eat, or desiring to give it to another—he rejects the food during that interval, he does not invite. Why? Because the state of having left the meal unfinished has been interrupted.

"In the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'Even for one who, desiring to eat after going elsewhere, swallows some food into his mouth, takes the remainder with him, and then refuses further food on the way, there is no *pavāraṇā*.
And as it is with the bowl, so it is with the hand; or even if food is present in the mouth, if he has no desire to swallow it,"
And at that moment, he rejects another [offering] and does not invite [him to eat]. For the characteristic stated in one instance must be understood to apply everywhere.
Moreover, this method is shown in the *Kurundi* itself; for it is said there: "Food has been swallowed into the mouth;
one wishes to give food in the hand to a scavenger (*vighāsāda*); one wishes to give food in the bowl to a monk."
"If he rejects it at that moment, he does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Regarding the phrase "standing within arm's reach": here, if the monk is sitting, it is measured from the rear edge of his seat;
if he is standing, from the tip of his heels; if he is lying down, from the far side of the direction in which he lies.
Starting from the donor— whether he is sitting, standing, or lying down—
the "hand’s reach" (*hatthapāsa*) should be understood as two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*), measured by delimiting the nearest limb excluding the outstretched hand.
An invitation (*pavāraṇā*) occurs only for one who refuses what is brought while standing within that range, and not beyond it.
"Brings forward" (*abhiharati*) means that while standing within arm's reach, one holds out [the bowl] for the purpose of receiving [food].

However, if even a monk sitting immediately next to him says, "Take the food," without having brought forward the bowl—which might be resting in his hand, on his thigh, or in a stand—there is no *pavāraṇā* (invitation) for one who refuses it. Having brought the food-basket and placed it on the ground in front [of him],...

The same principle applies even when it is said, "Take [some]. However, if one says, "Take," after having lifted up slightly or moved aside [the food], there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) for one who refuses.

When an elder monk sitting on the seat of the elders sends his bowl toward a young monk sitting at a distance and says, "Take rice from here," but having taken it, the other remains silent, [there is no offense].
A junior monk refuses, saying, "Enough for me," and does not invite [the elder to eat]. Why? Because the elder is far away and because the messenger has not brought the food.
However, if a monk who has come back with the food says, "Take this alms-food," then there is an invitation for one who refuses it.
At the serving hall, one person [serves] a rice-basket with one hand...
If a monk serves another monk while holding a ladle, and someone else arrives there and says, "I will carry the basket;
you give me the rice," and [the newcomer] merely takes hold of it, yet the server himself continues to carry it, then that [food] is indeed considered "brought forward" (*abhihaṭa*).
Therefore, for one who refuses to accept it from the giver out of a desire to give, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

However, if the food has only just been touched by the server and another person still holds it, then for one who refuses a person wishing to take it out of a desire to give, there is no *pavāraṇā* (invitation to take more). But if the food has been lifted with a ladle, then there is *pavāraṇā*.
For the mere lifting with a ladle constitutes its "lifting. Even in the case of two equal portions, one who refuses [the second] indeed performs the *pavāraṇā*.
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "When food is being given to one monk, if another covers his bowl with his hand, there is no *pavāraṇā*.
Why? Because it has been refused when brought to someone else. Regarding the phrase 'the refusal is made known':
here, for one who refuses what is brought by speech, there is no *pavāraṇā*; [but] for one who [refuses] by body..."
It should be understood that the invitation (pavāraṇā) is valid for one who rejects what has been brought forward by any means whatsoever, whether by body or by speech.
In this context, "rejection by body" means moving a finger, a hand, a fly-whisk, a corner of the robe, or making a gesture with the eyebrows, or looking on in anger. By speech...
"Refusal" means saying "enough," or "I will not take it," or "do not pour it," or "go away.
Thus, when a refusal has been made by body or speech in any such manner, the invitation (pavāraṇā) is valid. 119.
One who, fearing the invitation regarding food brought to him, withdraws his hand and repeatedly puts rice back into the bowl...
When someone is scattering [powder] and another says, "Scatter! Scatter! Grind it up, grind it up, and fill it!", how is this to be understood?
First, the Elder Mahāsumma said, "Because it was spoken for the purpose of not scattering, it constitutes an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, the Elder Mahāpaduma, having stated, "For anyone who says 'Scatter and fill,' there can be no such thing as an invitation," declared, "It does not constitute an invitation."
Another monk, having observed a bhikkhu bringing food, said, "Friend, will you take anything from here as well? I will give you something.
Regarding this case too, the Elder Mahāsumma said, "Because it was said, 'He will not come that way,' there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "For one who says, 'Will you take it? there is no such thing as an invitation."
Having said this, he replied, "There is no *pavāraṇā*.
One person brings a sauce containing meat and says, "Take the sauce"; having heard this, there is no *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it.
When it is said, "Fish and meat sauce," there is *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it; [but] when [he says], "Take this..."
Even when this was said, it remained so. Separating the meat [from the broth], he says, "Take the meat broth.

If there is even a piece of meat the size of a mustard seed in it, for one who refuses it, there is an invitation (to eat more). But if it has been strained, it is permissible—thus said the Elder Abhaya.
When the meat broth was being offered, the Great Elder said, "Wait a moment," and then said, "Friend, bring the bowl."
He asked, "How is it in this case? First, the Elder Mahāsumma said, "The departure of the one who brings the food has been interrupted; therefore, he performs the *pavāraṇā*.
But the Elder Mahāpaduma, having said, "Where is this man going? What kind of departure is this?
Even for someone who is actually taking [the food], can there be a *pavāraṇā*? replied, "He does not perform the *pavāraṇā*."
They cook meat mixed with bamboo shoots, jackfruit, and so forth; having taken it, they say, "Take bamboo shoot soup," or "Take jackfruit curry.
Even in this case, one does not invite [the donor to choose). Why? Because it is stated by name that which is not fit to be invited.
However, if they say, "Fish soup" or "meat soup," or "Take this," one does invite; such is the case with meat and *karambaka* (rice-and-sesame porridge).
It has such a name. Even if one who wishes to give it says, "Take some *karambaka* (rice-and-meat porridge)," it is permissible; this does not constitute an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, if it is said, "Meat *karambaka*," or "This [is meat]," then it constitutes an invitation. This same principle applies to all cases involving fish or meat. 120.
Furthermore, if one who is eating at an invitation rejects meat that has been brought to him, thinking, "This was prepared specifically for me" (*uddissakata*), [it is an offense].
"He is as if he has invited [the monks]," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, the discussion regarding mixed [food] is explained thoroughly in the *Kuruṇḍī*.
For it is said there: "If a monk who goes for alms brings rice gruel mixed with solid food and says, 'Take the rice gruel,' he does not invite [the monks];
but when he says, 'Take the solid food,' he invites them. Why? Because [he speaks] to that person from whom he was requested..."

Because of its existence. This is the intended meaning here: if one says, "Take this with the rice-gruel," and therein the gruel is either more abundant or equal [in quantity] to the rice, one does not invite [the guest to eat more). If the gruel is weak and the rice is more abundant, then one invites [the guest].
And because this has been stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it cannot be rejected; however, the reason for this is difficult to perceive.
If he says, “Take a mixture of food,” whether the food is more, equal, or less [than the other items], he still performs the *pavāraṇā*.

If, without touching the food or the rice-gruel, he says, “Take a mixture,” and therein the food is more or equal, he performs the *pavāraṇā*; if it is less, he does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. And this...
One should not accept it with *karambaka*. For *karambaka* may be mixed with meat or not mixed with meat; therefore, when "karambaka" is mentioned, there is no invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
But this [food] is mixed only with cooked rice. Here, the invitation occurs according to the method stated for that very case.
In the case of food with much flavor, one should say "flavor"; in the case of much milk, "milk"; and in the case of porridge with much ghee, "ghee."
If one gives after setting it aside, saying, "Take this," there is no *pavāraṇā* for one who refuses it.
However, if one extends the invitation while walking, he may eat while still walking.
Upon reaching mud or water, he must have the food declared as leftover (*atiritta*). If, meanwhile, a river is full, [he should go] to a grove on the riverbank.
One who is walking around should eat. If there is a boat or a bridge, one should also eat while walking upon it;

one must not interrupt the movement. Or, having sat in a vehicle, on the back of an elephant or horse, or in the mandala of the moon or the sun, once one has been invited to partake, even if those [vehicles] continue moving until midday, [one may still eat].
One must eat while remaining seated. If one who is standing invites [another] to eat, the latter must eat while standing; if one who is seated invites [another], the latter must eat while seated.
One who alters their posture while eating commits an offense of excess (*atiritta*).
If one who is squatting on their heels invites [another], the latter must eat while squatting on their heels. However, beneath that person, there should be a grass mat.
Or some kind of sitting mat should be given. Having sat upon a bench, one who has been invited to eat may eat while turning around in the four directions without moving the seat.
However, having sat upon a couch, one who has been invited to eat is not permitted to move here or there;
but if they lift the person along with the couch and carry them elsewhere, [it is permissible].
It is permissible. One who has invited [others] to eat while lying down must consume the food while remaining in that very position.
While turning over, one must not cross beyond the spot where one was originally lying.
121. But what should one who has invited [others] do? Having altered the posture in which one invited them—
If he eats using another posture, he must have it made "leftover" before eating.
However, if he eats or consumes any kind of food— whether solid or soft— that is included among the "timely" foods and has not been made leftover,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every mouthful swallowed.

In this context, "anatiritta" means not left over; the meaning is "not excessive. However, because it is either not performed by the seven modes of formal monastic acts (vinayakamma) beginning with "made allowable" (kappiyakata), or because it is not excessive for one who is ill, it is therefore stated in the word-commentary:
"What is called 'anatiritta' is that which has not been made allowable; it has not been accepted; it has not been formally declared;

it has not been done within arm's reach; it has been done by one who has not yet eaten; and it has been done by one who has already finished eating, who has refused further food, and who has risen from his seat."
“It has been made allowable; it has not been said, ‘This is enough for all’; it is not the remainder of one who is ill—this is what is called ‘not leftover’ (anatiritta).

In this context, “made unallowable” (akappiyakata) refers to whatever fruit or root-crop there is that has not been made allowable by the five monastic allowables (samaṇakappa), as well as any unallowable meat or unallowable food; this is what is called “unallowable.”
Even if something unallowable has been made "leftover" by saying, "This is enough for all," it should be understood as "made unallowable.
"Made unaccepted" means that it was made leftover in the aforementioned manner while still unaccepted by a monk.
"Made without being uttered" means that when a monk has come to have it made allowable, he has not raised his voice even slightly nor signaled with a gesture.
"Done outside the reach of the hand" means done by one standing outside the reach of the hand of the person who has come to have it made allowable.

"Done by one who has not yet eaten" refers to when someone makes food leftover, thinking, "This is enough for all," while that person has not yet consumed a meal sufficient to satisfy the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"Done by one who has finished eating, has been invited, and has risen from his seat" is self-evident. "This is enough... [The rest follows].
"Not mentioned as 'all'" means that by making a verbal distinction, it is thus not mentioned.

Therefore, by these seven modes of formal acts of the Vinaya, whatever is "leftover" (*atiritta*) that has not been made allowable (*kappiya*), and whatever is not "leftover from one who is ill" (*na gilānātiritta*), both of these should be understood as "not leftover" (*anatiritta*).
However, "leftover" should be understood by way of its opposite. For this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
“‘Leftover’ means: it has been made permissible; it has been accepted; it has been announced; it is within arm’s reach;
it has been made by one who has finished eating; it has been made by one who has finished eating and been invited to stop, yet has not risen from his seat;
it has been declared, ‘This is enough for all’; it is the leftover of one who is ill—this is what is called ‘leftover.’”
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it is done by one who has finished eating":

even if one eats a single grain of rice or a piece of meat from the almsbowl of a fellow monk seated immediately next to oneself, it should be understood that "it is indeed done by one who has finished eating.
Regarding the phrase "without having risen from one's seat," this is the explanation for the sake of clarity: two monks, at the very break of dawn...
When they have finished eating and are invited to stop, one person must remain seated right there;

the other, having brought either a regular meal or a ticket-ration, should pour half of it into that monk’s bowl, wash his hand, and then, having had the remainder made allowable by that monk, he may eat it. Why? Because whatever remains stuck to his hand is not allowable.
...it is so. However, if the monk who sat down first takes [the food] from his bowl with his own hand, there is no need for the act of washing hands.
But if someone says, "While he is eating after having had the *kappiya* made, pour some more sauce or solid food into his bowl," then that person by whom the *kappiya* was first made—
One may not perform it again. It must be performed by the one who has not yet performed it; and that which has not been performed must be performed.
"By the one who has not performed it" means it must be performed by another bhikkhu by whom it was not first performed.

"And that which has not been performed" means even by him by whom the *kappiya* (ritual authorization) was first performed, whatever has not been performed must be performed. However, regarding the first vessel, one may perform it...
It is not permitted. For if it were made there, it would be considered as having been made together with what was already made;
therefore, the intention is that it should be made in another vessel. However, once it has been made in this way, it is permissible for that monk to eat it together with what was first made.

When making something *kappiya* (allowable), it should not be done only over a bowl; it may also be done over a vessel, a basket, or anywhere else, provided the container is placed before one and tilted downward.
If a hundred monks have been invited to eat (*pavārita*), it is permissible for all of them to eat;
it is also permissible for those who have not been invited. However, it is not permissible for the person by whom the *kappiya* was made.

Even if, after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they take the bowl of a bhikkhu who has entered for alms and seat him at a celebratory invitation where food must necessarily be eaten, he may eat only after having it made *atiritta* (leftover).

If there is no other bhikkhu present there, he should have it made [into leftovers] by sending his bowl to the dining hall or the monastery; however, the one making it *kappiya* (proper) must do so through a person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
One must not do what is placed in one’s hand. If there is an incompetent monk in the assembly hall, one should go there oneself, have what is permissible (*kappiya*) prepared, bring it back, and eat.

Regarding "leftover from the sick" (*gilānātiritta*): here, "leftover from the sick" does not refer only to that which remains after the sick person has eaten; [it also includes food set aside for them].

Furthermore, whatever has been brought for the sake of one who is ill with the thought, "He shall eat it today or whenever he wishes," all that should be understood as *gilānātiritta* (leftover for the sick).
However, for one who consumes anything— whether *yāmakālika*, *sattāhakālika*, or *yāvajīvika*—
that is not *atiritta* for the purpose of food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every mouthful swallowed.

If, however, the items are mixed with food, such as those that may be kept for a watch of the night and so forth, then for one who accepts them and consumes them—whether for the purpose of nutriment or not—the offense is a *pācittiya*.
But if they are unmixed with food, there is no offense for one who eats them when a requisite condition exists.
Thus ends the compendium of legal determinations (*vinayavinicchaya*) extracted from the Pāḷi.
The Discussion on the Determination of the Pavāraṇā is finished.
22. The Discussion on the Determination of Going-forth (Pabbajjā) 123.
Regarding "going-forth" (*pabbajjā*): here, when one is ordaining a son of good family who desires going-forth, those [prohibitions] which are stated in the Canon as "not... [should be observed].
“Monks, one who is afflicted by five diseases should not be given the going forth,” and so on;
having excluded such persons, a person free from the defects of the going forth should be admitted. Herein is the analysis:
one afflicted by these five diseases—leprosy, boils, ringworm, consumption, and epilepsy—should not be given the going forth; for one who does give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
One incurs an offense because it is stated: "Whoever should give the going-forth [to such a person], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

In this context, "leprosy" (kuṭṭha) refers to either red leprosy or black leprosy; it is said that whatever variety there may be—such as skin eruptions, ringworm, scabies, and so forth—all of it is indeed leprosy.
If even a spot the size of a fingernail or the back of a finger is situated on a part of the body where it increases, he must not be given the going-forth.

However, if it is in a place naturally covered by the lower and upper robes, and it is no larger than the surface of a fingernail and situated on the side that does not require enlargement, it is permissible.

But regarding the mouth, or the backs of the hands and feet—even if situated on the side that does not require enlargement—it is not permissible at all if it is even slightly smaller than the surface of a fingernail; thus it is stated in the *Kurundi*. Having had it treated medically...

Even when granting the going-forth (pabbajjā), one should grant it only to those who possess their natural appearance; it is not permitted to grant the going-forth even to one whose body is covered with powder resembling the back of a monitor lizard.
As for "a boil" (gaṇḍa), whether it be a carbuncle or another kind, if it is of any size even as large as a jujube fruit and is on the side of increasing—

If a boil is present, he should not be ordained. However, if it is located in a concealed place and remains the size of a jujube fruit (*kolaṭṭhi*) and stays in a non-progressive state, it is permissible;
even if it remains in a non-progressive state, it is not permissible if it is in an unconcealed place such as the mouth and so forth.
Even when ordaining one after having them treated, he must be ordained only after having the body restored to its natural skin condition. [This applies to] boils with pus.
They are called "gothanakas," hanging here and there like little lumps or like fingers;
these too are indeed swellings (*gaṇḍa*), and when they are present, it is not permitted to grant the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
There are what are called milk-boils in childhood and harsh pustules in youth, which disappear in old age; these do not count as swellings, and when they are present, one may grant the going-forth.
It is permissible. However, there are others called "rough pustules" on the body, and others called "lotus-seed [eruptions]";
others called "mustard-seed eruptions," which are the size of mustard seeds and spread over the entire body—all of these are types of leprosy (*kuṭṭha*).
If these exist, one should not be ordained.
*Kilāsa* is a leprosy that does not break open or exude, having the color of a white lotus petal.
By means of this, the body becomes spotted like that of a cow; the analysis of this leprosy should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

*Sosa* is the disease of consumption (*śoṣa*). When this exists, one should not be ordained. *Apamāra* is either a derangement caused by bile (*pittummāda*) or a derangement caused by a spirit (*yakkhummāda*).
Alternatively, one seized there by a non-human being who holds a prior grudge is difficult to treat; moreover, if even a slight illness occurs, he should not be ordained.
"Monks, one who is in the king's service should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
By virtue of his status as a royal servant (*rājabhaṭa*), even one who is a mere verbal [servant] should not be ordained.

In this context, whether he be a minister, a high official, a servant, or one who has attained some rank or not—whosoever is supported by the king through food and wages, all such persons are reckoned as royal servants and must not be ordained. However, his sons, grandsons, or brothers...
It is permissible to ordain those who do not accept food or wages from a king.

However, if one returns to the king himself whatever fixed income or monthly or annual allowance he received from the king, or if he causes his son or brother to take over that position and informs the king, "I am no longer Your Majesty’s servant," or for whatever reason he has accepted the wages; [in such cases, it is permissible].
That deed has been committed; or, if one has been permitted by the king with the words, "Go forth," it is also permissible to ordain him.
125. Even a bandit who wears the insignia [of his crime] must not be ordained. For it has been said: "Monks, a bandit wearing the insignia must not be ordained.
Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In this context, he is so called because he wanders about as if having bound on a banner.
It is meant that he is well-known in the world, like Dhajabandha, Mūladeva, and others.

Therefore, one who wanders about committing village raids, highway robbery, or acts such as housebreaking in a city, and who is recognized by the saying, "So-and-so is doing this and that," should not be ordained.
However, one who is a prince seeking the kingdom—
If one commits acts such as plundering a village, he may be ordained; for kings are pleased when such a person has gone forth.

However, if they are not pleased, he must not be ordained. If a thief who was previously well-known among the public later abandons his criminal deeds and undertakes the five precepts, and if people know him thus, he may be ordained. As for those thieves who deal in mangoes, wood-apples, and the like—
Or, just like thieves who break into houses and so forth, they commit theft while remaining invisible; even afterwards, it is not known that "this person did this.
It is permissible to ordain them as well.
However, a thief who breaks into fortifications must not be ordained. [The Buddha said: "Monks, a thief who breaks into fortifications must not be ordained."
Because it is stated: “Whoever should cause [someone] to go forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In that context, *kāra* refers to a prison.

But here, whether it be a bond with a leather thong, a bond with a chain, a bond with a rope, a bond to a village, a bond to a town, a bond to a city, protection for a man, a bond to a province, or a bond to an island—[it is all included].
Alternatively, whoever among these, having broken, cut, released, or opened any bond whatsoever, flees while they are unaware, is reckoned as a "breaker of the prison.
Therefore, such a thief who has broken the prison and gone to another island must not be ordained. However, one who is not a thief—

If a person who has not committed any physical assault is bound by royal officials and others on the suspicion that "he will do it if we do not apprehend him," he may be ordained even if he escapes from confinement and flees.
However, one who has been imprisoned for failing to fulfill a contract after having taken villages,
market towns, ports, and so forth by means of a tax-levy, is not to be ordained even if he returns after escaping.
If someone who earns their living through agriculture and other such means is imprisoned by another person after that person spreads slander,
claiming, "He obtained this treasure," it is not permissible to ordain him right there;
however, if he has escaped and gone elsewhere, it is permissible to ordain him at his new location.
127. “Monks, a thief who is marked with a brand should not be given the going-forth; whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Because of this statement, a thief who is marked with a brand must not be given the going-forth.

In that context, one who is “marked with a brand” (likhitaka) refers to anyone who, having committed theft or some other serious offense against the king, has fled; and the king [has recorded him] on a leaf or in a book as “so-and-so.”

If he causes [the person] to be written down with such instructions as: "Wherever he is seen, he is to be seized and killed," or "His hands, feet, and so forth are to be cut off," or "He is to be made to pay such-and-such a fine," this is called one who has been written down; he is not to be ordained.
128. One who has been whipped and undergone punishment is also not to be ordained: "Monks, one who has been whipped and undergone punishment..."
"One who has been ordained [is not to be re-ordained]; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Because of this statement, one who is beaten for failing to perform tasks such as delivering messages is not one who has undergone punishment. However, one who, having received something by means of a bribe or otherwise, eats it and is unable to give it back, and is then beaten with whips because of the words "Let this itself be your punishment"—this person alone is one "beaten with whips."

One who has undergone corporal punishment: whether he has been struck with whips or by any other means such as the half-staff and so forth, he must not be ordained as long as the wound is still moist;
however, once the wound has healed, he may be ordained.
But if he has been released after being beaten with the knees, the head-knocker, or stones such as those from coconuts, and there are lumps on his body...
[If these] are seen, he should not be ordained; rather, he should be ordained only after [the wound] has been made comfortable and the knots have been tied together.
129. Furthermore, one who has been struck by a mark and has already undergone the penalty should not be ordained, because of the statement:
"Monks, one who has been struck by a mark and has undergone the penalty should not be ordained; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In this case as well—
The state of having performed the act of punishment (daṇḍakamma) is to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
However, if a mark has been branded on his forehead or on his thighs and other such parts with heated iron, he—if he is a free man—must not be ordained as long as the wound is still moist.
Even if the wounds have healed and the skin has grown back level, if the mark is no longer visible, he may be ordained provided the three circles [of the saṅgha] are present.
If he is clothed with the lower robe and the upper robe is put on, and the place is concealed, it is permissible to give him the going-forth; if the place is not concealed, it is not permissible.

130. Because of the statement, “Monks, one who is a debtor should not be given the going-forth; whoever should give him the going-forth incurs an offense of wrong-doing,” even a debtor should not be given the going-forth.
In this context, a “debtor” is one whose father or grandfather has taken a loan.
One who has incurred a debt himself, or for whom a debt was contracted by his parents on his behalf, is called a debtor (*iṇāyika*) because he owes that debt to others.
However, one for whom other relatives have taken something on his behalf is not a debtor;
for they have no authority to bind him, and therefore it is permissible to ordain such a person, whereas the other is not.
It is not permissible. However, if his relatives or blood kin take the debt upon themselves, saying, "We will pay it;
ordain him," or if someone else, having seen his excellence of conduct, says, "Ordain him; I will pay the debt," then it is permissible to ordain him.
In the absence of these, even if there is a lay supporter of such a kind, [the monk may ordain him].

It should be announced: "A being who has a cause for obstruction, such as a debt, does not go forth. If he agrees, he may be ordained. Even if he has his own allowable goods, he may be ordained with the understanding: "I will give this [to pay the debt].
But if neither his relatives and so forth agree, nor does he have wealth of his own, [the thought should be: "Having ordained him, through alms..."

"It is not permissible to ordain [someone] with the thought, 'Having worked [for the debt], I will release him. If one ordains him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even if he has fled, he should be brought back and given [to the creditor].
If he does not give him up, the entire debt becomes his personal liability (*gīvā*). There is no offense for one who ordains him without knowing [of the debt];
however, by one who sees [the debt], he must be brought back and shown to the owners of the debt. For one who does not see [the debt], there is no personal liability."

If a debtor goes to another country and, when questioned, says, "I owe nothing to anyone," and then goes forth into homelessness, and the creditor, while searching for him, arrives there; and the young man, seeing him, flees;
then the creditor approaches the elder and says, "Venerable sir, by whom was this man ordained? Having taken such and such an amount of wealth from me..."
If he says, "I have run away," the Elder should say, "Lay follower, I ordained you while saying, 'I am free from debt.
What can I do now? Look at my bowl and robes. This is the proper course in that situation. However, there is no liability for the debt if he has fled.
But if, having seen him in the presence of the Elder, he says, "This man owes me a debt," [the Elder should say], "To you..."
"You yourself must know about the debt," he should be told; even so, there is no liability for the debt. Even if he says, "This man has now gone forth as a monk, where will he go?
the Elder should tell him, "You yourself must know. Even if he flees after being told this, there is no liability for the debt.
But if the Elder says, "Where will he go now? Let him stay right here," [then the responsibility remains].
If he flees, it becomes a debt. If that person is well-behaved and fulfills his duties, the elder should say, "He is such as this.
If the creditor says, "Very well," and releases him, that is good; but if he says, "Give him half, half," he should be given [that].
At another time, if he becomes very serviceable, even when told, "Give him everything," [he should be released].

It must certainly be given. However, if he is skilled in recitation, interrogation, and so forth, and is of great benefit to the bhikkhus, then even if it must be sought through the practice of alms-gathering, the debt must still be paid. 131.
A slave also must not be ordained: "Bhikkhus, a slave must not be ordained; whoever should ordain one, there is an offense."

...because of the statement, "of a wrong-doing. In that context, there are four types of slaves: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, one brought as a captive, and one who has entered into slavery of his own accord.
Among these, one "born in the house" is a slave by birth, the son of a female slave of the household.
One "bought with wealth" is one for whom the price was paid—either for the son from the parents or for the slave from the owners—to enter into the condition of servitude.
Having been led away as a slave. These two also should not be ordained. One who ordains them must first have them undergo probationary service (cāritta) in various places before ordaining them.
One "brought from a foreign land" refers to those who, having committed plunder or extortion in another kingdom, are brought back from that foreign land as free men;
or it refers to someone who has committed an offense within their own kingdom.
If the king commands, "Plunder the village," and they bring back human beings from there, then all the men become slaves and the women become slave-girls.

Such a slave brought as a prisoner of war—whether he is living with those by whom he was brought, or is bound in prison, or is being guarded by men—should not be ordained; however, if he should escape...

One who has gone to a place where he is to be executed should be ordained. Or, when the king, being pleased, says, "Release those brought as victims," or when the release from bondage is effected by some other general means, he should indeed be ordained.
One who has entered into slavery of his own accord is one who, for the sake of life or for the sake of protection, says of himself, "I am your slave."
One who has entered into a state of servitude for kings—such as elephant-keepers, horse-keepers, cowherds, buffalo-herders, and so forth—is not to be ordained.
Likewise, a slave is not to be ordained. The sons of a king’s concubines (vaṇṇadāsī) are similar to the sons of ministers; they too are not to be ordained.
However, it is permissible to ordain the sons of free women who associate with unchaste concubines. If [the father] himself...

They apply a formal agreement (*paṇṇa*); this is not permitted. Even slaves belonging to groups such as those of hired laborers (*bhaṭiputtaka*) must not be ordained if they have not been given away by their masters.
In monasteries, there are those known as "monastery-attendants" (*ārāmika*) or "slaves" who have been granted by kings; it is likewise not permitted to ordain them.

However, it is permitted to ordain them once they have been made free men (*bhujissa*). In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "Having brought in those born within [the household] or those bought with money for the Saṅgha of monks..."
It is said: "If they give [the slave], saying, 'We give him as a monastery attendant (ārāmika),' they become like one who has had buttermilk poured over his head; it is permissible to ordain them.

However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "If they give him by means of a formal expression of suitability, saying, 'We give him as a monastery attendant,' regardless of the specific expression used, he must not be ordained.
Furthermore, destitute people might think, "We shall live depending upon the Saṅgha."

If there are authorized attendants (*kappiyakāraka*) in the monastery, it is permissible to give him the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). It is not permissible to give the going-forth to one whose parents are slaves, or whose mother is a slave while his father is not a slave.
However, it is permissible to give the going-forth to one whose mother is not a slave but whose father is a slave.
Or, if the relatives or supporters of a bhikkhu give a slave [to him], saying, "Give this person the going-forth," [it is also permissible].
"He will perform service for you," or if he has his own slave, he must be ordained only after he has been made free.
If the owners give the slave [saying], "Ordain him; if he finds it pleasing, he shall not be a slave.
But if he should disrobe, he will remain our slave," this is called "temporary" (tāvakālika), and it is not permitted to ordain such a person—thus it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
It has been stated. One who is a slave without an owner—even he must be made free before being ordained.
If one ordains or grants full admission [to the Saṅgha] without knowing [this status], but later finds out, it is permissible to make him free.
To illustrate this point, they cite this story: it is said that a certain family slave, together with a certain man...
Having fled from Anurādhapura and living in Rohaṇa, she obtained a son. After he had gone forth and received full ordination, he became modest and scrupulous.
Then one day he asked his mother, "Upāsikā, do you have no brother or sister?
I see no kinsman at all. She replied, "Dear son, in Anurādhapura I was a slave in a noble family."

“I shall flee with your parents and live here. The virtuous bhikkhu, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon thinking, “My going forth is indeed impure,” asked his mother for the name and clan of that family.
Having arrived at Anurādhapura, he stood at the door of that family’s house; even when they said, “Please enter, venerable sir,” he did not cross the threshold. They came forward...
“What is it, venerable sir? they asked. “Does a certain slave-girl of yours belong to you?
“She does, venerable sir. “I am her son; if you grant me permission, may I receive the going-forth; you are my masters.
They, being delighted and joyful, said, “Venerable sir, your going-forth is pure,” and having made him a free man, [they established him] in the Mahāvihāra.
They had him live there, looking after him with the four requisites. While the Elder was living supported by that family, he attained arahantship. 132.

"Monks, one who has had a hand cut off should not be given the going-forth. Nor one who has had a foot cut off, nor one who has had both hands and feet cut off, nor one who has had an ear cut off, nor one who has had an ear and nose cut off, nor one who has had a finger cut off, nor one who has had a toe cut off, nor one who has had a tendon cut off."
He was not one with webbed hands, nor hunchbacked, nor dwarfed, nor with a goiter;
he was not marked by disfigurement, nor scarred by whips, nor branded, nor afflicted with elephantiasis, nor suffering from a foul disease;

he was not a detractor from the assembly, nor one-eyed, nor with a crooked limb, nor lame, nor paralyzed on one side, nor impaired in his physical postures, nor weak from old age, nor blind, nor mute, nor deaf.
"Furthermore, from the statement: 'One who is not blind and mute, not blind and deaf, not mute and deaf, and not blind, mute, and deaf should be ordained;
whoever should ordain such a person incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' it follows that those with severed hands and so forth are also not to be ordained.
In this context, 'one with severed hands' refers to one for whom [the hand] has been cut off at the palm, at the wrist, at the forearm, or anywhere else."
"One or two hands are cut off. "One whose foot is cut off" refers to one for whom one or two feet have been cut off anywhere—at the toes, at the ankles, or in the shanks.
"One whose hands and feet are cut off" refers to one for whom, in the same manner as described above, two, three, or all four of the hands and feet have been cut off.
[They] exist. "One whose ears are cut off" refers to one whose one or two ears have been severed either at the base of the ear or at the earlobe.
However, if one's ears are torn at the helix (*kaṇṇāvaṭṭe*) and it is possible to join them together, he may be ordained after having his ears joined.
"One whose nose is cut off" refers to one [wherever]—at the nostril, at the tip, or at the single fold—where...
In some cases, the nose has been cut off. However, one whose nose can be rejoined should have it restored to health and then be ordained.
One whose ear and nose are both severed should be understood according to both conditions.

"One with severed fingers" refers to one for whom one or more fingers have been cut off such that no trace of a nail remains. But as for one [whose fingers are missing] even to the extent of a mere thread...
If only the nails remain visible, it is permissible to grant him the going-forth.
"One whose thumbs are severed" refers to one for whom one or several thumbs among the four have been cut off in the same manner as described for the fingers.
"One whose tendons are severed" refers to one for whom the large sinews called *kaṇḍara*—whether in the front or at the back—have been cut; because even one of these has been severed...
He walks on his toes or he walks on his heels; he is unable to place his feet flat on the ground.

Regarding the "webbed-hand": one whose fingers are joined together like the wings of a bat—if one wishes to ordain such a person, the webbing between the fingers must be cut away, all the intervening skin removed, and once it has been made functional, he may be ordained.
Even one who has six fingers should be ordained; if one desires to ordain such a person, the extra finger should be cut off and made functional before ordaining him.
A "hunchback" (khujja) is one whose body is bent because the chest, back, or side has protruded.
However, it is permissible to ordain one whose various limbs and members are slightly crooked. The Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa).
For indeed, one whose body is straight is called *brahmujugatto*; there is no remaining being who is not called "crooked.

A "dwarf" (*vāmana*) may be a dwarf in the shanks, a dwarf in the waist, or a dwarf in both. For one who is a dwarf in the shanks, the lower part of the body from the waist downwards is short, while the upper part of the body is well-proportioned.
For one who is a dwarf in the waist, the upper part of the body from the waist upwards is short.
The lower body is complete. In the case of one who is dwarfed in both parts, both bodies are short;
because of this shortness, his physical form is rounded like a living being and resembles a large pot-bellied jar. It is not permissible to ordain any of these three types.
"One with a goitre" (*galagaṇḍī*) refers to one who has a tumor on the neck like a *kumbhaṇḍa* fruit. This is merely an illustration; in whatever [case]...
However, if there is a tumor (gaṇḍa) in any part [of the body], one should not be ordained.
The detailed explanation regarding this is to be understood according to the method stated in the passage: "Monks, one who is afflicted by five diseases should not be ordained.

As for what should be said concerning those with disfigured marks, those struck by a club, those struck by a staff, and those with tattooed skin, that has already been explained above. A "sīpadī" is called a "burden-foot"; one whose foot is thick...
If a wart has grown and it is rough, he should not be ordained. However, if it has not yet become rough,
and it is possible to cause it to wither— by binding a tourniquet, immersing him in a water-pit, filling it with sand,
and applying pressure until the veins become visible and the leg becomes like an oil-tube— then, having treated his foot in this manner, [he may be ordained].
It is appropriate to grant him the going forth. If he should recover, then even when granting him full ordination, he must be ordained only after having been treated in that manner.

"One afflicted by a foul disease" refers to one who is constantly ill with any of the diseases such as hemorrhoids, fistula, bile-disorders, phlegm-disorders, cough, or consumption—diseases that are incurable, loathsome, and unpleasant;
such a person should not be granted the going forth.
133. "One who defiles the assembly" refers to one who, by reason of his own deformity, brings disgrace upon the gathering;
for instance, he may be excessively tall, reaching from the heads of others down to their navels; or excessively short, like a figure composed of two dwarfs joined together;

or excessively dark, like a charred stump in a burnt field; or excessively pale, with the color of copper or bronze polished with curd, buttermilk, and the like; or excessively emaciated, with little flesh and blood.
One who is like a body of bone, sinew, and skin; or one who is not too stout, yet has heavy flesh and a large belly resembling a great elemental being;
or one with an excessively large head, standing as if carrying a basket upon his head; or one with an excessively small head, endowed with a head so tiny it is disproportionate to the body;
or one with a peaked head, endowed with a head like the cluster of a palmyra fruit; or one with a crest-like head.
Or one who has a head that is gradually tapering from above; or one with a "tube-head," like the joint of a large bamboo;
or one with a "helmet-head" or a "sloping-head," meaning a head that is bent toward any one of its four sides;
or one with a "wound-head," a "putrid-head," or "tufted hair," like a field eaten by insects.
He is endowed with hair that has grown here and there like blades of grass; or he has a hairless head, or thick, stiff hair, or hair resembling the fibers of a palm tree;
or he has hair turned white with natural graying, or naturally tawny hair, or hair as if set ablaze;
or he has a head marked with whorls, like the upward-pointing whorls found on the bodies of cattle.
He is endowed with hair-whirls; or his facial hair, together with the hair of his head, is joined into a single mass, as if his forehead were covered by a net;
or he has joined eyebrows, or hairless eyebrows, or monkey-like eyebrows; or his eyes are too large, or his eyes are too small.
Or he is one who has eyes like those with holes made by being struck with a bamboo splinter or a piece of hide;
or he is "uneven-eyed," possessing one large eye and one small eye;

or he is "uneven-eyebrowed" (visamacakkala), having one eyebrow pointing upward and the other downward, thus possessing eyes and brows of unequal kind; or he is "squint-eyed" (kekara) with deep-set eyes.
Or one whose eye-iris appears like the reflection of water in a deep well;
or one whose eyes protrude so that the iris is visible like that of a crab; or one who has "elephant ears," being endowed with large ear-flaps;
or one who has "rat ears" or "bat ears," being endowed with small ear-flaps.
Or one whose ears are merely perforated, meaning that without ear-rings there is only a hole in the ear;
or one with unperforated ears. However, one born as a Yavana does not corrupt the assembly, for that is simply his nature.
Or one suffering from an ear-fistula, possessed of an ear that is constantly putrid; or one with a goitre-like ear, an ear from which pus perpetually drips.
He may possess ears like those of a *ṭaṅkitakaṇṇa* (a type of animal), or ears resembling the tips of a cow's fodder-stalk;
or he may have excessively tawny eyes, though it is permissible to ordain one whose eyes are honey-tawny.
Or he may have eyes free of film, or eyes with streaming tears, or blossoming eyes, or eyes affected by inflammation.
One who has an excessively large nose, or an excessively small nose, or a flat nose, or a crooked nose that does not stand straight but is bent to one side, or a long nose;
or one endowed with a nose from which mucus constantly drips, like a well-fashioned beak, such that it is capable of licking with the tongue; or one with a large mouth, like a grasshopper-frog.
The opening itself is large, but the mouth is like a gourd—excessively small—or it has a split opening, a crooked opening, or large lips;
or it is provided with thin lips, or with lips resembling the skin of a drum that are unable to cover the teeth; or it has a large lower lip.

Or having thin upper lips, or thin lower lips, or large upper lips, or severed lips, or a snout-like face, or a protruding mouth, or a beak-like mouth, or one endowed with lips that are white on the outside and excessively red on the inside;
or having a foul-smelling, corpse-like mouth; or having large teeth, or being endowed with teeth resembling those of a crow, or having the teeth of an *asura*.

Whether the tooth protrudes below or above, or externally; however, if it can be covered by the lips, and is visible only while speaking and not when not speaking, it is permissible to grant him the going-forth (pabbajjā).
If his teeth are decayed, or missing, or too small, or if the space between his teeth has fine teeth like those of a squirrel, [it is permissible].
It is permissible to ordain him. One who has a large jaw,
or one endowed with a jaw like that of a cow, or one with a long jaw, or one with a flat jaw, or one endowed with an excessively short jaw as if it were sunken within,
or one with a broken jaw, or one with a crooked jaw, or one whose teeth are without gums— [these are not to be ordained].
Or one whose face resembles that of a bhikkhunī; or one with a long neck, endowed with a neck like that of a crane;
or one with a short neck, as if the neck were drawn inward; or one with a split neck; or one with a collapsed shoulder-peak;
or one without a hand, or with only one hand, or with hands that are too short, or with hands that are too long; or one with a split chest; or one with a split back.
One whose body is itchy, or one whose body is scabby, or one whose body is afflicted with ringworm, or one whose body is like a lizard’s—

meaning from whose body powder falls off as if from a lizard’s— is described here in detail with reference to all such deformities; however, the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) in this regard should be understood according to the method explained under the five diseases (*pañcābādha*).
One who has hocks like those of a camel or a horse, or whose hock-flesh protrudes like the peak of a hearth;
one with large thighs, or a "wind-cripple" (vātaṇḍika), or one with large knees, or one with knees that touch [the ground], or one with long shanks, or one with shanks like a staff;
one who is deformed, or one with joined [limbs], or one with upturned calves—this is of two kinds: those with [calves] descending from below or those ascending from above.
Or he is endowed with very large calves; or he has large shanks, or thick, fleshy calves; or he has large feet, or large heels;
or his feet are turned backward, with the shanks rising from the middle of the feet; or he has crooked feet—this being of two kinds, with the feet turned inward or outward;
or he has knotted fingers, being endowed with fingers resembling the bulbous roots of ginger.
One with blind nails, or one possessed of black-colored, putrid nails—such a person is a defiler of the assembly in every way.
One who is a defiler of the assembly such as this should not be ordained.
134. "Blindeyed" means one who is blind from birth, or whose vision is impaired by cataracts and the like, or who is missing one or both eyes.

If he does not see, he should not be ordained. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, one with a single blind eye is called "blind" (*kāṇa*), while one blind in both eyes is included under the category of "blind" (*andha*).
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, one born blind is called "blind. Therefore, both [definitions] are appropriate according to their respective contexts.
"Lame" (*kuṇī*) means one who is lame in the hand, lame in the foot, or lame in the finger; for whomsoever there is such a defect in these [limbs], such as the hands and so forth...
Something crooked is perceived. "Lame" means one with bent knees, or one with a broken shank; or one with stunted feet due to the feet being contracted at the middle;
or one with stunted feet due to the feet being contracted at the tips, walking on the middle of the back of the foot;
or one who walks on the tip of the foot; or one who walks on the heel.
Or one who limps while walking with the outer side of the foot; or one who limps while walking with the inner side of the foot;
or one who limps while walking with the entire back of the foot due to a fracture above the ankles—all these are indeed limping persons and should not be ordained.

"One whose limbs are impaired" (*pakkhahata*) refers to one for whom one hand, one foot, or half the body does not function normally. "One whose modes of deportment are severed" (*chinniriyāpatha*)...
A "bed-crawler" (*pīṭhasappī*) is so called. "Weak through old age" means one who is weakened by the state of being aged and is incapable of performing even such tasks as dyeing his own robes.
However, one who is elderly yet strong and capable of taking care of himself may be ordained.
"Blind" refers to one born blind. "Dumb" refers to one whose vocal articulation does not function, or to one for whom...
[The person] acts [normally], but is unable to recite the formula for going for refuge in its entirety;

it is not permissible to ordain such a person even if they are otherwise competent. However, it is permissible to ordain one who is able to recite at least the formula for going for refuge in its entirety.
One who is deaf is one who does not hear at all. But one who hears loud sounds—

It is appropriate to grant him the going-forth (pabbajjā). Those such as the blind and the mute are mentioned by way of both defects. For those for whom the going-forth is prohibited, the full admission (upasampadā) is likewise prohibited.
However, if the Saṅgha should nevertheless confer full admission upon them, all of them become fully admitted;
yet the performing Saṅgha, as well as the preceptor (ācariya) and the teacher (upajjhāya), are not released from their offense.

135. Furthermore, these eleven persons—the paṇḍaka, the one with both sexual organs, the one living in communion by theft, the one who has gone over to another sect, the animal, the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an arahant, the shedder of blood, the schismatic, and the defiler of a bhikkhunī—[regarding] the paṇḍaka, monks, one who is not ordained should not be ordained; if he is already ordained...

Because of such statements as "he is to be expelled," they are incapable; neither their going forth nor their full ordination is valid. Therefore, they should not be given the going forth nor should they be fully ordained.
One who knowingly gives the going forth or grants full ordination incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even those who have been given the going forth or granted full ordination unknowingly must, once it is known [that they are ineligible], be expelled by the removal of their robes and signs.

In this context, "eunuch" (*paṇḍaka*) refers to five types of eunuchs: the drenched eunuch (*āsitta-paṇḍaka*), the envious eunuch (*usūya-paṇḍaka*), the surgically-induced eunuch (*opakkamika-paṇḍaka*), the periodic eunuch (*pakkha-paṇḍaka*), and the neuter eunuch (*napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*).
Among these, one whose fever is pacified by taking another's sexual organ into the mouth and being drenched with impurity is the drenched eunuch.
One for whom [the fever] arises through envy upon seeing another's transgression is the envious eunuch.
The fever subsides; this is the envious paṇḍaka. He whose seeds have been removed by means of an external effort is the one produced by artificial means (opakkamika-paṇḍaka).

Furthermore, a certain person becomes a paṇḍaka during the dark fortnight due to the influence of unwholesome karmic fruition, but his fever subsides during the bright fortnight; this is the fortnightly paṇḍaka (pakkha-paṇḍaka).
Finally, he who is devoid of the faculty [of masculinity] even at the moment of rebirth-linking—

This is not a *paṇḍaka* whose [sexual organ] has arisen. Among them, the admission into the order (*pabbajjā*) is not forbidden for the *āsittapaṇḍaka* and the *usūyapaṇḍaka*, but it is forbidden for the other three.
Regarding those as well, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: "For the *pakkhapaṇḍaka*, admission into the order is forbidden during whichever half-month he is a *paṇḍaka*."

136. Regarding the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*): because he possesses both female characteristics (*itthinimitta*) and male characteristics (*purisanimitta*), he is called a hermaphrodite due to the karma that produced the female signs and the karma that produced the male signs. He is of two kinds:
the female hermaphrodite and the male hermaphrodite. Among these, for the female hermaphrodite, the female characteristic is manifest.
The male characteristic of a hermaphrodite (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka) is manifest, while the female characteristic is concealed.

When a female hermaphrodite (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) assumes masculinity among women, her female characteristic becomes concealed and her male characteristic becomes manifest. When a male hermaphrodite assumes femininity among men...
When approaching [another], the male characteristic is concealed and the female characteristic is manifest.
A hermaphrodite female both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive;
however, a hermaphrodite male does not conceive himself, though he does cause another to conceive. This is the distinction between them. Now, regarding these two types...
For one who possesses both sexual organs (ubhatobyañjanaka), there is neither going-forth (pabbajjā) nor full ordination (upasampadā).

137. Regarding "one living in communion by theft" (theyyasaṃvāsaka), there are three types of such persons: one who takes the outward sign by theft, one who lives in communion by theft, and one who takes both by theft.
Among these, he who, having gone forth for himself and entered a monastery, does not count his years as a monk (bhikkhu-vassa) and does not observe seniority according to age...
He accepts veneration, does not decline a seat, and does not appear at the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies;
because he has stolen merely the outward signs [of a monk], he is called a "sign-stealer" (*liṅgatthenaka*).

Furthermore, one who, having been ordained as a novice by monks, goes to another country and, while being a novice, falsely says, "I am ten years or twenty years [ordained]," and [counts] the years of his monkhood...

"Counts in the assembly" means that he accepts veneration according to seniority, declines [being offered] a seat, and appears at the Uposatha, the invitation for criticism (*pavāraṇā*), and so forth;
because he has merely stolen the outward appearance of living together, he is called "one who has stolen the status of living together.
For in this context, every variety of action, such as the counting of a bhikkhu’s years since ordination, should be understood as "living together. Having renounced the training, [saying] "no..."
The same principle applies even if one continues to act in this way while thinking, "Does anyone know me? However, one who has gone forth himself,
goes to a monastery, counts his years as a monk, accepts veneration according to seniority, refuses a seat [for others], and appears at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other ceremonies—
this person is a "double-thief" because of his theft of both the outward sign and the communal life.
This person, though of these three kinds, being one who dwells in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), if unordained, must not be ordained; if already ordained, he must be expelled;
and even if he requests the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) again, he must not be admitted to the going-forth.
In this regard, for the sake of avoiding confusion, the following supplementary matter should be understood:
“Whether due to a king, famine, or a wilderness, or out of fear of disease and enemies,
or for the sake of obtaining robes— whosoever here assumes the outward mark,
as long as he does not consent to cohabitation, his mind remains pure.”
"He is not yet called one who lives in communion through theft.
Herein is the detailed method: In this case, a certain man is angry with a king;
thinking, "In this way my safety will be secured," he takes the [monastic] marks himself and flees. Seeing him, they report it to the king. The king says, "If he has gone forth..."
Thinking, "Nothing can be done about that," he should dispel his anger.

Then, thinking, "The danger from the king has subsided," even though he has not gone into the midst of the Saṅgha but has returned having taken up the marks of a householder, he should be granted the going forth.
Furthermore, if he has developed a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "I have obtained my life by relying on the Teaching; come now, let me go forth," then by that very [feeling]...
If, having arrived in the monastic robes, he does not consent to the duties of a guest, yet— whether questioned or unasked by the monks—
discloses his true identity as it is and requests ordination, he should be ordained after removing those robes. However, if he consents to the duties,
points out a place for those who have gone forth, and follows the entire procedure previously described, including the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth, [he may be ordained].
This person is not to be ordained.
However, there is someone here who, being unable to survive during a famine, takes the robes himself and eats the alms-food provided for all religious sects;
yet, when the famine has passed, he returns having taken up the marks of a householder without ever having entered the midst of the Saṅgha.
Everything is exactly as before.
Another person desires to cross a great wilderness, and the caravan leader is traveling while taking along renunciants.
Thinking, "The caravan leader will take me along in this way," he himself assumes the outward marks and [joins] the caravan leader.

Having together crossed the wilderness and reached a place of safety, he did not descend into the midst of the Saṅgha but returned having taken up the marks of a householder; all of this is exactly as before.
Another, when a danger of disease arose and being unable to live [as a monk], took the marks himself and [partook of] the alms-foods of all the various sectarians.
While he was eating, the danger of illness subsided; yet, without having returned to the midst of the Saṅgha, he came back having assumed the marks of a householder—all of this is exactly as before.
Another man had an enemy who was angry with him and wandered about seeking to kill him. He thought, "In this way, my safety will be secured."

Taking up the monastic emblem himself, he fled. His enemy, searching for him and hearing that he had escaped by going forth into homelessness, thought, "If he has gone forth, nothing can be done to him," and thus he let go of his anger toward him.
Thinking, "The danger from my enemy has been stilled," he returned without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, taking up the layman's emblem once again.
Everything is exactly as before.
Another [monk], having gone to his family’s home, renounced the training and became a householder, thinking: "These robes will be lost here;
even if I were to take them and go to the monastery, they would seize me on the way, calling me a 'thief. What if I..."
“Having made [myself] ready for the body, I shall go. Thus, having dressed and put on his outer robe for the purpose of fetching the robes, he goes to the monastery.
Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and young monks come forward and perform their duties (*vatta*).
He does not accept this; he reveals himself as he truly is. If the monks say, “Now...”
Thinking, "We shall release him," they desire to ordain him by force; having removed his saffron robes, he must be ordained again.

But if, thinking, "These people do not know my state of having returned to the lower life," he claims that very status as a bhikkhu and proceeds with all the previously mentioned formalities such as counting the years of residence and so forth, he is not to be ordained.
Another great novice went to his family home and left the order. Being oppressed by the necessity of performing manual labor, he thought, "Now I shall become a novice again;

moreover, the Elder does not know that I have left the order," and taking that very same bowl and robe, he went back to the monastery. He did not inform the monks of this matter, nor did he declare his status as a novice.
If he admits [to his offense], he is indeed one who dwells in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) and does not receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).

Even if, at the very time of being taken [into the Saṅgha], he thinks, "I will not tell anyone," yet having gone to the monastery he does report it, he is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* by that very act of taking.
Furthermore, even if at the time of being taken the thought "I will inform" has arisen in him, but having gone to the monastery [he asks], "Where..."
When addressed with the words, "Friend, you have gone [to the forest]," if he deceives them by saying, "They no longer know me," and does not disclose it, or if he thinks,
"I will not disclose it," and thereby abandons his responsibility, he too is one living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). However, if at the time of being caught he thinks,
"I will disclose it," and after going to the monastery he does disclose it, he receives the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) once again.
Another is a young novice, or perhaps one who is grown but incompetent.
Having gone forth according to the previous method, he does not wish to perform domestic tasks such as tending calves or guarding cattle.
His relatives, having clothed him in those very same saffron robes and placed an alms-bowl or a vessel in his hand, send him out from the house, saying, "Go; you shall remain a monk."

Thus he goes to a monastery; neither do the monks know him, thinking, "This man, having disrobed, has again gone forth by himself," nor does he himself know, "One who goes forth in this manner is called a thief-living monk.
However, if they grant him full ordination when his years are complete, he is well-ordained. But if [he is ordained] while still in the state of one not yet fully ordained—

While the formal decision on the Vinaya is being deliberated, if he hears it said, "One who goes forth in this manner is called a 'thievish co-resident' (theyyasaṃvāsaka)," he must declare to the monks, "I have done such-and-such.
In this way, he may receive the going-forth again.
But if, thinking, "Now no one knows me," he does not report it, he becomes a thievish co-resident at the very moment he abandons his responsibility.

A bhikkhu who, having renounced the training but not discarded the outward signs, performs an act of immorality— whether he does so or not— then undertakes again the entire procedure previously described,
such as the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth, becomes one who dwells in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). One who,

without having renounced the training and while remaining in the outward signs, engages in sexual intercourse [becomes one who dwells in communion by theft] through the procedure consisting of the calculation of the rains-residence and so forth.
One who commits [an offense] does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft); he receives only the status of one who has gone forth.
However, in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that "this person is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*"; that should not be accepted.
A certain bhikkhu, while still having an aspiration for the saffron robes, put on white garments, engaged in sexual intercourse, and then again [put on] the saffron robes.
If, having dressed himself, he undertakes the formal procedures such as the counting of the rains-retreat (*vassa*), he is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who dwells in communion by theft),
and he receives the mere status of one who has gone forth. However, if he sets aside the saffron robes, puts on white garments, engages in sexual intercourse,
and then again dresses in saffron robes and undertakes the formal procedures such as the counting of the rains-retreat, he becomes a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.
A novice (sāmaṇera), while remaining in his own robes, does not become one who dwells as a thief (theyyasaṃvāsaka) even if he commits an act such as sexual intercourse that renders him non-monastic.

Even if he, still with the intention [to remain a monk], takes off his saffron robes, engages in sexual intercourse, and then puts on the saffron robes again, he does not become one who dwells as a thief.
However, if he lays down the burden of the saffron robes and remains naked...

If one who was formerly a non-monk due to engaging in sexual intercourse and so forth puts on the saffron robe while still wearing white clothes, he is a thief-living-in-the-community (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).

However, if— desiring the state of a householder— he wraps the saffron robe as a loincloth or wears it in some other manner as a householder’s garment for the purpose of testing whether "this mark of a householder suits me or not," he is protected [from being a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*] for the time being.
Having accepted [the robe] with the thought, “It is beautiful,” if he then consents to the mark [of the robe], he becomes one who dwells in communion through theft.

The same principle applies even to the examination and acceptance [of the robe] after having put on a white cloth. However, if he examines it or accepts it after putting a white cloth over the saffron-colored robe already worn, he is indeed protected. The same applies to a bhikkhunī as well.

This is the method. Even she who, longing for the state of a householder, puts on the yellow robe worn by householders—if it is for the purpose of testing whether "the mark of a householder suits me or not," she still guards [her virtue]. But if she accepts it, thinking "it suits me," she does not guard it.
The same principle applies to putting on white robes and to both testing and accepting them. For one who has put on the yellow robe...
But if one puts on a white upper robe and either investigates or accepts [the food],
one indeed protects it. If someone who has gone forth at an old age, disregarding his years and not even staying by the Pāḷi [of the Vinaya], goes past with his side turned toward it,
and when a morsel of rice is lifted with a ladle from large bowls and the like, holds out his bowl and takes it like a hawk seizing a piece of meat, [he does not protect it].

One who is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion through theft) is not one who takes [the status] by counting his own years as a monk; rather, one becomes a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* by taking [the status] while falsely counting [the years].
A novice (*sāmaṇera*) who, being a novice himself, counts false years according to the sequence of novices and takes [the status] does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.
A monk who, being a monk, counts false years according to the sequence of monks and takes [the status] is to be dealt with according to the value of the stolen property (*bhaṇḍaggha*).
139. *Titthiyapakkantaka* (one who has gone over to the sectarians): one who has gone over to, entered among, the sectarians is a *titthiyapakkantaka*;

he also must not be ordained. Herein, this is the analysis: if an ordained monk, thinking "I shall become a sectarian," goes to their dwelling while still wearing his own [monastic] robes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every step taken; as soon as he has assumed their characteristic mark, [he becomes a *titthiyapakkantaka*].

He becomes one who has gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas*. Even one who, thinking for himself, "I shall become a *titthiya*," puts on robes made of *kusa* grass and so forth, is indeed one who has gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas*.
However, if one who is naked, while bathing, looks at himself and thinks, "The state of an Ājīvaka suits me;
I shall become an Ājīvaka," and goes to the dwelling of the Ājīvakas without taking up saffron robes, [he too becomes one who has gone over to their faction].

For every step taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if a sense of shame and moral dread (*hirottappa*) arises within him while on the way, he is released from those offenses after confessing them.

Even if he goes to their dwelling place and, either being exhorted by them or seeing for himself that "the life of these renunciants is exceedingly painful," turns back, he is likewise released. But if he says, "What is so superior about your renunciation?"—
Having been asked, if he says, "The plucking out of hair and beard, etc.," and causes even a single hair to be plucked;
or if he undertakes practices such as the exertion of squatting (ukkuṭikappadhāna); or if he wears garments such as peacock feathers; or if he adopts their distinctive marks (liṅga);

or if he regards this asceticism as supreme, thinking, "This renunciation is the best," and adheres to that state of supremacy—he is not released [from the offense], but becomes one who has gone over to the faction of the heretics (titthiyapakkantaka). If...
However, if one puts on garments of kusa-grass or the like, binds matted hair, or takes up a carrying-pole for the sake of investigation—thinking, "Does my renunciation as a sectarian look good?
Does it not look good?"—one remains protected until one accepts their tenets;
at the very moment of acceptance, one has gone over to the faction of the sectarians. But one whose robes have been stolen may [use] garments of kusa-grass or the like...
One who adopts the insignia of a sectarian out of fear of kings and the like does not become one who has gone over to a sect, because of the absence of such a conviction.
Regarding this, the *Kurundi* states: "This one called 'one who has gone over to a sect' is spoken of in reference to an ordained bhikkhu;
therefore, even if a novice (sāmaṇera) goes to the domain of a sect while still wearing his own insignia, he may again receive both the going-forth and the full ordination."
This has been stated. However, the former type of one living in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) was described as being [defined] by one who is not fully ordained;

therefore, even if a fully ordained monk counts fraudulent rains-residences (*kūṭavassa*), he does not cease to be a *samaṇa*. Even if one who is intent upon the outward signs (*liṅga*) commits a *pārājika* offense and takes the number of monks' rains-residences and so forth, he does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.
