140. "A beast" (*tiracchānagata*) means whether it be a *nāga*, or any other among the *supaṇṇas*, *māṇavakas*, and so forth—even including Sakka, the king of the gods—anyone belonging to the class of non-human beings (*amanussa-jāti*) should, in this context, be understood as a "beast.
Such a person may neither be ordained (*upasampādetabba*) nor given the going-forth (*pabbājetabba*); even if already ordained, he is to be expelled (*nāsetabbo*).

141. Regarding those such as matricides: one who, being himself of human birth, intentionally deprives of life his own biological mother who has become a human female—this person is a matricide by virtue of the immediate (*ānantariya*) kamma of killing a mother.
For him, both going forth and full ordination are prohibited. However, one who [kills] a woman who has become a human female but is not his biological mother...
If a foster mother, a stepmother, or even a biological mother who is not a human female is killed, his going forth is not forbidden, nor does it constitute an immediate offense (*ānantarika*).
Likewise, one who kills a human female mother while himself being an animal does not commit an immediate offense; however, because he is an animal, his going forth is prohibited.
The same principle applies even in the case of one who kills his father. For even if he is the son of a courtesan and does not know,
"This is my father," if he kills the man by whose procreation he was born, he is reckoned as a patricide and incurs an immediate retribution (ānantariya) kamma.
The "murderer of an arahant" should be understood specifically as one who kills a human arahant.

For even if one intentionally deprives of life a child—whether a boy or a girl—who belongs to the human race and has exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*), even if that child has not gone forth into homelessness, one becomes a murderer of an arahant, incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), and his going forth is forbidden. However, [this does not apply to] an arahant of non-human birth, nor to one of human birth...
Or, having killed any remaining noble person (*ariyapuggala*), one does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarika*);
his going forth (*pabbajjā*) is not forbidden, yet the kamma is powerful. Even a beast, having killed a human or an *arahant*, does not incur an immediate retribution;
however, the kamma is grave. This is the analysis (*vinicchaya*) in this matter.

However, one who, like Devadatta, with a malicious mind and a murderous intent, causes even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly to flow from the living body of a Tathāgata, is called a "shedder of blood.
For such a person, both going forth and full ordination are forbidden. But he who, for the sake of curing a disease, like Jīvaka, [uses] a knife...
"Having cut it open and removed the putrid flesh and blood, he makes it healthy; he generates much merit.

One who, like Devadatta, makes the Teaching contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya and splits the Saṅgha by means of one of the four formal acts (*kamma*)—this person is called a "schismatic of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghabhedaka*). His going forth and full ordination (*upasampadā*) are forbidden.
Furthermore, one who violates a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhunī in any of the three ways is a "defiler of bhikkhunīs" (*bhikkhunīdūsaka*).
[This is] the name. For him, both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*) are forbidden.
However, for one who brings about the destruction of virtue through physical contact, neither the going-forth nor the full ordination is forbidden.

Even one who, by force, makes [a person] wear white robes and defiles them while they are unwilling, is indeed a "defiler of a nun" (*bhikkhunī-dūsaka*); for even by force, [if he makes her] wear white robes...

One who defiles a woman who has already consented [to intercourse] does not become a "defiler of a bhikkhunī. Why? Because at the very moment she accepted it while still in the state of a householder, she ceased to be a bhikkhunī.
One who later defiles a woman whose virtue has once lapsed, or who commits misconduct with a *sikkhamānā* or a *sāmaṇerī*, does not become a defiler of a bhikkhunī;
he may even receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thus, these eleven types of persons should be understood as incapable [of full ordination].

Furthermore, for one less than twenty years of age, only full ordination (*upasampadā*) is prohibited, not the going forth (*pabbajjā*); therefore, one who has completed twenty years from the moment of conception should be fully ordained.
For even one who is twenty years old by the calculation of the womb is indeed considered "one who has completed twenty years."
It comes under reckoning. As the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, that first thought which arose in the mother’s womb, that first consciousness which appeared—based on that, there is birth for this person. I allow, bhikkhus, the conferring of full ordination upon one who has been in the womb for twenty weeks.
In this context, one who has dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months and is born on the Great Pavāraṇā day is counted from that point onward.
Up until the nineteenth year, there is the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā); having passed that, one should be ordained on the first day of the fortnight (Pāṭipada).

By this method, the decrease and increase [of the age] should be understood. However, the ancient Elders ordain a novice who is nineteen years old on the first day of the fortnight, after the full-moon day of the month of departure (Nikkhamanīya-puṇṇamāsi). Why? Because in one year...
There are six Uposatha days on the fourteenth; thus, over twenty years, four months are lost.
Kings postpone the rains retreat every third year; thus, over eighteen years, six months are added.
Then, having subtracted the four months lost due to the Uposatha schedule, two months remain. Those two...
Thinking, "Having taken [the candidate] for one month, twenty years will be complete," they become free from doubt and, having passed the full-moon day of the departure-month,
they confer full ordination on the first day of the waxing moon (pāṭipada).
However, in this context, the phrase "one who is nineteen years old" refers to one who will become twenty years old after the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).
Thus it was said. Therefore, one who dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months becomes twenty-one years old; one who dwelt there for seven months becomes twenty-seven years and seven months old.

However, one born after six months does not survive. But for one who ordains a person less than twenty years old under the perception that they are "twenty years old," there is no offense; yet the individual remains unordained.
It happens thus: if, however, after ten years have passed, he ordains another, and the quorum is completed by releasing that person, then the second is fully ordained.
And for him as well, as long as he does not know [the offense], there is neither an obstacle to heaven nor an obstacle to liberation;
but having known it, he must be ordained again.
143. Thus, even though he is free from these faults of going forth, one must not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father, because of the statement:
"Monks, a son must not be ordained without the permission of his mother and father. In this context, "by his mother and father" is said with reference to the biological parents.
If both are present, both must be asked for permission. If the father is deceased, [only the mother's permission is required].
Whether it be the mother or whoever else is living, that person must be asked for permission; likewise, those who have gone forth [as nuns] must also be asked.
When asking, one should either go oneself to ask or send another. Or he himself may be sent with the instruction: "Go, ask your parents for permission, and then return.
If he says, "I have been granted permission," then, having faith in him, one should let him go forth. If the father goes himself...
One who has gone forth may wish to have even his son go forth; he should ask his mother’s permission and then let him go forth.
Or, a mother who wishes to have her daughter go forth should likewise ask her father’s permission and then let her go forth.

If a father has fled because he is weary of his wife and children, and the mother gives her son to the monks, saying, "Let this one go forth," and they ask, "Where is his father? she says, "He is playing at dice."

If he says, "I have fled to play," it is permissible to give him the going-forth. If the mother has fled with some man, but the father says, "Give him the going-forth," the same principle applies here as well.

If the father is away on a journey, and the mother gives permission for the son, saying, "Give him the going-forth," and [the monk] asks, "Where is his father? and she replies, "What does his father have to do with you?"...
"If he says, 'I shall know [the truth],' it is permissible to grant him the going-forth," so it is stated in the *Kurundi*.

If his parents are deceased and the boy has been raised in the presence of his maternal uncles (*cūḷamātā*) and others, when he is being granted the going-forth, his relatives may either cause a quarrel or speak in dispraise;
therefore, for the purpose of preventing such disputes, he should be granted the going-forth after having obtained their permission.
However, there is no offense for one who ordains someone without having asked permission.
Those who take [a child] at a young age and raise him are called "parents," and the same principle applies to them as well. A son lives by depending on himself, not on his parents.
Even if he is a king, he must be ordained only after having asked permission. If, having been ordained with the consent of his parents, he later disrobes...
Even if he has gone forth a hundred times and then disrobed, he must be ordained only after being asked for permission again and again each time he arrives.
Even if they say, "This man has returned home after disrobing;
he does not do work for us, nor does he fulfill his duties toward you after going forth; there is no need to ask his permission; whenever he arrives..."
"Please let him go forth"—if he has been relinquished in this manner, it is permissible to let him go forth again even without asking for permission.
Furthermore, if someone was given [to the Saṅgha] at a very young age with the words, "This one is given to you;
when you wish, then let him go forth," he too may be let go forth each time he arrives, without having to ask for permission again. However, as for one who, while still a child...
“Venerable sir, please let him go forth. Having given his consent, they later refuse when he has reached maturity;
such a person must not be ordained without having asked permission. Another, having quarreled with his parents, comes saying, “Ordain me!
When told, “Come after you have asked permission,” he replies, “I will not go; if you do not ordain me, I shall burn down the monastery.”
If he says, "I shall strike you with a weapon, or I shall bring harm to your relatives or supporters by cutting down their groves and so forth,
or I shall die by falling from a tree, or I shall enter the midst of thieves,
or I shall go to another country," it is permissible to ordain him for the sake of protecting him. But if, for him...

If the parents come and say, "Why have you caused our son to go forth?", one should inform them of the matter and tell them, "We caused him to go forth for the sake of his protection; may you be supported by your son.
However, it is indeed permissible to admit one who climbs a tree thinking, "I will jump from the tree," but then lets go of his hands and feet.
If one person goes abroad and requests the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), he should be ordained if he has gone after having asked for permission.

If he has not, a young monk (*dahara-bhikkhu*) should be sent to ask for his permission, and then he may be ordained. If the distance is very great, it is permissible even to ordain him and then send him back with the monks so that he may see [his relatives].
However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: "If it is far away and the road is a great wilderness..."

“Having gone, I shall ask for permission,” thinking thus, it is permissible to grant the going-forth. But if the parents have many children and say, “Venerable sir, among these children, you may let whichever one you wish go forth,” then after examining the children, whichever one he desires should be allowed to go forth.
Even if the entire family or the whole village has given their consent...
“If, venerable sir, there is someone in this family or village whom you wish [to ordain], please let him go forth”—in such a case, whoever is desired may be ordained.

144. Even when one is ordaining someone who is free from the defects regarding going forth and has been permitted by his mother and father, if that person’s hair has not yet been cut and there are other monks within the same boundary, one must request the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*) for the purpose of cutting the hair.

In this regard, the procedure for seeking permission is as follows: having assembled the monks within the boundary and having brought the one seeking admission there, one should say three times, twice, or once:
"Venerable sirs, I seek permission from the Saṅgha for the shaving of this child's head.
And here, "I seek permission for the shaving of this child's head" means—
It is indeed permissible to say, “I ask permission for this person’s undertaking of the ascetic life,” or “This person wishes to become an ascetic,” or “This person wishes to go forth.
If it is a suitable location where ten, twenty, or thirty bhikkhus reside, and the limit of their dwelling is known—
whether by going to the place where they stand or sit— one should proceed in the same manner as previously described.

One must ask for permission. Even if one sends junior monks or novices instead of the person seeking admission, it is permissible to have them ask for permission by saying, "Venerable sir, there is a person seeking admission;
we ask for permission regarding his shaving," and so forth. If some monks have entered a dwelling or a thicket and are sleeping or engaged in the duties of a recluse...

Or they perform [the act], and even while seeking those who have not yet asked for permission, they perceive that "we have asked permission from everyone," thinking that ordination (*pabbajjā*) is a minor formal act (*lahukakamma*);
therefore, one who has gone forth is well-ordained, and there is no offense for the one who ordains.
However, if the monastery is large and the residence of many thousands of monks, even if they were to assemble all the monks...

It is difficult, let alone to ask for permission in the proper sequence; rather, he should be ordained while standing within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (a partial boundary) or after traveling to a river, the ocean, or similar locations.

However, for one who is newly shaven, or a renegade, or belongs to another group such as the Nigaṇṭhas, or whose hair is two finger-breadths long or less than two finger-breadths long, there is no need for the shaving of hair; therefore, the *bhaṇḍukamma* (tonsure) is performed.

It is permissible to give the going-forth even without having asked permission in such cases. However, one whose hair exceeds two finger-breadths—even if he wears it in a single tuft—must have his shaving performed only after asking permission;
and when giving the going-forth after having thus asked permission, one should give the going-forth only if he possesses a full set of bowl and robes. If he...
It is not prohibited; it is permissible to grant the going-forth even with borrowed bowl and robes, and it is also permissible to grant the going-forth after taking them on trust in a common place.

However, if one has come having taken an unbaked bowl and cloths intended for robes, then as long as the bowl is being baked and the robes are being made, for him staying in the monastery during that time, there is almsfood that has not been specifically requested.
It is permissible to give [food]; it is permissible to eat from shallow bowls (*thālaka*). Before the meal, it is permissible to give a portion of material goods equal to the *sāmaṇera*’s share;
however, the assignment of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*), as well as tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*), designated meals (*uddesabhatta*), invitations (*nimantana*), and so forth, are not permissible.
After the meal, it is also permissible to give a medicinal portion—such as oil, rice, honey, or molasses—that is equal to the *sāmaṇera*’s share.
If he is ill, it is permissible to prepare medicine for him and to perform all the duties of nursing, just as one would for a novice (sāmaṇera).
However, it is not permissible to confer full ordination (upasampadā) upon one who seeks it using borrowed bowl and robes.
“Monks, one should not be ordained with borrowed bowl and robes; whoever should ordain [in this manner], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Thus it was said. Therefore, he should be ordained only when he possesses a complete set of bowl and robes.

If he has none, and his preceptor and teacher are willing to give them, or if other monks give them after relinquishing them without expectation of return, then a bowl and robes sufficient for formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) must be provided.
However, there is an offense for one who ordains using a borrowed bowl or robe.
However, the formal act (*kamma*) does not become invalid.
146. Even when one is ordaining someone who possesses a complete set of bowl and robes, if there is the opportunity, one should perform the ordination oneself.
If one is occupied with reciting the scriptures (*uddesa*), questioning (*paripuccha*), and so forth, and thus finds no opportunity, a young bhikkhu should be instructed as follows:
“Ordain him. Even if the young bhikkhu has not been so instructed, it is permissible for him to ordain [the candidate] with the preceptor in mind.
If there is no young bhikkhu available, even a novice (sāmaṇera) should be told:

“Go, having led him to the broken boundary (khaṇḍasīma), ordained him, clothed him in the saffron robes, and then return. However, the refuges must be administered by oneself. Thus, he is ordained by a bhikkhu alone.
It happens thus. For no one other than a bhikkhu is permitted to ordain a man, nor anyone other than a bhikkhunī for a woman;
however, a novice (sāmaṇera) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī) are permitted to give the saffron robes by command. The shaving of hair may be performed well by anyone.
But if he is of suitable appearance, possessed of the causal factors, well-known, renowned, and of noble birth, then even after granting him leave, [the teacher] himself...
He should be ordained, [but] he must not be sent away with the instruction, "Take a handful of clay, bathe, and come back. For those who desire to go forth have a strong initial enthusiasm;
however, later on, upon seeing the saffron robes and the razor for shaving the hair, they become terrified and flee from that very place.
Therefore, having personally led him to a bathing ford—if he is not too young—
He should be told, “Bathe,” but his hair must be washed by himself using clay.
However, a young boy may bathe him by himself after descending into the water and rubbing him with cow-dung and clay.
Even if he has scabs or boils, he should attend to him thoroughly and without disgust, just as a mother does not feel disgust for her child.
He should be bathed by rubbing him repeatedly, starting from the hands and feet and proceeding to the head. Why?

Because through such service, sons of good family develop strong affection for their teachers, preceptors, and the Dispensation; they possess intense reverence and become those whose nature is not to turn back.
Having dispelled any discontent that has arisen, they reach the state of an elder and become grateful and mindful of what has been done for them.
Likewise, at the time of bathing or when shaving the hair and beard, one should not say, "You are well-known and famous;
now, by depending on you, we shall not suffer for lack of requisites. Nor should any other talk that does not lead to liberation be spoken.
Instead, having said to him, "Friend, reflect thoroughly; establish mindfulness," one should [teach] the skin-pentad meditation subject (*tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).

It should be explained. And when explaining, it should be explained by making manifest its impurity, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness—by way of its color, shape, smell, location, and source—or its lifeless and insentient nature.

For if he has previously practiced the preparatory exercises and developed his meditation, he will be like one who, having been pierced by a thorn, awaits the arrival of the sun for a fully ripened boil.

And as soon as he began to direct his attention to the meditation subject—the lotus that had fully blossomed—his knowledge proceeded, pulverizing the mountain of defilements just as Indra’s thunderbolt shatters a mountain; he attained Arahantship at the very tip of the razor.
Indeed, all those who have attained Arahantship at the tip of the razor did so after obtaining such an opportunity for hearing [the Dhamma] through a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta).
It must be based on the method given by the teacher, not without such a basis. Therefore, from the very beginning, he should be addressed with a discourse of this kind.
Furthermore, once his hair has been shaved, his head and body should be rubbed with turmeric powder or scented powder to remove the lay scent;
then he should be made to accept the saffron robes three times, twice, or once.
Furthermore, if the teacher or preceptor does not give it into his hand but robes him himself,
that is permissible. If he instructs another— whether a junior monk, a novice, or a lay follower— saying, "Friend,
take these saffron robes and robe this person," or if he instructs that person directly, saying, "Take these and robe him," all of that is permissible.

All of that has been given by the monk himself. However, whatever lower robe (*nivāsana*) or upper robe (*pārupana*) he wears without having been formally assigned to him must be removed and given back again.
For it is only a yellow robe (*kāsāya*) that has been given—either directly by hand or by formal assignment—that is permissible for a monk;
one that has not been given is not permissible. Even if it belongs to that very person [the donor], who...
But the discussion regarding those whose preceptor is the root [of their ordination] follows.

147. Having thus caused him to put on the saffron robes, having caused him to arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, having caused him to pay homage at the feet of the monks assembled there, and then having caused him to sit in the kneeling posture for the purpose of taking the refuges—
Having had him raise his hands in *añjali*, he should be told, "Speak thus," or "Speak what I say.

Then the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or the teacher (*ācariya*) should grant him the refuges (*saraṇa*) in the manner beginning with "I go for refuge to the Buddha," following exactly the sequence already mentioned, and not out of order. For if even a single word or a single syllable...
If one gives them out of order, or if after giving the refuge in the Buddha three times, one then gives each of the others three times,
the refuges have not been properly given. Furthermore,
having rejected this admission by going for refuge, the admission that was authorized is [based on] purity in one respect.
It is permissible; however, the going forth as a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is permissible only when there is purity on both sides, not when there is purity on only one side.

Therefore, regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*), if the preceptor (*ācariya*) performs the ritual while avoiding defects in the motion (*ñatti*) and defects in the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), it is well-performed.
But regarding the going forth, these three refuges [must be recited] with the consonants *bu*, *dha*, and so forth...
The teacher and the pupil must both speak without failing in the perfection of the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the places of pronunciation (*karaṇa*).
It is not permissible if the teacher is able to speak but the pupil is not; or if the pupil is able to speak but the teacher is not;
or if neither of them is able to speak. However, it is permissible if both are able to speak. And these—

While giving [the precepts], one should give them either by making them connected with a single nasalization, such as “Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī,” or by making them end in the letter *m* through separation, such as “Buddham saraṇam gacchāmī. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it says:
“Having announced his name: ‘Venerable sir, I, Buddharakkhita, for as long as life lasts...’”
As for the statement, “I go to the Buddha for refuge,” that is not found even in the *Ekaṭṭhakathā*, nor is it mentioned in the *Pāḷi*;
it is merely their own preference and therefore should not be accepted. For the refuge does not become invalid for one who does not speak in that way.
And by this much, one is established on the level of a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).
148. But if he is capable and of a wise nature, then the training rules (sikkhāpada) should be recited to him right there. How? Just as they were recited by the Blessed One. For this has been said:
"I allow, monks, ten training rules for novices (sāmaṇera), and that novices should train in them:
abstention from taking life, abstention from taking what is not given, abstention from unchaste conduct, abstention from false speech..."
“Abstention from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; abstention from eating at improper times;

abstention from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing unsuitable spectacles; abstention from wearing garlands, using perfumes and unguents, and the adornment and beautification by ornaments; abstention from high and large beds;
and abstention from accepting gold and silver.”

In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that the giving of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is like the giving of the refuges, as in: “Venerable sir, I, named so-and-so, undertake for as long as life lasts the training rule of abstaining from taking life. This is found neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the commentaries;
therefore, they should be recited exactly according to the Canon. For going forth (*pabbajjā*) occurs through the very act of going for refuge.
The training rules (*sikkhāpada*), however, need only be known for the purpose of fulfilling those very rules;
therefore, it is permissible to explain them by means of their meaning in any language whatsoever to one who is unable to learn them according to the method presented in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
This applies until one knows the training rules that must be observed by oneself regarding the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe, and regarding standing, sitting, and so forth.

Furthermore, as long as he is not skilled in the procedures for drinking, eating, and so forth, he should not be sent to the dining hall, the place where voting tickets are distributed, or any other such location;

he should be kept close at hand and treated like a young child. Everything that is allowable and unallowable must be explained to him, including matters concerning his undergarments, upper robes, and so on.
He is to be disciplined according to the *Abhisamācārika* rules.
Furthermore: "Monks, I allow you to expel a novice who possesses ten qualities:
he is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, one who practices unchastity, a speaker of falsehood, a drinker of intoxicants, and one who speaks dispraise of the Buddha..."

Having thoroughly avoided these ten grounds for expulsion as thus described— namely, speaking dispraise of the Buddha, speaking dispraise of the Dhamma, speaking dispraise of the Saṅgha, holding wrong view,
and being a defiler of bhikkhunīs— one who fulfills the higher conduct should train well in the tenfold virtue.
149. Furthermore, whoever commits even one of the ten acts leading to expulsion, such as the taking of life, must be expelled by the removal of his emblem (*liṅganāsanā*).
For among the three types of expulsion, it is only the removal of the emblem that is intended here.
And whereas monks incur various specific offenses for acts such as the taking of life, it is not the same for novices (*sāmaṇera*). Indeed, a novice, having killed even an ant or a termite...
Even a maṅgulaṇḍaka (one who has committed a grave offense) reaches the state of being destroyed once he has broken [the precepts];
at that very moment, his taking of refuge, his choosing of a preceptor, and his taking possession of a dwelling cease;
he no longer receives a share from the Saṅgha, and only the mere outward mark remains. If he is indeed full of faults, he will not [attain] restraint in the future.

He remains [in his position], and he should be expelled. But if, having suddenly become disenchanted and thinking, "I have done wrong," he wishes to stand once more in restraint, there is no need for the act of changing his robes;

the refuges should be given to him while he is still wearing his usual lower and upper garments, and a preceptor should be assigned. However, the training rules are fulfilled by the mere going for refuge alone. For the going for refuge of novices—
It is similar to the formal procedure for the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of monks;

therefore, just as with the monks, by this [act] the ten precepts are indeed undertaken along with the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). Nevertheless, they should be given again for the purpose of strengthening them and for establishing oneself in future restraint.
If the refuges were taken again during the earlier period, then during the later period...
He shall receive the rains-residence gift. If [the robes] were taken during the later [rains-retreat], the gain should be given after the Saṅgha has obtained permission.

One becomes a non-recluse—and is subject to expulsion—by the mere taking of what is not given even by way of a blade of grass, by misconduct in any of the three paths regarding unchastity, or by speaking a lie even with a sense of humor.

Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, however, for a bhikkhu who drinks intoxicants starting from the very seed—even if he does not know [that they are intoxicants]—there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
A novice (sāmaṇera), on the other hand, incurs a breach of virtue only if he drinks knowing [it to be intoxicants], not if he drinks unknowingly.
As for his other five training rules (sikkhāpada), if these are broken, he is not to be expelled; rather, a disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma) must be performed. Regarding the training rule...

However, it is permissible whether the act has been repeated or not; yet, having pressed him with disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma), it must certainly be given for the sake of establishing him in future restraint.

Regarding the speaking of dispraise, however, it refers either to the Buddha by way of the opposites of such qualities as "the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," or to the Dhamma by way of the opposites of such qualities as "well-expounded," or [to the Saṅgha] by way of the opposites of such qualities as "well-practiced."

If he speaks in dispraise of the Saṅgha or censures and reviles the Three Jewels, he should be restrained by his teachers, preceptors, and others, who should show him the danger in speaking such dispraise, saying, "Do not speak thus.
"If, even when told up to three times, he does not desist, he is to be expelled by the 'removal of thorns' (kaṇṭakanāsanā)," so it is stated in the *Kurundi*. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*...

However, it has been stated: "If, when being addressed in this way, he relinquishes that adherence, then after having him perform a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*), he should be made to confess his transgression.
If he does not relinquish it, but remains having taken up and maintained that very same [view], he should be expelled by the removal of his status (*liṅganāsanā*).

This is appropriate; for it is this very expulsion that is intended here. The same method applies even in the case of one with wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhika*). For regarding eternalism and annihilationism...

If a person holding a particular wrong view relinquishes [the view] when exhorted by his teachers and others, he should be made to undergo disciplinary action and then asked to confess his transgression;

however, if he does not relinquish it, he should be expelled. Furthermore, although a defiler of nuns is certainly included under the term "one who is unchaste," one who is unchaste but desires to abide in restraint for the future may be granted the refuges and then ordained.

It is permissible. It should be understood that this tenth factor, "one who has violated a bhikkhunī," is stated separately because it shows that even one who desires to abide in restraint for the future does not receive the going-forth (pabbajjā), let alone full ordination (upasampadā).
150. "Monks, I allow you to impose a disciplinary measure upon a novice (sāmaṇera) who possesses five factors."
"Because of the statement: 'He strives for the non-gain of the bhikkhus; he strives for the harm of the bhikkhus;
he strives for the displacement of the bhikkhus; he reviles the bhikkhus; he insults the bhikkhus;
he causes dissension among the bhikkhus,' these are five factors. Together with the last five training rules, beginning with eating at the improper time, there are ten."
Regarding the grounds for disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma-vatthūni*): "What kind of disciplinary action should be performed here? [The Buddha replied:

"Monks, I allow that a restriction be made wherever one dwells or from where one returns," because of this statement, a restriction must be made—saying, "Do not enter here"—wherever one dwells or enters. By both of these means, [one protects] oneself...
The cell and the lodging obtained by seniority have already been mentioned. Therefore, the entire Saṅghārāma must not be enclosed;
for one who does so, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred, because it has been stated: "Monks, the entire Saṅghārāma must not be enclosed;
whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Nor should food brought through the gate be enclosed.
And one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by doing so, because it has been said: "Monks, food should not be obstructed at the gateway of the mouth;

whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, for all such applications—including saying, "Do not eat today, do not consume," or even putting away the bowl and robes with the thought, "I shall prevent him from eating"—there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who behaves improperly.

However, it is permissible to administer a disciplinary measure (*daṇḍakamma*) to a difficult-to-correct novice (*dubbaca-sāmaṇera*), and having shown him the rice gruel, the meal, or the bowl and robes, to say, "When such a disciplinary measure has been brought upon you, you shall receive this.
For the Blessed One has stated that the disciplinary measure is indeed a deterrent (*āvaraṇa*).
But the Elders who compiled the Dhamma [stated]: "In accordance with the offense, [the punishment consists of] water, wood, sand, and so forth..."

It is said, "The act of making him bring [the robe] back should also be performed"; therefore, that too should be done, but out of compassion with the thought, "He will desist, he will abstain," and not through a wicked disposition proceeding in such a manner as thinking, "He will be ruined" or "He will disrobe.
And regarding the phrase "I am performing a disciplinary act," it means one should have him lie down on hot stones, or have bricks and the like placed upon his head, or [submerge him in] water...
or to cause [him] to enter, it is not permitted.
Even without asking the preceptor, disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma) must not be imposed, because of the statement: "Monks, one should not place an obstacle without asking the preceptor;
whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In this context, however, [regarding the words] "to you..."
When it has been said three times, "This is such-and-such an offense of the novice;
perform a disciplinary act against him," if that preceptor does not perform the disciplinary act, it is permissible for [the monk] himself to do so.
Even if the preceptor says from the beginning, "If there are faults among my novices, you should perform the disciplinary act," it is still permissible to do so. Just as...

And just as it is permissible to administer disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*) against novices (*sāmaṇera*), so too is it permissible to do so for co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and pupils (*antevāsika*).
However, one must not incite others’ assemblies; for one who incites them, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is incurred.
This is because of the statement: “Monks, one must not incite another’s assembly; whoever should incite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, [one should say]: “To you...”

Thinking, "We shall give him an alms-bowl; we shall give him a robe," one may win over others for the sake of receiving service from them—whether they be novices or fully ordained monks—even including a monk of immoral conduct—but it is not permitted to break up another's assembly and take [them] away.
However, it is permissible to speak of the danger, saying: "When you came here to bathe, you were smeared with excrement..."

"...as if living in dependence upon one who is immoral. If that person, having recognized [the situation] himself, requests formal affiliation (*upajjhā*) or dependence (*nissaya*), it is permissible to grant it.
Thus ends the compendium of Vinaya adjudications not found in the canonical texts (*pāḷimuttaka*).
The Discussion on the Determination of Going-forth is finished.
23. The Discussion on the Determination of Dependence.
151. Regarding "dependence" (*nissaya*): here, by whom should this dependence be given? By whom should it not be given? To whom...

To whom should it be given, to whom should it not be given; how is it received; how is it pacified; upon whom should one live in dependence, and upon whom should one not live in dependence? Regarding that, as for "to whom should it be given, to whom should it not be given," it is said here:
"Monks, I allow a learned, competent monk—whether ten years of standing or more than ten years—"

And because of the statement, "to grant full ordination or to give dependence," this [dependence] must be given by one who is competent and capable—namely, one who has ten years or more than ten years of seniority for the purpose of granting full ordination—and not by another. If another gives it, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
And here, by the term "competent," one who is learned and capable of supervising the assembly (*parisupaṭṭhāpaka*) is to be understood. By the supervisor...
Indeed, at the very least, one must master and have committed to memory the two Vibhaṅgas in order to guide an assembly in the Vinaya;

if one is unable to do so, one should prepare them for recitation together with three other persons. Furthermore, one must learn what constitutes a valid legal act (*kamma*) and what does not, as well as the rules of conduct (*vatta*) from the Khandhaka.
Moreover, for the purpose of guiding an assembly in the Abhidhamma, if one is a Majjhima-bhāṇaka...
The *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka* should be mastered; by a Dīgha-bhāṇaka, the *Mahāvagga*;
by a Saṃyutta-bhāṇaka, either the first three vaggas or the *Mahāvagga*; by an Aṅguttara-bhāṇaka, half of a *nikāya*, either from the beginning or from the end.
For one who is unable, it is also permissible to master it starting from the *Tikanipāta*. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, [it says]: "One..."
It is said: "For one who is learning, it is permissible to learn either the Catukka-nipāta or the Pañcaka-nipāta.
A reciter of the Jātakas must learn the Jātaka together with its commentary (Sāṭṭhakathā); less than that is not permitted. It is stated in the Mahāpaccarī:
"It is also permissible to learn the Dhammapada together with its narrative background (vatthu). Having compiled [the material] from here and there, [one may learn] at least the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka.
"It is permissible" or "it is not permissible"—this has been rejected in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*;
in the other [commentaries], there is no discussion at all. It is not stated that anything from the Abhidhamma should be taken up.

However, for one who is proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka along with their commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*), and for whom there is no such textual burden regarding the Suttanta, [he may] attend an assembly.
He does not obtain it. However, one who has mastered a body of texts of the prescribed measure from both the Suttanta and the Vinaya is indeed "learned" (bahussuta) as a supporter of an assembly;
such a person is a leader of the quarters, one who can go wherever he wishes, and is able to support an assembly—this is the one intended by the term "competent" (byatta) in this context.

However, one who is able to perform services such as nursing for a sick pupil (*antevāsika*) or co-resident (*saddhivihārika*) is intended here by the term "competent" (*paṭibala*). As for what was said:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not confer full ordination, should not give dependence, and should not have a novice attend upon him:
he is not endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (*asekha*)."
He does not possess the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training; he does not possess the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training;
he does not possess the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training; he does not possess the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Monks, a monk who possesses these five factors should not grant full ordination.
"One should not give dependence; one should not have a novice attend upon oneself.

Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five other qualities should not confer full ordination, should not give dependence, and should not have a novice attend upon himself: if he himself does not possess the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training..."
He does not himself possess the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, nor does he encourage others in the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training.
He does not himself possess the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, nor does he encourage others in the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training.
He does not himself possess the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, nor does he encourage others in the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training. Himself...
He does not himself possess the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, nor does he encourage others to attain the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training.

He does not himself possess the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training, nor does he encourage others to attain the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. It is by these five factors, monks, that...
“A monk who possesses [these] qualities should not grant full ordination, should not give formal support, and should not have a novice attend upon him.

Furthermore, monks, a monk who possesses five other qualities should not grant full ordination, should not give formal support, and should not have a novice attend upon him. He is faithless, he is shameless, and he is reckless.”

“He is ill-behaved, he is lazy, and he is muddle-minded. Possessed of these five factors, monks, a monk should not grant full ordination, should not give formal support, and should not have a novice attend upon him.
Furthermore, monks, possessed of another five factors, a monk should not grant full ordination...”

He should not give dependence; he should not have a novice attend upon him. He has failed in virtue regarding higher morality, he has failed in conduct regarding proper behavior, he has failed in view regarding excessive views, he is of little learning, and he is of poor wisdom.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should neither confer full ordination nor...
“Support should be given, but a novice should not be attended to.

Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five other qualities should not confer full ordination, should not give support, and should not attend to a novice. He is not competent [to care for] his pupil or his co-resident.”
or to attend to one who is ill or to have another attend to them; or to dispel dissatisfaction or to have another dispel it;
or to remove, in accordance with the Dhamma, remorse that has arisen; he does not know the offense, nor does he know the way to emerge from the offense.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not grant full ordination.
“Support should not be given; a novice should not be attended to.
Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five other qualities should not confer full ordination, should not give support, and should not attend to a novice.
He is not capable of [instructing] his pupil or his co-resident...”
or to train them in the training of proper conduct, to discipline them in the training fundamental to the holy life,
to discipline them in the Abhidhamma, to discipline them in the Abhivinaya, or to separate from what is contrary to the Dhamma any arisen wrong view. Monks,
a monk endowed with these five qualities should not grant full ordination, nor should he give formal support (nissaya).
A novice should not be attended by him.
"Furthermore, monks, a monk who possesses five other qualities should not confer full ordination, should not give formal support, and should not attend a novice.
He does not know what is an offense; he does not know what is no offense."
He does not know a light offense; he does not know a heavy offense;
furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have not been properly handed down to him in detail, nor well analyzed, nor well mastered, nor well determined, either by way of the rules or by way of the phrasing.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not confer full ordination.
“Dependence should not be given; a novice should not be attended to.
Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five other qualities should not grant full ordination, should not give dependence, and should not attend to a novice:
he does not know what is an offense, and he does not know what is not an offense.”
“He does not know what is a light offense; he does not know what is a heavy offense; he has fewer than ten years of seniority.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not grant full ordination, should not give dependence, and should not have a novice attend upon him,” and so forth. That too—
“I allow, monks, a competent and capable monk— whether ten years of standing or more than ten years—
to confer full ordination and to give formal dependence. This was stated for the purpose of showing the detailed characteristics of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and teacher (*ācariya*),
which had been mentioned only in brief in this way.
In this context, some things are rejected on account of being improper, while others are rejected on account of the factors of an offense.

For instance, in the three pentads—namely, "not with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training," "not oneself being one beyond training," and "being faithless"—the rejection is made on account of being improper, not on account of the factors of an offense.
This is because one who [possesses] the aggregates of virtue and so forth of one beyond training...

If one who lacks these qualities himself and is unable to encourage others toward them continues to lead a community while remaining possessed of faults such as lack of faith, his assembly will indeed decline in virtue and so forth rather than increase;
therefore, the statement "he should not grant full ordination" and so on was spoken by way of what is improper, not by way of being an offense-factor.
For the status of preceptor or teacher does not belong to one who has only destroyed the taints.
It was permitted by the Blessed One; had it been permitted for him alone, he would not have said, "If dissatisfaction has arisen in the preceptor," and so forth.
However, because a community whose taints are destroyed does not decline in virtue and the other qualities, it was therefore stated:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors may confer full ordination," and so on.

In such passages as "one who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue" (*adhisīle sīlavipanna*), one who has committed a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa* offense is called "one who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue.
One who has committed the other five classes of offenses is called "one who has failed in conduct regarding improper conduct" (*ajjhācāre ācāravipanna*).
Having abandoned right view and being possessed of an extremist view, one is called "one who has failed in view regarding excessive view" (*atidiṭṭhiyā diṭṭhivipanna*). As much as has been heard...

One who maintains a retinue should possess [learning], yet because he lacks it, he is "of little learning. Because he does not know what ought to be known by him—such as the nature of offenses—he is "of poor wisdom.
In this pentad, the first three terms are stated in terms of being improper, while the latter two are stated in terms of the factors of an offense.
“He does not know the offense” means that when it is said, “This is what was done by me,” he does not know, “This person has fallen into such-and-such an offense.
“He does not know the method of purification” means that he does not know, “The purification from this offense—whether it leads to rehabilitation or to confession—is as follows.
For in this pentad, the first two terms are used in the sense of being improper.
The [first] three have been stated; the latter three are by way of the factors of an offense (*āpattiaṅga*).
"In the training regarding proper conduct" (*ābhisamācārikāya sikkhāya*) means he is not capable of training [others] in the conduct of the Khandhakas.

"In that which pertains to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyakāya*) means he is not capable of training [others] in the training-rule formulations (*sekha-pannatti*) for those in training (*sekkha*). "In the Abhidhamma" means he is not capable of training [others] in the analysis of mind and matter (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda*).
"Not competent" means [he is] not capable. "In regard to the Abhivinaya" means he is not capable of guiding [others] in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
And "not capable of guiding" means everywhere it means he is unable to train [them].
"To separate from the Dhamma" means to cause [him] to be released by means of the Dhamma, that is, by means of a legal reason. In all instances within this group of five, there is an offense.
“In the detailed explanation of the fivefold set beginning with ‘he does not know the offense,’” refers to [the text] together with the two Vibhaṅgas.
“Not well-arrived” means not properly arrived. “Well-analyzed” means well-distinguished, being free from the faults of confusion regarding words, phrases, and sequences.
“Well-proclaimed” means they are mastered, come forth from the mouth, and well-determined. “From the Suttas” means from the Khandhaka and Parivāra.

They are well-determined by way of the suttas that must be cited. Regarding the "explanation of the phrasing" (*anubyañjana-sota*): they are well-determined through the completion of syllables and words;
they are unbroken and their syllables are not inverted. By this, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) is indicated, for this determination arises from the commentary.
In this group of five as well, there is an offense in all instances, even in the group of five at the conclusion of being less than ten years [of seniority].
The same method applies. Thus, in the first three sets of five, there are three items each; in the fourth, two items;
and in the fifth, two items—thus all four sets of five are stated by way of what is improper (*ayutta*). In the fourth set of five, there are two items; in the fifth, three;
and the sixth, seventh, and eighth are three sets of five—thus all four sets of five are stated by way of the factors of an offense (*āpatti-aṅga*).
In the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha), however, by way of the opposite of what was stated, eight sets of five [qualities] have indeed been handed down, beginning with:
"Monks, a monk endowed with five factors may grant full ordination, may give dependence, and may have a novice attend upon him;
he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekkha-sīlakkhandha)," and so forth. In all these instances, there is no offense.

152. Regarding the question of to whom it should be given and to whom it should not be given: here, it should be given to one who possesses a sense of shame (*lajjī*); it should not be given to the other. This is because of the statement:
"Monks, support (*nissaya*) should not be given to those who lack a sense of shame; whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even for one living in dependence (*nissāya*), one should not live in dependence upon someone who lacks a sense of shame. For this has been said: "Monks,..."
"One should live depending on those who are shameless; whoever should live [depending on them], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Here, "alajjīnaṃ" is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative; it means that one should not live depending on shameless persons.
Therefore, when one has gone to a new place and is told, "Come, monk, receive dependence," even for four or five days—
The dependence (nissaya) should be taken after examining the conscientiousness of the one granting the dependence.
For it is said: "I allow you, monks, to wait for four or five days until I know whether he is like the community of monks.
If, having heard from the monks that "the Elder is conscientious," one wishes to take the dependence on the very day he arrives, but the Elder says, "Wait for now..."
“Wait until spring, you shall know,” [the teacher says]. After observing his conduct for a few days, it is permissible for him to grant formal dependence (*nissaya*).
However, when one goes to the place where dependence is normally received, it must be taken on that very day; there is no allowance of even a single day’s delay.
If the teacher has no opportunity during the first watch of the night, and not obtaining an opportunity, [the student thinks], “I will take it at dawn.”

If he sleeps and does not even know that dawn has broken, there is no offense. However, if he sleeps without the intention (*ābhoga*) of "I will take it up," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the rising of dawn.
Having gone to a place never visited before and stayed for two or three days, one who wishes to depart must live there without formal dependence (*anissita*).
But for one who forms the attachment (*ālaya*) thinking, "I will stay for seven days," dependence is required.

It should be accepted. If the elder says, "What is the need for formal dependence (nissaya) for one staying for seven days?", from the time it is refused, he receives the same privileges as one who has received dependence.
"I allow you, monks, for a monk traveling on a journey who cannot obtain dependence to live without dependence."
However, because of the statement "the basis," if one traveling on a long journey does not find someone to grant dependence who is also traveling on that same journey,
it is permissible for him to travel for many days without dependence while remaining without formal reliance (*anissita*).
If he enters any monastery where he has previously lived after having received dependence there before, [he may stay] for one night.
One must also receive formal dependence (*nissaya*) during the summer retreat (*vassa*). If one stays for a few days while resting on the way or while searching for a caravan, there is no offense.
However, during the rains retreat, one must dwell in a fixed residence and receive formal dependence.
But for one traveling by boat, there is no offense if, even when the rains have arrived, one does not obtain formal dependence. If, however, on the way...
If one is ill, it is permissible for one who cannot obtain formal dependence (*nissaya*) to live without being under dependence.
Even a caregiver for the sick, when requested by the sick person, is permitted to live without being under dependence. For this has been said:
"Monks, I allow a monk who is ill, if he cannot obtain formal dependence, to dwell without being under dependence; I allow..."
“Monks, if a monk who is attending to the sick finds himself without formal support (nissaya) and is being asked for it, he may live without support.
However, if he is told, “Ask me,” yet being ill, does not ask because of pride, he must go [to another].
“I allow, monks, a forest-dwelling monk who is considering his own well-being to live without support.”
However, for one who does not obtain a formal support (nissaya) and remains independent, because of the statement, "When a suitable provider of support arrives,

then I shall live under his support," he should observe such a comfortable dwelling where, while residing there, there is ease through the attainment of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā); thus, not obtaining a support, he remains independent.
This must be understood. Furthermore, neither the stream-enterer, nor the once-returner, nor the non-returner, nor the arahant receives this exemption;

nor does one who has attained stable concentration or insight. As for the foolish worldling who has abandoned his meditation subject, there is no question at all. However, he whose serenity or insight is still tender receives this exemption.
The inclusion of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*) is also permitted for this very person.

Therefore, even after this individual has invited his teacher and the teacher has departed, it is permissible for him to dwell without formal dependence (*anissita*) until the full moon of Āsāḷhī, provided he maintains the intention:
"When a suitable provider of dependence arrives, I shall dwell depending upon him. However, if during the month of Āsāḷhī...
If the teacher does not come, one should go to where support (nissaya) can be obtained.

153. How is it received? Here, first, by one receiving the status of a pupil (upajjhāya) in the presence of a preceptor, having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at his feet, having sat down in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika), and having extended the hands in añjali, [he should say]: "Preceptor..."
“May you be my preceptor, venerable sir,” should be said three times.

When the student has spoken thus, if the preceptor indicates by body, by speech, or by both body and speech: “Very well,” or “Certainly,” or “It is appropriate,” or “It is fitting,” or “Accomplish it with a pleasing manner,” then the preceptor is accepted.

In this context, "acceptance by the preceptor" refers specifically to the verbal announcement of any one of these five points by the preceptor, or the making known of their meaning by means of the body.
Some, however, say it refers to the acceptance [by saying] "Very well," but that is not authoritative. For the preceptor is considered accepted merely by the act of being requested.
In this context, the factor is the formal acceptance. It is not only permissible for the co-resident student to know, "By this word, my preceptor has been taken [as mine]";
it is also permissible for him to know, "From this day forward, the Elder is my responsibility, and I am also the Elder’s responsibility. For this has been said:
“Monks, let the preceptor establish the thought of a son toward his co-resident pupil,
and let the co-resident pupil establish the thought of a father toward his preceptor. In this way, dwelling with mutual respect,
deference, and concordant conduct, they will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
This same analysis applies even to receiving dependence (*nissaya*) in the presence of a teacher (*ācariya*). However, there is this distinction here:
one receiving dependence in the presence of a teacher must sit in the squatting posture (*ukkuṭika*) and say three times, "Venerable sir, be my teacher;
I shall live in dependence upon you, venerable sir. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

154. Regarding the question, "How is it suspended?"—here, first of all, the suspension of dependence (*nissaya*) from a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) should be understood as occurring in five ways, and from a teacher (*ācariya*) in six ways. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five suspensions of dependence from a preceptor:
the preceptor has departed; he has disrobed; he has died; he has joined another faction; or the fifth is by formal authorization (*āṇatti*). These, bhikkhus..."
“Monks, there are these five ways in which dependence on a preceptor (upajjhāya) ceases.
Monks, there are these six ways in which dependence on a teacher (ācariya) ceases:
the teacher has departed, or he has disrobed, or he has died, or he has joined another faction, or the fifth is by formal authorization, or by the preceptor.”
“He has reached the state of being fully ordained. These, monks, are the six ways in which dependence on a teacher ceases.
Herein is the analysis: “He has departed” means he has gone away in some direction.

And when he has thus departed, if there is a giver of dependence in the monastery—whether it be one from whom dependence was previously received at another time, or one with whom he shares communal meals and requisites—[he may remain].
One must receive dependence (*nissaya*) from him; there is no exemption even for a single day.
If such a person is not available, and there is another who is modest and virtuous, one who knows that person’s virtue should request dependence on that very day.
If he grants it, all is well. But if he asks, "Will your preceptor (*upajjhāya*) arrive soon? [one should respond accordingly].
If the preceptor has spoken thus, one should say, "Yes, venerable sir. If he says, "In that case, wait for the preceptor's arrival," it is permissible.

However, if one does not know his natural disposition of being well-behaved, one should observe that monk's conduct for four or five days, and after having requested the opportunity, the formal dependence (nissaya) should be taken.
If, however, there is no one in the monastery to provide formal support (nissaya), and the preceptor has departed after saying, "I will return in a few days;
do not be disheartened," then he receives the exemption [from formal support] until his return.
Even if people there should keep him for five or ten days beyond that fixed period, he remains in the monastery.
A message should be sent: "Let the young ones not be distressed; I shall arrive on such-and-such a day. In this way, too, an exemption may be obtained.

Now, if on the way there is an obstacle for the one coming, such as a river in flood or an attack by thieves and the like, and the elder waits for the water to recede or searches for companions—if the young ones [hear] that news...
They hear [of the situation], and an exemption from the duty is granted until their arrival. However, if he sends word saying, "I shall stay right here," there is no exemption.
One must go to wherever one can obtain formal dependence (*nissaya*).
But if [the teacher] has disrobed, died, or joined another faction, there is no exemption for even a single day; one must go to wherever one can obtain formal dependence.
"Command" (*āṇatti*), however, refers to the dismissal from formal dependence (*nissayapaṇāmanā*). Therefore, whether by way of the canonical formula—
such as "I dismiss you," or "Do not return here," or "Take away your bowl and robes," or "I am not to be attended by you"— or by way of a non-canonical formula—
such as "Do not ask me for permission to enter the village"— it is that which constitutes the dismissal from formal dependence.
He has been dismissed; therefore, he must ask his preceptor for forgiveness.

If the preceptor does not forgive him at the outset, he should perform a formal act of penance (daṇḍakamma) and then ask for forgiveness himself three times. If he still does not forgive him, he should take the senior elders (mahātheras) of that monastery and ask for forgiveness through them.
If he still does not forgive him, he should take monks from the neighboring monasteries and ask for forgiveness through them.

If even this is not forgiven, one should go elsewhere and live in the presence of preceptors who are like-minded [with the teacher], thinking, "Perhaps, knowing that 'he is living in the presence of those who are like-minded with me,' he will forgive.
If even this is not forgiven, one should live right there. If it is impossible to live there due to a lack of food or other such faults, then that very [place]—
Having returned to the monastery, it is permissible to dwell after receiving formal dependence (*nissaya*) from another. This is the analysis regarding the formal instruction (*āṇattiya*).

Regarding the cessation of dependence from a teacher, in the cases where "the teacher has departed," some teacher departs after having requested leave, while others depart without having requested leave;
the resident pupil (*antevāsika*) does likewise. In that regard, if the resident pupil...
He asks his teacher, “Venerable sir, I wish to go to such-and-such a place for some business.

When the teacher asks, “When will you return? and he replies, “I shall return having risen either in the evening or at night,” and the teacher accepts by saying, “Very well,” at that very moment the formal dependence (nissaya) is dissolved.

But if, when he says, "Venerable sir, I wish to go to such-and-such a place," the teacher says, "After you have wandered for alms in such-and-such a village, you will know [the way] later," and he accepts this, saying, "Very well," then if he goes, it is well.
But if he does not go, the formal dependence (nissaya) is not dissolved. Furthermore, even if he says, "I am going..."
When the teacher says, "Do not go yet; let us deliberate during the night and then we shall know," and having deliberated, he departs, he is well-gone.

If he does not depart, the formal dependence (nissaya) is not dissolved. However, for one who departs without asking permission from the teacher, the dependence is dissolved upon crossing the boundary of the precincts (upacāra-sīmā); likewise, it is dissolved for one who turns back before reaching the boundary of the precincts.
It does not cease. However, if the teacher asks the resident pupil, "Friend,
I shall go to such-and-such a place," and when the pupil asks, "When?", he replies,
"In the evening or during the night," and the pupil accepts by saying, "Very well," at that very moment the formal dependence (nissaya) ceases.

If, however, the teacher says, "I will go tomorrow after wandering for alms," and the other agrees, saying "Very well," then for that one day the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not suspended; on the following day, it becomes suspended.
But if [the teacher] says, "I will wander for alms in such-and-such a village and then decide whether to go or not," then [the dependence remains in force].
He does not go, and the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not suspended. Furthermore, even if the teacher says, "I am going," and the pupil says, "Do not go for now;
having deliberated during the night, you shall know [what to do]," and even after deliberating he still does not go, the dependence is not suspended.
If both the teacher and the pupil, due to some business, [go] outside the boundary...

They go on their way. If, after the teacher has developed the intention to travel, he goes without having asked for permission and returns within the distance of two *leḍḍu-pātas* (the range of a stone’s throw), the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not dissolved. If he returns after having exceeded the distance of two *leḍḍu-pātas*, it is dissolved.
If the teacher and preceptor stay in another monastery after having exceeded the distance of two *leḍḍu-pātas*, [the dependence is likewise dissolved].
The formal dependence (nissaya) is suspended. When the teacher has departed, died, or joined another faction, the dependence is suspended at that very moment.
However, in the case of a formal dismissal (āṇatti), the teacher dismisses the pupil for the sake of sending him away while being desirous of letting him go;
yet the pupil remains full of longing, thinking, "Even though my teacher dismisses me, he is nevertheless soft-hearted toward me. Thus the dependence [is maintained].

It does not subside. Even if the noble one has attachment while the pupil is free from attachment, and the pupil lays down his burden, thinking, "I will no longer live in dependence on him," even then it does not subside.
However, if both have attachment, it certainly does not subside; it subsides only when both lay down their burden, or when [the pupil] has been dismissed.

Having performed the disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma), he must ask for forgiveness three times. If he does not forgive, one should proceed according to the method stated regarding the preceptor (upajjhāya).

However, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who dismisses a resident pupil (antevāsika) or a co-resident student (saddhivihārika) who fulfills the duties toward the teacher and preceptor as prescribed and is endowed with the five factors such as excessive affection;
there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing even for one who does not dismiss the other [the one who failed to fulfill his duties]. For this has been said:

“Monks, one who is conducting himself rightly should not be expelled; whoever should expel him commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). And monks, one who is not conducting himself rightly should not be left unexpelled; whoever should leave him unexpelled commits an offense of wrong-doing.
“Monks, if an instructor does not expel a pupil who possesses five qualities, he is at fault; if he expels him, he is not at fault.
[The pupil] has no excessive affection for the instructor, nor has he no excessive confidence in him.”
There is no excessive sense of shame, no excessive reverence, and no excessive cultivation.
Monks, if a teacher dismisses a pupil who possesses these five factors, he is at fault;
if he dismisses him, he is not at fault.
“Monks, when a preceptor possesses five qualities, he is at fault if he does not send away his co-resident student, and he is not at fault if he does send him away.
[These are: he has no excessive affection for the preceptor; he has no excessive confidence in the preceptor;
he has no excessive sense of shame regarding the preceptor; he has no excessive reverence for the preceptor; he has no excessive devotion toward the preceptor. These—”
“Monks, when a preceptor does not dismiss a student who possesses five qualities, he is at fault;
when he dismisses him, he is not at fault,” and so forth.

In that context, “there is no excessive affection” means there is no excessive affection based on worldly attachment toward the preceptor. “There is no excessive cultivation” means there is no excessive cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*); this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "or has come together with the preceptor (*upajjhāya*)," here "coming together" should be understood by way of seeing and hearing.

For if a student (*saddhivihārika*) living under the dependence of a teacher (*ācariya*) sees his preceptor—whether the preceptor is worshipping a shrine in the same monastery or walking for alms in the same village—the dependence is suspended. [Likewise if] the preceptor sees [the student].

The co-resident does not see [the preceptor], and thus it is not pacified. Or, having seen the preceptor walking on the path or traveling through the air, because of the distance, he perceives him as "a monk" and does not perceive him as "my preceptor," and thus it is not pacified.
If he does perceive him, it is pacified. The preceptor is staying in the upper story of the palace, while the co-resident is below.
If he drinks the gruel without even seeing him and then departs; or if, not seeing him seated in the assembly hall, he eats in a secluded spot and leaves;
or if, not seeing him even when seated in the Dhamma-preaching pavilion, he listens to the Dhamma and departs—the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended.
In this way, first of all, the convergence should be understood by way of sight.

Regarding the method of hearing: if, while the preceptor is preaching the Dhamma or offering an expression of thanks in his own dwelling or in a house among the laity, one hears the sound and perceives, "This is my preceptor's voice," the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended;
if one does not perceive it, it is not suspended. This is the detailed analysis in summary.
155. Regarding the question of who must live in dependence and who need not:
here, because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a learned and competent monk to live in dependence for five years;
one who is unlearned [must live in dependence] for as long as life lasts," whoever is unlearned must live in dependence for the rest of his life. If this person is older...

If one does not find a teacher, and has been ordained for sixty or seventy years, one should nevertheless sit in the kneeling position (ukkhuṭika) before a more junior but competent person, raise the joined palms (añjali), and say three times: "Friend, may you be my teacher;
with the Venerable One as my support, I shall live. In this way, the formal support (nissaya) must be taken. [This concludes] the section on entering a village.
Even when seeking permission, one should sit in the *ukkuṭika* posture, raise the joined palms, and say: "Teacher, I ask for permission to enter the village.
This same method applies to all instances of seeking permission.
However, one who is competent and has five years of seniority since full ordination (*upasampadā*) is permitted to live independently. Therefore:
One who has been released from dependence and has five years since full ordination—at the very least—must master and recite two Matikas;
on the fortnightly days, for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, four recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) from the Suttanta;
and for the purpose of preaching to the assemblies that have gathered, the Mahārāhulovāda, the Ambaṭṭha, and [the Andhakavinda].
There is one similar method of discourse: three expressions of thanks for the purpose of giving thanks after a meal provided by the Saṅgha, whether it be auspicious or not;
the determination of what constitutes a formal act and what does not, for the purpose of knowing the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies and so forth;
and a single meditation subject culminating in Arahantship, either by way of concentration or by way of insight, for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse. This much should be learned.
To this extent, indeed, he is one who is learned and impartial; wherever he may be, he is permitted to dwell by his own authority. As for what was said:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not live independently. Not..."
He is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, but he is not endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training...

nor with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training... nor with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training... nor with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live independently.
“Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five qualities should not live independently.
He is faithless, he is shameless, he is reckless, he is lazy, and he is muddle-minded.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not live independently.”
“Monks, a monk who possesses five other qualities should also not live independently.
He is deficient in virtue regarding higher morality; he is deficient in conduct regarding his behavior; he is deficient in view regarding extreme views;
he has heard little; and he is lacking in wisdom. Monks, a monk who possesses these five qualities [should not live independently].”
“A monk should not live independently.
Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with five other qualities should not live independently:
he does not know what is an offense; he does not know what is no offense; he does not know what is a light offense; he does not know what is a heavy offense.”

He does not know them; furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have not been properly handed down to him in detail, nor well analyzed, nor well mastered, nor well determined, either by way of the rules or by way of the phrasing.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should not live independently.
“Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities should not live independently.
He does not know what is an offense; he does not know what is not an offense; he does not know what is a light offense; he does not know what is a heavy offense;
and he has fewer than five years of seniority. Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities [should not live independently].”

"One should not live without being supported. Here too, it should be understood that the prohibition is made on the basis of the same previous method—namely, by way of what is improper and by way of the factors of an offense.
Furthermore, permission should not be granted to those who are foolish, incompetent, or traveling in different directions, nor to pupils (antevāsika) or co-residents (saddhivihārika).

If they give permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preceptor and the teacher. If they go without having been granted permission, there is also an offense of wrong-doing for them. For it has been said:
"In this case, monks, a number of foolish and incompetent monks who are traveling abroad ask leave of their preceptors and teachers.
Those monks, monks, should be asked by the preceptors and teachers: 'Where will you go? By whom..."

“You shall go together with them. If, monks, those fools who are incompetent should designate other fools who are incompetent [as their preceptors], they must not be authorized by their teachers and preceptors;
if they were to authorize them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, monks, those fools who are incompetent should go without having been authorized by their teachers and preceptors, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of dependence in the Compendium of Determinations on the Vinaya Excluding the Pāḷi. 24.
Discussion on the Determination of Boundaries (Sīmā).
156. Regarding the boundary (*sīmā*): here, this so-called "boundary" is twofold—namely, the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) and the unestablished boundary (*abaddhasīmā*).

Among these, a boundary that has transcended the eleven types of defective boundaries, is endowed with the threefold perfection, and is formally authorized by binding sign to sign, is called an "established boundary.
