[The eleven defects are: too small, too large, having broken signs, having shadow-signs, having no signs, ...
Because of the statement: "Legal acts fail by way of the boundary in these eleven ways— those performed standing outside the boundary, those performed on a river,
those performed on the ocean, those performed on a lake, those performed on a natural pond, those performed by one who merges one boundary with another boundary,
and those performed by one who oversteps one boundary with another"— these are called "boundaries of failure."
In this context, "too small" means one where twenty-one bhikkhus are not able to sit down.
"Too large" means one that is designated as exceeding three *yojanas* by even the measure of a hair's tip. "A broken sign" (*khaṇḍanimittā*) is said to be an incomplete sign.
Having designated the sign in the eastern direction, [one proceeds] successively to the southern direction and the western direction...
Having described the northern direction, it is permissible to describe again what was previously described for the eastern direction and then establish [the sign] there;

in this way, it becomes an unbroken sign (*akhaṇḍanimitta*). However, if one brings [the descriptions] in sequence and, having described the sign in the northern direction, establishes it right there, it becomes a broken sign (*khaṇḍanimitta*). There is yet another kind called a broken sign.

That which is designated by making any one of the following—such as a tree with solid bark, a stump, a heap of earth, or a heap of sand—situated between oneself and a signless object, is called "designated by a sign.
That which is designated by making any shadow, such as the shadow of a mountain and so forth, a sign is called "designated by a shadow-sign.
That which is designated without mentioning any signs whatsoever is called "signless."
“Consent given by one standing outside the boundary” means: having proclaimed the boundary marks, it is consent given by one who stands outside those marks.

“Consent given within a river, the ocean, or a lake” means: consent given within these [areas], such as rivers and so forth. For even though it is given in this way, it is indeed not valid consent because of the statement:
“Bhikkhus, every river is without a formal boundary; every ocean is without a formal boundary; every lake is without a formal boundary.”
[It] exists. Regarding "one who merges one boundary with another boundary": this refers to one who, while within his own boundary, merges it with the boundary of others.

For if, in the eastern direction of an ancient monastery, there are two trees—an *amba* and a *jambu*—whose branches are intertwined with one another, and if the *jambu* tree is on the western side of the *amba*, [then] the monastery boundary...
It was bound having included the rose-apple tree and excluding the mango tree.
Later, when a monastery was built to the east of that monastery, the monks binding the boundary included that mango tree and excluded the rose-apple tree; thus, one boundary overlapped the other.
Therefore, if the boundary of the monastery built earlier has not yet been formally established, [the second may be established].

If it exists, the precinct of the boundary must be established. If it has been formally authorized, a boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*) measuring at least one cubit must be established at its western limit.
In the *Kurundi*, it is stated that "even a span's width" is sufficient; in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is said that "even a four-finger's width is permissible.
Furthermore, even a single tree can serve as the marker for two boundaries; however, if it grows larger, it causes a confusion of boundaries.
Therefore, it should not be done. Regarding "one who oversteps the boundary with the boundary":
this refers to one who, while establishing their own boundary, oversteps the boundary of others.
For if they establish their own boundary by including either the entire boundary bound by others or a portion of it within it, it is called "overstepping the boundary with the boundary."
However, it is permissible to establish a boundary for monks within a boundary that already encompasses the boundary of the bhikkhunīs.
The same principle applies to the boundaries of the bhikkhunīs within the boundary of the monks.

For they do not serve as a quorum for one another’s formal acts (*kamma*), nor do they render a formal act deficient by their presence. Thus, a boundary should be established only after transcending these eleven types of defective boundaries.
157. "Endowed with the threefold perfection" means endowed with the perfection of the site (*nimitta*), the perfection of the assembly (*parisa*), and the perfection of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
Among these, "endowed with the perfection of the site" refers to what is stated as follows:
the mountain site, the rock site, the forest site, the tree site, the path site, the anthill site, the river site, and the water site.

Regarding the eight signs, in each respective direction, the signs that have been obtained and brought forward should be correctly announced according to the method beginning with: "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
'A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the sign,'" and so forth.
Herein, this is the detailed explanation: the holder of the discipline (vinayadhara) should ask, "What is the sign in the eastern direction?"
“‘A mountain, venerable sir,’ [he says]. Whether it is one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or one who is not fully ordained who points this out, it is indeed permissible.
Furthermore, the holder of the Vinaya must designate the landmark (*nimitta*) in this way: ‘This mountain is the landmark. Likewise: ‘We are making this mountain the landmark;
we shall make it so; the landmark has been made; let there be a landmark; there is one; there will be one. Thus [it should be said].
But it is not appropriate to praise [it]. The same principle applies to stones and so forth as well.

"In the eastern direction, in the intermediate eastern direction, in the southern direction, in the intermediate southern direction, in the western direction, in the intermediate western direction, in the northern direction, and in the intermediate northern direction—what is the cause? "Water, venerable sir. This...

The water should be designated as the sign (*nimitta*). However, in this case, after first setting it aside and then designating the previously designated sign—asking, "What is the sign in the eastern direction?
A mountain, venerable sir; that mountain is the sign"—it should then be set aside. For in this way, one sign is joined with the sign; the signs [are thus linked] once.

Those things that have been designated remain designated as such. However, in the *Andhaka-ṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The sign must be designated by one who is binding the boundary-circle three times. 158.
Now, the mountains and other features that serve as signs should be understood—there are three kinds of mountains: a mountain of pure soil...
There are mountains of pure rock and those composed of both [rock and sand]. All three types of these are permissible; however, a heap of sand is not permissible.
As for the other [rocky mountain], one smaller than the size of an elephant is not permissible, but from the size of an elephant upwards—even up to the size of Mount Sineru—it is permissible.
If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three in three directions, they may consist of either four or three [mountains].
It is permissible to designate [the boundary] by means of mountain signs, but it is not permissible to designate it by means of two signs or even one.
This same principle applies to the subsequent [signs], such as stone signs and so forth. Therefore, when making a mountain sign, one must ask:
"Is it a single continuous unit, or is it not a single continuous unit? If it is a single continuous unit, it should not be made; for that—
Even when praising [the landmarks] in the four or eight directions, only a single sign is praised;

therefore, having praised that mountain—which stands surrounding even the monastery in the shape of a wheel—in one direction, one should praise other signs inside it, excluding it from the other directions. If, regarding the mountain...

If they wish to include one-third or a half within the boundary, they should designate a sign—such as a tree, an anthill, or the like—growing on that very mountain, beyond whatever portion of the mountain they wish to include inside;
provided that they do not intend to include the entire mountain, even if it measures one or two *yojanas*. If, however, they wish to include the whole mountain within the boundary...
On the ground beyond the mountain, signs such as trees and anthills that have grown there should be described.
Regarding a stone sign, even an iron ball is counted as a stone; therefore, any kind of stone is suitable.
As for its size, one that has reached the dimensions of an elephant is considered a "mountain," and thus it is not permitted; however, one the size of a large bull or a large buffalo is acceptable.
However, it is permissible. At its minimum limit, it must be the size of a ball of molasses weighing thirty-two *palas*;

anything smaller than that is not permissible, whether it be a brick or even a large one. A heap of stones that have not yet been shaped into specific forms is not permissible, much less a heap of dust or sand.
It may be like a flat stone on the ground similar to a threshing floor, or like a stump protruding from the earth.
Or it may be a protruding rock; if that too is of the proper size, it is permissible.

Even a back-rock (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*), though very large, is still reckoned as a rock; therefore, if they wish to designate one part of a large back-rock within the boundary, they should not designate that [part], but another rock should be designated on top of it.
If they build a monastery around the back-rock, [it is likewise permissible].
If a rock slab passes right through the middle of the monastery, such a rock slab is not permissible.

For if they were to mark that [rock], the monastery would be situated upon the boundary marker (*nimitta*); and since the boundary marker itself is outside the formal boundary (*sīma*), the monastery would consequently also fall outside the boundary.
A rock slab standing so as to encircle the monastery may be marked at one point...
It should not be praised elsewhere.
Regarding "a forest landmark": a grass forest or a forest of trees such as *tacasāra*, palm, or coconut is not permitted;
however, a forest of trees such as *sāka* or *sāla* that have inner pith, or trees mixed with those having inner pith, is permitted, provided it meets the minimum requirement.
Even the size of four or five trees is permissible, but less than that is not allowed; more than even a hundred yojanas is permitted.
However, if they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, the forest itself must not be designated as the boundary.

Even for those wishing to include a portion of it within the boundary, they should designate the trees, rocks, and so forth therein without designating the forest. This applies to the forest standing around the perimeter of the monastery.
Having praised it in one place, it should not be praised elsewhere.
Regarding the sign of a tree: trees such as the *tāla* or coconut are not permitted;
however, the inner heartwood of a living tree—even if only eight finger-breadths in height and the thickness of a needle’s shaft—is permitted. Anything smaller than that is not permitted.
However, even a well-established banyan tree (*suppaṭṭhita-nigrodha*) up to twelve *yojanas* in size is permissible.
A tree that has been grown by planting its seed in bamboo, reeds, or bowls, even if it has reached the proper size, is not permissible;

but having removed it from there, it is permissible to plant it in the ground at that very moment, construct a fence around it, water it, and then perform the consecration (*kitteti*). This concludes the section on the emergence of new roots and branches.
This is not the case for a stump; however, it is appropriate when a trunk has been cut down and replanted.
Furthermore, when praising, it is permissible to call it simply "a tree," or "a *sāka* tree," or "a *sāla* tree.
But having praised it as a single connected whole—such as a well-established *nigrodha* tree—it is not permissible to praise it in one place and then praise it again elsewhere.
Regarding the signs of a path, forest tracks, fields, rivers, ponds, main roads, and so forth are not permitted;

however, a footpath or a cart-track is permitted. This applies to one who, having turned away [from the village], goes two or three villages' distance, or to one who, having descended from a footpath or a cart-track, returns again to that very cart-track, or to those footpaths and cart-tracks that are not accessible [to carts].
They are not permitted; they are only permitted when being traversed by a caravan on foot or by a caravan of carts.

If two roads diverge and later merge like the yokes of two carts, then having once designated [the boundary] at the point where they split or at the point where they join, it should not be designated again, for this constitutes a single continuous landmark. If [the road] encircles a monastery...
The four paths go out in the four directions; having designated one in the center, it is not permissible to designate another.
For this is a single, continuous sign. However, it is permissible to designate that which has gone out after passing through a corner.
But a path that has gone out by passing through the middle of the monastery should not be designated; [for if it were], it would be on top of the sign already designated.
It becomes a monastery (vihāra). If they mark the sign at the track of the last wheel of a cart-track, the road is outside the boundary;
if they mark the sign at the track of the outer wheel, the outer wheel-track is outside the boundary, while the remainder belongs to the interior boundary.
When designating the road, [one should use] the ten terms such as "road" (maggo), "path" (pantho), "way" (patho), "track" (pajjo), and so forth.

It is permissible to mark it by any name whatsoever; however, having enclosed the monastery with a ditch-shaped boundary, it is not permissible to mark the path at one place and then mark it elsewhere.
Regarding the ant-hill landmark, even if it is only eight finger-breadths high—born on that very day—and as large as a cow’s horn, it serves as the lower limit.
An anthill is permissible; anything smaller than that is not permissible. Even something as large as the Himavat mountain is permissible;
however, if it stands surrounding a monastery in a single continuous mass, one may designate it in one place, but it is not permissible to designate it elsewhere.
Regarding the river boundary: [it is so designated] during the time of righteous kings every half-month, every ten days, or every five days.
Thus, when it rains so that the clouds have just cleared away, the current is cut off, and this does not count as a river.
But for that [river] whose current is not cut off during such a period of good rain— the four months of the rainy season— wherein, whether by a ford or a non-ford,
one who has come with the characteristic of having fulfilled his training covers the three circles, [this is a river].

If the inner robe of a nun crossing [the river] becomes wet even by the measure of one or two finger-breadths without having been tucked in, this river serves as the boundary-mark for those establishing a boundary.

This same river applies whether the nun is going to the far bank, performing a formal act of the Saṅgha such as the Uposatha, or demarcating the boundary on the far side of the river. As for the path...
If they have gone surrounding the monastery in the shape of a cart-pole or in the shape of a moat, it is not permissible to mark that [boundary] in one place and then mark it elsewhere.

The same rule applies even to a group of four rivers that flow past the four directions of the monastery, branching off from one another. However, if the four rivers are unmixed, all four may be marked.

It is permissible. If, as if building a fence, they bury [a boundary marker] at the foot of a tree and block the river current with creepers, straw, and so forth, such that the water overflows and the obstruction remains in place, it is permissible to establish the sign (*nimitta*).
However, once a dam has been constructed so that the water no longer flows, it is permissible to establish the sign for the river where the flow has ceased.
It is not permissible; however, it is permissible to establish a river-mark at a place where water flows and a water-mark at a place where it does not flow.
But that which does not flow due to being waterless during a time of drought or in the summer heat is permissible.
When they divert a channel from a great river, it becomes like a small stream, providing for three crops and flowing constantly.
Even though it may be flowing, it is not permissible to make it a landmark. However,
if a river that was once diverted from its main course by being channeled away at its source later returns to break through the embankment along that same original path and flows on its own—
becoming a river further downstream teeming with crocodiles and the like, where boats and such must navigate— it is permissible to make that a landmark.
It is not permissible to mark the water-sign by filling a boat or a barrel and the like with water in a place where there is no water;

it is permissible only for water situated on the ground. Furthermore, that must be water that does not flow away, such as that found in pits, lotus ponds, tanks, lakes, natural pools, salt mines, or the ocean;
however, water that is not so situated—such as water in floods, rivers, flowing streams, or canals—is not permissible. This is stated in the *Andhakatthakathā*.
However, as for what was said—that "in deep pits and such, water that has been drawn out should not be made a sign"—that is poorly stated;

it is merely one's own personal opinion. But even in the case of standing water, whether in a pit dug by pigs or in a village children’s play-pool, if at that very moment a hole is made in the earth and it is filled with water brought in jars, [it may be used].
If he remains until the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā), it is permissible whether [the duration] be short or long.
However, at that spot, for the purpose of establishing a perception of the boundary-mark (nimitta), a heap of stones, sand, or soil, or a stone pillar or a wooden pillar, may be made.
It is permissible for a monk to make or cause such a thing to be made; however, this is not permissible within the boundary of acquisitions (lābhasīmā).
A boundary for common residence does not cause obstruction for anyone; it merely effects the formal legal acts (*vinayakamma*) of the bhikkhus.
Therefore, it is permissible here.
Furthermore, a boundary may be established by means of these eight types of marks, whether they are unmixed with one another or mutually mixed.
It is indeed permissible. Once it has been thus appointed, when it is being bound, it may be unbound by one or two signs;
however, starting from three, it may be bound even by a hundred of the types of signs mentioned.
It may be triangular with three corners, square with four, or shaped like a crossroads, a half-moon, a mudiṅga drum, and so forth; or with more than that.
They are of various shapes. Having thus described the signs according to the method stated, they should be understood as "endowed with the perfection of signs.

159. "Endowed with the perfection of the assembly" means that at least four monks have gathered, and as many as are situated within that village boundary—whether it be a fixed boundary, a river, the ocean, or a lake—without having crossed over them.
Those monks are all either within arm’s reach of one another or have brought their consent; they are thus formally appointed.
160. What is meant by "accompanied by the perfection of the formal proclamation" (*kammavācā*)?—"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:

as far as the boundaries have been designated on all sides, if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should, by means of these markers, appoint a boundary for common residence and a single Uposatha; this is the motion (*ñatti*)."

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: as far as the boundaries have been proclaimed on all sides, the Saṅgha designates this area by these marks as a boundary for common residence and a single Uposatha.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the designation of this boundary for common residence and a single Uposatha by these marks, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
“The boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha with these markers as a common residence and a single Uposatha; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.

When the motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) has been spoken in this way and is pure, the boundary is authorized. At the conclusion of the proclamation, the boundary lies within the markers, and the markers are outside the boundary. 161.

Once the boundary has been thus established, the authorization for non-separation (*avippavāsasammuti*) should be made for the sake of the comfort of being separated from the three robes and for the sake of strengthening the bond. That, moreover, should be performed in this way:

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as one where one is not separated from one’s three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts. This is the motion.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha—let the Saṅgha authorize that boundary as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts.
Whosoever of the venerable ones approves of the authorization of this boundary as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts...”
And [the phrase] "the village and its precincts" is silent. Whoever does not approve should speak.

"This boundary has been approved by the Saṅgha as one where one is not separated from the three robes, with the exception of the village and its precincts; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
And here, it should be understood that towns and cities are included within the term "village. "The precinct of a village" refers to that which is enclosed...

An enclosure, or the space for an enclosure where there is no enclosure. Regarding these villages and village precincts, however, a monk who has resolved upon the three robes does not receive the privilege [of being outside them].

For this non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā), because it is stated as "excluding the village and the village precinct," it does not cover over the village or the village precinct; rather, it covers over only the common-observance boundary (samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā). This is the common-observance boundary.
And herein, it extends according to its own nature; however, the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) extends only where there is a common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*).
For there is no separate proclamation of signs for that [non-separation boundary].

In that case, if there is a village at the time of the formal authorization (*sammuti*) for non-separation, it does not encompass it. But if a village exists after the boundary has been authorized, [it is encompassed].
That which is settled later also goes by the name of "boundary. And just as with what is settled later, even an area expanded after someone has first settled there goes by the name of "boundary.

If houses were built at the time of the formal act for establishing the boundary, and although there was an intention to enter—thinking, "We shall enter"—but people did not actually enter, [it remains part of] the ancient village.
Or, if they have abandoned their homes and gone elsewhere, this is indeed a non-village (*agāma*), and the boundary (*sīmā*) extends over it.
But if even a single family has entered [the area] or has not departed, it is indeed a village, and the boundary does not extend over it. This is the summary here. 162.
As for the detailed explanation: one who wishes to establish a boundary must [inform] the monks in the neighboring monasteries (*sāmantavihāra*). Each of them...
Having asked about the boundary delimitation of the monastery, and having set aside the interval between boundaries for monasteries with established boundaries,

or the precinct of the boundary for monasteries without established boundaries, if those wishing to establish a boundary within a single village district do so at a time when monks traveling from various directions are not moving about, they should inform the monks in the monasteries there that have established boundaries: "Today we..."
"You shall bind [the boundary]; do not go outside the limits of your own parish," this should be sent.
In those monasteries where the boundaries have not been bound, the monks should be assembled together, and the consent of those entitled to give it should be obtained.
"If they wish to include other village territories as well, the monks who reside in those villages must also come; for those who do not come..."
“Consent must be brought,” said the Elder Mahāsumana. But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, “Various village districts are like separately bound boundaries;
consent and purity do not come from them. However, monks who have gone within the boundary markers must come.
He further said, “At the time of delimiting the boundary for common affiliation, their coming [is required].”

"It is also permissible for them not to come; however, at the time of demarcating the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsa-sīmā), those who have gone within the marks must return, and for those who do not return, their consent (chanda) must be brought.

Thus, when the monks have assembled and the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, [the procedure is to be performed] on various paths, at river crossings, village gates, and so forth.
And for the sake of quickly pointing out the hand-signs to visiting monks and for the sake of establishing the external boundary,

having appointed monastery attendants and novice monks and having given the signal by means of a drum or a conch, the boundary should be bound using the formal proclamation beginning with "Let the Sangha,
venerable sirs, hear me," as stated immediately after the delineation of the signs. At the very conclusion of the formal proclamation—
Having excluded external signs and having established the lower limit at the water that supports the earth, the boundary is reached.

163. However, by those who are establishing this common-ordination boundary (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*), a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) must first be tied off for the sake of making the sangha-acts (*saṅghakamma*) such as going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*) easy to perform. Those tying it off must know the proper procedure (*vatta*).
For if they construct [the boundary] in a monastery already built after having established all the sites such as the Bodhi-tree shrine, the dining hall, and so forth,

they should not bind it in the middle of the monastery where many people gather, but rather in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery. When constructing [the boundary] in a monastery that has not yet been built,
they should first mark out the locations for all the sites such as the Bodhi-tree shrine, and then— so that...
When the sites have been determined, it should be established in a secluded place on the outskirts of the monastery; thus it should be bound.
As for its lower limit, it is permissible if it includes twenty-one monks, but not if it is fewer than that; even if it includes a thousand monks, it is permissible.
Those binding it should place boundary-marking stones around the perimeter of the boundary enclosure (*sīmāmaḷaka*).
Those standing within a minor boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) must not establish a major boundary (mahāsīmā); those standing within a major boundary must not establish a minor boundary.
However, standing only within a minor boundary, a minor boundary may be established.
The procedure for establishing it is as follows: having designated the boundary markers all around, saying, "This rock is the marker," and so forth.

The boundary should be formally designated by means of a *kammavācā*. Then, for the sake of strengthening that very designation, a *kammavācā* regarding non-separation (*avippavāsa*) should be performed.
For in this way, those who have come with the intention, "We shall abolish the boundary," will not be able to abolish it.
Having designated the boundary, stones should be placed outside the boundary-marking stones (*sīmantarika*). The boundary-marking stone at the western limit should measure one *ratana*.

It is permissible. According to the *Kuruṇḍī*, "even one measuring a span (*vidatthi*) is permissible," while the *Mahāpaccarī* states, "even one measuring four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) is permissible.
However, if the monastery is large, two, three, or even more than that many fragmentary boundaries (*khaṇḍasīma*) should be established.

Having thus demarcated the fragmentary boundaries, at the time of the formal authorization for the great boundary (*mahāsīma*), one should emerge from the fragmentary boundary and [enter] the great boundary.
Standing there, those who are walking around the perimeter must designate the boundary-stones (*sīmantarika-pāsāṇa*);

then, having designated the remaining signs, they—without letting go of hand’s reach (*hatthapāsa*)—must formally establish a common residence zone (*samānasamvāsaka-sīmā*) by means of the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*).

Furthermore, for the sake of strengthening that [boundary], the ritual proclamation regarding non-separation (*avippavāsa-kammavācā*) must also be performed. For it was with this very purpose that those who had come saying, "We shall abolish the boundary," arrived.

They will not be able to abolish it. However, if they first designate the boundary marks for a *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary), then designate the boundary marks for a *sīmantarikā* (intermediate boundary), and finally designate the boundary marks for a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary)—thus having designated the marks in these three places—it is permissible to bind whichever boundary they desire first. Even so, according to the method already described...
It should be bound starting from the boundary of the sub-territory (*khaṇḍasīma*).

When the boundaries have been bound in this manner, monks standing within a sub-territory do not invalidate a formal act (*kamma*) performed by those in the great territory (*mahāsīma*), nor do those standing in the great territory invalidate one performed by those in a sub-territory;
however, those standing in the intermediate space between boundaries (*sīmantarikā*) invalidate neither. If a formal act is performed while standing within the precinct of a village...
However, when they are performing the ceremony, those standing in the intermediate space (sīmantarikā) cause it to fail. For the intermediate space belongs to the village precinct (gāmakhetta).
Now, this boundary (sīmā) is not bound only on the surface of the earth;
rather, it is indeed bound even on a stone slab, in a hut, in a cave, in a palace, or on a mountain peak. Among these, regarding a stone slab:
One should not establish a boundary mark by carving a line on a stone surface or by digging a mortar-hole;
rather, having placed stones as boundary marks, the marks should be designated.

At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), the boundary descends, making the limit of the water that supports the earth its extent. The boundary-mark stones [should remain] in their respective places.
They remain; therefore, a line should be established all around, or stones should be pierced at the four corners, or letters should be carved, saying, "This is the boundary limit.
Some envious people, thinking, "We shall burn down the boundary," set fire to it; however, only the stones burn, not the boundary.
Even in the case of a house with a roof, one should establish the boundary by not including the wall itself, but by designating stone markers to enclose a space sufficient for twenty-one monks;

thus the boundary exists only within the walls. If there is no space for twenty-one monks within the walls, it should be established by placing stone markers at the front entrance. Even if this is so...
If it is not sufficient, boundary markers should be established even outside at the place where the water falls away;
when it has been authorized in this way, the entire hut and house becomes included within the boundary.

Even in a rock cave with four walls, those establishing it must not mark the plastered walls but must mark the stones themselves; if there is no space inside, the markers should be placed at the entrance; in this way, the boundary exists both inside and outside the cave.
On the upper terrace as well, the boundary should be demarcated by not plastering the wall and placing stones inside it.
If that is not possible, it should be demarcated by placing stones even at the front entrance. A boundary demarcated in this way exists only on the upper terrace itself and does not descend below.
However, if there is a wall on the lower floor of a palace constructed over many pillars and beams...
Just as there is a limit to signs, so too, having risen up, it stands connected to the measuring-ropes;
it also descends below. However, the boundary is fixed upon the upper surface of a single-pillared palace.
If there is space for twenty-one monks at the top of the pillar, it descends below. If [the boundary] extends to the balconies and such that project out from the walls of the palace...

Having placed stones [as markers], they bind the boundary; the wall of the palace is within the boundary. However, whether it descends below or not should be understood according to the method already stated.
Even when the lower part of the palace is being measured, the wall and the wooden pillars must not be measured; [only] what is attached to the wall...
However, it is permissible to mark the boundary by inscribing it upon stone pillars. A boundary thus marked remains strictly within the limits of the pillars at the base of the lower palace.
But if the wall of the lower palace is connected with the upper floor, it extends upward to include the upper palace as well.
If they establish the marks outside the palace at the place where water falls off, the entire palace comes to be included within the boundary.
On the summit of a mountain there is a level space sufficient for twenty-one bhikkhus;
there they bind the boundary as if on a flat rock, and the boundary extends downwards into the lower part of the mountain by that very same demarcation.
On Mount Tālamūlaka as well, the boundary bound above extends downwards. However, in the case of one that has the shape of a canopy, [the boundary] for twenty-one [bhikkhus] above...
There is space for the monks [above], but none below; the boundary fixed above it does not descend below.

Thus, whether it be shaped like a drum (*mudiṅga*) or shaped like a small drum (*paṇava*), the boundary fixed above that which has no measure of the boundary either below or in the middle does not descend below.
However, in the case of one where two peaks are situated close together, [the situation is different].

If even for one [mountain] the space above it is not sufficient for the measure of the boundary, one must pile up or fill in its gaps and make it a single solid mass before the boundary can be formally established above it. If there is a mountain resembling a cobra’s hood, they establish the boundary because there is sufficient space above it;
however, if there is a hollow chasm beneath it, the boundary does not descend into it.
If, however, in the middle there is a porous rock the size of the boundary, it is included; and that rock remains within the boundary itself.
Or if the wall of the lower cave stands touching its upper edge, it is included;
both below and above, it remains within the boundary itself. But if, below, inside the cave beyond the limit of the upper boundary...
[The boundary] exists, but it does not extend outside the boundary. Or again, if there is a cave outside the interior of the upper boundary-limit, it does not enter within the boundary.
Or again, if the upper boundary-limit is small while the cave below is large and situated beyond the boundary-limit, the boundary exists only above and does not extend below. But if...
If the cave is small, measuring only the full extent of the boundary, while the boundary above it remains large, covering it, then the boundary descends [into it].
But if the cave is too small and does not measure the full extent of the boundary, and the boundary remains only above it without descending below,
then even if half of it should break away and fall, it still does not constitute the measurement of the boundary.
What falls outside is not within the boundary (*asīmā*). However, if what has not fallen [outside] is of the same measure as the boundary, it remains indeed a boundary.
And when a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) has a low foundation, if they fill it in and make it high-foundationed, it is still a boundary.

If they build a house within the boundary, it belongs to those who stand within the boundary (*sīmaṭṭhaka*). If they dig a lotus pond within the boundary, it is still the boundary itself. The flood [does not carry away] the circle of the boundary.
Having covered [the area], one goes; it is permissible to perform the formal act after erecting a watchtower at the boundary-marker.
If there is a river below the boundary, and a monk possessing supernormal powers sits there—if that river flowed first and the boundary was established later, it does not invalidate the formal act.
But if the boundary was established first and the river flowed later, the formal act [is valid].
If one stands upon the surface of the earth below, however, one certainly causes [the boundary] to be disturbed.
There is a banyan tree in the precinct of the boundary-mark; its branches or the shoots emerging from them touch the ground within the great boundary or the trees growing there.
Having cleared the great boundary, the formal act (kamma) should be performed.

Alternatively, those branches and shoots should be cut off and placed outside. Monks who have climbed onto branches and such that stand without touching [the ground] should be brought within arm’s reach.
Thus, in the case of a tree grown within the Great Boundary (mahāsīmā), a branch or a shoot must be established in the boundary enclosure (sīmāmāḷaka) according to the method already stated;
or, having cleared the boundary according to the stated method, the formal act (kamma) should be performed. Or else, those branches and shoots...

Having cut them down, they should be placed outside. If, while work is being done on the platform, some monk enters inside the platform and sits on a branch standing in the air, or if his feet touch the ground, or his lower garment or upper robe touches the ground, it is not permissible for him to do the work.
However, having had his feet and his lower and upper garments lifted up...
It is permissible to perform the act; this characteristic should also be understood according to the previous method. However, this is the distinction:
there, it is not permissible to perform it after having caused [the object] to be lifted up;

it must be brought within the reach of the hand. If a rock rises up from within the boundary, the monk standing there must be brought within the reach of the hand. Even when one has entered inside the rock by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), [the same rule applies].
The same principle applies here. For while being bound, the boundary does not enter a place that lacks a fixed measure;
however, once the boundary is established, whatever has arisen within it—no matter where—and which is connected as one, comes to be reckoned as part of the boundary.

Furthermore, when one is establishing a boundary with a maximum extent of three *yojanas*, standing in the center, one must ensure that it extends for one and a half *yojanas* in each of the four directions.
It must be designated in this way. However, if they stand in the middle and designate three *yojanas* from each direction, it becomes six *yojanas*, which is not permitted.
One who designates it as either square or triangular must designate it so that the distance from corner to corner is three *yojanas*.
For if, by any boundary whatsoever, even by the measure of a hair-tip...
If one exceeds three *yojanas*, one incurs an offense and the boundary becomes no longer a boundary.

164. Because of the statement, "Monks, a river-crossing boundary (*nadīpārasīmā*) must not be authorized; whoever should authorize it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," a river-crossing boundary must not be authorized.
However, where there is a permanent boat or a permanent bridge, [the boundary] is indeed right at the landing place.
"It is permissible, monks, to designate such a river-bank boundary where there is either a permanent boat-landing or a permanent bridge. For this has been said.
If there is no permanent boat-landing or permanent bridge at the landing-place facing [the monastery], one must ascend slightly upward and then descend.

Or having descended [from the boat], it is also permissible even if [the boundary] exists [only there]. However, the Elder Karavikatissa said, "It is permissible even within the distance of a *gāvuta*.

Furthermore, when one is establishing this river-bank boundary, one should stand on one bank, designate a landmark (*nimitta*) on the upper bank of the river, and then, starting from that point, encircle oneself as far as the limit one desires.
At its conclusion, having marked a sign on the riverbank at the downstream end, one should mark a sign on the opposite bank directly facing it.
From that point onward, according to whatever extent of boundary one desires,
one should mark signs along the riverbank as far as the upstream end opposite the first sign already marked, and then return.

It should be joined with the boundary-mark first mentioned. Then, having brought all the monks standing within the boundary-marks into hand’s-reach, the boundary should be formally established by means of the *kammavācā*. Those standing on the river, even if they have not yet arrived, do not invalidate the act;
at the conclusion of the formal authorization, excluding the river itself, [the area] on the far bank and the near bank is included within the boundary-marks.
And it becomes a single boundary; however, a river does not fall under the category of a "bound boundary. For that is simply a separate river-boundary.

If there is an island within the river, one who wishes to include it within the boundary should, in the same manner as before, mark the boundary signs on the bank where he himself stands, and then mark boundary signs on both the near shore and the far shore of the island. Then...
On the opposite bank of the river, at the spot facing the sign on this side, one should define the sign;
then, starting from there, in the same manner as before, one should define signs all the way upstream until reaching the sign first defined at the mouth of the upper stream.
Then, having defined a sign at both the far and near ends of the island, one should return.

First, it should be connected with the previously mentioned boundary markers. Then, having brought all the monks within arm’s reach on both banks and on the islands, the boundary (sīmā) should be formally established by means of the ritual proclamation (kammavācā).

Even those standing in the river who do not come forward do not invalidate the act; for at the conclusion of the formal agreement, the river is excluded, and [the area] between the two banks is included within the markers.
An island constitutes a single boundary, whereas a river is itself the river boundary.

However, if the island extends further than the delimitation of the monastery boundary—either above or below—then one should designate a boundary marker on the near shore of the island directly opposite the marker that defines the monastery boundary;
from that point onward, [the boundary follows] the crest of the island.
While encircling it, one should again designate the boundary-mark on the far side of the island opposite the boundary-mark [already] designated.
Thereafter, in the same manner as before, having designated the boundary-marks on the far shore starting from the boundary-mark directly opposite,
as well as the boundary-marks on the far side of the island and the boundary-marks at its near side and far side, together with the boundary-mark first designated—
The arrangement of the boundary markers must be performed. Having thus proclaimed it, the boundary established by formal agreement takes the shape of a mountain.

However, if the island extends further both above and below the limits of the monastery boundary, the arrangement of the boundary markers must be performed by proclaiming the markers while encircling both peaks of the island in the same manner as previously described. Thus...
Having thus designated it, the boundary established is shaped like a drum (*mudiṅga*).
If there is a small island within the limits of the monastery boundary, the markers must be designated on that island according to the very first method.
Having thus designated it, the boundary established is shaped like a small drum (*paṇava*). In this way, the delimitation of the boundary should be understood.
165. But when a boundary thus established becomes a non-boundary? It becomes a non-boundary when the Saṅgha abolishes the boundary. How, then, should it be abolished?
"Monks, when establishing a boundary, first the boundary for common affiliation (samānasaṃvāsasīmā) must be established;
afterwards, the non-separation from the three robes (ticīvarena avippavāsa) must be established. [Regarding] the boundary..."
"Monks, by one who is abolishing [the formal acts], first the non-separation from the three robes must be abolished; afterwards, the common boundary of the same communion must be abolished.
Because of this statement, the non-separation must be abolished first, and the boundary afterwards.
How so? A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as ‘not being separated from the three robes’—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rescind that authorization of not being separated from the three robes. This is the motion (*ñatti*).

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. That which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as ‘not being separated from the three robes’—the Saṅgha now rescinds that authorization of not being separated from the three robes.
Whichever venerable one approves of this rescinding of the authorization of not being separated from the three robes...”
It has been abolished; it is for those who are silent. Whoever does not approve should speak.
"The non-separation from the three robes has been abolished by the Saṅgha; it is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way, first of all, the non-separation [from the robes] is to be abolished.

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha—if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha abolish that boundary as a common residence with a single Uposatha. This is the motion (*ñatti*).

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. That boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence with a single Uposatha—the Saṅgha abolishes that boundary as a common residence with a single Uposatha. To whichever venerable one this is agreeable...”
The abolishment of the boundary for common residence and a single Uposatha is as follows: "It is abolished for him who is silent. He to whom it is not pleasing should speak.
"That boundary has been abolished by the Saṅgha for common residence and a single Uposatha; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent;
thus do I understand this. In this way, the boundary should be abolished.
Furthermore, the monk who is abolishing [the boundary] must know the proper procedure (*vatta*). Herein, this is the procedure:

standing within a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), one must not abolish a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*); likewise, standing within a non-separation boundary, one must not abolish a broken boundary.

However, standing within a broken boundary, only a broken boundary may be abolished; likewise, standing within the other, only the other may be abolished. This is what is called a "boundary" (*sīmā*).

They abolish [the boundary] for two reasons: either to enlarge a naturally small one by making it large for the sake of increasing the residence, or to make a naturally large one small again for the sake of giving space for other monasteries.
In that regard, if they know both the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*), they will be able both to abolish and to bind it.
However, those who know of the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) but do not know of the non-separation (*avippavāsa*) will be able both to abolish and to bind it.

Those who do not know of the broken boundary but do know of the non-separation may perhaps be able to abolish it by standing in places free from apprehension, such as the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*), the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa*), or the Uposatha hall; but as for binding it, they will not be able to do so.
They will certainly not be able [to do so]. If they were to bind it, they would have to create a division of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*) and turn the monastery (*vihāra*) into a non-monastery;
therefore, it must not be abolished. However, those who do not know both [the method of abolishing and binding] will be unable either to abolish or to bind it.

For this so-called boundary (*sīmā*) ceases to be a boundary either through a formal act of proclamation (*kammavācā*) or through the disappearance of the Teaching (*sāsanantaradhāna*), but not otherwise.
Furthermore, it is not possible for those who do not know the boundary to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*);

therefore, it should not be abolished. Rather, only after having thoroughly understood it should it be abolished, as well as bound. This, then, is the exposition regarding the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*).

166. The unestablished boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), however, is threefold: the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the seven-abhantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), and the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). Regarding these:

To the extent that there is one village field, this is called a "village boundary" (*gāmasīmā*); and here, by the mention of "village," both town (*nagara*) and market town (*nigama*) are also included.

In that regard, whatever area the village headmen of each respective village receive as tax, whether that area be small or large, it is reckoned precisely as a village boundary. This applies to the boundaries of towns and market towns as well.

The same principle applies here. Even when a king demarcates a certain portion within a single village district, thinking, "Let this be a separate village," and bestows it upon someone, that too indeed becomes a separate village boundary.
Therefore, both that [new] boundary and the other—the natural boundaries of villages, cities, and market towns—are exactly like established boundaries;
however, they simply do not receive the exemption from the offense of being separated from one's three robes (*ticīvara-vippavāsa*).
In a forest devoid of villages (*agāmaka*), however, the area extending seven *abbhantara*s on all sides is called a "seven-*abbhantara* boundary" (*sattabbhantarasīmā*).
Therein, "a forest devoid of villages" is found in places such as the Vindhya wilderness or in islands in the middle of the ocean that are not accessible to fishermen.
"Seven *abbhantara*s on all sides" means that, measured from the center, it extends seven *abbhantara*s in every direction.
There are fourteen [rods]. Among them, one internal [rod] measures twenty-eight cubits. This boundary increases according to the extent of the assembly;
therefore, the internal limit must be established starting from the edge of the surrounding assembly.
However, if two Saṅghas perform the Uposatha separately, there are two internal [rods] of seven [cubits each].
In between, another internal boundary should be established for the purpose of the precinct (upacāra). 167.
Furthermore, after having rejected the notion that rivers and so forth constitute fixed boundaries by stating, "Bhikkhus, all rivers are not boundaries; the entire ocean is not a boundary;
every natural lake is not a boundary," [the Buddha] then said: "Or, bhikkhus, regarding a river..."
"In the ocean or in a lake, the area within the distance of a man's water-splashing all around is what is called there 'common residence' and 'a single observance-day'";
this is what is known as the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*). In that regard, a river has the same characteristics as those described for the river-markers;
the ocean is also clearly evident. However, that which is not made by anyone digging it out, but is self-arisen—
A pool that remains filled with water coming from all directions—where water collects during the rainy season as described for a river—is called a "natural lake" (*jātassara*).
Furthermore, even a pool that has been excavated by water flowing out after breaking through a river or the ocean attains this characteristic;
this too is indeed a natural lake. Among these, such as rivers and so forth, whichever location...
An area delimited on all sides by the splash of water from a man of medium strength is called a "water-splash boundary" (*udakukkhepasīmā*).

How, then, is the water-splash to be made? Just as gamblers throw a wooden ball, so should one take either water or sand in the hand and throw it with all one's might using the strength of a man of medium build.
Wherever water or sand thrown thus falls, this constitutes one "water-splash" (*udakukkhepa*).
Standing within the range of an arm’s reach from that point, one commits the formal act (*kamma*). As long as the assembly increases, the boundary (*sīmā*) also increases;
the measure is precisely the water-splash extending to the limit of the assembly, and this is obtained only within these [specified] rivers and so forth, not outside them.
Therefore, in a river or a lake, whatever area is flooded by water during the four months of the natural rainy season,
or in the ocean, whatever area the natural waves reach and settle upon— that from that point onward is *kappiya-bhūmi* (permissible ground).
It is allowable to perform the Uposatha and other rites while standing there, whether during a time of drought or in the summer heat.
Or, even when rivers and natural lakes have dried up, that very spot remains a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an allowable ground).

However, if they dig a pond or a reservoir in a dried-up natural lake or catchment area, or cultivate it, that place becomes village territory (*gāma-khetta*). As for what is called a "kappiya-bhūmi," the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (the boundary determined by the throwing of water) does not extend beyond it;
it extends only within. Therefore, from the inside of those [natural lakes], up to the edge of the assembly...
Starting from that point, a boundary defined by the splash of water should be established all around; this is the summary here.

This, however, is the detailed explanation: if a river is not very long, such that the Saṅgha can sit everywhere from its source down to its mouth, there is no need for a formal act (*kamma*) regarding a water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), for the entire river belongs to them alone.

It is appropriate for monks [to build a hut]. However, that which was stated by the Elder Mahāsumma—namely, "Even in the case of a river flowing for a *yojana*, it is permissible to perform the work after leaving half a *yojana* above and below"—was refuted by the Elder Mahāpaduma himself.
For the Blessed One said: "Having covered the three circles, where..."
The statement, "In some places, the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) of a bhikkhunī crossing [the water] becomes wet," refers to the measurement of a river, not one *yojana* or half a *yojana*.

Therefore, it is permissible to perform a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) starting from the source of that river which possesses the characteristics previously described according to this rule. However, if there are many bhikkhus here...
Each person performs the ritual separately;

however, between the boundary established by all of them for their own respective water-sprinkling, another water-sprinkling must be set aside to serve as the boundary-line (*sīmantarikā*). It is stated that more than this is permissible, but less is not allowed.
This same principle applies to natural lakes and the ocean as well.

However, when those who have gone to a river thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha ceremony," find that the river is full and level with its banks, they should put on their bathing robes and perform the ceremony right within the river.
If they are unable to do so, it may be performed even while standing in a boat;
yet, it is not permitted to perform it while the boat is moving. Why? Because the boundary is merely the distance of a stone's throw in water. That...
A boat does not remain stationary for long; such being the case, there would be a formal motion (*ñatti*) within one boundary and the proclamation (*anusāvanā*) within another.
Therefore, having moored the boat with a rudder, or having weighed it down with stones, or having tied it to a tree growing within the river, the legal act (*kamma*) should be performed.
It may also be performed by those standing on a raft tied within the river or by those standing on a tree growing within the river.

It is permissible. However, if the branch of a tree or a shoot growing from it is established on the bank outside the river, or within the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*), or within the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*), the work may be performed either by clearing the boundary or by cutting the branch.
Or, in the case of a tree grown on the bank outside the river, one may tie a boat to its branch or shoot that has entered into the river.
It is not permissible to perform formal acts (kamma); those who do so must either clear the boundary (sīmā) or destroy its status by cutting it away so that it stands outside [the territory].
However, on a riverbank, it is likewise not permissible to perform acts for a boat tied to a post driven into the ground.
If they build a bridge over a river, and both the bridge and the bridge-piers are entirely within the river, then for those standing upon the bridge, the act is permissible.
It is permissible to perform the work. However, if the bridge or the bridge-piers are established on the outer bank, it is not permissible to perform the work;
the boundary must be cleared away before it may be done. But if the bridge-piers are on the inner side and the bridge itself stands in the air above both banks, it is permissible.
In a riverine area (*antonadiya*), there may be either rocks or sandbanks;
therein, whatever extent of ground is submerged by water during the four months of the rainy season at the time of natural rainfall as previously described, that is reckoned as a river itself.
During times of excessive rain, the area submerged by a flood should not be included, for that is reckoned only as a village boundary.
When they are removing earth from the riverbed, they create a dam in the river;
if the water flows over or through that dam, it is permissible to perform the work everywhere the water is flowing.
However, if the current is cut off by the dam or by a structural embankment so that the water does not flow, then in that place where there is no flow—
It is not permissible to do it; it is not permissible even to do so by way of a mere obstruction.
If some area for obstruction is completely submerged by water—just as the previously mentioned rock-island area was—it is permissible there, for that indeed counts as a river.
They destroy the river and construct a pond; when the water comes from below and reaches the pond, which is bounded by an embankment...
"Having filled [the tank], it remains standing": in this case, it is not permitted to perform work [on the tank].

However, it is permitted starting from the place where the water, having flowed down from the upper reaches and being discharged below, enters the river. Even when there is no rain, during the winter or summer seasons, it is permitted even for a dry river.
It is not permitted [to use water] from a channel diverted from the river. If, after some time, that...

If it breaks apart and becomes a river, it is permissible. If a certain river rises up and flows over the boundary of a village or town, it remains a river, and it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*) there.
However, if it overflows the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*), it is reckoned simply as the monastery boundary.
Even in the ocean, for those performing the formal act, whatever area is reached by water rising from below or by the force of natural waves—
If the waves come and spread over it, it is not permissible to perform the work there.
However, in whatever place the natural waves roll in and settle, that area from the water’s edge inward is called the "sea"; those standing there may perform the work.
If the force of the waves is oppressive, they should perform it while standing on a boat or a platform. The detailed explanation regarding these matters is found in the section on rivers.
This should be understood in the same manner already stated. In the ocean there is a rock on the surface; sometimes waves come and submerge it, and sometimes they do not.
It is not permissible to perform work there, for it is merely reckoned as belonging to the village boundary.
However, if it is submerged by the natural water—whether waves have arrived or not—it is permissible. An island [is also included].
Or there may be a mountain; if it is distant and not on a path accessible to fishermen, it is reckoned as belonging to the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*).
However, on this side of the limit of their access, it is reckoned as belonging to the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*);
in such a case, it is not permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) there without first clearing away the village boundary. If the ocean overflows onto a village boundary or a town boundary...
It remains; it becomes like the ocean, and it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*) there.
However, if it overflows the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*), it is reckoned as belonging to the monastery boundary itself.
When those performing the formal act at a natural pond (*jātassara*) have just finished the rain during the rainy season—provided the conditions previously mentioned are met—
If there is no water for drinking or for washing the hands and feet, and it dries up, this is not a natural pond (*jātassara*);
it merely counts as village-field land, and no work [of construction] should be done there.
However, where water remains during the aforementioned rainy season, that alone is a natural pond. In whatever area the water remains during the four months of the rains, therein—

It is permissible to perform the ritual. If the water is deep, it is also permissible to build a platform and perform it while standing upon it—even on a platform built over a tree growing within a natural pond (*jātassara*).
Regarding back-stone islands (*piṭṭhipāsāṇadīpaka*) here, the determination is exactly as stated for the river.
However, even if there is sufficient water in a natural pond during a year of normal rainfall, if it is a time of drought—
Or if it dries up in the summer or winter and becomes waterless, it is permissible to perform a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) there.
As for what is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā—that "every natural pond that has dried up and is without water belongs exclusively to the village territory"—that should not be accepted.
However, if they dig a well or a lotus pond, etc., here for the purpose of obtaining water, [it is permissible].
That place becomes an *ajātassara* (a natural pond) and is reckoned as part of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
The same principle applies even when it is filled with creepers such as *lābu* or *tipusa*.

However, if they fill it up and make it dry land, or if they build a bank on one side and turn the whole area into a large reservoir (*mahātaḷāka*), then the entire area becomes an *ajātassara* and is reckoned as part of the village boundary.
Even salt water is reckoned as "natural water" (jātassara). During the four months of the rainy season, it is permissible to perform work in a place that has become a body of water.
This is the exposition regarding the unbound boundary (abaddhasīmā).
Thus ends the compendium of the Vinaya exposition not found in the Pāḷi.
The Discussion on the Determination of the *Sīmā* is finished.
25. The Discussion on the Determination of the Observance (*Uposatha*) and the Invitation (*Pavāraṇā*). 168.
Regarding the phrase "the observance and the invitation": here, by way of days, there are three observances—the fourteenth-day and the fifteenth-day.
"Uposatha by assembly. In this context, there are twenty-four Uposathas in one year:
six on the fourteenth day—counting two each in the third and seventh fortnights of the three seasons of winter, summer, and the rains—and the remaining ones on the fifteenth day.
This, first of all, is the normal practice. However, when such a cause exists, the Uposatha may also be held on another fourteenth day.
It is appropriate to do so. However, for those who have completed the previous rains residence, the full moon of the former Kattika month is [the first day].

If they, being harassed by quarrelsome persons, postpone their invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), then either the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika or the full moon of the latter Kattika month is [the first day];

and for those who have completed the subsequent rains residence, only the full moon of the latter Kattika month is [the first day]. Thus, these three days are also the initial days for the invitation ceremony.
These are [the normal practices]. This too is simply the natural conduct (*pakaticāritta*).
When such conditions exist, it is permissible to perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) on the two preceding fourteenth days of the two full-moon days of Kattika.

However, when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been split according to the method described in the Kosambaka-kkhandhaka, and that bhikkhu has been reinstated, the Saṅgha, for the sake of settling that matter—
When he effects the harmony of the Saṅgha, at that very moment the Uposatha should be performed.
Because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha should be recited," any day other than the fourteenth or fifteenth is indeed called an Uposatha day;
however, within the month of Kattika for those who have completed the rains residence, this specific day is known as the day of the Pavāraṇā for the sake of harmony.
Thus, the Uposatha should be observed during these three days. When performing it, if it falls on the fourteenth day, one should say:
"Today is the Uposatha of the fourteenth. If it is a Uposatha for the sake of communal harmony (*sāmaggī*), one should say:
"Today is the Uposatha for harmony. On the fifteenth day, however, one should say: "Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth," according to the method transmitted in the Canon.
169. "Uposatha in the Saṅgha, uposatha in a group, and uposatha with an individual"—thus three other types of uposatha have been mentioned by way of the performers.

However, by way of the manner in which it is to be performed, there are yet three other types of uposatha: the recitation of the Sutta, the uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi), and the uposatha of formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
Therein, the "recitation of the Sutta" refers to [the formula] beginning with: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs."
The recitation of the Pātimokkha is spoken according to this method. As for the other two Uposatha observances, among them, first, the Uposatha of pure confession (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) is twofold:
by way of declaring it in the presence of others and by way of mutual declaration. Therein, that which is performed in the presence of others is also twofold:
by way of performing it in the presence of those who have already invited (*pavārita*) and those who have not yet invited. Therein—

It should be performed by one who has entered the later rains-residence—whether or not he has approached those who have already performed the Great Pavāraṇā—or by one whose rains-residence has been interrupted;

or else, by one who has not approached those who have performed the four-month Pavāraṇā or whose rains-residence has been interrupted, after having offered physical harmony and said three times: "Venerable sirs, I am pure; may you remember me as pure."
However, except on the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), at any other time, when the *pātimokkha* has merely been recited by the resident monks,
whether the assembly has not yet risen, or some have risen, or all have risen, those others who arrive— whether they are equal in number or fewer—
should announce their purity in the presence of those [resident monks] according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, that which is performed by means of mutual announcement is twofold: by way of performing [the act] after having established a motion (*ñatti*), and by way of performing it without establishing a motion.

In this regard, when three bhikkhus are dwelling in a certain residence and have assembled on the Uposatha day, one bhikkhu should say: "Venerable sirs, listen to me; today is the Uposatha of the fourteenth."

Or, having said "the fifteenth day," and after the motion has been established with the words, "Venerable sirs, if it is timely for you, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purification," the senior monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika), raise his joined palms, and say:
"Friends, I am pure; may you consider me to be pure."
It should be recited three times. The others, having addressed him as "Venerable Sir," should recite in the same manner. Having thus established the motion (*ñatti*), it should be performed.
However, where two monks reside, the motion need not be established; rather, purity should be announced in the manner already described.
This is the Uposatha of Purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*).
If, however, there is only one monk, he should perform all the preliminary duties, ascertain that no others are coming, and having said, "Today is my Uposatha;
it is the fourteenth" or "the fifteenth," he should say, "I resolve. This is the Uposatha by resolution.
Thus, the three types of Uposatha should be understood according to the manner in which they are to be performed. Up to this point—
Nine types of Uposatha are explained. Among these, by way of day: the fifteenth-day [Uposatha];
by way of the performing agent: the Saṅgha-Uposatha; by way of the manner in which it is to be performed: the recitation of the Sutta.

When such an Uposatha, endowed with these three characteristics, is being observed, if one does not perform the Uposatha on that very Uposatha day, but instead goes to another monastery that is either without monks or inhabited by monks of a different affiliation—
If one goes to a place that is not a residence for the purpose of staying there—unless it is with the Saṅgha or unless there is an obstacle—it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

170. When the Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of performing the Uposatha, if someone who has performed the Uposatha elsewhere arrives and, having gone to the place of assembly, does not grant his physical presence (kāyasāmaggi), he must give his consent (chanda). This applies even if he is ill or occupied with some duty.
One who gives the purity must also give consent (*chandam*). How so? In the presence of a single monk, this meaning—“I give consent;
take my consent; announce my consent”—must be made known either by body, by speech, or by both;
thus is consent given. [This applies even] when one has not performed the Uposatha, or is ill, or is preoccupied with business.
Or, the purity (pārisuddhi) may be given. How? In the presence of a single bhikkhu, the meaning—“I give my purity; take my purity;
announce my purity”—must be made known by means of body, speech, or both.
In this way, the purity is considered given. Furthermore, when giving it, consent (chanda) must also be given. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“I allow you, monks, when giving formal purity (*pārisuddhi*) on the Uposatha day, to give consent (*chanda*) as well, provided there is business for the Saṅgha.
In this context, the giving of formal purity accomplishes both the performance of the Uposatha for the Saṅgha and for oneself, but not the remaining duties of the Saṅgha;
whereas the giving of consent accomplishes both the performance of the Uposatha for the Saṅgha and its remaining duties.
He fulfills [the observance], yet his own Uposatha remains unperformed; therefore, when giving purification, one must also give consent (*chandam*).

It is permissible for a single person to bring forward either the pure consent (*suddhika-chanda*) mentioned previously, or the purification (*pārisuddhi*), or this combined consent and purification (*chandapārisuddhi*), even on behalf of many. However, if he sees another bhikkhu along the way...
If he has received the consent (*chanda*) or the purity (*pārisuddhi*) of those [monks], he gives his own consent and purity to them as well;
it returns to him alone. However, that which is called "cat's chain" consent and purity does not return;
therefore, one must go to the place of assembly oneself and announce it. But if, intentionally...

If he does not announce it, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); however, his consent and purification (*chandapārisuddhi*) are considered conveyed as soon as he has come within arm’s reach.
171. But by means of a deferred giving of consent, no formal act of the Saṅgha whatsoever may be performed.

In this regard, there are four kinds of deferral: deferral of the assembly (*parisapārivāsiya*), deferral of the night (*rattipārivāsiya*), deferral of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*), and deferral of intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).
Among these, "the assembly being dispersed" means: monks have gathered for some business, and then either a cloud arises, a signal is given to clear out, or people come crowding in;
the monks, thinking, "We have no space here, let us go elsewhere," rise up without having sent forth their *chanda* (consent). This is "the assembly being dispersed."
Even though there is a delay in the assembly, it is permissible to perform the formal act (kamma) because the consent (chanda) has not been withheld.
Furthermore, monks might gather at night, intending to perform the Uposatha and other rites, and request one among them, saying, "Let us listen to the Dhamma until everyone has assembled.
While that person is still delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, the dawn breaks.
It rises. If they have sat down thinking, "We will perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day," it is permissible to perform it on the fifteenth.
If they have sat down to perform it on the fifteenth, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the fortnight (*pāṭipada*), which is not an Uposatha day;
however, it is permissible to perform other business of the Saṅgha. This is called "overflowing by night" (*rattipārivāsiya*).
Again, some monks sat down thinking, "We shall perform some formal act of the Saṅgha, such as a rehabilitation (abbhāna).
There, one monk who was an astrologer said, "Today the constellation is unfavorable; do not perform this.
Because of his words, they relinquished their consent and remained sitting right there. Then another [monk] arrived and said, "The constellation..."
Having said, "While he was honoring [the assembly], the matter passed the fool by," he says, "What is the use of the lunar mansion?

Do it! This is both *chandapārivāsiya* (suspension of consent) and *ajjhāsayapārivāsiya* (suspension of intention). In this case of suspension, it is not permitted to perform the formal act (*kamma*) without first bringing back the purity of consent (*chandapārisuddhi*).
172. If any monk who is ill is unable to give his consent and purification, he should be brought into the midst of the Saṅgha on a bed or a chair.
If it occurs to the monks who are nursing the sick, "If we move the sick man from this place, his illness will either increase or he will pass away," [they need not move him].
That bhikkhu must not be removed from his place; the Saṅgha should go there and perform the Uposatha.
If many such sick persons are present, the Saṅgha should stand in a row and bring them all within arm’s reach.
If they are far away and the Saṅgha is unable to do so, the Uposatha should not be performed on that day. However, it must never be performed by a factional Saṅgha.
The Uposatha should be performed; if one were to perform it [without doing so], there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If, while four monks are residing in a single monastery, three perform the purity-Uposatha after bringing the consent and purity of one, or if three are residing [there] and they perform it after bringing the consent and purity of one...
If two recite the Pātimokkha, it is an Uposatha procedure that is illegal and performed by an incomplete assembly.
However, if four have gathered together and perform the Uposatha of mutual purity, or if three or two recite the Pātimokkha, it is called "legal but performed by an incomplete assembly.
If, among four persons, one brings their own purity and the other three recite the Pātimokkha...

They recite the Pātimokkha; or, having brought the purity of one among three persons, they perform the Uposatha of purity for two—this is called a "legitimate but incomplete" (dhammena vagga) assembly.

However, if four who are dwelling together all assemble and recite the Pātimokkha, or if three perform the Uposatha of purity, or if two perform the Uposatha of purity with one another, [these are also legitimate assemblies].
It is called "in accordance with the Dhamma and in concord.

173.
