Regarding the formal acts of invitation (*pavāraṇā-kamma*), however, if five monks are residing in a single monastery, they may perform the invitation by bringing the invitation of one monk and then performing it after four have established the motion for the assembly; or, if four or three are residing [there].
If they bring the invitation of one person and then perform the invitation by establishing a motion for the Saṅgha— whether three or two people do so—
all this is an invitation procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma and is a discordant (vagga) act.
But if all five persons gather together and perform the invitation by establishing a motion for a group (gaṇañatti), or if four, three, or two who are residing together gather together...

If they perform the invitation ceremony by establishing a formal motion (*saṅghañatti*) while excluding one person from among five, this entire invitation procedure is an illegal act performed by a unanimous assembly.
Or, if four people perform the invitation by bringing the invitation of one person and establishing a formal motion,
or if three or two people perform the invitation by bringing the invitation of one person and establishing a group motion (*gaṇañatti*).
All this is a factional *pavāraṇā* procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma. However, if all five persons assemble together and perform the *pavāraṇā* after establishing a motion for the Saṅgha;
or if four or three assemble together and perform the *pavāraṇā* after establishing a motion for a group (*gaṇa*);
or if two perform the *pavāraṇā* with one another; or if one staying alone performs a *pavāraṇā* by formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-pavāraṇā*).
All this is called a *pavāraṇā* procedure that is lawful and in harmony.
Herein, if it is the fourteenth-day *pavāraṇā*, one should resolve thus: "Today is my fourteenth-day *pavāraṇā*";
if it is the fifteenth-day [pavāraṇā], one should resolve thus: "Today is my fifteenth-day *pavāraṇā*. Furthermore, by the one granting the *pavāraṇā*, [it should be said]: "I grant the *pavāraṇā*."
"Bring my invitation; invite on my behalf"—this meaning must be conveyed by means of body, speech, or both body and speech.
Once the invitation has been thus given, the one who brings the invitation should approach the Saṅgha and invite in this manner:
"Venerable sirs, this bhikkhu invites the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."
Or rather, let the Saṅgha, out of compassion, speak to him, venerable sir; seeing [his fault], he will make amends. For a second time, venerable sir...
[as before] ...For a third time, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Saṅgha... [as before] ...he will make amends.
But if he is senior, one should say, “Venerable sir, the venerable Tissa. For in this way, on his behalf—
The invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has been performed. However, when one is giving the invitation, consent (*chanda*) must also be given;
the manner of giving consent should be understood according to the method explained below. Here too, the giving of consent is for the sake of the remaining formal acts.

Therefore, if one who is giving the invitation also gives consent, then by the invitation being brought forward in the manner described and by that monk, the invitation ceremony is indeed completed by the Saṅgha.

Now, if he gives only the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) and not the consent (*chanda*), then when his invitation has been announced and the Saṅgha has performed its invitation, the invitation of all is well-performed;

however, other formal acts (*kamma*) are invalidated. If he gives only the consent and not the invitation, the Saṅgha’s invitation and the remaining formal acts are not invalidated; nevertheless, that monk has not invited.
However, on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, even if one has arrived after resolving to perform the *pavāraṇā* outside the boundary, consent (*chanda*) must be given;
by doing so, the *pavāraṇā* procedure of the Saṅgha is not invalidated.
If five monks have entered the rains retreat during the first period and another five during the second period, [the resident monks] should, with the former, propose a motion...
Except when the invitation has been performed, the Uposatha of purity should be carried out in their presence by those who arrive later;

one should not propose two motions at a single Uposatha site. Even if there are four, three, two, or only one person who has arrived during the later period, the same rule applies. Furthermore, if there are four during the earlier period and also four, three, or two during the later period...
Or there may be only one; the same method applies. Furthermore, if there were three in the earlier period, then in the later period there may also be three, two, or one;
the same method applies. This is the defining characteristic here:
if those who have entered the rains residence in the later period are fewer than, or equal in number to, those who entered in the earlier period, [the same rules apply].
And since they complete the quorum for a formal invitation of the Saṅgha, a motion must be put by way of a formal invitation of the Saṅgha.

However, if there is only one person during the later period, and together with him they become four, it is not permitted for them to perform the invitation after putting a motion for a Saṅgha of four.
But in the case of a motion for a group, he becomes the completer of that group; therefore, the motion is to be put by way of a group.

Excluding those [who have already performed the invitation ceremony], one should perform the *pavāraṇā* with the others; for those [remaining], the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* should be performed in their presence.
This same method applies whether there are two in the first period (*purimikā*) and two or one in the second period (*pacchimikā*).

If there is one in the first period and one in the second period, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* in the presence of the other, and the other should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*. If, by the first...
If those who entered the rains residence later are even one person more numerous than those who entered first, then after the Pātimokkha has been recited by the former group,
the latter should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony in their presence.
However, regarding the four-month Pavāraṇā at the end of the Kattika month, if the first group who entered the rains residence has already performed the Great Pavāraṇā:
If those who have entered the rains residence later are more numerous or equal in number, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) should be performed after setting aside the formal motion (*ñatti*).
When they have invited, the others should subsequently perform the Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*).

Now, if many have invited during the Great Invitation (*mahā-pavāraṇā*), and those who have entered the rains residence later are few or even only one, then after the Pātimokkha has been recited, [the procedure for] them...
He should perform the *pavāraṇā* in their presence. But should this *Pātimokkha* be recited in its entirety, or even just in part?
It is permissible to recite even a part. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of reciting the *Pātimokkha*: having recited the introduction (*nidāna*), the remainder may be announced by way of summary."

This is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Nidāna and having recited the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by way of summary; this is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha.

Having recited the Nidāna, having recited the four Pārājikas, and having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, the remainder should be announced by way of summary; this is the third recitation of the Pātimokkha.

"Having recited the Nidāna, having recited the four Pārājikas, having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, and having recited the two Aniyatas, the remainder should be announced by way of summary; this is the fourth method of reciting the Pātimokkha. The fifth is by way of full detail.
Therein, "having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by way of hearing" means: "Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs... [etc.]".
Having recited this introduction: "For one who has confessed, there is ease," [he says]: "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited.
Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask... [as before] ... Thus do I understand this to be.
Furthermore, the four *pārājika* rules have been heard by the venerable ones... [as before] ... You should train yourselves without disputing."
In this way, the remainder should be announced by means of recitation. By this method, the other four recitations of the Pātimokkha are also to be understood.
174. “I allow you, monks, when there is an obstacle, to recite the Pātimokkha in brief.
Monks, when there is no obstacle, the Pātimokkha must not be recited in brief; whoever should so recite it, there is an offense.”
However, because of the statement, "It is an offense of wrong-doing," the Pātimokkha should not be recited in brief when there are no obstacles.

In this regard, these are the obstacles: a royal obstacle, a thief obstacle, a fire obstacle, a water obstacle, a human obstacle, a non-human obstacle, a beast obstacle, a creeping-creature obstacle, a life-threatening obstacle, and an obstacle to the holy life.
In that regard, if while the monks are seated, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha," a king arrives, this is an obstruction caused by a king (*rājantarāya*).

If thieves arrive, this is an obstruction caused by thieves (*corantarāya*). If a forest fire approaches, or a fire breaks out in the monastery, this is an obstruction caused by fire (*aggiantarāya*).
If a cloud arises, or a flood arrives, this is an obstruction caused by water (*udakantarāya*). Or if many people...
They come; this is a human obstacle. A *yakkha* seizes a bhikkhu; this is a non-human obstacle.
Fierce wild animals such as tigers and the like approach; this is a wild-beast obstacle. Snakes and the like bite a bhikkhu; this is a reptile obstacle.
A bhikkhu becomes ill, or passes away, or enemies wishing to kill him seize him; this is—
A threat to life. When people, whether one or many, seize monks with the desire to cause them to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*), this is a threat to the holy life.

In the presence of such threats, the *Pātimokkha* should be recited in brief, or the first section (*uddesa*) should be recited—namely, the first two, three, or four sections. Herein, regarding the second and subsequent sections:

If an obstacle arises before the [Nidāna] has been completed, that too must be announced by means of the Sutta. However, when the recitation of the Nidāna has not yet been finished, there is no such thing as announcing by means of the Sutta.
Even in the case of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, if an obstacle occurs, it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā by means of two statements, one statement, or by way of equal seniority (*samānavassika*).
In this case, even when laying down the motion (*ñatti*), one should say: "If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by means of two statements.

For a single-statement invitation, one should say: "Let [the Saṅgha] perform the invitation by means of a single statement"; and for those of equal seniority (*samānavassika*), one should say: "Let [the Saṅgha] perform the invitation for those of equal seniority.
And in this regard, even many who are of equal seniority may perform the invitation together. "May the venerable ones listen to me."
“Sangha, today is the fifteenth day of the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā). If it is agreeable to the Sangha, let the Sangha perform the invitation ceremony.
When this all-inclusive formal motion (ñatti) has been established, it is permissible to perform the invitation ceremony by three statements, two statements, or one statement;

however, it is not permissible to do so according to the number of years since ordination (samānavassika). But when it is said, “Let [the Sangha] perform the invitation ceremony by three statements,” then it must be performed by three statements alone.

The [second] is permissible; the other is not permissible. When it is said, "One should invite with two utterances," both the two-utterance and the three-utterance methods are permissible, while the one-utterance and the same-year methods are not permissible.

However, when it is said, "One should invite with one utterance," the one-utterance, two-utterance, and three-utterance methods are permissible, but only the same-year method is not permissible. Regarding the term "same-year":
When all has been spoken, everything is valid.

175. But by whom should the Pātimokkha be recited? Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow the Pātimokkha to have the Elder as its head," the Pātimokkha should be recited by the Elder, or—monks, I allow whichever monk is there... [to recite it].
Or it may be by one who is junior, because of the statement: "He is competent and capable; the Pātimokkha is dependent upon him.
And here, although the recitation of the Pātimokkha is permitted even for one who is junior provided he is competent, nevertheless, this is the intended meaning:
if five, four, or three recitations of the Pātimokkha do not come from the Elder, but two [recitations] are unbroken...
The words become very clear, and the Pātimokkha depends entirely upon the Elder.
However, if one is unable to make even this much clear, it depends upon a learned monk; therefore, either he himself should recite it, or another should be requested.
"Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be recited in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been requested."
Because of the statement, "Whoever should recite it [when not requested] commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," the Pātimokkha must not be recited by one who has not been requested.
Not only the Pātimokkha, but even the Dhamma must not be spoken; for there is the statement: "Monks, the Dhamma must not be spoken in the midst of the Saṅgha by one who has not been requested;
whoever should speak it commits an offense of wrong-doing."
In this context, "request" (*ajjhesanā*) refers either to dependence on a Dharma-requester appointed by the Sangha, or to dependence on the Elder of the Sangha for the sake of the Sangha;
therefore, in the absence of a Dharma-requester, one may speak after having requested permission from the Elder of the Sangha, or when invited by him.
Even by the Elder of the Sangha, if there are many preachers of the Dharma in the monastery, it should be said according to the sequence of turns: "You..."
When told, "Recite the Dhamma" or "Give the gift of Dhamma," one may speak the Dhamma in all three ways (chanting, reciting, and explaining).

However, when told, "Recite [from memory]," one is permitted only to recite; when told, "Speak," one must speak; and when told, "Recite the *sara-bhañña*," one must recite the *sara-bhañña* specifically.
Furthermore, even the senior elder of the Saṅgha, if seated on a higher seat, is not permitted to request [the Dhamma].
If the preceptor is also the resident pupil, and the preceptor sits on a high seat and says, "Recite," one should recite after having resolved upon the lesson.
However, if there are junior bhikkhus present there, one should recite thinking, "I am reciting for them.
If the senior of the Saṅgha in the monastery has his own dependents recite, [one should do so].
If he does not even request other sweet-spoken monks [to speak], he may be told by others: "Venerable sir, please have such-and-such a person speak.
If he says, "Please have them speak," or remains silent, it is permissible to have him speak.
But if he refuses, one should not have him speak. However, if the Saṅgha elders have already begun the hearing of the Dhamma before he has arrived, then—

When [the Sangha] has arrived, there is no need for the formal act of asking permission (*āpucchanakicca*) except for the purpose of suspending the recitation. However, once the recitation has been suspended, one who wishes to speak must either ask for permission or speak even without having asked.
This same rule applies even when he returns after having spoken.
In the case of informal conversation while seated together as well, the Elder of the Sangha alone is the master; therefore, either he himself should speak or another [should be authorized].
A bhikkhu should be told, “Speak,” but not by one sitting nearby in a higher position; however, it is permissible for people to say, “Please speak.
When people ask a bhikkhu who knows [the answer], he should speak even after having requested permission from the elder (thera).
If the senior of the Saṅgha is asked, “Venerable sir, these people are asking questions,” [he may respond accordingly].
If he says, “Speak,” or if he remains silent, it is permissible to speak. This same principle applies to giving thanks (*anumodanā*) and so forth while inside a house.
If the senior of the Saṅgha grants permission, saying, “You may speak in the monastery or inside a house even without asking me,” then it is deemed allowable;
in all such cases, it is permissible to speak. Even when one is engaged in recitation (*sajjhāya*), the senior...
One must indeed ask for permission. If another person arrives while one has already asked permission and is reciting, there is no further need to ask for permission.
Even if someone arrives while one has set aside the recitation thinking, "I shall rest," one must ask for permission again when beginning once more.
This same rule applies even when one has begun reciting before the Sangha-thera has arrived. By one Sangha-thera...
When permission has been granted with the words, “Recite as you wish even without asking me,” it is permissible to recite as one wishes;
however, when another person arrives, one must ask that person for permission before reciting.
But in whatever monastery all the bhikkhus are foolish and incompetent, not knowing how to recite the Pātimokkha, [the following applies].
In that case, what should be done? Those monks should immediately dispatch one monk from the neighboring residence, saying:
"Go, friend; having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, return.
If they should succeed in this way, that is good. If they do not succeed, then all those monks [should go] wherever...
Such are the monks [who must be present]; that residence must be visited every half-month for the purpose of performing the Uposatha;

for those who do not go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). And this applies only during the dry season; however, during the rains, one should not enter the rains retreat without a reciter of the Pātimokkha.
If he departs or disrobes while they have entered the rains retreat, or if he dies...
If one does so, it is permissible to stay for the later period only if there is another [monastery]; if there is not, one must go elsewhere.
For those who do not go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if one departs during the later period, or renounces the training, or dies, one must stay for two months.
But where those foolish, incompetent monks dwell, if some monk should come there who is learned, one who has mastered the tradition,
a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent,
modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, those monks should welcome, assist, and encourage that monk.

He must be attended to with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, and water for rinsing the mouth. If they do not attend to him, do not assist him, and do not provide for him by attending to him with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, and water for rinsing the mouth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for all of them.
Herein, neither the elders nor the juniors are exempt; he must be attended to by everyone in turn. [One should attend] to oneself...

There is an offense for one who does not attend upon him on his day of rest. Furthermore, he must not accept from the great elders such things as the sweeping of their courtyards or the offering of tooth-sticks;
even so, the great elders must come to attend upon him in the evening and in the morning.
However, having learned of their arrival, he himself should go to attend upon the great elders earlier than they do. If he is traveling together with them...
If there are resident monks (*upaṭṭhāka*), he should say: "I have resident monks; you may dwell free from anxiety.

Even if he has no companions traveling with him, if one or two other monks who are perfected in their duties (*vattasampanna*) reside in that very same monastery and say, "We shall perform what must be done for the Elder;
let the rest dwell in comfort," there is no offense for anyone.
176. “He who has an offense should reveal it,” according to these and other such words, the Uposatha should not be performed by one who is guilty of an offense;
therefore, on that very day of the Uposatha, one who remembers an offense must confess it.
And when confessing, he should approach a single bhikkhu, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit down on his heels, raise his joined palms, and speak as follows:
“I, friend, have fallen into such-and-such an offense; I confess it. If he is junior, he should say, “Venerable sir, I...
As for the phrase “I confess it,” it is perfectly correct to say, according to what is appropriate for each individual, “I confess it in your presence” or “I confess it before you. The receiver, too—
According to what is appropriate for each individual, one should say, "Venerable sir, see that offense; friend, do you see that offense?
The confessor should then reply, "Yes, friend, I see it; yes, venerable sir, I see it.
Again, the receiver should say, "Venerable sir, restrain yourself in the future; friend, restrain yourself in the future."

Or it may be said. When this has been said by the instructor, [the other] should say, "Very well, friend, I will restrain myself thoroughly; very well, venerable sir, I will restrain myself thoroughly.
If he is doubtful regarding an offense, he should approach one monk, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit down on his haunches, and raise his joined palms in salutation.
He should speak thus: "Friends, I am uncertain regarding such-and-such an offense;
when I become certain, I will then make amends for that offense. Having said this, the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be heard;
on no account should an obstacle to the Uposatha be created on that account. "Monks, a shared offense should not be confessed."
"Whoever should confess [such an offense], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, a similar offense (sabhāgā āpatti) must not be accepted;

whoever should accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Because of this statement, an offense that two people incur through a common basis—such as eating at an improper time—is neither to be confessed nor accepted. This refers to offenses based on eating at an improper time.

However, it is permissible to confess an offense that has been committed—which is similar in nature—to one who has also committed an offense similar to it on account of eating food that is not leftover.
But if the entire Saṅgha commits a light offense through a common basis, such as eating at an improper time, what should be done in that case?
Those monks should immediately dispatch one monk from a neighboring residence, saying: "Go, friend..."
“Having expiated that offense, come back; we shall expiate the offense in your presence.
If this can be arranged, it is well. If it cannot be arranged, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This entire Saṅgha has fallen into a shared offense. When another...”
Having said, "He will see a pure bhikkhu who is free from offense, and then he will confess that offense in his presence," the Uposatha should be performed.
But if he is uncertain, [he should say]: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this entire Saṅgha is uncertain regarding a common offense; when I become certain, then I shall [confess] that offense."

Having said, "I will make amends," the Uposatha should be performed. However, if someone there, thinking that "it is permissible to confess that similar offense," confesses it in the presence of one person, then once confessed, it is indeed well-confessed.
But otherwise, both the confessor on account of the confession and the receiver on account of the receiving incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That [offense] has various bases; therefore, it must be confessed to one another. Up to this point, they become free from offense;
in their presence, the remaining similar offenses must be confessed or announced by the others.

If they perform the Uposatha without doing so, according to the method beginning with, "Venerable sirs, announce your purity," and so forth, then regarding the performance of the Uposatha by one who possesses an offense:
They incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If any bhikkhu, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, remembers an offense, that bhikkhu should speak thus to a neighboring bhikkhu:
"Friend, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense; having emerged from this [recitation], I shall deal with that offense."
"I shall make amends. Furthermore, the monk who is a neighbor should be one who is similar [in status].

For if it is said to one who is dissimilar, quarrels, strife, schisms in the Saṅgha, and so forth may arise; therefore, without speaking to him, one should perform the Uposatha while forming the intention: "Having emerged from this [seclusion], I shall make amends.
However, if someone becomes doubtful regarding an offense while the Pātimokkha is being recited...
If there is a neighboring monk who is similar in this regard, he should be addressed thus:
"Friend, I am uncertain regarding such-and-such an offense; when I become certain, I shall then make amends for that offense.
Having spoken thus, the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be heard; one must not, on that account, cause an obstruction to the Uposatha.
177. From the words, “I allow you, monks, to sweep the Uposatha hall,” and so forth:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.”
Having performed the fourfold preliminary duty (*pubbakaraṇa*) as thus described, the Uposatha should be carried out. But by whom should it be performed? From such statements as:
“I allow you, monks, for the senior monk to command a junior monk; monks, that which has been commanded by the senior monk must not be neglected by one who is not ill.
Whoever does not sweep, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). And so forth.

Whoever is commanded by the Elder must perform the task. Furthermore, when assigning duties, one should not appoint someone who is currently performing some other work, nor one who is always alone, nor a burden-bearer, nor anyone among the reciters or preachers of the Dhamma;
rather, the remaining monks should be appointed in turn. If one has been appointed and [takes] the broom even for a short time...
If he does not obtain it, he should have branches broken off and made allowable, and then sweep; if even that is not obtained, it becomes allowable for him once it has been acquired.

Furthermore, if there are no seats in the Uposatha hall when one who has been commanded to prepare the seats goes there, he should bring them from the Saṅgha’s residence, arrange them, and then take them back again. In the absence of seats, he may even arrange straw mats or wooden planks.

It is permissible; even if there are no trays, splinters from branches should be prepared by having them made allowable (*kappiya*) and then set out. For one who cannot find a person to make things allowable, anything already made allowable is acceptable.
However, when ordering [materials] for the purpose of making a lamp, one should say: "In such-and-such a place, oil, or a wick, or a bowl..."
Or, if there is [something], take that and do it. If oil and such items are not available, they must be sought;
for one who has sought them but cannot obtain them, what has been obtained becomes permissible. Furthermore, a fire should also be kindled in a pan.
“Consent, purity, the announcement of the season, the number of monks, and the exhortation;”
“These are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.

Thus, although these four kinds of preliminary duties have been described, they must be performed after the *pubbakaraṇa* (the formal announcement). For even without performing those, the Uposatha should not be carried out.
This is because of the statement: “If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha. When [it is time] for the Saṅgha...
The Uposatha transaction is fit to be performed when it is the proper time; and this "proper time" is comprised of four factors.
Therefore, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā said:
"The Uposatha, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the transaction..."
“Shared offenses do not exist,
and there are no persons to be avoided therein;
it is therefore called ‘the right time.’”
In this context, "Uposatha" refers to any one of the three Uposatha days.

For when such a day exists, this formal act of Uposatha for the Saṅgha is said to be "timely and appropriate," but not when it does not exist. As it has been said: "Monks, Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day."
"As many bhikkhus as are entitled to the formal act" means:

however many bhikkhus are eligible, fit, and suitable for that Uposatha act—at the very least, four regular bhikkhus—and who, moreover, stand within the same boundary without having left the reach of one another's hands.
For it is only when those four bhikkhus are standing within the same boundary without having left the reach of one another's hands [that the act is valid].
That Uposatha procedure of the Saṅgha is said to be "fit" (pattakalla), and not otherwise. As it was said:
"I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha for four [monks].
And regarding the phrase "no common offenses exist": here, when the entire Saṅgha [is gathered] by way of a common ground such as eating at the wrong time, etc.
One incurs a light offense; such cases are called "similar in substance" (*vatthusabhāgā sabhāgā*).
Even when these similar cases are absent, it is indeed appropriate (*pattakalla*) even when they are present.
Furthermore, since the persons to be avoided are not present there, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, the Pātimokkha is not [to be recited] in an assembly that includes householders..."

Because of the statement, "It should be recited," it refers to a householder; and because of the method stated in such passages as, "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited to an assembly where a bhikkhunī is seated," it refers to a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, one who has renounced the training,
one who has committed an ultimate offense, one suspended for not seeing an offense, or [one suspended] for not making amends for an offense...
One who has been suspended for failure to make amends, one who has been suspended for not relinquishing an evil view, a paṇḍaka, one living in communion by theft,
one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī,
a schismatic of the Saṅgha, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, and one who is a hermaphrodite— these twenty together with the aforementioned [one] make twenty-one persons.
"Those to be avoided" (vajjanīyā) means they are to be excluded by being kept outside the reach of one's hand.
For when these three types of suspended persons (ukkhitaka) are present, the Saṅgha incurs a *pācittiya* offense if it performs the Uposatha; in the remaining cases, there is a *dukkaṭa*.
And here, "an animal" (tiracchānagata) refers to one for whom full admission (*upasampadā*) has been forbidden. Heretics (*titthiya*) are included among householders; for they too are to be avoided.
Thus it should be understood that this is appropriate when comprised of these four factors.
And all of this should also be applied to and shown in relation to the *pavāraṇā* ceremony: “Monks, the reciter of the Pātimokkha must not intentionally fail to announce [the time].
Whoever should fail to announce it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Monks, I allow the reciter of the Pātimokkha to make an effort.”

"Because of the statement, 'There is no offense for one who makes an effort, [thinking], "How might I announce it to the assembly?"', the reciter of the Pātimokkha must make an effort to announce it to the assembly.
Thus ends the summary of the Vinaya analysis not found in the canonical texts (*Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*).
The Discussion on the Determination of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā is finished.
26. The Discussion on the Determination of the Entrance into the Rains Retreat (Vassūpanāyika) 179.

Regarding the term "entrance into the rains retreat" (*vassūpanāyikā*): there are two such entrances, namely the earlier (*purimikā*) and the later (*pacchimikā*). Among these, [the first begins] from the full moon of Āsāḷhī...

On the first day of the following month, the earlier period (*purimikā*) should be entered; however, the later period (*pacchimikā*) is entered on the first day of the month immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī.
When entering, one should tend to the monastery, provide drinking water and water for washing, complete all acts of reverence such as the worship of the *cetiyas*, and [declare]: "In this..."
One should enter the rains residence by uttering the words once or two or three times: "I enter the rains residence for these three months in this monastery.
Even if one has the underlying intention, "I will dwell here," if one does not enter the rains residence due to a lack of mindfulness, the lodging already taken is well-taken;
one does not become one whose rains residence is broken, and one is indeed permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony. Even without...
For even by the mere act of making a verbal declaration or establishing a residence, one has indeed entered the rains residence.
In this context, the "establishment" (*ālaya*) is simply the arising of the thought:
"I shall dwell here for the rains. "Monks, on the day of the invitation for the rains, one who does not wish to enter the rains residence must not intentionally pass beyond his dwelling."

"Whoever should cross [the boundary], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). According to this statement, if one who does not wish to enter the rains residence crosses the monastery boundary on the day of the commencement of the rains, there is a *dukkaṭa* for each monastery.
For if on that day he enters the precincts of a hundred monasteries and crosses them, there are a hundred offenses. But if, having crossed one monastery, he goes to another...
If he turns back without even having entered the vicinity of the monastery, it is a single offense.
If one has not entered for the earlier period due to some obstacle, one may enter for the later period.
“Monks, the rains residence must not be entered by one who does not have a dwelling place; whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
According to the words of the Buddha, one for whom there is no lodging with its door fastened and secured by any one of the five types of coverings must not enter the rains residence.
From such statements as, “Monks, the rains residence must not be entered in a charnel-house;
whoever should enter it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it follows that [one must not stay] in a charnel-house, under a canopy, or in a water-pot.
It is not permissible to enter there. In that context, a "shroud-hut" (*chavakuṭikā*) refers to a small hut consisting of various types such as those with iron frames or beds.
It is not permissible to enter into that very [shroud-hut]. However, it is permissible to enter after having built another hut within the charnel ground.
Even under a canopy, it is permissible to enter after setting up the canopy upon four pillars, providing a screen, and securing a door.
This is what is called a "parasol-hut. It is permissible to enter a hut made from a large wooden bowl or a large potsherd in the manner described for a parasol.

However, because of the statement, “Monks, one should not enter the rains residence in the hollow of a tree; whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is not permissible to enter a clean tree-hollow; but as for a large tree-hollow—
It is permissible to approach after having constructed a small hut with a tiled roof inside and fitted it with an entrance door;
it is likewise permissible even if one constructs a small hut with a tiled roof on top of a tree stump after cutting down a tree.
Because of the statement beginning with, “Monks, not upon a tree-branch,” it is not permissible to approach a mere clean branch, but [it is permissible] on a large branch...
However, having constructed a frame, made a small hut there with a thatched roof, and fitted it with a door, one may enter [the rains residence].
Because of such statements as, "Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence in a cattle-pen," it is permissible to enter the rains residence in a cattle-pen, in a caravan, or on a boat.
In this context, "cattle-pen" (vaḷa) refers to the dwelling place of cowherds. When the cattle-pen has been vacated, [one may enter] by means of the cattle-pen.
There is no offense for one who breaks the rains-retreat while traveling together, because it was said: “Monks, I allow you to go wherever there is a caravan.
However, by one entering the rains-retreat with a caravan, lay followers should be told on the day of the commencement of the rains:
“It is necessary to obtain a hut. If they build one and give it, he should enter it and declare: “I enter the rains-retreat here.”
It should be requested three times. If they do not give it, one should go beneath a cart stationed near the hall.
If even that is not obtained, one should make a formal resolve (*ālaya*). However, it is not permitted to enter the rains residence (*vassa*) within a caravan.

A "resolve" (*ālaya*) is merely the arising of the thought, "I will dwell here for the rains. If the day of the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*) falls while the caravan is still on its journey along the road...

If it is so, the invitation (pavāraṇā) must be performed right there. If the caravan, while still within the boundary, passes beyond the place where the monk intended to stay, he should stay at that intended place and perform the invitation there together with the monks.
Furthermore, if the caravan, while still within the boundary, stops at a certain village along the way or breaks up, [he should perform the invitation] in that very village.
Having stayed together with the bhikkhus, one must perform the *pavāraṇā*; it is not permitted to depart from there without having performed the *pavāraṇā*.
Even for one entering the rains residence on a boat, one must enter a hut; if, after searching, none is found, one should establish a temporary dwelling (*ālaya*).
If during the three months the boat remains only at sea, the *pavāraṇā* must be performed right there. Then...
If a boat reaches a shore and this person wishes to go further, it is not permitted to go;
having stayed only in the village reached by the boat, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* together with the monks.
Even if the boat goes elsewhere along the bank and the monk wishes to stay only in the village already reached, let the boat go; the monk [should remain] right there.

Having stayed [there], one should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony together with the monks. Thus, in the case of a caravan, a military expedition, or a boat—these three situations—there is no offense in interrupting the rains residence, and one is permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
"Monks, having entered the rains residence, one should not depart before completing either the first three months or the last three months."

"Because of the statement, 'The journey should be undertaken; whoever should undertake it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' one who has entered the rains residence during the earlier period must not set out on a journey without having completed the first three months, nor one who has entered during the later period without having completed the latter three months.
However, having entered the rains residence, even if one does not wait for dawn to rise, one may [depart] on that very day for a seven-day business."

There is no offense for one who departs and returns within seven days; how much less so for one who stays for two or three days and then departs on business lasting seven days and returns within seven days.
“Monks, I allow you to go when sent on business lasting seven days by seven [types of persons], but not if you are not sent.”
"Of a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā"— from these words,
it follows that for the sake of any one of these five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, or for oneself, one may have a monastery (vihāra),

a gabled house (aḍḍhayoga), a mansion (pāsāda), a watchtower (hammiya), a cave (guha), a courtyard (pariveṇa), a storehouse (koṭṭhaka), or a service hall (upaṭṭhānasālā) built, intended for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Having had a fire-hall, a kitchen, a privy, a walking path, a cloister for walking, a well, a well-house,
a bathhouse, a bathhouse hall, a lotus pond, a pavilion, a monastery, or a site for a monastery built, and having sent word by specifying, "Let the bhikkhus come;
I wish to give gifts, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the bhikkhus."

One may go on account of business to be done during seven days, but certainly not without having sent word beforehand. A lay follower (upāsaka) or a lay follower woman (upāsikā), having had one of the dwellings such as a monastery (vihāra) built for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual;
or having had one of the residences, beds, houses, and so forth built for their own sake;
or having pointed out some other task or duty to be performed; or being ill—[sends] a messenger to the presence of the monks.

If someone should send word: "May the venerable ones come; I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the bhikkhus," one may go on account of a seven-day business, but not if no such message has been sent.
"I allow you, bhikkhus, to go on account of seven kinds of seven-day business even if no message has been sent, let alone if one has been sent."
Based on the statement, "Of a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, and of one’s mother and father," [the intention is]:

"I shall seek out, or inquire after, either sick-food or food for those attending the sick, or medicine, specifically for these fellow practitioners— beginning with the bhikkhu— and for my parents, only when they are actually ill."
For this reason—one thinking, “I will attend to him”—one may go even when not sent for, let alone when sent for.
However, in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “It is also permissible to go unbidden to those who are relatives or non-relatives acting as attendants to one’s parents.
This was stated neither in the *Aṭṭhakathā* nor in the *Pāḷi*; therefore, it should not be accepted.
But if a monk’s brother or another relative is ill, and he should send a messenger to the presence of that monk saying, “I am ill;

may the venerable one come, for I desire the venerable one’s arrival,” he may go on account of this seven-day business, but not if he has not been invited. If [he is] in a single monastery together with other monks...
If a lay follower who supports the monks falls ill, and he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks saying, "I am ill;
let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks," one may go on account of a seven-day business, but not if one has not been invited.
If a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice experiences dissatisfaction or anxiety...
Or if a state of wrong view has arisen, even if one has not been sent for, one may go on account of a duty to be performed within seven days, thinking:
"I will dispel his discontent, or have it dispelled; I will remove his remorse, or have it removed; I will separate him from that state of wrong view, or have him separated from it;
or I will give a Dhamma talk. How much more so if one has been sent for! If...

If some bhikkhu has committed a grave offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation, subject to being sent back to the beginning, subject to the trial period (mānatta), or subject to rehabilitation, one may go even if not sent for, thinking:
“I will make an effort regarding the granting of probation and so forth; I will perform the proclamation;
or I will serve as the one who completes the quorum,” let alone if one is sent for. This also applies to a bhikkhunī who is subject to the trial period or subject to being sent back to the beginning.

The same method applies to one who is worthy of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*). If a novice (*sāmaṇera*) wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), or wishes to ask about the rains-retreat (*vassa*);
or if a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) wishes to receive full ordination, or her training has been interrupted;
or if a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*) wishes to undertake the training, or wishes to ask about the rains-retreat—one should go even if not sent for, let alone if one is sent for.

If the Saṅgha intends to carry out a formal act against a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī—whether it be one of censure, demotion, banishment, reconciliation, or suspension—one should go even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha refrain from performing this act, or perhaps transform it into a lighter one? Even if it has already been performed...

There is a case where there is a formal act (*kamma*), and one should go even if not invited, thinking: "How might he conduct himself properly, grow in virtue, and conduct himself so as to reach deliverance, such that the Saṅgha might suspend that formal act?
(181) Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to go for the sake of a matter concerning the Saṅgha," this includes even a matter concerning the Saṅgha related to lodgings.

It is permissible to go. For in this context, whatever is to be done in the Uposatha hall and other such dwellings, or at shrines, parasols, railings, and so forth—even down to a private dwelling belonging to an individual monk—is all intended as "a matter for the Saṅgha" (saṅghakaraṇīya).
Therefore, it is permissible to bring building materials and the like, or to employ carpenters and others, for the purpose of accomplishing that work.
Or one may go to give alms-food, wages, and so forth. Furthermore, this method not found in the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka-naya*) should also be understood here:
it is not permissible to go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma if one has not been invited;
however, if a prior agreement (*katikā*) has already been made in a large residence that "one must assemble on such-and-such a day," then one is indeed considered as having been invited.
It is permissible to go. It is not permissible to go thinking, "I will wash my belongings. However, if the teacher or preceptor sends one, it is permissible.
If the monastery is not too far away, but one is unable to reach it and return on the very same day, thinking, "Having gone there, I will return this very day," it is permissible.
One does not even obtain permission to go for the sake of recitation, questioning, and so forth; [one must remain with] the teacher...
However, he is permitted to go [thinking], "I shall see [them]. If his teacher says to him, "Do not go today," it is permissible;
yet, he is not permitted to go to see a family that supports him or a family of his own relatives.
If, when the monks have entered the rains retreat, the village is raided by bandits, what should be done there? [He should go] to where the village is...
He should go there. If a village is split into two parts, he should go where the greater number of people reside.
If the majority there are faithless and lack confidence, he should go where those who are faithful and confident reside.
And in this case, if the village is not far away, he may wander for alms there and then return to dwell in the monastery itself.
If he has gone far away, dawn should be made to rise every seven days; if that is not possible, he should remain right there in a suitable place.
If people continue to give regular offerings such as *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) and so forth, he should say, "We did not stay in that monastery.
[They may reply,] "We do not give for the sake of that monastery or that palace; we give for you."
But when it is said, "Having stayed anywhere, eat," then one may eat as one pleases;

that [gift] accrues to those very people. However, when it is said, "Having had it delivered to your place of residence, eat," then one must take it to where they are staying, have it delivered according to the *vassa* (rainy-season) period, and then eat.
If, at the time of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), the *vassāvāsika* (gift for the rainy season) [is offered]...
Regarding the teeth: if they have caused dawn to rise on the seventh day, they may take them.
However, those whose rains-residence has been interrupted should say, "We did not dwell there; our rains-residence was interrupted.
If they say, "Let those to whom our lodgings were assigned take them," then they may take them. But as for that which was deposited in the monastery—do not...
"Let it be destroyed!"—regarding such items as robes and other goods brought here that are subject to distribution, they should be taken back to that very place, announced, and divided there.

When things such as fields or land are given to the *kappiyakārakas* with the instruction, "Give these four requisites to the noble ones from here," the same procedure applies to those sources of income.
For communal property subject to distribution, whether within the monastery or outside the boundary, [is to be treated in this manner].

Let it be: it is not permissible for those standing outside the boundary (*bahisīma*) to divide [the property] after merely obtaining permission from those standing inside. However, even if they are standing in both places, it is indeed permissible to divide it after obtaining permission from those standing within the boundary.
But if the monks who have entered the rains retreat are harassed by wild beasts, which seize them and even trample them, or by reptiles...
Or they are harassed by gadflies and mosquitoes, which bite them and sting them; or they are harassed by thieves, who plunder them and beat them;
or they are harassed by *pisāca* demons, who possess them and kill them—if [thinking], "This very thing is an obstacle," he should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat. If a village has been burned by fire or swept away by water. [If] the monks...
If they are exhausted by the alms-food, thinking, "This indeed is an obstacle," they may depart; there is no offense in interrupting the rains residence.
If the lodging has been burnt by fire or swept away by water, and the monks are exhausted by the lack of lodging, thinking, "This indeed is an obstacle," they may depart;
there is no offense in interrupting the rains residence. If the monks who have entered the rains residence do not obtain coarse food...

Or, if they obtain as much as they need and in full measure of coarse or refined food, yet do not obtain suitable food, they should depart, thinking, "This very thing is an obstacle. Even if they obtain as much as they need... of coarse or refined food... [and so on].
Or, if they obtain an abundance of excellent food to their heart's content,
yet do not obtain suitable medicinal requisites, thinking, "This is indeed an obstacle," one should depart. If, however,
they obtain an abundance of coarse or excellent food to their heart's content, and obtain suitable food, and obtain...
If they do not obtain suitable medicines, or if they do not obtain a suitable attendant, thinking, "This is indeed an obstacle," they may depart;
in all such cases of interrupting the rains residence, there is no offense.
However, if a woman invites a monk who has entered the rains residence, saying, "Come, venerable sir, I will give you gold or..."
“I will give you gold, or a field, or a dwelling, or a bull, or a cow, or a male slave, or a female slave;
or I will give you my daughter for the sake of a wife; or I myself will become your wife, or I will bring another wife for you”—if, in that situation, it occurs to the bhikkhu:
“The mind has been described by the Blessed One as quick to change; it might even happen to me...”
“...is an obstacle to the holy life,” one should depart; there is no offense in interrupting the rains retreat.

In the same manner as stated above, if a prostitute invites him, or a courtesan invites him, or a paṇḍaka invites him, or relatives invite him, or kings invite him, or thieves invite him, or rogues invite him—the same rule applies. If...

If a monk who has entered the rains residence sees a treasure-trove that has no owner, and if it occurs to him, "The Blessed One has said that the mind is quick to change; there might be an obstacle to my holy life," he should depart;
there is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
If a monk who has entered the rains retreat sees many monks striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, or hears that "many monks are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha," and it occurs to that monk:
"A schism in the Saṅgha is said by the Blessed One to be a grave matter; let the Saṅgha not split while I am present."
One may depart; there is no offense in breaking the rains residence. If a monk who has entered the rains residence hears:
"It is said that in such-and-such a residence, many monks are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha," and if it occurs to that monk:
"Those monks are my friends; I shall speak to them, saying: 'Friends, a schism in the Saṅgha is said to be a grave matter.'"

If [a monk thinks], "The Blessed One has said, 'May it not please the Venerable Ones to cause a schism in the Saṅgha,' they will follow my word, they will listen, and they will lend an ear," he may depart;
there is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat. However, once the Saṅgha is split, there is no business for him to go there.
But if some monk, having promised when told, "Stay here for the three months of the rains," should then fail to keep his word, [he commits an offense].
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It is not only for the breach of that specific promise that there is an offense of wrong-doing;

even for the breach of various other promises made such as, "Take almsfood for these three months," "We both shall dwell here for the rains retreat," or "We shall recite the *uddesa* together," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
And that occurs when one was initially pure-minded but later...
On account of deception, there is a *pācittiya* offense for the first instance of making a promise with an impure mind.
Regarding "in the case of deception there is a *dukkaṭa*," this means that a *dukkaṭa* is joined with the *pācittiya*.
182. Having established the fixed duties during the rainy season for those who have entered the rains retreat, the monks who have entered the rains retreat [should attend to] the brooms...
"You should tie them," they should be told. If sticks and tally-sticks are easily available, one person should tie together six or five handful-brooms, or two or three stick-brooms.
If they are difficult to obtain, two or three handful-brooms and one stick-broom should be tied together. Five each [should be tied] by the novices.
Either torches must be struck out, or a stain of dye must be applied to the dwelling places. Those performing the duties must not recite the Pāṭimokkha, nor cause it to be recited;

they must not engage in study, nor grant the going-forth, nor grant full ordination, nor give formal support (nissaya), nor hold a hearing of the Dhamma. For all these are elaborations; [the state] is free from elaboration.

One should not establish such unrighteous rules as: "Having sacrificed [worldly concerns], let us practice only the duty of a recluse," or "Let everyone undertake all thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas)," or "Let them spend their time standing or walking without preparing a bed," or "Let them observe the vow of silence," or "Let those who have gone on a seven-day mission receive the goods to be shared. Rather, it should be done in this way:
The Dhamma of the scriptures establishes the Triple Gem;

therefore, recite it yourselves and have others recite it, and perform its study. While residing in the meditation hall, do not cause disturbances, but sit within the monastery and recite, have others recite, and ensure that the hearing of the Dhamma flourishes.
When ordaining others, ordain them after having purified them; confer full admission after having purified them; grant formal dependence after having purified them.
For even a single son of good family, having obtained both the going-forth and full admission, establishes the entire Dispensation.
According to your own strength, undertake as many ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) as you are able. This is indeed the rainy season retreat.
One should be heedful throughout the entire day and during the first and last watches of the night, and exert energy.
The ancient great elders also, having severed all worldly attachments, fulfilled the practice of wandering alone during the rainy season;
knowing the proper measure for recitation, they taught the discourse on the ten bases, the ten foulness subjects, the ten recollections, and the thirty-eight meditation objects.

It is proper to perform the duties; it is proper to perform the duties for newcomers; and it is proper to grant leave to those who have gone on a seven-day errand. Such duties as these should be performed.
Furthermore, the monks should be exhorted: "Do not speak words that are contentious, malicious, or harsh; day by day..."
“Recalling the precepts, not neglecting the four protections, and dwelling frequently with attention, you should practice. The rule regarding the use of tooth-sticks should be explained:
while worshipping a cetiya or the Bodhi tree, offering perfumes or garlands, or putting the alms-bowl into its bag, one must not speak.
The rule for the alms-round within the village should be explained.
One should not engage in talk concerning requisites or discordant talk with laypeople;
one must keep the sense faculties guarded, and fulfill both the Khandhaka-vatta and the Sekhiya-vatta. Such numerous discourses leading to liberation should be explained.
Thus ends the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
The discussion on the determination of the commencement of the rains residence is finished.
27. Discussion on the Determination of Duties Toward Preceptors and Others. 183.
Regarding "duties" (*vatta*), this duty consists of the duty toward a preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*), the duty toward a teacher (*ācariya-vatta*), and the duty toward a guest (*āgantuka-vatta*).

The duties for residents, the duties for those departing, the duties regarding the meal hall, the duties for alms-gathering, the duties for forest-dwellers, the duties regarding lodgings, the duties for the sauna, and the duties for the restroom—these are of many kinds.
Among these, first, the duty toward the preceptor should be understood as follows:
the co-resident, having risen early, should remove his sandals, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, and...
The tooth-stick should be given to the preceptor, and water for rinsing the mouth should be given.

In that regard, when giving the tooth-stick, one should present three types—large, medium, and small—and from the fourth day onward, one should give the same size as that which he has been taking for the preceding three days. If, however, he makes no fixed choice and takes whichever...
Or he may take it himself; then, whatever kind he receives, that same kind must be given back.

When providing water for rinsing the mouth, one should bring both cold and warm water, and from whichever of these he uses for three days, from the fourth day onward, that same kind of water for rinsing the mouth must be given. If he uses both kinds, then both should be brought.
Having set water for washing the face in its proper place, one should sweep starting from the latrine.
Once finished there, one should sweep the courtyard; in this way, the courtyard is not left empty.
Before leaving the latrine, one should prepare a seat. Having performed the bodily needs and returned, if there is rice gruel for the person sitting there, [one should serve it].
Having washed the vessel, rice-gruel should be offered. When he has drunk the gruel, water should be given to him;
then, having received the vessel, holding it low and washing it carefully without scraping it, it should be put away. When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be removed.
If that place is dirty, being strewn with any refuse, that place [should be cleaned].
It should be swept. However, if there is no other refuse, and there are only drops of water, it should be wiped with the hand.

If the preceptor wishes to enter the village, the inner robe should be given to him, the outer robe received back, the waistband should be given, the upper robes should be given after being folded together, and the bowl should be washed and returned with some water in it.

It should be given. If the preceptor desires an attendant monk, [the candidate] should cover the three circles, put on the lower robe properly, fasten the waistband, arrange the upper robes with their folds tucked in, put on the outer cloak, fasten the toggle, wash the bowl, take it up, and act as the preceptor’s attendant monk; he should not walk too far behind.

One should not go too near. In this regard, it should be understood that if one reaches [the teacher] by one or two steps while the preceptor has turned back and is looking around, then one has gone neither too far nor too near.
If, during the alms-round, the bowl is filled with rice gruel or cooked food by the preceptor, and it is either hot or heavy...
If [the preceptor] has one, he should give his own bowl to him and receive that bowl back;

he must not interrupt the preceptor’s speech with talk in between. From this point forward, wherever a prohibition is made by means of the word "not" (*na*), it should be understood in all such cases as an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If the preceptor speaks near an offense, he should be stopped.
And when restraining him, he should be restrained as if one were asking, "Venerable sir, is it permissible to speak such a thing? Is there no offense?
However, having resolved, "I shall restrain him," one should not say, "Elder, do not speak thus.
If the village is nearby, or if there is a sick monk in the monastery, one must return from the village earlier than [the other].
If the village is far away and there is no one coming along with the preceptor, he should depart from the village together with him,
wrap his bowl in his robe, and arrive first from the middle of the road. Having arrived first in this manner,
he should prepare a seat and set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone.
Having gone out to meet him, one should receive his bowl and robe; one should give him an inner garment and receive his lower robe.
If the robe has become damp with sweat, it should be dried for a short while in the sun, but the robe must not be left in the heat;
the robe should be folded. When folding the robe, one should turn back the edge by four finger-widths before folding the robe.
It should be rolled up evenly. For what reason? Lest there be a break in the middle.
For if it is rolled up after being made even, there will be a break in the middle; thus, by breaking constantly, it becomes weak. This was said for the purpose of preventing that.
Therefore, day by day, it should be done in such a way that it does not break tomorrow at the very same place where it broke today.
Having rolled it up four finger-widths, it should be folded; the waistband should be fastened across the fold.
If there is almsfood and the preceptor wishes to eat, the student should offer the almsfood after giving water, and the preceptor should be asked for drinking water.
When asking, he should say three times: "Venerable sir, let drinking water be brought."
He should be asked for water. If there is time, he should eat after his preceptor has eaten.
If the time is drawing near, he should place the water near his preceptor and eat himself.
After the preceptor has finished eating, he should give him water, receive the bowl, hold it low, and wash it carefully without scratching it.
Having washed it with water, it should be dried for a short while in the sun, but the bowl must not be placed directly in the heat; rather, the bowl and robe should be set aside.

When setting down the bowl, one should grasp the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, feel for the lower part of a bed or the lower part of a chair before placing the bowl down; it must not be placed on mats, pieces of leather, or similar surfaces.
The bowl should be placed on ground that has not been recently cleared.
However, if the ground is blackened, plastered with lime, or consists of dustless clay, it is permissible to place it on such ground; it is also permissible to place it on washed sand.
It is not permissible on soil, dust, gravel, and the like. In that case, however, one may use a leaf or a stand.

Or, having set it aside, it should be placed there. When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, arrange the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then place the robe down.
This [should be done] by inserting the hand beneath the robe-stand or similar object and facing it directly.

This was said for the purpose of placing it down slowly with the hand. However, if one takes hold of it by the edge and hurls it over the robe-pole and so forth with the shoulder, the shoulder strikes against the wall; therefore, one should not do it in that manner.
When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be put away, and the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-wiping cloth should be stored.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.
If the preceptor wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared. If he needs cold water, cold water should be prepared; if he needs warm water, warm water should be prepared.
If the preceptor wishes to enter the sauna, the powder should be kneaded and the clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should follow closely behind his preceptor;
having offered the sauna-bench and received the robe, he should place it aside in a smoke-free spot. He should provide powder and provide clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna; when entering, he should smear his face with clay.
One should enter the sauna having covered oneself both in front and behind.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks, nor should one block junior monks from their seats. In the sauna, service should be rendered to one’s preceptor.
"Service in the sauna" refers to all necessary tasks, such as providing charcoal, clay, and hot water.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench and depart from the sauna after covering oneself both in front and behind.
In the water as well, one should perform services for the preceptor, such as massaging his limbs; having bathed, one should emerge first.
Having emerged from the bath, dried his limbs, and dressed himself, he should wipe the water from the preceptor’s body, give him his lower robe, and give him his upper robe.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should return first and prepare a seat;
he should set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scraper. [Then] the preceptor...
He should be asked for water; for in a sauna there is thirst due to the heat.
If he wishes to have [the preceptor] recite [the Pātimokkha], he should be made to recite it. If he wishes to question him, he should be questioned.
If the dwelling where the preceptor resides is dirty, if he is able, by someone...
He is not overcome by illness; he must be purified. For a co-resident who is not ill must perform the entire duty toward the preceptor even if he is sixty years old.
For one who performs it without respect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty.
However, regarding those sections connected with the word "not," even for one who is ill, performing an action that is prohibited results in an offense of wrong-doing. While purifying the dwelling:
First, having taken out the bowl and robes, they should be placed to one side; having taken out the sitting mat and sheet, they should be placed to one side;
having taken out the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side;
and having lowered the bed, one should take it out carefully without scraping it or knocking it against the door frame.
It should be set aside to one side. Having lowered the stool, one should carry it out without scraping it or knocking it against the door-sill, and set it aside to one side.
Having carried out the bed-legs, they should be set aside to one side.
Having carried out the spittoon, it should be set aside to one side. Having carried out the leaning-board...
It should be set aside to one side. Having observed the floor-covering as it was laid out, it should be removed and set aside to one side.
If there is cobwebs in the dwelling, they should first be removed from the ceiling; the light-fittings, joints, and corners should be wiped clean.
If the wall treated with red-ochre plaster has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened and wrung out...
It should be swept. If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be swept after moistening a cloth and wringing it out.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled with water again and again and then swept, thinking, "Lest the monastery be covered in dust.
Having cleared away the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having dried the ground-covering, cleaned it, shaken it out, and brought it back, it should be spread exactly as it was spread before.

For it is for this very purpose that it is said: "Having observed how it was spread, having taken it out, it should be placed aside in one corner. However, if it was spread previously by someone who did not know [the proper way], [then...]
It should be prepared by leaving a gap of two or three finger-breadths all around the wall. This is the procedure for its preparation:
if the frame is too large, it should be cut down, the corners turned back, and tied together before being set up.
If one does not know how to turn back the corners and tie them, [one should not do so].
It should be cut. Having dried the bed-legs and wiped them, they should be placed back in their proper position.

Having dried the bed, cleaned it, and beaten it [to remove dust], and having lowered it, one should carefully carry it in without scraping or knocking against the door-sill, and then set it out as previously arranged.
Having dried the stool, cleaned it, and beaten it, and having lowered it...
Having done so carefully, without knocking or jarring the door-panel, he should carry it in and spread it out as arranged.
Having dried the mattress and pillow-covers, cleaned them, beaten them, and carried them in, he should spread them out as arranged.
Having dried the sitting mats and rugs, cleaned them, beaten them, and carried them in, he should spread them out as arranged.
It should be laid out; the spittoon, having been dried, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place;
the leaning board, having been dried, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes should be put away; when putting away the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and... with the other hand.
Having touched either the lower part of a bed or the lower part of a seat, the bowl should be set down; however, the bowl must not be set down on bare ground.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, and with the other hand wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string, [placing] the edge toward oneself and the fold toward the front.
Having done so, the robe should be laid aside.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If they blow from the west, the north, or the south, the southern windows should be closed. If it is the cold season...
If it is hot, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night. If it is the hot season, they should be closed by day and opened at night.

If the area is dirty, the courtyard should be swept, the storehouse should be swept, the assembly hall should be swept, the fire-hall should be swept, the restroom should be swept, and drinking water and water for washing should be provided.
He should attend to his preceptor; he should pour water from the rinsing-pitcher.
If dissatisfaction arises in the preceptor, the student should lead him elsewhere, or he should tell another monk, "Take the elder and go elsewhere," or he should give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If remorse arises in the preceptor, it should be dispelled by the student, or he should have it dispelled by another,
or a discourse on the Dhamma should be given to him. If a wrong view arises in the preceptor,
it should be resolved by the student, or another should be told, "Please have the Elder resolve his wrong view."

Or a discourse on the Dhamma should be given to him. If the preceptor has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation, the student living with him (saddhivihārika) must make an effort; he should approach various monks and request that probation be granted to him.
If he himself is capable, he should grant it himself. If he is not capable, [he should have it granted] by another.

He should cause [the Sangha] to grant it. If the preceptor is subject to sending back to the beginning, subject to the trial period (mānatta), or subject to rehabilitation, the student should make an effort in the manner already described.
If the Sangha wishes to perform a formal act against the preceptor—whether a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the student [should likewise make an effort].
One should make an effort, thinking: "By what means might the Saṅgha not carry out a formal act against the preceptor, or might it transform it into something lighter?

For when the student learns that "the Saṅgha intends to carry out a *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) against his preceptor," he should approach each individual monk and say: "Venerable sir, do not [carry out] this act against our preceptor..."

He should request them, saying, "Please perform the formal act. If they are indeed performing it, he should request them, saying, "Perform either a censure (tajjanīya), a demotion (niyassa), or a light formal act.
If they are indeed performing it, then the preceptor should request them, saying, "Venerable sirs, behave properly.
Having thus caused him to behave properly, he should request the monks, saying, "Venerable sirs, please suspend the formal act."
If the preceptor’s robe needs washing, it should be washed by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking,
"How can my preceptor’s robe be washed? If the preceptor’s robe needs to be made,
or dye needs to be boiled, or the robe needs to be dyed, [it should be done] by the student.
Everything should be done, or an effort should be made, thinking, "How might my preceptor’s robe be dyed?
When dyeing the robe, it should be dyed by turning it over thoroughly; one must not depart while there are still drops of dye remaining.
Without asking permission from the preceptor, one must not give a bowl to anyone, nor must one receive a bowl from anyone.
One should not give a robe to some, nor should one receive a robe from some;
one should not give requisites to some, nor should one receive requisites from some; one should not shave the hair of some, nor should one have the hair shaved by some;
one should not perform services for some, nor should one have services performed by some.
One should have [work] performed; one should not perform services for some, nor should one have services performed by some;
one should not act as an attendant for some, nor should one take someone as an attendant;
one should not carry out almsfood for some, nor should one have almsfood carried out by some; one should not [act] without having asked permission from one's preceptor.
The village must be entered. One who wishes to enter for alms or for any other purpose must do so only after having asked for permission.
If the preceptor has risen early and intends to go on a long alms-round, one should say, "Let the juniors enter for alms," and then depart.
If one departs without saying this, and upon reaching the monastery compound does not see the preceptor, [one should wait].
It is permissible to enter a village. If one sees [the preceptor] while entering the village, it is likewise permissible to seek permission starting from the point where he was seen.
One must not go to a cemetery for the sake of staying there or for the purpose of contemplating the foul without asking the preceptor’s permission, nor should one depart for another region;
however, one who wishes to depart should announce their business [and seek permission].
It should be requested up to three times. If he grants permission, that is well;

if he does not grant permission, and while living under him the student’s recitation, questioning, or meditation subject does not succeed, and the preceptor is ignorant and incompetent, refusing to let him go away merely out of a desire to have him live in his own presence—even in such a case of one who prevents him from leaving—[the student may leave].
It is permissible to go. If the preceptor is ill, he must be attended to for as long as life lasts;

one must wait for his recovery and not go anywhere else. If there is another monk who can act as attendant, one may go after having sought medicine and placed it in his hands, saying, "Venerable sir, this person will attend to you. This...
This concludes the duties toward the preceptor (upajjhāya).
184. And because these very same duties must be performed by the resident pupil (antevāsika) for the teacher (ācariya), they are called the "duties toward the teacher.

Here, the difference is merely one of name. In this regard, as long as the dyeing of the robes has not been completed, if the duties are not performed, [the fault falls upon] the preceptor and the teacher.
And there is a falling away [from the training]; therefore, for one who does not perform it, there is an offense whether he is released from dependence or not.

For some, however, the offense occurs starting from the giving of the bowl, even while still not released from dependence. If the preceptor or the teacher consents to the duty, then even if there are many co-residents or pupils, all of them incur an offense. If the preceptor...
