If the teacher says, "I have an attendant; you should apply yourselves to your own recitation, mental attention, and so forth," there is no offense for the resident pupil (saddhivihārika) and others.

If the preceptor or the teacher does not know whether [the pupil] consents or does not consent, or if he is ignorant, and there are many resident pupils and others among them, then one monk who is perfect in his conduct (*vatta*)—
“If I shall perform the duties for my preceptor or teacher, may you live free from anxiety”—
if he thus takes the burden upon himself and dismisses the others, then from the moment he assumes that burden, there is no offense for them. In this regard, among the resident pupils,
as long as one who is under formal dependence (*nissaya*) lives in dependence upon the teacher, [the responsibility] belongs entirely to him.

The duties toward the teacher must be performed. However, for those who have gone forth, received full ordination, or are dhamma-pupils—even if they are not under formal dependence (nissaya)—the duties must be performed from the beginning up until the dyeing of the robes. Yet, there is no offense for these individuals in cases such as giving away their alms-bowl without first asking permission.

Among these, the one who has gone forth as a pupil (*pabbajjantevāsika*) and the one who has received full ordination as a pupil (*upasampadantevāsika*) are a burden to the teacher for as long as they live.

As for the one who lives under dependence (*nissayantevāsika*) and the one who is a pupil in the Dhamma (*dhammantevāsika*), as long as they dwell in the vicinity, the teacher and preceptor must likewise support and assist their pupils and co-residents with recitation, interrogation, exhortation, and instruction. If [the teacher] regarding the pupils and co-residents...
If he has no bowl, robe, or any other requisite, but does have his own extra bowl, robe, or extra requisites, they must be given.
If not, he should make an effort to seek them by means of a righteous method.
If the resident pupil or co-resident student is ill, tooth-sticks should be given according to the method stated in the duties toward a preceptor.
Starting from the beginning up to the end of sprinkling water from the rinsing-pitcher, the entire routine must indeed be performed;
for those who do not perform it, there is an offense. Therefore, teachers and preceptors must also behave properly toward their resident pupils and co-residents.
For whichever among the teachers, preceptors, and others does not behave properly, that person incurs an offense. This concludes the discussion on the duties toward preceptors and others.
185. Now, the duties for incoming monks and so forth should be understood.

An incoming monk, having gone near the boundary of the precincts, should remove his sandals, set them down low, shake them out, take hold of them with the sandal-strap, lower his sunshade, uncover his head, place his robe over his shoulder, and enter the monastery carefully and without haste.
One should enter; when entering the monastery, one should observe: "Where do the resident monks assemble?

Having gone to where the resident monks assemble—whether it be in the assembly hall, under a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—one should set aside one's bowl to one side and set aside one's robe to one side in a suitable manner.
Having taken a seat, one should sit down; one should ask for drinking water and ask for water for washing;
[one should specify] "Which is the drinking water? Which is the water for washing? If there is need for drinking water, one should take the drinking water and drink it.
If there is need for water for washing, one should take the water for washing and wash one's feet. While washing the feet—
Water should be poured with one hand, and the feet should be washed with the other;
water should not be poured with the same hand as that used for washing the feet.
Having wiped the foot-wiping cloth, the sandals should be wiped. When wiping the sandals, they should first be wiped with a dry cloth.
Afterwards, when it is wet, he should wash the cloth for wiping sandals and spread it out to one side.
If the resident monk is senior, he should pay him homage; if he is junior, he should have himself paid homage by him.
He should ask about the lodging, saying, "Which lodging falls to me?"—whether it has been already occupied or not yet occupied.
Or he should ask: "Is the village for alms-seeking near or far? Must one go for alms early in the morning, or during the day?
In this way, the practice of alms-round should be asked about; the non-range should be asked about, and the proper range should be asked about.
A "non-range" means a village of those with wrong view, or a village where alms are restricted, where [there is enough] for only one or two.

Or, when alms are being given, one should ask about families that honor those in training (*sekha*), one should ask about the place for excrement, one should ask about the place for urination, and one should ask about both drinking water and water for use, such as:
"Do they drink only the water from this lotus pond, or do they also use it for bathing and other purposes?
One should also ask about a walking stick (*kattaradaṇḍa*).

One must inquire about the Sangha’s established regulations; for in certain places there may be wild beasts or non-human beings, therefore one should ask, "At what time should we enter, and at what time should we depart?
If the monastery is unoccupied, one should knock on the door, wait a moment, and then open the latch and the door.
Having paid his respects, he should look around while standing outside.

If that dwelling is dirty—if a bed has been placed upon a bed, or a bench upon a bench, or if bedding has been piled on top of the furniture—he should, if he is able, clean the entire dwelling; if he is unable, [he should inform the resident monk].

One must clear one’s own living quarters. However, if one is able to clean everything thoroughly, one should take out the floor coverings, beds, chairs, and so forth, according to the method prescribed for the duties toward a preceptor;
having cleaned the dwelling, they should be brought back in again and arranged in their proper places.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed. If [they blow] from the west, [the western windows should be closed].
Northern and southern winds blow; the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night. If it is hot, they should be closed by day and opened at night.
If it is dirty, the courtyard should be swept, the storehouse should be swept, and the assembly hall [should be swept].
The floor must be swept; the fire-hall must be swept; the restroom must be swept; drinking water and washing water must be provided;
and water must be poured into the rinsing pitcher. This is the duty for a guest. 186. Regarding the duties for a resident:
when a resident monk sees a visiting monk who is senior, he [should offer] a seat.
A seat should be prepared; water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone should be set out.
Having gone forward to meet him, one should receive his bowl and robes. He should be asked if he wishes for drinking water;
however, if he drinks all the water brought once when asked, he should simply be asked again, "Shall I bring more? He should also be fanned with a fan; while fanning him...
Having fanned him once on the soles of his feet, once in the middle [of his body], and once on his head, when told "Enough," he should fan more gently;
when told "Enough" again, he should fan even more gently;
when told a third time, the fan should be set aside, and his feet should also be washed. If he has oil of his own, with that oil...
It should be smeared [with oil]. If there is none, it should be smeared with what belongs to him. If he is able, the sandals should be wiped.
When wiping the sandals, they should first be wiped with a dry cloth and afterwards with a wet one;
having washed the sandal-wiping cloth, it should be set aside to one side.
A visiting bhikkhu should be greeted with a formal salutation, and a dwelling place should be assigned to him, saying, "This dwelling is available.
Whether it has been previously occupied or not, it should be pointed out; the alms-resort should be pointed out, and the non-alms-resort should be pointed out;
families designated as "for those in training" should be pointed out; the place for defecation should be pointed out, and the place for urination should be pointed out.
The drinking water must be pointed out; the water for washing must be pointed out; the walking stick must be pointed out;
and the Sangha’s agreement on the schedule must be pointed out: "One should enter at this time;
one should depart at this time."
If the newcomer is a junior, the resident monk must point it out while remaining seated: "Place your bowl here;

place your robe here; this is the seat; sit down. He must point out the drinking water, point out the water for washing, and point out the cloth for wiping sandals. The incoming monk must be made to pay his respects.
Even lodgings and such things should be pointed out while one is seated. However, when a more senior person arrives, a seat should be prepared;
all such duties—including those related to robe-making or new construction—should be performed except for those specifically excluded.
When sweeping the cetiya courtyard, one should set aside the broom and begin to perform its proper service. For a wise visitor should think: "Sweep it..."

He will say, "First, [attend to] the shrine courtyard. However, when preparing medicine for a sick person, if the patient is not very ill, one should perform the duties first without yet making the medicine;
but for one who is severely ill, the medicine must be prepared first. For a wise visitor will say, "Prepare the medicine first. This is the duty toward residents.

187. When departing on a journey, a monk who is traveling must put away all wooden articles such as beds and stools, as well as earthenware such as dye-vessels and the like, in the fire-hall or some other secure place.
Having closed the doors and windows and taken leave of the lodging, he should depart.
If there is no monk present, a novice should be asked for permission.
If there is no novice, a monastery attendant should be asked for permission.
If there is neither a monk, nor a novice, nor a monastery attendant, one should arrange a bed upon four stones, place bed upon bed, and stool upon stool;
having stacked the lodgings on top and put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, [one should close] the doors and windows.

Having closed it, one should depart. If the dwelling is leaking and one has the strength, the whole of it should be covered, or an effort should be made with the thought, "How can this dwelling be roofed? If this can be accomplished, that is good.
If it cannot be accomplished, then in a place that is not subject to rain, having prepared a bed upon four stones—
Having moved bed from bed and bench from bench, having stacked the lodgings on top, having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, and having closed the doors and windows, one should depart.
If the monastery is leaking and if one is able, the lodgings should be carried to the village, or an effort should be made [to repair them], thinking: "How might this be?"
“...you should carry the lodgings to the village. If you should obtain this, it is well.

If you do not obtain this, having arranged a bed upon four stones in the open air, having placed bed upon bed and chair upon chair, having made a pile of lodgings on top, and having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, [you should cover it] with grass or leaves.
Or, having covered [the body], one should depart with the thought, "Perhaps even some limbs might remain visible. This is the procedure for those departing. 188.

Regarding the procedure for the meal hall: if the time has been announced at the monastery, one should cover the three circles, put on the lower robe properly, fasten the waistband, fold the upper robes together, put them on, and fasten the toggle.
Having washed the bowl and taken it, one should enter the village carefully and without haste.
One should not go out ahead of the elder monks. One should walk within the village well-covered, well-restrained, with eyes cast down, and with little noise;
one should not walk within the village with the body exposed or laughing loudly.
One should not walk among the houses shaking the body, shaking the arms, or shaking the head;
nor should one walk with hands on the hips, nor with the head covered, nor squatting while walking among the houses.
One should sit among the houses well-covered, well-restrained, with eyes cast down, and with little noise.
One should not sit in an inhabited area with one’s body raised, nor laughing loudly;
one should not sit in an inhabited area swaying the body, swaying the arms, or swaying the head;
one should not sit in an inhabited area with hands on the hips, with the head covered, or with the knees bound together; and one should not sit encroaching upon senior bhikkhus.

One should sit down. If the seat is equal in height to that of the senior elder (*mahāthera*), one should sit down after setting aside one or two seats when there are many available. Having counted the monks, one should not sit on the prepared seats until the senior elder says, "Sit down.
If the senior elder does not say so, [one should wait], saying: "Venerable sir, this..."

It should be said, "The seat is high. One who is told, "Sit down," must sit down. However, if [the elder] does not speak even after being thus requested, there is no offense for the one sitting down; the offense belongs to the senior elder alone.

For it is the junior monk who incurs an offense by sitting on such a seat without asking permission, while the elder incurs an offense by not granting permission after having been asked. It is not the junior monks who [are at fault regarding] the seat...
One should ward it off; one must not sit in an inhabited area having spread out one’s outer robe.
When water for rinsing the bowl is being offered, one should receive the water by taking the bowl with both hands.
However, when the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*) is offered, one should place the bowl on a stand in front and receive it, holding it low so as to avoid making a sound with the water.
The bowl should be washed by one who does not rub it or strike it against anything.
If there is someone to receive the water, he should lower the bowl and pour the water into the hands of the water-receiver, thinking: "May the water-receiver not be splashed with water;
may the neighboring monks not be splashed with water; may the outer robe not be splashed with water. If there is no water-receiver...
It should be held low and water poured onto the ground, thinking: "May the neighboring monks not be splashed with water;
may the outer robe not be splashed with water.
When rice is being given, the bowl should be received with both hands, and the rice accepted. As for the soup...

When there is an opportunity, rice should be taken in such a measure. If there is ghee, oil, or additional curry, the senior monk should say, "Distribute it equally among everyone. This instruction applies not only to the ghee and so forth, but should also be said regarding the rice.
However, in the case of ghee and the like, that which is small—sufficient for only one or two—[should be treated accordingly].
When it is said, "Distribute that equally among all," it would cause distress to the people;
therefore, having taken such [an amount] once or twice, the remainder should not be taken. Almsfood should be received with care;
almsfood should be received with awareness of the bowl; almsfood should be received with equal curry and equal broth.
The Elder must not eat until the rice has been served to everyone.
This was said with reference to a dining hall where the number of monks is limited, and where people, having served everyone, wish to pay their respects.
However, this does not apply to a great dining hall where they eat in one place and water [is served] in another.
It is being given; there, one should eat as is convenient.
Almsfood should be eaten with care; almsfood should be eaten with mindfulness of the bowl; almsfood should be eaten in regular order;
almsfood should be eaten with an equal amount of curry; almsfood should not be eaten by scooping it up from a heap.
One should not cover the curry or the condiment with rice out of a desire for more;
one who is not ill should not eat curry or rice that has been requested for one's own sake;
one should not look into another’s bowl while intending to find fault; one should not make a mouthful too large; and a mouthful should be made round.
One should not open the mouth until a morsel has been brought to it; while eating, one should not put the entire hand into the mouth;
one should not speak with a morsel in the mouth; one should not eat by tossing morsels into the mouth; one should not eat by breaking off pieces from the mass of food;
one should not eat stuffing out the cheeks; one should not shake the hand; one should not scatter the rice; one should not lick the tongue.
One should not eat making a *capucapu* sound, nor making a *surusuru* sound, nor licking the hands, nor licking the bowl, nor licking the lips.
One should not receive the water vessel with a hand soiled by food; the elder should not [give] the water for washing the hands until...
It may be accepted until all have finished eating. If people say, "Venerable sir, wash your bowl and hands," or if the monks say, "You take some water," it is permissible.
When water is being given, one should receive the water while holding the bowl with both hands, keeping [the bowl] low.
Having made [the bowl] ready, the bowl should be washed by one who makes no sound with water and does not strike [it].
If there is a water-receiver, one should pour the water into the water-receiver while holding it low, thinking: "May the water-receiver not be splashed by the water;
may the monks nearby not be splashed by the water; may the outer robe not be splashed by the water. If...

One should not be a water-receiver; rather, having lowered [the bowl], one should pour the water on the ground, thinking, "May the neighboring monks not be splashed with water, and may the outer robe not be splashed with water.
One should not discard bowl-washing water containing rice-grains within an inhabited area.
When those who have gone to the dining hall are rising to leave, the junior monks should return first, and afterwards...
"By those [paths]. For in crowded houses, there is no room for the great elders (mahātheras) to exit; therefore, it was said thus.
However, when the novices (navakas) are returning in this manner, they should stand at the door of the house and proceed in single file as the elders exit.
But if the great elders are seated in the front and the novices are inside the house, [they should wait] from the seat of the elders...
One must depart in the proper sequence starting from the beginning; one should walk along a sparse path so that people can pass between the bodies without physical contact.

Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow the senior monk to give the blessing of appreciation (*anumodanā*) in the dining hall," the senior monk of the Saṅgha must give the blessing in the dining hall. One should not depart leaving him alone, but rather together with the rest.
“Monks, I allow four or five senior and junior monks to follow [the meal] in the dining hall.
Because of this statement, when the Sangha’s senior elder is seated for the purpose of giving the thanksgiving (anumodanā), four [junior monks] should sit below him in order;
when a junior elder is seated, three [monks] should sit below him, including the great elder; and when a fifth is seated, [those] above...
Four [monks] must sit; even if the junior monk below the Sangha-thera is requested [to leave], the four must indeed sit starting from the Sangha-thera.
However, if the monk who offers the thanksgiving says, "Go, venerable sirs, there is no duty to wait," it is permissible to go. When the Great Elder says, "Let us go, friend..."
If, when this has been said, he says, “Go,” it is likewise permissible.
Even if he forms the intention, “We shall return outside the village,” and having gone outside the village, tells those dependent on him, “Wait for his arrival,” it is still permissible to go.
However, if people have someone else perform the *anumodanā* according to their own preference, that does not belong to him.
If he gives the blessing, there is an offense; it does not become a burden for the Great Elder.
For while people are conversing, the Elder should be requested only during the course of seated conversation. And the Great Elder, having been requested to give the blessing, should wait;
this is the characteristic in this matter. “I allow you, monks, when there is business to be done, to request the monk sitting next to you.”

However, from the statement "one should go," it follows that when one is oppressed by the need for defecation or other such necessities, one should go only after first informing the monk immediately following.
This is the duty regarding the refectory. 189.

Regarding the duty of the alms-collecting monk (*piṇḍacārika*), when a monk intending to enter a village for alms thinks, "I shall now enter the village," he should [perform] the three circles (*timaṇḍala*).
One who is entering [the village] should put on the lower robe evenly all around, fasten the waist-band, arrange the upper robes with their folds intact,
put on the outer cloak, fasten the toggle, wash the bowl, take it up, and enter the village carefully and without haste.

"One should walk in inhabited areas well-covered," and so forth— all this should be understood here in the same manner as explained in the section on the duties regarding the meal hall (*bhattagga-vatta*).
One entering a dwelling should observe: "By this way I shall enter; by this way I shall exit.
One should not enter too hastily; one should stand neither too far away nor too close; one should not stand for too long; one should not turn back too abruptly.
While standing, one should observe: "Do they wish to give alms, or do they not wish to give? If...
One should stand [thinking], "I wish to give," whether one sets down the food, rises from the seat, takes up the spoon,
takes up the vessel, or sets it aside. When the alms-food is being given, one should lift up the outer robe with the left hand,
tilt the bowl with the right hand, and receive the bowl with both hands.
Alms should be accepted; whether it be a woman or a man, at the time of giving alms, one must not look at their face, but should observe:
"Does she wish to give curry or not? If she touches the spoon, or touches the vessel, or sets it down, one should remain [patient], thinking, "She wishes to give. When the alms have been given...
Having covered the bowl with his outer robe, he should turn back carefully and without haste.
Whoever returns first from the village for alms should prepare a seat, set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone;
he should wash the bowl for refuse and set it out, as well as drinking water and water for rinsing.
It should be set out. When one returns from the village after the alms round, if there is food remaining from the meal and if he so desires, it should be eaten.
If he does not desire it, it should be discarded where there is no greenery, or thrown into water that contains no living beings.
Then the seat should be lifted up, as well as the foot-water, the footstool, and the foot-washing stone.
It should be put away; the bowl for refuse should be washed and put away; the drinking water and the washing water should be put away;
the dining hall should be swept. Whoever sees that the water jar, the washing-water jar, or the chamber-pot is empty or void should refill it.
If it is too heavy for him to carry, he should signal a second person with a gesture of the hand.
Having addressed [the attendant], he should have him supported by means of hand-to-hand carrying, and he must not break his speech for that reason.
This is the conduct for one who goes for alms. 190.
Regarding the conduct for forest-dwellers: a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having risen early, should place his bowl in its bag.
Having draped the robe over the shoulder, having put on the sandals,

having put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, and having closed the doors and windows, one should depart from the dwelling place. Thinking, "Now I shall enter the village," one should take off the sandals,
lower them, dust them off, place them in the bag, hang the bag over the shoulder, and [arrange] the three circles...
While concealing [the body], one should put on the lower robe evenly all around, fasten the waistband, arrange the upper robes so they have folds,
put on the outer cloak, fasten the toggle, wash the bowl, take it up, and enter the village carefully and without haste.
"One should walk within inhabited areas well-concealed," and so forth— all the rules for walking apply here as well.
The procedure for the meal hall (*bhattagga*) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
When entering a residence, one should observe: "By this way I shall enter; by this way I shall exit," and so forth;
the entire protocol for the alms-round should be understood in the same manner as stated in the *Piṇḍacārika-vatta*. For a forest-dweller (*āraññika*),...
A monk should provide drinking water and water for washing. If there are not enough vessels, he should provide drinking water by making it serve as water for washing as well.
If he cannot obtain a vessel, he should provide it even with a bamboo tube.
If he cannot obtain that either, he should act so that there is a water pool nearby. Fire should also be provided.
One should keep fire-sticks ready; when fire-sticks are available, it is permissible even not to make a fire.
And just as for a forest-dweller, so too for one traveling through a wilderness, fire-sticks should be desired. However, for those living in a community, it is permissible even without them.
A walking stick should be kept ready, and the constellations should be learned, either in their entirety or in part.
Or, one should be skilled regarding the directions. This is the duty for forest-dwellers. 191.
Regarding the duty concerning lodgings: in whichever monastery one dwells, if that monastery is dirty, it should be cleaned if one has the strength to do so.
When cleaning the monastery, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having taken out the sitting mat and rug, they should be placed to one side; having taken out the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side;
having lowered the bed, it should be taken out and placed to one side by one who is careful not to strike or bump it against the door frame;
having lowered the bench, it should be [taken out] by one who is careful not to strike...
Without knocking, one should take out the door-sill and set it aside;
the bed-legs should be taken out and set aside; the spittoon should be taken out and set aside;
the leaning-board should be taken out and set aside; and the floor-covering should be removed as it was arranged.
Having observed it and removed it, it should be placed to one side.
If there is mold on the dwelling, the ceiling should first be cleared, and the light openings, joints, and corners should be wiped clean.
If a wall treated with red ocher has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean. If the floor is stained black...
If it is dusty, the cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to sweep.
If the ground has not been prepared, one should sprinkle it repeatedly with water and then sweep, thinking, "Lest the monastery be covered in dust.
Having cleared away the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
One should not shake bedding within the vicinity of the bhikkhus, nor should one shake bedding within the vicinity of the vihāra,
nor should one shake bedding within the vicinity of drinking water, nor should one shake bedding within the vicinity of washing water;
one should not shake bedding in an open courtyard where the wind blows against it, but one may shake bedding downwind.
Having dried the ground-covering, cleaned it, and shaken it out, one should bring it back and spread it according to its proper arrangement.
Having dried the bed-legs, wiped them, and brought them back, they should be placed in their respective positions.
Having dried the bed, cleaned it, and shaken it out, one should lower it and carefully move it without scraping it along the floor.
Without knocking against the door-socket, one should carry the stool inside and arrange it as prescribed;

having set the stool aside, cleaned it, brushed it, lowered it, and carefully carried it inside without knocking or striking the door-socket, one should arrange it as prescribed; and having set the mattress and pillow aside...
Having washed it, shaken it out, and brought it back, it should be spread out as prescribed;
having dried the sitting mat and the rug, shaken them out, and brought them back, they should be spread out as prescribed;
the spittoon should be dried in a corner, wiped clean, brought back, and placed in its proper position; the leaning board [should be placed] in a corner.
Having dried it and wiped it, it should be placed in its proper position. The bowl and robe should be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, and with the other hand touch the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the chair, and then place the bowl down;
the bowl must not be placed on the ground where there is no covering. When putting away the robe...
Holding the robe with one hand and wiping the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other, one should lay out the robe by making the edge face away and the fold face toward oneself.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed. If [they blow] from the west...
Northern and southern winds blow with dust; the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold weather, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night. If it is hot weather, the windows should be closed by day and opened at night.
If it is dirty, the courtyard must be swept, the gateway must be swept, the assembly hall must be swept, the fire-hall must be swept, and the restroom must be swept.
If there is no drinking water, drinking water must be provided. If there is no water for washing, water for washing must be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water must be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
If one dwells in the same monastery as an elder, one should not give a recitation, nor give an interrogation,
nor engage in study, nor speak on the Dhamma, nor light a lamp without having asked the elder’s permission.
The lamp must not be extinguished; the windows must not be opened, nor must the windows be closed.

Since a door is a place of great public access, there is no requirement to seek permission regarding it; however, all other matters, such as giving a recitation and so forth, must be done only after seeking permission.
It is also appropriate to seek permission on a daily basis. Furthermore, [if one says], "Venerable sir, permission has already been sought..."
When this is said, if the elder accepts by saying "Very well," or if he himself says, "Dwell as you please," it is likewise permissible.
It is also permissible even through the trust of one who is similar [in status].
If he walks the walking-path together with the elder, he should walk in the opposite direction to the elder; nor should he [walk] with the corner of his outer robe [covering the elder].
It should be struck. This is the procedure regarding lodgings. 192.
Regarding the procedure for the sauna: whoever goes first to the sauna, if the ashes have accumulated, the ashes must be discarded.
If it is dirty, the sauna must be swept and the surrounding floor must be swept.
The courtyard should be swept; the gateway should be swept; the sauna hall should be swept; the powder should be prepared;
the clay should be moistened; water should be poured into the water-tub.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and back [with leaves], and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks, nor should one block the junior monks from their seats.
If one is able, one should perform services for the senior monks in the sauna.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna bench and exit the sauna while shielding it both in front and behind.
If one has the strength, one should also perform services for the elder bhikkhus even in the water;
one should not bathe in front of the elder bhikkhus, nor should one bathe above them. When emerging after bathing, one who has bathed should give way to those entering.
Whoever leaves the sauna last, if the sauna is muddy, should wash it.
Having washed the clay trough, put away the bench in the sauna, extinguished the fire, and closed the door, one should depart.
This is the proper conduct regarding the sauna. 193.
Regarding the proper conduct for the restroom: whoever goes to the restroom should cough while standing outside; the one sitting inside should also [respond].
One should cough; having placed the robe on the robe-stand or the robe-string, one should enter the restroom carefully and without haste.
One should not enter too abruptly, nor should one enter with the robe tucked up. While standing on the toilet-stool, the robe should be tucked up.
One should not defecate while snorting, nor while chewing a tooth-stick.
Feces must be disposed of [in the latrine], but one must not discharge feces outside the feces-receptacle;
urine must not be discharged outside the urine-receptacle; saliva must not be spat out on the urine-receptacle.
One must not scrape with wood that is split, rough, knotted, thorny, hollow, or putrid. [This refers to] the scraping-stick.
However, there is no offense for one who has entered without taking [the tooth-stick]; the tooth-stick used for scraping should not be thrown into the cesspool;
it should be covered while standing on the toilet-shoe; one should not exit too hastily; one should not exit by lifting up [the lid];
one should lift it up while standing on the washing-shoe; and one should not rinse with a slurping sound.
No water should be left remaining in the rinsing bowl. This is stated with reference to a place that is common to all;
for since various people come there one after another, no water should be left.

However, it is permissible in the case of a place within a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha that has been set aside for the regular use of a specific individual, or in a place belonging to a private person.
It is also permissible for one who has drunk a purgative to enter again and again. One standing on the rinsing-slat should cover [the opening].
If the latrine is overflowing and smeared with excrement outside, it should be washed after bringing water.
If there is water but no vessel, this is called "non-existent. If there is a vessel but no water, this too—
If it is not there: when both are absent, it is simply not there; one should go after wiping with a piece of wood or something else.
If the waste-basket is full, the scraping-stick should be discarded.
If there is refuse, the latrine should be swept, the floor should be swept, and the courtyard should be swept.
The privy should be swept. If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water should be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.

Because of the statement, “Monks, having defecated, one must rinse with water if water is available; whoever does not rinse commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” there is an offense for one who does not perform the water-rite when water is present. If water is available, [one should go to] a concealed place.
However, there is no [water] [in the bowl]; one must rinse by pouring it out with a vessel. If there is no vessel, it must be poured out with the bowl;
if there is no bowl either, it is called "non-existent. If, thinking, "This is too far open;
there will be other water ahead," he goes and does not find water, and the time for the alms-round has already arrived, he should wipe it with a piece of wood or something else.
It is permissible to go there, to eat, and to offer words of thanksgiving (*anumodana*).
Because of the statement, “Monks, defecation must not be performed in the latrine according to seniority; whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monks, I allow you to defecate according to the order of arrival,” one who enters the latrine must enter according to the order of arrival. In the latrine...
In the case of the place for urination and the bathing ford, the sequence as it has been handed down is the authority even among these three.
This concludes the duties regarding the privy. Thus ends the discussion on the determination of the duties toward preceptors and others in the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
28. Discussion on the Analysis of the Distribution of the Four Requisites (Catupaccayabhājanīyavinicchayakathā) 194.
"The distribution of the four requisites" (*catupaccayabhājana*) means the distribution of the four requisites, beginning with robes.
In that regard, first, in the distribution of robes, one must understand the receiver of robes, the depositor of robes, and the storekeeper.
The storehouse must be known; the distributor of robes must be known; the distribution of robes must be known.
In this regard, "I allow you, monks, to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the receiver of robes:
one who would not fall into partiality through favoritism, nor fall into partiality through ill will, nor fall into partiality through delusion..."

"One should not go to a state of fear, and one should know what has been accepted and what has not been accepted"—according to this statement, a robe-acceptor endowed with these five factors should be appointed.
In that regard, one who accepts first those who arrive later, such as his own relatives;
or who accepts by showing partiality toward certain individuals; or who, due to a greedy disposition, appropriates for himself—[these are the faults to be avoided].
Or he goes by way of favoritism (*chandāgati*). This refers to one who, out of anger, takes [an item] later even though he arrived earlier;
or one who takes it while showing contempt for those of low status; or one who creates an obstacle to the Saṅgha’s gain by saying, "Do you have no place to store it in your house?
Take what belongs to you and go!"—this is going by way of ill-will (*dosāgati*).
It is called "going. However, one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacks clear comprehension is said to go by way of delusion (*moha*).

One who receives [offerings] earlier out of fear of powerful people who arrive later, or who does so out of trepidation thinking, "This place for receiving robes is a heavy responsibility," is said to go by way of fear (*bhaya*). [Thinking,] "I have already accepted this and that..."
One who knows, "This and that have not been accepted," is said to know what has been accepted and what has not. Therefore, one who does not proceed by way of favoritism (*chandāgati*) and the like,
but accepts according to the order in which they arrive— making no distinction between relatives and strangers, or the wealthy and the poor— and who is endowed with virtue,
conduct, and right practice, being mindful, wise, and learned, is able to [dispose of] the gifts entrusted by the donors.
One who expresses appreciation with speech that is well-rounded in its words and phrasing, in order to inspire confidence, should be appointed in this way.
And he should be appointed as follows: First, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the receiver of robes. This is the motion."
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the receiver of robes.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the receiver of robes, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
“Such-and-such a monk has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the receiver of robes; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.

By means of this formal act (*kammavācā*) or by means of a motion (*apalokana*), it is indeed permissible to appoint him within the monastery, in the midst of the entire Saṅgha, or even within a limited boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
And one who has been so appointed must not remain on the outskirts of the monastery or in the meditation hall.
Furthermore, in a principal monastery where people who have come and gone see him with ease, one should place a fan behind [the seat] and sit down well-robed and well-covered. 195.
Regarding the robe-keeper as well: "Monks, I allow a monk endowed with five qualities to be a robe-keeper."

Because of the statement, "One should appoint [a monk] who would not fall into favoritism, would not fall into ill-will, would not fall into delusion, would not fall into fear, and would know both what is deposited and what is not," a monk endowed with these five factors [should be appointed]. He says:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of robes. This is the motion."
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the robe-storer.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the robe-storer, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
“Such-and-such a monk has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the robe-designator; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way, he should be appointed either by this formal act (*kammavācā*) or by a motion (*apalokana*), according to the method already stated.
196. Regarding the storekeeper as well: “Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as storekeeper.”

Because of the statement, "One should appoint [a monk] who would not fall into partiality through favoritism, nor fall into partiality through hatred, nor fall into partiality through delusion, nor fall into partiality through fear, and who would know what is guarded and what is unguarded," a monk endowed with these five factors [should say]:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so..."
He should be appointed by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) or by a motion (*apalokana*), according to the method beginning with the words, "One should appoint a storekeeper.
And herein, that which has no defect in its roofing or other aspects is "guarded" (*gutta*).
However, where the thatching grass or the roof-tiles have fallen anywhere, such that it leaks or there is entry for mice and the like, [it is not guarded].
If there is a hole anywhere in the walls or other parts, or if termites are emerging, all of that is called "unprotected.
Having noticed it, the storekeeper must repair it. During the cold season, the doors and windows must be well-shuttered;
for by the cold, the robes become stiff with moisture. During the hot season, from time to time...
It should be opened for the purpose of allowing air to enter. For by doing so, one indeed knows what is secured and what is unsecured.

197. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to appoint a storehouse—whether it be a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, or a cave—whichever the Saṅgha desires," having appointed a storehouse, [one should act accordingly].

It should be set aside. In this context, however, that monastery or *aḍḍhayoga* which is located in the middle of the monastery grounds, not secluded from monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) or novices (*sāmaṇera*), and serves as a meeting place for everyone, is to be formally authorized. But a remote dwelling (*paccantasenāsana*) is not to be authorized.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to authorize this storehouse after having gone to the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) while sitting within that broken boundary.

Right in the midst of the monastery, it should be appointed either by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) or by a motion (*apalokana*), according to the following method: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint such-and-such a monastery as a storehouse.
Furthermore, all three—the receiver of robes and the others—must know their respective duties. Therein, by the receiver of robes:
Whatever people give— whether it be called "timely robe-cloth," "untimely robe-cloth," "urgent robe-cloth," "rainy-season robe," "sitting mat," "bedspread," or "face-towel"—
all that should not be accepted by making them into one heap and mixing them; rather, they should be kept separately.

Having received it, one should inform the robe-storer exactly as it was described and give it to him. The robe-storer, when giving it to the storekeeper, must also give it after describing it, saying: "This is the timely robe... [and so on] ...this is a face-cleaning cloth.
The storekeeper, in turn, should likewise place each item separately after making a mark for identification. Then, by the Saṅgha: "The timely robe..."
When it is said, “Bring [this],” only a timely robe-cloth should be given... and so on... when it is said, “Bring a face-towel,” that very thing should be given.
Thus the Blessed One has authorized a receiver of robes, authorized one who lays out robes, authorized a storekeeper, and authorized a storehouse;
not for the sake of abundance, nor for the sake of lack of contentment, but rather for the benefit of the Saṅgha.

For if the monks were to distribute the requisites by taking whatever had been brought, they would not know what was brought and what was not brought, what was given and what was not given, what was obtained and what was not obtained;

they might either give what was brought to those in the seats of the elders or take it after cutting it into pieces. This being so, there would be improper consumption, and there would be no inclusion of all.
It has been done. However, when the robes have accumulated after being stored in the storehouse, they will give three robes, or two each, or one robe to each bhikkhu;
they will know who has received them and who has not, and having learned those who have not received them, they will think to provide for them.

198. Regarding the distributor of robes, it is said: "I allow you, monks, to appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of robes—one who would not act out of favoritism, nor act out of ill will, nor act out of delusion, nor act out of fear, and who would know what has been distributed and what has not been distributed.
Therefore, [the candidate] must indeed be endowed with these five qualities.
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of robes.
Having been appointed by means of such a formal act (*kammavācā*) or by means of a motion (*apalokana*), he should be established [in that office].
In this regard, one who gives a costly robe even when it does not reach monks of similar standing falls into favoritism (*chandāgati*).
It is called "going to the wrong course through hatred" when one does not give a costly robe to others who are more senior, even though it has reached them, but instead gives one of little value.
It is called "going to the wrong course through delusion" when one, being utterly bewildered and ignorant of the proper conduct regarding the giving of robes, acts out of delusion.

It is called "going to the wrong course through fear" when one gives a costly robe only to those novices who are talkative, out of fear of them, even though it does not reach those [who are more senior].
One who does not act in such a way—who is impartial toward all, serving as their scale and authority—should be appointed.
By that person, while distributing the robes, one should first [examine them] thus:
"This is coarse, this is fine, this is thick, this is thin, this has been used, this has not been used, this is this much in length, and this much in width."
Having examined the robes and determined their value by saying, "This is worth this much;
that is worth this much," if each person receives exactly ten [robes] worth ten [units], that is well.
If that is not possible, then whatever is worth nine or eight [units] may be combined with another robe worth one [unit] and another worth two [units].
Having bound [the robes] by this method and placed them upon level ground, the *kusa*-grass should be cast down.
If the day is not sufficient for distributing the robes one by one, ten monks should be counted together;
ten portions of robe-cloth should be bound together, made into a bundle, and one such portion of robe-cloth should be set aside. When the portions of robe-cloth have been set aside in this manner...
A blade of *kusa* grass must be cast [to determine the portion]. Those monks, having also performed the casting of the *kusa* grass, must then divide [the property].

Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to give half a share to the novices," those novices who are independent and do not perform the duties to be done for the Saṅgha of monks—being devoted to recitation and interrogation [of the Dhamma] under their own teachers and preceptors—[are entitled to this].
They perform their duties and counter-duties for some, but not for others; a half-share should be given to these alone.
However, to those who perform the duties to be done for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus both before and after the meal, an equal share should be given.
And this refers specifically to out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*) that have arisen during the post-harvest period and have been stored in the storehouse.
It has been said that, however, the robe for the [specific] time must be given equally.

The *tatruppāda-vassāvāsika* (the rainy-season gift arising from that source) and items such as brooms and binding materials should be taken after performing the service for the Saṅgha. This is the duty for everyone here.
Regarding the robes in the storehouse, if novice monks come and say, "Venerable sir, we are cooking rice-gruel, we are cooking a meal, we are cooking snacks..."
“Let us take green leaves; let us bring tooth-sticks; having made dye-skin allowable, let us give it—what indeed have we not done?
they cry out. It should be given in equal shares.
If they act by neglecting this very rule, and with reference to those whose status as makers is not evident, it was said: “I allow, monks, [the work] of novices.”

"...to give them half a share. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "But if the novices should request, saying, 'Venerable sir, why do we not perform the formal acts of the Saṅgha? We shall perform them,' then an equal share must be given.
If any monk, having taken his own portion and obtained a boat, crosses a river or a wilderness...
When he wishes to depart for another region, because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to give one's own share to one who is departing," once the robes have been brought out from the storehouse,
the bell has been struck, and the Saṅgha of monks has assembled, the robe-distributor,
having estimated that "this monk’s portion must be this much," [proceeds] by way of a guiding principle.
The robe-cloth should be distributed in equal shares. For it is impossible to distribute it with absolute mathematical precision, as if weighed on a scale;
therefore, whether it be slightly less or slightly more, what is given according to this method is well-given.
One should not give again what was short, nor should one accept what is in excess. If there are ten monks and ten cloths, yet among them one [monk] has twelve...

The rest are worth ten [units]. When the *kuśa* grass has been cast down for all [the monks] by way of their value being ten units each, whichever monk’s *kuśa* grass was worth twelve units may take that extra portion after giving whatever suitable article belonging to himself is worth as much as the excess in that lot. If [this is done] for all...
There are five robes and five bowls; there are others as well, but each individual does not receive them all. They should be cut and given out.
When cutting them, they should be made into pieces sufficient for half-moons and so forth, or for sandals, bags, and the like.
At the very least, even a piece four finger-breadths wide and long enough to reach downwind [to cover the body] may be given.
It is proper to give [the robes] after having cut them up, but they must not be left as unusable.
Even if one or two robes are insufficient for the portion of a single bhikkhu, one should set aside other requisites for novices there;
then, having divided that portion for whoever is satisfied with it, the cutting up [of the remaining cloth] should be performed afterwards. If there are ten bhikkhus each time...
When they count them and form groups, one group does not reach the full number; there are eight or nine. To those eight or nine, [the robes] should be given with the instruction:
"Take these and distribute them separately. Having given them in this way, the drawing of lots (kusapāta) should be performed afterwards.
199. Now, "Bhikkhus, there are these eight headings for the arising of robes: one gives within the boundary, by agreement..."

The detailed exposition should be understood according to those eight headings (mātikā) which were stated for the purpose of showing the fields for obtaining robes: "He gives," "he gives by means of the distribution of alms-food," "he gives to the Saṅgha," "he gives to both Saṅghas," "he gives to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence," "he gives specifying [a particular robe]," and "he gives to an individual."
In this context, when one gives while referring to the boundary by saying, "I give to the boundary," it is called giving to the boundary.
What is given to the boundary in this manner must be shared among all those bhikkhus who have entered within the boundary.

Now, as for this boundary, there is the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), the common-assembly boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*), the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*), the profit boundary (*lābhasīmā*), the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the town boundary (*nigamasīmā*), and the city boundary (*nagarasīmā*).

The boundary is of fifteen kinds: the internal boundary, the water-splash boundary, the district boundary, the kingdom boundary, the realm boundary, the island boundary, and the world-system boundary.
Among these, the fragmented boundary has already been explained in the discussion on boundaries.
As for the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), it is defined by the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or, in the case of an unenclosed one, by the area suitable for an enclosure.

Furthermore, the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) should be understood as being within two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of two stone-throw) from the place where the monks regularly assemble, or from the dining hall situated at the edge, or from the permanent dwelling; this is for a man of medium strength.
Moreover, that boundary expands when the dwellings expand and contracts when they contract. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
It is said: "When the bhikkhus increase, [the boundary] increases.

Therefore, if they sit down together with the bhikkhus assembled in the monastery, forming a single continuous line even across a hundred yojanas, that hundred yojanas becomes a *upacāra-sīmā* (functional boundary), and the gains (*lābha*) reach all of them.
Both the *samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā* (boundary of common residence) and the *avippavāsa-sīmā* (boundary of non-separation) have already been explained. [Now follows] the *lābha-sīmā* (boundary of gains).
It was neither authorized by the Perfectly Enlightened One nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma;
rather, kings, royal ministers, or great officials, having had a monastery built, demarcated an area of a quarter-league, half a league, or a full league on all sides,
and having driven stakes inscribed with the name "This is the boundary for the acquisitions of our monastery" into the ground, [established it].
“When whatever arises within this interval, we give it all to our monastery,” they establish a boundary; this is called a *lābhasīmā* (boundary for acquisitions).
The boundaries for villages, market towns, cities, interiors, and the throwing of water have already been explained.
As for a *janapadasīmā* (national boundary), there are many districts within kingdoms such as Kāsī and Kosala; therein, each individual district-limit is [a *janapadasīmā*].
The boundary of a district (*janapada-sīmā*). The boundary of a kingdom (*raṭṭha-sīmā*) refers to the territorial limits of kingdoms such as Kāsi, Kosala, and so forth.
The boundary of a realm (*rajja-sīmā*) refers to the area where the authority of a single king prevails, such as "the province of Coḷa" or "the province of Kerala.

The boundary of an island (*dīpa-sīmā*) refers to both the great islands and the intermediate islands, which are delimited by the edge of the ocean. The boundary of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-sīmā*) is delimited by the World-System Mountains (*cakkavāḷa-pabbata*) themselves.

Thus, regarding these boundaries: when one sees the Saṅgha assembled for some business within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (sub-boundary) and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha right here within the boundary," it should be divided among as many bhikkhus as have entered within that *khaṇḍasīmā*.
For that gift accrues only to them; it does not belong even to those standing in the *sīmantarikā* (intermediate space) or the *upacārasīmā* (proximate boundary).

It reaches [the recipient]. However, for one standing on a tree or a mountain situated within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (a partial boundary), it reaches those who are below or situated in the middle of the earth.
But what is given with the words, "I give this to the Saṅgha within this *upacārasīmā* (proximate boundary)," reaches even those standing in the intervals between the *khaṇḍasīmās*.
Furthermore, what is given with the words, "I give this to the *samānasaṃvāsasīmā* (boundary of common communion)," [reaches] those in the intervals between the *khaṇḍasīmās*.

It does not reach those who are standing outside [the boundary]. What is given within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) or the robe-keeping boundary (*lābha-sīmā*) reaches those who are inside those boundaries.

What is given within village boundaries (*gāma-sīmā*) and so forth reaches even those standing within a formally established boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) inside them. What is given within an inner boundary (*abbhantara-sīmā*) or a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) reaches only those who are inside that very area.
This also applies to the boundaries of a district (*janapada*), a province (*raṭṭha*), a kingdom (*rajja*), an island (*dīpa*), and the world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷa-sīmā*).
The legal determination regarding village boundaries and so forth is exactly as previously stated.
However, if one staying in Jambudīpa says, "I give this to the Saṅgha in Tambapaṇṇidīpa," even a single person coming from Tambapaṇṇidīpa is entitled to receive it on behalf of all.
Furthermore, if in that very place there is a single bhikkhu who is a companion [to those in Tambapaṇṇidīpa]... [he may also act for them].
He takes a share; he is not to be prevented. Thus, first, the decision regarding the gift of one who gives after touching the boundary should be understood.

However, as for one who does not know how to say "in such-and-such a boundary," but knowing only the mere word "boundary," comes to the monastery and says, "I give to the boundary," or "I give to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary":
He should be asked: "There are many kinds of boundaries; which boundary do you have in mind?
If he says, "I do not know which specific boundary it is; let the Saṅgha residing within the boundary divide and take [the goods]," then within which boundary should they be divided?
The Elder Mahāsīva reportedly said, "Within the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā). Thereupon, they said to him: "The non-separation boundary..."
It is said that [the distance] is three *yojanas*. This being so, those standing at three *yojanas* will receive alms;
standing at three *yojanas*, they must fulfill the duties for visitors and enter the monastery; a traveler, having gone three *yojanas*, must take leave of his lodging;
for one under formal dependence (*nissaya*), the dependence is suspended upon exceeding three *yojanas*; and by one on probation (*pārivāsika*)...
"The dawn must be made to rise after having passed three yojanas; a bhikkhunī standing within three yojanas must obtain permission to enter the monastery.
All of this is permissible only by way of defining the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīmā);
therefore, it should be divided according to the precinct boundary."

200. Regarding the phrase "gives by agreement" (*katikāya deti*): here, "agreement" (*katikā*) refers to an agreement for equal distribution of gains. In this regard, the agreement should be made as follows:

when the monks have assembled in a certain monastery, those who wish to maintain that monastery and desire to establish an equal distribution of gains should take its name and say, "Such-and-such a monastery is ancient," or "It was inhabited by the Buddha."
Or, having stated some reason such as "there is little gain," one should announce three times:
"Does it please the Saṅgha to make that monastery have a common share with this monastery? Up to this point, even one sitting in that monastery is as if sitting here.
In that monastery as well, the Saṅgha should act in exactly this same way. Up to this point, even one sitting here [is as if sitting there].
He remains seated right there. When alms-food is being distributed in one monastery, it is permissible for one who is standing in another to take a share.
In this way, even many dwellings may be made to have a single distribution of alms by means of a single monastery.
And when this is done, if [the portion] is given in one dwelling, it is as if it were given everywhere.
201. "Designation of Alms-food" (*bhikkhāpaññatti*) refers to a place where one's own relinquishment is designated, wherein regular services are performed for the Saṅgha.

In this context, it refers to whichever monastery belongs to this donor of robes where the Saṅgha’s meal-provisions are maintained, or whichever monastery the monks, taking upon themselves the responsibility, always dine at the house, or wherever—
If he has had a residence built, or has established regular offerings such as *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals) and the like, these are called "regular benefactors" (*dhuvakāra*).
However, there is no need to say anything at all regarding one who has established an entire monastery;
therefore, if he says, "I give [the gift] wherever my regular benefactors are serving," or "Give it there," even if there are many [such places], [it is valid].
They become permanent recipients in those places, and thus it is as if given everywhere.
However, if there are more monks in one monastery, they should say, "In your permanent allotment, there are many monks in one place and few in another.
If he says, "Take it according to the number of monks," it is permissible to divide and take it accordingly.
And here, even small items such as bedding and medicine are easily distributed.
However, if there is only one bed or one chair, one should ask whose monastery it belongs to; or, even if it is a single monastery, whose lodging it is, and it should be given there.
Even if someone says, "Let such-and-such a bhikkhu take it," it is permissible. Now...
If, after saying, “Give it to my permanent attendant,” he goes away without further consideration, it is permissible for the Saṅgha to investigate.
It should be investigated in this way: one should say, “Give it to the dwelling place of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
If the lodging there is already full, it should be given where there is space available. If a single bhikkhu says, “To me...”
If he says, "There is no furniture for the use of lodgings in the place where one dwells," it must be given there.

202. Regarding the phrase "he gives to the Saṅgha": if, having entered the monastery, he gives saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha," they are to be distributed by the Saṅgha standing within the boundary (upacārasīmā) after striking the gong and announcing the time.
One who takes a share from a monk belonging to the boundary, even if he has not arrived, is not to be prevented.

If a monastery is large and, while robes are being distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*), the indolent great elders arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sir, [robes] for those of twenty years' standing are being given;
your turn has passed. Rather, having set aside the turn, one should give them [the robes].
It should be given from the place where they stand after arriving. Hearing that "much robe-cloth has arisen in such-and-such a monastery," monks come even from a monastery a *yojana* away;
it should be given starting from the spot where each person arrives.
Even for those who have not yet arrived, but have entered the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), it must certainly be given when their pupils and others receive it. Outside the precinct boundary...
If they say, “Give it to those who are staying [here],” it should not be given.

However, if they have entered the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) and, being connected as one, are at the door of their own monastery or even inside the monastery itself, the boundary is said to have expanded by way of the assembly;
therefore, it should be given. Even when it has been given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, it must still be given to those who arrive later. In the second portion...
However, when the Elder’s seat has been ascended, if the first portion does not reach those who have arrived, it must be given by way of the *vassagga* from the second portion.
If there are ten bhikkhus in one monastery and they give ten robes saying, "We give these to the Saṅgha," they should be divided individually.
If they take them, thinking, "All of these will reach us," and then depart, they have improperly distributed them.

And those that were wrongly grasped belong to the Saṅgha alone at whatever place they have gone to. However, having set aside one [robe] and presented it to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, saying, "This belongs to you," it is permissible to take the remainder, thinking, "The rest belong to us.
If they bring even a single robe, saying, "We give this to the Saṅgha," it is permissible to take it without dividing it, thinking, "It belongs to us."

They take it, but it is poorly distributed and poorly grasped. Having made a mark with a needle or with turmeric and so forth, it is permissible to give one portion to the senior of the Saṅgha, saying, "This place falls to you," and then take the remainder for oneself, saying, "The rest falls to us.
However, whatever is merely a flower or a fold of the cloth itself, by that [mark] one should define the boundary.

It is not permissible to do so. However, if they remove a single thread and give that portion to the Elder, saying, "This place belongs to you," and then take the remainder for themselves, saying, "The rest belongs to us," it is permissible. It is likewise permissible if the cloth is divided by cutting it into pieces.
In a monastery with only one monk, if robes accrue to the Saṅgha, if that monk—according to the method previously described—[acts accordingly...]
If one takes them thinking, “All of these shall come to me,” they are properly taken, but the distribution does not remain stable.
If, however, one takes them by drawing out each one individually, thinking, “This one comes to me,” then the distribution remains stable.
In that case, if the distribution has not remained stable and another robe arises, and a monk arrives, [the robe] should be cut in the middle.
It should be accepted by both. If, while standing in one's turn, another robe arises and a junior monk arrives, the turn descends;

if a senior monk arrives, the turn ascends. If there is no other [monk], it should be accepted again after bringing it back to oneself, saying, "We give it to the Saṅgha," or "To the community of bhikkhus."
Furthermore, anything given by touching the Saṅgha in any manner whatsoever—such as saying "demā" (give me)—is not permitted for those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*), because it has been stated:
"I reject householder’s robes; I undertake the practice of wearing rag-robes. This is not, however, because they are unallowable (*akappiya*).
Even that which is given after the Bhikkhu Saṅgha has sought permission must not be accepted. As for that which belongs to a monk himself...
If one gives it, that which is given by monks (bhikkhudattiya) is permissible, though it does not count as a rag-robe (paṃsukūla). Even so, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is not broken.
However, if it is said, "We give this to the monks," or "We give this to the elders" (theras), it is also permissible for those who wear rag-robes;
yet if it is said, "We give this cloth to the Saṅgha; with this [cloth], [make] sandals, bags for robes, bags for bowls, waist-bands, shoulder-straps, and so forth..."

It is permissible even if [the cloth] was given with the words, “Let them make [it]. Even if many cloths were given for the purpose of making alms-bowl bags and so forth, they are sufficient for the purpose of robes;

therefore, it is permissible to make a robe from them and wear it. However, if the Saṅgha divides the surplus cloths after distribution and then divides them for the purpose of sandals, bags, and so forth, it is not permissible to take them from there.

Only that which has been deliberated upon by the owners is permissible, not otherwise. Even if it is said of a rag-robe, "We give this for the sake of the Sangha’s Dhammakaraṇa-cloth and so forth," it is permissible to accept it; for requisites are desired even by those who wear rag-robes.
Whatever surplus there may be therein is also permissible to apply toward robes. [If] they give thread to the Sangha...

It should also be accepted by those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*). This, first of all, is the decision regarding robes given after entering a monastery with the words, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha.

However, if one sees monks traveling on a journey road outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) and announces to either the senior monk of the Saṅgha or the junior monk of the Saṅgha, saying, "I give [these] to the Saṅgha"—even if it is a *yojana* away—

When the assembly stands surrounding [the recipient], if they are joined together as one, it reaches all of them. However, for those who do not reach the assembly within twelve hand-spans, it does not reach them.
Regarding the phrase "gives to both Sanghas": even if one says, "I give to both Sanghas," it means "to the Sangha in two parts."
If it is said, “I give,” or “I give to the two Saṅghas,” or “I give to both the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha,” it is indeed given to both Saṅghas.
In that case, even if there are many bhikkhus and only one bhikkhunī, half must be given;
the meaning is that having divided [the gift] into two equal parts, one part is to be given.
If there are many bhikkhunīs but only one bhikkhu, half [of the portion] should be given. When it is said,
"I give to both Saṅghas and to you," if there are ten bhikkhus and ten bhikkhunīs each, having made twenty-one portions,
one portion should be given to the individual, ten to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, and ten to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha.

Whatever has been obtained for an individual, that person is permitted to take it for themselves according to their own seniority. Why? Because it was taken by means of a distribution to both Saṅghas.
The same principle applies when it is said, "I give this to both Saṅghas and to the Cetiya.
However, in this case, there is no portion that accrues to the Cetiya from the Saṅgha; it is exactly like a portion obtained by a single individual.

It becomes a portion. However, when it is said, "For both Saṅghas, for you, and for the Cetiya," one should divide it into twenty-two portions and give ten to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, ten to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, one to an individual (puggala), and one to the Cetiya.
In that case, the individual may also take [a share] from the Saṅgha according to their own seniority (*vassaga*), whereas for the Cetiya there is only one [share].
But when it is said, “I give to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and to the bhikkhunīs,” one should not divide it in the middle;

rather, having counted both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, it should be given. However, when it is said, “To the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, to the bhikkhunīs, and to you,” the individual does not receive separately;
he receives only one portion from the place where the distribution reaches. Why? Because by the mention of the “Saṅgha of bhikkhus,”...

Because it has been taken [as a share]. Even when it is said, "For the Saṅgha of monks, for the nuns, for you, and for the cetiya," a single individual's share is obtained for the cetiya, but no separate share is obtained for the individual;
therefore, having given one share to the cetiya, the remainder should be divided by counting the monks and the nuns.
Even when it is said, “I give to the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs,” one must not divide it in the middle;
it should be distributed according to the number of individuals.

Even when it is said, “To the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs and to you,” or “To the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs and to the cetiya,” or “To the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs and to you and the cetiya”—in such cases, [the portion] for the cetiya...
It is obtained as a twenty-first; there is no separate portion for an individual person. It should be divided only by counting both the monks and the nuns.
And just as the method was set forth beginning with the community of monks, so too it should be applied beginning with the community of nuns.
When it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for you,” an individual share is not obtained separately; it must be taken as part of the total distribution.
However, when it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for the cetiya,” a separate share for the cetiya is obtained.
Even when it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for you, and for the cetiya,” [the share] belongs to the cetiya alone separately.
It is obtained for the Saṅgha, not for an individual. Even when it is said, “for the bhikkhus and for you,” it is not obtained separately for the individual;
however, when it is said, “for the bhikkhus and for the cetiya,” it is obtained for the cetiya.

Even when it is said, “for the bhikkhus, for you, and for the cetiya,” it is obtained separately for the cetiya alone, not for the individual. This same principle should be applied starting from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha as well.

In the past, people gave alms to the Saṅgha of both monks and nuns headed by the Buddha; the Blessed One sat in the center, with the monks sitting on his right and the nuns on his left. The Blessed One was the senior elder of both Saṅghas;
at that time, he himself consumed the requisites he received and also caused them to be given to the monks. But nowadays, wise people...
Having established an image or a shrine together with its constituent elements (sadhātuka), they give alms to the Saṅgha of both sides headed by the Buddha; or,
having placed a bowl on a stand before the image or the shrine and having offered water for the dedication, saying,
"We give to the Buddhas," they first give there hard food and soft food, or having brought it to the monastery...
If people give alms-food, garlands, perfumes, and so forth, saying, "We give this to the cetiya," how should one proceed in that case?
First, the garlands, perfumes, and so on should be offered upon the cetiya; banners should be made with cloth, and lamps with oil.
As for the alms-food, honey, molasses, and so on, however, they should be given to whichever monastic or layperson is the appointed caretaker of the cetiya.
Or, they should be given to him. If there is no appointed attendant, it is permissible to perform the duties and consume the food brought after setting it aside;
even when the time for eating has nearly passed, it is still permissible to eat first and then perform the duties afterwards.
Regarding garlands, perfumes, and so forth, if someone says, "Take this and offer it as worship at the cetiya," one should carry it even a great distance and offer it in worship.
Even if it is said, “Bring it for the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha),” it should be brought. However, if he says, “I am walking for alms; there are monks in the dining hall (āsanasālā);
they will bring it,” and [the donor] replies, “Venerable sir, I give it to you alone,” it is permissible to eat it.
But if, while bringing it with the thought, “I shall give it to the community of monks,” the time [for the meal] passes while he is on his way, [he may not eat it].
When it is near [the end of the rains), it is permissible to take [the robes] for oneself and enjoy them. 204.

Regarding the phrase "gives to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains": here, if one enters the monastery and gives, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains," then as many bhikkhus as have not broken the rains retreat in that residence—
Those who have completed the previous rains-residence must share [the gift] among themselves; it does not accrue to others.

Even for one who has departed for another region, as long as there is a recipient, the gift must be given until the dismantling of the *kaṭhina*. However, experts in the characteristics of the law state:

"But when the *kaṭhina* has not been dismantled, if it is given during the winter season after saying this, it accrues even to those who have completed the subsequent rains-residence. Thus it is said in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

But this has not been investigated. However, if one standing outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) says, "I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," it accrues to all those who have arrived.

If, on the other hand, he says, "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence at such-and-such monastery," it accrues only to those who completed the rains residence there, up until the suspension of the Kathina. But if, during the summer...
If one speaks thus starting from the very first day, it reaches all those who are present there.
