Why? Because it arises at the time of the back-season (piṭṭhisamaya). If one says, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," only those who have actually spent the rains receive it;

those whose rains-residence was interrupted do not receive it; only those who have completed the rains-residence receive it. However, during the robe-month, if one says, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," [it applies to everyone].

When it is so stated, the gift accrues only to those who have entered the rains residence during the later period; it does not accrue to those who entered during the earlier period or to those whose rains residence has been interrupted.

From the beginning of the robe-month until the last day of winter, if it is said, "We give the *vassāvāsika*," then regardless of whether the *kaṭhina* has been spread or not, it accrues only to those who have completed the rains residence of the past year.
Starting from the first day of the summer season, however, the following schedule (mātikā) should be set forth:
"Five months of the past residence have elapsed; four months of the future [residence] remain until its completion. To which residence do you belong?
If he says, "I give it to those who have completed their residence in the past," then it accrues only to those who have completed their residence within that very rainy season.
Those who have departed for other regions may also receive their share from those remaining.

If someone says, "I give the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering) for the future," it should be set aside and received on the day of the formal entry into the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*). However, if it is said, "The monastery is unprotected; there is danger from thieves;
it is not possible to set it aside or to carry it about," and he then says, "I give it to those who are present," [it should be taken immediately].
It should be taken after having been divided. If he says, "Venerable sir, I did not give my *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering) for the third year from here;
I give that now," it falls to those monks who have resided during that particular rainy season. If they have departed for other regions and another person of trust takes it, it must be given.
Now, if only one remains and the others have passed away, everything belongs to that one alone.
[He] obtains it. If not even one [of these] exists, it belongs to the Saṅgha; it should be divided among those who are present.

205. "He gives by specifying" means: here, when he gives by pointing out and delimiting—whether it be rice-gruel, cooked food, fresh food, a robe, a lodging, or medicine—it is called "giving by specifying. In this regard, the following is the analysis.
If, having invited monks for today’s meal or for tomorrow’s, one gives them rice gruel after they have entered their house,

and after giving the rice gruel, once it has been drunk, says, “I give these robes to those by whom my rice gruel was drunk,” then it accrues only to those who were invited and drank the rice gruel. But as for those [monks] who [were there] by way of the practice of going for alms—
If rice porridge is obtained by those going out through the house door or by those who have already entered the house;
or if it has been brought from the dining hall in bowls and carried away by people; or if it has been sent by the elders—it does not reach them.
However, if many others besides the invited monks arrive and fill both the interior and exterior of the house...
While they are seated, the donor says: "Whether they were invited or uninvited, let these robes belong to all those to whom I gave the rice-gruel.
It reaches everyone; however, it does not reach those who received the gruel from the hands of the elders.
Then he says: "Let it belong to all those by whom my gruel was drunk."
When he says [this], it accrues to all. The same principle applies to meals and hard foods as well.
Regarding robes, however, if he has previously spent the rains retreat with the monks and given them robes, and then, after feeding the monks, says:
"To those to whom I have previously given robes, let this robe, or thread, or ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth [belong]," [then it accrues to them].

Or let them be,” then all of it accrues to them alone. Regarding lodgings as well, if one says, “Let this belong to whoever dwells in the monastery or the cell built by me,” it belongs to that person alone.
Regarding medicines as well, if one says, “We give ghee and other medicines to the elders from time to time; let this belong only to those by whom they were received,” then it belongs to them alone.

206. Regarding the phrase "gives to an individual": here, he gives either in the person's absence, saying, "I give this robe to [so-and-so]," or in their presence, having placed it at the feet [of the recipient], saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you.
That [robe] belongs to that very person alone. However, if he says, "I give this to you and to your students," [it belongs to both].
It reaches both the Elder and his resident pupils. There are those who come to receive the recitation and depart after having received it;

for them, too, it reaches. When it is said, "I give this to the bhikkhus who travel in regular association with you," it applies to all those who, having performed the duties toward their recitation-pupils, travel about receiving the recitations, the questioning on the meaning, and so forth.
[He] attains [the merit]. This is the analysis of the phrase, “he gives to an individual.
If a certain monk dwells alone for the rains retreat, and people there give robes saying, “We give to the Saṅgha,” what should be done in that case?
“I allow you, monks, those very robes for him until the Kathina [ceremony].”
Because of the statement, "They are [robes] set aside," if the kaṭhina has been spread after obtaining monks to complete the quorum, they belong to him for five months;
if it has not been spread, even if they have been taken elsewhere during the one month of robe-season, those robes still belong to him alone, and no one else has authority over them.
For whatever is given with the words, "We give to the Saṅgha," or "With reference to the Saṅgha..."

If they give it saying, "We give it to the Saṅgha," or "We give it to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence," or "We give it as a gift for the rains residence," even if he enters that monastery without having divided the deceased monk's robe-cloth, all of it belongs to that very bhikkhu.
This applies also to whatever he has set aside from the investment he put out for the purpose of the rains residence, or from the specific endowment for that purpose.
If one accepts the *vassāvāsika* (the robe-offering for the rainy season residence), everything is properly accepted. This is the defining characteristic here:

in whatever manner cloth arises for the Saṅgha, it reaches the Saṅgha whose *kathina* has been spread during the five months [of the rains], and it reaches the Saṅgha whose *kathina* has not been spread during the one month of the robe-season.
However, if some bhikkhu should dwell alone at a time other than the rains-retreat, there—
If people give robes saying, "We give these to the Saṅgha," that bhikkhu must resolve upon them, thinking, "These robes are for me.
Furthermore, the one making the resolution must know the proper procedure.
Therefore, that bhikkhu—having either struck the gong or announced the time, and having waited a short while—if, by means of the sign of the gong or the sign of the time...

When monks arrive, [the robes] should be shared with them. If another monk arrives while those monks are in the process of dividing that robe-cloth before the *kusa*-grass markers have been cast, an equal share must be given to him.
If another monk arrives after the *kusa*-grass markers have already been cast, a share need not be given against his will.
For even in the case of a single portion, as soon as the *kusa*-staff has been cast— even if...
There is a thousand bhikkhus; the robe-cloth has indeed been accepted. Therefore, a share should not be given against their will.
But if they wish to give it out of their own inclination, let them do so. This same principle applies to the subsequent portions as well.
Now, if other bhikkhus do not arrive due to the sound of a bell or the perception of the time, [one should think]: "These robes are for us."
One should resolve: "May they come to me. When resolved in this way, all of them belong to him, yet the turn of succession does not remain fixed.
If, however, one takes them up one by one, saying, "This first portion comes to me;
this is the second portion," then what is taken is well-taken and the turn of succession remains fixed. Even for one who takes them after having caused them to come to him in this manner:

It is indeed determined. However, if one takes them—whether by striking the bell or not, whether by making an announcement or not—thinking, "I alone am here; these robes are mine alone," they are wrongly taken.
But if one takes them thinking, "There is no one else here; these fall to me," they are rightly taken. Then...

If, without making a formal resolution (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*), one takes those robes and goes toward another monastery with the intention, "I will share them there with the monks," those robes belong to the Saṅgha wherever they go. In this case, the mere fact that the monks have seen them is the determining factor.
Therefore, if some people coming from the opposite direction ask, "Friend, where..."
Having asked, "Are you going? and having heard that matter, [they think], "Friend, are we not the Saṅgha?

and they divide and take it right there; these are well-taken. Even if he, having left the road, enters some monastery or a sitting-hall while wandering for alms, or enters only a single house, and the monks see him there and [inform] him of that matter...
If they take [the robes] after having asked [for permission] and divided them, they have indeed taken them correctly.
Because of the statement: “Monks, one who has completed the rains residence elsewhere must not accept a share of robe-cloth elsewhere;
whoever should so accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” if one who has completed the rains residence elsewhere takes a share elsewhere, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
In this case, although the offense is light, nevertheless the robes that were taken must be returned to the place from which they were taken.

Even if they have been lost or worn out, the liability for their value falls upon him alone. If, when told "Give them," he does not give them, he is to be made to pay the value of the goods once he has abandoned his defense.
A certain bhikkhu dwells for the rains retreat in two residences, thinking, "In this way, much robe-cloth will accrue to me.

He receives only his individual share from one [residence]. Therefore, if he stays for one day at a time—or for up to seven days—in each monastery, he receives half of what one person would receive from each respective monastery.

It should be given. For in this way, a share for a single individual has been given. However, if one who is living in one monastery causes the dawn to rise [within the seven-day period] while staying in another, a larger share from the monastery where he stayed longer must be given to him.
Even in this case, it is indeed a share for a single individual that has been given. And this applies when there are different acquisitions and different jurisdictions.

This has been explained regarding those residing within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*). However, when residing in different boundaries (*nānāsīmā*), the formal taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*) ceases.
Therefore, the distribution of robes (*cīvarapaṭivīsa*) does not apply there; however, all other items such as food and medicine belong to everyone who is within the boundary.
207. "Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes; furthermore, those who attended to the sick [are also entitled to them]."
"It is of great benefit, monks; I allow you, monks, to give the triple robe and the bowl to those who have attended to the sick.
Whatever light goods or light requisites there may be in that regard, those shall be distributed by the assembled Saṅgha.
Whatever heavy goods or heavy requisites there may be in that regard, those shall not be disposed of, but shall belong to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future."
Because of the statement, "it is not to be divided," when a monk has passed away, one should either seek permission or say:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. The monk named so-and-so has passed away; this is his triple robe and his bowl.
If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this triple robe and this bowl to those who attended the sick. This is the motion."
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: the bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away; this is his triple robe and his bowl.
The Saṅgha gives this triple robe and this bowl to those who attended the sick.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of giving this triple robe and this bowl to those who attended the sick, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”
“‘This triple robe and bowl have been given by the Saṅgha to the attendants of the sick; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.

Having thus announced the formal act (*kammavācā*) and having given the bowl and robes to the attendants of the sick, the remaining light requisites should be distributed and taken by the assembled Saṅgha. 208.
Regarding the distribution of gains to the attendants of the sick, this is the rule: if the entire community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) attends upon them...

If he dies while all [the duties] have been performed, all [the monks] are owners [of the merit]. Now, if he dies when some have performed their turn and others have not yet performed theirs, regarding this, some teachers say: "All should perform [their duty] when their own turn arrives; therefore, all are owners. Others say:
"Only those by whom he was tended receive [the merit]; the others do not receive it. This applies even in the case of a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).
When he has passed away, if there is a robe-cloth, it should be given to those who attended to him while he was ill.
If there is none, whatever else there is should be given. If other requisites are present, they should be divided and a portion set aside for the robe-cloth before being distributed.
If both a bhikkhu and a sāmaṇera have attended to him equally, an equal share should be given. But if only the sāmaṇera has attended to him, [the share] for the bhikkhu...
It is merely for the purpose of cooking; the senior portion should be given to the novice.
If the novice merely performs the task of having rice-gruel cooked by the monk using water brought by him, while the monk attends to the service, the senior share should be given to the monk.
If many monks all attend together in harmony, it is equal for all.
A share must be given. However, for one who attends specifically and with distinction, a special portion should be made.
Furthermore, whoever—even for a single day—has provided rice-gruel or cooked rice as an attendant to the sick, or has prepared a bath, he too is indeed an attendant to the sick.
But as for one who, without coming near, [provides] medicines, rice, and so forth...
If he merely sends [someone], this person is not a nurse. One who, having sought and secured [an attendant], returns, is indeed a nurse.
One attends out of a sense of duty, while the other attends out of expectation; at the time of death, both expect [to receive something], and it should be given to both.
One attends, but having finished his duties for the sick person or his own personal business, goes elsewhere; [if he thinks], "Again..."

"I will come and attend to him," for such a person it should also be given. If one who has attended for a long time, saying "I am no longer able," casts off the burden and departs—even if he dies on that very day from illness—the portion for an attendant should not be given.
Whether he be a layperson or a monastic, even down to a woman, all are called "attendants of the sick."
They receive a share. If that monk has nothing but his bowl and robes, and there is nothing else, everything must be given to the attendants of the sick.
Even if it is worth a thousand [pieces of gold], they do not receive any other requisites;
it belongs to the Saṅgha alone. Any remaining goods, whether numerous or of great value, [including] the three robes—
Taking from that [value] what is of little worth, the requisite of the three robes (ticīvaraparikkhāra) should be given; all of this is obtained only from what belongs to the Saṅgha.

However, if he, while still alive, has relinquished his entire personal property and given it to someone, or if someone took it on trust, then it belongs only to the one to whom it was given or by whom it was taken, and only according to his own wish.
Those who attend to the sick receive [the requisites]. Even the requisites placed far away, without having been given to others, belong to the Saṅgha in each respective case.
When something belongs to two persons and has not been divided, the other becomes the owner when one has passed away. This same principle applies even when many [persons] own it.
When all have died, it belongs to the Saṅgha. Even if, without dividing it, [it is intended for] the *saddhivihārika* and so forth...

The robe-cloth remains ungiven; however, if it is distributed, then it is well given. Even when they have died, it belongs only to the resident pupils (*saddhivihārika*) and others, not to the Saṅgha.

If a monk who has completed the rains retreat departs while the robe-cloth has not yet arisen or has arisen but not yet been distributed—and if he is insane, deranged, overwhelmed by pain, or suspended—then, provided there are suitable recipients, a share must be given. If...
But if he disrobes, or dies, or acknowledges himself to be a novice, or one who has renounced the training, or one who has committed an offense involving defeat,
or a paṇḍaka, or one living in communion by theft, or one who has gone over to another sect, or an animal, or a matricide,
or a patricide, or a murderer of an arahant, or a defiler of a bhikkhunī, or a schismatic, or one who has shed blood—
Or if one who claims to be a hermaphrodite is recognized as such, the Saṅgha is the owner; no share should be given.
If, before the robe-material has been distributed among the monks who have completed the rains residence, the Saṅgha splits—as happened with the Kosambī monks—there are two factions.
In that case, people offer the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*) and perfumes and other items to one side.

If they give [robes], giving robes to one [group] saying, "We give them to the Saṅgha," or wherever water was offered, or to whichever faction they give the robes saying, "We give them to the Saṅgha," those robes belong to the Saṅgha alone;
they accrue to both portions and, having struck the gong, must be distributed together by both factions. But if people...
In one fortnight they give the water for the offering and perfumes and so forth, and in the other fortnight they give robes, saying, "We give them for the fortnight.
Those robes belong to that very fortnight. For when it is given in this way, whatever portion received the water belongs to that water alone;
whatever received the robe belongs to that robe alone. In whichever place the water for the offering was given...
If it becomes a matter of equal measure, then since one side has received the water for the dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*), they receive robes;
and since the other side has received the robes themselves, both sides, having come together as one, should divide them according to seniority.
"This, it is said, is the rule regarding the foreign ocean," so it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. If the robes are [to be divided] in the very same side where the water was given...
If they say, "We shall give them during the fortnight," those robes must indeed be distributed within that very fortnight; the other fortnight is not one over which [the monks] have authority.
However, if the Saṅgha splits while the robes have arisen for the monks who have completed the rains residence but have not yet been distributed, they must be distributed equally among all.

If, while many bhikkhus are traveling along a highway, some bhikkhus enter a cemetery for the sake of rag-robe material while others depart without waiting, no portion need be given to those who departed without waiting against their will;
however, a portion must be given to those who waited, even if it was against their will. But if people say, "Let those who have come here take it," [then it should be given].
Or, having made a mark with their teeth, they go away, thinking, "Let those who arrive take it";
in that case, it belongs to all those who arrive. If they have gone after discarding [the mark], whoever takes it is the owner.
If some monks enter the charnel ground first and others later, there, those who entered first obtain the rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), not those who came later.

Those who enter later do not receive [a share]. Because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, not to give a share against the will of those who enter later,” a share must not be given against the will of those who enter later.
However, if all have entered at the same time, some receive and some do not. “I allow you, monks, for those who have entered simultaneously, even against their will...”
Because of the statement, "A portion must be given," a portion must be given even against one's will to those who have entered the charnel ground together.

However, if they enter the charnel ground after making an agreement outside, such as, "We shall take whatever rag-robes we find after dividing them among all," and some obtain them while others do not, [the Buddha said]:
"I allow you, monks, for those who have entered after making an agreement, even against their will..."
Even for those who have entered [the monastery] after making an agreement based on the words "to give a share," the share must be given even against their will.

This concludes, for now, the discussion on the distribution of robes (*cīvarabhājanīya*). 209. Regarding the distribution of alms-food (*piṇḍapātabhājana*), however: "Monks, I authorize a meal for the Saṅgha, a designated meal, and an invitation."

Regarding the distribution of meals such as *saṅghabhatta* (meals for the entire Sangha) and so forth, which have been thus authorized—namely, *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals), *pakkhika* (fortnightly meals), *uposathika* (Uposatha-day meals), and *pāṭipadika* (first-of-the-month meals)—this is the analysis:
"Meal for the entire Sangha" (*saṅghabhatta*) means a meal that must be given to the whole Sangha. Therefore, there is no fixed order of seniority (*ṭhitikā*) regarding a meal for the entire Sangha;
and for that very reason, [one may say]: "Today we have been eating for ten or twelve days; now, from elsewhere..."
One should not say there, "Bring the bhikkhus," nor is it even permitted to say, "We did not receive [it] on previous days;
now please take it for us. For that [food] reaches those who arrive one after another.
However, this is the procedure regarding *uddesabhatta* (food designated for a specific group) and so forth: when a king or a royal minister has designated [food] from the Saṅgha...
When it is announced, "Bring so many bhikkhus," the time should be proclaimed and the standing line should be asked about.
If there are [seats], distribution should begin from that point; if not, it should begin from the seat of the elders. The reciter must not let even the alms-collecting bhikkhus pass by;
however, those who observe the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) will pass by of their own accord. While being distributed in this manner—
When great elders of the Alasanda clan arrive later, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, the distribution for those of twenty years' standing is being taken;
your turn has passed. Rather, having set aside their turn, one should distribute to them first, and afterwards distribute according to the [regular] order of seniority.
Having heard that "much *uddesabhatta* (meal by assignment) has arisen in such-and-such a monastery," even from a monastery a league away...
When monks arrive, the portion should be assigned starting from the place where each person has stood upon arrival.
Even for those who have not yet arrived, if they have entered the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) and their students or others are receiving portions, it must indeed be assigned.

If they say, "Assign portions to those standing outside the boundary of the precinct," it should not be assigned. However, if [the area] is connected as one unit with those who have entered the boundary of the precinct...

Having been offered, it comes to be either at the door of one’s own monastery or within the monastery itself; this is called a boundary that has increased by way of overflow, and therefore it must be distributed.
Even if it was given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, it must still be distributed to those who arrive later.

However, regarding the second portion, once the seat of the Elder has been ascended, the first portion does not reach those who arrive again; from the second portion, it must be distributed according to seniority (*vassagga*).
In a single monastery, having demarcated one place for the assignment of meals (*bhattuddesa*),
the designated meal (*uddesabhatta*) announced anywhere within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), even if it measures a *gāvuta*, must be received at that very place where the meal was assigned.
If one person sends word to another monk, saying, "Tomorrow, having been assigned from the Saṅgha, send ten monks," by him—
That matter must be announced to the meal-designator. If he forgets on that day, it must be announced early in the morning on the second day.

If, having forgotten, he remembers while entering for alms-food before he has crossed the boundary of the precinct, it should be assigned according to the usual standing position in the dining hall. Even if [he remembers] within the boundary of the precinct...
When [the boundary] has been crossed and the monks are in a continuous line with those standing within the precinct boundary (upacārasīma),
they should be included according to their natural position, provided they do not separate from one another by more than twelve cubits. However, if there is no such continuous line among the monks,
they should be included by establishing a new position at whatever spot outside the precinct boundary they remember [the boundary].
If one remembers [the meal] while in the village, one must have it announced at the sitting hall.
Wherever one remembers, one must certainly have it announced; it is not permissible not to announce it. For this is not available on the following day.
If, seeing monks going from their own monastery to another monastery, someone has them announce a meal for recitation (*uddesabhatta*), [one should accept it].

As long as [the monks] are within the precincts, or are connected as one unit with those standing at the boundary of the precincts according to the method already stated, they should be included by virtue of their residence in their own monastery.
However, for those standing outside the precincts, when it is said, "Venerable sirs, designate so many monks from the Saṅgha," they should be included as each person arrives. In that regard:
It should be understood that even those standing at a distance are considered "arrived" provided they do not exceed a distance of twelve *hattha*s and remain connected as a single group.
If they announce their arrival upon entering the monastery where they are going, it should be accepted according to the status of that monastery.
Furthermore, if they see monks at a village gate, on a street, at a crossroads, or within a house...
If someone announces it by means of a formal designation for the Saṅgha (saṅghuddesa), it should be given to those who have entered within the precincts at each respective location.

Furthermore, the "house precinct" (gharūpacāra) here should be understood according to these four types: a single house with a single precinct; a single house with multiple precincts; multiple houses with a single precinct;
and multiple houses with multiple precincts. Among these, that which is the house of a single family with a single access point...
That which exists within the boundary of the *suppapātapaṭicchanna* (the area where one can throw a porridge bowl) is called a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*).

The portion of the recitation (*uddesalābha*) obtained there reaches all those who stand even within a single precinct according to the practice of wandering for alms. This is what is meant by a single house with a single precinct.
However, as for a single house where a wall has been erected between two wives for the sake of their comfortable living—
When various doors have been constructed, the portion of food obtained there does not reach one who is separated by a wall;
it reaches only those sitting in their respective places. This is called "a single house with different precincts.
However, in a case where many monks are invited to a house, and starting from within the house, they are made into a continuous line including even the neighboring houses—
Having filled [the space], they cause them to sit; whatever portion of the recitation (*uddesa*) arises there reaches everyone.
Even in the case of a residence belonging to various families where, without a wall in the middle, they move about through a single door, the same principle applies.
This is what is called "various houses with a single common area" (*nānāghara-ekūpacāra*). However, as for the portion of the recitation obtained by monks sitting in separate residences...
It arises; even though the monks are seen through a gap in the wall, it reaches them only when they are seated in their respective dwellings.
This is what is called "different houses" and "different precincts.
However, if one receives a meal for recitation at any one of the places such as the village gate, the street, or the crossroads, and [then goes] elsewhere...

If there is no other monk, having caused it to reach oneself, and if on the following day one obtains another portion at that same place, one should give it to whichever other monk one sees, whether junior or senior.
If there is no one at all, one should eat it after having caused it to reach oneself. If, while sitting in the assembly hall, they are waiting for the time [of the meal]...

If anyone comes among the bhikkhus and says, “Give me a bowl designated for the Saṅgha,” or “Give me a designated bowl,” or “Give me a bowl designated from the Saṅgha,” or “Give me a bowl belonging to the Saṅgha,” then a designated bowl should be given after it has been drawn by lot. [Likewise,
if they say,] “Give me a bhikkhu designated for the Saṅgha,” or “Give me a bhikkhu designated from the Saṅgha,” or “Give me a bhikkhu belonging to the Saṅgha...”
The same procedure applies even when it is said, "Give a bhikkhu.

Furthermore, the reciter (uddesaka) here should be one who is pleasant, modest, and wise; having asked three times for a person standing by (ṭhitika), if there is no one who knows such a person, he should take [the bowl] from the seat of the elders. But if [he thinks], "I know [such a person],"...
If someone says, "I have received it for ten years," one should ask, "Friend, are there other bhikkhus with ten years' seniority?
If, upon hearing him, many come forward saying, "We have ten years, we have ten years," they should not go about saying, "It belongs to you, it belongs to you.
Instead, one should say, "All of you be quiet," and have them stand in order.
Setting those aside, the lay follower should be asked, "How many monks do you require? When he replies, "So many, venerable sir," one should not say, "It falls to you;
it falls to you. Instead, the seniority, the season, the time of day, and the shadow must be inquired about for every single junior monk.
If, even while the shadow is being inquired about, another elder arrives, [the procedure must be repeated].
It should be given to him. However, if one asks about the shadow and, when it is said, "It falls to you," an elder arrives, he does not receive it.
For even if one has been sitting for a long time or sleeping due to a lengthy conversation, what has been taken is well-taken, and what has passed over is well-passed-over.
This is because such goods to be distributed go only to those who are present; in this matter, being present is the decisive factor.
It is to be delimited by the precinct (upacāra). The interior enclosure of the assembly hall (*āsanasālā*) constitutes the precinct; for one standing within it, the distribution of alms is obtained.
Suppose someone has eight bowls brought from the assembly hall—seven filled with choice foods and one filled with water—and sends them back to the assembly hall;
those who have taken them and returned, without saying anything, [place them] in the hands of the monks.
Having established [the distribution], they depart; whatever is obtained by whom, that belongs to him alone.
However, for one who has received water, even if he has passed the time limit, another designated meal (*uddesabhatta*) must be set aside for him;
whether he receives coarse food or fine food, or even the requisites for the three robes, that belongs to him alone. For such is his particular merit.
However, because water is not considered "food-stuff" (*āmisa*), one receives a separate designated meal (*uddesabhatta*).
But if those who have brought it arrive and say, "Venerable sir, please divide all of this and eat," then after everyone has divided and eaten it, the water should be drunk. [One should say:
"Having designated it from the Saṅgha, give eight portions to the eight Great Elders; to the middle-ranking..."

If someone says, "Give it to the newcomers! Give it to the novices! Give it to the novices who have completed their years of training! Give it to the middle reciters and so forth! Give it to my kinsmen-monks!
one should say, "Lay follower, you speak thus, but according to the established order (*ṭhitikā*), it does not reach them," and it must be given strictly according to that established order.
However, in the case of meals for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) provided by young novices...
If, when the alms have been obtained, there is a festive occasion in the donors' house, one should say: "Please send [some] for your teachers and preceptors.

However, in the case of a meal provided for recitation where the first portion falls to the novices and the subsequent portion to the great elders, the novices do not get to go ahead simply because they received the first portion; rather, they must follow the established order of seniority.

It should be distributed in this manner. When it is said, "Having designated [the portion] from the Saṅgha, you come," one should distribute it according to the established order (*ṭhitikā*), saying, "You will know for me on another occasion; however, the order proceeds in this way.

Then, having said, "Give the bowl designated by the Saṅgha," if someone takes the bowl of anyone at all—even before the bowls have been formally received—and fills it and brings it back, even that which has been brought back...
It should be understood precisely according to the established rule.
Suppose one person, sent with the instruction, "Bring a bowl for the community's designated meal," says, "Venerable sir, give me a bowl; I shall bring the meal from the invitation.
If the other, knowing that "this man has come from the house where the designated meal is kept," [says], "But surely, monks—"

When asked, "Have you come from such-and-such a house? and he replies, "Yes, Venerable Sir, it is not an invitation-meal (nimantana-bhatta), but a designated meal (uddesa-bhatta)," it should be accepted on the spot.
However, when told, "Bring one bowl," and he asks, "Saying what should I bring it?
and upon being told, "As you please," he comes; this person is called a messenger who has been sent off (*vissaṭṭha-dūta*). [This refers to] the designated bowl (*uddesa-patta*).
Whether it be the bowl in the regular sequence or a personal bowl, whichever he desires should be given to him.
A single fool who is incompetent, being sent with the instruction, "Bring the bowl for the recitation," does not know how to speak and remains silent;
he should not be asked, "Whose presence have you come to? or "Whose bowl will you carry? For if he were addressed in such a way, it would be tantamount to asking a question.
He might say, “I have come into your presence,” or “I will take your bowl.
Then, other monks, feeling disgust, would not look at that monk; instead, they should say to him, “Where are you going? What are you wandering about doing?
When he replies, “I have come for the sake of the bowl for recitation,” they should give him the bowl after having it handed over.
There is one called a "peak-assignment" (*kūṭaṭṭhitikā*). In the house of a king or a royal minister, eight very choice meals are regularly provided;
these, having been made into individual portions, are consumed by the monks according to their separate assignments.
Some monks, observing their own assignment and thinking, "They will reach us tomorrow," departed.
While those [monks] were still future, other visiting monks arrived and sat down in the assembly hall.
At that very moment, royal messengers arrived and said, "Give us bowls of fine rice. The visiting monks, not knowing the established rule (*ṭhitika*), accepted them;
at that very same moment, other monks who knew the rule arrived and asked, "Why are you taking these?"
"Exquisite food at the royal palace. "From how many years [of seniority] onwards? "From such-and-such a number of years.
Having stopped them with the words, "Do not take it," they should be made to take it while standing.

When it has been taken, those who arrive—whether at the time of arrival, at the time when the bowls are being distributed, at the time of distribution, or at the time when the bowls have been filled and brought back from the royal palace—the King says, "Today let only the bhikkhus come."
Having sent [food], she gives alms-food directly into the hands of the monks themselves.

When they have taken the alms-food thus given and returned, those monks who are aware of the standing order must stop them from eating by saying, "Do not eat," and it should be distributed only according to that standing order.
Then, if the king feeds them and gives them their bowls filled with food, whatever has been brought should be distributed according to the standing order.
However, if only a small amount has been placed in the bowls so that they do not go away empty-handed, that should not be made subject to forfeiture.
"If they come back with empty bowls after eating, what they have eaten becomes their liability," said the Elder Mahāsumma.
But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "There is no requirement for forfeiture here."
"However, those who do not know the duration [of the meal] should remain seated until those who do know it arrive.
Even so, the food eaten by the monks has been well-eaten; now it should be distributed according to the place where the bowls are kept.
One bowl, worth one hundred coins and accompanied by a set of three robes, was the alms-bowl of a monk who had never used one before, and in the monastery...
They wrote, "Alms-food of this kind was obtained by one who had lived for sixty years," and set it aside.

Then, after the passing of sixty years, another such alms-food arose. [The question was: "Should this be assigned to the one who has lived for sixty years, or to the one who has lived for seventy years?
It was said: "To the one who has lived for seventy years. For this monk grew up having already taken up the standing of a bhikkhu. One.
Having eaten the *uddesabhatta* (designated meal), he becomes a *sāmaṇera*; he may then take back the bowl for that meal according to his status as a *sāmaṇera*.

This, it is said, is called the "one who stands in between. However, if a *sāmaṇera* who has completed his full year of training, thinking "I shall receive the *uddesabhatta* tomorrow," receives the higher ordination (*upasampadā*) this very day, his period of standing [in that status] has passed. For one person...
If a monk has received a meal for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) in his bowl, and that bowl is not empty, he causes it to be given to another person sitting nearby;

if they take it away with intent to steal, he is liable for the offense. However, if that monk gives it himself, saying, "Give my bowl," he is not liable. Furthermore, if he has no need for that food and says, "Enough..."
If one says something else, such as, "This food is for me; give it to me, having sent the bowl," whatever is brought from there belongs entirely to the owner of the bowl.
If the bowl is stolen, it is well-secured; because the food has already been given away, there is no liability for its loss.
In a certain monastery there were ten bhikkhus; among them, nine were alms-food eaters (piṇḍapātika) and one was an acceptor of invitations.
When it was said, "Give ten portions in the alms-bowl," the alms-food eaters did not wish to take [the food].

The other bhikkhu took it all, thinking, "It all comes to me," and thus the established order was not maintained. If he takes it after assigning one portion to each, the established order is maintained. Having taken it in this manner...
Having had food brought in ten bowls, he says, "Venerable sirs, please accept my hospitality," and gives nine bowls to the alms-collecting monks;

this is known as "that which is given by a monk," and it is permissible for them to accept it. If that lay follower says, "Venerable sir, you must come to my house," and that monk says to those monks, "Come, venerable sirs, be my companions," [and leads them] to his house...
He goes [to the house], and whatever he receives there, all that belongs to him alone; the others receive what has been given by him.

Then, having had them sit right in their own house and having offered the water of hospitality (*dakṣiṇodaka*), they give rice gruel, solid food, and so forth, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept whatever people give.
It is permissible for the others solely by virtue of that monk's word. After they have finished eating...
If they fill their bowls, take them, and give them to him for the purpose of going, all that belongs to that monk alone; what is given by him is permissible for the others.

However, if those people go to the monastery itself because that monk has said to them, "Venerable sirs, please accept my almsfood; it is permissible to comply with the request of these people," then whatever they eat there [belongs to them].

Whatever they bring out and carry away, all that belongs to them alone. Furthermore, even if they have not been told, "Accept my alms," but go thinking, "It is proper to do what people say," and there,
upon hearing one person offering a blessing with a sweet voice and becoming confident in the tranquility of the elders, [one gives] much requisites for ascetics...
Dutiya: "Venerable sirs, this is called 'unassigned' (akatabhāga) because it arose through faith in the elders; therefore, it belongs to everyone.
One person, having had it assigned from the Saṅgha, takes the bowl received by way of distribution, fills it with excellent hard and soft foods, brings it back, and gives it, saying:
'Venerable sir, let the entire Saṅgha consume this. Then all divide it."
It should be consumed. However, for the owner of the bowl, even if the period has elapsed, other designated food (uddesabhatta) should be set aside, excluding the *ṭhitika*.
Now, if someone says right from the beginning, "Give all the bowls belonging to the Saṅgha," a bowl belonging to a single modest monk should be given.
Once it has been brought back and the words "Let the entire Saṅgha consume it" are spoken, it should be distributed and then consumed.
If one person brings food in a bowl and says, "I give this for the Saṅgha," it should be given by standing and making it sufficient for one person, without giving each individual a mouthful.

Then, if he remains silent after bringing the food, not knowing what to say, one should not ask, "For whom was this brought? To whom do you wish to give it? This is because such questioning would be inappropriate.

For if one were to say, "This has been brought for you; I wish to give it to you," then other monks, feeling disgust toward that monk, would not even think to look at him by turning their necks. But if, when asked, "Where are you going?
What are you wandering about doing? he replies, "I have come after receiving alms-food for recitation (uddesabhatta)," then [he may be accepted] by a single modest monk.
It should be distributed by means of a standing order (*ṭhitikā*). If what has been brought is so much that it suffices for everyone, there is no need for a standing order;
the bowls should be filled and given out starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*).
When it is said, "Give the bowl designated for the Saṅgha," one should distribute it according to the established standing order, without asking, "What will you bring?"
However, for milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) or a meal of savory juices (*rasapiṇḍapāta*) that are obtained regularly, a separate fixed price (*ṭhitikā*) should be set for such superior foods;
likewise for rice-gruel (*yāgu*) with its accompaniments, expensive fruits, and choice snacks (*khajjaka*).
A single fixed price should be set for ordinary rice, gruel, fruits, and snacks. When it is said, "I shall bring ghee (*sappi*),"...

For all types of ghee, only one portion is permitted; likewise for all oils. When it is said, "I shall bring honey," however, only one portion of honey is permitted, as well as for molasses and medicinal substances such as *laṭṭhi-madhuka* and so forth.
But if they offer scents and garlands for the sake of the Saṅgha, is it permissible or not for a forest-dweller (*piṇḍapātika*)? [It is] only for food.
Because it has been refused, it is permissible. However, they say that because it was given specifically for the Sangha, it should not be accepted.
The discussion on designated food (*uddesabhatta*) is finished. 210.
If the invitation is for an individual, he himself is the master. But if it is for the Sangha, it is according to the method already stated regarding designated food.

It should be accepted. However, if the messenger here is competent and, instead of saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept a meal for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the king’s residence," says, "Please accept almsfood," it is permissible even for those who subsist on almsfood.
But if the messenger is incompetent and says, "Accept a meal," and the distributor of meals is competent and, instead of saying "a meal," says, "Venerable sirs..."
If he says, "Give this to you, give that to you," it is permissible even for those who live on alms-food;
however, when it is said, "Venerable sir, the meal reaches you in turn," it is not permissible.
If the person who has come to invite [the monks] enters the dining hall and says, "Give eight bhikkhus" or "Give eight bowls," [it is permissible].
In this way, it is also permissible for alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*); they should say, "Go, you and you.
If someone says, "Give eight monks [alms]; take the food," or "Give eight bowls; take the food," it should be distributed in order.
However, while distributing, one who does not break the flow by saying "food" [at every step]—[you]...
When it is said, "And you may go as well," it is permissible for those who live on alms-food. However, when it is said, "Venerable sir, give us your bowl;
come, you too," one should go, saying, "Very well, lay follower. Even when it is said, "Come from the Saṅgha's portion;
you may go," it should be accepted according to one's standing.

Furthermore, when someone comes from the house where he was invited for a meal to receive alms, the bowl should be given to him while standing, according to the same method described for the *uddesabhatta* (meal by assignment). If one person,
instead of saying "the bowl in order from the Saṅgha," simply says "give me a bowl," and before the bowls have been taken,
takes the bowl of anyone at all, fills it, and brings it back, it belongs only to the owner of that bowl.

It is so. Just as with a meal provided by enumeration (*uddesabhatta*), one must not insist on a fixed order of seating. Here too, if someone comes and stands in silence, he should not be asked, "Whose presence have you come to? or "Whose bowl will you carry?
For, in accordance with the nature of the inquiry, he would say, "I have come to yours; I shall carry your bowl. Then that bhikkhu...
He would be an object of loathing for the monks. However, when asked, "Where are you going?
What are you wandering about doing?", if he replies, "I have come for his bowl," the bowl should be taken from the line where the alms-food is being distributed and given to him.
Even if he says, "Give me the bowl for carrying food," it should still be given from that same line where the alms-food is being distributed.
If, having brought it, one says, "Let the entire Saṅgha eat," it should be eaten after it has been divided.
For the owner of the bowl, setting aside even that portion which exceeds the limit, another meal in the regular sequence should be assigned.
If one person brings rice in a bowl and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha," starting from the portion of rice sufficient for a mouthful...
It should be divided by means of mouthfuls. However, if he remains silent, one should not ask, "For whom was it brought for you?
To whom do you wish to give it? But if, when asked, "Where are you going? What are you wandering about doing?
he replies, "I have brought food for the Saṅgha" or "I have brought food for the elders," then [having taken it], one should divide it.

It should be distributed by means of a standing distribution of mouthfuls of food. However, if the food brought in this manner is so abundant that it suffices for the entire Saṅgha, it is called "food brought as alms" (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*);
it is permissible even for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*), and there is no need to ask for a standing distribution.
Starting from the seat of the Elder, one should give after filling the bowl.
If a lay follower sends [a message] to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, or to one renowned for his mastery of the scriptures and ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or to the meal-designator, saying,
"Please come taking eight bhikkhus with you for the purpose of receiving our meal"—
even if this has been sent by relatives or attendants— these three persons do not obtain permission to ask; the rule has already been established.
Having had eight bhikkhus designated from the Saṅgha, one should go with oneself as the ninth. Why?

Because it is by depending on these bhikkhus that gain arises for the bhikkhu-saṅgha. However, a resident bhikkhu who is not well-known for his mastery of the texts or his ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) may obtain permission to depart;
therefore, he should ask: "Shall I take [bhikkhus] from the Saṅgha, or those whom I know?"
Having made the announcement, "I am coming," one should act according to what the donors say.
However, when it is said, "Go taking with you those who depend on you or those whom you know," one may go together with whoever wishes to go.
If they send word saying, "Send eight bhikkhus," they must be sent from the Saṅgha itself. [If] by oneself...
If it is possible to obtain almsfood in another village, one should go to that other village.
If it is not possible to obtain it, one should enter that very village for alms.
When invited monks are seated in the dining hall, if people come there saying, "Give us [alms] in bowls," [one should give].
Food should not be given to those who have been invited; it should be said, "These monks have already been invited. However, if they say, "You may also give," then it is permissible to give.

During festivals and similar occasions, people themselves go to the monastic courtyards (*pariveṇa*) and meditation halls (*padhānaghara*), and invite [the Sangha] along with the masters of the Three Piṭakas and the Dharma-preachers, even if there are hundreds of monks; at such times, those who know [this situation]...
It is appropriate to take them and go. Why? Because people who need the Great Saṅgha of Bhikkhus do not go to the individual cells or the meditation huts;
rather, they go from the assembly hall itself, taking as many bhikkhus as their means and strength permit.
However, if it is the Elder of the Saṅgha, or one renowned for his mastery of the scriptures or the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or the distributor of meals, [they may be taken] elsewhere...
Or, having spent the rains retreat or having gone elsewhere, he returns again to his own place;
and since people offer hospitality to a visitor, he should go taking with him those who knew him on that one previous occasion.
From the time he becomes bound [to the community], when the second period begins, he must go taking only the Saṅgha. Being a brand-new visitor, [thinking] "relatives..."
If they go thinking, “I will see [my] relatives or attendants,” and if their relatives and attendants there pay them honor,
it is permissible for those who know [the situation] to take [them] and go. However, one who receives excessive gains,
for whom his own place and a guest’s place are exactly the same, [should go only] where people have prepared a meal for the Saṅgha.
They sit down; therefore, one must go taking only the *saṅghabhatta*. This is the distinction regarding an invitation (*nimantana*).

The remainder of the entire question should be understood according to the method already stated for the *uddesabhatta*. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is said: "When it is said, 'Give eight great elders,' only eight great elders are to be given.
This same principle applies to the middling [elders] and so forth. But if, without making such a distinction...
“If one says, ‘Give eight bhikkhus,’ it should be given from the Saṅgha.
The Discussion on Invited Meals is finished. 211.
However, regarding meals by ticket, [the Buddha said]: “I allow you, monks, to fasten [tickets] with a tally-stick or a strip of cloth...”

According to the statement, "having piled them up, one should designate the meal," one should attach characters such as "the ticket-meal of so-and-so" using either a ticket made of heartwood or a slip made of bamboo,
cane, palm leaf, or similar materials; then, having placed them in a basket or on the edge of a robe,
and having piled all the tickets together, one should mix them repeatedly by turning them upside down and right side up.
The distributor of meals endowed with the five factors should distribute the voting sticks (*salākā*) starting from the standing place if there is one;

if not, starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*). For those who arrive later, they should be given in a continuous sequence, and even for those standing far away, they should be given according to the same method prescribed for the designated meal (*uddesabhatta*).
If there are many alms-villages surrounding the monastery but not many monks, the voting tickets (*salākā*) are distributed according to the villages.
One should distribute them by way of the villages, saying: "The ticket-food (*salākabhatta*) for you falls due in such-and-such a village.
When distributing in this manner, even if there are various kinds of sixty types of ticket-food in each individual village, all [of them]— [...should be assigned accordingly.]
They are indeed taken [by him]. Near the village where he has received his bowl, there may be two or three *salākā*-tickets for meals;
these must be given to him alone. For it is not possible to send another monk on account of those tickets.
If, having observed many *salākā*-tickets in certain villages, [one intends to provide] for seven or eight monks...
They should be given. When giving them, however, one should tie together slips for four or five meals and give them as a single unit.

If there is another village beyond that village, and if there is only one meal-slip (*salākabhatta*) for that [second] village, but they give it in the morning, then having assigned that to one of these monks by means of a formal act (*niggaha*), [one should say]: "Having taken that in the morning, afterwards..."

He should be told, "Take the other meals in the last village. If he goes with the perception that they have already been taken when the *salākā*-meals in the last village have not yet been received, he must take the *salākā*-meal in the next village, return again to the monastery, take the others, and then go to the last village.
For it is not permitted to receive the Saṅgha’s alms-food outside the boundary.

This method is stated in the *Kurundi*. However, if there are many monks and the voting sticks (*salākā*) do not suffice on a village-by-village basis, they should be distributed according to street, or by a single house on a street, or by a single family.
And among the streets and so forth, wherever there are many meals, there the food for many monks should be distributed according to the same method prescribed for the villages.
If voting sticks are not available, they may be distributed even by merely pointing them out.
Furthermore, the distributor of the sticks must know the proper procedure.
He should rise early, take his bowl and robe, go to the dining hall, sweep the unswept areas, and prepare the drinking water and water for washing.
Having had [the meal] prepared, and observing the time, thinking, "Now the duties will be performed by the monks," he should strike the bell.
When the monks have assembled, the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) for the village of rest must first be distributed.
He should say, "The ticket for you falls to such-and-such a village of rest; go there. If...
If there is a village one *gāvuta* away, those traveling there on that day will become exhausted; thinking, "Tomorrow you will reach your own village," [the meal] must be sent today.
If someone who has been sent to the village does not go, but seeks another voting-ticket (*salāka*), it should not be given.
For if it were, there would be a loss of merit for the faithful people and a cutting off of gains for the Saṅgha; therefore—
On the second and third days as well, no other voting ticket (salākā) should be given to him; he should be told, "Go to your own place and eat.
However, if he does not come for three days, the voting ticket should be cast for him in the village on the near side of the river from the village on the far side.
If he still does not accept it, from that point onward it is not permitted to give him another voting ticket.
The disciplinary task (daṇḍakamma) must be performed rigorously; it must not be reduced from sixty or fifty [days].
Having assigned the turn for the village, the turn for the monastery (vihāravāra) should be assigned, and it should be said: "Your turn for the monastery has come.
Two or three rice-sticks (yāgusalākā) and three or four food-sticks (bhattasalākā) should be given to the monastery steward (vihāravārika), having established a fixed routine.
It should not be given [to them]. For those who provide rice gruel and meals might become resentful, thinking, "The monastery guardians are eating our rice gruel and meals.
Therefore, it should be given to other families.
If the monastery attendants (*vihāravārika*) bring it and give it because they are on friendly terms [with the recipients], that is well. If not, one should take turns.
They should have rice gruel and alms-food brought for them; for as long as they are merely performing the distribution of voting sticks (*salākā*), this is their duty.
However, at the place where the *vassaga* (seniority) is reached, they are indeed permitted to take other voting sticks for superior food as well.

Separate voting sticks should be given for extra-allowance food (*atirekauttaribhaṅga*) and for food intended for those traveling alone (*ekacārikabhatta*). If [the food] has been obtained by means of a voting stick...
If he does not receive that meal on that day, it must be sought again on the following day.
If he receives only the meal and no further food (uttaribhaṅga), it must likewise be sought again. The same rule applies to a ticket for milk-rice.
However, if he receives only milk and no rice, then starting from the time he receives the milk, it need not be sought again. Two.

Three meals for solitary wanderers accrue to one person alone; during a time of famine, when they are obtained by a junior member of the Saṅgha, they should be distributed separately after being disentangled.
Even for one who has not received the regular ticket-meal, it should be distributed on the following day.
If the monastery is small and all the bhikkhus share in common, then when distributing sugarcane tickets, for whichever—
It is permissible to give [the food] after serving it to whoever is present, such as the great elders (mahāthera) and others, having sliced it during the day.
After serving the ladle of broth, even after the meal, one may strain it or have it made into molasses (phāṇita) and give it to those who live on alms-food (piṇḍapātika) and others;
once it is known whether newcomers have arrived or not, they should be included in the distribution. In a large monastery, it should be distributed by establishing a standing committee (ṭhitika).
It is permissible to bring even *takkasālaka* (a type of medicinal plant) to a common distribution point, smoke it, or cook it, and then give it to the elders.
One should proceed according to the method described for the *mahā-āvāsa*. Voting sticks (*salāka*) for fruits, cakes, medicines, perfumes, and garlands should also be distributed separately.
Furthermore, although voting sticks for medicines and the like are permitted even for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*), [they must still be distributed separately].
However, because it is distributed by means of voting sticks (*salāka*), it should not be accepted [as a personal favor].

When they give a *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) of the measure of a single portion, one should distribute it after asking for the seniority list (*ṭhitika*). If the seniority list is not available, it should be distributed starting from the seat of the Elder (*therāsana*).
If there are many such meals, two or three should be given to each monk; if not, [one each].
Having given one portion each, they proceed in order; then it should be given again starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*).
If it is interrupted in the middle, the sequence must be noted. However, if such food is regularly provided, whoever it reaches should be told:
"Whether you have received it or not, you should take it tomorrow as well. One [type of meal] is not fixed.
On the day it is obtained, however, one receives as much as needed. Days when it is not obtained are more numerous;
if it reaches someone who has not received it, he should be told, "You may take it tomorrow.
If someone arrives after the voting sticks (*salākā*) have already been distributed, the sticks that have already passed him by must not be set out again for him to receive.
Regarding the "lot" (salāka): starting from the moment the bell is struck, one receives it while still extending the hand as the person approaches;

even if another has already arrived and is standing nearby, [the lot] is considered "passed over" for that person. However, if there is someone else taking [the lot] on his behalf, he receives it even if he himself does not come;
having learned in the assembly hall that "so-and-so has not come," [one assigns it thinking], "this is for him."
It is permissible to set aside [the portion] as "salākā" (voting sticks). If they make an agreement that "it should not be given to one who has not arrived," it is unrighteous (*adhammika*).
For the shareable goods belong to one who stands within the precincts (*upacāra*).
However, if they raise a loud cry saying, "Give to those who have not arrived," a disciplinary measure (*daṇḍakamma*) must be imposed, and they should be told, "Come and take it. Six.

If the five voting sticks have been lost and the distributor of meals does not remember the names of the donors, he may, having obtained the lost sticks from either the senior elder or himself, tell the monks: "I have assigned meal-tickets for such-and-such a village;
you may eat the meal-tickets you receive there. This is permissible, provided they were not assigned at the monastery itself.
However, it is not permissible to receive that meal in the dining hall, bring it right there, and eat it.
If one says, "From today onwards, please accept my ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*)," it is not permissible to distribute it there in the dining hall;
it must be brought to the monastery and distributed. But if one says, "Starting from tomorrow," then it should be announced to the meal-designator (*bhattuddesaka*).
“From this day forward, such-and-such a family gives *salākabhatta* (ticket-food);

you should remember this at the time of drawing the tickets. During a famine, they suspend the *salākabhatta*, but when a time of plenty arises, seeing some bhikkhu, they reinstate it, saying, “From today onward, accept our *salākabhatta*,” and having brought [the food] from within the village to the monastery—
It should be distributed. For this so-called *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) is not like *uddesabhatta* (food by assignment);

it is given specifically for the monastery, and therefore it is not permitted to distribute it outside the precincts. However, when it is said, "Starting from tomorrow," it must indeed be distributed within the monastery.
If a monk who intends to travel has received a ticket for another village in the direction he wishes to go, [he may take it there].
Having taken that [ticket], it is permissible for him to say to another monk, "Please take my bowl-ticket," and then depart.
However, he must give him the ticket while the latter has not yet crossed the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīma).

When people, having stayed in an abandoned monastery, establish "ticket-food" (salākabhatta) with the thought, "Let them enjoy it after they have tended the Bodhi-tree shrine and other sites," [the procedure is as follows].
It is permissible for monks who have stayed in common quarters to go there early, perform the duties (*vatta*), and eat that meal. If,
after those [resident monks] have gone having secured their own portions for the following day,
a visiting monk stays in an abandoned monastery, performs the duties early, strikes the bell, secures his own portion of the ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*), and [goes to] the dining hall...

He who goes [to receive alms] is the master of that meal. However, if one who is in the midst of monks performing their duties gives two or three strokes with the broom on the ground, strikes the bell, and then departs thinking, "The *salākabhatta* from the village ahead has reached me," it does not reach him because he took it by stealth;
rather, it reaches him only after he has performed his duties and delivered it.
It belongs only to the monks who have arrived later.
If there is a village that is too far away and the monks do not wish to go there constantly,
and the people say, "We would be excluded from merit," then those monks who are of like status in a monastery near that village should be told:
“On the coming day, you should eat with these monks,” [one should say]. However, the voting sticks (*salākā*) must be presented every day.
Furthermore, they are not considered properly presented merely by the striking of a bell or the mere shaking of the basket;
rather, having taken up the basket, the voting sticks must be poured onto a stool, but the basket itself must not be held by its rim. If...

For there might be a snake or a scorpion there, which would cause pain; therefore, having taken it down and turned the basket away from oneself, the sticks should be scattered with the thought, "Even if it be a snake, it will flee from this very spot.
Having thus scattered the sticks, one should draw lots according to the previously mentioned method by way of village and so forth.
Furthermore, having given one portion to a senior elder and thinking, "The remainder shall fall to me," he takes his own portion, performs the customary duties, and worships the Cetiya.

When the monks standing in the Vitakkamaḷaka (the Hall of Reflection) say, "Friends, the voting tickets have been distributed," he should reply, "Yes, venerable sirs; you may take the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) in whichever village you go. For it is thus:

Even those who have committed minor offenses become very grave offenders. When monks go to another monastery all night long for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, they do not take voting tickets, thinking, "We will return after wandering for alms in our own alms-resort village without having received any gifts there.
Yet, they arrive at the monastery to eat the ticket-food from the Elder's bowl.
It is permissible. Then, the Mahāthera also thinks, "What am I doing here? and goes along with them.
When they have arrived at the village for alms-food without having eaten in the monastery where they stayed, and say, "Give us the bowls, venerable sir;
we shall bring the *salākayāgu* (rice-gruel with sticks) and so forth," the bowls must not be given. Why not, venerable sir? Because it is the meal intended for those staying in the monastery.
[If someone says,] "The one staying in this monastery has reached the end of his term; we have stayed in another monastery," [it is not permissible].
However, when it is said, "Venerable sir, give [us food]; we do not give from the monastery storehouse, we give to you; please accept our alms-food," it is permissible.
The discussion on tickets for meals is finished.

213. Regarding the *pakkhika* (fortnightly) and other types of food: that which is given for the purpose of providing mindfulness so that those intent on wholesome deeds may observe the Uposatha on these specially marked days—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the fifth, and the eighth of the fortnight—is called *pakkhika*.
It follows the same procedure as *salākabhatta* (ticket-food); it must be distributed and then consumed. If both *salākabhatta* and *pakkhikabhatta* [are available]...
It passes through many, piercing through all; even two meals must be distributed separately.
If the community of monks is large, having first distributed the fortnightly meal, one should distribute the ticket-meal according to its sequence;
or, having had the ticket-meal distributed, one should distribute the fortnightly meal according to its sequence. Those to whom it does not reach should [seek] alms.

They will go about for alms. If there are two meals and many [invitations], and the bhikkhus are slow [to respond], and a *salākabhatta* (ticket-meal) is obtained daily, then setting that aside, one should give only the fortnightly meal, saying, "Friends, eat the fortnightly meal.
If they give a choice fortnightly meal, a separate standing place (*ṭhitikā*) must be made; [one should not say] "Tomorrow is the fortnight," and thus omit the fortnightly meal today.
It should be accepted. However, if the donors say, "Tomorrow there will also be coarse food in our house;
designate today’s meal as the fortnightly meal," then it is permissible.
What is called "Uposathika" is that which one has undertaken oneself on the Uposatha day of the half-month after having observed the Uposatha precepts.
He eats it, and that very same thing is given. Regarding the "first-day-of-the-month gift" (*pāṭipadika*): on the Uposatha day, many faithful and devoted people offer hospitality to the monks;
however, on the first day of the month, the monks are weary. A gift given on the first day of the month is like a gift given during a famine—it is of great fruit.
Or, a gift given on the second day to those whose virtue is purified by the Uposatha observance is of great fruit.
Having observed, “It happens,” [he gives] the alms-food being offered on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*). That too belongs to the same category as the *salāka-bhatta* (ticket-food).
Thus, these seven types of meals are not permissible for those who practice the alms-round (*piṇḍapātika*); they indeed constitute a breach of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*). 214.
Furthermore, there are others given after Visākhā requested a boon in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*: the meal for newcomers (*āgantuka-bhatta*) and the meal for those departing (*gamika-bhatta*).
The four types of meals mentioned in the Pāḷi are: *gilānabhatta* (meals for the sick), *gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta* (meals for those attending the sick), and so on.
Among these, the meal given to newcomers is *āgantukabhatta*. The same principle applies to the others.
However, if there are many newcomers and not enough meals for them, one portion must be assigned to each person. If the meals are insufficient, [they should be distributed] by turn.

It should be distributed. If one newly arrived monk comes first and, having taken all the food for newcomers for himself, sits down, it belongs to him alone. Those who arrive later must eat what has been given by him.
He too, having taken one portion for himself, should give the rest away. This is its excellence. But if, even though he arrives first...
Without taking [a portion] for oneself, one should sit in silence; it is to be taken in turn together with those who arrive later.
If guests come regularly, they should eat on the very day they arrive.
If they come at intervals, they may eat for two or three days. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It is permissible to eat for seven days."
It has been said: a resident monk who has gone elsewhere and returned must also eat the meal intended for a guest (*āgantuka-bhatta*).

However, if that meal has been assigned to the monastery, it should be distributed within the monastery. If the monastery is far away, but the assignment was made to the assembly hall (*āsana-sālā*), it should be distributed in the assembly hall.
Furthermore, if the donors say, "In the absence of guests, the residents [should also receive it]..."
If they say, "Please eat," it is permissible; however, if they do not say so, it is not permissible.
This same line of reasoning applies to food for travelers as well. But this is the distinction:
a visitor receives only visitor’s food, whereas a traveler receives both visitor’s food and traveler’s food. An resident monk who wishes to depart is also considered a traveler.

...there is [the meal]; he receives the meal for those going on a journey (*gamikabhatta*). However, unlike the meal for guests (*āgantukabhatta*), this one is not received for two, three, or seven days.

Even if one who has eaten with the intention "I will go" does not go that day due to some reason, it is permissible to eat again on the following day because of the prior resolve (*saussāha*). For one who has eaten with the intention "I will go," even if robbers [obstruct] the path...
If they are obstructed—whether by water, or if the god rains, or if the caravan does not proceed—one may eat with enthusiasm.
"It is permissible to eat for two or three days while observing these calamities," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
However, one does not receive permission to eat by making a pretext such as, "I will go, I will go."
If there is enough medicine for the sick to go around, it should be given to all. If not, it should be distributed by establishing a fixed portion.
If one sick person is able to go into the village while another is unable, the latter is called a "greatly ill" person;
medicine for the sick should be given to him. If there are two greatly ill persons, and one is a recipient of renown...
One obtains much food, both hard and soft; another, being destitute and receiving little, enters the village.
For this person, sick-food should be given. There is no time limit for the sick-food; it should be eaten as long as the illness does not subside.
If one cannot survive without eating suitable food, then one should eat. However, when there is mixed rice-gruel...
Even for one who has eaten mixed food, if the illness does not flare up, then from that point on he should not eat.
As for the meal provided for the attendants of the sick, if it suffices for all, it should be given to all.
If it does not suffice, it should be distributed by making a fixed portion. This too should be given to the chief attendant among two attendants of the sick.

Regarding the two great illnesses, for one who does not attend to a patient who is without a protector: in a family that provides both food for the sick and food for the attendant, wherever the food for the sick reaches, it must be distributed there to the attendant of that specific patient as well.
Even regarding the food for the attendant, there is no daily limit; as long as the patient receives it, so too shall his attendant receive it.
"He receives. If these four types of meals are given in this manner:
"May those who are newcomers, those who are departing, the sick, and those who attend the sick, take my almsfood," it is permissible even for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika).
However, if they are given in this way: "I am setting aside meals for the four—newcomers and so forth; may they take my meal"—it is not permissible for alms-collectors.
215. There are also three kinds of meals: *dhurabhatta* (regular meal), *kuṭibhatta* (hut meal), and *vārakabhatta* (turn-based meal).
Among these, *dhurabhatta* refers to a regular meal; it is of two types: that belonging to the Saṅgha and that belonging to an individual.
Of these, that which is designated by the formula, “We give this as the Saṅgha’s regular meal,” falls under the category of *salākabhatta* (ticket-meals). [As for] “my regular alms-food...”

Having said, "Please take it," what is given is permissible even for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*). Regarding property belonging to an individual (*puggalika*), if one says, "I give you your regular meal (*dhurabhatta*)," it is not permissible if [the recipient] is an alms-food eater;
however, if one says, "Take my fixed portion of alms (*nibaddhabhikkha*)," it is permissible and may be accepted. If, after some days have passed, [the donor] later says, "Take the regular meal,"...
He says: because it was properly accepted at the outset, it is permissible.
What is called "hut-food" (*kuṭibhatta*) is that which, having had a dwelling built for the Saṅgha, one has stipulated thus:
"Let those who reside in our lodgings take food from us alone. That falls under the same category as ticket-food (*salākabhatta*); having distributed it...
It may be eaten. However, when it is said, "Let only those who reside in our lodgings take our almsfood," then it is also permissible for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika).

But as for that which is given out of faith in a particular person after building a dwelling for him, saying, "We give this to you," that belongs to him alone; when he has gone elsewhere, it should be eaten by those dependent upon him.
