“Turn-taking food” (*vārakabhatta*) refers to food given from the house of the host, starting from the first day, with the thought, “We shall take turns serving the monks during a time of famine.
This is permissible for alms-collecting monks (*piṇḍapātika*) if it is given under the designation of “alms-food” (*bhikkhā*).

However, when it is specifically called “turn-taking food,” it falls into the same category as “ticket-food” (*salākabhatta*). If they send rice and other provisions, saying, “Let the novices cook and give them,” [it is permissible].
It is permissible for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*). Thus, these three, together with the four beginning with *āgantuka-bhatta*, make seven;
these, along with *saṅgha-bhatta* and the others, constitute fourteen types of meals.
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it mentions *vihāra-bhatta*, *aṭṭhaka-bhatta*, *catukka-bhatta*, and *guḷhaka-bhatta*.
Four other types of meals are also mentioned. Among them, "monastery meal" (*vihārabhatta*) refers to a meal provided for that specific monastery;

it is included within the category of "sangha meal. However, because it was accepted in such a way that even those who are alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*) could partake of it—just as those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and are free from taints (*khīṇāsava*) did at places such as the Tissamahāvihāra and Cittalapabbata—it is permissible for them to consume.

In such places, it is permissible even for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*). However, if food is given specifically saying, "We give this for eight monks," or "We give this for four," that is "food for eight" (*aṭṭhakabhatta*) and "food for four" (*catukkabhatta*);
even that, when given by means of the word "alms" (*bhikkhā*), is permissible for those who live on alms-food.
[This applies even to] what is given after filling the bowl with a large amount of preparation, such as an excessive quantity of fried cakes (*atirasaka-pūva*).
"Guḷhakabhatta" (lump-food) means this. These three belong to the same category as *salākabhatta* (ticket-food). There is another kind of *guḷhakabhatta*:
here, some people, having arranged for a great hearing of the Dhamma and a worship of the monastery, [think], "We are not able to give to the entire Saṅgha;
let two or three hundred bhikkhus receive our almsfood. For the purpose of knowing the limit of the bhikkhus, they...
They give it in a small container; this is also permissible for those who subsist on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*).
The section on the distribution of alms-food (*piṇḍapātabhājanīya*) is finished. 217.

However, the section on the distribution of medicinal requisites (*gilānapaccayabhājanīya*) should be understood as follows: regarding medicinal substances such as ghee, kings, royal ministers, and high officials...
Regarding ghee, they may send even a hundred or a thousand jars to the monastery;
having struck the bell, it should be given by filling the vessels starting from the seat of the senior elder (therāsana). This is also permissible for those who live on alms-food (piṇḍapātika).
If the elder monks, being of a lazy nature, arrive late, one should say: "Venerable sirs, [the ghee] is being given to those with twenty years of seniority; your turn has passed."
It should not be said that it must be given only after setting aside a portion; rather, having given to them [who have arrived], it should be given from the remainder of the portion set aside.
Having heard that "much ghee has been produced in such-and-such monastery," even monks from a monastery a *yojana* away come there;

to those who arrive one after another, it should be given starting from the place where they have stood. Even for those who have not yet arrived, but have entered the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*), it should be given among their pupils and others.
When they are taking [the robes], one must simply give them. If they say, "Give them to those standing outside the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*)," they should not be given.

However, if they have entered the precincts boundary and become connected as one unit, being either at the door of their own monastery or inside the monastery itself, the boundary is said to have expanded by way of the assembly; therefore, they should be given. Even when given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha...

It must indeed be given to those who arrive later. However, if those who arrived after the second portion has already been assigned to the senior seats (therāsana), the first portion does not reach them;

it must be distributed from the second portion according to the period of residence (vassagga). Whatever is given anywhere after entering within the precinct boundary (upacārasīma) must all be divided at the very place of assembly.
In whichever monastery ten bhikkhus reside and ten pots of ghee are given, it should be divided according to each pot.
There being one pot of ghee, it should be taken by dividing it among the ten bhikkhus.
If they take it thinking, "It falls to our share exactly as it stands," that is a wrong grasp; wherever they go, it remains the property of the Saṅgha alone. However, the pot—
Having reflected on this, one should place a small amount of ghee in a dish and say, "This portion falls to the Great Elder;
the remainder falls to us. Having said this, one should pour that [ghee] back into the pot, take as much as desired, and depart.
If the ghee is thick, one should make a line and say, "The portion beyond the line falls to the Great Elder; the remainder..."

Even if it is taken [thinking], "It is for us," it is rightly taken. Among the monks, whether they are fewer or more than the stated number, and among the pots of ghee, it should be distributed by this very same method.
However, if there is one monk and one pot, it is permissible to strike the bell and take it [thinking], "This falls to my share.
Or [one may think], "This first portion falls to me; this..."
"the second portion"—in this way, it is permissible to give even small amounts. This same method applies to butter and other such items.
However, whatever sesame oil or similar liquid is perfectly clear and in which no streaks remain, that should be set aside and divided.

As for medicinal substances such as ginger and black pepper, as well as all the requisites of the monks such as remaining almsbowls and ladles, all should be carefully examined according to the very method already described.
"It should be distributed. This concludes the discussion on the distribution of requisites for the sick. 218.
Now, the determination regarding the assignment of lodgings (*senāsana*) should be understood:

this assignment of lodgings is of two kinds, namely, that for the [appropriate] season (*utu-kāla*) and that for the rainy-season residence (*vassa-vāsa*). Regarding these, first, during the [appropriate] season, some visiting monks arrive before the meal.
Some [arrive] after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch.
Whenever anyone arrives, the monks must be roused at that very moment and the lodgings assigned; there is no such thing as "the wrong time.
However, the assigner of lodgings must be wise; he should set aside one or two places for beds. If [he does so] at an improper time...

If one or two elders arrive, they should be told: "Venerable sirs, if [the dwellings] were assigned starting from the beginning, all the monks would end up with no belongings; therefore, please stay in our residence.
However, when many have arrived, after assigning them, it should be given out in order. If each individual cell is sufficient, [it should be assigned accordingly].
Each individual cell (pariveṇa) should be given. Therein, the fire-hall, the long hall, the pavilion, and so forth—all these belong to that person alone.
If this is insufficient, it should be given by way of the palace; if there are not enough palaces, by way of the rooms;
if there are not enough rooms, by way of the beds; and if there are not enough beds, by way of the place for couches.

It should be given; if there is insufficient space for beds, it should be given according to the space available for chairs, but one must not allow even the mere standing room of a monk. For that is not what is called "lodging.
However, if there is insufficient space for chairs, then either one bed-space or one chair-space should be given to three people with the words, "Venerable sirs, rest by turns."
Indeed, it is not possible to dwell entirely in the open air throughout the entire night during the cold season.
After the senior elder has rested during the first watch, he should go out and say to the second elder, "Friend, please enter here.
If the senior elder is heavy with sleep and does not know the time, the other should cough and knock on the door, saying, "Venerable sir, the time has come; it is cold."
It should be said, "She burns [with fever]. Therefore, having gone out, space must be given; it is not permitted not to give it.

The second elder, too, having rested during the middle watch of the night, must give it to the other in the same manner as before. One who is heavy with sleep must be roused in the manner already described.
In this way, for one night, the space on a single bed and in a single place must be given to three people. However, in some parts of Jambudīpa...
The monks think, "What is called 'lodging' (senāsana) is suitable for some in the place of a bed or the place of a chair,
but unsuitable for others," and so they take up lodgings every day, whether newcomers have arrived or not.
This is what is known as the taking of lodgings during the [appropriate] season.
219. Furthermore, during the rains residence (*vassāvāsa*), there is the duty of the newcomer (*āgantuka*) and there is the duty of the resident (*āvāsika*).
First, regarding the newcomer who wishes to leave his own place and go elsewhere to dwell: he should not go there on the very day of the commencement of the rains.
For the dwelling place there might be crowded, or alms-round (*bhikkhācāra*) might not be successful; therefore—
One would not dwell in comfort; therefore, thinking, "In about a month from now, the entry into the rains residence will take place," one should enter that monastery.
While staying there for about a month, if one is seeking formal instruction, one should observe whether the instruction is available;
if one is a practitioner of meditation, one should observe whether the meditation subject is suitable; and if one is seeking requisites, one should observe the availability of requisites.
Having observed this, he will dwell happily during the rains retreat. When going there from his own place, he must not bypass the village where he seeks alms.
He should not say to the people there: "Because of you, there is no distribution of tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*), nor rice gruel, nor solid food, nor the *vassāvāsika* offering;
this is the property of the shrine, this is for the Uposatha hall, and this..."
“Accept a gong and a needle for your monastery. However, after having tended to the lodgings, put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, and fulfilled the duties of one departing, one should go.
When going in this manner, the juniors should be made to carry up their bowls, robes, and bundles, as well as the oil-tubes, walking sticks, and so forth.
Having taken up the alms-bowl and holding the umbrella, one should not go by way of the village gate showing oneself;
rather, one should go by way of a concealed forest path. If no forest path exists, one should not go crushing bushes and the like;
instead, having fulfilled the duties of one going on a journey, having cut off discursive thoughts, and with a pure mind, one should go precisely according to the procedure for traveling. But if...

The road passes through a village gate; seeing him going along with his retinue, people run after him, thinking, "He is like our own Elder," and ask, "Where are you going, venerable sir, taking all these requisites?
If one among them says, "This is the time for entering the rains retreat; it is the period when alms-round is restricted to within the rainy season."
“Storage for goods is also available there, and monks go there.
Having heard this, those people said, “Venerable sirs, in this village as well, people both eat and provide clothing; do not go elsewhere.
Then, having summoned their friends and kinsmen and consulted with them all, they established a regular schedule of offerings at the monastery, such as tickets for meals and other provisions.
Except for the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe, if they request, “Venerable sir, please stay right here,” it is permissible to accept [the invitation] from all of them.
All of this is both allowable (*kappiya*) and blameless (*anavajja*). However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: “When asked, ‘Where are you going?
one should say, ‘To such-and-such a place. When asked, ‘Why are you going there? the reason should be explained.”
Thus it was said. Both of these, however, are blameless precisely because they arise from a pure mind.
This is called the duty for guests. Now, this is the duty for residents. Indeed, the monastery must be maintained by the residents beforehand;

repairs for what is broken or dilapidated must be carried out, as well as plastering and whitewashing. [They must maintain] the night-quarters, the day-quarters, the restroom huts, the urinal areas, the meditation hall, and the path to the monastery.
All of these must be looked after. Plastering the cetiya, oil-anointing of the circular railing, and the maintenance of the beds and benches—all this should be done with the thought:
"May those who wish to dwell for the rains come and dwell in comfort, engaging in recitation, interrogation, and application to their meditation subjects.
Once the preparatory work has been done, starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷhī, the rainy-season residence (vassāvāsa) [should be entered].
It should be asked. Where should it be asked? It should be asked where [the gift] is normally obtained. However, it is not permissible to ask those from whom it has never been given before.
Why should it be asked? For sometimes people give, and sometimes they do not give due to being afflicted by famine and so forth;
in that case, if one does not ask those who will not give, then when the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gifts are taken, [there may be trouble for] the monks who have already received them.
There may be an obstacle to their gain; therefore, it must be accepted only after asking.
When asking, one should say: "Venerable sirs, the time for you to receive the *vassāvāsika* has approached.
If they say, "Venerable sir, this year we have been afflicted by drought and other calamities; we are unable to give," or [if they say], "What was previously..."
Or thinking, "We shall give less than what we gave before," or "Now cotton is easily obtained;

we shall give more than what we gave before"—having observed this, one should distribute the *vassāvāsika* (rain-retreat gift) to the monks in their respective lodgings according to that appropriate method.
If people say, "Whoever receives our *vassāvāsika* [should stay] for three months..."
"If [it is said], 'Let him provide drinking water; let him tend the path to the monastery; let him tend the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard;
let him pour water on the Bodhi-tree,' it should be assigned to whoever that task falls upon.
Furthermore, if there is a village located one or two *yojanas* away, and if families there have established a deposit for the maintenance of the rains-residence..."
If he stays there after having asked permission from those families and performed the duties regarding their lodgings, the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) should be assigned to him.

However, if a *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearer) is staying in those lodgings and, upon seeing him arrive, says, "We shall give you the *vassāvāsika*," he should inform the Saṅgha. If those families [intend to give it] to the Saṅgha...
If they do not wish to give it, saying, "We shall give it to you alone," then the bhikkhu who shares a common lot should be told, "Go and receive it after performing the proper service.
However, this is not permitted for a paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer). Thus, the laypeople who have offered the gift out of faith should be asked;
alternatively, the stewards (kappiyakāraka) regarding the source of the funds should be asked. How should they be asked? "Friends, what belongs to the Saṅgha..."
"Will there be cloth for the stores? If they say, "There will be, Venerable Sir; we shall give each person a nine-cubit robe;
please accept the rainy-season gift," it should be accepted. Even if they say, "There are no robes, but there is the value of them;
please accept it, Venerable Sir," it is indeed permissible to accept it even when only the value exists. For [the purpose of] the attendants...
Regarding the items placed in the hand with the instruction, “Use these allowable articles,” it is permitted to use whatever among them is allowable.

However, as for that which is given specifically for the purpose of almsfood or for the purpose of medicinal requisites for the sick, those who present it to the robes must first seek permission for the welfare of the Saṅgha before presenting it; but as for that intended for lodgings—
That which is given specifically for [a particular person] is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

However, there is no requirement for a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) for those who present [an item] as robe-cloth or as one of the four requisites when it was given for the purpose of robe-cloth.

Furthermore, when performing an act of seeking permission, it must be done with respect to the individual [recipient], and not with respect to the Saṅgha. This applies equally to gold and silver, as well as to raw grain.
It is not permissible; however, it is permissible by way of allowable goods (*kappiya-bhaṇḍa*), such as cloth and rice. That [request] should be made in this way:
"Now there is good food and alms are easily obtained, yet the monks are distressed for lack of robes;
would it please the monks if such an amount of rice were used to make robes for them? Or: "The requisite of medicine is easily obtained, but the sick person..."
"Or there is not; such an amount of rice-portion is sufficient for the monks to make robes.
Having thus ascertained the requirements for robes, when the time for lodgings has been announced and the Saṅgha has assembled, an assigner of lodgings should be appointed.
It is said that two should be appointed; for in this way, the junior [monk] [serves] the elder.
"An elder shall cause a novice to grasp [the bowl]. However, in a large monastery similar to the Mahāvihāra, three or four persons should be appointed.
In the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "It is permissible to appoint eight or even sixteen persons.
The appointment of these individuals may be effected either by formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*) or by a motion of consent (*apalokana*). By those monks thus appointed...

The lodging should be inspected. For these are not lodgings: a shrine hall, a Bodhi-tree house, a refectory, a storehouse for broomcorn, a wooden shed, a privy, a brick hall, a carpenter’s workshop, a gatehouse, a water-shed, a path, and a lotus pond. However, these are lodgings:
a monastery, a gabled house, a multi-storied mansion, a cell, a cave, a pavilion, the foot of a tree, and a bamboo grove.
"These lodgings must be assigned.
And regarding the one who assigns them, because of the words beginning with, "Monks, I allow you first to count the monks;
having counted the monks, to count the beds; having counted the beds, to assign them by way of the beds," first, in the monastery, the monks—
Having counted [the number of monks], the bed-places must be counted; then, one bed-place should be assigned to each individual monk.
If there are more bed-places than [monks], they should be assigned by way of the dwellings (*vihāra*).
If there are even more dwellings, they should be assigned by way of the courtyards (*pariveṇa*). If there are still more courtyards, yet another portion should be given.
For among the *atimanda* monks, two or three cells should be assigned to each individual monk.
However, when a second portion has been taken and another monk arrives, that portion must not be given to him against one's own will.
But if the one who took it gives away that second portion—or even the first portion—of his own accord, it is permissible.
“Monks, one must not assign a lodging to someone standing outside the boundary; whoever should so assign it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Because of this statement, [the assignment] must not be given to one standing outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*); however, it is indeed permissible for one who stands even at a distance within the precinct boundary.
“Monks, I allow a suitable bed to be given to one who is ill,” because of this statement,
for one who is ill with coughs, asthma, fistula, dysentery, and so forth— for whom spit-pots, chamber-pots, and the like must be placed—
or for one who is a leper and defiles the lodging, a separate lodging such as a lower story of a palace, a leaf-hut, or similar place, should be assigned to him.
In whichever season a lodging is not in disrepair, a superior bed should indeed be given to that person.

Furthermore, whoever administers any kind of medicine—whether for an oil enema, a purgative, an eye ointment, or otherwise—that person is also considered ill. A suitable lodging should also be assigned to him after careful consideration.
This is because of the statement: "Monks, two [monks] must not be excluded from a lodging by one [person]; whoever should exclude them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
One person should not take two lodgings. Even if one were to take them, the prior taking is nullified by the subsequent taking.
For by a taking, a taking is nullified; by a taking, attachment is nullified; by attachment, a taking is nullified;
and by attachment, attachment is nullified. How so? Here, a certain person...

On the day of entering the rains residence, if one takes a lodging in one monastery and then goes to a neighboring monastery and takes a lodging there as well, his previous taking is superseded by this taking.

Another person, having merely formed the intention, "I shall dwell here," goes to a neighboring monastery and takes a lodging there; for him, it is by this very taking [that the previous one is superseded].
The former attachment subsides. One person, thinking "I shall dwell here," takes up a lodging or forms an attachment;
then, having gone to a neighboring monastery, he forms an attachment, thinking "I shall now dwell right here.
Thus, by means of his attachment, there is either a grasping or an attachment [to the new place]; in every case, it is in this final grasping or attachment that [the former one] subsides.

Or he remains. However, for one who has taken a lodging in one monastery and goes to another thinking, "I will dwell in that other monastery," his possession of the lodging lapses once he has crossed the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīma*).
But if, having gone there with the thought, "It will be comfortable there; I shall stay; if not, I will return," and subsequently learns that it is not comfortable...
...or goes, it is permissible.
After the assigner of lodgings has assigned the lodgings, he must assign the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-cloth).
While assigning it, if there are two types of requisites for robes—those belonging to the Saṅgha and those offered by the faithful—he should let the monks take whichever they wish to receive first.
Having taken that [share], the other [portion] should be distributed starting from the place where it was located. "If, due to a scarcity of monks, when lodgings are being distributed by courtyard,
one courtyard yields great profit such that ten or twelve robes are obtained,
that should be divided and added to other residences where there is no profit, and then distributed to other monks as well."
The Elder Mahāsumma said: "It should not be done in this way.
For people give requisites for the purpose of maintaining their own residence; therefore, other monks should enter there. 221.
But if the Elder Mahāpaduma objects here, saying: "Friend, do not take it thus; [this is] the instruction of the Blessed One..."
“Do so. For this was said by the Blessed One: “I allow you, monks, to take [the requisites] by way of the *pariveṇa* (monastic cell).
Without standing on his protest, one should persuade him, saying, “Venerable sir, there are many monks and the provisions are meager;
it is right to provide for them,” and then take them. And when the appointed monk takes them, he should go into the presence of the Great Elder...
Having gone there, one should say: "Venerable sir, your lodging has been reached; please accept the requisites. [The other replies:
"Venerable sir, the requisites from such-and-such family and such-and-such lodging have reached me. [He says: "They have reached me, venerable sir;
take them. [He replies: "I take them, friend. It is accepted. But if [the other says], "Venerable sir, they have been taken by you..."

When it has been said, "I have taken it," or when it has been said, "I will take it, venerable sir," and he replies, "I will take it," it is not yet taken," said the Elder Mahāsumma. But the Elder Mahāpaduma said:
"Whether it be a statement regarding the past or the future, or a statement regarding the present, here the mere arising of mindfulness and the mere forming of an attachment are the criteria."
"Therefore, it is indeed considered taken.
Even a monk who is a wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika), having taken possession of a dwelling and relinquished his requisites, should not have those requisites placed in another residence;
they should remain in that very same courtyard, in the fire-hall, in the long hall, or at the foot of a tree.
Or it is permissible for another to take it. The paṃsukūlika will tend to the lodging thinking, "I am staying here," while the other will do so thinking, "I am receiving requisites.
Thus, by these two reasons, the lodging will be better tended.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "When a paṃsukūlika takes a lodging for the purpose of staying, the receiver of the lodging should say:"
“Venerable sir, there is a requisite here; what should be done with it? He should be told, “Have someone else take it down.
However, if he stays without saying anything, and they give him a robe-cloth after placing it at the feet of the monks who have completed the rains residence in that monastery, it is permissible.
But if they say, “We are giving you the *vassāvāsika* (the end-of-rains gift),” [it is not permissible] for the monks who have completed the rains residence in that lodging.

"...attains [the merit]. However, for those who have no lodging and give only the requisites, it is permissible to assign those requisites to a lodging where there is a resident during the rains retreat (*vassāvāsa*).
When people build a stupa (*thūpa*) and cause a rains-retreat gift to be assigned, the stupa itself is not a lodging;
therefore, the gift should be tied to a tree or a pavilion in its vicinity and then assigned.

That bhikkhu must maintain the cetiya. The same rule applies to the Bodhi tree, the Bodhi house, the sitting-hall, the refuse-heap, the wood-shed, the privy, the gatehouse, the water-house, the water-pavilion, and the tooth-stick pavilion.
As for the dining hall, however, it is simply a lodging; therefore, it is permissible to assign it to one person or to many by apportioning it.
All of this has been stated in detail in the Mahāpaccarī.
The assigner of lodgings, however, must assign them starting from dawn on the first day of the month until the next dawn breaks;

for this is the proper time limit for the assignment of lodgings. If, after the lodgings have been assigned early in the morning, another monk who wanders about with discursive thoughts arrives and requests a lodging, one should say:
"Venerable sir, the lodgings have already been assigned; the Saṅgha has entered the rains residence."
"You should dwell wherever you wish—be it at the foot of a tree or elsewhere—in this delightful monastery," he should be told.

On the day of the later invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), however, if someone announces the time and the Saṅgha has assembled, and someone brings a ten-cubit cloth and offers it as a gift for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*), it should be given to the visiting monk if he is the senior of the Saṅgha;
if he is junior, it should be given by one who has been appointed.
The monk should say to the senior of the Saṅgha, "Venerable sir, if you wish, please set aside the first portion and take this cloth.
If he does not let go of it, it must not be given. But if he lets go of what was previously taken and takes this, it should be given.
By this same method, having exchanged [the portions] starting from the second senior, [the cloth] should come to the newcomer in its proper place.

It should be given. However, if those who have entered the first rains retreat received two, three, four, or five robes, then each robe they received should be distributed by this same method until it is equal to that of the newcomer;
once it has been made equal, the remaining portion should be given to the senior’s seat. Regarding present acquisitions:
It is permissible to make an agreement to determine [the residence] by means of a lottery.
If there is a famine, and the monks who have entered the rains retreat during both the two periods of the commencement of the rains find themselves exhausted from seeking alms, they may say:
"Friends, while all of us living here are suffering, it would be well if we were divided into two groups; those who have places where their relatives have invited them..."

If they say, "There is [a residence]; having stayed there, come for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) and take your own rainy-season robe (*vassāvāsika*)," then for those among them who stay there and return for the invitation ceremony, the rainy-season robe must be given after obtaining their permission.
For even those who consent are the owners of that very rainy-season robe, and the resident monks do not lose their ownership.
They obtain [the robe] without having to give anything. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: “A formal agreement (*katikavatta*) should be made:
‘If there is not enough rice-gruel and alms-food for all of us here, stay together in a common place and then come;
you shall receive your share of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe). If one person objects to this, it is properly objected to. If he does not object, the agreement is well-established.”
"Afterwards, when they have stayed there and returned, it should be given to them after they have requested it; at the time of their requesting, it is not permitted to refuse.
Furthermore, it is said: "If, among those who have entered the rains residence, some do not receive their share of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-benefit), the monks make an agreement:
'For those whose rains residence has been interrupted, [we shall provide] both the *vassāvāsika* and the *vassāvāsika* that will now arise.'"
"Once an agreement has been made thus, 'It is pleasing to give to these [monks],' it is exactly as if they had already received it; whatever arises should be given to them alone.

Having provided drinking water for the three months, having tended the monastery path, the shrine courtyard, and the Bodhi courtyard, and having sprinkled water on the Bodhi tree—even if one has departed or defected, one still receives the *vassāvāsika* (the robe-offering at the end of the rains retreat).

For what has been "placed under deposit" by him is indeed obtained even by one who has left the rains residence (*vassa*), provided it was taken after performing an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*) for the Saṅgha;
however, they say that what was taken on account of personal requisites (*paccaya*) is not obtained.
If a monk who has completed the rains residence and is traveling abroad receives any kind of allowable article from the hand of a resident monk...
If, having taken [the bowl] and said, “In such-and-such a family my *vassāvāsika* bowl is kept;
take it,” he departs from the place where he was, the *vassāvāsika* becomes the property of the Saṅgha. But if he goes after having caused the people to accept it in their presence, he obtains it.
When it is said, “We give this *vassāvāsika* to the bhikkhu who has stayed in our lodging,” to whomever—

Once it has been taken, it belongs to that very person. However, if the owner of the lodging, out of a desire to please [the resident], brings many robes such as those for sons, daughters, and so forth, and gives them saying, "We give these for our lodging," then among those, only one robe should be given to the one who has entered the rains residence;
the rest belong to the Saṅgha. They should be distributed by means of a lottery for the rainy-season residents; by means of the lottery...

If there are none, they should be taken starting from the senior monk’s seat. Even if many robes have been brought with a mind of confidence arising from dependence on a monk who has entered the rains residence at that lodging, and given with the thought, "We give them to the lodging," the same rule applies.
However, if they place them at the monk's feet and say, "We give them to this monk," they belong to him alone.
In one person’s house there were two *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gifts. The first portion was taken by a novice (*sāmaṇera*), and the second was for the seat of the elder (*therāsana*).
He sent one robe-cloth ten cubits long and another eight cubits long, saying, “Give the *vassāvāsika* to the monks who have received their alms.
Having sorted them out, the superior portion should be given to the novice, and the remaining portion should be given to the seat of the elder. If...
However, having led both of them to the house and fed them, he places [the gift] at their feet himself;
whatever is given to one belongs to that very person. Hereafter follows the method as it appears in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
if the rainy-season robe (*vassāvāsika*) falls to a young novice (*daharasāmaṇera*) in a certain house, and he asks, "Whose rainy-season robe is ours?", [the answer is]: "It is the novice's."
Without taking it [the bowl], saying, "You shall know at the time of giving," one should send a great elder on the day of the offering and have it brought out.
If he for whom the rains-residence bowl was intended should disrobe or pass away, and people ask, "Whose rains-residence bowl is ours?", they should be told the truth as it is. If they say:
If they say, "We give it to you," it accrues to that individual monk.
If they give it to the Saṅgha or to a group (gaṇa), it accrues to the Saṅgha or to the group.

If those who have entered the rains residence are exclusively pure paṃsukūlika monks, then what has been brought and given should be set aside as rain-season bedding and requisites, or pillows and so forth should be made from them.
This, first of all, is the discourse on the taking of lodgings according to the day of the entry into the rains during the rainy season. 222.

This other kind of taking of lodgings, known as "intermediate-release" (*antarāmuttaka*), should also be understood as occurring at other times. For the taking of lodgings is threefold according to the day: the prior, the subsequent, and the intermediate-release. Indeed, this has been said:
“Monks, there are three ways of taking up lodgings: the first, the last, and the intermediate-release.
On the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, the first should be taken up; on the month after the full moon of Āsāḷha, the last should be taken up;
and on the day after the Pavāraṇā ceremony has passed, the intermediate-release should be taken up for the purpose of the upcoming rainy-season residence.”
Among these three ways of taking up lodgings, the first and the last—these two modes of taking—are permanent;
however, the "intermediate release" was permitted by the Blessed One for the purpose of maintaining the lodgings.

For instance, if there is a large and highly valuable lodging in a monastery, the owners of that lodging might attend upon the monk who has entered the rains retreat with all requisites and great care.

At the time of departure after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they give away much of the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha. Great elders, having come from afar, take possession of these on the day of entering the rains retreat;
they dwell there in comfort, and once the rains have ended, they depart taking the gains with them. The resident monks think, "We do not receive the gains arising here;
it is always the visiting great elders who receive them, for they themselves come and—"
Thinking, "They will look after it," they did not even look at it while it was falling into ruin. For the sake of looking after it, the Blessed One said:
"When the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) has passed, a temporary dwelling (antarāmuttaka) should be assigned for the purpose of the upcoming rainy-season residence.
When assigning it, the Elder of the Saṅgha should be addressed: "Venerable sir, please accept this temporary dwelling."
If he accepts it, it must be given to him. If not, then by this same method, starting from the most senior monk down to whoever accepts it—even if it be a novice (sāmaṇera)—it must be given to him.
He must maintain that lodging for eight months; whatever is broken or decaying in the roof, the walls, or the floor, all of that must be repaired.
[He should also attend to] the recitation of the scriptures, questioning on the Dhamma, and so forth.
Having spent the day [elsewhere], it is permissible to stay there during the night; having stayed in the pariveṇa during the night, it is also permissible to spend the day there;
and it is even permissible to stay right there for the entire day and night. One must not turn away elder monks who have arrived during the proper season.
However, when the day of entering the rains retreat has arrived, if the Saṅgha-thera says, "This [place] is mine..."

If one says, "Please give us a dwelling," one does not receive it. Having said, "Venerable sir, this [dwelling] was taken as a 'rain-breaker' (antarāmuttaka) and looked after by a single monk," it should not be given; for it has been taken by the very monk who looked after it for eight months.
However, in whichever dwelling they provide requisites twice a year, at the end of six months—
If they give it every four months, that intermediate gift must not be included;
if they give it three times every four months, or if they give it four times every three months, that intermediate gift must not be included.
For it will receive its maintenance through the very requisites [already provided]. However, in the case of one who gives for one year...
"If they give many requisites all at once, this should be understood as the 'intermediate-release' [gift]. 223.
"Monks, I allow you to assign uncompleted or partially completed building work.
In the case of a small vihāra, after inspecting the work, one may assign five or six years of building work; in the case of an *aḍḍhayoga*, after inspecting the work..."
Based on the statement, "One may grant seven or eight years of *navakamma* [for repairs], or, having inspected the work in a large monastery or palace,
one may grant ten or twelve years of *navakamma*," one may dwell while performing *navakamma* on a dwelling that is unfinished or partially completed—
having announced it to a single bhikkhu either by means of a formal motion (*apalokana*) or a formal act (*kammavācā*)— in accordance with the aforementioned time limits.
It must be given. If a monk who is overseeing new construction (navakammika) obtains that residence during the rainy season, he is not permitted to refuse it during the [subsequent] weather-season.
However, a monk who has obtained the assignment of new construction should not perform the work himself after taking up tools such as axes, hatchets, or chisels;
rather, he should ascertain what has been done and what remains to be done. If that residence falls into decay, [the responsibility lies with] the owner of the residence or with him...
It should be told to anyone born in that lineage: "Your residence is being lost; look after this residence.
If he is unable to do so, it should be looked after by having monks, relatives, or supporters take responsibility for it.
If they too are unable, it should be looked after with requisites belonging to the Saṅgha. If even that is not available, one residence should be relinquished.
The remainder must be maintained; even if many are relinquished, it is permissible to establish one [monastery].

When food is scarce and monks depart, all monasteries perish; therefore, after relinquishing one, two, or three monasteries, those who consume the gruel, alms-food, robes, and so forth from them must indeed maintain the remaining monasteries.
However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: "In the absence of requisites belonging to the Saṅgha, a single monk [should think]: 'Your place for one bed..."
Having taken it, he should be told, "Look after it. If he desires more, he should be made to look after it even after being given a third or a half-share.

If, however, he does not wish for it because only a mere pillar remains there and much work must be done, it should be given to him with the words, "Look after it as your own private property. For in this way, [it is for] the Saṅgha...
He should be made to look after [the property] with the thought: ‘He will obtain the place for storing the belongings and the dwelling place for the novices.
When he has been looked after in this way, as long as he is alive, it remains the personal property of that individual; when he is dead, it belongs to the Saṅgha.
If he wishes to give it to his co-residents, he should be made to look after it after considering the work [required], setting aside either a third part or a half as his personal share.
"For it is thus that one is permitted to give [a share] to co-residents (*saddhivihārika*).

However, when there is no one to look after it, it should be made to be looked after by the method beginning with 'having assigned one dwelling,' and so forth. This too was stated elsewhere in that very same place:
"Two monks, having taken a piece of land belonging to the Saṅgha and cleared it, construct a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha; by means of which land..."
If he takes possession first, he is the owner. If both take it as their own private property, he alone is the owner.

If one makes it the property of the Saṅgha while the other makes it his own private property, if there is another abundant place for lodgings, even the one making it his own private property should not be prevented.
However, if no other such suitable place exists, [the latter] must be stopped and it should be made the property of the Saṅgha.
It must be done by the one who is building it himself. However, whatever construction work has already been done there by him should be given back.
But if, in the dwelling already built or at the site where the dwelling is being constructed, there are trees that provide shade or bear fruit, they should be removed after seeking permission.
If they belong to an individual, the owner should be asked. If he does not give them up, one should ask him up to three times.
“Let us give the value of the tree,” they should say, and it must be removed.

However, if someone, without taking even a single creeper belonging to the Saṅgha, builds a private dwelling on land belonging to the Saṅgha using imported materials, half belongs to the Saṅgha and half belongs to the individual. This applies if it is a palace (*pāsāda*).
There is a case where the lower story belongs to the Saṅgha and the upper story belongs to an individual. If one desires the lower story, it belongs to him;
if he desires both the lower and the upper, he receives half in each place. He has two lodgings built:
one for the Saṅgha and one for an individual. If he builds them using building materials obtained from the monastery, [it is so].
He receives one-third. If he builds a foundation or a front porch on a site not yet prepared, outside the enclosure wall, half belongs to the Saṅgha and half belongs to him.
But if it is built after filling in a large uneven area and providing a path where there was none, the Saṅgha has no ownership over that place.
If a monk takes rafters and other such materials from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha and installs them in another dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, they are considered properly installed.
However, those who install them in a private dwelling must either pay for the original materials or restore them to their former state.
If one takes beds, chairs, and so forth from an abandoned monastery with the intent to steal, he is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods, as in the case of theft.

If one takes [an item] thinking, “I will give it back at the time of the residents' stay,” and then uses it as communal property of the Saṅgha, then if it is lost or ruined, or worn out or completely worn out, it is as if it were never lost or ruined. However, if it is healthy, it must be restored to its original state;

but if one uses it as private property, then if it is lost or worn out, it becomes a debt for which one is liable. Furthermore, regarding doors, windows, and so forth, whether in a communal residence of the Saṅgha or a private residence...

Or if they have been assigned [to a specific person], they must indeed be returned. If a certain monastery belonging to the Saṅgha falls into disrepair, it is permissible to move items such as beds and chairs from there elsewhere for the sake of protection.
Therefore, if one moves them elsewhere and uses them as personal property of the Saṅgha, then if they are lost, they are truly lost;
if they are worn out, they are truly worn out. If, however, they remain intact once that monastery has been repaired...
It must be restored to its original state. If one uses [the lodging] for private enjoyment, then whatever is lost or worn out becomes his personal liability;
once it has been repaired, it must simply be returned. This concludes the discussion on the assignment of lodgings. 225.
Now follows here the discussion on the common use of the four requisites—by one appointed as the distributor of minor items.
When a bhikkhu is making robe-cloth and says, "Give me a needle," two needles should be given—one long and one short.
There is no need to ask whether it is "unapportioned property belonging to the Saṅgha.
To one who needs a thimble, one thimble; to one wishing to set out on a wilderness journey, a pair of sandals; to one who needs a waistband...
A waistband; for one who has arrived [saying], "My shoulder-strap is worn out," a shoulder-strap should be given.
To one in need of a water-strainer, a water-strainer should be given; to one in need of a water-vessel, a water-vessel should be given.
If there is no cloth-strip, the water-vessel should be given together with a cloth-strip. To one requesting it [saying], "I shall place my bowl among the incoming monks,"...
A sufficient amount of *kusī* and half-*kusī* cloth should be given. To one who has come because the *maṇḍala* is insufficient, one *maṇḍala* should be given;
two half-*maṇḍalas* should be given. However, two full *maṇḍalas* should not be given to one who asks for them.
To one who requires a border (*paribhaṇḍa*) for a robe due to the wind, a sufficient amount for one robe should be given. [Likewise] to one who requires ghee, fresh butter, and so forth...
Having prepared one medicinal substance for the sick person in the measure of a *nāḷi*, a third portion from that should be given.
Having thus given [the medicine] for three days until the *nāḷi* is full, from the fourth day onward, it should be given after having requested permission from the Saṅgha.
In the case of lumps of sugar as well, a third part should be given on one day. When the lumps have been finished in this way over three days, then—

However, after requesting permission from the Saṅgha, it should be given. Furthermore, those appointed and established as rice-milk distributors (*yāgu-bhājaka*) and so forth must give half a portion to people who have come to the distribution place even without asking for permission; but by those not so appointed, it should be given after having asked for leave.
This applies to what is being given by those appointed by the Saṅgha, or by monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others acting under their orders, as well as to what belongs to laypeople.
If one takes what is being given by the owner or by one authorized [by him], saying to a non-existent person, "Give another's share," there is *bhaṇḍādeyya* (theft).
One who takes what is being given by another must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
Or, when it is being given by one who is neither authorized nor commissioned, if one says, "Give another share as well," or counts false years [of seniority]...
One who takes [the food] must be made to pay the value of the goods as a fine for theft. For one who takes it while others are giving it, the "non-payment of goods" (bhaṇḍādeyya) applies;

however, if the owner has caused it to be given by saying, "Give this to him," or if he gives it himself, it is considered "well-given. This is the essence derived from the adjudication in all the commentaries.
Even for one who has entered for alms, it is permissible to take a portion of rice while standing within the boundary of the vicinity (upacārasīmā).
However, if the donors say, "Venerable sir, please accept even that which is within the outer boundary (bahiupacārasīma),
for they will come and consume it," then it is permissible to accept even that which is within the village boundary.
A discerning person, having examined both the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā, [should act accordingly].
"In this way, one should distribute the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha while being heedful.
Thus ends, in the Compendium of Decisions on the Vinaya Excluded from the Pāḷi,
the Discourse on the Decision Concerning the Distribution of the Four Requisites in all its aspects.
29. Discussion on the Determination of the Spreading of the Kathina 226.
Regarding the term *kathina*: here, who is entitled to spread the *kathina*, and who is not?
By way of number, first of all, at the minimum limit five persons are entitled; above that, even up to a hundred thousand, but below five, they are not.
They do not obtain it. Those who have spent the rains and entered for the earlier rains-retreat, and have performed the first invitation (*pavāraṇā*), obtain it.

Those whose rains-retreat has been interrupted, or those who entered for the later rains-retreat, do not obtain it. "Even those who have spent the rains in another monastery do not obtain it," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
However, for all those who entered for the earlier rains-retreat, [all] are fillers of the quorum.
They do not obtain the benefit; the benefit belongs only to the others.
If those who entered during the first period are four, three, two, or even one, the kaṭhina should be spread by making the others fulfill the quorum.
Now, if four monks have entered and one novice (sāmaṇera) is of full age, and he receives full ordination (upasampadā) during the second period—

He both completes the quorum and receives the benefit. The same principle applies here as well for the cases of three bhikkhus and two sāmaṇeras, two bhikkhus and three sāmaṇeras, or one bhikkhu and four sāmaṇeras.
If those who entered during the first period are not skilled in the spreading of the kaṭhina, one should seek out elder theras who are reciters of the Khandhaka and are skilled in the spreading.
They should be brought back. Having announced the formal act (*kammavācā*), having had the *kaṭhina* spread, and having partaken of the gift, they shall depart;
however, the merit belongs only to the others.
By whom may the *kaṭhina* be given? It is permissible for anyone—whether a deva or a human, or by one of the five who share the same Dhamma.
What has been given by anyone is permissible. There is a duty for the donor of the *kaṭhina*;
if he, not knowing it, asks, "Venerable sir, how should the *kaṭhina* be given?", he should be instructed thus:
"It is permissible to give a cloth sufficient for one of the three robes at the time of sunrise, saying, 'We give this as a *kaṭhina*-robe.'"
“For the purpose of its preparation, it is fitting to provide this many needles, this much thread, this much dye,
and rice porridge and meals for so many monks who are performing the preparation.
The one who spreads the *kaṭhina* must also know the proper conduct regarding the *kaṭhina* that has been procured in accordance with the Dhamma and in a righteous manner.
For it is not permissible to wear a robe brought from a weaver’s house that is still stained with chaff, nor is a soiled robe permissible;

therefore, having obtained a cloth for the Kathina ceremony, one should wash it thoroughly, prepare the requisites for sewing such as needles and so forth, and together with many bhikkhus, sew it on that very day. Once the needlework is finished, it should be dyed and marked with the *kappa-bindu*.

Having been given, the kaṭhina should be spread. If, while that one has not yet been spread, another person brings a kaṭhina-cloth and gives many other items that constitute the requisites for the benefits of the kaṭhina, then it should be spread using the property of whoever gives the greater benefit.
The other person should be exhorted and persuaded in such a way.
By whom, then, should the kaṭhina be spread? By him to whom the Saṅgha gives the kaṭhina-cīvara. To whom, however, should it be given by the Saṅgha? To one whose robes are worn out.
If there are many whose robes are worn out, it should be given to the senior.
Even among the seniors, it should be given to one who has a large following and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day. If [there is] a senior...
If he is unable, but one who is younger is able, it should be given to him. Furthermore, it is appropriate for the Saṅgha to show hospitality to a senior elder;
therefore, one should say: "Venerable sir, you take [the robe]; we shall make one and give it to you.
Among the three robes, that which is worn out should be given for its sake. For one who normally wears a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭa*), it should be given as a double-layered robe.

It should be given. Even if his single-layered robe (*ekapaṭṭacīvara*) is thick and his *kathina* cloth is thin, for the sake of propriety, only enough for a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭa*) should be given;

it is even permissible to give a double-layered robe to one who says, "I will wear a single-layered robe if I do not receive [more]. However, it should not be given to one whose nature is characterized by greed. By him also, [the *kathina*...]
One should not accept [the cloth] with the thought, "Having spread it out and later sewn it apart, I will make two robes. However, for the one to whom it is given, [the formal motion is as follows]:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this cloth for the kaṭhina to the monk named so-and-so, in order to spread the kaṭhina. This is the motion."
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha;
the Saṅgha gives this cloth for the kaṭhina to the monk named so-and-so in order to spread the kaṭhina.

Whoever among the venerable ones approves of giving this cloth for the kaṭhina to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the kaṭhina, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.”

“This kathina-cloth has been given by the Saṅgha for the purpose of spreading the kathina for the bhikkhu named so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way it should be given with the second formal act (*kammavācā*).
But when the kathina has been thus given, if that kathina-cloth has already had its preliminary work completed, then this is so.
It is wholesome. If the preliminary work has not been completed, it is not permitted for even a single person—whether on account of being an elder or being learned—to say, "I will do it";
rather, everyone must assemble and complete the washing, sewing, and dyeing.
For this is called the Kathina duty, praised by the Buddha. In the past, even the Blessed One Padumuttara [praised] the Kathina duty...
He performed it. It is said that his chief disciple, the elder named Sujāta, received the *kaṭhina*.
The Teacher, having sat down together with six million eight hundred thousand monks, performed it.
Once the *kaṭhina* had been finished and taken up, if the monk who spread the *kaṭhina* [uses] the *kaṭhina* with the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*)...
If one wishes to spread the *kaṭhina* with an outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), the old outer robe must be relinquished, the new outer robe must be determined upon, and the speech must be uttered:

"With this outer robe, I spread the *kaṭhina*. If one wishes to spread the *kaṭhina* with an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), the old upper robe must be relinquished, the new upper robe must be determined upon, [and the speech must be uttered].
The speech should be uttered: “With this upper robe, I spread the kaṭhina.

If one wishes to spread the kaṭhina with an inner robe, the old inner robe must be relinquished, the new inner robe must be determined upon, and the speech should be uttered: “With this inner robe, I spread the kaṭhina.”

That monk who has spread the *kathina* should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms in salutation, and speak thus: "Venerable sirs, the *kathina* has been spread for the Saṅgha; it is a lawful spreading of the *kathina*.
May you give your approval. Those monks who are to give approval should likewise arrange their upper robes over one shoulder.
Having raised his joined palms, he should speak thus to him: "Friends, the kaṭhina has been spread for the Saṅgha; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma;

let us give our approval. Then that monk who has spread the kaṭhina, having approached several monks, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and raised his joined palms, should speak thus to them: "Venerable sirs, the kaṭhina has been spread..."
“The kaṭhina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma; please give your approval.
Those monks who are to give approval, having arranged their upper robes over one shoulder and extended their hands in reverential salutation, should say to him:
“Friend, the kaṭhina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma; we approve. Then that monk who has spread the kaṭhina—
A monk, having approached another monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus to him:
"Friend, the kaṭhina has been spread for the Saṅgha; the spreading of the kaṭhina is in accordance with the Dhamma; please express your appreciation.
Then that monk who expresses appreciation, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to him thus:
He should be addressed thus: "Friend, the *kaṭhina* of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is in accordance with the Dhamma;
I give my approval. In this way, the *kaṭhina* is considered spread for all. For this is said in the *Parivāra*: "The *kaṭhina* is spread for two persons:
for the one who spreads it and for the one who gives approval. Furthermore, it is said: "The Saṅgha does not [spread] the *kaṭhina*..."
"It is spread; it is not the group that spreads the kaṭhina, but the individual who spreads the kaṭhina.
Through the sangha’s expression of appreciation, through the group’s expression of appreciation, and through the individual’s spreading, the kaṭhina becomes spread for the sangha;
the kaṭhina becomes spread for the group; the kaṭhina becomes spread for the individual."

But when the kaṭhina has been spread in this way, if the donors give the benefit brought along with the kaṭhina-cloth, saying, "We give it only to him by whom our kaṭhina was accepted," the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has no ownership over it.
However, if they depart after giving it without making such an inquiry, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus does have ownership. Therefore, if there are other robes belonging to the one who spread the kaṭhina...
They become weak; having obtained the permission of the Saṅgha, robes should be given for their sake as well, but only a single formal act (*kammavācā*) is required.
As for the remaining benefits of the kaṭhina, strong robes should be given by means of a distribution lot (*ṭhitikā*) for the rainy-season residence;
in the absence of a distribution lot, they should be given starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*). Heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*) must not be divided. If...
However, if there are many monasteries within a single boundary, the kaṭhina should be spread by all the bhikkhus having assembled together in one place;
it is not permitted to spread it separately.
"For you, bhikkhus, who have spread the kaṭhina, five things will be allowable: wandering without having been invited, wandering without taking [the robes] along, eating in a group..."

"Whatever robes are required and whatever robe-cloth arises there shall belong to them"—from this statement, the five benefits, such as wandering without having informed [other monks], are obtained for those monks whose *kaṭhina* has been spread.
In that context, "wandering without having informed" means wandering without having asked permission;
it is stated that as long as the *kaṭhina* has not been dismantled, there is no offense regarding the training rule on wandering.
...occurs. "Wandering without having taken up [the robe]" means wandering without having taken up the robe;
the meaning is "separation from the robe. "Eating in a group" refers to the non-offense stated by the training rule concerning eating in a group.

"Robe as much as required" means that as much as is needed for a robe, that much is permissible provided it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned to another (*vikappita*). And whatever robe-offering arises there...
Whether it be a robe for the deceased within the boundary where the *kathina* has been spread, or one given specifically for the Saṅgha,
or brought in by means of funds intended for that purpose— in whatever manner a robe belonging to the Saṅgha arises, the meaning is that it shall belong to them.
Thus ends the summary of the Vinaya analysis not found in the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*).
The Discussion on the Determination of the Kathina Spreading is finished.
30. The Discussion on the Determination of Valuable Articles 227.
Regarding "valuable articles" (*garubhaṇḍa*): here it is said, "Monks, these five things are not to be relinquished; they must not be given away."
Whether by the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, [these items] remain unalienated even if they have been alienated;

whoever should alienate them incurs a thullaccaya offense—thus it is shown by way of such passages. These include: an ārāma and the site of an ārāma, a vihāra and the site of a vihāra, a bed, a bench, a mattress, and a pillow;
a bronze cauldron, a bronze vessel, a bronze bucket, a bronze pan, and an adze.
An axe, a hatchet, a spade, a pickaxe, a creeper, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden ware, and earthenware—these are called the five heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa).
Therein, a "grove" (ārāma) means either a flower grove or a fruit grove. A "site for a grove" (ārāmavatthu) refers to the ground of those very same groves.
A "site" (*okāsa*) refers to a space set aside and demarcated for a specific purpose, or, when those monasteries have fallen into ruin, their former ground area.
A "monastery" (*vihāra*) refers to any dwelling such as a palace (*pāsāda*) and so forth. A "monastery site" (*vihāravatthu*) refers to the location where that [dwelling] is established.

A "bed" (*mañca*) refers to these four types of beds: the stuffed-cotton bed (*masāraka*), the bound-fiber bed (*bundikābaddha*), the crab-legged bed (*kuḷīrapādaka*), and the bed with removable legs (*āhaccapādaka*).
"Another. A "bench" (*pīṭha*) refers to any one of the four types of benches, such as the *masāraka* and so forth.

A "cushion" (*bhisi*) refers to any one of the five types, such as the woolen cushion and so forth. A "bolster" (*bimbohana*) refers to any one of the materials such as tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or silk-cotton.
An "iron pot" (*lohakumbhī*) is a pot made of any kind of iron, whether black iron or copper. This also applies to iron pans and similar vessels.
The same method applies here. In this context, however, "bhāṇaka" refers to a water-carrier (arañjara); "vāraka" refers to a jar; and "kaṭāha" is simply a basin.

Among the axes and so forth, as well as among the creepers and so forth, there is nothing that is difficult to understand. The word "five" is stated by way of a group, but according to their individual forms, these are of twenty-five kinds. For it has been said:
“The second consists of two groups; the third, of four groups;
the fourth, of nine sections; and the fifth, of eight divisions.
Thus, with these five collections, he whose eyes are the fivefold stainless vision—”
“The Lord has declared twenty-five kinds of heavy goods. Regarding this, here is the analytical explanation:
for all these heavy goods are stated in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* as “not to be disposed of,” and they are shown in the *Kīṭāgiri-vatthu* as “not to be shared out. However, in the *Parivāra*:
“Not to be disposed of, not to be shared out...”
“Five [cases] have been declared by the Great Seer:
there is no offense for one who distributes or consumes [the food].
This question was contemplated by those skilled in the Dhamma.”

It has been brought. Therefore, because it must not be released or distributed by way of cutting off the root, there is no offense for one who exchanges it or uses it by way of barter; this is how the intended meaning here should be understood.
228. Herein, this is the sequential explanation: first of all, it is not permitted to offer even these five kinds [of goods] for the sake of robes, almsfood, or medicine;
nor is it permitted to exchange durable goods for durable goods, or heavy goods for heavy goods.

It is permissible. However, in the case of immovable property, such as a field, a building site, a pond, or a watercourse, it is not permissible for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to deliberate upon, accept, or approve of them;
rather, once they have been deliberated upon by the kappiyakārakas (stewards), such items become permissible goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*).
But regarding these four—namely, a monastery for a monastery, a site for a monastery, a dwelling for a dwelling, and a site for a dwelling—[they are permissible].
It is permissible to exchange [the produce].
Herein is the method of exchange: the monastery’s coconut grove belongs to the Saṅgha, but it is situated at a distance;
the kitchen attendants eat most of it, and even what they do not eat, they bring back only a small amount after having paid the cart-driver’s wages from it. For others...
However, if near that monastery there is another monastery belonging to village-dwelling people,

and they approach the Saṅgha and request that monastery by means of their own [land], it should be accepted by the Saṅgha after obtaining the formal consent with the words, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha.
Even if there are a thousand trees belonging to the monks and five [trees] belonging to the people...
“Six hundred [trees]; you should not say, ‘Your grove is small. For although this is small, it nevertheless yields more income than the other.
Even if it yields exactly the same amount, it must still be accepted, because one is able to enjoy it whenever one wishes.
However, if there are more trees belonging to the people...”
“Surely you have more trees,” one should say. If they say, “May our merit be even greater;
we give them to the Saṅgha,” it is permissible to accept them after making this known. The trees belonging to the bhikkhus bear fruit, whereas the trees belonging to the people do not yet bear fruit;
although they do not yet bear fruit, [one may accept them] thinking, “They will bear fruit before long.”
It must indeed be accepted. While trees bear fruit for laypeople, monks do not yet take fruit from those trees;
one may say, "Do not your trees bear fruit? If they give it, saying, "Venerable sir, please take it;
it will become merit for us," it is permissible to accept it after making them understand [the situation]. Thus, by means of the monastery...
The monastery (ārāma) may be exchanged. By this same method, the site of a monastery (ārāmavatthu), a dwelling (vihāra), or the site of a dwelling (vihāravatthu) may be exchanged for a monastery;
and by means of a large or small site of a monastery, a monastery, its site, a dwelling, or its site may be exchanged.
How is a dwelling to be exchanged for a dwelling? Suppose there is a house belonging to the Saṅgha within a village, and people...
There is a palace in the middle of the monastery; both are equal in value. If people ask for that house in exchange for the palace, it is permissible to accept it.
Even if the monks' house is more valuable, when they say, "Our house is more valuable," [one should reply:
"Although it is more valuable, it is unsuitable for those who have gone forth; it cannot [be kept]."
If they say, “It is suitable for those who have gone forth to dwell there; please accept this,” it is permissible to accept it even in this way.
However, if the gift is of great value to the people, one should say, “Is your own house not of great value?
But if they reply, “Let it be, venerable sir; it will be a merit for us, so please accept it,” then it is permissible to accept it.

In this same way, one dwelling-place (*vihāra*) should be exchanged for another dwelling-place. By this same method, a site for a dwelling (*vihāravatthu*), a monastery (*ārāma*), and a site for a monastery (*ārāmavatthu*) should also be exchanged for a dwelling-place;
and by means of a site for a dwelling—whether of great or small value—one should exchange dwellings, sites for dwellings, monasteries, and sites for monasteries.
Thus should the exchange of stable things for stable things be understood.
Regarding the exchange of heavy goods for other heavy goods, however, whether a bed or a chair be large or small—
even one with legs only four finger-breadths high, or even one made by village children playing in sand-pits—
from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha, it becomes a heavy good. Even if kings, royal ministers, and others [should give them] all at once...
If they give a hundred couches or a thousand couches, all of them should be accepted as allowable couches. Having accepted them, they should be given out with the instruction:
"Use them for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha according to seniority. They must not be given out on an individual basis.
It is also permissible to place extra couches in storehouses and such places, and to deposit one's bowl and robes upon them.
A bed given outside the boundary with the words, "We give it to the Saṅgha," should be placed in the dwelling place of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
If there are many beds there, it need not be used as a bed. It should be given to whoever has work in that place, saying, "Use this for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha.
Whether it is of great value, worth a hundred or worth a thousand [coins], it should be so used.
Or, if one receives another hundred beds in exchange for a bed, it may be accepted after bartering. It is not only beds that may be exchanged for beds;
it is also permissible to exchange monasteries, monastery sites, dwellings, dwelling sites, stools, couches, and pillows.
This same principle applies to stools, couches, and pillows as well. However, among these items, anything that is unallowable (akappiya) must not be used.
What is allowable (*kappiya*) may be used for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha.

Or, having exchanged what is unallowable or of great value for what is allowable, the aforementioned items should be taken. However, there is no such thing as a mattress or bolster made from non-heavy materials.
229. Iron pots, iron pans, and iron basins—these three may be either large or small.
Or, even those items that hold only a handful of water are indeed "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

However, a metal vessel made of any kind—whether black iron, copper, round iron, or bell-metal—that holds a *pāda* in the island of Sri Lanka is to be distributed. A *pāda*, by the Magadhan *nāḷi* measure, amounts to five *nāḷis*;
anything holding more than that is a heavy good. These, first of all, are those mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*).

Iron vessels. However, those not mentioned in the Pāḷi—such as water-pitchers (bhiṅgāra), receiving-bowls (paṭiggaha), large basins (uḷuṅka), small ladles (dabbika), spoons (kaṭacchu), bowls (pāti), plates (taṭṭaka), saucers (sarakasa), boxes (samugga), charcoal-baskets (aṅgārakapalla), incense-spoons (dhūmakaṭacchu), and so forth—whether small or large, all are heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa).
But the alms-bowl (patto), iron pots (ayathālaka), and copper-iron pots (tambalohathālaka)—these are items to be used (bhājanīya).
Whether they are made of brass, copper, or tin, if they are intended for the communal use of the Saṅgha or are offered by householders...

It is permissible [to use it] as such, but it is not permissible for private personal use. For even if a vessel made of bronze, copper, or other metals has been given to the Saṅgha, it is not permissible as a personal possession (*pārihārika*);
rather, it must be used only according to the householders’ method of handling forbidden items (*gihivikaṭanīhāra*). This is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
However, setting aside vessels and their derivatives, other articles made of allowable metal (*kappiyaloha*)—such as an ointment box, an ointment stick, or an ear-cleaner—are also permitted.
A needle, a needle-case, a small pair of pincers, a small awl, a key, a mallet, a staff, a probe, a blowpipe, a slingshot,
an iron hammer, an iron chisel, an iron ball, an iron lump, an iron wheel, and any other miscellaneous iron implements that are not finished products and are subject to distribution.
A smoke-tube, an iron lamp, a wooden lamp, a hanging basket-lamp, a suspended lamp, and images of women, men, or animals.
Furthermore, all other metal articles—whether they are to be applied to walls, roofs, doors, and so forth, or even as small as a metal peg—are indeed "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Even those obtained by oneself must not be used for private personal consumption after being kept;
rather, it is permissible to use them for communal monastic use or as items provided by householders. This also applies to the three types of medicinal substances.
The same principle applies here. Trays, plates, and the like made of milk-stone are indeed heavy articles.

However, a small jar or an oil vessel is a heavy article only when it exceeds the size of a foot-measure. Furthermore, vessels made of gold, silver, brass, or crystal are not permitted even if they belong to a layperson;
how much less so if they are for communal use by the Saṅgha or for private use by an individual.
Regarding the use of lodgings (*senāsana*), however, everything is permissible, whether it has been formally assigned (*āmāsa*) or not yet assigned (*anāmāsa*).
Among tools such as axes and the like, an axe with which one cannot perform any major work other than cutting tooth-sticks or stripping sugarcane is to be shared (*bhājanīya*);
any axe larger than that, regardless of how it was made, is indeed heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).

As for the axe (*pharasa*), even a surgeon’s lancet used for venesection is indeed a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*). The determination regarding the hatchet (*kuṭhāriya*) is exactly the same as for the axe.
However, that which is fashioned as a compact weapon is not an untouchable object (*anāmāsa*). As for the pickaxe (*kudāla*), even one measuring only four finger-breadths is indeed a heavy object.
Whether the chisel (*nikhādana*) has a square face, a scoop-like face, or is curved or straight—[it is always a heavy object].
Or, even if it is as small as a broom-handle or a wooden peg, if it is bound with a handle, it is indeed "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

However, the tool for carving a broom-handle, being handleless and consisting of mere wood, is not [heavy property]. That which can be carried by placing it inside a small box is "to be shared" (*bhājanīya*).
The top-knot [of a peg] is also included by virtue of its being driven into the ground. By those people who [provide] axes and so forth in the monastery...
If they have been given [to the Sangha], and their house is burned down or plundered by thieves, and they say, "Venerable sirs, give us back our requisites;
we shall restore them to their former state," they should be given. If they bring them back, they should not be prevented; nor should those who do not bring them back be reprimanded.
[This applies to] the tools of smiths, carpenters, turners, basket-makers, reed-workers, jewelers, bowl-binders, and the like—such as anvils, mallets, pliers, and scales.

All iron implements become "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*) from the moment they are given to the Saṅgha. The same principle applies to the tools of the goldsmiths working with tin and lead, the goldsmiths, and the leather-workers.
However, there is this distinction: among the tools of the tin and lead workers, it is the small knife used for cutting tin;

among the tools of the goldsmiths, it is the small knife used for cutting gold; and among the tools of the leather-workers, it is the small knife used for cutting leather that has already been prepared.

These are articles that may be shared. Among the implements of barbers and tailors as well, with the exception of the large knife, the large pair of scissors, and the large thimble-block, everything else is an article to be shared; the large knife and the others are heavy articles.
Regarding creepers and such, any creeper such as the rattan-creeper measuring half an arm’s length, whether given to the Saṅgha or grown there, [is an article to be shared].
Or, if it is guarded and protected, it is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*);

when used for the business of the Saṅgha or the business of a shrine (*cetiyakamma*), if there is a surplus, it is permissible to apply it toward personal business as well. However, that which is unguarded is not considered heavy property at all.
Ropes or cords made of thread, cotton, bark, coconut husk, or leather—whether made by twisting cotton, bark, or coconut husk into a single strand or a double strand—are [permissible].
