From the time they are given to the Saṅgha, these are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*). However, thread that has been spun and given, as well as cotton, wool, coconut husks, and seeds, are to be shared out.
Those by whom these ropes, cords, and so forth have been given may take them away for their own business and are not to be stopped.
Any bamboo, even as small as the eight-finger-long shaft of a needle, whether given to the Saṅgha, grown there, or protected and guarded, is considered "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).
Even such an item may be used when tasks for the Saṅgha or the Cetiya have been performed, and it is permissible to give it away for personal use provided there is a surplus.
However, a tube for oil to be applied to the feet, a walking staff, a sandal-stand, or a parasol-staff [are not heavy property].
"Sixty-four sticks"—this is the property subject to distribution here. When people taking goods from a burnt house depart, they are not to be stopped.

One who takes bamboo that has been protected and guarded must take it either of equal value or more than its value, having made compensation even for a mere creeper worth that much; one who takes it without making compensation...
It should be used right there. When departing, one should go after having placed it in a communal dwelling;
if one has gone while taking it with the intention of forgetting it, it must be sent back once one has reached the destination.

One who has traveled to another region should place it in a communal dwelling upon reaching a monastery. "Grass" refers to any grass whatsoever, excluding *muñja* and *pabbaja*. However, where there is grass...
There is none; they cover it there with leaves, therefore leaves are also included within grass.

Thus, any grass the size of a handful among *muñja* and other such grasses, or even a single leaf among *tāla* leaves and the like, if given to the Saṅgha, or if grown there, or if it is grass grown from what was designated as a grass-plot for the Saṅgha outside the monastery, or if it has been protected and guarded—it constitutes "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
When that [material] has been used for the business of the Saṅgha or for the business of a cetiya, it is permissible to give the remainder for personal (puggalika) work;
those people taking away what was taken from a burnt house should not be stopped. Even an empty book measuring eight finger-breadths is indeed a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).
As for clay—whether it be natural clay, five-colored clay, lime, or substances such as Sajjurasa, kaṅgu, and silesa—[it is likewise].
Or whatever has been brought from a place where it is difficult to obtain and given— whether grown there or protected and guarded—
even if it is as heavy as a ripe palm fruit, it is permissible to give it for personal work once the work for the Saṅgha and the work for the Cetiya have been completed;
however, asafoetida, vermilion, yellow orpiment, realgar, and antimony are items to be shared.

Regarding wooden articles (*dārubhaṇḍa*), the *Kurundi* states: "Any wooden article, even if it is merely eight finger-breadths long like a needle-handle, which has been given to the Saṅgha in a place where wood is scarce, or which grows there naturally, and is protected and guarded—this constitutes a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*).
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, all products made from wood, bamboo, leather, stone, and so forth, are included within the category of wooden articles.
The determination of wooden articles beginning with the *āsandi* (stool) has been stated. Herein is the method:

among these—namely, the *āsandi*, the seven-limbed throne (*sattaṅga*), the *bhaddapīṭha*, the bench (*pīṭhikā*), the one-legged stool, the stool with a curved handle, the plank, the brush-mat (*koccha*), and the straw mat (*palālapīṭha*)—whatever there may be, whether small or large, if it has been given to the Saṅgha, it is a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*).
[It] exists. And here, by the term "straw mat" (palālapīṭha), mats made of plantain leaves and so forth are also included.
A couch covered with a tiger skin, encircled by animal figures, and inlaid with gems is indeed a "heavy article" (garubhaṇḍa).
Furthermore, there are crooked boards, long boards, boards for washing robes, rubbing boards, mallets for rubbing, and knots for cutting tooth-sticks.
A staff, a club, a basket, a dye-vat, a water-receptacle made of wood, ivory, or bamboo—
whether with feet or without feet— a casket, a chest, a box larger than the size for holding [personal] feet,
a water-vat, a water-basin, a ladle, a spoon, a water-cup, and a water-strainer: whatever among these belongs to the Saṅgha...
A heavy article (garubhaṇḍa) has been given. However, a conch-shell bowl is to be shared; likewise, a wooden water-pot.
Whether the foot-scraper and the circular foot-rest are made of wood or of cloth, leaves, and so forth, all such items are heavy articles.
Also, a stand, a bowl-cover, a palm-leaf fan, a whisk, a small box, a basket, a stick-brush, and a hand-brush.
Among these as well, whether it be small or large, anything made from wood, bamboo, leaves, hide, or other materials, is indeed "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
This includes any structural component of a house such as pillars, scales, stair-rungs, or planks— whether made of wood or stone—
as well as any kind of bed-frame, any kind of floor-covering, or any kind of unallowable hide.
Any heavy article given to the Saṅgha may be used as a floor-covering.
However, sheepskin falls under the category of bedspreads, and that too is a heavy article. Permissible hides are to be distributed.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated: "All hide measuring the size of a bed is a heavy article."

The mortar, pestle, winnowing fan, grindstone, small grinding stone, stone trough, stone basin, spinning wheel, shuttle, loom, and so forth— all such articles of the weaver, all such articles of the farmer,
and all vehicles equipped with wheels are indeed "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
As for the legs of a bed, the frame of a bed, the legs of a stool, the frame of a stool, and the handles of axes, hatchets, and so forth— whichever among these [is stolen]:

Woodwork for which the planing has been partially done but is not yet finished is *bhājanīya* (common property); however, once it has been planed and polished, it becomes *garubhaṇḍa* (heavy property).

Furthermore, among permitted items: a staff, a parasol, a handle, a walking stick, sandals, a set of fire-drills, a water-strainer, a foot-bath, a vessel for *āmalaka* fruit that is not excessive, a jar for *āmalaka* fruit, and a vessel for *lābu* fruit.
A gourd-pitcher, a horn-vessel, and a water-jar—all these are items that may be used; anything larger than those is "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).
An elephant tusk or any kind of horn, if unworked, may be used exactly as it was found. The same determination applies to bed-legs and other items made from them.
Even if worked and finished, a casket for asafoetida, a toggle, a needle-case, or a collyrium-box [are heavy property].
The eye-salve box, the applicator stick, and the water-wiper—all of these are indeed items to be shared.
Among earthenware vessels, everything used for human enjoyment and utility—including jars, pots, and other pottery;
bowls and basins; charcoal pans; incense burners; oil-lamp trees; lamp-stands; tiles for the roof; tiles for the ceiling; and pinnacle-tiles—is included.
From the time it was given to the Saṅgha, it is a "heavy article" (garubhaṇḍa);

however, from the time it is taken up [as a gift], a water-pot (*ghaṭaka*) that is not exceeding the measure for what is not left over (*anatiritta*), as well as a bowl (*patta*), a dish (*thālaka*), a golden vessel (*kañcanaka*), and a water-flask (*kuṇḍikā*)—these here are the articles to be shared (*bhājanīyabhaṇḍa*).

And just as with earthenware vessels, so too among iron vessels, the water-flask belongs exclusively to the category of those to be shared; this is the sequential explanation (*anupubbikathā*) in this matter.
Thus ends the section on the determination of heavy articles in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi. 31.
The Section on the Determination of Formal Accusation and Other Matters.
230. Regarding the "determination of the accusation and so forth": here, who is permitted to accuse and who is not?
First, taking the case of the words of a weak accuser, no one is permitted [to act on them].

A "weak accuser" is one who, while several people are sitting together in conversation, speaks regarding another person—addressing him generally—concerning a matter involving defeat (*pārājika*); and another, having heard this, [speaks] to the other...
Having gone, he reports it; he approaches him and says, "It seems you said this and that to me.
He replies, "I do not know anything of the sort; however, in the course of conversation, I spoke generally without referring to anyone in particular.
Had I known that this would lead to such suffering for you, I would not have said even so much. This is the weak accuser.
Regarding this, the Elder Mahāpaduma said that once one has accepted such a formal discussion, no one is permitted to censure that bhikkhu;
however, without accepting it, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue may censure a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, and a bhikkhunī endowed with virtue may likewise censure a bhikkhunī.
The Elder Mahāsuma, however, [said] that even those who are fellow practitioners of the Dhamma...
[The opponent] said, "They obtain [the offense]. The Elder Godatta replied, "No one fails to obtain it," and cited this sutta: "Having heard it from a bhikkhu, he accuses;
having heard it from a bhikkhunī... [and so on] ...having heard it from followers of other sects, he accuses.
According to the assertions of all three elders, the matter must be decided based solely on the admission of the one who has been accused.
This so-called "accusation" (codanā) is threefold: an accusation based on what has been seen, one based on what has been heard, and one based on suspicion.

There is also another fourfold classification: an accusation regarding failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), an accusation regarding failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), an accusation regarding failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), and an accusation regarding failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti).
Among these, an accusation regarding failure in virtue should be understood by way of the two heavy classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha); as for the remaining...

The censure for failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*) should be understood by way of [the rules concerning] misconduct; the censure for failure in view (*diṭṭhi-vipatti*) by way of wrong view and extremist views;
and the censure for failure in livelihood (*ājīva-vipatti*) by way of the six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood.

Furthermore, there is another fourfold [classification]: the pointing out of the basis (*vatthu-sandassanā*), the pointing out of the offense (*āpatti-sandassanā*), the prohibition of communal living (*saṃvāsa-paṭikkhepo*), and the prohibition of proper treatment (*sāmīci-paṭikkhepo*).
In this context, "exposing the basis" refers to statements such as: "You engaged in sexual intercourse, you took what was not given, you killed a human being, or you spoke what was untrue.
"Exposing the offense" refers to statements proceeding by way of such formulas as: "You have fallen into an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for sexual intercourse.
"Prohibition of communal residence" refers to [the declaration]: "There is no Uposatha with you."
It proceeds thus: “Is it an invitation (*pavāraṇā*), or a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*)? This is what is meant by the refusal of proper courtesy.

The refusal of proper courtesy consists in not performing such acts as salutation, rising from one’s seat, joining the palms in reverence, or prostrating. This should be understood to occur when one who is performing salutations and so forth in successive order fails to do so for one person while performing them for the others.
Even at this stage, there is what is called a “formal charge” (*codanā*). However, if one asks for whatever one desires, such as rice gruel or food, there is no formal charge by that much alone.
In the *Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*, another [section], beginning with "Monks, there is one illegitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha and one legitimate [suspension]," and so forth,

up to "ten illegitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha and ten legitimate [suspensions]," thus fifty-five illegitimate and fifty-five legitimate [cases] are stated; this constitutes one hundred and ten charges (*codanā*).
For one who accuses by what is seen, there are one hundred and ten; for one who accuses by what is heard, one hundred and ten;
and for one who accuses by suspicion, one hundred and ten—thus there are three hundred and thirty.
These, when multiplied by three for one who accuses by means of body, by means of speech, and by means of both body and speech, become nine hundred and ninety.
These remain the same whether one reproves oneself or causes another to reprove; thus, there are two thousand less twenty.

Furthermore, it should be understood that when divided by way of what has been seen and so forth, and according to the presence or absence of a basis (*samūlaka*/*amūlaka*), there are many thousands of ways of reproving.
Regarding these various types of reproving already mentioned, by means of any one of them, in the midst of the Saṅgha—
When the matter has been brought forward, the one who is reproved and the one who reproves should be told: "You will be satisfied with our decision.
If they say, "We shall be so," the Saṅgha should accept that legal case.
But if they say, "First decide it, venerable sirs; if it is acceptable to us, we will accept it," [then the Saṅgha may proceed], as in the case of a cetiya...
Having said, "Worship them for so long," and so forth, one should release [the case] by making a long discourse.
If, after having been exhausted for a long time and having had their assembly depart and their wings cut off, they request again, one should refuse them up to three times;
when they have become humbled, then their legal case should be adjudicated. And while adjudicating it, if the assembly is full of those who are shameless...
There is an assembly; that legal issue must be adjudicated by a committee.

If the assembly is deficient in wisdom, one should have them seek out a master of the Vinaya who is like-minded with them, and then settle that legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—exactly as it should be settled.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the factual basis; "Vinaya" refers to both the formal charge and the subsequent reminder;

and "the Teacher’s instruction" refers to the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). Therefore, when the accuser has announced the matter, the accused should be asked:
"Is this true, or not? Having thus examined the matter and having charged him with the factual basis, [the procedure continues].
Having brought it forward, that legal issue should be settled through the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*).
If, in that case, a shameless person accuses a conscientious person, and that shameless person is foolish and incompetent, the way [of proceeding] should not be granted to him;
rather, he should be asked: "On account of what do you accuse him? He will certainly say: "What is this, Venerable Sir? On account of what..."
"You do not even know his name! [one should say]. "How can you, being such a fool, find it proper to accuse another?

Thus he should be dismissed, and no further questioning should be granted to him. However, if he is shameless yet wise and competent, and is able to overwhelm and substantiate his case through what has been seen or heard, then after granting him the opportunity for questioning, [the matter should be handled] by one who is modest.
The formal act (kamma) should be carried out based on his admission.

If a conscientious person accuses an unconscientious person, and that conscientious person is ignorant and incompetent, being unable to provide a proper cross-examination, then this method should be given to him:
"On what grounds do you accuse him—on failure in virtue, or on failure in conduct, and so forth, regarding one or another?"
But why should this method be applied only to this case and not to the other? Is it not improper for those who uphold the Vinaya to follow a wrong course?
It is indeed not improper. However, this is not a wrong course; rather, it is what is called "supporting the Dhamma.
For the training rule was established for the purpose of restraining the shameless and supporting the conscientious. In that regard, the shameless...

Having found an opportunity, the shameless one will come forward aggressively; however, the modest one, having found an opportunity, will speak after establishing himself upon what was seen by means of what was seen, and upon what was heard by means of what was heard. Therefore, it is appropriate to provide him with assistance through the Dhamma.
But if that modest one is wise and competent, he speaks while remaining established; yet the shameless one thinks, "Even this does not exist."
He does not give the admission, saying, "This too does not exist.
In the case of one who is shameless, it must be done by means of an admission. To illustrate this point, the following story should be understood:
it is said that the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, after teaching the Vinaya to the bhikkhus below the Lohapāsāda, would emerge at the time of evening; at the moment of his emergence, two...
How did his adversaries proceed? One said, "This too does not exist, that too does not exist," and refused to give a formal admission.

Then, when only a small portion of the first watch of the night remained, the Elder thought of that person: "This one speaks by relying on [the scriptures], but this one refuses to give a formal admission;
many points have been brought forward; surely this must be the work of Māra."

The conviction that it was impure arose. Then, having signaled with the handle of his fan to the footstool-bearer, he said, “Friend, I am not fit to adjudicate this; have someone else decide it. “Why so, Venerable Sir?
The Elder explained the matter to him. A burning fever arose in the body of the person being accused, whereupon he paid homage to the Elder.
“Venerable sir, one who is fit to adjudicate must indeed be like you, a Vinaya-expert;
likewise, the accuser must also be like this,” he said. Then, having put on white robes and apologized, saying, “You have been wearying yourselves for a long time because of me,” he departed.
Thus, when one who is conscientious urges him, the unconscientious person does not give a confession even when many grounds for offense have arisen.
He should be described neither as "pure" nor as "impure"; he is called a "living corpse" or a "raw corpse.
If another similar ground for offense arises for him, it need not be adjudicated; he will be expelled in that manner.
But if one who is shameless accuses another who is shameless, he should be told: "Friend, what can be done by your word?
Having spoken thus to the other as well, they should be dismissed with the words: "Both of you live together, sharing the same enjoyment and use.
No formal investigation should be made for the sake of their moral discipline (*sīla*), but rather what is appropriate for the sake of their bowl, robes, dwelling cell, and so forth.
"It should be done after obtaining a witness.

Now, if one who is modest accuses another who is modest, and their dispute concerns only a very minor matter, they should be made to understand the situation, be made to confess their transgression by saying, "Do not act thus," and then be dismissed. However, if in this case the accused acts impulsively—
It has been transgressed; from the very beginning, there is no such thing as one who is shameless.
Yet, for the sake of protecting his own faction, he does not give a formal admission. Many people stand up, saying, "We believe him, we believe him.
Let him be pure once or twice on their account by means of their admission; however, from the moment the transgression occurred, he does not remain in his position.
A formal adjudication (vinicchaya) must not be given.
However, when one is adjudicating a case involving taking what is not given, twenty-five modes of theft (avahāra) must be carefully observed.
And among these, a skilled Vinaya-master, without hastily adjudicating the case once it has been brought forward, [should consider] five points.
These things are to be considered, with reference to which the ancients said:
"Having weighed five points— the object, the time, the place, the value, and fifthly, the use— the wise person should wear [the robe] for the sake of its purpose."
In this context, "the object" (vatthu) means the goods (bhaṇḍa).
For even when the thief says, "I have stolen such-and-such," the offense must not be charged until those goods have been investigated to see whether they have an owner or are ownerless.
Even if they have an owner, it must be investigated whether the owners are still attached to them or are detached from them. If, at the time they are still attached...

When goods have been carried away, one must determine their value and then determine the offense. If it was during a time when there were no inhabitants, the offense should not be determined as a *pārājika*.
However, when the owners of the goods are having the goods brought back, the goods must be returned; this is the proper procedure in this matter.
To illustrate this point, there is this story: it is said that during the time of King Bhātikarāja, at the festival for the Mahācetiya...
From the southern direction, a certain bhikkhu entered the courtyard of the cetiya carrying a yellowish-pale robe over his shoulder.
At that very moment, the king also arrived for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya. Then, as the clearing of the way proceeded, a great crush of the crowd occurred.
Consequently, that bhikkhu, oppressed by the press of people, departed without even noticing that the robe was slipping from his shoulder.
Having gone out and not seeing the saffron robe, he thought, "Who will get the saffron robe amidst such a crowd of people?
It is no longer mine," and having thus abandoned his effort, he departed. Then another monk, arriving later, saw that saffron robe;
seizing it with a thieving mind, he subsequently became remorseful and thought, "I am no longer a monastic now; I shall disrobe."
When that thought arose, he reflected, "I shall find out by questioning one who holds the Vinaya.
At that time, there lived in the Mahāvihāra a monk named the Elder Cūḷasumana, a master of the entire Piṭaka and a preeminent teacher of the Vinaya.
That monk approached the Elder, paid homage, requested his leave, and [disclosed] his own remorse.

He asked. The Elder, having arrived after the crowd had dispersed and realizing he had been caught, thought, "Now there is an opportunity here," and said, "If you could bring a monk who owns the saffron robes, it would be possible for me to establish your innocence.
"Venerable sir, how shall I see him? "Go here and there and look about."
Thus, having looked at all five great monasteries, he did not see him. Then the Elder asked him, "From which direction are many monks coming?
"From the southern direction, venerable sir. "In that case, measure out a yellow robe both in length and breadth and set it down;
having set it down, search through the sequence of monasteries in the southern direction until you find him."
“Bring the bhikkhu,” he said. Having done so, and having seen that bhikkhu, he brought him into the presence of the elder.
The elder asked, “Is this your yellow robe? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “Where did you find it? He explained everything.
Having heard what the other had done, the elder asked the other, “Where did you see this and take it?”
He related everything. Then the Elder said to him: “If you had taken it with a pure mind, there would have been no offense for you;
however, because you took it with a thieving mind, you have committed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). After confessing that, you shall be free from offense.
And as for this yellow robe, make it your own property and give it to this very monk.”
Thus the bhikkhu was as if anointed with the Deathless and attained supreme consolation. In this way, the object (vatthu) is to be examined.
As for "time" (kāla), it refers to the time of the theft. For that very same article may at one time be of little value and at another time of great value.
Therefore, by whatever value that article had at the very time it was stolen, by that value [the offense is determined].
An offense must be adjudicated. In this way, the time must be considered.
"Place" refers to the place of theft. For that stolen property, one must adjudicate the offense according to its value at the very place where it was stolen;
for in the place where the goods were located, the goods may have been of little value.
It is of great value elsewhere.
And to illustrate this point, there is this story: it is said that in the midst of the ocean, a certain bhikkhu obtained a coconut of excellent shape;
having hollowed out the husk, he fashioned a beautiful drinking vessel resembling a conch-shell bowl.
Having done so and placed it right there, he went to Cetiyagiri.
Another monk, having gone across the intermediate ocean and residing in that monastery, saw that bowl; taking it with a thieving mind, he returned to Cetiyagiri itself.
While that [first] monk was drinking rice-gruel there, he saw the bowl, and the monk who was the owner of the bowl said: "From where..."

“They have obtained this,” he said. “I brought it from the intermediate ocean. He [the official] dragged him into the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, “This is not yours; you took it by theft. Not obtaining a decision there, they went to the Mahāvihāra.
There, having had the drum beaten and having convened an assembly near the Great Cetiya, they reached a decision.
They began [the proceedings]. The elders who were experts in the Vinaya made the claim known.
In that assembly, there was an elder named Ābhidhammika Godatta, who was skilled in the Vinaya;
he asked, "Where was this bowl taken by him? "It was taken into the middle of the ocean," [they replied]. He then asked, "What is its value there?"
Nothing has any value there. For in that case, having broken open a coconut and eaten the kernel, one discards the shell;
but it is used for the sake of wood. What value does the manual labor of this bhikkhu have here? A māsaka or less than a māsaka.
But is there anywhere where the Perfectly Enlightened One has declared a *pārājika* offense for [stealing] a māsaka or less than a māsaka?
“‘It is designated. When this was said, there was a single cry of ‘Excellent! Excellent!’—well-spoken and well-determined.
At that time, King Bhātiya, having departed from the city for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya, heard that sound.
Asking, “What is this? and having heard everything in its proper sequence, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “While I am present...”
“Whether it be a legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning monks, nuns, or laypeople, it has been well-ascertained by the Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta;
I establish that which does not abide by his ascertainment by royal decree. In this way, the place (*desa*) should be examined.
As for value (*aggha*), it is the value of the goods. For whatever value a new good has, that subsequently diminishes, just as [the brightness of] freshly washed [cloth fades].
An alms-bowl worth eight or ten [units] later becomes of little value if it is broken, cracked, or damaged by a knot;
therefore, the value of an article must not always be determined solely by its original price. Thus should the value be examined.
"Use" refers to the use of the article; for even through use, the value of articles such as axes and the like diminishes.

Therefore, it should be investigated in this way: if someone steals an axe worth one quarter of a coin from another, the owner of the axe should be asked, "At what price was this axe bought by you? [The thief replies,] "For a quarter, venerable sir.
[He asks further,] "Did you keep it after buying it, or did you use it? If he says, "One day I used it as a tooth-stick..."
Or if a dye-skin, or a wooden vessel-cooking ladle, is cut, or has been sharpened by being whetted,
it should be understood that its original value is lost. And just as with an adze, so too with a collyrium box,
or a collyrium stick, or a key, or with straw, or with husks, or with brick-dust— if they have been whetted even once and merely washed— [the value is lost].
It is worth a high price. Even by the mere wiping of a triple-circle design with a shark-tooth comb,
or by the mere wearing of a water-cloth once as an undergarment or upper robe, or by the mere placing of it on the shoulder or the head,
or by the shaking off of rice and so forth, or even by removing one or two grains from it, or at the very least by picking up a single pebble or stone— [it is worth a high price].
The value is forfeited by merely discarding it; by turning over the container of ghee, oil, or similar substances;
by removing even a single fly or ant from it and then discarding it;
or by scratching with a fingernail and taking even a minute amount for the purpose of testing the sweetness of a lump of sugar. Therefore, anything worth even one *pāda*— [End of fragment]
In the manner already stated, the value is reduced by the owners through their own use; a monk who has taken it away should not be charged with a *pārājika* offense.
In this way, the value must be examined.

Having thus weighed these five points, a discerning person should maintain them, and should place an offense or a non-offense, whether grave or light, in its proper place. Regarding this, the teachers of the commentaries said:
“The training rule is equal to that; nothing else exists [to compare].
It is interwoven with many methods and provides a determination of its profound meaning.
Therefore, when a matter has arisen, a monk who knows the Vinaya—”
In this matter, while making a formal determination for the sake of supporting the discipline,
one who is diligent should plunge into the entire Pāḷi and its commentary, together with their underlying intent, and carry out the determination.
“One should never make an effort to see an offense,
thinking in one’s mind, ‘I shall see that there is no offense.
And even after seeing an offense, one should not speak of it again and again.”
Having investigated and reconciled this with the wise, speak thus:
"Even regarding permissible matters, through the influence of a mind that is fickle,
the qualities of a recluse fall away from worldlings here."
“Therefore, perceiving the requisites of others as a venomous snake or like a fire, a wise person should not honor them.
Furthermore, when one is investigating a claim regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), [one should ask]: “What have you attained? How did you attain it? etc.
"What has been attained? When was it attained by you? Where was it attained by you? Which defilements have been abandoned by you?

Of which qualities are you a possessor?"—these six points must be cleared up. For even if some bhikkhu were to declare the attainment of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), he should not be honored on that account alone; rather, it is for the purpose of clearing these six points [that he should be examined].
He should be asked: “What have you realized? Is it a jhāna, or one of the liberations (vimokkha), and so forth?
For whatever Dhamma has been realized by someone becomes clear to that person. If he says, “I have realized this,” then he should be asked, “How was it realized by you?
[And he should be asked: “Among the characteristics such as impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) and the rest, which did you take as the primary focus among the thirty-eight [meditation subjects]?”
"Or by what means has he become obsessed with phenomena (dhammas) classified as objects, or as form and formless, internal and external, and so forth?
For whatever one's obsession is, that becomes manifest to him. If he says, "This is my obsession;
this is how it was attained by me," then he should be asked, "When was it attained? Was it in the morning, or rather..."
"At one of the times such as midday," etc. For the time at which one has attained [realization] oneself is evident to everyone.
If he says, "I attained it at such-and-such a time," he should then be asked, "Where did you attain it?"—namely, "Was it in a daytime place, or in some other location such as a night-place?
For the place where one has attained it oneself is evident to everyone.
It becomes evident. If he says, "I have attained it in such-and-such a place," then he should be asked, "Which defilements have you abandoned?
and "Are they those to be abandoned by the first path, or rather those to be abandoned by the second path and so forth?
For to everyone, the defilements abandoned by the path they themselves have attained become evident.
If he says, "I have abandoned these specific defilements," then he should be asked, "Of which states are you a possessor?
Is it of the stream-entry path, or of one of the others, such as the once-return path?
For the state attained by oneself is evident to everyone. If he says, "I am a possessor of these specific states," [then he should be questioned further].
To this extent, his word should not yet be trusted. For monks who are learned and skilled in inquiry can verify these six points; however, the path by which this monk has come must be verified.
If that path of arrival is not verified, one should conclude: "By means of this path, the supramundane Dhamma cannot be attained."

It must be removed. However, if his path of progress is found to be pure—such that he is seen to have long been diligent in the three trainings, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwelling with a mind like the palm of the hand in the sky—then that bhikkhu’s declaration accords with his actual practice. It is just as if it were the water of the Ganges.
It is just as it has been said: "The Yamunā river flows together and merges with [the Ganges]; even so, the path leading to Nibbāna has been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One for his disciples;
the path and Nibbāna flow together and merge. Nevertheless, one should not offer honor based on this alone. Why?
Because there are some ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) whose practice is similar to that of those who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
Since such behavior occurs, that bhikkhu must be intimidated by various means.

For one whose taints are destroyed, there is no fear, trepidation, or horripilation even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon his head; yet for an ordinary person, such things occur even at the slightest provocation.
In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that the Elder Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, being unable to take charge of a certain alms-collector (piṇḍapātika), gave him a signal.
While the latter was bathing, he submerged himself at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī river and seized his feet.
The alms-collector, thinking "it is a crocodile," let out a great cry; at that time, they recognized him as an ordinary worldling (puthujjana).
During the time of King Candamukhatissa, however, the senior elder of the Saṅgha at the Mahāvihāra, who was an arahant with failing eyesight, remained within the monastery itself.

When the monks had gone out for alms, the king, thinking, “I shall seize the elder,” approached quietly and grasped his feet like a snake. The elder, remaining as motionless as a stone pillar, said: “Who—”
“Is it here? he asked. “I am Tissa, venerable sir. “Do you smell the fragrance, Tissa? Thus, for one whose taints are destroyed, there is indeed no fear.
However, even a certain worldling may be exceedingly brave and fearless; he can be tested by means of an object that excites passion.
King Vasabha, while testing a certain elder, had him seated in his house and [offered] jujube shoots in his presence.
He sat down, chewing. A drop of saliva moved from the Great Elder; the state of being an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) became manifest.
For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), craving for flavors is indeed well-abandoned, and there is no attachment even toward divine tastes.
Therefore, having examined him through these means, if fear, trepidation, or craving for flavors should arise in him, [he would think], "And you..."

The phrase “an arahant” must be removed. However, if he sits like a lion—fearless, undaunted, and unafraid—and does not give rise to attachment even toward divine objects, this bhikkhu should be understood as one who possesses the capacity for exposition and is worthy of the honor sent from all sides by kings, royal ministers, and others.
Thus, first of all, the proclamation of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) should be judged.
234. Furthermore, one who desires skill in the entire determination of the Vinaya must understand the fourfold Vinaya.
For the great elders of old, possessed of great psychic power, having extracted it, proclaimed the fourfold Vinaya as the compilers of the Dhamma.

What are the fourfold [methods]? They are: the discourse (sutta), that which is in conformity with the discourse (suttānuloma), the teacher’s tradition (ācariyavāda), and one’s own opinion (attanomati).
It is with reference to this that it was said: “By the ‘striking word,’ O Great King, by the ‘flavor,’ by the ‘teacher’s lineage,’ and by the ‘intention.
For here, the ‘striking word’ intends the discourse; the ‘flavor’ intends that which is in conformity with the discourse; and the ‘teacher’s lineage’ intends the teacher’s tradition.
"Intention" (*adhippāya*) means one's own opinion.
In this context, "sutta" refers to the Pāḷi of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Suttānuloma" (conformity with the suttas) refers to the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), which were spoken by the Blessed One as follows:
“Monks, that which has not been prohibited by me with the words, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to what is unallowable and opposes what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
Monks, that which has not been prohibited by me with the words, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to what is allowable and opposes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you. That which...”
“Monks, whatever I have not authorized by saying, ‘This is allowable,’ if it conforms to what is unallowable and contradicts what is allowable,
that is not allowable for you. Whatever I have not authorized by saying,
‘This is allowable,’ if it conforms to what is allowable and contradicts what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.”

The "Teacher’s Word" (*ācariyavāda*) refers to the tradition of commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) established by the five hundred Arahants who compiled the Dhamma; it is distinct from the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) and consists of the explanations that have descended through oral transmission.

"One’s own opinion" (*attanomati*) refers to the statement of a perspective established through one's own analytical grasp (*nayaggāha*) and personal insight, based on inference while setting aside the Suttas, the Suttas’ concordances, and the Teacher’s Word.
Furthermore, every traditional doctrine of the Elders (*theravāda*) found in the commentaries on the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya is also termed "one’s own opinion."
Furthermore, one who speaks while relying on their own judgment should not express themselves with dogmatic insistence;

rather, having observed the underlying reasons, they should speak by correlating the meaning with the text and the text with the meaning. One’s own judgment must be brought into alignment with the teachings of the masters.
If it enters into and accords with them, it may be accepted. If it does not...
If it does not descend [into the text] and does not accord with it, it is not to be accepted. For this so-called "personal opinion" (*attanomati*) is the weakest of all;
the teacher's doctrine (*ācariyavāda*) is stronger than personal opinion.

Even the teacher's doctrine must be made to descend into conformity with the Sutta. Therein, only that which descends and accords should be accepted; the other is not to be accepted. For the Sutta-conformity is stronger than even the teacher's doctrine.
Even that which conforms to the Suttas must be tested against the Suttas themselves. In doing so, only that which fits and is consistent with them should be accepted;
the other should not be accepted. For the Sutta itself is more authoritative than even what conforms to the Suttas.

Indeed, the Sutta is unalterable, like a formal assembly of judges, and like the established law during the time of the Buddhas. Therefore, when two monks debate, the proponent should take up the Sutta.

He speaks in accordance with the Sutta; the opponent [speaks] in accordance with the Sutta. Without casting aspersions or reproaches upon one another, that which is in accordance with the Sutta should be integrated into the Sutta.
If it integrates and accords, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should remain by the Sutta itself.
Then, if this person takes up the Sutta and speaks, the other [takes up] the teacher’s tradition (*ācariyavāda*). By those [means], too, without casting aspersions upon one another...
Without offering either praise or blame, the teacher’s statement should be compared with the Sutta. If it fits and accords with the Sutta, it should be accepted.
If it does not fit and does not accord, the teacher’s statement is to be criticized and should not be accepted; one must remain steadfast in the Sutta itself.
Now, if this person speaks by taking the Sutta as authority, while the other speaks according to his own opinion, there may be mutual derision or blame between them.
Without forming one's own opinion, it should be compared with the Sutta. If it fits and accords, it should be accepted;
if not, it should not be accepted, and one must remain by the Sutta alone.
Furthermore, if this person speaks having taken what conforms to the Sutta, the other [should] compare that with the Sutta; if it conforms to the Sutta, it should be accepted. If...
If it descends into and accords with [the Dhamma], and is recognized as having been included in the three councils and entered into the Canon (pāḷi), it should be accepted.

If it is not so recognized, and does not descend into or accord with [the Dhamma]—whether it be an external sutta, a verse (siloka), or some other censurable sutta brought from among the Guḷha, Vessantara, Guḷhavinaya, Vedalla, or others—it should not be accepted; rather, it should be accepted only if it conforms to the Suttas.

One must remain firm. Now, if this person speaks while adhering to the conformity with the Sutta, and the other speaks according to the teacher’s tradition (*ācariyavāda*), then the teacher’s tradition must be brought down into the conformity with the Sutta.
If it descends and accords, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one must remain firm in the conformity with the Sutta.

Furthermore, if this person speaks while adhering to the conformity with the Sutta, and the other speaks according to his own opinion (*attanomati*), then that personal opinion [must be compared] with the conformity with the Sutta.
It should be compared. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one must remain strictly in accordance with the Sutta.
Now, if this person speaks by taking up the teacher’s doctrine (ācariyavāda) while the other speaks from the Sutta, the Sutta should be compared with the teacher’s doctrine.
If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted. The other, being a censurable Sutta, should not be accepted; rather, one should remain in the teacher’s doctrine itself.

One should remain firm. Now, if this person speaks by adopting the teacher’s doctrine while the other speaks in accordance with the Sutta, the teaching in accordance with the Sutta must be brought down into the teacher’s doctrine.
If it fits and is consistent, that alone should be accepted; the other should not be accepted, and one should remain solely within the teacher’s doctrine.
Now, if this person speaks by adopting the teacher’s doctrine while the other speaks according to his own opinion...
One's own opinion should be compared with the teacher’s doctrine. If it fits and accords with it, it should be accepted;
if not, it should not be accepted, and one should remain solely within the teacher’s doctrine.
However, if this person speaks while adhering to their own opinion, and the other cites a discourse (sutta), that discourse should be compared with one's own opinion.
If it descends and accords, it should be accepted. Otherwise, that which is a censurable discourse should not be accepted;

one should simply abide by one's own judgment. Now, if this person speaks having taken their own judgment as the standard, and the other [speaks] in accordance with the Sutta, then that which is in accordance with the Sutta should be made to descend into one's own judgment.
If it descends and indeed accords, it should be accepted; otherwise, it should not be accepted, and one should simply abide by one's own judgment.

One must remain steadfast. Now, if this person speaks while relying on their own opinion, whereas the other speaks from the perspective of the Teacher’s tradition (*ācariyavāda*), the Teacher’s tradition should be compared with one's own opinion.
If it fits and accords, it should be accepted. Otherwise, that censurable Teacher’s tradition should not be accepted;
one should simply remain steadfast in one's own opinion and give weight to one's own conviction alone. And in all instances...
"Neither praise nor blame should be given.

However, if someone says something taking it to be allowable (*kappiya*), while another says it is unallowable (*akappiya*), then it must be compared with the Sutta and that which accords with the Sutta.
If it is allowable, one should stand by what is allowable; if it is unallowable, one should stand by what is unallowable.
Now, if this person presents many reasons and legal determinations from the Suttas to establish its permissibility (*kappiya*),
and the other does not find a reason [to refute it], one must remain in the position that it is indeed permissible. Then,

if the other person presents many reasons and legal determinations from the Suttas to establish its impermissibility (*akappiya*), one should take this as an occasion for one's own grasp [of the truth] and hold firmly.
One should not remain [with the gift] after having accepted it, saying "Very well"; rather, after having accepted it, one should remain only with what is unallowable (*akappiya*).
Now, if the shadow of the reason for both [accepting and remaining] is seen, then the very state of having refused is better; one must remain with what is unallowable.
For once the Vinaya has been reached, through the investigation of what is allowable and what is unallowable, one must restrain oneself, act firmly, and cut off the stream [of desire].
One should remain firm only in what is weighty.

However, if this person speaks while taking something as "unallowable" (akappiya), but another takes it as "allowable" (kappiya), the matter must be tested against the Sutta and that which is in conformity with the Sutta.
If it is allowable, one should remain firm in the allowable; if it is unallowable, one should remain firm in the unallowable.
Now, if this person demonstrates the state of being unallowable through many reasons for determining the Suttas, and the other finds no reason [to refute it], one should stand by what is unallowable.
If the other person demonstrates the state of being allowable through many reasons for determining the Suttas, and this person finds no reason [to refute it], one should stand by what is allowable.
If, however, the shadow of a reason appears for both, [one should investigate further].
One must not relinquish one's own grasp [of the matter].

Just as this exposition has been stated regarding what is allowable and what is unallowable, and what is unallowable and what is allowable, so too should the exposition be understood regarding the discussion of non-offenses and offenses, and the discussion of light and heavy offenses, as well as the discussion of heavy and light offenses;
for here there is only a difference in name, but no difference in the method of application.
Therefore, it has not been elaborated.

Thus, when a determination regarding what is allowable and what is unallowable arises, one should stand by the position of whoever finds a superior reason among the Sutta, the Suttānuloma, the teachers' doctrines, or one's own reflection;
however, by one who finds no such determination of reasons whatsoever, [the decision must be made otherwise].
"The Sutta must not be abandoned; one must stand firm in the Sutta itself. Thus, by one who aspires to skill in the entire determination of the Vinaya, this fourfold Vinaya must be understood.
Furthermore, even after knowing these four kinds of Vinaya, the person who upholds the Vinaya must be endowed with the three characteristics.
It must be so. For three characteristics of one who is a bearer of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) are required. What are the three?
His *sutta* is well-received, well-practiced, and well-determined according to the *sutta* and according to the phrasing—this is the first characteristic.
Furthermore, he stands firm in the Vinaya and is unshakable—this is the second. Moreover, his lineage of teachers...
"It is well grasped, well attended to, and well retained"—this is the third [point].
In this context, "sutta" refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "It has come to him well" means it has been properly acquired.
"Well-proclaimed" means it has been well-practiced, mastered, or brought to the lips through recitation. "Well-determined" means according to the suttas and according to the phrasing (anubyañjana).
It is well-determined through the Pāḷi, through questioning, and through the commentaries, having been mastered by cutting away doubt.
"But he stands firm in the Vinaya" means he is established in the Vinaya through a sense of moral shame (*lajjā*).

For one who lacks shame, even if he is very learned, might—out of a desire for gain and honor—distort the tradition (*tanti*) and teach what is contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
Having illuminated [the teaching], he creates a great calamity for the Sāsana, even causing a schism in the Saṅgha or a division within the Saṅgha.
But one who is modest, conscientious, and desirous of training does not deceive the tradition even for the sake of his life;
he illuminates only the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and establishes the Teacher’s instruction as something weighty. For thus, in the past, the Great Elders [recited] three times...

They uttered these words: "In the future, one who possesses a sense of shame will protect [the discipline]; one who possesses a sense of shame will protect it; one who possesses a sense of shame will protect it.
Thus, whoever possesses a sense of shame, by not abandoning and not overstepping the Vinaya, stands well-established in the Vinaya precisely through that state of shame.
"Irreversible" means: one who is reversible is one who, in the Canon (pāḷi) or in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā), [misunderstands] from below or from above, or the sequence of the words...
Or, when questioned, he dilates and wavers; he is unable to remain steady, and whatever is said by another, he assents to it;

having abandoned his own position, he adopts the opponent's view. But he who, when questioned according to the text or the commentary, whether in reverse order or in the sequence of the words, does not dilate and does not waver—
One who answers as if plucking out a single hair with tweezers, saying, "This is what we say;

this is what our teachers say," and in whom both the scripture and the interpretation of the scripture remain without being exhausted or depleted— like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel— is called "unshakable" (asaṃhīra).
"Furthermore, his succession of teachers has been well grasped" means that his lineage of elders and lineage of the tradition have been properly mastered.
"Well attended to" means it has been thoroughly brought to mind; upon mere reflection, it is like a lamp that has already been lit.
"Well retained" means it has been properly held in mind through the connection of what precedes and follows, both in terms of the meaning and the underlying reasons.
It was thus upheld. Having abandoned his own opinion, he acted for the sake of the purity of the lineage of teachers (*ācariyasuddhi*): "My teacher learned it from such-and-such a teacher;

he [learned it] from such-and-such. In this way, having brought forth the entire succession of teachers—which is a constituent part of the Theravāda—down to the Elder Upāli, who learned it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, he established it. Having further brought it down from there...
The Elder Upāli learned it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Elder Dāsaka learned it from his preceptor, the Elder Upāli;
the Elder Soṇa learned it from his preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka; the Elder Siggava learned it from his preceptor, the Elder Soṇa;
and the Elder Moggaliputtatissa learned it from his preceptor, the Elder Siggava, and from the Elder Caṇḍavajjī.
And so, having brought forward the entire lineage of teachers as a constituent of the Theravāda tradition and having established his own teacher at the end, he places him there.
For when the lineage of teachers is thus learned, it is well-learned.
However, one who is unable to do so must certainly learn two or three rounds [of the lineage]. For by the very last method, just as the teacher, the teacher’s teacher, and so on...
They speak of the Pāḷi and the interrogation; it is fitting to understand it in that way.

Furthermore, when a Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of deciding a case by means of a Vinaya expert endowed with these three characteristics, and the matter under consideration has been introduced, and what was to be said has been stated by both the accuser and the accused, [the expert], without deciding hastily, [should proceed].
Six points should be examined. Which six? The subject matter should be examined; the matrix should be examined;
the word-by-word commentary should be examined; the section on the triads should be examined; the intermediate offenses should be examined; and the non-offenses should be examined.
For even while examining the subject matter, one sees: "One should come having covered oneself with grass or leaves, and certainly not naked."
"One must come; whoever does not come incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In this way, he perceives a particular offense;
having cited that sutta, he will settle that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).

Even while consulting the *Mātikā*, he perceives one of the five types of offenses by way of such rules as "an intentional lie is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)," and having cited that sutta, he will settle that legal issue.

Even while examining the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*), one sees one of the seven offenses according to the method beginning with: "If one engages in sexual intercourse while the body is unimpaired, it is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*);
if one engages in sexual intercourse when the body is mostly impaired, it is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*)," and so forth;
having then brought the discourse (*sutta*) from that word-by-word commentary, [one applies it].
He will settle that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).

Even when looking at the section on triads (*tikapariccheda*), if he sees in the section on triads any offense—whether it be a triad of *saṅghādisesas*, a triad of *pācittiyas*, a triad of *dukkaṭas*, or another type—he will bring that sutta forward and settle that legal issue.

Even when looking at the intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*), if he sees an intermediate offense among the intervals between the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) such as, "If one suspends [the Saṅgha] after having withdrawn [the motion], there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," he will bring that sutta forward and settle that legal issue.
Even when looking for a non-offense, he sees the non-offense specified in each respective training rule (sikkhāpada) thus:

"There is no offense, O Bhikkhu, for one who does not consent, who has no intent to steal, who does not intend death, who does not intend to misrepresent, and who does not intend emission—provided it was unintentional, done through lack of mindfulness, or done unknowingly. Having brought forward that Sutta, he will settle that legal issue.
For whatever monk, skilled in the fourfold Vinaya and endowed with the three characteristics, shall settle a legal dispute after examining these six points,
his judgment is irrefutable and is like that which was judged by the Buddha himself sitting in person.
If anyone, having transgressed a training rule, [approaches] such a monk who is thus skilled in adjudication...
A monk, having approached, should ask about his own remorse. Having carefully examined it, if there is no offense, he should say, "There is no offense.
But if there is an offense, if it is one that requires confession, he should say, "It is one that requires confession.
If it is one that requires rehabilitation, he should say, "It is one that requires rehabilitation. Then, for him—
The shadow of a *pārājika* offense is seen, yet it should not be said that there is a "pārājika offense. Why?

Because the transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) are coarse, whereas the transgressions of taking what is not given and the grasping of hands are subtle and light in mind.
One commits these through subtlety and guards against them through subtlety; therefore, by way of distinction—
When asked about that matter of remorse, if he does not say "it is an offense" but rather says, "Our teacher maintains [that it is not]," then that monk should be sent by him with the message:
"Ask our teacher. If he returns again and says, "Your teacher, having examined it according to the suttas and the methods of reasoning, told me it is 'curable,'" then he should say: "Very well..."
"You should say, 'Do exactly what the teacher says.
However, if he has no teacher, but there is an elder with whom he studied together, he should be sent to him with the instruction: 'The elder with whom we studied together is the leader of the group;
go to him and ask. When that elder has also determined, 'This case is curable,' [one should say]: 'Excellent, very well.'"
"You must do as he says. If he has no elder with whom he has studied, but does have a wise pupil, he should be sent to him with the instruction:
"Go to such-and-such a junior monk and ask him. If that person also determines that the case is "curable," he should be told:
"Very well, you must do exactly as he says. Now, even if the junior monk appears to be in the shadow of a *pārājika* offense...
It manifests; therefore, he should not be told, "You are one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and even rarer than that are the going forth and full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, he should be told:
"Having swept a secluded place, having sat down for the midday rest, and having purified your moral discipline (*sīla*), first attend to the thirty-two aspects [of the body]. If he is healthy...
Virtue meshes with the meditation subject; formations appear clearly; the mind becomes one-pointed as if it had reached access or absorption;
even when a day has passed, he does not know it. When he returns to the place of attendance after the passing of the day, he should be asked:
"What was the state of your mental activity? And once the state of his mental activity has been reported, he should be told:
“Going forth is for the sake of purifying the mind; be diligent and practice the duty of a recluse.
But for one whose virtue is broken, the meditation subject does not succeed;
his mind wavers like that struck by a goad, he is consumed by the fire of remorse, and at that very moment he is as if sitting on a red-hot stone.
He emerges. When he has arrived, he should be asked, "What was the movement of your mind? Once the movement of his mind has been reported, [he should be told]:
"There is no such thing as secrecy in this world for one who performs an evil deed. For when first committing an evil act, one knows it oneself;
thereafter, the protective deities, those ascetics and brahmins who know the minds of others, and other deities come to know it. You yourself..."
"Now, seek your own well-being," he should be told. This is the procedure to be followed when a bhikkhu who has committed an offense comes and reports it himself.
Now, regarding that very censure (codanā) previously described in its various classifications, for the purpose of knowing its success and failure:
The analysis should be understood by way of the beginning, middle, and end, and so forth. For example: what is the beginning of an accusation, what is its middle, and what is its end?
In the case of an accusation, the formal granting of permission—saying, "I wish to speak to you; may the venerable one give me the opportunity"—is the beginning.
Having accused [the person] regarding the matter at hand and having reminded them of it, the formal decision is the middle. Regarding the offense...
The settlement reaches its conclusion by establishing [the accused] either in innocence or in guilt.
How many roots, how many bases, and how many grounds are there for a formal charge (*codanā*)? There are two roots for a formal charge:
one with a root and one without a root. There are three bases: what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected. I shall speak of the five grounds at the proper time.
"I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; I shall speak what is true, not what is false; I shall speak gently, not harshly;
I shall speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial; I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of ill-will.

Furthermore, by means of this method of exhortation, the person who exhorts [another] should reflect according to the sequence in the *Upāli-pañcaka*: "Am I indeed pure in bodily conduct? and so forth.
One should be established in the fifteen qualities that have been stated. The one who is reproached should be established in two qualities:
truthfulness and imperturbability.
And the investigator should ask the reproacher: "Friend, for what reason do you reproach this bhikkhu?"
“You are accusing him; you are accusing him of failure in virtue, you are accusing him of failure in conduct, you are accusing him of failure in view.
If he should say, “I am accusing him either of failure in virtue, or of failure in conduct, or of failure in view,” he should be addressed thus:
“But do you, venerable sir, know what failure in virtue is? Do you know what failure in conduct is?”

"Do you know what failure in view is? If he should say, "I know, friends, what failure in virtue is, I know what failure in conduct is, and I know what failure in view is," he should be asked, "But what, friend, is failure in virtue?
What is failure in conduct? What is failure in view? If he should say, "The four..."

“The thirteen *pārājika* offenses and the *saṅghādisesa* offenses—this is failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*). A serious offense (*thullaccaya*), an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*), an offense entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*), an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and an offense of improper speech (*dubbhāsita*)—this is failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*). Wrong view and extremist views—this is failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*).
He should be addressed thus: “Friend, when you accuse this bhikkhu, do you accuse him on account of what has been seen?”
"Do you accuse him on account of what has been heard, or do you accuse him out of suspicion?
If he should say, "I accuse him on account of what has been seen, I accuse him on account of what has been heard, or I accuse him out of suspicion," he should be addressed as follows:
"Friend, as for the fact that you accuse this bhikkhu on account of what has been seen, what have you seen? How have you seen it? When did you see it?"
“Where have you seen this? Have you seen one committing a *pārājika* offense? Have you seen one committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense?
Have you seen one committing a *thullaccaya*, a *pācittiya*, a *pāṭidesanīya*, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *dubbhāsita* offense?
Where was this monk? Where are you? What are you doing? And what is this monk doing?”
If he should say, "Friend, I do not accuse this bhikkhu on account of what was seen;
rather, I accuse him on account of what was heard," he should be addressed thus: "Friend, regarding that which you accuse this bhikkhu on account of what was heard—what have you heard?
How have you heard it? When did you hear it? Where did you hear it? That he has committed an offense entailing expulsion?"
"I have heard that he has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense; I have heard that he has committed a *thullaccaya*, a *pācittiya*, a *pāṭidesanīya*, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *dubbhāsita* offense;

it was heard by a bhikkhu, heard by a bhikkhunī, heard by a *sikkhamānā*, heard by a *sāmaṇera*, heard by a *sāmaṇerī*, heard by a lay male devotee (*upāsaka*), heard by a lay female devotee (*upāsikā*), or heard by kings."
"It was heard by the king’s ministers, it was heard by the sectarians, it was heard by the disciples of the sectarians.

If he should say, "Friends, I do not reproach this bhikkhu on account of what has been heard, but rather I reproach him on account of suspicion," he should be addressed thus: "Friend, as for the fact that you reproach this bhikkhu on account of suspicion..."
What do you suspect? How do you suspect? When do you suspect? Where do you suspect? Do you suspect that he has committed an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)?

Do you suspect that he has committed an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa), a serious offense (thullaccaya), an offense requiring confession (pācittiya), an offense requiring acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), or an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita)? Do you suspect this having heard it from a bhikkhu? From a bhikkhunī?
"Having heard... [and so on] ...having heard from the disciples of the sectarians, one suspects.
What has been seen accords with what has been seen; what has been seen meets with what has been seen.
Because it does not accord with what has been seen, it is suspected of being impure.
Such a person, by his own admission, must perform that Uposatha.
What has been heard accords with what has been heard; what has been heard coincides with what has been heard.
Because it does not accord with what has been heard, and because he is suspected of being impure, [the assembly] should not proceed.
Therefore, by the admission of that person, the Uposatha should be performed.
What is perceived accords with what is perceived; what is perceived flows together with what is perceived.
One does not go beyond what is perceived; it is suspected to be impure.
Therefore, on the basis of that person’s admission, the Uposatha should be performed by him.
An admission is valid among those who are conscientious; it does not exist in the case of those who are unconscientious.
Even if an unconscientious person should speak at great length, one should have the matter carried out by means of a formal inquiry into the sequence of events.
Furthermore, when a monk belonging to the order of battle approaches the Saṅgha, he should approach with a humble mind, with a mind like a dust-sweeping broom;

he should be skilled in [choosing] a seat and skilled in sitting down. He should not encroach upon the elder monks nor obstruct the junior monks from their seats; he should sit on a seat that is appropriate for him.
One should not be a speaker of various kinds of worldly talk, nor a speaker of frivolous chatter;
one should either speak the Dhamma oneself, or request another to do so, or one should not despise noble silence.
When the Saṅgha has authorized an individual as an investigator who wishes to investigate, he should not ask his preceptor for permission.
One should not ask about the teacher, one should not ask about the co-resident, one should not ask about the pupil,
one should not ask about the co-superior, one should not ask about the co-teacher, one should not ask about birth, one should not ask about the name,
one should not ask about the clan, one should not ask about the place of origin, nor about the family lineage.
He should be questioned, but his place of birth should not be questioned. Why is that? Because there might be affection or aversion toward him;
and when affection or aversion exists, one might act out of favoritism, or act out of hatred, or act out of delusion, or act out of fear.
Therefore, a person authorized by the Saṅgha who wishes to investigate as an investigator must be respectful toward the Saṅgha.
One should not be one who values the person, but one who values the true Dhamma; one should not be one who values material things, but one who is intent on the welfare of others;
one should not be one who seeks out a following, but one should investigate at the proper time, not at the improper time; one should investigate based on what is factual, not on what is unfactual;
one should investigate gently, not harshly; one should investigate in a way that is connected with the welfare of others.
One should investigate with a mind of loving-kindness, not with what is unbeneficial;
one should not whisper into the ear, nor look askance, nor squint the eyes,
nor raise the eyebrows, nor nod the head, nor make gestures with the hands, nor display hand-signs.
One should be skilled in sitting and skilled in posture; looking only the distance of a yoke,
conforming to the purpose, one should sit on one's own seat, neither rising from it nor shifting about,
not following a wrong path, not speaking with flailing arms, being unhurried, not reckless, and not impetuous.
One should be patient in speech, possessing a mind of loving-kindness and being compassionate toward others' welfare;
one should be merciful, seeking the welfare and protection of others; one should not engage in idle chatter, but speak with moderation;
one should be free from enmity and devoid of malice; one should examine oneself, examine others, examine the accuser, and examine the accused.

One who accuses improperly must be investigated; one who has been accused improperly must be investigated; one who accuses properly must be investigated; one who has been accused properly must be investigated.

Without letting what was said fall away and without failing to clarify what was not said, having thoroughly mastered the words and phrases that have been brought forward, and having questioned the other person, one should deal with him according to his admission.
One who is dull-witted should be made to laugh (at his own inconsistency).
One who is timid should be reassured; one who is fierce should be restrained; one who is impure should be made to reveal it.
One should not follow a course of action out of favoritism, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear.
One should maintain equanimity toward both teachings and persons. And thus, while investigating, the investigator acts as a teacher...
And he becomes one who carries out the teaching; he is dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by his wise fellow-celibates.
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of the *codanā* (formal admonition) and so forth, in the Compendium of Determinations on the Vinaya Excluded from the Sutta Pitaka.
32. Discussion on the Decision Concerning Emergence from Grave Offenses (Garukāpattivuṭṭhānavinicchayakathā) 236.
"Emergence from a grave offense" means emergence from a grave offense by means of disciplinary acts such as probation (parivāsa) and penance (mānatta).

In this regard, there are three kinds of probation: probation for concealed offenses (paṭicchannaparivāsa), probation for pure ends (suddhantaparivāsa), and probation for combined periods (samodhānaparivāsa).
Among those, first of all, the probation for concealment (paṭicchanna-parivāsa) should be granted according to the offense as it was concealed.
For one person’s offense may have been concealed for one day, while another’s for two days; likewise, one person may have one offense, while another has two, three, or more than that.
Therefore, when granting probation for concealment, the period of concealment must first be determined.
For this so-called offense is concealed in ten ways.
Herein, this is the matrix: there is an offense, and one perceives it as such; one is a regular monk, and one perceives oneself as such;
there is no obstacle, and one perceives it as such; one is capable, and one perceives oneself as such; and one desires to conceal it.

"And there is an offense, and he conceals it. In this context, "there is an offense, and he perceives it as an offense" means that whatever he has committed is indeed an offense, and he likewise perceives it as such.
Thus, knowing this, he conceals it; it is then concealed. However, if he perceives it as no offense in that instance, it remains unconcealed.
But regarding what is not an offense, it is so regardless of whether one perceives it as an offense or as no offense.
By concealing it, it becomes as if unconcealed; or, when one conceals what is light as heavy, or what is heavy as light, one stands on the side of the shameless, yet the offense remains unconcealed.
If, thinking a heavy offense is light, one confesses it, it is neither confessed nor concealed.
If, knowing a heavy offense to be heavy, one conceals it, it is concealed. [This applies to] the state of being heavy or light.
If one does not know [the offense], yet conceals it with the thought, "I shall conceal this offense," it is indeed concealed.

"A regular monk" (*pakatatta*) refers to one who has not been subjected to the three kinds of acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). If he conceals it while perceiving himself as a regular monk, it is concealed.
However, if he conceals it while perceiving himself as not a regular monk, thinking, "An act has been performed against me by the Saṅgha," [it is not concealed].

It is concealed. However, if one who has not been expelled conceals [an offense] while perceiving himself as one who has been expelled—or even while perceiving himself as one who has not been expelled—it remains unconcealed.
And this has been said: "One incurs a grave offense with remainder..."
"He conceals it out of disrespect;
yet the nun would not incur an offense.
This question was thought out by those skilled in wisdom.
For this question was asked by one who had been suspended (*ukkhitto*).
"Without obstacle" (*anantarāyiko*) means that for whom not even one of the ten obstacles exists;

if such a person conceals [the offense] while perceiving it as being without obstacle, it is concealed. Even if, due to a timid nature, he [is in] darkness out of fear of non-human beings or fierce wild animals...
If one conceals [an offense] while perceiving it as an obstacle, it is as if it were not concealed at all. Even for one dwelling in a mountain hermitage,
where he must report [his offense] after crossing a ravine or a river, if there is danger on the way from fierce beasts,
non-human beings, and so forth, or if pythons lie across the path, or if the river is full— provided such an obstacle exists, one who perceives it as an obstacle [is exempt].
He conceals it; thus it remains unconcealed. However, for one who conceals a matter that is an obstacle while perceiving it as an obstacle, it is indeed unconcealed.
If he is capable of going to the presence of a monk and reporting it, yet conceals it while perceiving himself as capable, it is concealed.
If there is even a slight boil in his mouth or a jaw-cramp piercing him, [it is unconcealed].
Whether his teeth ache, or he receives meager almsfood, he is unable to speak or go because of that;
yet, he perceives, "I am not able. This is called being one who, though capable, has the perception of being incapable.
By this [perception], even what is covered is uncovered. However, by one who is incapable of speaking or going due to being insufficient, yet possesses the perception of being sufficient—

Whether she conceals it by means of a small amount [of cloth] or with a sense of inadequacy, it is as if it were not concealed at all. "He desires to conceal it and he conceals it"—this is of plain meaning.

However, if, having set aside his responsibility with the thought, "I shall conceal it," he falls into a state of shamefulness either before the meal, after the meal, or during the first watch of the night and so forth, yet [conceals it] before dawn itself—
If one reports [the offense], this is called "one who wishes to conceal but does not conceal.

However, for one who has committed an offense while staying in a place where there are no monks, and who lets half a month or even a full month pass while waiting for a fellow monk to arrive or going to the presence of a fellow monk, this is called "one who does not wish to conceal but conceals"; yet this too is indeed not concealed.

However, if one, as soon as the offense has been committed, flees in haste like a man who has stepped on fire and then goes to a place where there are companions and confesses it, this is called "not concealing" because he does not wish to conceal it.

But if, even upon seeing his companions, he does not report it out of shame, thinking, "This person is my preceptor or teacher," the offense remains concealed. [The status of being] a preceptor and so forth...
For here, the immeasurable is not the measure; rather, only that which is of a similar nature is the measure. Therefore, it should be reported in the presence of one who is of a similar nature.
However, it should not be reported even in the presence of a preceptor who is of a dissimilar nature and would, upon hearing it, wish to proclaim it.
In this regard, whether one has fallen into an offense before the meal, after the meal, by day, or by night—until [the confession].
One should report it before dawn has risen. Once dawn has risen, the offense is concealed; by reason of that concealment, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
However, it is not permissible to disclose [the offense] in the presence of one who has incurred a similar *saṅghādisesa* offense.
If one discloses it, the offense is disclosed, but one is still not released from the *dukkaṭa*. Therefore, [it should be confessed] in the presence of one who is pure.

It must be disclosed. And when disclosing it, one may say, “I disclose one offense in your presence,” or “I declare it,” or “I announce it,” or “Know that I have fallen into one offense”; or one may speak by way of such phrases as “I disclose one grave offense.
