In all these ways, it remains indeed undisclosed [as a concealed offense], according to the *Kurundi*.
It has been stated. However, if one speaks in such a manner as, "I shall disclose a light offense," and so forth, it remains concealed.
Whether one reports the *vatthu* (the underlying fact), reports the *āpatti* (the offense), or reports both, it is considered reported in all three ways.
237. Thus, having examined these ten reasons, when granting a *paṭicchanna-parivāsa* (probation for concealment), [the procedure] must first...
The state of concealment must be understood; then, having observed both the day of concealment and the offenses, if it has been concealed for one day, one should request thus:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day.
Having thus made the request and spoken the formal act (*kammavācā*) according to the method set forth in the *Khandhaka*, the probation (*parivāsa*) [is granted].
It should be granted. Now, if it has been concealed for two or three days and so forth, one should apply the calculation according to the number of days up to fourteen days, as follows:
"concealed for two days," "concealed for three days," "concealed for four days," "concealed for five days," and so on... up to "concealed for fourteen days.
For that which has been concealed for fifteen days, it is "concealed for a fortnight" (*pakkhapaṭicchanna*).
The application [of the rules] should be made as follows: from then until the twenty-ninth day, it is "concealed for more than a half-month";

after that, one should apply the rules in this way: "concealed for a month," "concealed for more than a month," "concealed for two months," "concealed for more than two months," "concealed for three months...
[and so on] ... up to concealed for more than eleven months. When the year is full—

Regarding the phrase “concealed for one year,” one should apply the same construction by adding “more than one year,” “two years,” and so on, up to “sixty years” or “concealed for more than sixty years,” or even beyond that.
If, however, there are two, three, or more than that number of offenses, then just as it was said, "one offense," one should say, "two offenses" or "three offenses.
Beyond that, whether there be a hundred or a thousand, it is permissible to say "many.
Even in the case of various bases [of offenses], one may say: "Venerable sir, I have committed many *saṅghādisesa* offenses..."
“I have committed offenses: one emission of semen, one bodily contact, one lewd speech, one act of self-indulgence, and one act of matchmaking;
each was concealed for one day”—thus by way of enumeration; or: “Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses of various bases, each concealed for one day”—thus.

Alternatively, the construction should be made either by way of describing the subject matter—as in, "Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses concealed for one day"—or by way of the name alone.
In this context, the name is twofold: that which is shared with its own class (*sajātisādhāraṇa*) and that which is common to all (*sabbasādhāraṇa*).
Therein, "saṅghādisesa" is shared with its own class; "offense" (*āpatti*) is common to all. Therefore, "several... [and so forth].
"I have committed offenses concealed for one day"—it is likewise permissible to state this by way of a name common to all.
Indeed, these disciplinary acts such as *parivāsa* may be performed by way of the offense (*vatthu*), the clan (*gotta*), the name (*nāma*), and the specific offense (*āpatti*).
In that regard, "emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) is both the offense and the clan; "Saṅghādisesa" is both the name and the offense.

In this context, by the expression “emission of semen, bodily contact,” and so forth, as well as by the expression “of various bases,” both the *vatthu* (the physical act) and the *gotta* (the category) are included.
By the expression “an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*),” as well as by the expression “offenses,” both the name and the offense itself are included.
Therefore, the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) may be performed according to whichever of these [terms] is appropriate.
Now, however, we shall demonstrate the formal act (*kammavācā*) by applying it everywhere according to the common method for all offenses and the method for a plurality.
For even when one who has committed a single offense performs a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) for "a plurality," he is rehabilitated;
this is because without a single [offender], there can be no plurality. But when one who has committed a plurality [of offenses] performs [the act] for "one who has committed [an offense],"...
If it does not emerge while he is performing it, we shall therefore apply it according to the method for multiple offenses. For example:
when granting probation for concealed offenses, if there is an offense concealed for one day, [the applicant says]:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several offenses, each concealed for one day; I, venerable sirs, [approach] the Saṅgha..."
"I request a one-day probation for several offenses concealed for one day. Venerable Sir, I have committed several offenses concealed for one day;
for a second time, Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for a one-day probation for several offenses concealed for one day. Venerable Sir, I [have committed] several offenses..."
"I committed [these offenses] concealed for one day; for a third time, venerable sir, I request from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for these many offenses concealed for one day."—
Having had him request this three times in this manner:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhu named so-and-so has committed several offenses concealed for one day;
he now requests from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for those several offenses concealed for one day.
If it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha [should grant] to the bhikkhu named so-and-so, for those several offenses concealed for one day...”
“Let the Saṅgha give him a one-day probation; this is the motion.
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has committed several offenses concealed for one day;
he requests from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha—’”
The Saṅgha grants a one-day probation for the concealment of one day for the numerous offenses of the monk named so-and-so.

Whoever among the venerable ones approves of granting a one-day probation for the concealment of one day for the numerous offenses of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.

“A second time I speak this matter… [as before] …A third time I speak this matter… [as before] …‘The Sangha has granted a one-day probation for several offenses concealed for one day to the monk named so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Sangha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this manner, the formal proclamation (kammavācā) should be performed by calling out the name of each individual who has committed an offense.

And at the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), that bhikkhu must undertake the duties right there within the *māḷaka* boundary, saying: “I undertake the probation; I undertake the duties. Having undertaken them, he must announce it to the Saṅgha right there.
And while announcing it, he should say: “Venerable sirs, I committed numerous offenses concealed for one day.
I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those numerous offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha granted me...”
“Having granted me a one-day probation for offenses concealed for one day, I am now undergoing that probation;
I acknowledge it, venerable sirs; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who acknowledges it.
Thus should he announce it. And having grasped this meaning, it is indeed permissible to announce it by whatever means of speech.
Having announced this, if he wishes to suspend it, he should suspend it by saying, "I suspend the *parivāsa*; I suspend the duties.
Here, the *parivāsa* is suspended even by a single word, but it is properly suspended by two. The same method applies to the undertaking as well.
From the moment it is suspended, he stands in the position of one who is in his original status (*pakatatta*). [Regarding] the monks in the assembly hall...

When they have departed, it is permissible to deposit [the bowl] in the presence of even one person. Having emerged from the hall, one who has regained mindfulness should deposit it in the presence of someone who is departing together with him.
If that person has also gone away, one should inform another person to whom it has not yet been announced in the hall, and then deposit it.
And when announcing it, at the end one should say: "The Venerable One acknowledges me."

One should say, "May [the Venerable] bear it in mind. When announcing to two, one should say, "May the Venerables bear it in mind"; when announcing to three, one should say, "May the Venerables bear it in mind.
If the monastery has few monks, but like-minded monks are residing there, the demarcation of the night should be made right there in the monastery without setting aside one's duties.
If, however, it is not possible to clear the area, [one should go elsewhere].
Having laid aside the duties in the manner already described, at dawn one should sit down with a single bhikkhu—
having passed two stone-throw distances beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the place where an unenclosed monastery would require an enclosure—
having descended from the main road, in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence.
Having performed the duties at dawn according to the method already described, he should announce [the time].
When announcing it, if he is junior, he should say, "Friend"; if he is senior, he should say, "Venerable Sir.
If another monk comes to that place for some business and sees him, he should call out.
If he hears rain, it must be reported; for one who fails to report it, there is both a breach of the night-period and a transgression of the duty.
Now, if he enters the twelve-fathom precinct and departs while still unaware [of the rain], there is indeed a breach of the night-period, but there is no transgression of the duty;
at sunrise, the duty must be relinquished. If that bhikkhu, for some business...
If he has departed, he should report it to the first person he sees and then set it down.
Even after going to the monastery, he should report it to the first person he sees and then set it down. This is the procedure for one who has set down [the bowl]. 238.
Thus, for as many days as the offense was concealed, for that many days—or even more—[he must undergo the penance].
Or, having observed the probation for the purpose of dispelling remorse, one should approach the Saṅgha, undertake the duties (*vatta*), and request the trial period (*mānatta*).
For it is only when the duties have been undertaken that one becomes eligible for the *mānatta*, because the probation was completed while undertaking those duties.
However, for one who has not undertaken the duties, there is no further need to undertake them; for he [becomes eligible] simply by the passing of the days of concealment.
He becomes one deserving of the trial period (*mānatta*); therefore, the trial period must indeed be granted to him.
By the one granting it, [he should say]: "Venerable sirs, I committed several offenses concealed for one day;
I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*parivāsa*) for those several offenses concealed for one day, and the Saṅgha granted me..."

He granted me a one-day probation for those offenses concealed for one day; I, venerable sir, having completed that probation, now request from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for many offenses concealed for one day.
Venerable sir, I... [as before] ...I, having completed that probation, for a second time, venerable sir, request from the Saṅgha [the same] for many offenses...
“I request a six-night *mānatta* penance for these numerous offenses concealed for one day. Venerable sir… [as before] …Now that I have completed my probation,
venerable sir, for a third time I request a six-night *mānatta* penance from the Saṅgha for these numerous offenses concealed for one day.”
Having thus caused him to request three times:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so has committed several offenses concealed for one day;
he has requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha..."
The Saṅgha granted a one-day probation for several offenses concealed for one day to the monk named so-and-so;
he, having completed that probation, now requests from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those same several offenses concealed for one day.

And at the conclusion of the *kammavācā*, that bhikkhu must undertake the observance (*vatta*) right there within the *māḷaka* boundary, saying: "I undertake the *mānatta* penance; I undertake the observance. “I am practicing it, venerable sir; I am experiencing it. May the Saṅgha remember me as one who experiences it.
In this way it should be announced. Furthermore, having grasped this meaning, it is permissible to announce it using any form of speech whatsoever.
Having announced it, if he wishes to relinquish it, he should say in the midst of the Saṅgha: “I relinquish the *mānatta* penance; I relinquish the duties.”
It should be deposited. When the monks have departed from the hall, it is permissible to deposit it in the presence of even a single one.
Having exited the hall, one who regains mindfulness should deposit it in the presence of someone accompanying him.
If that person has also departed, one should inform another to whom it has not yet been announced in the hall and then deposit it.
When announcing [the offense], at the end one should say: "May the Venerable One bear me in mind. When two are announcing, one should say:
"May the two Venerable Ones bear us in mind. When three are announcing, one should say: "May the Venerable Ones bear us in mind.
From the moment it is laid down, he stands in the position of a regular monk (*pakatatta*). If the monastery has few monks, the monks who are of like standing...
If they are staying [there], the nights must be counted while remaining within the monastery itself without laying down the duties (*vatta*). If it is not possible to purify [the offense],
then having laid down the duties according to the method already stated, at the time of dawn, together with four or five bhikkhus, from the enclosure of an enclosed monastery,
or from the place where an enclosure would be required for one that is unenclosed— two...
Having passed beyond the range of a thrown clod, one should descend from the main road and sit in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence.
Before dawn, having undertaken the duties in the manner already described, one should announce them.
If another monk comes to that place for some business, and if he sees him, [he should] make a sound.
If he hears rain, it must be reported. For one who does not report it, there is both a breach of the night-period (*ratticcheda*) and a transgression of the rule (*vattabheda*).
However, if he enters within a twelve-fathom radius and then departs while still unaware [of the rain], there is indeed a breach of the night-period, but no transgression of the rule.
From the time of reporting onwards, with the exception of a single monk, the others may go if they have business to attend to.
It is permissible; when the sun has risen, the formal act (vatta) must be relinquished in the presence of that monk.

If he too departs on some business before dawn, one should relinquish the formal act after announcing it in the presence of whichever other monk one first sees—whether he has come out from his own residence or is a guest. And this is because...

Having informed the community and observed whether other monks are present, he may stay; thus, even if his group is incomplete, there is no fault of wandering alone or being separated from the community.
If he sees no one, he should go to the monastery and, having informed whoever he first encounters, deposit it there.
This is the exemption for one who has deposited the bowl.
239. Having thus practiced the *mānatta* penance for six nights without interruption, that bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated (*abbhetabbo*) wherever there is a Saṅgha of at least twenty bhikkhus.

And those performing the rehabilitation must first make him eligible for rehabilitation. For he stands in the position of a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu because he has completed his duties; and it is not permitted to perform rehabilitation for one who is already a regular bhikkhu.
Therefore, he should be made to undertake the duties; once the duties have been undertaken, he becomes worthy of rehabilitation.
Having likewise undertaken the duties and announced them, he should request rehabilitation. For one who has not abandoned the duties, there is no further need to undertake the duties.
Indeed, by the mere lapse of six days, he becomes worthy of rehabilitation; therefore, he is to be rehabilitated. And by the one rehabilitating him—
“Venerable sir, I committed several offenses concealed for one day.

I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day, and the Saṅgha granted me a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day. Having completed that probation, I [approach] the Saṅgha...”
I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for several offenses concealed for one day;
the Saṅgha granted me that six-night *mānatta* penance for those several offenses concealed for one day.
Venerable sirs, having completed the *mānatta*, I now request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. Venerable sirs... [as before] ...having completed the *mānatta*, for a second time...

“Venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. Venerable sirs, [I have fulfilled the probation]...pe... having completed the mānatta penance, for the third time, venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.”—Having thus caused him to request three times:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhu named so-and-so has committed several offenses, each concealed for one day.
He has requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for those several offenses, each concealed for one day.
The Saṅgha [grants] a one-day probation for the bhikkhu named so-and-so for those several offenses, each concealed for one day.”
He gave [it]. Having completed his probation, he requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for numerous offenses concealed for one day;
the Saṅgha granted a six-night *mānatta* penance to that monk named so-and-so for numerous offenses concealed for one day.
Having practiced the *mānatta*, he requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha, if it is the Saṅgha’s...
It is the proper time for the Saṅgha to rehabilitate the bhikkhu named so-and-so; this is the motion.

“Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhu named so-and-so has committed several offenses concealed for one day, and he has requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day; the Saṅgha...”
The Saṅgha granted a one-day probation (parivāsa) for several offenses concealed for one day to the monk named so-and-so;

having completed that probation, he requested from the Saṅgha a six-night period of penance (mānatta) for those same several offenses concealed for one day; the Saṅgha [granted] to the monk named so-and-so [the mānatta] for those several offenses concealed for one day...
He was granted the *mānatta* discipline for four nights; having completed the *mānatta*, he requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named so-and-so. Whoever among the Venerable Ones approves of the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“A second time I speak this matter... [as before] ...A third time I speak this matter...
[as before]. ‘The Saṅgha has suspended the monk so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way the formal act (kammavācā) should be performed.

In this way, first, the probation (*parivāsa*), the granting of the trial period (*mānatta*), and the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) for an offense concealed for one day are to be understood. By this same method, the appropriate formal acts (*kammavācā*) should be performed even for offenses concealed for two days or more.

But if the offense is unconcealed, then without granting probation, one should grant the trial period itself; once the trial period has been undergone, he is to be rehabilitated. How so? When granting the trial period, [the applicant] should first say:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several unconcealed offenses. Therefore, venerable sirs, I [approach] the Saṅgha..."
I request a six-night *mānatta* penance for numerous offenses that have not been concealed.
Venerable sirs, I... [as before] ...For a second time, venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for a six-night *mānatta* penance for numerous offenses that have not been concealed.
Venerable sirs, I... [as before] ...For a third time, venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for numerous offenses that have not been concealed.
“I request the *mānatta* penance for four days.
Having had him request this three times, [the monk] says:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so has committed numerous offenses that were not concealed...”
He requests from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* discipline for several unconcealed offenses.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a six-night *mānatta* discipline to the monk named so-and-so for several unconcealed offenses.
This is the motion (*ñatti*).
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so has committed several unconcealed offenses.
He requests from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconcealed offenses.
May the Saṅgha grant a six-night *mānatta* penance to this monk named so-and-so for those several unconcealed offenses.”

[The Saṅgha] grants it. Whichever venerable one approves of granting the *mānatta* penance for six nights for the many unconcealed offenses of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve should speak.
For the second time I state this matter... [as before] ...For the third time I state this matter... [as before].
“The Saṅgha has granted the probationer named so-and-so, for many unconfessed offenses, the six-night *mānatta* penance; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent;
thus do I understand this.”—In this way the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) should be made.

At the conclusion of the formal proclamation, the undertaking of the duties, the relinquishing of those duties, and the practice of the *mānatta* penance—all should be understood according to the method already stated. However, by the one announcing [the decision]:
“Venerable sir, I committed several offenses that were unconfessed.
I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconfessed offenses, and the Saṅgha granted me a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconfessed offenses.
I am now practicing the *mānatta* penance; I experience [the effects].”
“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who has completed the *mānatta* penance”—thus should it be announced.

When announcing to one, two, or three [monks], it should be announced in the same manner as prescribed for when the period of concealment has been completed. And once the *mānatta* has been performed, he should be rehabilitated (*abbhānetabbo*) wherever there is a community of monks numbering twenty. And by the one rehabilitating him—
“Venerable sir, I committed several offenses that were unconfessed.
I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconfessed offenses, and the Saṅgha granted me a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconfessed offenses.
Having completed the *mānatta*, I now request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.”
“I request it. Venerable sirs... [as before] ... Having completed the mānatta penance, for a second time, venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.
Venerable sirs... [as before] ... Having completed the mānatta penance, for a third time, venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.”—Having thus caused him to request three times—
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so has committed several unconfessed offenses;
he has requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconfessed offenses.
The Saṅgha [grants] a six-night *mānatta* penance for the several unconfessed offenses of this monk named so-and-so.”

He has completed the *mānatta* penance and requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rehabilitate the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion (*ñatti*).
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so committed several offenses that were not concealed."
He requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for several unconcealed offenses;
the Saṅgha granted that monk named [so-and-so] a six-night *mānatta* penance for those several unconcealed offenses.
Having completed the *mānatta*, he requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named [so-and-so].
"Whichever venerable one approves of the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the second time I state this matter... [as before] ...For the third time I state this matter... [as before].
The monk named so-and-so has been rehabilitated by the Saṅgha; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
Having spoken these words of the formal act (*kammavācā*) in this way, he is to be rehabilitated. Thus should the restoration from an unconfessed offense be understood.

241. If someone has one offense that is confessed and one that is unconfessed, after granting him probation for the confessed offense, when he has completed his probation, the *mānatta* penance should be granted to him [with the condition] regarding the unconfessed offense.
It is also permissible to grant it by combining concealed offenses. How so? If a concealed offense has been concealed for one day, [one should say]:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several offenses, each concealed for one day;
I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses, each concealed for one day; the Saṅgha granted me... [and so forth].
He granted me a one-day probation for those offenses concealed for one day;
having completed that probation, venerable sir, I committed numerous offenses that were unconcealed.
Therefore, venerable sir, I beg the Saṅgha for a six-night period of penance (mānatta) for those numerous offenses, both those concealed and those unconcealed.”
Having had him request it three times:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This bhikkhu named so-and-so has committed numerous offenses concealed for one day;
he has requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those numerous offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha—”
The Saṅgha granted a one-day probation (*ekāha-parivāsa*) for the various offenses concealed for one day of the monk named so-and-so;
he has completed that probation. This monk named so-and-so committed several offenses that were unconcealed;
he now requests from the Saṅgha a six-night penance (*chāratta-mānatta*) for those various offenses, both concealed and unconcealed.

He requests the *mānatta* discipline: "If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant the six-night *mānatta* discipline to this monk for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed. This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk, so-and-so, has committed many offenses, one of which was concealed for one day..."
He requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for several offenses concealed for one day;
the Saṅgha granted that monk named [so-and-so] a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day.
Having completed his probation, this monk named [so-and-so] committed several offenses that were unconcealed.
He requests from the Saṅgha the *mānatta* discipline for six nights for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed;
the Saṅgha grants the *mānatta* discipline for six nights for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed, to the monk named [Name];
whichever venerable one approves of granting the *mānatta* discipline to the monk named [Name]...
For those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed, there is the granting of the *mānatta* penance for six nights;
he who approves of this should remain silent. He who does not approve should speak.
For the second time I state this matter... [as before] ...For the third time I state this matter... [as before].
“The Saṅgha has granted the *mānatta* penance for six nights for those many offenses—both concealed and unconcealed—to the monk named so-and-so;
it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way, the formal act (*kammavācā*) should be performed.
And at the conclusion of the *kammavācā*, everything beginning with the undertaking of the duties is exactly as previously described. However, the one announcing [the decision] should say:
"Venerable sirs, I committed several offenses concealed for one day;
I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for those several offenses concealed for one day, and the Saṅgha granted me..."
He granted me a one-day probation for those offenses concealed for one day;
having completed that probation, venerable sir, I committed numerous offenses that were unconcealed.
Therefore, venerable sir, I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for those numerous offenses, both those concealed and those unconcealed.
“The Saṅgha granted me, for those many offenses both concealed and unconcealed, the mānatta penance for six nights.
I am now practicing that mānatta; I am experiencing it, venerable sirs.
May the Saṅgha bear me in mind as one who experiences it.”
It should be announced in this way.

Having fulfilled the *mānatta* penance for six nights in the manner prescribed without omission, and having completed that *mānatta*, he should be rehabilitated (*abbhetabbo*) in a place where there is a community (*saṅgha*) of at least twenty monks. And by the one performing the rehabilitation, [he should say]:
"Venerable sirs, I committed several offenses concealed for one day; I [approach] the Saṅgha regarding those several offenses..."

I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for several offenses that had been concealed for one day, and the Saṅgha granted me a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day.
Having completed that probation, venerable sirs, I committed several offenses that were unconcealed; I now request the Saṅgha for [the probation] regarding them.
“I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* penance for many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed;
the Saṅgha granted me that six-night *mānatta* penance for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed.
Venerable sirs, having completed the *mānatta*, I now request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.”
Having thus caused him to request three times:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so has committed several offenses concealed for one day;
he requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those several offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha..."
The Saṅgha granted a one-day probation (*ekāha-parivāsa*) for the many offenses of the monk named so-and-so that were concealed for one day;
he has completed that probation. This monk named so-and-so committed several offenses that were unconcealed;
he [now] requests from the Saṅgha a six-night penance (*chāratta-mānatta*) for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed.
He requested the *mānatta* penance; the Saṅgha granted that monk [named] So-and-so a six-night *mānatta* penance for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed.
Having completed the *mānatta*, he now requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rehabilitate the monk [named] So-and-so. This is the motion (*ñatti*).
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so has committed several offenses, each concealed for one day.
He has requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for those several offenses, each concealed for one day.
The Saṅgha [grants] a one-day probation for the monk named so-and-so for those several offenses, each concealed for one day.”
He granted it. Having completed his probation, this monk named so-and-so committed numerous offenses that were unconfessed;
he requested from the Saṅgha a six-night *mānatta* discipline for those numerous offenses, both confessed and unconfessed.
The Saṅgha [granted] for this monk named so-and-so, for those numerous offenses, both confessed and...
He granted a six-night *mānatta* penance for those offenses that had not been concealed; having completed the *mānatta*, he requests rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.

The Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named so-and-so. Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“A second time I speak this matter... [as before] ...A third time I speak this matter... [as before].
‘The Saṅgha has granted rehabilitation to the monk so-and-so; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
Having performed the formal act (*kammavācā*) in this way, he should be rehabilitated.

The Discussion on the Concealed Probation is finished. 242. There are two remaining types: probation to the end of purity (*suddhanta-parivāsa*) and simultaneous probation (*samodhāna-parivāsa*). Among these, probation to the end of purity is of two kinds:

the minor probation to the end of purity (*cūḷa-suddhanta*) and the major probation to the end of purity (*mahā-suddhanta*). Both of these [durations] involve the delimitation of nights, either in their entirety or...
It should be given to one who does not know some [of the offenses], who does not remember them, or who is doubtful about them.
As for the limit of the offenses, however, it is irrelevant whether he knows, "I have committed this many offenses," or not;

in that regard, starting from the day of his full ordination by way of direct order, or starting from the day the [offenses] were confessed by way of reverse order, [he should declare]: "Such-and-such... and..."
When asked, "Do you know that on such-and-such a day, or fortnight, or month, or year, your state was pure?
and he replies, "Yes, venerable sir, I know; for this long a time I have been pure," the probation granted to him is called the "minor purification-limit" (cūḷasuddhanta).
Having taken that [period] and living in probation for as long as he recognizes his own purification, he should remove that much and live out the remainder—
whether it be one month or two months. If he took it thinking,
"I am impure for only a month," but while living in probation he remembers another month, that month must also be lived out in probation.
Furthermore, there is no need for a further granting of the probation period (*parivāsa*).

Suppose one takes it up after reflecting, "I have been impure for two months," but while on probation, one reaches the conclusion, "I was impure for only one month"; then only one month must be spent on probation, and there is no need for a further granting of the probation period.
This is indeed called "probation to the limit of purity" (*suddhantaparivāsa*); it extends both upwards and downwards.
He descends. This is its characteristic. However, regarding the emergence from other offenses, this is the characteristic:

if one performs a legal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) declaring an unconfessed offense to be "confessed," that offense is cleared for him. If one performs a legal act of the Vinaya declaring a confessed offense to be "unconfessed," it is not cleared for him. [Likewise,] if one declares an offense concealed for a short time to be "concealed for a long time"...
If one confesses a long-concealed offense as "not long concealed," it is not cleared; if one confesses a short-concealed offense as "long concealed," it is not cleared.
Having committed one offense, if one says "many," it is cleared, because without one there can be no "many.
However, having committed many offenses, if one says "I committed one," it is not cleared.
However, if one who is questioned according to the aforementioned method of direct and reverse order neither knows nor remembers the limit of the nights,
or is uncertain about it, the *suddhantaparivāsa* granted to him is called a "great *suddhantaparivāsa*" (*mahāsuddhanta*).
Having taken that [period], one should dwell in probation by counting the nights from the day it was accepted until the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This does not ascend upward, but rather descends downward.

Therefore, if one who is undergoing probation makes a determination regarding the limit of the nights, thinking, "Whether it be a month or a year for me who has committed [an offense]," then one must undergo probation for that month or that year.
Furthermore, the characteristic of requesting and granting probation here should be understood as follows: that monk, having approached the Saṅgha...

Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down on his heels and extended his hands in reverential salutation, he should speak to them thus:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several offenses involving communal restoration (saṅghādisesa); I do not know the limit of those offenses."
“I do not know the limit of the nights; I do not remember the limit of the offenses; I do not remember the limit of the nights;

I am uncertain regarding the limit of the offenses; I am uncertain regarding the limit of the nights. Therefore, I request from the Saṅgha purification through the end-of-the-nights (suddhantaparivāsa) for those offenses.”
He should be asked a second time; he should be asked a third time.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk, named so-and-so, has committed several offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)."
He committed [an offense], he does not know the limit of the offense, he does not know the limit of the night;
he does not remember the limit of the offense, he does not remember the limit of the night; he is doubtful about the limit of the offense, he is doubtful about the limit of the night.
He requests from the Saṅgha a *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation until the end of purification) for those offenses. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha...
“Let the Saṅgha grant to the monk named so-and-so a *suddhantaparivāsa* for those offenses. This is the motion.
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so has committed numerous *saṅghādisesa* offenses;
he does not know the limit of the offenses, he does not know the limit of the nights, and he does not remember the limit of the offenses.’”
He does not remember the limit of the night, he is uncertain about the limit of the offenses, and he is uncertain about the limit of the night;
he requests from the Saṅgha a *suddhantaparivāsa* for those offenses, and the Saṅgha grants a *suddhantaparivāsa* for those offenses to the monk named so-and-so.
To whichever venerable one it is pleasing [to grant] the monk named so-and-so...
The granting of the *suddhanta-parivāsa* for those offenses is as follows: He who approves of this should remain silent;
he who does not approve should speak. A second time I state this matter... [as before] ...A third time I state this matter... [as before].
The *suddhanta-parivāsa* for those offenses has been granted by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it to be thus.
In this way, the probation for purification (*suddhantaparivāsa*) should be granted.

At the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), everything beginning with the undertaking of the duties follows the same method already described. However, by the one announcing it, [the words] should be spoken thus:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several offenses involving suspension (*saṅghādisesa*); I do not know the limit of those offenses."
"I did not know the limit of the nights; I do not remember the limit of the offenses; I do not remember the limit of the nights;
I am doubtful regarding the limit of the offenses; I am doubtful regarding the limit of the nights.

Venerable sirs, I requested from the Saṅgha purification through the end of the night (suddhantaparivāsa) for those offenses, and the Saṅgha granted me that purification through the end of the night for those offenses."
“I am living it out; I am experiencing it, venerable sir. May the Saṅgha remember me as one who experiences it”—thus should he announce it.
The announcement to one, two, or three [monks] is in the same manner. When granting the *mānatta* discipline to one who has completed the *parivāsa*, [the monk] should say:
“Venerable sir, I committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses; I do not know the limit of the offenses.”
"I do not know the limit of the nights; I do not remember the limit of the offenses; I do not remember the limit of the nights;
I am uncertain as to the limit of the offenses; I am uncertain as to the limit of the nights.

Venerable sirs, I requested from the Saṅgha purification through the end of the night (suddhantaparivāsa) for those offenses, and the Saṅgha granted me purification through the end of the night for those offenses."
“Venerable sir, having completed my probation, I beg the Saṅgha for six nights’ and seven nights’ probation for those offenses.
Having thus caused him to beg three times, [the monk] should say:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so has committed numerous offenses entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).”
He committed [an offense], but he did not know the limit of the offense, nor did he know the limit of the night;
he did not remember the limit of the offense, nor did he remember the limit of the night; he was uncertain about the limit of the offense, and he was uncertain about the limit of the night.
He requested from the Saṅgha a *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation until purification) for those offenses. The Saṅgha [granted] for that monk named so-and-so...
He granted a *suddhantaparivāsa* for those offenses; having completed that probation, he now requests a six-night *mānatta* penance from the Saṅgha for those same offenses.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a six-night *mānatta* penance to the monk named [Name] for those offenses. This is the motion (*ñatti*).
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhu named so-and-so has committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses;

244. What is called the “combination by value” (*agghasamodhāna*) refers to [the case] where, among many offenses, one, two, three, or several [offenses are combined].

Or, when all the offenses have been concealed for a very long time, having combined them according to their value and by way of delimiting the number of nights, probation is granted for the remaining offenses that were concealed for a shorter duration; this is called "combination by value" (*agghasamodhāna*).
Furthermore, in the case of one who has one hundred offenses concealed for ten days, and another hundred offenses also concealed for ten days...

Having combined them all together, one must undergo probation for ten days. In this way, by means of a single ten-day period, even a hundred days of probation are effectively completed. And this has also been said:
“Having concealed one hundred offenses for ten nights and one hundred offenses for ten nights,
and having lived for ten nights, one who is on probation shall be released.
This is called “aggregation by value.”

245. "Mixed combination" (missakasamodhāna) refers to that which is granted after various bases of offenses have been made into one. Herein is the method:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
one emission of semen, one bodily contact, one lewd speech, one act of self-will, one act of matchmaking, and one building of a hut."

“One who has committed one offense involving a dwelling, one offense involving a corrupt fault, one offense pertaining to another case, one offense involving schism in the Saṅgha, one offense involving siding with a schism in the Saṅgha,
one offense involving being difficult to speak to, and one offense involving defiling families— Venerable Sir, I, being such a person,
request from the Saṅgha a simultaneous probation for all those offenses.”
Having had him request it three times, the probation (parivāsa) should be granted by means of a formal act (kammavācā) corresponding thereto.

And herein, according to the method previously stated— whether by way of the basis, the clan, the name, or the offense— one should say either, "He has committed various saṅghādisesa offenses," or simply, "He has committed saṅghādisesa offenses."
It is indeed permissible to perform the formal act (kamma) after having joined [the formula]; therefore, we shall not present a separate formal act here.

Since it is possible to emerge from even those offenses belonging to different bases by means of the very same formal act previously presented as applicable to all offenses in common, that formal act alone is sufficient in this case.
The Discussion on the Parivāsa for Combined and Mixed Offenses is finished. 246.
If any bhikkhu, while undergoing parivāsa, disrobes or becomes a sāmaṇera, the parivāsa does not count for one who has disrobed or for a sāmaṇera.
If he receives full ordination again, his previous granting of parivāsa remains valid.
The probation that was granted is well-granted; the probation that was undergone is well-undergone; the remainder must still be undergone.

Even if one who is subject to the *mānatta* penance, while practicing the *mānatta*, or one who is subject to rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), should disrobe, or become a novice (*sāmaṇera*), and if he later receives full ordination again, for him that same previous granting of probation remains: the probation that was granted is well-granted.
The probation has been undergone, it has been well undergone; the *mānatta* that was assigned has been properly assigned;
the *mānatta* that was practiced has been well practiced—that monk is to be rehabilitated.
If any monk, while undergoing probation, becomes insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by pain, [then for] the insane...
For one whose mind is deranged, who is afflicted by pain, probation does not take effect.

If he later becomes no longer insane, no longer deranged in mind, and no longer afflicted by pain, then that previous granting of probation—whatever probation was granted, well-granted; whatever probation was undergone, well-undergone—is valid, and the remainder must still be spent.
This same principle applies to those who are eligible for the *mānatta* (penance) and other such stages.
If anyone who is undergoing probation (*parivāsa*) is suspended (*ukkhitaka*), the probation of one who is suspended does not count.

If he is subsequently reinstated, his previous granting of probation remains valid; whatever probation was granted was well-granted, and whatever was completed was well-completed, and only the remainder is to be undergone.
This same principle applies to those who are eligible for the trial period (*mānatta*) and so forth.
If the female sex organ of any bhikkhu becomes manifest, she is his very own preceptor and that is his very own full ordination;
no further preceptor need be taken and no further full ordination need be performed.

From the time of his bhikkhu full ordination until the counting of the years of seniority, that alone is the reckoning of his years of seniority; from this point on, a new reckoning of years of seniority must not be made. This is improper.
It is not fitting for her to live in the midst of the monks; therefore, she should go to the nuns' quarters and live together with the nuns.
Regarding those offenses that lead to confession or lead to rehabilitation which are common to both monks and nuns, they must be dealt with by the nuns;
indeed, the formal disciplinary act (vinayakamma) must be performed in the presence of the nuns.
However, regarding those offenses that are not shared by monks with nuns—such as the emission of semen and so forth—one incurs no offense for those offenses when the gender changes;
those offenses are considered already cleared. Even when the original gender reappears, one remains free from those offenses.
The same principle applies even when a nun manifests the male gender. And this has been said:
Now at that time, a certain monk’s female characteristics appeared.

They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, I allow him to take that very same person as his preceptor, that very same person for his full ordination, and to associate with the bhikkhunīs for those same years;
as for those offenses which are common to both monks and bhikkhunīs, [he shall be dealt with accordingly].”
Offenses may be cleared in the presence of bhikkhunīs. There is no offense for those offenses that are not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the male characteristic appeared in a certain bhikkhunī. To the Blessed One...
They reported this matter [to the Blessed One]. "I allow you, monks, to reunite with that very same preceptor, that very same full ordination, and those very same years of seniority;
and for those offenses of nuns that are common to monks, they may be cleared in the presence of monks. But for those offenses of nuns that are not common to monks..."
"From offenses, there is non-offense.
247. Now, here is the analysis independent of the canonical text (pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya):
Of these two genders, the male gender is superior and the female gender is inferior; therefore, the male gender is eliminated by powerful unwholesome [kamma], while the female gender...
It is established by weak wholesome [kamma]. However, the female sex organ disappears through weak unwholesome [kamma], while the male sex organ is established by strong wholesome [kamma].
Thus, both disappear through unwholesome [kamma] and are obtained through wholesome [kamma].
In that regard, if two bhikkhus, having performed recitation or discussion on the Dhamma together, [enter] a single dwelling...
When two people have lain down and fallen asleep, the female characteristic appears in one; both incur the offense of sleeping together.
If he wakes up, sees his own misfortune, and becomes pained and dejected, and reports this to the other during the night itself, he should be comforted by him thus:
"Let it be; do not worry. This is merely a fault of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); by the Perfectly Enlightened One..."
“The door is opened; whether it be a monk or a nun, the Dhamma is not closed off, and the path to heaven is not barred.
Having thus reassured her, he should say: “It is permissible for you to go to the nuns’ quarters.
Do you have any nuns whom you know personally? If she has such nuns, she should say, “I do. If not...
If they say, "There is none," that bhikkhu should be told: "Please show me favor;

take me first to the bhikkhunīs' dwelling. Taking her with him, that bhikkhu must go into the presence of those bhikkhunīs whom he has known personally, or whom she has known personally. And he must not go alone.

One should go together with four or five bhikkhus, taking a torch and a walking stick, having arranged the journey and released from the obligation [to stay], and proceed thinking, "We are going to such-and-such a place.

If the monastery is far outside the village, there is no offense regarding the transgressions of crossing a river midway, staying overnight apart from one's companions, or departing from the group. [Regarding] the nuns' quarters...
Having gone there, those bhikkhunīs should be asked: "Do you know the bhikkhu named so-and-so? If they say, "Yes, noble lady," [the messenger] should say:
"The female characteristics have appeared in him; please give her support. If they say, "Very well, noble lady;
now we too shall recite the scriptures and listen to the Dhamma; you may go," and they provide support, they are successful.

If they are modest and are supporters, one must not go elsewhere after having provoked them; if one does go, one is not exempt from the offenses of traveling between villages, crossing a river, staying overnight apart [from the group], or abandoning the group.
However, if they are modest but not supporters, it is permitted to go elsewhere.
Even if they are immodest, if they nevertheless provide support, it is permitted to go elsewhere after abandoning them as well. If they are modest...
And although she is a caregiver, she is not a relative; however, in the nearby village there are other relatives who act as caregivers, and they say it is permissible to go to them as well.

Having gone, if one was already under formal dependence (*nissaya*) even during the state of being a monk, one should receive dependence from a suitable nun; or, if the *Mātikā* or the *Vinaya* has been well-mastered, [one may proceed].

There is no further reason for learning [the precepts]. If one was a member of the assembly even during the time of being a bhikkhu, those who received full ordination in his very presence have been properly ordained;
however, he must receive dependence (nissaya) from another. Even those who previously lived depending on him must receive dependence from another.
A novice monk (sāmaṇera) who has reached the full age must also choose a preceptor (upajjhāya) from another.
However, the triple robe and the bowl that were determined for him during his status as a monk lose their formal determination;
they must be determined anew. The *saṅkaccikā* and the *udakasāṭikā* must also be taken up.
Furthermore, whatever extra robe or extra bowl has been set aside after a formal legal act (*vinayakamma*) was performed, all of that also loses its legal status.
It must be accepted again. Even oil, honey, molasses, and so forth that have already been accepted lose their status as "accepted" [once the seven-day period has passed].
If one's gender changes on the seventh day from the time of acceptance, it is permissible to accept them again for another seven days.
However, that which was accepted while one was a monk, belonging to another monk, does not lose its status as "accepted. This also applies to both...
That which is set aside as common property without being divided, that the one of natural status (pakatatta) protects.
But that which has been divided and belongs to him alone, he loses his right of acceptance over it. And this has been stated in the Parivāra:
"Oil, honey, molasses, and even ghee—if one should take these oneself and store them..."
“There is an offense for one who consumes [food] when seven days have not yet passed, provided there is a valid reason.
This question was conceived by those skilled in the Dhamma.
This was indeed said with reference to a change of sex. “Acceptance” means [the invalidation of the gift] through a change of sex or through death.

One loses [the status of a monk] by renouncing the training, by returning to the lower life, by giving [the robe] to one who is not ordained, by discarding it without regard, and by taking it back after having seized it away.

Therefore, even if there is something belonging to him that has been accepted and set aside, such as a piece of myrobalan, his entire act of acceptance is lost. However, whatever belongs to him in a bhikkhu’s dwelling, having accepted it—
Whether it was placed there without being formally accepted, she is the mistress of it all; having had it brought, it may be taken.
However, whatever here is permanent—such as a dwelling or a garden belonging to her—these should be given to whomever she wishes.
Among the thirteen formal permissions (*sammuti*), any permission obtained during the time of being a bhikkhunī ceases entirely with the *purimikā* (the first rains-residence).

The assignment of lodgings is suspended. If, after lodgings have been assigned during the later period, one's gender changes, and the Saṅgha of monks wishes to give her the gains that have arisen, it should be given after obtaining their formal consent.
If, while one is undergoing probation for a concealed offense shared with the bhikkhunīs, one's gender changes...
Furthermore, the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight must be granted again. If the sex changes while she is practicing the *mānatta*, the *mānatta* for a fortnight must be granted again.
If the sex changes after the *mānatta* has been practiced, the nuns must perform the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*) for her.
If, when the unwholesome karmic result has been exhausted and during the period of the fortnightly *mānatta*, the sex changes once more, [she must undergo] six days...

Only *mānatta* penance should be granted. If, after the *mānatta* period has been observed for a fortnight, she changes her sex, the monks must perform the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*) for her.
Even in the case of a nun changing her sex, the entire legal analysis should be understood according to the same method already stated.
However, this is the distinction: if the offense of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta-āpatti*), committed during the time she was a nun, was concealed, the granting of *parivāsa* [is required].
It does not exist; only a *mānatta* of six nights should be given. If her gender changes while she is practicing the *mānatta* for a half-month, that [half-month] is of no account;
only a *mānatta* of six nights should be given. If it changes after she has already practiced the *mānatta*, the monks should rehabilitate her (*abbhetabba*) without giving the *mānatta* again.
But if her gender changes again before the monks have given the *mānatta*, [the procedure must begin anew].

The *mānatta* penance for a fortnight must be granted by the bhikkhunīs. If, while he is practicing the six-day *mānatta*, there is again a change of gender, the *mānatta* for a fortnight must likewise be granted.
However, when a change of gender occurs after he has completed the *mānatta*, the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) must be performed by the bhikkhunīs.
And if there is another change of gender, even though she remains in the state of a bhikkhunī, as for those offenses...
"Those [defilements] previously subsided are indeed well-subsided. 248.

“Ask for permission. Even if they continue to do so after this has been said, there is no offense, even though they are acting from the time they were forbidden.
One must not accept the formal authorization as a teacher of bhikkhunīs, nor should one who has been authorized teach the bhikkhunīs.

If one acts with the thought, “Go into the presence of those who hold the Vinaya,” neither of these two things should be done.
One should not take the place of seniority in the monastery; one should not act as the reciter of the Pātimokkha or the proclaimer of the Dhamma;

One should not go or sit down [within the boundary]; having left a twelve-fathom precinct, one may both go and sit down alone.
Whatever constitutes the limit of the Saṅgha’s seating, the limit of the beds, or the limit of the dwellings, that should be given to him.
In this context, "limit of the seating" refers to the seat for the newest member of the Saṅgha in the dining hall and other such places; that should be given to him. In that regard—
He should sit down. "The limit of the bed" (*seyyāpariyanto*) means the limit of beds; it refers to the most inferior bedstead or stool.
For he is not permitted to take a bed for himself in his own allotted place according to the seniority of the rains-residence (*vassagga*);

rather, he must be given an inferior bed that remains after all the monks have searched for and taken their own, one filled with filth and excrement and woven with rattan vines and the like. Just as...
And just as with a bed, so too a dwelling place is not permitted for him in his own allotted spot according to the *vassa* (rainy-season) assignment;
however, he should be given a leaf-hut that has been selected by all the monks and remains over, or a ground cleared of dust, or one filled with bats and mice.
If all the regular monks (*pakatatta*) are tree-root dwellers or open-air dwellers and do not take up a roofed shelter, then all [of them] [must share the available dwellings].
By these [means], they are said to have "given up their residence," and among them, one receives whatever one desires.
On the day of entering the rains retreat, if one stands to one side and requests the requisites, one may receive them for the duration of the rains; however, one does not receive a formal lodging.
One who wishes to take a fixed residence for the rains must do so after having set aside the formal observance (*vatta*).
In a place where one has been invited by relatives with the words, “Come taking such-and-such number of bhikkhus,” one should not,

having made an arrangement such as, “Venerable sir, a certain family has invited bhikkhus; come, let us go there,” approach families acting as a forerunner or a follower of the bhikkhus, saying, “Venerable sir, at such-and-such [place]...”

"If the people in such-and-such a village wish for the arrival of the bhikkhus, it would be good indeed if you were to provide them with support"—it is permissible to speak in this way by way of the Vinaya.

One who feels ashamed to announce [the arrival] to those who come and go should not undertake the forest-dweller's ascetic practice (*āraññika-dhutanga*). Even one who has already undertaken it by nature [should not do so].
Taking a second monk, one should cause dawn to rise in the forest; one must not dwell alone.

Likewise, in the dining hall and other such places, even if one feels embarrassed by sitting at the end of the row of seats, one should not undertake the alms-food-eater’s ascetic practice (*piṇḍapātika-dhutanga*).
However, for one who is already an alms-food eater by nature, there is no prohibition; nor, on that account, is alms-food [to be refused].

He should have the almsfood removed [from the monastery], thinking, "Let them not recognize me. Having had the almsfood removed and sitting down to eat right there in the monastery, he should not have the almsfood brought out for this reason:
"I will count the nights; if I see a monk passing by and do not inform him, there would be a break in my count," and also with the thought, "Let not even a single monk recognize me."
If, due to one's own inclinations, one causes novices to prepare food in the monastery, one is not even permitted to eat it; one must enter the village for alms.

However, for one who is ill, or occupied with duties such as being a master of construction work (*navakamma-ācariya*) or a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), it is permissible to remain in the monastery itself.
Even if hundreds of monks are wandering about in the village and it is impossible to announce [one's presence], one may go to the village residence (*gāmakāvāsa*).
It is appropriate to dwell in a place where there is a community (*sabhāga*). Since it has been said: "Monks, a monk who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) must inform an incoming monk;
he must inform an incoming monk; he must inform [the community] on the Uposatha day; he must inform [the community] at the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*);
if he is ill, he must inform even by means of a messenger"—therefore, by an incoming monk who has gone to some monastery...
In that case, it must be announced to the monks. If he sees them all standing in one place, it must be announced while remaining in that very place.
But if they are standing separately at the foot of trees and so forth, he must go to each respective location and announce it;
for one who intentionally fails to announce it, there is a breach of the night-period and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the violation of the proper conduct. Then, while searching—
Some do not see [the resident monks]; there is merely a breach of the night [limit], but no *dukkaṭa* offense for the breach of the duty (*vatta*).
Even for a guest who has come to his own dwelling-place, whether one or many, it must be announced in the manner already stated;
here too, the breach of the night limit and the breach of the duty are to be understood in the manner already stated. If the guests, having rested for a moment...
Or if they pass through the middle of the monastery without having rested, one must inform them as well.
If they depart without his knowledge, but he finds out after they have gone, one should go and inform him;

for one who is unable to reach him or to make himself heard, there is only a breach of the night-period (ratticchedo), and no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for breaking the rule of conduct. This also applies to those who do not enter inside the monastery.

If they enter the boundary of the precincts and depart, and he, having heard the sound of their parasols, the sound of their coughing, or the sound of their sneezing, recognizes that they are guests, he must go and inform them; even if he recognizes it only after they have left, he must still follow them and inform them.
For one who is unable to reach them, there is a breach of the night-period (ratticcheda), but no breach of the proper conduct (vattabheda).
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even one who arrives at night and departs that very same night causes a break in the continuity of the night for him;

however, because he was unaware [of the rules], there is no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the proper conduct (*vatta*). If he performs the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) without even knowing [the requirements], it is as if it were not done at all—thus it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
Therefore, it should be performed by including the additional nights. This is the "unerring practice" (*apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā*).
If one sees a bhikkhu traveling by boat on a river and so forth, standing on the opposite bank, moving through the air,
or situated far away on mountain slopes, in forests, and the like, and if there is the recognition that he is a "bhikkhu," one must go by boat or the like,
or raise a loud cry, or pursue him with speed, and inform him; for one who does not inform him, there is a breach of the night-period (ratticcheda).

And there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the duty. However, if one strives but is unable either to reach [the person] or to inform them, there is only the breaking of the night [of the observance], but no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the duty. Yet the Elder Saṅghasenābhaya speaks in terms of what constitutes a proper domain and what does not:

"It is said that for one who does not report within the proper domain, there is both the breaking of the night and the offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the duty; whereas in what is not the proper domain..."
"But neither of these two exists," [said another]. The Elder Karavīkatissa said, "The mere determination that 'this is a recluse' is the authoritative criterion.
Even if it is outside one's range, there is no *dukkaṭa* offense for a breach of the rule; however, there certainly is a violation of the night [limit].
On the day of the *uposatha*, visiting monks arrive, thinking, "We shall attend the *uposatha* ceremony. By means of psychic power (*iddhi*)...

Even while traveling, if they learn that it is the Uposatha day, they descend and perform the Uposatha; therefore, even on the Uposatha day, one must announce [the matter] for the purpose of purifying those who have arrived.
The same procedure applies to the Pavāraṇā ceremony. One who is ill and unable to go should send a monk to make the announcement;
it is not permissible to send one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).

A monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) should not go from a residence or non-residence containing monks to a residence or non-residence that is either devoid of monks or belongs to a different community (nānāsaṃvāsaka), except in the company of a regular (pakatatta) monk or except when there are obstacles.
For where there is not even a single monk, one must not dwell there; indeed, nights spent dwelling there do not count toward the probationary period.

The nights are counted [as part of the *pārivāsika* period]. However, regarding the ten kinds of obstacles (*antarāya*), even if the nights are not counted, one must certainly go for the sake of being freed from those obstacles.
Therefore it is said: "except in the case of an obstacle. It is not permitted to perform a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) together with those of a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*);
yet, even if one does not inform them, there is no interruption of the night count, as it is exactly like a residence where no monks are present.
Therefore it is said: “or [a dwelling] with monks belonging to a different communion.
A monk who is on probation must not live under the same roof as a regular (pakatatta) monk, whether in a residence (āvāsa) or a non-residence (anāvāsa).
In this context, a “residence” means a lodging constructed for the purpose of dwelling; a “non-residence” means a shrine-hall (cetiyaghara).
The Bodhi-house, the broom-shed, the wooden shed, the water-shed, the privy, and the gateway—these and others are such places. Regarding these, the *Mahāpaccarī* states:
"In any one of these, one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka) is not permitted to dwell even in a space enclosed by a roof and bounded by the place where water falls;
however, one who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) is not permitted [to stay] within the very same residence."
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated without qualification that [the probationer] is "prevented by the pouring of water. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
"Among these many places bound by five-colored canopies, the one undergoing probation and the one who has been suspended are prevented from [meeting] with the regular monk by the pouring of water.
Therefore, even if they are in different precincts, it is not permitted if they are under the same canopy.

But if, in this case, even though one who has been ordained that very day, or one who is a regular monk (*pakatatta*), has first entered and lain down, and a *pārivāsika* who has been [in probation] for sixty years enters later and lies down knowing [of the other], there is both a breaking of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of the rule.
For one who does not know, there is only a breaking of the night, but no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the rule. But if, after he has sat down...
If one who is in his original status enters and lies down, and the one on probation knows it, there is both a breaking of the night and an offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the proper conduct.
If he does not know it, there is only a breaking of the night, but no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of the proper conduct.
A monk who is on probation, upon seeing a monk in his original status—even one ordained on that very day—must rise from his seat.
And having risen, one should not even go out of sight [of the senior] thinking, "I was made to rise while sitting comfortably here";
rather, a bhikkhu who is of regular standing (*pakatatta*) must certainly invite him to a seat by saying, "Teacher, this is the seat; please sit here.
However, a junior bhikkhu should not go to a senior elder who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) with the thought, "I shall cause the great elder to be humiliated."
A monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) must not sit on the same seat as a regular (pakatatta) monk;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, may he sit on a high seat; nor, while sitting on the ground, may he sit on a seat.
However, it is permissible for him to sit at a distance of twelve cubits, having left that space between them. A monk who is undergoing probation [must act] together with a regular monk...
One should not walk on a walking-path when another is walking on a walking-path; one should not walk on a high walking-path when another is walking on a low walking-path;
one should not walk on a walking-path when another is walking on the ground.
However, in this case, even if it is low, [one may walk] on a constructed walking-path where a boundary has been made on the unenclosed ground, sand has been spread, and a support has been fixed.
One should not practice walking meditation there, much less on one that is constructed with brickwork and surrounded by a railing.
However, if it is enclosed by a wall, provided with a gateway, or well-concealed within mountain clefts, forest thickets, or groves, it is permissible to practice walking meditation on such a path;
even if it is not concealed, it is permissible provided one leaves a sufficient margin of space around it.

A monk undergoing probation (pārivāsika) must not dwell under one roof— whether in a monastery or outside a monastery— with a monk who is senior to him in the duration of his probation, nor with a monk deserving of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha),
nor with a monk deserving of the trial period (mānattāraha), nor with a monk practicing the trial period (mānattacārika),
nor with a monk deserving of rehabilitation (abbhānāraha). However, in this case, if the senior monk undergoing probation has already lain down first...
The other, knowing [the situation], lies down afterwards; for him there is a breach of the night-period and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the violation of the duty.

For the senior, however, there is only a breach of the night-period, but no offense of wrong-doing for the violation of the duty. If he lies down without knowing, there is no violation of the duty for either of the two, but there is a breach of the night-period.
Now, if the junior one who is on probation has already lain down first, and the senior...
If he lies down afterwards, the junior monk knows [of it], his night is cut short, and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty.

For the senior monk, however, there is only the cutting short of the night, not a breach of duty. If he does not know [of it], there is no breach of duty for either of them, but the night is still cut short.
If they lie down without one being before or after the other, there is only the cutting short of the night for the senior monk.
"In the case of the other, there is also a breach of the duty (*vattabhedo*)"—this is stated in the *Kurundi*.
Two *pārivāsikas* of equal seniority lie down together; one lies down first, while the other, knowing [the rule], lies down afterwards.

For the latter, the night is cut short and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty. For the one who lay down first, there is only the cutting short of the night, not a breach of duty.
If even the one lying down later does not know [of the offense], there is no breach of the observance for either of them, though there is a breaking of the night.
If both lie down without regard for who came first or last, there is only a breaking of the night for both, but no breach of the observance.
For if two who are on probation were to live together, they might learn of each other’s transgression and become disrespectful.
Or, having become remorseful, they might commit that same offense or one even more grave than that, or they might fall away from the faith;
therefore, sleeping together with them is prohibited in every respect.

Furthermore, it should be understood that those subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) and others occupy the position of a regular monk (pakatatta) relative to those on probation (pārivāsika). Therefore, by a monk who is on probation or subject to being sent back to the beginning...
A monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline, one who is practicing the *mānatta*, or one who is eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), shall not sit on the same seat as another such monk;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, shall he sit on a high seat; nor, while sitting on the ground, shall he sit on a seat;
nor shall they walk up and down in the same walking path; nor, while walking on a low walking path, shall he walk on a high walking path.
One should not walk back and forth on the ground where walking meditation is to be performed.
"Monks, a monk who is on probation must not consent to being saluted by,
rising up for, joining his palms to, performing respectful duties toward, offering a seat to, offering a bed to, providing water for washing the feet for, or providing a footstool for regular monks."
"Because of the statement: 'For a foot-bench, for receiving the bowl and robes, for bathing, and for back-massage— whosoever should consent to these,

there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who consents to salutation and so forth from regular bhikkhus— excluding only those who are junior, those on probation, and the rest including even those subject to being sent back to the beginning— and also from one's own pupils."
For one who accepts [the invitation], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, they should be told: “I am performing a disciplinary act (vinayakamma);

do not perform the duties for me; do not ask me for permission to enter the village. If sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith say, “Venerable sir, you yourself perform your own disciplinary act,” and yet they still perform the duties and even ask for permission to enter the village, [then it is permissible].
From the time it was prohibited, there is no offense.
“Monks, I allow monks who are on probation to greet one another according to seniority;
I allow them to rise for one another, to perform the añjali-salutation, to perform acts of respect, to offer seats, to offer beds, to offer water for washing the feet, footstools, and footrests.”

Furthermore, because of the statement, "The receiving of the bowl and robes, bathing, and the rubbing of the back [are permitted]," it is permissible for monks who are on probation (pārivāsika) to accept salutations and other such courtesies from one another according to seniority—that is, whichever one is senior must perform salutation and so forth toward the more junior.
"I allow, monks, for monks who are on probation, five things according to seniority: the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā..."

Because of the statement, "the rains-bathing cloth, the meal, and the food," it is permissible to perform these five [duties], such as the Uposatha, according to seniority even with those who are ordinary (pakatatta);
therefore, it is permissible to sit within arm's reach while the Pātimokkha is being recited.
