However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is said: "Without sitting apart from the text, and without leaving the text, one should not release the arm’s reach."

"It should be sat upon," it is said. When the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* (confession of purity) is being performed, one should sit in the junior position of the Saṅgha and, remaining seated right there, perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* according to one's own recitation.

At the *pavāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) as well, one should sit in the junior position of the Saṅgha and, remaining seated right there, perform the *pavāraṇā* according to one's own recitation. After the Saṅgha has struck the gong...
It is permissible to take even a *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloak) that is being distributed for one's own allotted place.

"Offering" (*oṇojana*) is said to mean distribution. For if two or three designated meals (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth fall to a *pārivāsika* monk, and he has an expectation of a private meal (*puggalika-bhatta*), he may take those [designated meals] in order and say: "Venerable sir, please take the lower ones."
Having said, "Today I have expectations for food; I will take it tomorrow," they should be released.
In this way, one is permitted to receive them on subsequent days. However, the *Kurundi* states: "On the following day, they must be given to him first.
But if he does not take them and does not release them, he does not receive them on the next day. This is the *oṇojana*.
This [allowance] was specifically authorized for one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) alone. Why?
Because when he sits in the junior position in the Saṅgha during the meal, rice gruel, solid food, and so forth may or may not reach him;
therefore, this was specifically authorized for the sake of providing for him, thinking, "May he not suffer from lack of alms-food."
"Bhatta" refers to the food for the Saṅgha in the quadrangle of the monastery, which is to be taken by those who have arrived in order of seniority.
One receives this according to one's seniority; however, one is not permitted to go or stand according to the sequence of the *pāḷi* (the line).
Therefore, stepping back from the *pāḷi*, standing within arm’s reach, and extending the hand—just as a hawk swoops down and seizes its prey—one should take it in that manner.
It should be accepted. One may not have it brought by monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) or novice monks (*samaṇuddesa*);
however, if they bring it themselves, it is permissible. The same rule applies even to the king’s great communal meal (*mahāpeḷabhatta*).
But regarding the four-hall meal (*catussālabhatta*), if one wishes to partake, when the alms-food has been set aside for oneself, one should say: "I have food today; I will take it tomorrow."

“It receives two alms-meals on the following day,” so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. Even meals designated for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) and the like must be accepted only after being set aside from the formal list (*pāḷi*).
However, in a place where they serve food after seating [the monks], one should sit as the eldest among the novices and as the most junior among the monks.
This is the duty of one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-vatta*).

It should be understood that this same procedure applies to those who deserve to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), those who deserve the trial period (mānattāraha), those undergoing the trial period (mānattacārika), and those deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha).
However, regarding the conduct for one undergoing the trial period, there is the specific distinction: "It must be announced daily.
Furthermore, concerning the interruptions of the night-count: "Upāli, there are three ways in which the night-count of a monk on probation (pārivāsika) is interrupted: living together..."
According to the statement, "separation and failure to announce," the breaking of the night for a monk under probation occurs through any one of these three causes:
the co-residence described by the method beginning with "in the same enclosed space together with a regular (pakatatta) monk," the residence of one alone,
and the failure to announce oneself as a guest and so forth.

However, for one undergoing the *mānatta* penance, there is a break in the night-counting due to even one of these four causes, according to the statement: "Upāli, there are four breaks in the night-counting for a monk undergoing the *mānatta*:
living together [with those not yet purified], living apart, failure to announce [one's status], and wandering in a group that is incomplete.
Here, a "group" (*gaṇa*) means four or more. Therefore, even if [he is with] three...
He dwells together with the bhikkhus; thus there is indeed a breaking of the night.
Thus ends the discussion on the determination of the emergence from grave offenses in the Compendium of Determinations on the Vinaya Excluding the Pāḷi Text.
33. Discussion on the Determination of Valid and Invalid Acts (Kammākammavinicchayakathā) 249. Regarding the phrase "valid and invalid acts" (*kammākamma*):

here, "acts" (*kamma*) refers to four types—namely, an act by announcement (*apalokanakamma*), an act by a motion (*ñattikamma*), an act by a motion and one resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and an act by a motion and three resolutions (*ñatticatutthakamma*).
In how many ways do these four types of acts fail? They fail in five ways.
They fail—either by reason of the subject matter, or the motion, or the proclamation, or the boundary, or the assembly.

How do formal acts fail by reason of the subject matter? One performs a formal act that ought to be done in the presence of the parties in their absence; this is an illegal act that fails by reason of the subject matter.
One performs a formal act that ought to be done with interrogation without interrogation; this is an illegal act that fails by reason of the subject matter.
If one performs a formal act that should be done by confession without confession, it is an illegitimate legal act with a defective basis.

If one grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of mindfulness, it is an illegitimate legal act with a defective basis. If one performs a legal act of further penalty against one who deserves a verdict of past insanity, it is an illegitimate legal act with a defective basis.
[Likewise] a legal act of censure against one who deserves a legal act of further penalty...
It performs an illegal act that fails in its basis. It performs a *niyassakamma* (act of demotion) against one deserving a *tajjanīyakamma* (act of censure);
it is an illegal act that fails in its basis. It performs a *pabbājanīyakamma* (act of banishment) against one deserving a *niyassakamma*; it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
It performs a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation) against one deserving a *pabbājanīyakamma*; it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
An illegal act: to carry out a *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) against one who deserves a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation) is an illegal act because it fails in its basis.
To grant a *parivāsa* (probation) to one who deserves a *ukkhepanīyakamma* is an illegal act because it fails in its basis.
To send back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassati*) one who deserves a *parivāsa* is an illegal act because it fails in its basis. [To do so] to one who deserves a sending back to the beginning...

To grant the *mānatta* penance [to one who does not deserve it] is an illegal act (adhamma-kamma) with a defective basis (*vatthu-vipanna*). To rehabilitate (*abbheti*) one who deserves the *mānatta* penance is an illegal act with a defective basis.
To confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon one who deserves rehabilitation is an illegal act with a defective basis.

To perform the Uposatha on a day other than the Uposatha day is an illegal act with a defective basis. To perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) at a time other than the invitation ceremony is an illegal act with a defective basis.
An illegal act: ordaining a paṇḍaka is an illegal act because the basis is defective.

[Likewise is it for] one living in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who has shed blood [of a Buddha], a hermaphrodite, or one less than twenty years of age.
If one ordains a person who lacks the requisite basis, it is an illegal act (adhammakamma) because the basis has failed. Thus, legal acts fail by way of the basis.
How do legal acts fail by way of the motion (ñatti)? Legal acts fail by way of the motion in five ways:
when one does not refer to the basis, when one does not refer to the Saṅgha, when one does not refer to the person, and when one does not refer to the motion.
Or one puts forward the motion later. In these five ways, formal acts fail because of the motion.
How do formal acts fail because of the proclamation? Formal acts fail because of the proclamation in five ways:
one does not specify the subject matter, one does not specify the Saṅgha, one does not specify the individual, or one omits the proclamation.
Or one makes the proclamation at the wrong time. By these five ways, formal acts fail because of the proclamation.
How do formal acts fail because of the boundary? Formal acts fail because of the boundary in eleven ways:
one establishes a boundary that is too small; one establishes a boundary that is too large; one establishes a boundary with a broken mark; one establishes a boundary with a shadow-mark...
One delimits a boundary; one delimits a boundary that lacks defining marks; one delimits a boundary while standing outside the boundary; one delimits a boundary across a river;
one delimits a boundary across the ocean; one delimits a boundary across a lake; one causes a boundary to intersect with another boundary;
one causes a boundary to be submerged by another boundary. By these eleven modes, formal acts (kamma) fail due to the boundary.
How do formal acts fail in an assembly? Formal acts fail in an assembly in twelve ways:

(1) when a formal act that requires a quorum of four is to be performed, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have not arrived; (2) the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought forward;
(3) those present raise an objection; (4) in a formal act requiring a quorum of four, as many bhikkhus...
Those who have reached the stage for the formal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought forward; those present raise an objection.
In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four, those who have reached the stage for the formal act have arrived;
the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought forward; those present raise an objection.

In a formal act performed by a group of five... [as before] ...in a formal act performed by a group of ten... [as before] ...in a formal act performed by a group of twenty: if as many bhikkhus as are required for that formal act have not arrived;
if the consent of those entitled to give consent has not been brought forward;

and if those present raise an objection—[then it is invalid]. In a formal act performed by a group of twenty: if as many bhikkhus as are required for that formal act have arrived... [as before] ...if those present raise an objection—[then it is invalid].
The consent of those who ought to give consent has not been brought; those present raise an objection.
In a formal act requiring a quorum of twenty, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived, and the consent of those who ought to give consent has been brought;
yet those present raise an objection. By these twelve ways, formal acts fail within the assembly.

In a formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a quorum of four, there are four regular monks (*pakatatta*) who are eligible for the act; the remaining regular monks are those entitled to give their consent (*chandāraha*).
He for whom the Saṅgha performs the act is neither eligible for the act nor entitled to give consent, but rather he is one who is the object of the act (*kammāraha*).
In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of five, there are five regular monks who are eligible for the act; the remaining regular monks are those entitled to give their consent.

Regarding one for whom the Saṅgha performs an act: he is neither one who has attained to the act (*kammappatta*) nor one who is entitled to give consent (*chandāraha*), but rather one who is entitled to the act (*kammāraha*).
In an act performed by a group of ten, ten bhikkhus who are regular members (*pakatatta*) have attained to the act; the remaining regular members are entitled to give consent.
Regarding one for whom the Saṅgha performs an act: he is neither one who has attained to the act nor one who is entitled to give consent, but rather one who is entitled to the act.

In a formal act (*kamma*) performed by a group of twenty, there are twenty regular monks (*pakatatta*) who are eligible for the act; the remainder are regular monks who are entitled to give their consent (*chandāraha*).
He for whom the Saṅgha performs the act is neither eligible for the act nor entitled to give consent, but rather he is one for whom the act is intended (*kammāraha*). 250.

To how many types of formal acts does a *ñattikamma* (an act consisting of a motion) belong? To a *ñattikamma*, a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation), and a *ñatticatutthakamma* (an act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation).
To how many matters does it apply? The *apalokana-kamma* (act of notification) applies to five matters.

The *ñatti-kamma* (act consisting of a motion) applies to nine matters. The *ñattidutiyakamma* (act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) applies to seven matters. The *ñatticatutthakamma* (act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) applies to seven matters.

Which are the five matters to which the *apalokana-kamma* applies? Reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), shaving the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*), the *brahmadaṇḍa* (penance of silence), and the characteristic of the act itself as the fifth. The *apalokana-kamma* applies to these five matters.
To what nine matters does a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) apply?

It applies to reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), the Uposatha, the Invitation (*pavāraṇa*), formal authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), receiving (*paṭiggahaṇa*), postponement (*paccukkaḍḍhana*), and the characteristic of the formal act itself as the ninth.
A formal act consisting of a motion applies to these nine matters.

To what seven points does a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) apply? Restoration (*osāraṇa*), sending away (*nissāraṇa*), formal authorization (*sammuti*), giving (*dāna*), rescinding (*uddharaṇa*), confession (*desana*), and the characteristic of the act itself (*kammalakkhaṇa*) as the seventh. A *ñattidutiyakamma* applies to these seven points.
To what seven points does a *ñatticatutthakamma* (an act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) apply? Restoration, sending away, formal authorization... [and so forth].

Giving, censure, formal admonition, and the characteristics of legal acts—these seven constitute the seventh [category]. The legal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) proceeds through these seven bases. This, then, is the method of the text (*pāḷinaya*). 251.
Now, here follows the exposition of the analysis starting from the beginning: a "legal act of seeking permission" (*apalokanakamma*) refers to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary (*sīmaṭṭhaka*).

The formal act (kamma) to be performed after having cleared away [the objections], having brought forth the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it, and having announced it three times with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha.
A *ñattikamma* is a formal act to be performed with a single motion (*ñatti*) with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, in the manner already described.
A *ñattidutiyakamma* is a formal act to be performed with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha... in the manner already described.
"With one consent, one motion, and one proclamation"— this is the formal act to be performed by means of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

A "formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations" (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is a formal act to be performed by means of a motion and three proclamations, following the same method as stated above, with the consent of a united Saṅgha.

In that regard, a *apalokana-kamma* (act by way of announcement) must be performed only after announcing; it must not be performed by way of a *ñatti-kamma* (act consisting of a motion) or other such methods.
A *ñatti-kamma* must also be performed by establishing only a single motion; it must not be performed by way of an *apalokana-kamma* or other such methods.

However, regarding a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation), there are cases where it may be performed after announcing and cases where it may not. Among these, the formal authorization of a boundary (*sīmā-sammuti*), the removal of a boundary (*sīmā-samūhana*), and the offering of the *kathina* robe-material [are examples].
These six formal acts—the lifting of the *kaṭhina* robe, the designation of a site for a hut, and the designation of a site for a monastery—are heavy;
they must not be performed by merely seeking permission (*apaloketvā*), but must be carried out after proclaiming the motion and the second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

The remaining thirteen permissions—such as the permission to appoint a distributor of lodgings, a distributor of robes, and so forth—are light formal acts; these may be performed even by merely seeking permission.
They may be performed; however, they must certainly not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñatti*) or a motion followed by a third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*).
Some say: "That which is performed by way of a *ñatticatuttha-kamma* is more firm; therefore, it should be performed. But if that were so, there would be a confusion of formal acts (*kamma-saṅkara*);
therefore, it is strictly rejected as something that should not be performed. However, if [the formula] is deficient in syllables or deficient in words...
If there is a word that has been poorly uttered, it is permissible to repeat it again and again for the sake of correcting it.

This constitutes the strengthening of an irreversible formal act (*akuppakamma*); in the case of a reversible formal act (*kuppakamma*), it remains as a formal act. A formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*) must be performed only after announcing the motion and the three proclamations;
it must not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of mere intimation (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth.
"An act that ought to be performed in the presence [of the assembly] is performed in the absence [of the assembly]; it is an illegal act because the matter is defective.

In this regard, there are acts that ought to be performed in the presence [of the assembly], and there are acts that ought not to be performed in the presence [of the assembly]. Among these, "that which ought not to be performed in the presence" refers to:
ordination by messenger, the overturning of the alms-bowl, the setting upright of the alms-bowl, and the authorization for a mad monk to be considered mad.
There are eight kinds [of formal acts]: the authorization for trainees (*sekkhasammuti*) among families of trainees; the "divine punishment" (*brahmadaṇḍa*) against the monk Channa;
the act of proclamation (*pakāsanīyakamma*) against Devadatta; and the act of non-prostration (*avandiya-kamma*) to be performed by the Saṅgha of nuns against a monk who displays contempt.
These eight kinds of formal acts, when performed in the absence of the subject, are well-performed and irreversible; so too are all other formal acts.

They must be performed in the very presence [of the parties involved]. Having brought them under this fourfold *sammukhāvinaya*—namely, presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals—they must be performed.

For when performed in this way, they are well-performed; however, if performed otherwise, they are defective in their basis (*vatthuvipanna*) because they have been done without this matter known as *sammukhāvinaya*.
Thus they are called [by those names]. Therefore it was said: "A legal act that ought to be performed in the presence of the assembly is performed in their absence;

this is an illegal act because it is deficient in its basis (*vatthu*). In the case of acts that ought to be performed with interrogation and so forth, the very performance of the interrogation and so on constitutes the basis;
since these are performed without that basis, they too should be understood as being deficient in their basis. Furthermore, regarding one who is less than twenty years of age, or the final basis...

Or, even when one ordains someone who has previously committed an offense or any one of the eleven types of persons incapable [of the path], it is an illegal act (adhammakamma) because the subject matter (vatthu) is deficient.
This is the analysis regarding failure in the act (kammavipatti) by way of the subject matter.

Regarding failure by way of the motion (ñattivipatti), however, one does not grasp the subject matter; that is, [one fails] in respect to the person for whom one performs the act of ordination and so forth.
He does not misrepresent that person, nor does he take his name. When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this Dhammarakkhita is desirous of full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
[I am] desirous of full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita. In this way, he does not misrepresent the subject matter.
"He does not misrepresent the Saṅgha" means he does not seize upon the name of the Saṅgha. When one should say, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me;
this is Dhammarakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable sirs, let him hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita.
In this way, he does not misrepresent the Saṅgha.
"He does not misrepresent the person" means that he does not misrepresent the preceptor of the one seeking full ordination;
he does not take his name. When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
this Dhammarakkhita seeks full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this Dhammarakkhita seeks full ordination."
He speaks. In this way, he does not misapprehend the person.
"He does not misapprehend the motion" means he does not misapprehend the motion in every respect;

that is, in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), having set aside the motion, he performs the act of proclamation twice through the ritual formula alone; and likewise in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*).

Having set aside the motion (*ñatti*), he performs the formal act of proclamation (*anussāvanakamma*) by means of the ritual formula (*kammavācā*) four times. In this way, he does not touch upon the motion.

Or, "he sets aside the motion afterwards" means that having first performed the formal act of proclamation by means of the ritual formula, he says, "This is the motion," and then says, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha;
therefore, it is silent; thus do I understand this. In this way, afterwards...
He puts forward the motion (*ñatti*). Thus, in these five ways, formal acts (*kamma*) fail on account of the motion.
Regarding failure on account of the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the basis and so forth should first be understood in the manner already stated. However, their non-grasping occurs as follows:
at the first proclamation, [one says] "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," or at the second proclamation...
"I speak this matter... [and so on] ...for a third time I speak this matter.

Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs"—in these second and third proclamations, when it should be said, "This Dhammarakkhita is seeking full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," if one says instead, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs, [regarding] the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he is said to have failed to specify the subject matter.
When it should be said, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita,” if one says instead, “Venerable sirs, let [the Saṅgha] hear me;
this is Dhammarakkhita,” one is said not to have designated the Saṅgha. When it should be said, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me;
this is Dhammarakkhita [acting on behalf] of the Venerable Buddharakkhita,” if one says, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me...”
By saying, "This Dhammarakkhita is seeking full ordination," one does not misrepresent the person.

To omit the proclamation means that one does not perform the proclamation at all within the formal act (*kammavācā*); in a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), one performs only the motion twice;
in a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*), one performs only the motion four times.

In this way, one omits the proclamation (*sāvana*). Furthermore, even in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), if one sets forth the motion but then, while reciting the single formal statement (*kammavācā*), drops a syllable or mispronounces a word, this too constitutes omitting the proclamation.

However, in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), even if one sets forth the motion and then performs the proclamation of the formal statement only once or twice, [it is still considered valid].
It should be understood that even if one omits a syllable or a word, or utters something incorrectly, it still constitutes a failure in the proclamation (*anussāvana*). 252.

Regarding the phrase "he utters something incorrectly," this is the analysis: for if one says something other than what ought to be said regarding a particular syllable, this is called "uttering something incorrectly. Therefore, when a monk performs the formal act (*kammavācā*), he must consider the following:
"The lax and the firm, the long and the short, the heavy and the light, and the nasal stop (*niggahita*);..."
“The classification of the phoneme-intellect is tenfold: related, fixed, and liberated. This has been stated; it should be well observed.
For here, “soft” refers to the first and third consonants in each of the five groups.
“Hard” refers to the second and fourth in those same groups. “Long” refers to vowels such as *ā* that must be pronounced over a long duration. “Short” refers to—

Then, in half the time, the forms beginning with *vattabba* should be stated. "Heavy" (*garuka*) refers specifically to a long vowel, or that which is spoken followed by a conjunct consonant, such as:

“Āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa nakkhamatī. “Light” (*lahuka*) refers specifically to a short vowel, or that which is spoken not followed by a conjunct consonant, such as: “Āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa na khamatī.”
*Niggahita* (the nasal stop) is that which, having restrained the vocal organs and not releasing them, is to be uttered with the mouth unclosed and with a nasal resonance.
*Sambandha* (connected) is that which is joined with a subsequent word and is pronounced either as "tuṇhissā" or "tuṇhassā.
*Vavatthita* (separated) is that which is not joined with a subsequent word, but is uttered by making a pause, as in "tuṇhī assā."
Or it is called “*tuṇha assā*. That which is called “liberated” (*vimutta*) is spoken with the vocal organs unrestrained, released, with the mouth open, and without nasalization.
In that regard, where one should say “*suṇātu me*,” by changing the letter *ta* to the letter *tha*, the expression becomes “*suṇāthu me*”; this refers to the relaxed [articulation].

Making a harsh sound (*dhanita*) means, for example, saying "this motion (*ñatti*) is appropriate" when one should say "this motion is timely (*pattakalla*)," or saying "this matter (*ñatthi*) is desirable (*patthakalla*).
Making a soft sound (*sithila*) means, for example, saying "bante saṃgo" by changing the *bha*-sound and *gha*-sound of "bhante saṅgho" into the *ba*-sound and *ga*-sound.
Furthermore, when one should speak with an open mouth, saying "May it be heard from me," [to speak otherwise is an offense].
When one should say “suṇantu me” (let them hear me) or “esā ñatti” (this is the motion),
saying “esaṃ ñatti” with the mouth not opened and without nasalization is called speech with a suppressed *niggahīta*.

When one should say “pattakallaṃ” (it is opportune) with the mouth not opened and with nasalization, saying “pattakallā” with the mouth opened and without nasalization is [speech with a released *niggahīta*].
The *niggahīta* (the nasal stop) is called a "word of release. Thus, when a soft consonant (*sithila*) ought to be used, a hard one (*dhanita*) is used;
when a hard one ought to be used, a soft one is used; when a word of release ought to be used, a *niggahīta* is used; and when a *niggahīta* ought to be used, a word of release is used.
These four types of syllables (*byañjana*) corrupt the formal act (*kamma*) within the *kammavācā*. For by speaking thus, when another syllable ought to be uttered...
One is said to "speak otherwise" or "utter what is ill-spoken.
However, regarding the other six consonants—*dīgha*, *rassa*, and so forth—one should speak that very same syllable in its proper place:
a long vowel in the place of a long vowel, and a short vowel in the place of a short vowel; thus, one should not violate the traditional lineage handed down in succession.
The formal proclamation (kammavācā) must be performed. However, if one fails to do so and speaks a short vowel where a long one should be spoken, or a long vowel where a short one should be spoken;
likewise, if one speaks a light syllable where a heavy one should be spoken, or a heavy syllable where a light one should be spoken;
or if one speaks a distinct term where a connected one should be spoken, or a connected term where a distinct one should be spoken—
Even when spoken thus, the *kammavācā* is not invalidated. For these six phonetic substitutions do not invalidate the ritual act:
namely, that the *suttantika*-Theras say, "the letter *da* becomes the letter *ta*; the letter *ta* becomes the letter *da*; the letter *ca* becomes the letter *ja*;
the letter *ja* becomes the letter *ca*; the letter *ya* becomes the letter *ka*; and the letter *ka* becomes the letter *ya*."
Therefore, they say that when it is necessary to speak with the letter *da* and so forth, speaking with the letter *ta* and so forth is not contradictory;
however, this is not permissible when it comes to the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*). Consequently, the Vinaya master must neither change a *da*-sound to a *ta*-sound...
nor a *ka*-sound to a *ya*-sound. Rather, having purified the phonology according to the canonical text, he should avoid the faults mentioned regarding the tenfold phonological system of syllables.
The formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) must be performed. Otherwise, it is said that one omits the announcement.

Or, "one announces at the wrong time" means that at an improper time or place for the announcement, one fails to establish the motion (*ñatti*) first, but instead performs the act of the first proclamation and only afterwards establishes the motion. Thus, by these five ways, formal acts fail due to the proclamation.
253. Regarding failure by way of the boundary (*sīma*), there is what is called a "too small boundary," which does not accommodate twenty-one monks.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated: "Where twenty-one monks are unable to sit.
Therefore, such a boundary (*sīmā*), even if formally authorized, is as if unauthorized and is like a village field; any formal act (*kamma*) performed therein is invalid.
This same principle applies to the other types of boundaries as well. Here, however, what is called "excessively large" is that which exceeds three *yojanas* by even the breadth of a hair.
Having passed beyond [the boundary], it is considered approved. "A broken sign" (khaṇḍanimitta) is said to be a sign that has not been joined together.
After designating the sign in the eastern direction, one may designate them in sequence for the southern, western, and northern directions;
then, having designated back toward the previously designated sign in the eastern direction, it is permissible to establish [the boundary]. Thus...

It is an unbroken sign (*akhaṇḍanimitta*). However, if one brings [the parts] in succession, designates the sign in the northern direction, and then places it right there, it is a broken sign (*khaṇḍanimitta*).
Furthermore, another kind of broken sign is that which occurs when, between [the parts], there is a tree with no heartwood, a stump, a heap of earth, a heap of sand, or some other such thing.
It is designated by making a sign (*nimitta*). "By a shadow-sign" means it is designated by making any kind of shadow—such as the shadow of a mountain—as the sign.
"Without a sign" means it is designated without indicating any signs whatsoever.
"Standing outside the boundary, one designates the boundary" means that after having indicated the signs, [one designates] the boundary of those signs...

One standing outside is authorized. Regarding the statement, "One authorizes a boundary in a river, the ocean, or a lake," whatever is authorized within these rivers and so forth remains unauthorized even if so authorized, because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, every river is without a boundary;
every ocean is without a boundary; every lake is without a boundary. Regarding the phrase "one confounds a boundary with a boundary": one's own...
One merges one’s own boundary with the boundary of others. "One overflows one boundary with another" means one overflows the boundary of others with one’s own boundary.
In this regard, how both the merging and the overflowing occur has already been explained entirely in the *Sīmākathā*.
Thus, these eleven types of boundaries are indeed non-boundaries, just like village-fields; whatever is performed while sitting within them [is invalid].
The formal act fails. Therefore it was said: "In these eleven ways, formal acts fail by way of the boundary.

As for failure of the formal act due to the assembly (*parisā*), there is nothing particularly obscure about it. Even that which ought to be stated regarding the characteristics of being eligible for and entitled to the formal act therein, that too will be explained later in the manner beginning with:
"Four monks who are regular members (*pakatatta*) are entitled to the formal act."

This has already been stated. Regarding that, "those who are regular members (pakatatta) and have attained the status for the formal act" means that for a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four, four bhikkhus who are regular members—neither suspended nor expelled, possessing pure virtue—are "attained for the formal act"; they are worthy of the act, suitable for it, and its masters.
Without them, that formal act is not carried out; neither their consent nor their purity is required [for the act itself], as the rest [of the requirements] are fulfilled by them.

However, even if there are as many as a thousand, provided they are all of the same communion and all are entitled to give consent—if they have given their consent and formal purity (pārisuddhi), whether they actually come or not, the legal act (kamma) stands valid.

But he for whom the Saṅgha performs an act such as probation (parivāsa) is neither eligible for the act nor entitled to give consent; nevertheless, since that person is made the subject of the matter (vatthu), [the act proceeds].
The Saṅgha performs the formal act (*kamma*); therefore, it is called the "performer of the act" (*kammārahā*). The same principle applies to the remaining formal acts as well. 254.
The *apalokanakamma* (act of seeking permission) pertains to five points:

reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), banishment (*nissāraṇa*), shaving the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*), the *brahmadaṇḍa* (the censure of being excluded from the community), and the characteristic of the formal act itself as the fifth. Here, the expression "reinstatement and banishment" is used for the sake of metrical elegance (*padasiliṭṭhatā*).
It has been said: first there is the sending away (*nissāraṇā*), and afterwards the readmission (*osāraṇā*).
In this context, that which was the formal act of suspension (*daṇḍakamma-nāsana*) against the novice Kaṇṭaka should be understood as "sending away.
Therefore, even now, if a novice speaks in dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; if he proclaims what is improper as "proper"; or if he holds wrong views—
If he is possessed of views that grasp at extremes, he should be made to relinquish that adherence after being restrained up to three times.
If he does not relinquish it, the Saṅgha should be convened and he should be told, "Relinquish it.
If he still does not relinquish it, a competent monk, having performed an act of formal announcement (*apalokanakamma*), should expel him. And this is how the formal act should be performed:
“Venerable sir, I ask the Saṅgha: ‘This novice named so-and-so speaks dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and holds wrong view.

Does the Saṅgha approve of his expulsion so that he may not receive—along with other novices—the privilege of sleeping two or three nights together with the bhikkhus? A second time... A third time, venerable sir.”
"I ask the Saṅgha: 'This novice named so-and-so... [as before] ...it is pleasing to the Saṅgha. Go away, perish!
At a later time, when he asks for forgiveness, saying, "Venerable sirs, through my foolishness, ignorance, and lack of fortune I acted thus;
therefore, I ask the Saṅgha for forgiveness," he should be reinstated by means of a formal act of notification (*apalokana-kamma*) after having been made to request it up to three times.
And furthermore, he should be reinstated in this manner: In the midst of the Saṅgha, a competent monk, with the permission of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: this novice named so-and-so has spoken in dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
he holds wrong view. Whatever other novices receive from the monks for two or three nights..."

"He was suspended for not relinquishing cohabitation; now, however, he is gentle, humble in conduct, has entered into a sense of shame, is established in moral dread, and having undergone the penalty, confesses his transgression.
Does it please the Saṅgha to grant this novice the restoration of physical communion as before?"

This should be stated three times. In this manner, the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) applies to both reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and expulsion (*nissāraṇa*). The shaving ceremony (*bhaṇḍukamma*) has already been explained in the discussion on the determination of going forth (*pabbajjāvinicchaya*).
As for the "divine punishment" (*brahmadaṇḍa*), however, it was not prescribed solely for one who conceals [an offense];
it should also be imposed upon any other monk who is talkative and dwells harassing, reviling, and mocking monks with harsh words.
And it should be given in this way: In the midst of the Saṅgha, a competent monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"Venerable sirs, the monk named so-and-so is talkative; he dwells harassing, reviling, and mocking the monks with ill-spoken words.
That monk may say whatever he wishes; [therefore] the monks [should address] the monk named so-and-so..."
"He should neither be spoken to, nor exhorted, nor instructed. Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha:
'Does the Saṅgha approve the imposition of the brahma-punishment upon the monk named so-and-so? A second time I ask... a third time I ask:
'Does the Saṅgha approve the imposition of the brahma-punishment upon the monk named so-and-so?'"

At a later time, when he has conducted himself properly and asks for forgiveness, the *brahmadaṇḍa* should be lifted. And it should be lifted in this way: A learned monk should announce it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha of monks imposed the *brahmadaṇḍa* upon the monk so-and-so;

that monk is gentle, humble in conduct, has entered into a sense of shame, is established in moral dread, and stands with reflective discernment for restraint in the future. [He requests] the Saṅgha..."
"Venerable sir, I ask: does the Saṅgha approve of the lifting of the brahmadaṇḍa for that bhikkhu?
Having spoken thus up to three times, the brahmadaṇḍa is to be lifted by means of a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of one motion and one proclamation).
The fifth [act] is indeed characterized as a formal act (*kamma*), which was stated by the Blessed One in the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka:
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks splashed the bhikkhunīs with muddy water, thinking, "Perhaps they will become infatuated with us.
They exposed their bodies and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; they exposed their thighs and showed them to the bhikkhunīs;
they exposed their private parts and showed them to the bhikkhunīs. The bhikkhunīs were scandalized.
They consorted with the bhikkhunīs, thinking, "Perhaps they might develop a sense of attachment toward us.
Regarding these matters, after prescribing an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for those bhikkhus and stating, "Bhikkhus,
I authorize you to carry out disciplinary action against that bhikkhu," a doubt arose as to what kind of disciplinary action should be performed.
When [the offense] has arisen, it was thus authorized as a *avandiya-kamma* (act of non-reverence): "Monks, that monk is to be made one who is not to be reverenced by the community of nuns.
That is the fifth [type of act], characterized precisely by the formal act (*kamma*). It is the basis for this *apalokana-kamma* (act of notification).
For its characteristic is the formal act itself, not [acts such as] reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and so forth; therefore, it is called "characterized by the formal act. Of that—
We shall explain in detail the formal act together with its pacification.
With the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs assembled at the bhikkhunī’s quarters, a competent bhikkhunī should announce:
"Venerable ladies, the venerable one named so-and-so displays what is unpleasing to the bhikkhunīs; this is the formal act of non-prostration toward this venerable one."

"I ask the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs: 'Venerable ladies, does it please you that the formal act of non-prostration be performed against the venerable one named so-and-so, who displays what is unpleasing to the bhikkhunīs? A second time... A third time I ask the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
Having thus announced this three times, the formal act of non-prostration should be carried out by means of a *apalokana-kamma* (an act of seeking permission).
From that time forth, that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the bhikkhunīs.
If, while not being saluted, he maintains a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing and conducts himself properly, he must ask the bhikkhunīs for forgiveness.

When asking for forgiveness, he should not go to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters, but rather approach the Saṅgha, a group, or a single bhikkhu right there in the monastery, sit down on his heels, and [proceed].
Raising his hands in *añjali*, he should ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable sirs, reflecting upon this, I stand here in restraint for the future;
I will not again show myself in an unpleasing manner. May the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs forgive me.
Then, having sent a single bhikkhu from that Saṅgha or group, or having gone himself, that one bhikkhu should say to the bhikkhunīs: "This... [text continues]"
“The monk, having reflected and established himself in restraint for the future, has confessed this transgression and asked forgiveness from the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs;
let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs grant this monk the status of one to be venerated. He should be granted the status of one to be venerated, and it should be done in this way:
with the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs assembled at the nunnery, an experienced bhikkhunī should announce:
“Venerable lady, a certain venerable one named so-and-so was declared ‘not to be saluted’ by the Sangha of bhikkhunīs because he displayed what was unpleasing to them.
Having fallen into a state of shame, he reflected and established himself in restraint for the future;

having confessed his transgression, he asked the Sangha of bhikkhunīs for forgiveness. I ask the Sangha of bhikkhunīs: does it please you to restore that venerable one to the status of being saluted?”
It should be recited three times. In this manner, the one to be saluted should be made so by means of a *apalokana-kamma* (an act of formal announcement).
255. Furthermore, here is a determination of the characteristics of the legal act (*kamma*) even apart from the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

For this characteristic of the legal act is indeed prescribed as being rooted in the community of nuns (*bhikkhunī-saṅgha*), yet it is certainly applicable to the community of monks (*bhikkhu-saṅgha*) as well. For that which...

The Saṅgha of bhikkhus also performs an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*) regarding the distribution of tickets for meals and the observance of the Uposatha day; this too is indeed a characteristic of a formal act.

For it is proper to assemble the Saṅgha and, after a competent bhikkhu has announced the matter up to three times, to perform an act of formal authorization and give robe-cloth to those whose robes have been stolen, whose robes are worn out, or whose robes have been lost. By the distributor of minor requisites...
However, for one making a robe, the requisites such as needles and so forth—of the types mentioned in the discussion on the distribution of requisites—should be given even without seeking permission.
In the giving of these, he alone is the master; but when giving anything beyond those, it must be done after seeking permission.
For regarding any gift exceeding that, the Saṅgha is the owner. Medicines for the sick of the kinds mentioned therein should also be given by oneself.
To one who desires an extra portion, it should be given after seeking permission (*apaloketvā*).

Furthermore, for one who is weak, or whose physical activities are impaired, or whose path for alms-gathering has been cut off, or who is severely ill, one should give—whether from the great storehouses or from local produce—one *nāḷi* or half a *nāḷi* daily, or even five or ten *nāḷis* of rice on a single day;
this should be given only after performing the formal act of seeking permission. For one who is well-behaved...
It is permissible for a monk to grant, by means of a formal act of notification (*apalokana-kamma*), a debt-obligation arising from income at that place,

as well as the obligation to provide lodgings that need not be personally attended to by a learned monk who has relieved the burden of the Saṅgha, and even the food and wages for the kitchen assistants and others while they are performing duties for the Saṅgha.
It is permissible to have a Saṅgha residence maintained using specific offerings given for the sake of the four requisites;

however, in order to put an end to talk such as "this bhikkhu is managing it out of a sense of lordship," he should have it maintained only after having requested permission from the Saṅgha at the voting hall or during an intermediate assembly.
This also applies to specific offerings given for the purpose of robes or almsfood.
Having obtained permission, the residence should be maintained; however, it is also permissible without obtaining permission.

Yet, for the purpose of cutting off talk that might arise—such as, "This bhikkhu is indeed a hero, for he maintains the residence specifically because it was given for the sake of robes and almsfood"—one should have it maintained only after performing the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*).
Regarding a cetiya, whether one is constructing a parasol, a railing, a Bodhi-house, or a seat-house that has not yet been made, or [repairing] one that is dilapidated...
Or, while making repairs or performing whitewash work, it is permissible to have it done by enjoining people [to help].

If there is no one to do it, it should be made from items deposited at the cetiya. If there is nothing deposited, it should be made from funds arising for that purpose after performing an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*).
It is also permissible to perform work for the cetiya after obtaining authorization regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha.

Even after seeking permission from the property of a cetiya, it is not permissible to perform what belongs to the Saṅgha; however, it is permissible to take something on loan and restore it to its original state.

Furthermore, for those performing plastering work and so forth at a cetiya who do not obtain enough for their subsistence from alms-rounds or from the Saṅgha, they may take just enough for their subsistence from the property of the cetiya and consume it.
It is proper to perform the duties (*vatta*). However, it is not proper to provide a meal for the Saṅgha using fish, meat, and so forth, under the pretext of "performing the duties.
As for fruit trees planted in the monastery that have been formally accepted by the Saṅgha, they receive the labor of tending them.
Regarding those [trees], one need not perform the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) before eating their fruits after striking the gong and distributing them.
However, regarding those who are unclaimed, a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) must be performed;

this may be done even at the head of the voting sticks, the head of the sacrificial offerings, the head of the meal, or within the boundary of the monastery, and it is certainly permissible at the head of the Uposatha hall.
For there, the consent and purity of those who have not arrived are also brought forward, and thus that [act] becomes thoroughly purified. And it should be performed in this way: by a learned monk...
With the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it should be announced:
“Venerable sirs, whatever belongs to the Saṅgha within the boundary of this monastery—roots, bark, leaves, sprouts, flowers, fruits, fresh foods, and so forth—I ask the Saṅgha:
does it please you that all of this may be used at will by whichever bhikkhus arrive?”
It should be asked three times.

What is performed by four or five bhikkhus is indeed well-performed. Even in a monastery where only two or three people reside, what is performed by them sitting together is exactly like what is performed by the Saṅgha. However, in a place where there is only one bhikkhu, by him—

When a bhikkhu has performed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks on the Uposatha day and sits down, even a formal agreement (*katikavatta*) made by him is exactly as if it were made by the Saṅgha.

When performing it, it is permissible to do so either by dividing it according to shares of fruit—delimiting it for four months, six months, or one year—or even without such delimitation. When it is delimited...
Having enjoyed [the fruit] according to the distribution, it must be done again. If there has been no distribution, it is permissible as long as the trees remain standing.
Even for other trees planted from the seeds of those [original] trees, the same agreement applies.
However, if they have been planted in another monastery, the Saṅgha [has authority] over them only in the monastery where they were planted.
Venerable sir, even those seeds which were brought from elsewhere and planted later in the original monastery, another agreement (*katikā*) must be made regarding them.
Once the agreement is made, they remain in the status of private property; it is permissible for them to enjoy the fruits and so forth as they please.
However, if they maintain the grounds by constructing and enclosing various areas such as monastic cells (*pariveṇa*), then [the produce belongs] to those monks.
They remain in a place belonging to an individual; others do not obtain the right to use it. However, after giving a tenth part to the Saṅgha, they may be used by them.
The same rule applies even to one who protects a tree in the middle of the monastery by surrounding it with branches.
When a venerable monk has gone to an ancient monastery, people bring fruits and other produce, thinking, "The Elder has arrived."
If a learned bhikkhu who has mastered the entire scriptural tradition (pariyatti) resided there at the root [of that tree], one may consume [the fruit] without scruple, thinking:
"Surely a long-standing agreement must have been made here. Fruit from a monastery is permissible even for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika);
it does not violate the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). Novices give many fruits to their own teachers and preceptors.
If other monks do not receive [alms], they become critical; that is merely a matter of criticism.
If there is a famine, even sixty people can survive depending on a single jackfruit tree; at such a time, it should be shared and eaten for the sake of supporting everyone.
This is the proper conduct (*sāmīci*). However, until the established agreement (*katikavatta*) is rescinded, [the practice continues].
What has been eaten by them is indeed well-eaten. But when does the formal agreement (*katikavatta*) cease?
When a harmonious Saṅgha, having assembled, proclaims: "From now on, let them eat after dividing [the food]";
however, in a monastery with only a single bhikkhu, even if this proclamation is made, the previous agreement ceases nonetheless. If the agreement has ceased...
The novices neither knock fruit down from the trees nor pick it up from the ground to give to the monks;
instead, they wander about striking fallen fruits with their feet. From the tenth part of those fruits, up to the point where half the fruit portion is reached, the compensation must be made.
Surely, out of greed for this compensation, they will bring and give them once again when a time of plenty arises.
When those who prepare what is allowable (kappiyakāraka) come and protect the trees by pruning branches and so forth, no special service need be rendered to the novices;
rather, [the fruit] should be divided and consumed.
If people from neighboring villages, thinking, "There is fruit in the monastery," bring it for the sake of the sick or for pregnant women...
When they arrive and beg, saying, “Give us a coconut! Give us a mango! Give us a jackfruit!”, should it be given or not?

It should be given. For if it is not given, they become dejected. However, when giving, one must first convene the Saṅgha, announce the matter up to three times, and perform an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*) before giving;
or else, having established an agreement regarding the proper conduct (*katikavatta*), it may be set aside for distribution.
And it should be done in this way: A learned monk, with the permission of the Saṅgha, should announce:
"People have come from the neighboring villages and request various fruits for the sake of the sick and others;
there shall be no prohibition against those who take two coconut fruits, two palm fruits, two jackfruit, five mangoes, and five plantain fruits."
“Does the Saṅgha of bhikkhus approve the non-prohibition for those taking fruit from such-and-such a tree and such-and-such a tree?”—this should be stated three times.
From that point on, when those who are ill or in similar circumstances take [fruit] by mentioning its name and asking, they should not be told, “Take it”;
rather, the proper procedure (*vatta*) should be explained: “For those taking coconuts and so forth within this specific limit...”
“No prohibition has been made against those taking fruit from such-and-such trees and such-and-such trees.
However, after having investigated, one should not say, “This mango tree has sweet fruit; take from this one.
But at the time of distributing the fruit, half the portion should be given by one who is appointed, and by one who is not appointed, [only] after having obtained permission.

It should be given. If one whose travel expenses are exhausted, or a caravan leader traveling on the road, or some other powerful person comes and requests it, it should be given only after taking leave [of the owner]. One should not prevent him from taking and eating it by force;
for if he is angry, he might even cut down the trees or cause other harm. If he comes to a private dwelling and [requests it] in the name of a sick person...
When they ask, one should say: "This was planted by us for the sake of shade and so forth; if there is any [fruit], you know that.
However, if the trees are already laden with fruit and people tie thorns to them to take the fruit by turns, it should be given without expecting anything in return.
One who takes it by force should not be stopped; the reason for this is exactly as stated previously.

If he has a grove belonging to the Saṅgha, but does not receive its maintenance, it belongs to the Saṅgha. If someone looks after it on account of his duties (*vattasīsa*), it still belongs to the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, if the Saṅgha entrusts the responsibility to a capable monk, saying, "Good man, look after this and give it back," and if he looks after it on account of his duties, even in that case it belongs to the Saṅgha. This is the procedure for compensation (*phātikamma*).
However, for one who expects a return, a reciprocal service (*phātikamma*) should be performed to the extent of a third or a half-share.
If, after saying "This is a heavy task," he still does not wish to do it with that much, he should be told: "Make it all yours;
take charge of it after giving me only the tenth part as the basic fee. Yet, because it is a valuable object (*garubhaṇḍa*), it must not be taken by way of total confiscation.

It must be given. Having given the root-portion, while eating it, he either makes an unprepared dwelling or maintains a prepared dwelling and then hands over the monastery to those who are dependent on him;
by them also, the root-portion must indeed be given. But when the monks themselves are capable of maintaining it, then they should not be made to maintain it at that time of maintenance.
However, they should not be forbidden [altogether]; rather, they should be forbidden only at the time of the watch.
One should say: "You have eaten much; do not keep watch now; the Saṅgha itself will keep watch.

But if there is no one keeping watch either by way of duty or by way of service, and the Saṅgha is unable to keep watch, then one person may, without asking permission, keep watch and perform the service.
Having increased [the penalty], he awaits [the formal act]; it must be granted only after the preliminary work (*phātikamma*) has been increased by means of a *apalokana-kamma*.
Thus, all of this constitutes the very characteristic of a formal act (*kamma*). The *apalokana-kamma* pertains to these five points.
Regarding the classification of the points for a *ñatti-kamma*:

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: such-and-such a person desires full ordination from the Venerable such-and-such; he has been instructed by me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let such-and-such a person come;
he should be told, ‘Come. This is the formal admission of one seeking full ordination;
this is what is called “admission. “Let the Venerable ones hear me: this monk such-and-such is a preacher of the Dhamma; for him there is no [need for] the Sutta...”
He arrives, but not with the Suttavibhaṅga; failing to discern the meaning, he misrepresents the meaning based on the mere shadow of the phrasing.
[The others say: "Venerable sirs, if it seems appropriate to you, let us resolve this legal issue after having had the monk named so-and-so removed.
In this way, the removal of a monk who speaks according to the Dhamma during a decision by a committee is what is called "removal."

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha.”—thus, a motion established by way of the Uposatha ceremony is called “Uposatha.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth day. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā.”—[thus, a motion established by way of the Pavāraṇā ceremony is called “Pavāraṇā”].
Thus, the motion established by means of the formal act of invitation (*pavāraṇa-kamma*) is called the "invitation-motion" (*pavāraṇā-ñatti*). [The formula is:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. So-and-so desires the full ordination from the Venerable so-and-so.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, may I instruct so-and-so," and, "If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha..."
“Let [so-and-so] instruct [so-and-so],” “If it is timely for the Saṅgha,
I would question [so-and-so] regarding the obstructing factors,” “If it is timely for the Saṅgha,
let [so-and-so] question [so-and-so] regarding the obstructing factors,” “If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I would [question] [so-and-so] regarding the Vinaya.”
“...should ask,” “If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let so-and-so ask so-and-so about the Vinaya,” “If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha,
when asked about the Vinaya by so-and-so, I would answer,” and “If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let so-and-so, being asked about the Vinaya by so-and-so, answer.”
Thus, a motion (*ñatti*) established to authorize oneself or another is called an authorization (*sammuti*).
"Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs: this robe-cloth, which is subject to forfeiture by the monk so-and-so, has been forfeited to the Sangha.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, let the Sangha [give] this robe-cloth to the monk so-and-so..."

“May they give [it]”; “Venerable sirs, when it is appropriate for you, may you give this robe-cloth to the monk named so-and-so”—such giving of relinquished robe-cloth, bowls, and so forth, is called “giving.
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so remembers an offense, reveals it, and makes it plain.”

He makes the motion and declares: "If it is timely for the Saṅgha, may I accept the offense of the bhikkhu named so-and-so," or, "Venerable sirs, if it is timely for you, may I accept the offense of the bhikkhu named so-and-so.
He [the bhikkhu] should be asked: "Do you see [it]? "Yes, I see it. "You should exercise restraint in the future."
In this way, the acceptance of an offense is called "acceptance. [One should say:

"Venerable sirs, let the residents listen to me. If it is agreeable to the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the invitation ceremony (Pavāraṇā) at the next dark fortnight.
If those monks, O bhikkhus, are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and [disruptors] in the Saṅgha...
If those involved in a legal dispute should remain there for that period of time, the resident monk who is competent and capable must inform the resident monks:

"Venerable sirs, may the residents listen to me. If it is appropriate for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the following full moon.
In this way, the postponement of the Pavāraṇā is called "postponement."
Everyone must assemble together in one place. Having assembled, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. While we have been living in a state of mutual quarreling, disputing, and contending, we have habitually engaged in much that is unbecoming of a recluse, speaking and repeating such things. If, regarding these offenses..."
"We shall deal with it among ourselves; for that legal issue might lead to harshness, to violence, and to schism.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha settle this legal issue by means of 'covering over as with grass,' excepting grave offenses and matters connected with householders."

Thus, having settled the matter by the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) method, the very first motion that encompasses all is called the "characteristic of legal action" (*kammalakkhaṇa*).

Likewise, following that, there are two motions, each made for one side. Thus, including the reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and the exclusion (*nissāraṇa*) according to the aforementioned divisions... [and so on]... up to the ninth, which is the "characteristic of legal action" itself; this motion-based legal act (*ñattikamma*) proceeds through these nine points. 257.
Regarding the classification of legal acts consisting of a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), there is the case of the overturning of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi’s bowl.
The overturning of the bowl, as taught in the Khandhaka, and the restoration of it by means of turning it upright again, should be understood as also taught in the Khandhaka. For this has been said:
"Monks, the bowl of a lay follower endowed with eight factors should be overturned. Of the monks..."
He strives for the non-acquisition [of requisites], he strives for the harm of the bhikkhus, he strives for the displacement of the bhikkhus,
he reviles and abuses the bhikkhus, he causes dissension among the bhikkhus,
he speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha. I allow you, bhikkhus, by these—
The bowl of a lay follower endowed with eight qualities should be overturned.
And thus, monks, it should be overturned: A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. Vaḍḍha the Licchavi has [accused] the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of groundless [sexual misconduct]."
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha overturn the bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi and enact non-association with him; this is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: Vaḍḍha the Licchavi has [accused] the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta with groundless [charges of] failure in virtue..."
He has proclaimed the failure of Vaddha the Licchavi’s virtue. The Saṅgha overturns the bowl of Vaddha the Licchavi and effects non-association with him.

Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the overturning of the bowl of Vaddha the Licchavi and the effecting of non-association with him by the Saṅgha, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi has been turned upside down by the Saṅgha; it is not to be shared with the Saṅgha. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I hold it.
“Monks, the bowl of a lay follower endowed with eight factors should be turned upright.
He does not strive for the non-acquisition of gains for the monks; he does not strive for the harm of the monks... [and so on] ...he does not speak dispraise of the Saṅgha.”
He speaks thus: "I allow you, monks, to overturn the bowl of a lay follower who is endowed with these eight qualities.
And furthermore, monks, it should be overturned in this way:
That Licchavi Vaḍḍha, monks, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the monks, and having sat down in the kneeling position..."
Having raised his joined palms, he should speak to him thus:

"Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha has overturned my bowl; I am excluded from communion with the Saṅgha. Therefore, venerable sirs, I conduct myself properly, I behave in accordance with the rules, and I act toward rehabilitation; I beg the Saṅgha for the overturning of my bowl.
He should beg a second time, and he should beg a third time.
A competent monk who is learned should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha has overturned the bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi and suspended his communion with the Saṅgha.
He now conducts himself properly, he behaves with humility, and he acts toward deliverance; he requests the Saṅgha to overturn his bowl."
He requests: "If it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha overturn the bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi and restore communal sharing with him. This is the motion.
"Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: the Saṅgha has overturned the bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi; there shall be no communal sharing."
The Saṅgha [has acted]. He conducts himself properly, he behaves with humility, he conducts himself in a way that leads to deliverance, and he requests the Saṅgha to overturn his bowl.
The Saṅgha overturns the bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi; he shares in communion with the Saṅgha.
For whichever venerable one it is pleasing, let him approve the overturning of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi’s bowl and his sharing in communion with the Saṅgha.
This is the formal act; he who approves should remain silent. Whoever does not approve should speak.
"The bowl of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi has been overturned by the Saṅgha; its use has been suspended by the Saṅgha. It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by your silence, we hold it to be so.
And herein, the formal act of overturning a bowl may be performed against one who possesses even a single one of these eight factors.
It is permissible; it is indeed permissible to overturn [the bowl] within the boundary, or having gone outside the boundary, or in rivers and such places.

However, when the bowl has been thus overturned, no gift should be accepted from anyone in that person's house. One should send messengers even to other monasteries, saying, "Do not accept alms in the house of so-and-so.
But at the time of righting [the bowl], one must have the request made up to three times.
Having caused him to leave the reach of hand-contact, he should be reinstated by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma).

These are: the authorization for the boundary (sīmāsammuti), the authorization for not being separated from the three robes (ticīvarena avippavāsasammuti), the authorization for the rug (santhatasammuti), and the authorizations for the designator of meals, the assigner of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the distributor of robes, the distributor of rice gruel, the distributor of hard food, the distributor of fruit, the distributor of minor items, the assigner of upper robes, the assigner of alms bowls, the supervisor of monastery attendants, and the supervisor of novices.
Conventional designation (sammuti) should be understood by way of these conventional designations.

Giving should be understood by way of the giving of the *kaṭhina* robe and the giving of a robe as a funeral gift (*mataka-cīvara*). Suspension (*uddhāra*) should be understood by way of the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. Designation (*desanā*) should be understood by way of the pointing out of the site for a hut (*kuṭi*) and the site for a monastery (*vihāra*).

Furthermore, regarding the settlement by "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*), [it should be understood] by way of the motion that includes all [offenses] and by way of each individual [offense].

Having established three motions—namely, one motion for each side plus one motion [for the whole]—it is further stated that there are two formal acts consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*), one for each side.

The characteristics of the formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*) should be understood by way of these. Thus, the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) covers these seven points.

258. Regarding the classification of the formal acts consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*), it is by way of the seven formal acts beginning with the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*).
Expulsion (*nissāraṇā*) should be understood as such; reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) should be understood by way of the subsiding of those very same offenses.

Authorization (*sammuti*) should be understood by way of the authorization to exhort bhikkhunīs. Granting (*dāna*) should be understood by way of the granting of the probationary period (*parivāsa*) and the period of penance (*mānatta*).

Discipline (*niggaha*) should be understood by way of the formal act of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanākamma*). These are: one who follows a suspended person, the eight matters that must be brought up a third time, Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷī.
"Up to the third time": by way of these eleven formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*), the "admonition" is to be understood.

By way of the act of ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) and the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), the characteristic of the formal act (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*) is to be understood. Thus, the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) proceeds through these seven points. In this way, [the exposition of] the formal acts, the failure of formal acts, and the delimitation of the Saṅgha that performs those formal acts [is concluded].
And the determination of the different grounds for those actions that are free from failure should also be understood.
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of what constitutes a formal act and what does not,
within the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Excluding the Pāḷi Text.
The Matrix of the Miscellaneous Chapter:
Eating in a group, [eating] in succession, not asking permission, [wearing] rag-robe material;
taking what has been stolen, [speaking] inspired speech, and designating what has been left unfinished.
A long seat for three years, the description of attending to the sick;
not looking after one’s own fall, stone-pounding and plastering.
Wrong view, the taking up of a cow’s footprint, protection by the Dhamma, and excrement and so forth.
Bathing, eunuchs and the like, long hair and so forth, slaves and the like;
dancing and the like, cutting off limbs, supernormal power; the bowl, all kinds of rag-robes;
the water-strainer, nakedness; flowers, perfumes, and ointments.
A bowl with a handle, a cloth for wiping the feet,
a fan, a sunshade, nail-clippers and so forth, a waist-band, and a lower garment;
a remedy for hemorrhoids, tooth-sticks, climbing trees, and the application of ointments.
Lokāyata philosophy is to be rejected, and garlic is not to be eaten.
A cotton mattress is not to be venerated, as are stuffed pillows, couches, and the like;
high seats, large seats, robes, and unrighteous dwellings [are likewise forbidden].
The gift of faith, what is better than peace, deposits such as the work of a teacher,
the barber, the tenth part, provisions for a journey, the Great Authorities, and the benefits—
this is the summary outline (mātikā).
34. Discussion on Miscellaneous Determinations (Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya-kathā) 1.
Now, the miscellaneous discussion should be understood. It has been stated: “In eating in a group, except on an occasion, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This eating in a group arises in two ways: either through solicitation or through invitation. How does it arise through solicitation?
Does he incur an offense? If four bhikkhus, standing or sitting together, see a lay follower and request,

“Give us all four our meal,” or if they see him individually and request, “Give me [one], give me [one]”— whether requesting thus together or separately— and then go either together or separately, even after having received the meal...
They may eat together or separately. If they take [the food] together, it constitutes a *gaṇabhojana* (group meal), and there is an offense for all of them.
For in this case, the act of receiving [the food] itself is the criterion. Thus it arises from solicitation. How does it arise from an invitation?
Having approached four monks, [one says]: "Venerable sirs, you [should eat] with rice..."

"I invite you; take rice, desire it, look upon it, accept it, and partake of it"—in this way, by whatever synonym or other language one uses, having taken the name of the five kinds of cooked food, one invites.
Thus, being invited together, they go together on either the same day or the following day, according to the limited time specified.
If they take [the food] from one side and eat from one side, it constitutes a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*), and all incur an offense.
If those invited from one side go either together or separately, and they take [the food] from one side and eat from one side—or from one side or separately—they still incur an offense.
If those invited from one side go either together or separately, and they take [the food] from separate sides, or eat from one side or separately...

If they eat, there is no offense. Having gone to four separate courtyards or monasteries, even if invited separately, if they remain in one place—such as one with his son and another with his father—even though invited separately, let them go together or separately, and let them eat together or separately;
if they take their food together, it constitutes a *gaṇabhojana* (group meal).
This is an offense for all. Thus, first of all, it arises from an invitation.

Therefore, if someone sent by one wishing to provide a meal for the Saṅgha comes to the monastery and, instead of saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept almsfood at our house tomorrow," says, "Please accept a meal," or "Please accept a meal for the Saṅgha..."
If he says, "Take it," or "Let the Saṅgha take the meal," the distributor of food must be wise.
He must release those who accept invitations from the offense of group-meals, and those who are alms-seekers from the breach of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). How so?
First, he should say, "It is not possible [to provide] tomorrow, lay followers. On the following day, he asks, "Venerable sir? [The reply is: "It is not possible even tomorrow."
In this manner, even after he has carried it off for as long as half a month, he should be asked again: "What did you say?

If he says again, "Take the meal for the Saṅgha," then one should create a diversion by saying, "Lay follower, first make these flowers allowable, and this grass," and then he should be asked again: "What did you say? If he still does exactly the same...
He says, "Friend, you will not get it from the alms-collectors or the elder monks; you will get it from the novices.
When he replies, "Venerable sir, did they not feed the Bhadantas in such-and-such and such-and-such villages?
Why do I not receive it? they know how to invite them, but you do not. How did they invite them?
“Venerable sir? they ask. They say, “Venerable sir, please accept almsfood from us. If he also speaks in that same way, it is permissible.
But if he says again, “Please accept a meal,” one should say to him, “Friend, you will not receive many monks now;
you will receive only three, friend. [If he asks], “But venerable sir, in such-and-such a village and such-and-such a village...”
“They fed the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus; why do I not receive [an invitation]? “You do not know how to invite.
