“How, venerable sir, did they invite? They said this: “Venerable sir, please accept almsfood from us.
If he also says exactly the same thing, “Please accept almsfood,” it is permissible. But if he says again, “Only the meal,” [it is not].
If he says this, one should tell him: “Go away; we have no need for your alms-food.
This is our regular alms-round; we shall wander here for alms ourselves. When he has returned after saying, “Wander on, venerable sirs,” they ask him:
“Well, sir, did you get any alms? What is the use of that? There is much to be said about this. The elders [say]: “Tomorrow...”
“We shall go for alms,” they said. “Do not neglect this now.

On the second day, after performing the duties toward the shrine (cetiyavatta), the monks standing there were addressed by the senior of the Saṅgha: “Friends, there is a meal for the Saṅgha in the village ahead, but a foolish person went [there instead].
Let us go; we shall go for alms in the village ahead. When the monks heard the elder’s words, they...
One should act thus; one should not be difficult to speak to. Without standing at the village gate, one should wander for alms.
When they take up the bowls, seat [the monks], and serve the food, one should eat.
If, having set aside the meal in the dining hall, they go wandering along the streets and announce, "Venerable sirs, in the dining hall..."

If they say, "Take the meal," it is not permissible. However, if they say, "Take the meal and go here and there to receive food," or if they have already brought the meal to the monastery and placed it in a suitable location so that they give it to whoever arrives, this is called "brought-along alms" (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*) and is permissible. But if they prepare a gift in the dining hall and...
If they send him to that cell, saying, "Take your meal in the dining hall," it is permissible.
However, those people who, upon seeing monks going for alms, sweep out the sitting hall, have them sit there, and feed them, should not be refused.
Furthermore, those who, seeing monks coming out of the village after failing to obtain alms in the village...
If they say, "Venerable sir, please accept food," they should be refused; one must not turn back.
If they say, "Please turn back, venerable sir, and accept food," it is permissible to turn back at the words "please turn back.
If they say, "Please turn back, venerable sir; food has been prepared at home; food has been prepared in the village," [one may turn back].
If there is food belonging to anyone at all in a house or in a village, it is permissible to turn back.
They say, connecting the words as "Turn back and take food," [implying it is not for them]; in that case, it is not permissible to turn back.
The same principle applies even when, upon seeing monks departing from the assembly hall to wander for alms, someone says, "Sit down, venerable sirs, and take food."

Regarding the phrase "except at the proper time": because of this statement, there is no offense during any one of these seven proper times: the time of illness, the time of giving robes, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of boarding a boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a meal for recluses.
Therefore, just as meat might be seen beyond the hide of a large animal, even if one's feet are cracked, [it is still permissible].
When even a mere touch with sand or gravel causes pain, and it is no longer possible to wander for alms within the village, one may eat during such an illness, considering it a time of sickness;
one must not, however, resort to the "trace-allowance" (*lesakappiya*).
What is called "the time for giving robes" refers to the last month of the rainy season when the Kathina has not been spread, or whenever the Kathina has been spread.
Five months. Within this interval, one may eat [at the invitation of others] on the grounds that it is "the time for giving robes.
When robes are being made, one may eat on the grounds that it is "the time for making robes.

For when, having obtained both cloth and thread, they make a robe, this is called "the time for making robes"; there is no separate "time for making robes" apart from this. Therefore, whatever must be done regarding those robes—
One performs the work; for it is said in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "At the very least, even one who pierces with a needle.
By that [rule], one may eat during the "time for making robes" (*cīvarakārasamaya*). However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated in detail:
"He who distributes the robe-cloth, cuts it, lays down the false thread-mark, lays down the incoming patch, sews what has been brought back, [and lays down] the incoming patch..."
He binds it, cuts it following the grain, joins it, and mounts it; there he sews what has come back together, makes the thread, and weaves it;
he fixes the toggle and performs the turning-over—all this is indeed called "making the robe.
However, one who sits nearby reciting the Jātaka or the Dhammapada is not a robe-maker; this is [not included].
"Excepting these, there is no offense for eating in a group with the rest.

At the time of traveling on a journey, even one intending to go only half a *yojana* may eat [thinking], "I will go half a *yojana*"; while traveling, he may eat; and once arrived, he may eat for one day.

At the time of boarding a boat, he may eat [thinking], "I will board the boat"; having boarded, he may eat as long as he has not disembarked, even after reaching his desired destination; and once disembarked, he may eat for one day.

A "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) is that place where even two or three bhikkhus, having gone for alms, can barely sustain themselves, and where they cannot even sustain themselves when a fourth has arrived;
this is a great assembly. However, where a hundred or a thousand gather, there is no need to say anything further.
Therefore, at such a time, one may eat after determining it to be a "great assembly."
The "time for alms-food from recluses" (samaṇabhattasamaya) refers to when anyone who has entered the order of wanderers prepares food; this is indeed the time for alms-food from recluses.

Therefore, when food has been prepared by any member whatsoever—whether among those of the same Dhamma or among those of other sects—it may be eaten [thinking], "This is the time for alms-food from recluses.
There is no offense at such a time, provided two or three eat together, having gone on alms-round and gathered together in one place.

Because of the statement, "There is no offense in all cases except for the five kinds of food— whether eating a regular meal, a ticket meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha meal, or a meal on the first day of the lunar half-month"—
there is likewise no offense even for those who, having accepted an improper invitation, eat two or three [meals] together.

In this regard, the determination should be understood by way of five types of "fourth persons": one who is not invited as the fourth, one who is a forest-dweller (*piṇḍapātika*) as the fourth, one who is not ordained as the fourth, one who has a bowl as the fourth, and one who is ill as the fourth. How so?
Here, someone invites four bhikkhus, saying, "Please accept food. Of them, three have gone, but one has not gone. [Then] a lay follower...
“Venerable sir, where is one elder? he asks. “The lay follower has not arrived.
He then invites another person who happens to arrive at that moment, saying, “Come, venerable sir,” and leads him into the house and gives food to all four; for all of them, there is no offense. Why?
Because the one who completed the group was not invited. For only three were invited there, and it was they who received [the meal]; by them, the group was formed.
"It does not fill [the quorum], and the one who completes the group has not been invited; thus the group is split.

This is the "fourth consisting of one who has not been invited. Regarding the "fourth consisting of an alms-food eater": at the time of the invitation, there is one alms-food eater who does not accept.
However, at the time of departure, when it is said, "Come, Venerable Sir," although he does not come because he did not accept, [the others say] "Come, you will receive alms-food."
They go taking [the bowl], and he breaks that group; therefore, there is no offense for anyone.
When they are invited together with a novice as the fourth member of a group not yet fully ordained, he too breaks the group.
When one comes himself as the fourth member of a group [carrying] bowls and sends back a bowl, even in this way the group is broken; therefore, there is no offense for anyone.

In the fourth case regarding the sick, they have been invited together with the sick person; therein, there is no offense for the sick person alone, but for the others, he serves as the one who completes the group.
For the group is not broken by the sick person; therefore, there is an offense for them.

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated without distinction: "One who has obtained [the meal] at the proper time is himself released, but because he acts as the one who completes the group for the rest, he incurs an offense."
...it happens. Therefore, fourfold sets should be understood by way of those who receive [offerings] at the time of giving robes, and so forth.
However, even if the four people have departed after having accepted [the invitation], if one wise bhikkhu says, “I shall break your group;
please accept the invitation,” and then, at the conclusion of the rice gruel and solid food, holds out his bowl for the sake of a meal—
If he sits down without giving to those who are taking [the food], saying, "First feed these monks and then dismiss them;

I will go after I have performed the thanksgiving (anumodanā)," and after they have eaten and departed, he takes his bowl from the lay follower, saying, "Give it, venerable sir," and having eaten when the food is given, he departs after performing the thanksgiving— there is no offense for anyone.
For regarding the five kinds of cooked food alone, there is no ambiguity in the case of eating in a group;
even those who, having been invited with rice, take gruel, incur an offense, for those [five foods] were not taken by them together.

However, there is ambiguity regarding rice-gruel and so forth, for those were taken by them together. Thus, one wise person effects the non-offense for others as well. "A regular meal" (niccabhattaṃ).
“Fixed meal” (*dhuvabhatta*) means they say, “Take a regular meal”; it is permissible to take it from many people at once.
The same principle applies to “ticket meals” (*salākabhatta*) and so forth. 2.
Regarding what is stated as, “In eating in succession, except on an occasion, there is an offense of expiation” (*pācittiya*), “eating in succession” refers specifically to invitations.

It gives rise to [an offense]. For one who has been invited with words such as, “Take your meal with any one of the five kinds of cooked food,” yet eats another of those five kinds of cooked food instead of that [specific one], for him that food is called “successive eating” (*paramparabhojana*).
For one eating in this manner, except at the time of illness...
Since it has been stated that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at other times regarding the occasion of giving robes and the occasion of making robes,
one must therefore eat according to the sequence of invitations and not out of order.
From the statement, "Monks, I allow you to eat successive meals after having assigned them," [the first invitation...]
It is permissible to consume [the food] even after having assigned it to another. This act of assignment (vikappanā) is permitted both in the presence of the person and in their absence.
If one sees them in person, one may say, "I assign my expected portion of food to you," or "I give it to you," and then eat;
if one does not see them, one may take the name of any one among the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika) and say, "My..."
Having said, "I dedicate this food to [so-and-so]," or "I give it," one may eat.
However, it is permissible to place two or three invitations into a single bowl, mix them together, and treat them as one before eating;
for it is said: "There is no offense in eating two or three invitations together. This applies even if one has been invited by two or three families.
Having seated him in one place, they bring food from here and there and heap it upon him;
they heap on curry and condiments so that it becomes a single mixture—in this case also, there is no offense.
However, if the original invitation was below and the subsequent ones were above, then starting from the top...

There is an offense for one who eats [in this manner]. However, there is no offense for one who, having inserted the hand inside [the bowl], takes out even a single mouthful after the first invitation and then eats in whatever way, starting from the time it has been eaten.
Even if they pour milk or broth there, provided that the food covered by it becomes of a single flavor, [one may eat] starting from the edge.
"There is no offense for one who is eating," as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* it is said:

"If, after one has received either milk-rice or curry-rice and is sitting down, others pour more milk-rice or curry-rice right there upon him, there is no offense for one drinking the milk or the curry;
likewise, for one eating, there is no offense regarding the first piece of meat received."
"Or, having placed a morsel of food in the mouth, it is permissible to eat starting from the tip; the same rule applies even to rice gruel with ghee.

When a great lay follower invites a bhikkhu, once he has entered that person's house, the lay follower, as well as his sons, wife, brothers, sisters, and others, each bring their own portion and place it in the bowl;
[the bhikkhu] must not eat what was first given by the lay follower without [first eating the other portions].
"An offense occurs for one who eats what was obtained later," so it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. In the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated, "It is permissible.

In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "If they cook separately and give [food] by taking portions from their own respective cooked rice, then for one who eats first that which was brought later, there is a *pācittiya* offense. But if..."
It is said: "For all [monks], there is but one single meal; there is no eating in succession.

When a great lay follower (mahā-upāsaka) has invited [the Sangha] and they are seated, if another person takes a bowl, [the food] must not be given. [The other asks: "Venerable sir, why do you not give? [He replies:
"Is it not true, lay follower, that you have invited us? [The other says: "Very well, venerable sir; whatever is obtained, eat what is obtained."
"It is permissible to eat. According to the *Kurundi*, it is also permissible to eat after someone else has brought food and given it to one, even if one has asked for it.
Those desiring to hear the Dhamma from a monk who is departing after giving a blessing invite him, saying, "Venerable sir, please come again tomorrow.
On the following day, it is permissible for him to eat whatever he receives. Why? Because all [have invited him].

Because of being invited. Even if a single bhikkhu, while wandering for alms, obtains food, and another lay follower invites him and has him sit down at home, yet the meal has not yet been prepared—if that bhikkhu eats the food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense.
If he does not eat and remains seated, and is asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not eat? [he may then eat].
Having said, “Because he was invited by her,” if it is then said, “Venerable sirs, eat whatever you have received,” it is permissible to eat.
For one who has been invited by an entire village acting as one body, there is no offense in eating wherever [in that village] one may choose.
The same rule applies to a guild (pūga). “There is no offense for one invited by an entire village who eats anywhere in that village.”
"He eats": if invited by an entire group, he eats anywhere within that group;

if being invited, he says, "I shall take alms-food"; and in the case of regular meals, ticket-meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha meals, or meals on the first day of the lunar half-month—excluding the five kinds of soft food—in all such cases it is said, "there is no offense."

Regarding the phrase, "If, being invited there, he says, 'I will take almsfood'": here, when invited with the words, "Take food," he says, "I have no need for your food; I will take almsfood. The meaning is that there is no offense.
On this point, however, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "One who speaks thus is able to constitute a non-invitation under this training rule."
"But since an opportunity has been made for eating, one is released neither from the offense of group-eating (gaṇabhojana) nor from improper conduct (cāritta).
The Elder Mahāsumma said: "At the very moment one is able to make an invitation, at that very moment there is neither group-eating nor improper conduct."
In this context, "visiting" (*cāritta*) refers to the following rule:

"If a monk, having been invited for a communal meal, should visit families before or after the meal without informing a monk who is present—except on an appropriate occasion—it is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*). In this regard:"
“The proper occasion is the occasion for giving robes, the occasion for making robes. This is the proper occasion therein.

Thus the training rule concerning going on a journey has been handed down. For by this training rule, one who is invited with an improper invitation—such as by saying, “Take food,” and so forth—with any one of the five kinds of cooked food, [is not at fault] with respect to that very meal of the invitation...

Having already finished his meal, if he goes to the house of such-and-such a person or enters upon a journey without having informed a present bhikkhu with words such as these, then— whether he has eaten that meal for which he was invited or not—
he should not, before midday has passed, go from the family where he was invited to other families.
If one were to enter [a house], having set aside both types of permitted times (samaya) described for him, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated for doing so elsewhere.
Therefore, if one being invited by an improper invitation says, "I will accept alms-food," there is no offense even under this training rule (sikkhāpada).
3. Regarding the phrase "without having asked a bhikkhu who is present": herein, to what extent is one "present," and to what extent is one "not present"?
One is "present" from the point where, while staying within the monastery, the thought of visiting families has arisen;
from that point on, whoever he sees either to his side or in front of him, and to whom it is possible to announce [the matter] with ordinary speech—this person is "present."
There is no need to search here and there for the purpose of making a formal announcement; for whoever must be sought in such a manner is simply not present.
Furthermore, having seen a monk within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), one goes thinking, "I shall ask for permission.
In that case, whoever he sees should be asked for permission. If he does not see anyone, he has entered without asking permission of a non-existent monk.
This is the name [of the offense]. This same method applies to entering a village at an improper time as well.
However, if a large group enters a village for some business, they must all ask one another for permission, saying, "I ask for permission to enter the village at an improper time.
If that business is not accomplished in that village, they may go to another village.
They may go; let there even be a hundred villages, yet there is no further need for taking leave.
However, if they lose their enthusiasm and, while going to the monastery, wish to enter another village along the way, they must indeed take leave again.
Or, having performed the meal-duty at a family home or in a dining hall, one who wishes to go out for alms of oil or alms of ghee [must likewise take leave].
If there is a monk present, one must go after having asked for permission. If no monk is present, one may go thinking, "There is none.
If, having descended to the path, one sees a monk, there is no need to ask for permission; even without asking, one may simply proceed.
If the road passes through the middle of a village, for one traveling by that way with the thought, "I will go about for alms such as oil," etc., [the same applies].
If a thought arises that there is a monk present, one must go out after having asked for permission.
However, for one who goes on almsround without leaving the path, there is no requirement to ask for permission.
If a lion or a tiger approaches, or if a storm arises, or if some other danger occurs—under such circumstances as these, even without asking permission, one may leave from outside the village.
It is permissible to enter the village. 4.
"And, monks, a rag-robe must not be taken while the body is unseparated; whoever should take one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, a rag-robe must not be taken while the body is fresh and moist; one who takes it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Furthermore, dangers arise for it; however, it is permissible to take [the robe] once it has been torn.
To what extent is it considered "torn"? Even by the mere act of being slightly split by the beak or the fangs of crows, kites, cranes, jackals, and so forth.
But when, through the friction of falling, even a mere layer of skin is cut away, [it is considered torn].
The skin is "unbroken" (*abhinna*); it is indeed not broken as long as the skin itself is not cut. However, once the skin is cut, it is "broken.
Furthermore, if a boil, leprosy, carbuncle, or ulcer has already burst while the body was still alive, this too is "broken.
From the third day onward, even when it has reached the state of a corpse through the stages of bloating and so forth, it is likewise "broken. Yet, even when it is entirely unbroken in every respect—
It is permissible to have it taken by cemetery guards or other people. If no one else is available, one may take it after making a wound with a knife or some other instrument.

However, in the case of a body of the opposite sex, it is permissible to take it provided one maintains mindfulness, arouses the perception of a monk, and makes a wound on the head or on the back of the hands or feet.
5. How should a monk whose robe has been stolen proceed? "I allow you, monks, for one whose robe has been stolen or whose robe has been lost, to ask an unrelated householder or housewife for a robe.
If he first goes to a certain residence and there happens to be a robe belonging to the Saṅgha..."
Or a bedspread, or a floor-covering, or a mat of reeds—having taken one of these, he may put it on, thinking, "I will lay it aside after I have received [permission].
If there is no robe belonging to the Saṅgha, nor a bedspread, nor a floor-covering, nor a mat of reeds, he should come having covered himself with grass or leaves; but he must not come naked.
"One must come; whoever does not come incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of this statement, one should proceed according to the method explained here.

Now, this is the sequential account: If, upon seeing the thieves, the young monks take their bowls and robes and flee, and the thieves go away taking only the under- and upper-robes of the elders, then the robe [of the elder] has not yet been... by the elders.
One should request [the items], but one must not break off branches or foliage.

Then, if the young monks flee, abandoning all their belongings, and the thieves depart taking the robes and the belongings of the elders, the young monks who have returned must not yet give their own robes to the elders; for they are not those whose robes have been stolen.
They are permitted to break off branches and foliage for their own sake, and they are permitted to do so for the sake of those whose robes have been stolen.
Those whose robes have been stolen may break them off for the sake of both themselves and others;

therefore, the elders should either break off branches and foliage themselves and tie them with grass or similar materials to give to the juniors, or the juniors should break them off for the sake of the elders.
Having tied it up, whether he gives it into their hands or not, he should himself put on his own lower and upper robes and give them to the elders;
in this way, there is no offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for destroying living plants, nor is there an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for their wearing [the robes].
If, however, on the way there is a dyer’s cloth or they see other such people, [he should leave] the robe...
It should be requested. And whatever robes those people for whom they have been requested, or other people,
give out of inspiration upon seeing the monks dwelling among the branches and foliage— whether they have fringes or are fringeless, or are of various colors such as blue and so forth,
whether they are allowable or unallowable— all of them may be worn by them, because they stand in the place of one whose robe has been stolen.
And it is permissible to wear them.
This too has been stated in the Parivāra:
"That which is not made allowable, nor dyed with a dye..."
Clad in that, one may go wherever one wishes; there is no offense for him,
and this is the Dhamma taught by the Sugata.
“This question was contemplated by the wise.
For this question was spoken with reference to a bhikkhu whose robe had been torn.
However, when they encounter members of other sects (titthiya), and those give them robes made of kusa grass, bark, or wood-shavings, they may wear them even without adopting [the formal] tenets.
They are permitted; even after putting it on, one should not form the conviction that it is one's own.

Whatever robes, dwellings, or other requisites exist in the monastery where they first arrive, they may take them and wear them as an undergarment or an upper robe even without asking permission, provided they think:
"Having received this, I shall return it, and I will restore it again."
This is done with the intention [of preservation], not for the purpose of cutting off the root.
Once it has been obtained, however, one should restore it to its original state from relatives, attendants, or anyone else.

If, while traveling abroad, one leaves it in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha for the purpose of using it as property belonging to the Saṅgha, and if through that very use it becomes worn out or lost, there is a debt to be paid.

There is none. However, if one does not obtain any of these aforementioned items for household use, down to a piece of leather from a snake’s skin, one may come having covered oneself with grass or leaves.
6. “Monks, a lifelike painting should not be commissioned, whether in the form of a woman or a man. Whoever should commission one, [is guilty of an offense].”
Because of the statement, "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to make or cause to be made an image of a woman or a man.
Not only an image of a woman or a man, but even an animal form— even as small as an image of a leech—
it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to make it himself or to say, "Make one," such as, "Lay follower, make a door-keeper."
One may not even speak of it. However, one may have others perform inspiring deeds such as giving—which are unlike those described in the *Jātaka* collection—or matters connected with disenchantment;
one may also perform these oneself, such as making flower garlands and the like.
7. "Monks, a monk who has left his meal unfinished must not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense."

Because of the statement, "it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," a monk eating anywhere—whether in a village, a monastery, or in the forest—must not be made to leave before his meal is finished. If one arrives later in a village, he may take alms and depart.
If people or monks say, "Please enter," [he should reply: "If I enter, the monks..."
One should say, "They will rise. But when it is said, "Come, venerable sirs, there are seats," one may enter.
If no one says anything, one should go to the hall for seating and stand in a suitable place, not too close.
When space has been made and one is told, "Enter," one should enter. However, if a seat falls to one's lot, [one should sit].
In that case, it is permissible to ask a monk who is sitting there without eating to rise.

However, if he has drunk or eaten anything at all—such as rice gruel, dry food, or the like—it is not permissible to ask him to rise even if his hands are empty while he remains seated until another person arrives;
for he is still considered one whose meal is unfinished.
But if he nevertheless causes [the other] to leave even after the offense has been committed, and this monk has already finished his meal, he should be told:
"Go, fetch some water. This is the only occasion for ordering a senior monk.
If he does not even fetch the water, [he should be made to] swallow the rice morsels carefully and [then attend to] the elder.
A seat should be offered. And this has also been said:
"If he causes [the senior] to rise and he has already been invited [to eat], he should be told, 'Go, fetch water.
If it can be obtained in this way, that is good. If it cannot be obtained, having carefully swallowed the rice, a seat should be offered to the elder."
“Monks, I do not say that for any reason whatsoever should a seat be withheld from a more senior monk;
whoever should withhold it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow a junior monk who is reciting to sit on a seat equal [in rank] to that of his teacher.”
Based on the statement, "Or, out of reverence for the Dhamma, one may sit on a higher seat when being exhorted by an elder bhikkhu,
or on an equal or lower seat out of reverence for the Dhamma," it is permissible for a junior bhikkhu who is exhorting to sit on a higher seat,
and for a senior bhikkhu who is having [the junior] exhorted to sit on a lower seat.

9. “I allow you, monks, to sit together with one who is within three years [of seniority],” because of this statement, it is permissible for a monk to sit on the same seat as one who is within three years [of seniority].
One who is “within three years” is one who is either greater than two years or less than two years; whereas one who is greater than or less than one year, or...
If they have been ordained for the same number of years, there is no need to say anything further; all of them may sit two by two on a single bed or bench.
For it has been said: "I allow, monks, a bed for a group of two and a bench for a group of two."
10. However, whatever is sufficient for three people—whether it be portable or non-portable—even on such a mere wooden plank, it is permissible to sit together with one who is not fully ordained.
For it has been said: “Monks, I allow that which is sufficient for three; this much is the minimum length for a long seat. “Monks, I allow...”

However, based on the statement, "Excepting a paṇḍaka, a woman, and a hermaphrodite, one may sit on a long seat together with those who do not share a common seat," it is likewise not permitted to sit on a long seat together with a paṇḍaka or others. 11.
When attending to the sick, [the Buddha said]: "Bhikkhus, you have no mother, you have no father, who might attend to you."
“Bhikkhus, if you do not attend upon one another, who then will attend?
Bhikkhus, whoever would attend upon me should attend upon the sick. Recalling this instruction of the Blessed One, one should attend with care.
If there is a preceptor, he should be attended to by the pupil for as long as life lasts; his recovery must be awaited.
If there is a teacher, he should be attended to by the pupil for as long as life lasts; his recovery must be awaited.
If there is a co-resident student, he should be attended to by the pupil for as long as life lasts; his recovery must be awaited.
If he is a resident pupil, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts by that resident pupil, and his recovery should be awaited.
If he has the same preceptor, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts by one who shares that preceptor, and his recovery should be awaited.
If he has the same teacher, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts by one who shares that teacher, and his recovery should be awaited.

One must go to him. If there is no preceptor, teacher, co-resident, pupil, fellow-preceptor, or fellow-teacher, he should be attended by the Saṅgha. If one does not attend to him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
According to the statement, if one's preceptors and others are not present in that monastery, and he is a visiting monk traveling alone, he is a burden to the Saṅgha;
therefore, he must be looked after by the Saṅgha. If they do not look after him, there is an offense for the entire Saṅgha.
However, among those who take turns looking after him, the offense belongs only to the one who does not look after him during his own turn.

Even the senior monk of the Saṅgha is not exempt from his turn of duty. If the entire Saṅgha takes up the burden for one person, or if a single monk endowed with proper conduct takes care of him, thinking, "I alone shall look after him," then the Saṅgha is released from the offense.
However, in the case of one who is ill—
“Monks, a patient endowed with five factors is difficult to attend to. He does what is unwholesome;
he does not know moderation regarding what is wholesome; he does not take his medicine;

he does not describe his illness as it truly is to the caregiver who desires his welfare, saying, ‘When I am moving forward, I am moving forward,’ or ‘When I am moving backward, I am moving backward.’”
Or he moves back when [the monk] has moved back; or, standing, he says, ‘He is standing.

He is by nature one who does not endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, harrowing, disagreeable, and life-threatening.”—Having thus avoided from afar these five unbecoming factors which have been mentioned:
“Monks, a patient endowed with five factors is well-attended. He acts in accordance with what is beneficial;
he knows the proper measure regarding what is beneficial; he consumes medicine;
he reveals the illness as it truly is to the attendant who desires his welfare, saying, ‘When I am moving forward, I am moving forward; when I am moving backward, I am moving backward.’”

"Or standing, he stands"— thus one must be endowed with these five factors as they have been described, being "one who is by nature patient toward arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening."
And by the attendant of the sick:
"Monks, one who possesses five qualities is not fit to attend to the sick.
He is not capable of providing medicine; he does not know what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he offers what is unsuitable."
“He diverts himself toward what is suitable for his own gain; he attends to the sick with a motive for material things rather than with a mind of loving-kindness;
he feels disgust at removing excrement, urine, spittle, or vomit;
and he is not capable of instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with talk on the Dhamma.”
Having avoided from afar these five unsuitable factors thus described—“Bhikkhus, a nurse endowed with five factors is capable of attending to the sick. He is able to provide medicine;
he knows what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he sets aside what is unsuitable and [provides] what is suitable...”
He brings [medicine] forward; with a mind of loving-kindness he attends to the sick, not for the sake of material gain;
he is not disgusted by removing excrement, urine, spittle, or vomit; and he is capable of instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with talk on the Dhamma.”
One should be endowed with these five factors thus spoken.

And while delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, one should speak to the sick bhikkhu regarding the excellence of death, saying: "You are indeed virtuous and skilled in what has been done; why do you fear dying?
Is not heaven for the virtuous dependent upon nothing more than death itself? Thus [should he speak].

He should not be praised. For if, having heard praise of him, one were to die prematurely through some means such as the cessation of food while there is yet only a single conscious moment remaining of his life-span, he would have been killed by that very person.
However, a wise bhikkhu should give instruction in this manner: "The arising of the paths and fruits is no wonder for one who is virtuous; therefore, in monasteries and so forth..."
“Without forming attachments, one should establish mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the body, and apply diligence to mental attention.

Even when the description of death is being recounted, if he makes no effort on account of that description, he dies according to his own nature, according to his lifespan, and according to the natural sequence of events; because of that, [he does not die prematurely].
One who praises [himself] should not be made to undergo an offense.
13. “And you, monks, must not throw yourselves down; whoever should throw himself down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, even a sick monk must not, by any means whatsoever—even by the cessation of food—throw himself down.
He is to be killed. Even in the case of one who is ill and, while medicine and attendants are available, cuts off food because he desires to die, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa* offense.

However, if there is a monk with a severe, long-lasting illness, such that the monks who attend to him become exhausted, feel disgusted, and are distressed, thinking, "When indeed shall we be freed from this sickness?", and if that person [thinks], "Even though this body is being cared for..."
"If [the life-force] does not persist and the monks are becoming exhausted," it is permissible for one to cut off food, not use medicine, and so forth.

Furthermore, if one thinks, "This illness is severe, the formations of life do not persist, and this attainment of distinction appears as if already within my grasp," and thus cuts them off, it is likewise permissible.
Even for one who is not ill, if a sense of spiritual urgency has arisen, [to think,] "The search for food..."
"It is mere conceptual proliferation; I shall devote myself solely to the meditation subject"—it is permissible for one who cuts off [the meal] under the pretext of the meditation subject.
However, it is not permissible if one cuts off the food after announcing the attainment of a specific distinction.
For it is permissible to speak thus to fellow bhikkhus who possess a sense of shame.
14. “And, monks, one should not sit on a seat without having examined it; whoever should so sit commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, one must not sit on a seat without having scrutinized it. But what kind of seat is to be scrutinized, and what kind is not to be scrutinized?
That which is a mere seat, clean and without any spread, and that which—
If it is spread out while people have arrived and are looking on, that should not be reviewed; it is permissible to sit there.
Even if people themselves step onto it with their hands and offer it, saying, "Venerable sir, please sit here," that is also permissible.
Even if those who had already arrived and were sitting there later move upward or downward, [it remains permissible].
There is no need for inspection. Even that which is covered by a thin cloth such that the palm is visible through it, there is likewise no need for inspection.

However, that which has been prepared beforehand with a cloak, a quilt, or the like, should be sat upon after feeling it with the hand and examining it. But in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "Even with a thick robe..."
It is said: "That upon which no fold (wrinkle) is visible when it is laid out should not be scrutinized.

15. Because of the statement, "Monks, a stone must not be pierced for sport; whoever should pierce one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," a stone must not be rolled about with the intention of making a joke.
And this applies not only to a stone, but to whatever else [might be used].
It is not permitted to pierce anything with the hand or with a tool, whether it be a piece of wood or a piece of brick.
However, when stones and such are rolled, thrown, or lifted up while laughing for the sake of a cetiya or similar structure, it is permissible, as it is considered "the time of work.
This also applies to those performing other such new construction or washing articles.
It is permissible to drive them away by throwing up a tree or a washing-brush;
it is also permissible to scare them away at times such as during the meal break by throwing a stick or a pebble at crows or jackals.
16. "Monks, a forest grove must not be set on fire; whoever should set one on fire incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," because of this statement.

Fire must not be set to a forest. However, if one sets fire with the thought, "Let whatever being lives within this area die," there is an offense according to the respective categories of *pārājika*, *ānantariya*, *thullaccaya*, or *pācittiya*, as well as a heap of unwholesome states (*akusalarāsi*) such as *pārājika* and so forth.
For one who sets fire with the thought, "May all grasses and trees burn," it is a *pācittiya*.
For one who sets fire with the thought, "May the wooden implements be destroyed," it is a *dukkaṭa*. Even if done with the intention of mere play...

“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*. Regarding one who gives fire with the thought, “Let whatever is wet or dry, whether possessing sense-faculties or lacking them, be consumed,” the offenses—Pārājika, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, and Dukkaṭa—are to be understood according to the specific object involved.
However, the Blessed One has permitted the giving of a counter-fire and the performance of protective charms; therefore, [this applies] when forest workers in the wilderness...
Or, seeing a fire approaching—whether given by others or arisen spontaneously—one may light a counter-fire against it so that "the grass huts do not perish.
This is permissible so that the fire coming with it may merge with the counter-fire and be extinguished for lack of fuel.
"It is also permissible to make even a small [protection]" refers to smoothing the ground around the grass huts or digging a trench.

Or, just as a fire that has started goes out when it finds no fuel, all of this may also be done by oneself once the fire has already arisen, provided no one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) is present.
However, if the fire has not yet arisen, it must be caused to be extinguished by those who are not fully ordained using appropriate terminology;
furthermore, those extinguishing it with water must pour only water that contains no living beings.

17. Having received respectful and excellent food from families that lack faith and hold wrong views, one should neither consume it oneself nor give it to others without first investigating them. For such families may offer alms mixed with poison.
Furthermore, whatever food—whether stale rice or snacks—one receives from them, that too must not be consumed.
For those families give as things to be discarded even food covered with cloth that has been inhabited by snakes, scorpions, and the like.
Furthermore, almsfood smeared with perfumes, turmeric, and so forth, should not be accepted; for they think that even food set aside after wiping it on their bodies may be given.
18. “Monks, there is no offense in giving to a cowherd,” it was said. In this regard, which kind of gift to a cowherd is permissible, and which is not? To this, the Elder Mahāsiva said:
“Only that which has been specifically assigned to the cowherd—such as when one says, ‘Take this much every day’—is permissible; anything beyond that is not permissible.”
But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Is there anything given after having had a leaf placed [as a sign] by cowherds, or after making a sign of a mark?
These people are the masters of what has been left in their hands; therefore, whatever they give, even if it is much, is permissible.
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "When children [take] a monastery belonging to people, or other fruits and crops..."
"It is permissible to accept what is given by those who guard [the property], but one must not take it after having had it brought.

However, in the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha or to a Cetiya, it is permissible for one who guards it by means of a fee; but for one who guards it for a wage, only that which is his own share is permissible.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it says: "Those who are garden-keepers for householders... [regarding] the monks...
Teeth—this is also permissible. As for garden-keepers belonging to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, what they give after having broken off [fruit] as their own wages is permissible.
Even one who guards half a monastery or a few trees after receiving wages, it is permissible for him to give from the very trees he has received;
however, for one who guards them by taking a fee (keṇī), [it is not].
"Everything is also permissible," it is said. However, all of this is a difference in phrasing; in meaning, it is one and the same.
Therefore, it should be understood by knowing the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
Furthermore, this specific determination (*vinicchaya*) should also be known here: where the residents do not give [food] to the newcomers during the fruit-season.
Furthermore, when others have not arrived and they see their absence, they eat it themselves by stealing it;

in such a case, it is proper for newcomers to strike the gong and, having shared it out, consume it. However, where resident monks guard the trees and, when the fruiting season arrives, share and eat them while properly providing for the four requisites, there the newcomers have no authority.
Even regarding those trees that have been specifically designated for the purpose of robes, the newcomers have no authority over them.

This same principle applies to those designated for the sake of other requisites as well. However, as for those given without such designation, which the residents enjoy by stealing after having guarded and protected them, one should not abide by the agreement made among the residents in such cases. As for those given for the purpose of enjoying their fruit—
If the resident monks, having guarded and protected [the goods], hand them over properly, one must abide by their agreement regarding those very items.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "One who uses with a thieving mind what has been given after the four requisites have been assigned must be dealt with according to the value of the goods;
for one who uses them after dividing them by way of consumption, there is the obligation to pay the value of the goods."

"However, regarding that which has been designated here for the purpose of lodgings, for one who distributes it solely for the purpose of personal use and consumes it, there is a thullaccaya offense and the value of the goods must be paid.
That which is given specifically for the purpose of robes should be applied only to robes. If there is a famine, the monks—
If they are distressed by almsfood, but robes are easily obtained, it is permissible to offer almsfood after performing an act of formal authorization for the welfare of the Saṅgha.

If they are distressed by lodgings or medicinal requisites for the sick, it is also permissible to offer them for that purpose after performing an act of formal authorization for the welfare of the Saṅgha.
[This applies] specifically for the sake of almsfood and medicinal requisites for the sick...
And the same principle applies even when [the robe] has been given. However, that which is specifically given for the purpose of a dwelling is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*);

it must be protected, guarded, and used solely for that purpose. But if there is a famine and the monks cannot subsist on alms-food—where, due to fear of kings, disease, thieves, and so forth, they go elsewhere and their monasteries fall into ruin—[then it may be otherwise].
While things such as palm trees and coconut palms perish, it is possible to subsist by depending on the requisite of lodgings;
at such times, even if one relinquishes the lodging, the Blessed One has permitted its use for the purpose of maintaining the dwelling.
Therefore, having set aside one or two excellent lodgings, the others—even those of the lowest quality—should be used for the sake of alms-food.
It is permissible to sell [the produce], but it must not be brought [to the monastery] after cutting off its root or source.
However, in the case of a monastery that has been designated and given for the purpose of the four requisites, a formal act of consultation (*apalokanakamma*) need not be performed there.
It is, however, permissible to bring in what is lacking for the sake of those requisites; the monastery must be maintained, and wages [should be paid].
Even after giving [the fruit], it is permissible to have it preserved. However, if those who, having received wages, live in the monastery itself after building houses there,
protect [the property] and give coconuts or palm fruits to the monks who have arrived,
they may give only that which has been authorized for them by the Saṅgha, saying, "Eat this much every day."

They may accept it, but beyond that, it is not permissible for them to accept even what those donors give. However, if someone acquires a monastery by purchase and gives only allowable goods for the sake of the Saṅgha’s four requisites, this person is permitted to give as much as they wish.
This also applies to a monastery given for the purpose of lighting lamps at a cetiya or for the repair of dilapidated parts.
It must be looked after; it may even be made to be looked after by paying wages. And here, it is permissible to give wages from the property of a *cetiya* as well as from the property of the Saṅgha.

This case should be understood according to the method already stated regarding those who live right there in that monastery while guarding it for wages, those who take it on lease, and those who provide allowable goods, as well as the gift of fruits produced there.
19. For one requesting protection for the righteous, it is not permitted to specify and describe [the danger] by referring to either the past or the future.
Regarding the past, there is both specified description and unspecified description;
regarding the future as well, there is both specified description and unspecified description. How is there specified description regarding the past?

What is it? When village boys, ruffians, or anyone else misbehave in the monks’ dwelling—whether they cut down trees, take fruits and flowers, or steal requisites—the monk approaches the judges and says, "This or that has been done in our dwelling.
When asked, "By whom?", he replies, "By so-and-so..."
and by so-and-so,” he declares. Such specific declaration concerning the past is not permissible.
If, having heard this, those judges impose a penalty on them, the entire liability falls upon the monk;
even if his intention is merely, “They will take the penalty [from them],” the liability still falls upon him. However, if he says, “Take the penalty from him,” [it is permissible].
He speaks; when even five māsakas have been taken, it becomes a *pārājika* offense. However, when asked, "By whom?", he should say:
"It is not permissible for us to say 'by such-and-such a person'; you yourselves shall know. We merely ask for protection;
give that to us, and have the stolen goods brought back. This is an unspecified pointing out. That—

It is permissible. When this has been said, even if those judges seek out the perpetrators and inflict punishment upon them, and even if all their property is confiscated, there is neither liability nor an offense for the monk. Furthermore, it is not permissible to say "Thief!
Thief! out of a desire to cause harm to those who are seen carrying away requisites. For even when this has been said, whatever punishment they inflict upon them [falls upon them alone].
A monk may have a debt. However, it is permissible for him to say to someone who obeys his word, "This person has taken my requisites;

make him bring them back, and do not inflict punishment upon him. But when people gamble for the sake of male and female slaves, etc., this is called an improper gambling match (*akappiya-aḍḍa*), and it is not permitted.

How is there a specific declaration concerning the future? In the same manner already described, when others commit misconduct and so forth, a bhikkhu says to the judges: "They are doing this and that in our monastery; grant us protection so that they may not do it again in the future.
When asked, "By whom was this done?", he declares: "By such-and-such a person and by such-and-such a person."
Thus, there is a specific announcement concerning the future; that too is not permissible.
For when a punishment is imposed on them, as in the previous case, the entire liability falls upon the monk. The rest is exactly as before.

If the judges, having caused a drum to be beaten with the command: "We shall impose such-and-such a punishment on those who commit such misconduct in the monasteries of the monks," [issue this order...]
If they do not stop, one may search for them and impose a fine; however, there is neither a debt nor an offense for the monk.
It is not permissible to take axes, hatchets, and so forth, and strike trees and such within the boundary of a monastery with stones while cutting them down.
If the blade breaks, it must be repaired and returned. If they run up and seize their requisites, that too is not permissible.
It must be done. For the mind is quick to change; once the intention to steal has arisen, it might even lead to the cutting off of one's roots [of merit].
It is not permissible to discard or cause to be discarded excrement, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or over a fence.
Even for one who discards all four of these items in a single action, there is only one [offense].

It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who discards [things] individually, there are offenses of wrong-doing according to the number of items. The same principle applies to giving an order [to discard them]. There is also an offense of wrong-doing for discarding tooth-sticks.
However, there is no offense for one who discards excrement and so forth after looking [for a suitable place] or in a place where there is no danger [of harm].
Even if it is a field planted by humans as their property for use and enjoyment, such as a grove of coconut trees and the like—
Or, even there, it is not permissible to discard these things in any place where green vegetation grows.
For one who discards them, the classification of the offense should be understood according to the same method as before.

If, while sitting in a field or a monastery and eating, or while chewing sugarcane and the like, one goes along and discards leftover water, dregs, and so forth, in a place where green vegetation grows;
Even if one discards a coconut that has been cut at the top after drinking its water, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Even when sprouts have emerged—or even if they have not—among seeds sown in a ploughed field, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing. However, it is permissible to discard them in places where seeds have not been sown, such as the corners of a field, or on the boundaries of a field where no planting has occurred;
it is also permissible to discard them in a place where people throw away their rubbish.
It is permissible. When humans have harvested the grain and departed, it is what is called an abandoned field; there it is permissible.
However, where they guard it with the thought, "Even if the early rice and so forth are gathered, it will grow again," there it is not permissible.
21. "Monks, a monk who is bathing must not rub his body against a tree. Whoever should rub [his body against a tree],"

Because of the statement, "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one who is bathing must not rub the body against a tree, or against a pillar set up after being buried at a bathing place, or against any kind of wall made of brick, stone, wood, or plaster.
Because of the statement, "Monks, one must not bathe in an improper place; whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
It is not permitted to bathe at a *aṭṭhāna*. What is called an *aṭṭhāna*?
They cut down a tree like a plank and, having carved lines in the shape of a checkerboard (*aṭṭhapada*), they bury it at a bathing place; there, people sprinkle scented powders and rub their bodies.
“Monks, one must not bathe with a fragrant hand-bath (*gandhabbahatthaka*). Whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).”
At bathing places, people take powder with wooden ladles placed there and rub their bodies;
therefore, it is not permissible to bathe [with that].
“Monks, one must not bathe with *kuruvindaka* soap. Whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).”
According to the textual tradition, it is not permitted to bathe with *kuruvindaka* powder.
*Kuruvindaka* powder refers to a bundle of pills made by binding *kuruvindaka* stone dust with lac; one holds these at both ends and rubs them against the body.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "Monks, one should not have massage performed while quarreling; whoever should have it done so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," it is not permitted to rub each other's bodies against one another.
“Monks, one must not bathe using a *mallaka* (a tooth-stick scraper). Whoever should so bathe incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Monks, I allow an unworked *mallaka* for one who is ill. Because of this statement, that which is made by cutting off the shark-fins [of a tooth-stick] and shaping it like the base of a *mallaka* is called a “*mallaka*”;
this is not permitted even for one who is ill. An “unworked *mallaka*” refers to [one made from] ivory...
What is made by tearing [cloth] apart is not permitted for one who is not ill; however, a fragment of brick or a fragment of a skull is permitted.
Because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a *ukkāsika* and a *puthupāṇika*,” both the *ukkāsika* and the *puthupāṇika* are permitted.
A *ukkāsika* is a roll of cloth; therefore, it refers to any roll of a bathing garment for one who is bathing.
It is permissible to rub the back. "Broad palms" refers to hand-massage; therefore, it is permissible for everyone to perform back-massage with the hands.
This, however, is the rule for bathing here: having gone to a water-crossing and having laid aside one's robe anywhere there, [one should bathe].

One should not descend with haste as if one were standing still; rather, having looked in all directions and ascertained that the place is secluded, and having identified stumps, thickets, creepers, and so forth, one should clear the throat three times and, while standing with the body bent forward, remove the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and spread it out.
Having loosened the waistband (*kāyabandhana*), it should be placed right on top of the robe. If there is no bathing cloth (*udakasāṭikā*), [one should do so] at the water's edge.
Having sat down in the squatting posture and removed his lower garment, if there is a sloping place, it should be spread out in the sun;

if not, it should be folded up and set aside. When descending, one should descend slowly to the depth of the navel, and then, without creating ripples or making a sound, turn back and submerge oneself facing the direction from which one came.
In this way, the robe is protected. When emerging from the water, one should emerge slowly without making a sound;

at the conclusion of the bath, one should sit in the squatting posture at the water’s edge, put on the lower garment, stand up, dress in the lower garment very neatly, fasten the waist-band, and only then put on the upper robe before standing still.

22. “Monks, a creeper-garland must not be worn… a waist-belt must not be worn… a neck-thread must not be worn… a hip-string must not be worn… a breast-ornament must not be worn… an armlet must not be worn… a hand-ornament must not be worn… a finger-ring must not be worn.
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
According to the textual tradition, no ornament whatsoever—such as earrings and the like—is permitted.
In this context, "pendants" (*vallikā*) is a designation for things such as tassels or hanging ornaments that emerge from the ear.
Not only pendants, but any kind of ear-ornament—even so much as a palm leaf—is not permitted. "Necklaces" (*pāmaṅga*) refers to any kind of hanging string of beads.
“Necklace” (*kaṇṭhasuttaka*) refers to any ornament worn on the neck. “Waistband” (*kaṭisuttaka*) refers to anything worn around the waist, even if it is merely a single thread.
“Anklet” (*ovaṭṭika*) refers to a bracelet. Bracelets (*kāyūra*) and so forth are already well known.
23. “Monks, long hair must not be worn. Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). I allow—”

Based on the statement, "Monks, [the hair] shall be two months old or two finger-breadths long," if the hair reaches two finger-breadths within two months, it must be cut within those same two months;
it is not permitted to let it exceed two finger-breadths.
Even if it is not long, one is not allowed to let it exceed [the limit] by even a single day beyond two months. In both cases, this is the maximum limit.
Thus it was said; beyond that, however, there is no state of being permitted.
From the statement: "Monks, hair should not be caused to be cut with scissors; whoever should cause it to be cut, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to have hair cut with scissors on account of illness," [it follows] because of illness...
It is not permitted to have the hair cut without a razor.
“Monks, the hair must not be smoothed with a brush... the hair must not be smoothed with a comb... the hair must not be smoothed with a hand-comb...
the hair must not be smoothed with beeswax... the hair must not be smoothed with oil mixed with water.”
Because of the statement, “Whoever should comb [the hair] commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” the hair should not be combed with a brush or similar tools for the sake of beautification;

however, for the purpose of smoothing down the hair that grows upward, one may moisten the hand and wipe the head, and it is also permissible to wipe the head with a moist hand even when it is covered in dust from being heated by the sun.
24. “Monks, one should not look at the reflection of one’s face in a mirror or in a bowl of water;
whoever should look, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, I allow you to look at the reflection of one’s face in a mirror or in a bowl of water on account of illness.
Because of this statement, one should not look at one’s face in a mirror or in a bowl of water without being ill. In this regard:

Furthermore, bronze plates and other such items upon which the reflection of the face appears all fall under the category of mirrors; likewise, sour gruel and similar liquids fall under the category of water bowls.
Therefore, for one who looks at anything [other than these], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, it is permissible for the purpose of knowing, due to an illness, whether a wound has healed over or not yet done so.
It is said that it is even permissible to examine the constituent of life (*āyusaṅkhāra*) by thinking, "Am I old, or am I not?
[However: "Monks, the face must not be smeared... the face must not be massaged... the face must not be powdered...
the face must not be marked with red arsenic (*manosilika*)... no body-paint (*aṅgarāga*) must be applied... no facial makeup (*mukharāga*) must be applied... [and so forth].

"Body-unguents and face-unguents must not be applied; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Monks, I allow you to smear the face [with ointment] only on account of illness.
Because of this statement, facial smearing and the like must not be performed in the absence of illness.
25. "Monks, one must not go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music; whoever should go..."
"Because of the statement, 'There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' one must not go to see dancing and such.
And here, 'dancing' means whether it be actors and the like who dance, or drunkards, or even as little as peacock feathers or monkeys—even all this is indeed dancing;
therefore, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who goes to see even a peacock’s dance. [The same applies] for one who dances oneself."
Or for one who causes [others] to dance, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding "song": whether it be the song of actors and the like;
or the well-performed song associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the Noble Ones' parinibbāna; or the chanting of Dhamma by unrestrained monks;
or even a "tooth-song" (dantagīta)—that is, whatever they do beforehand while making grunting sounds, thinking, "We shall sing"—all of this is included.
It is indeed singing; for one who sings himself or causes others to sing, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa* offense.
“Monks, there are these five disadvantages for one who sings the Dhamma with a drawn-out melodic voice:
he himself becomes infatuated with that melody, others become infatuated with that melody, householders grumble, [he develops] a habit of melodic intonation...”
“While one is desiring concentration, it is destroyed; and later generations follow that example.
These, monks, are the five dangers for one who sings the Dhamma in a drawn-out, melodic voice.
Monks, the Dhamma should not be sung in a drawn-out, melodic voice. Whoever should sing it so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Even the Dhamma must not be sung with a drawn-out, melodic voice.
A "drawn-out" melodic voice is one that proceeds by breaking the regular cadence and distorting the syllables.
However, regarding the Dhamma, there is indeed the cadence of the Suttantas, the cadence of the Jātakas, and the cadence of the Gāthās.
Having removed that [excess], it is not permissible to make it too long; rather, the words and phrases should be displayed in a circular manner with a square arrangement.
However, because of the statement, "I allow you, monks, the chanting of the Dhamma in melody" (*sarabhañña*), it is permissible to recite the Dhamma with a melodic tone.
Indeed, in the *sarabhañña*, there are thirty-two [modes of recitation], such as the wave-pattern (*taraṅgavatta*), the wash-pattern (*dhota-vatta*), and the flow-pattern (*galita-vatta*).
There are various modes of recitation; among these, one may perform whichever one desires.
The characteristic [of this] is simply the proceeding according to the fourfold method in a manner befitting a recluse, without destroying the words and phrases and without making any alteration.
As for "instrumental music" (*vādita*), it refers to musical instruments bound with strings and so forth, whether they be struck by hand or sounded like a drum, even down to—

Even the sounding of water-drums or other musical instruments—all of this is not permitted. However, there is no offense if one is spitting, or standing in a place of danger, snaps one’s fingers, or claps one’s hands;
likewise, there is no offense for one standing within the monastery grounds who merely watches.
But there is indeed an offense for one who goes from one dwelling to another thinking, "I will watch. [This applies] in the assembly hall.
If he sees [them] while sitting, there is no offense. If he rises and goes with the intention, "I will see [them]," there is an offense;
even if he stands in the street and turns his neck to look, there is likewise an offense.

If he sees or hears [them] after having gone for the sake of a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*) or some other business, there is no offense. In cases of emergency (*āpadā*), such as when beset by such a calamity...
If one enters a festival site while being harassed, there is no offense for one who has entered in such a manner and sees or hears [the performance].
One may not say, "Lay followers, give an offering to the shrine," nor may one accept it when it is said, "We shall make an offering to your shrine.
Nor may one accept it when it is said, "We shall perform service for your shrine."
However, it is permissible to say that "providing assistance is indeed good.

26. Because of the statement, "Monks, one's own *aṅgajāta* (genital organ) must not be cut off; whoever should cut it off, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*," for one who cuts off the *aṅgajāta*, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; but as for other parts such as the ear, nose, finger, and so forth—whatever [is cut]...
There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who cuts anything or causes such pain.
However, there is no offense for one who causes blood to flow or cuts [a wound] on account of a snakebite, an insect bite, or other similar afflictions.
27. “Monks, a superhuman state or a miracle of psychic power must not be displayed to laypeople; whoever—”

Because of the statement, "If one should show [such powers], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," it is not permitted for monks to display the transformative power (*vikubbaniddhi*) to householders;
however, the power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is not prohibited. 28.
"Monks, a bowl made of gold must not be used... nor one made of silver... nor one made of gems... and so forth.
"Neither a bowl made of beryl... nor one made of crystal... nor one made of bronze... nor one made of glass...
nor one made of tin... nor one made of lead... nor one made of copper should be used; whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, bowls made of gold and so forth are not permitted. Even if a householder [places] gold plates and such in the dining hall...
Having made a handle, they offer it; even touching it is not permitted.
However, trays and other vessels made of crystal, glass, or bronze are not permitted for individual use;
they are permitted either for communal use by the Saṅgha or as items provided by laypeople. Even a plate made of copper is not permitted, but a shallow dish (thālaka) is.
It is permissible. “I allow, monks, two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl”; thus, only two types of bowls were authorized.
Because of the statement, “Monks, one must not wander for alms with a gourd-vessel;
whoever should so wander, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is not permissible to carry around a gourd-vessel; however, having obtained one, it may be used temporarily.
It is permissible. The same principle applies to a bowl-shaped basin (*ghaṭikaṭāha*).

Because of the statement, "Monks, a bowl with a human skull design must not be carried; whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," a bowl made from a human skull is also not permissible.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I authorize a bowl-rest," [it is permissible] for one made of earth, wood, bamboo, rattan, or similar materials.
It is permissible to place the bowl on a ground-rest or on a wooden stand.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kuruṇḍī* that "it is permissible to place three bowls one above another on a ground-rest, and two bowls on a wooden stand or a staff-stand.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "There is no room for three bowls on a ground-rest; it is permissible to place two. This also applies to wooden stands and staff-stands."
The same method applies to those that are well-prepared. However, a wooden stand resembling a turner’s lathe is bound with three sticks;
as for a stick-stand, there is no room even for a single bowl. Having placed it there, one must sit while holding it with the hand;
otherwise, it should be placed on the ground alone, turned upside down.
“Monks, an almsbowl must not be placed on a shelf; whoever should place it there incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Because of this statement, it is not permitted to place it at the edge of a porch shelf or similar surface. However, if it turns over and remains stable right there, it is permissible to place it on such a wide shelf.
"Monks, an alms-bowl should not be placed on a ledge; whoever should place it there, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, the same rule applies to the interior of a shallow cover made of thin cloth on the outer side.
"Monks, I allow a cloth (*coḷaka*)," because of this statement, it is permissible to spread out a cloth and place [the bowl] upon it. However, if that is not available...
It is permissible to place [the bowl] on a wooden shelf, a board, a clay surface, or on ground that has been plastered so that it does not get dirty, or on sand of such a kind.
However, for one who places it on dust, dirt, or similar rough ground, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Because of the statement, “Monks, the bowl must not be hung up; whoever should hang it up incurs an offense of wrong-doing,” it is not permissible to hang it anywhere on pegs or the like, nor is it permissible to place it by tying it to a robe-stand.
“Monks, an alms-bowl must not be placed on a bed; whoever should place it there incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Because of this statement, whether it was made for the purpose of storing belongings or for the purpose of sitting or lying down, there is an offense of wrong-doing for anyone who places it on any kind of bed or chair. However, it may be placed tied together with other belongings.
It is permissible to tie it with a loop and hang it, but even after tying it, it is not permissible to place it on top [of other items].
However, if a bed or a chair has been lifted and placed upon a robe-stand or similar object so that it is covered by a canopy, it is permissible to place it there.
It is also permissible to hang it from the shoulder using a shoulder-hanger and place it in one's lap.
It is not permitted to place [the bowl] on the lap, nor even to rest it upon the shoulder with the bowl-handle attached.
However, it is permitted for anyone to place it there if it has been tied together with other requisites and arranged as a bundle.
“Monks, one should not push open a door with the bowl in hand; whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
One should not push open the door with the bowl in hand. In this context, "one with bowl in hand" does not refer only to one who has the bowl in his hand.
Furthermore, it is not only the door that one is not permitted to push;
rather, wherever there is a bowl—whether in the hand, on the back of the foot, or in any other part of the body—one must not push with the hand or the foot.
“Whether with lead, or with any other part of the body, one is not permitted to push open a door-panel, lift up a latch, or open a door with a key;
however, having hung the bowl on the shoulder, one is permitted to open it as one pleases.
‘Monks, one must not carry out scraps of food, bones, or used water in the bowl.’”
"Whoever should carry [these] out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of this statement, it is not permitted to carry out scraps of food and the like with the bowl.

In this context, "scraps" (*calaka*) refers to bits of meat that have been chewed and discarded. "Bones" (*aṭṭhika*) refers to fish bones and the like. "Leftover water" (*ucchiṭṭhodaka*) refers to water used for rinsing the mouth.
For one who carries any of these out with the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing. [The same applies to carrying] the bowl or the alms-bag.
Having done so, he does not even get to wash his hand. It is not permitted to pour water from the washed hands or feet into the bowl and carry it out;
nor is it permitted to take hold of the clean, unwashed bowl with a hand that has been used for eating.
However, in this case, one may pour water with the left hand, take a single mouthful of water, and [rinse] with the hand that has been used for eating.
It is permissible to take it up. For even at this point, that bowl is considered "leftover" (ucchiṭṭha); however, after washing one's hand with water from outside, it is permissible to take it up.
And when eating fish, meat, fruits, or other such foods, whatever bone or core one wishes to discard there, one is not allowed to place that in the bowl. But as for what one wishes to chew again...
If there is [food], he is permitted to place it in his bowl. It is allowable to chew bone-thorns and the like right there, pull them out with the hand, and eat them.
However, one who wishes to eat again anything that has been removed from the mouth is not permitted to place it back in the bowl;
yet, having bitten off pieces of ginger, coconut, and so forth, he is permitted to place them back.
29. “And you should not, monks, be one who wears only rag-robes; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Because of this statement, one should not be a wearer of only rag-robes. In this context, however, it is permissible for both robes and bedsteads/chairs to be made of rags, but as for food to be swallowed, only that which has been given may be accepted.
30. “Monks, when a monk who has set out on a journey is asked for a water-strainer, he must not refuse;
whoever should not give one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Because of this statement, it is not permissible not to give a water-strainer to one who asks when one does not possess one. However, if someone asks even though a water-strainer is already in their own hand, [it is not an offense].
It must not be given to him against his will.
Because of the statement, “And monks, a monk who does not have a water-strainer should not set out on a journey;
whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” one should not travel on a road without a water-strainer, even if one does not possess one.
A water-strainer or a water-purifier (dhammakaraṇa) must be determined [as one's own] with the thought: "Having strained with this, I shall drink.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a staff-strainer," a staff-strainer is also permitted.
A staff-strainer is that which has a ladder-like structure bound to its four legs, like the lye-strainer used by washermen.
Having tied a cloth (sāṭaka) with a stick in the middle, they pour water into it; having filled both sections, it filters.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a strainer-cloth (ottharaka)," a strainer-cloth is also permitted as a filter.
A "strainer-cloth" (ottharaka) is that which, having been spread out over water, one takes up water from with a jar; for that [is placed] upon four sticks.
