Having tied a cloth [to a rope], they sink four stakes into the water, tie it to them, release all the ends from the water, and having submerged the middle, they draw up water with a jar. 31.
“Monks, one who is naked must not be saluted by one who is naked; whoever should so salute him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” and so forth, according to these words.
One who is naked must not pay homage to one who is naked; one who is naked must not cause one who is naked to pay homage;
one who is naked must not be made to pay homage by one who is naked; one who is naked must not perform service for one who is naked;
one who is naked must not give to one who is naked; one who is naked must not receive from one who is naked; one who is naked must not eat; one who is naked [must not...].
One should eat; one should not consume [food] naked, nor drink [liquids] naked.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow three coverings: a sauna covering, a water covering, and a cloth covering," these three coverings are permitted. And herein, regarding the sauna covering:
A water-strainer is permitted only for one who is performing the preparatory service; it is not permitted for the other acts, such as paying homage and so forth.
However, a cloth strainer is permitted for all formal acts.
32. “Monks, one must not lie down on beds strewn with flowers. Whoever should so lie down, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”

One must not lie down on beds covered with flowers; however, it is permissible to take the fragrance of the scent and apply it to the door with the five fingers, or to take a flower and place it aside in the monastery.
33. “Monks, one must not eat from a vessel that has been smeared [with food]. Whoever should so eat, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
According to the rule, one must not eat having placed food upon a vessel with a pouring lip (*āsittakūpadhāna*).
"Vessel with a pouring lip" is a designation for a box made of copper or silver; however, because it is prohibited, even one made of wood is not permitted.
34. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a *maḷorikā*," it is permissible to eat having placed food upon a *maḷorikā*.
“Maḷorika” refers to a staff-rest. A stand for a walking stick, a leaf-stand, a back-rest, a stool, and so forth, are also included herein.
From the point when they come under the general designation of “rests,” it is permissible whether they have holes or not, and whether they are pierced or not. 35. Because of such statements as:
“Monks, one should not eat from a single vessel; whoever should so eat, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” and so on.
One should not eat from the same vessel, nor should one drink from the same bowl.
However, if one monk takes fruit or a cake from the vessel and departs, it is permissible for the other to eat what remains once he has gone;
likewise, it is permissible for the first monk to take more once his portion is finished.
“Monks, one must not lie down on the same bed; whoever should so lie down incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of such statements, one must not lie down on the same bed, nor must one lie down on the same sheet.
However, for those who lie down after having established a boundary by placing a yellow robe, a walking stick, or at the very least a waist-band in between, [there is no offense].

There is no offense. One should not lie down with those who have only a single upper garment (*ekapāvuraṇa*) or with those who share both a single spread and a single upper garment (*ekattharaṇapāvuraṇa*).

"Those who have a single spread and a single upper garment" refers to those for whom there is one and the same thing that is both a spread and an upper garment. This is a designation for those who lie down after spreading out one end of portable rugs, blankets, mats, and so forth, and covering themselves with the other.
36. “Monks, a cloth-mat (celappaṭikā) must not be stepped upon; whoever should step upon it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Because of this statement, a cloth-spreading (celasanthāra) must not be stepped upon. However, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow that when requested by householders for the sake of an auspicious ceremony, one may step upon a cloth-mat,” [it is permitted] if a certain woman is either one whose pregnancy has passed or one who is heavily pregnant.
Alternatively, it is permissible for one who is requested to step on such places for the sake of an auspicious blessing.

Because of the statement, "I allow you, monks, to step on a washed-foot mat," it is permissible to step on a spread covering placed down for the purpose of stepping with feet that have been washed in a foot-washing place.
37. “Monks, a *kataka* [foot-scrubber] must not be used; whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, a *kataka* is not permitted. A *kataka* is something made in the shape of a lotus pericarp with spikes protruding for the purpose of rubbing the feet.
Whether it is circular or of a square or other variety, it is strictly prohibited because it involves indulgence in luxury.
It is not permissible to accept it, nor is it permissible to use it. However, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow three kinds of foot-rubbers:
gravel, pebbles, and sea-foam,” rubbing the feet with gravel and the like is permitted.
By “gravel” (sakkharā) is meant a stone; thus, even a stone-foam (pāsāṇaphenaka) is likewise permitted.
38. “Monks, a yak-tail fan must not be carried; whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, a fan made with yak-tail handles is not permitted.
“Monks, I authorize a mosquito fan. Monks, I authorize three kinds of fans: one made of wool, one made of *uśīra* grass, and one made of peacock feathers. Monks, I authorize—”
From the statement, “a fan and a palm-leaf fan,” the use of a mosquito fan and similar items is permitted. In this context, “fan” (vidhūpana) refers to a handheld fan.
As for the “palm-leaf fan” (tālavaṇṭa), whether it is made of palm leaves, bamboo, ivory, feathers, or leather products, all are permitted.
A mosquito fan with a handle made of ivory or horn is also permitted.
It includes those made of woven grass, as well as those made of *ketaka* shoots, *kuntāla* leaves, and so forth.
39. “Monks, an umbrella must not be carried. Whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monks, I allow an umbrella for one who is ill. Because of this statement, an umbrella must not be carried by one who is not ill. For whom...
However, if a bodily fever or a disturbance of bile occurs, or if the eyesight is weak, or if some other affliction arises—whether in a village or in the forest—an umbrella is permitted for him.

Furthermore, during the rainy season, it is permitted both for the purpose of protecting one's robes and for the purpose of protecting oneself from the fear of wild beasts and thieves; indeed, even a single-leaf umbrella is permitted in all circumstances.

“Monks, I allow even one who is not ill to carry a sunshade within a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery,” because of this statement, it is permissible for even one who is not ill to carry a sunshade within a monastery or its precincts. 40.
“Monks, long nails must not be worn; whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). I allow—”
Because of the statement, "Monks, one should clip the nails to the size of a grain of rice," long nails are to be clipped.
Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not have them polished to a shine like a mirror; whoever should have them so polished, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to remove only the dirt," one may have even twenty nails polished.
It is not permitted; however, it is permissible to remove merely the dirt from the nails.
Based on the statement: “Monks, the hair in the private parts must not be removed. Whoever should have it removed commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to have the hair in the private parts removed for the sake of a medical condition,” one may do so in cases of illness such as abscesses, wounds, and the like.
It is not permitted to have the hair removed from the private parts unless there is a necessity. Because of the statement, “Monks, long nose-hair must not be worn;
whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is permitted to have the nose-hair removed with tweezers.
There is no offense even in having the nose-hair plucked using pebbles and the like; however, for the sake of protection, [the Buddha said]: “I allow...”
"Monks, a pair of tongs," [it is said], and thus a pair of tongs was permitted. "Monks, one must not have grey hair plucked out;
whoever should have it plucked out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," because of this statement, it is not allowed to have grey hair plucked out.
However, that hair which has grown on the eyebrows, the forehead, or the beard, and remains looking hideous—such hair is what is called "grey hair" (palita).
Or it is permissible to have one’s grey hair dyed. 41.

Because of the statement, “Monks, a village must not be entered without a waistband; whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” one must not enter a village without a waistband.
When leaving without having fastened it, wherever one remembers [to do so],...
In that case, it must be tied up. It is permissible to go with the intention, "I will tie it up in the assembly hall.
Once one has remembered, one should not go on almsround until it has been tied up.
42. "Monks, one should not wear the clothing of a householder; whoever should so wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
According to the primary injunctions: one should not wear lay clothing such as that with an elephant-trunk hem;
one should not put on lay-style coverings such as those wrapped in white cloth; and one should not wear clothes with the waist tied like laborers, such as wrestlers or manual workers.
It is not permissible to dress in this manner even when ill or when traveling on a journey. Furthermore, regarding those traveling on a road...

If one lifts up one or two corners and hangs them over the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), or if one wears one saffron robe inside in that manner and then puts another robe on over it outside—all this is not permitted.

However, one who is ill is allowed to wear another robe over the top after showing the waistband (*ovaṭṭika*) of the inner saffron robe; one who is not ill, when wearing two robes, must do so with the upper robe folded over.
Having prepared them, they should be worn.

43. Because of the statement, “Monks, one should not carry a load on both shoulders; whoever should so carry it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is not permitted to carry a load on both shoulders.
“I allow you, monks, to carry a load on one shoulder, an intermediate load, or a head-load.”
Because of the statement, "It is permissible to carry a load on the shoulder, a load on the hip, or a hanging load," it is allowable to carry items such as a bundle of firewood. 44.
Because of the statement, "Monks, a long tooth-stick must not be used; whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," a long tooth-stick must not be used.
[The Buddha said: "Monks, I allow [a tooth-stick] up to eight finger-breadths in length."
“Dental wood. I allow you, monks, dental wood that is at least four finger-breadths long.
Because of this statement, one should chew dental wood that is eight finger-breadths at most and four finger-breadths at least, according to the measurement of a human finger.
45. “Monks, one must not climb a tree; whoever should climb one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). I allow you—”
Monks, because of the statement, "When there is a task to be done, one may climb a man-sized tree as much as necessary in times of distress," one should not climb a tree [ordinarily];
however, when there is a necessity such as gathering dry wood and so forth, it is permissible to climb one that is the height of a man. Regarding "in times of distress":
this refers to seeing wild beasts and the like, or being lost on the road, or desiring to look at the directions while a forest fire is raging.
Or, upon seeing a flood of water approaching, it is permissible to climb even a very tall tree.
46. "Monks, the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) must not be set to meter; whoever should so set it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to master the word of the Buddha in its own language (sakāya niruttiyā)," because of this statement, [the Veda...]
It is not permissible to announce the path of recitation for the Buddha’s word in the Pāli language as if it were in the Māgadhi language; rather, it should be mastered in its own Māgadhī idiom.
47. “Monks, the Lokāyata system should not be studied; whoever should study it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”

Based on their initial assertions, the teachers of other sects—known as the Lokāyatikas—possess scriptures associated with useless arguments, such as: “Everything is impure; everything is pure; a crow is white; a crane is black—for this and that reason.
Such works should neither be mastered nor taught to others. Furthermore, one should not master base sciences (tiracchānavijjā).
One must not cause another to recite it.
48. “Monks, when someone sneezes, one should not say ‘Live!’; whoever should say so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow that when householders say ‘May you live long, venerable sir,’ one should reply ‘May you live long. Because of this statement.
When [someone] has been spat upon, one should not say, "Live! However, when a householder says, "May you live," it is permissible to reply, "May you live long.
49. "Monks, garlic must not be eaten; whoever should eat it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to eat garlic on account of illness. Because of this statement, it is not permitted to eat garlic without being ill.
It is not permitted; however, it is permitted when added to things such as curry or condiments.

For that is permitted when added to anything whatsoever—be it boiling green-gram soup and the like, or fish and meat preparations, or oil, or jujube pickles and the like, or sour vegetables and the like, or even to supplementary foods (uttaribhaṅga), down to rice gruel and boiled rice.
50. “Monks, one must not step onto a lodging with unwashed feet; whoever should so step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, one must not step onto a prepared floor or a lodging such as beds and chairs with unwashed feet.
“Monks, one must not step onto a lodging with wet feet; whoever should so step...”

Because of the statement, “There is an offense of wrong-doing,” one must not step on ground or a dwelling that has been plastered with such damp feet from which water is still visible in the places trodden upon.
However, if only the moisture of the water is visible and no actual water remains, it is permissible. Furthermore, it is indeed permissible to step on a foot-wiping cloth even with damp feet.
“Monks, one should not step onto a lodging while wearing sandals; whoever should so step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, it is not permitted to step with sandals onto a place that is to be stepped upon with washed feet.
“Monks, one should not spit on ground that has been prepared; whoever should spit, there is an offense...”
Because of the statement, "It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one must not spit on ground that has been prepared.
When it was thus permitted, "Monks, I allow a spittoon," one may spit into a spittoon.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to wrap [it] with a cloth," [one may place] a bed or chair on either a plastered floor or a paved floor.
When putting it away, if there is no mat or wooden board, the legs of the bed and chair must be wrapped with a cloth;
if that is unavailable, it is permissible to spread out even a leaf. However, for one who places it down without spreading anything at all, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
But if the resident monks place it on the bare ground because there is nothing else, or use it while their feet are unwashed, [there is no offense].
It is likewise permissible to use it in that manner.

Because of the statement, “Monks, a prepared wall must not be leaned against; whoever should lean against one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” a prepared wall—whether it be a white-plastered wall or one decorated with paintings—must not be leaned against.

And it is not only the wall; one is not permitted to lie down without seeing even the door, the window, the window-sill, the stone pillar, or the wooden pillar, without having covered them with the robe or some other material.
However, because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to lie down after spreading a mat," one may step on [the floor] after washing the feet, provided it has been made into a border (paribhaṇḍaka).
One must lie down only after having covered the ground, a ground-covering, a lodging, or a bed or bench belonging to the Saṅgha with one’s own own covering-cloth.
Even if one falls asleep, if any part of the body touches the bed or the bench because the covering-cloth has shrunk, there is indeed an offense;
however, if it touches only the hairs, there are as many offenses as there are hairs touched.

The same rule applies even for one who does not see [the object] under the heading of "use" (*paribhoga*). However, it is permissible to touch or step upon [it] with the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet;
if it strikes against the body of one who is carrying a bed or a chair, there is no offense.
51. “Monks, these ten are not to be saluted: one who was ordained later is not to be saluted by one who was ordained earlier;”

It should be understood that these ten are not to be saluted, based on the statement: "One who has not received full ordination is not to be saluted; one of a different communion, even if senior, who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be saluted;

a woman is not to be saluted; a paṇḍaka is not to be saluted; one undergoing probation is not to be saluted; one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be saluted; one deserving the trial period (mānatta) is not to be saluted;
one undergoing the trial period is not to be saluted; and one deserving rehabilitation is not to be saluted."

“‘One who has been ordained later is to be saluted by one who was ordained earlier; one of a different affiliation who is senior and speaks according to the Dhamma is to be saluted; the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is to be saluted’—according to this statement, these three are to be saluted.
52. “I allow, monks, three kinds of cotton: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and moth-cotton”—according to this statement, these three kinds of cotton are allowable.
Therein, “tree-cotton” refers to that of any kind of tree, such as the *simbali* tree, etc.
“Cotton of trees” refers to the cotton of any kind of creeper, such as the milk-creeper (*khīravalli*) and so forth.
“Silk-cotton” refers to the cotton of any kind of grass, such as *poṭakī* grass and so forth, including even sugarcane, reeds, and the like.
By these three [categories], all types of living organisms (*bhūtagāma*) are included; for, apart from the classes of trees, creepers, and grasses, there is no other class of living organism.
There is no such restriction; therefore, cotton from any kind of living plant is permitted for a cushion.
However, once it has reached the stage of being a mattress (*bhisī*), all of this is called "unallowable cotton.

Furthermore, it is not only this cotton that is permitted for a cushion; the feathers of all birds, such as swans and peacocks, and the fur of all four-footed animals, such as lions, are also allowed, as are flowers such as the *piyaṅgu* and *bakula*.
However, no flower whatsoever is permitted. A *tamāla* leaf is not permitted if it is pure [unmixed], but it is permitted if it is mixed.
Regarding mattresses (*bhisī*), the five kinds of stuffing—wool and so forth—are also permitted. 53.
“Monks, I allow five kinds of mattresses: a wool mattress, a cotton mattress, a bark-fiber mattress, a grass mattress, and a reed mattress.”
From the statement "a mattress of leaves," five mattresses filled with wool and other materials were permitted.
Indeed, their number is stated according to the count of the stuffing. In that context, by the mention of "wool" (*uṇṇā*), not only sheep’s wool is included;
rather, with the exception of human hair, all the feathers or fur of birds and quadrupeds—whether of a permissible or impermissible species—is included.

Here, it is included by the very mention of "wool. Therefore, it is permissible to make a woolen mattress by using either one of the six types of robes or one of the six types of under-robes as the covering material, and then stuffing it with all of that.
However, even if sheep’s wool is not stuffed inside, if one merely stuffs a fourfold or fivefold layer of blanket-wool and makes it, it still counts as a woolen mattress.
A cotton mattress is one made by gathering any kind of new or old cotton and stuffing it inside.
A reed mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of reeds inside. A grass mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of grass inside.
A leaf mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of leaf inside, with the exception of pure *tāla* leaves.
It should be understood that *tamāla* leaves are permissible only when mixed with other materials, but not when used alone.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Kurundi* commentary that whatever five kinds of cotton, such as wool and so forth, are permitted for a mattress (*bhisi*), they are also permitted for a bolster (*masūraka*).
By this, it is established that it is permissible to use a bolster. There is no fixed measurement for a mattress.

Regarding the mattress for a bed, the mattress for a bench, the mattress for a floor, the mattress for a walking path, and the foot-wiping mattress—one should determine their size according to one’s own preference after observing what is appropriate for each. However, a bolster must be of a suitable size.
54. “Monks, you should not use bolsters that are half the body’s length. Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Having prohibited pillows that were half the size of the body—such as those which reach from the waist up to the head—the Buddha declared:
"Monks, I allow a pillow the size of the head. As for what is called "the size of the head":
when measured across the three corners [of the head], the distance between two corners is its width.
It is one span and four finger-breadths [in width], with the middle part being a fist’s breadth.
However, according to the *Kurundi*, "In length, it is one and a half cubits or two cubits. This is the maximum limit for the size of a headrest;
more than this is not permitted, but less is allowed. For one who is not ill, there is both a head-rest and a foot-rest.
Only two things are permitted: it is also permitted for one who is ill to lie down after spreading out pillows and placing a coverlet on top.
However, the Elder Phussadeva said: "It is also permitted to have a large pillow made with those five kinds of allowable stuffing materials that were authorized for mattresses.
But the Elder Vinayadhara-Upatissa said: "Thinking, 'I shall make a pillow'..."
"Whether one inserts allowable cotton or unallowable cotton, for one who makes [a seat], only the prescribed measure is permitted," he said.
55. "Monks, I allow a chair (āsandika)," because of this statement, a chair known as a square stool is permitted;
and because of the statement, "Monks, I allow even a high chair," it may be eight finger-breadths [in height].
A seat with high legs is also permitted. For it is specifically a long bench that is not permitted when its legs exceed eight finger-breadths on one side;
therefore, a square seat is permitted even if it exceeds the standard measurement.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow a seven-limbed [rest]," a couch constructed with a support on three sides is also permitted. "I allow... [the rest of the passage follows].
Monks, because of the statement, "even one as tall as seven spans," this [type of seat] is also permissible even if it exceeds the standard measurement.
Furthermore, that which is authorized in the Pāḷi by such passages as, "I allow you, monks, a bhaddapīṭha," refers to a seat made of cane,
a seat bound with rags, and a sheep's-foot stool (*eḷakapādapīṭha*)— shaped like an *āmalaka* fruit— constructed by placing the feet upon a wooden strip, similar to a food-tray.

A multi-legged stool, a stool with a circular frame of raw bamboo, a straw mat, a wooden plank seat, and whatever other wooden seats are not mentioned in the text, are all permissible. This is because of the statement:
"Monks, one should not lie down on a high bed; whoever should so lie down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

For one who lies on a bed that exceeds the prescribed measure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for one who makes it or causes it to be made, there is a *pācittiya* involving cutting down.
Having obtained one made by another, one who uses it must use it after cutting it down.
If he does not wish to cut it down, he should bury it in the ground so that the measure is visible above, or turn it upside down.
If one makes [a frame], uses it, or having lifted it and placed it upon a collection of scales, uses it after making a mark, it is permissible.
Because of the statement: “Monks, high bed-legs must not be kept; whoever should keep them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow bed-legs at most eight finger-breadths,” by means of the human standard finger-breadth—
A bed-leg support is permitted only up to eight finger-breadths in height; beyond that, it is not permitted.
56. “Monks, high and luxurious beds and seats are not to be used, such as:

a divan, a couch, a woolen coverlet, a variegated coverlet, a long-fleeced coverlet, a short-fleeced coverlet, a stuffed mattress, a bolster, a woolen rug with long fleece on both sides, one with long fleece on one side only, a deer-skin rug, silk, or embroidered cloth.”

Because of the statement: “Whoever should use a quilted rug, an elephant rug, a horse rug, a chariot rug, a rug of antelope hide, a rug of reed-matting, a rug of fine *kadalī* or *migapavara* deer-skin, provided with a canopy and red pillows at both ends—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”—high beds and grand seats are not permitted.
In this context, a "high bed" (*uccāsayana*) refers to a couch that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.
A *mahāsayana* (great bed) is an improper spread. Among items such as the *āsandī*, an *āsandī* is a seat that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.
A *pallaṅka* is one made by placing animal figures on its legs. A *gonaka* is a large woolen rug with long hair;
it is said that its pile is more than four finger-breadths thick. A *cittaka* is a woolen spread adorned with various jewels. A *paṭika* is a white woolen spread.
*Paṭalikā* is a thickly padded woolen mattress, which is also called an *āmalakapaṭa*.
*Tūlikā* is simply an ordinary stuffed mattress. *Vikatikā* is a woolen mattress variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth.
*Uddalomī* is a woolen covering with the fleece raised on one side. *Ekantalomī* is a woolen covering with the fleece raised on both sides.
They will spread out a rug made of silk (*koseyya*) interwoven with jewels. "Silk" refers to a rug made of silk thread interwoven with jewels;
however, plain silk is also permissible.
"Woolen rug" (*kuttaka*) refers to a woolen carpet suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand upon while performing a dance. There are also elephant rugs and horse rugs.
The coverlets on the backs of elephants and horses are indeed [special] coverlets. The same method applies to the coverlets on chariots.
"Antelope-skin rugs" (*ajinapaveṇī*) refers to rugs made by sewing together antelope skins to the size of a bed.
"Exquisite spread of kadali-deer skin" means there is a specific kind of deer skin called the *kadali-miga*, and a superior spread made from that; it is said that this was [spread] over white cloth.
They spread out the skin of a Kadali deer above, sew it together, and thus construct it. "With an upper canopy" means together with the upper covering;
the meaning is: together with the red canopy tied above. Even a white canopy is not permitted if there is an improper under-covering beneath it, but it is permitted when there is none.
"Red pillows on both sides" refers to both the head-pillow and the foot-pillow.

A bed with red pillows on both sides is not allowable. However, if there is only one pillow, whether it is red on both sides, the color of a lotus, or variegated, it is permissible provided it is of the correct measure;
but a large pillow is prohibited. As for woolen covers (gonaka) and the like, whether in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or in a private dwelling, [they are not to be used] on beds or stools.
It is not permissible to spread them out and use them; however, they may be obtained for a Dhamma seat by way of a layperson’s gift, yet even there it is not permissible to lie down.
“Monks, I allow you to sit upon anything except three things: a high couch, a luxurious couch, and a stuffed mattress—provided they are gifts from laypeople.”

However, according to the statement, "but one must not lie down," with the exception of the three types of high seats (the *āsandi*, etc.), it is permissible to sit on the remaining household items such as woolen rugs (*gonaka*), or on a Dhamma-seat, or in the dining hall, or within a house;
however, it is not permissible to lie down. But a bed or chair upholstered with cotton is permitted to be used for sitting in the dining hall or within a house.
It is permissible to lie down even there. However, for one who has a bed or chair upholstered with cotton down made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for tearing it out.

But because of the statement, "Monks, I allow an upholstered bed and an upholstered chair," it is permissible to have beds and chairs upholstered with leather and so forth. "Monks, I allow a woolen cloak. Monks, I allow a silk woolen cloak."
"I allow, monks, a woolen rug (*kojava*). I allow, monks, a blanket (*kambala*).

Because of these words, it is permissible to use items such as *pāvāra* robes—whether belonging to the Sangha or to an individual—as one pleases, either in a monastery or in a village, wherever they may be.
However, in this context, only a standard woolen rug is permitted; a large back-strap rug (*mahāpiṭṭhiyakojava*) is not permitted.
“Monks, I allow the use of all palace furnishings,” because of this statement, doors decorated with gold, silver, and so forth;
couches and stools; palm-leaf fans; water-jars and water-basins made of gold and silver; and whatever is fashioned with painted designs—all such things are permitted for use in lodgings.
[Also permitted are] the male and female slaves, fields and lands, and the palace itself.
If they say, "We are giving a cow or a buffalo," there is no need for separate acceptance; when the mansion is accepted, it is indeed accepted.
"I allow you, monks, sandals with a single layer of leather... Monks, sandals with double layers of leather must not be worn...
sandals with triple layers of leather must not be worn... sandals with multiple layers of leather must not be worn... whoever should wear them, there is an offense."
Because of the statement, "There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) [for using more]," sandals with only a single layer are permitted;
however, those with two layers or three layers are certainly not permitted. Sandals with multiple layers (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*) are said to begin from four layers;
these, moreover, are not permitted in the Middle Country alone. "Monks, I allow sandals with multiple layers in all outlying countries," it is said.
—According to the words [of the Vinaya], in border regions it is permissible to wear sandals with multiple straps (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*), whether they are new or used.
However, in the Middle Country, because of the statement: “Monks, I allow you worn-out sandals with multiple straps.
Monks, new sandals with multiple straps must not be worn; whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”; having fastened them...
A multi-layered sandal that has already been used is permitted; one that has not been used is strictly prohibited.
However, a single-layered sandal—whether used or unused—is permitted in all cases.
Furthermore, with the exception of human skin, sandals made from any other kind of skin are permitted. The same rule applies to the pouch for sandals, the sheath for a knife, and the case for a key.

“Monks, sandals that are entirely blue should not be worn… sandals that are entirely yellow should not be worn… sandals that are entirely red should not be worn… sandals that are entirely madder-red should not be worn… sandals that are entirely black should not be worn… sandals that are entirely dyed with mahāraṅga should not be worn.
Sandals that are entirely dyed with mahānāma should not be worn.”

"Sandals are to be worn; whoever should wear [forbidden ones], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of this statement, sandals that are entirely blue and so forth are not permitted.
In this context, "blue" (*nīlikā*) is the color of the flax flower; "yellow" (*pītikā*) is the color of the *kaṇikāra* flower; "red" (*lohitikā*) is the color of the *jayasumana* flower;
"madder-red" (*mañjiṭṭhikā*) is simply the color of madder; "black" (*kaṇhā*) is the color of burnt bricks; and "dyed with a great dye" (*mahāraṅgarattā*)...
It has the color of the back of a centipede... it is reddish-brown like a *mahānāma* flower, with mottled colors, having the appearance of a withered leaf.

However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated that "it has the color of a lotus flower. Having obtained any of these, it is permissible to dye it by wiping it with a cloth and wearing it once the color is altered;
even if the color is altered by only a small amount, it is indeed permissible.

“Monks, sandals with blue straps should not be worn… sandals with yellow straps should not be worn… sandals with red straps should not be worn… sandals with madder-red straps should not be worn… sandals with black straps should not be worn… sandals with straps dyed with a strong color should not be worn.”
"High-soled leather sandals with fringes must not be worn... whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, those sandals that are high-soled and colored blue or otherwise are also not permitted; however, it is permissible to wear them after altering their color.
"Monks, sandals with heel-protectors must not be worn... sandals with enclosed tops must not be worn..."

Sandals with leather covers must not be worn… sandals stuffed with cotton must not be worn… sandals with partridge-feather straps must not be worn… sandals with ram-horn heel-props must not be worn… sandals with goat-horn heel-props must not be worn… sandals with scorpion-patterns must not be worn… sandals woven with peacock feathers must not be worn.
"Sandals should be worn... variegated sandals should not be worn; whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Because of this statement, even sandals such as those with leather straps are not permitted.

In that context, "those with leather straps" refers to those made by binding leather to the soles for the purpose of covering the toes. "Those with compartments" refers to Yavana-style sandals, which extend as far as the shins.
It covers the entire foot. "Paliguṇṭhimā" means made by being wrapped around; it covers only as much as the foot above, not the calf.
"Tūlapuṇṇikā" means made by stuffing with cotton wool. "Tittirapattikā" means decorated and bound in a manner resembling the feathers of a partridge.
"Meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikā" means having fastened projections shaped like the horns of a ram at the position of the ear-rings.
[They] have been made. This same principle applies to those made from goat horns and so forth;

even scorpion-stingers are made by joining them to a horn shaped like a scorpion’s tail. "Covered with peacock feathers" means sewn with peacock feathers resembling thread onto either the leather or the horn.
"Variegated" means multicolored. Having obtained any of these, if one removes the leather patches and so forth—
They are capable of being used; they ought to be used. However, for one who uses them when such [forbidden] items are present, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Monks, sandals decorated with lion skins must not be worn... sandals decorated with tiger skins must not be worn...
sandals decorated with leopard skins must not be worn... sandals decorated with antelope skins must not be worn."
"Sandals are to be worn... sandals trimmed with ox-hide are not to be worn... sandals trimmed with cat-skin are not to be worn...
sandals trimmed with black-skin are not to be worn... sandals trimmed with deer-skin are not to be worn;
whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—from this statement, it follows that even those trimmed with lion-skin and so forth [are prohibited].
Footwear is not permitted. In this context, "lined with lion-skin" means that the lion-skin has been joined along the edges of the robe as if it were an inner lining;
this same principle applies in all cases. "Lined with otter-skin" refers to being lined with the skins of birds or cats.
In these cases as well, any such skin must be removed before the robe is worn.

“Monks, wooden sandals should not be worn… palm-leaf sandals… bamboo-leaf sandals… grass sandals… muñja-grass sandals… pabbaja-grass sandals… hintāla-reed sandals… kamala-grass sandals… woolen sandals… golden sandals… silver sandals… nor sandals made of jewels… nor sandals made of beryl.”
“Neither sandals made of crystal... nor those made of bronze... nor those made of glass... nor those made of tin... nor those made of lead... nor those made of copper...
nor any sandals that are merely for walking upon should be worn; whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Because of this statement, no sandals whatsoever made of grass or anything else that are merely for walking upon should be worn. “I allow...”
However, according to the statement: “Monks, there are three kinds of sandals that are fixed in place, not to be moved— namely, the toilet sandal, the urinal sandal,
and the rinsing sandal”— it is permissible to use these three types of sandals, such as the toilet sandal and the others, provided they are well-set on the ground, stationary, and immovable.
“Monks, one should not enter a village wearing sandals; whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Because of this statement, one should not enter a village wearing sandals. However, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow a sick monk to enter a village wearing sandals,” [this applies] to one whose feet are cracked or who has an affliction such as a corn on the foot.
If one's feet are painful such that one is unable to enter a village without sandals,
it is permissible for such a sick person to enter the village wearing sandals. Furthermore, because of the statement, "I allow you, monks, to wear sandals,
carry a torch, a lamp, and a walking stick within the monastery precincts," it is permissible even for one who is not sick to wear sandals within the precincts of the monastery.
“Monks, when teachers, those who are merely teachers, preceptors, or those who are merely preceptors are walking back and forth without sandals, one must not walk back and forth wearing sandals.
Whoever should so walk commits an offense of wrong-doing.

Because of this statement, when teachers and others are walking back and forth without sandals, one must not walk back and forth wearing sandals. And herein, the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjā-ācariya*)...
The preceptor for full ordination (*upasampadā-ācariya*), the tutor (*nissaya-ācariya*), and the instructor (*uddesa-ācariya*)—these four are indeed "teachers" (*ācariya*) in this context.

One who has been ordained for six years is merely a teacher for a novice (*avassika*). For he would have relied upon that teacher during his fourth year. Likewise, one of one year [is a teacher] for one of seven years;
one of two years for one of eight years; one of three years for one of nine years; and one of four years for one of ten years.

These too are merely teachers (*ācariya-matta*). However, those monks who are friends of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), having seen him and being his companions, or whoever else is senior to ten-year [seniority] monks—all these are called "merely teachers.
When these many monks are walking about barefoot, for one who walks about wearing sandals, there is an offense.
“Monks, large skins are not to be worn—namely, the skin of a lion, the skin of a tiger, or the skin of a leopard;
whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, cow-hide is not to be worn;
whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, no skin whatsoever is to be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
According to the words [of the Vinaya], in the Middle Country it is not permitted to take up or carry about any hide whatsoever, such as a lion’s hide and so forth.
The prohibition regarding lion hides and the like applies specifically to their being carried about;
however, for the purpose of spreading on the ground, it is permitted to use any hide whatsoever provided one does not carry it elsewhere.
“I allow you, monks, in all border regions, skins as coverings: sheepskin, goatskin, and deerskin.
Regarding this statement, in border regions it is permissible to lie down or sit upon any kind of sheepskin or goatskin.
As for deerskin, it refers to the skin of the eni-deer or the vata-deer.
The skins of only these are permitted: the *pasada* deer, the *kuruṅga* deer, the *migamātuka*, and the *rohitaka* deer.
However, for others— The monkey and the black lion, the *sarabha* and the *kadalī* deer;
whatever wild beasts there may be—their skins are not permitted.
In this context, "wild beasts" refers to lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas.

Not only these, however, but—setting aside those whose hides are permitted—all others, down to cows, buffalo, hares, cats, and so forth, should be understood as "wild beasts" for the purposes of this rule. Indeed, the hides of all of them are not permitted.
“Monks, one should not travel by vehicle; whoever should so travel commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow a vehicle for one who is ill. Because of this statement, a monk who is not ill must not go by vehicle.
Now, which kind of vehicle is allowable and which is not? “Monks, I allow a handcart yoked with men.”
"Monks, I allow a palanquin and a sedan chair," because of this statement, a hand-carriage drawn by men—whether it be a *sivikā* or a *pāṭaṅkī*—is permitted.
In this regard, whether the hand-carriage is drawn by men with a female driver or a male driver, it is permitted;
however, one drawn by cows is not permitted. As for the hand-carriage, it is indeed permitted whether women or men drive it.

57. “I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), a single-layered upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and a single-layered inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) made of unwashed cloth that is as good as new;
or a four-layered outer robe, a double-layered upper robe, and a double-layered inner robe made of cloth that has been washed out of season;
or as much rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) material as required; or effort may be made for cloth from a shop.”

According to the statement, "it must be made," for robes that have not been washed or have been washed only once, the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) should be made of double thickness, while the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) should be made of single thickness.

However, for rags (*pilotika*) taken from the weathered cloth of a hat, the outer cloak should be made of fourfold thickness, and the upper robe and the inner robe should be made of double thickness; this applies to refuse-rag robes (*paṃsukūla*).
However, it may be made according to one's preference. One should make an effort and conduct a search even for rags fallen from a marketplace;
there is no fixed limit, and even a hundred pattas is permissible. All of this is stated regarding a monk who consents [to the robe].
But among the three robes, they should be made by cutting two or even one; if that is not sufficient, the incoming cloth (āgantukapatta) [may be used].
It should be given. For it has been permitted for [a bowl] that does not suffice as an incoming bowl. Indeed, this was said:
"I allow you, monks, two cut [bowls] and one uncut.
When [the bowls] were not sufficient—two cut and one uncut—they reported this matter to the Blessed One. He said: "I allow you, monks, two uncut [bowls]."
"One [robe] has frayed edges; two have unfrayed edges. One with frayed edges is not sufficient. They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow you to add an extra piece as well. But, monks, you must not wear one that is entirely unfrayed;
whoever should so wear it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
Therefore, if it is possible to obtain a bowl for a guest, it is not permitted [to use the old one];
it must indeed be cut down. “Monks, a cloth made of *potthaka* grass must not be worn as an undergarment; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monks, robes that are entirely blue must not be worn… nor entirely yellow… nor entirely red… nor entirely madder-red…”
"One should not wear robes that are entirely black... nor entirely dyed with maha-raṅga... nor entirely dyed with maha-nāma...
nor with frayed borders... nor with long borders... nor with flower-patterned borders... nor with fruit-patterned borders... nor a bodice...
nor a tirīṭaka garment... nor a turban; whoever should wear such, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."—from this statement.

Cloth and other such items should not be worn. In this context, "cloth" (*potthaka*) refers to what is made of *makaci* fiber; likewise, fabrics made of *akkadussa*, *kadalidussa*, and *erakadussa* are also included under the category of cloth.
All garments that are entirely blue or otherwise dyed must be washed and then re-dyed before being worn.
If they cannot be washed, they should be made into bedspreads (*paccattharaṇa*). Or, in the case of a three-layered robe (*tipaṭṭacīvara*), [the middle layer...]
These are to be given. Their various descriptions follow the same method as that stated for sandals.
If robes with ten strips or long strips are obtained, they should be worn after cutting the strips. If a tunic is obtained, it is permissible to tear it apart, dye it, and then use it.
The same rule applies to a turban. However, *tirīṭaka* cloth is made from tree bark; it is permissible to use it to make a foot-wiping cloth.
58. “Monks, an illegitimate legal act (adhamma-kamma) must not be performed; whoever should perform one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Monks, I allow you to protest when an illegitimate legal act is being carried out. Because of this statement, an illegitimate legal act must not be performed, and one that is being carried out must be prevented.
And by those who prevent it, [it is said]: “Monks, I allow [you] with four or five...”

Because one may protest, two or three may reveal their view, and one may resolve, saying, "This does not please me," a monk should not attempt to stop [an illegal act] alone in a place where they cause trouble for the monk who tries to prevent it.
If there are four or five, he should stop it. However, if there are only two or three, [thinking] "this is an illegal act..."
“This is so, this is not acceptable to me”—in this way one’s own view should be disclosed in the presence of another.
If one is alone, one should resolve: “This is not acceptable to me. All of this has been stated for the sake of ensuring their safety. 59.
“Monks, a monk who has not been granted an opportunity should not be accused of an offense; whoever should so accuse him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”

When reproving by means of speech, the one reproving should first cause the other to grant leave by saying, "Venerable sir, please give me leave; I wish to speak to you," and only then should he reprove him.
Furthermore, the different types of intention (*adhippāya*) should be understood here. For this so-called intention is of seven kinds:

the intention to cause to fall away, the intention to abuse, the intention to perform a formal act (*kamma*), the intention to cause to emerge [from an offense], the intention to suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, and the intention to investigate.

The intention regarding a Dhamma discourse is of many kinds. In that regard, for one who does not grant an opportunity [to speak] regarding the first four intentions, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even if an opportunity has been granted, for one who accuses another in their presence with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense, there is a formal act involving the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*);

for one who accuses another with a groundless charge of a *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); and for one who accuses another with a groundless charge of failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), [there is an offense of wrong-doing].

It is a *dukkaṭa* offense; for one who speaks with the intention of reviling, it is a *pācittiya*. However, for one who speaks [of faults] in the absence [of the person], even if using all seven classes of offenses, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
likewise, for one who performs any of the seven kinds of formal acts (*kamma*) in the absence [of the person], it is only a *dukkaṭa*.
But according to the *Kurundi*, for one who says with the intention of restoration, "You have fallen into such-and-such an offense; you should make amends for it," [it is not an offense].
It is said: "There is no need for a formal motion (okāsakicca). Even for one who suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā, there is no formal motion;
however, the grounds for the suspension must be known [by the words]: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha."

For in this case, it is permissible to stop while the syllable *re* has not yet been passed; however, once the syllable *yya* is reached, it is no longer permissible. This same principle applies to the *pavāraṇā*.

Even for an investigator (*anuvijjaka*), when a matter has come before him, there is no formal announcement of the occasion if he speaks with the intention of investigating, saying, "This belongs to you.
Likewise, for a preacher of the Dhamma who, having sat upon the Dhamma-seat, says: "Whoever does this and that..."
There is no formal act of granting leave for one who teaches the Dhamma indiscriminately in such a manner as, "This bhikkhu is not a samaṇa," and so forth.
However, if one speaks specifically and restrictively, saying, "So-and-so and so-and-so are not samaṇas and not upāsakas," one must descend from the Dhamma-seat, confess the offense, and depart.
[The Buddha said: "Bhikkhus, [there is no offense] for pure bhikkhus who are without transgression."
"An opportunity must not be granted without cause or basis; whoever should grant one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
From this statement, it follows that an opportunity must not be granted to pure monks without cause or basis.
Furthermore, from the statement, "Monks, I allow you to grant an opportunity after weighing the individual," [one must consider]: "Does he speak of an actual offense, or one that is non-existent?"
Having investigated in this manner, the opportunity [to accept] should be made.

60. Because of the statement, "Monks, one must not squander what has been given out of faith; whoever should squander it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," that which is given out of faith must not be squandered.
Even when giving to kinsmen other than one's mother and father, [one must act with care].
One should indeed cause them to fall [into ruin], but if one's parents are established in sovereignty, they should be granted their wish; it must be given. 61.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not enter a village wearing only an inner and an upper robe; whoever should so enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one should not enter a village wearing only an inner and an upper robe.
62. "Monks, there are these five reasons for laying aside the outer robe (saṅghāṭī): one is ill, or there is a rainy-season agreement..."
"Or it may be that he has gone across a river, or he is staying in a dwelling secured by a bolt, or the kaṭhina has been spread.
These, monks, are the five conditions for the laying aside of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*).

Furthermore, according to this statement, one who is unable to go after having taken [the robe] is either ill, or there is some other reason such as the rainy-season agreement (*vassika-saṅketa*) and so forth; in such cases...
Having placed the *saṅghāṭi* robe in a monastery protected by a bolt, it is permissible to go out wearing only the inner and upper robes (*santaruttara*).
For in all these cases—being ill, during the rainy season, having made an appointment, crossing a river, or when the *kaṭhina* has not been spread—the protection of the bolt is the sole criterion;
it is permissible to go outside after depositing the robe in a protected monastery, but not in one that is unprotected. However, for a forest-dweller...
If the dwelling is not well-guarded, one should place the bowl inside a basket and set it down in well-concealed places such as hollows in rocks or hollows in trees before departing.
These same five conditions should also be understood to apply when setting down the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).
63. “Monks, surgical treatment or vaginal treatment must not be performed within two finger-breadths of the constriction.
Whoever should have it performed, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
Because of this statement, within the delimited area, by means of any instrument whatsoever—whether a knife, a needle, a thorn, a small sword, or a stone splinter—[one must not act].
One must not perform cutting, scraping, piercing, or scratching with the fingernail; all such acts constitute surgical treatment (*satthakamma*).
Furthermore, one must not perform vaginal compression with any skin or cloth;
all such acts constitute vaginal treatment (*vatthikamma*). And in this context, "two finger-breadths around the constriction" refers to...
This was said specifically with reference to surgical treatment (*satthakamma*); however, vaginal dilation (*vatthikamma*) is prohibited in the case of the narrow passage itself.
In that regard, it is permissible to apply caustic alkali or to bind [the area] with any kind of cord;

if it is cut by that means, it is a "good cut. Even in the case of the disease of testicular enlargement (*aṇḍavuḍḍhi*), surgical treatment is not permitted; therefore, [one should say]: "Having incised the testicle..."
One must not think, "I will remove the seeds and make it free from disease"; however, there is no prohibition against heating it with fire,
applying medicinal ointments, or using a medicinal-impregnated applicator-stick (*ādānavatti*) or bamboo tube inserted into the rectum,
by means of which one performs the alkaline treatment (*khārakamma*) or introduces oil.
64. “Monks, one who was formerly a barber must not carry about a barber’s kit; whoever should so carry it commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because of this statement, it is not permitted for one who was formerly a barber to take up and carry about a barber’s kit;
however, it is permitted to have one’s hair cut by someone else’s kit. If he cuts it while taking wages, [he commits an offense].

It is not permissible. It is permissible for one who has never had their hair shaved before to have it done; or, having taken either that [comb] or another, it is also permissible to shave the hair. 65.
"Monks, seeds belonging to the Saṅgha that have been planted in land belonging to an individual should be used after giving a portion [to the owner]."
"Seeds belonging to an individual that have been planted on land belonging to the Saṅgha should be used after giving a portion," according to this statement,
when seeds belonging to the Saṅgha are planted on land belonging to an individual, or when seeds belonging to an individual are planted on land belonging to the Saṅgha,
one should use them after giving a tenth part. This, it is said, was the ancient custom in Jambudīpa.
Therefore, having divided it into ten portions, one portion should be given to the owners of the land.
66. “Monks, there are wilderness roads that are waterless, lacking food, and not easy to travel without provisions.
Monks, I allow you to seek out provisions: rice for one who needs rice, mung beans...”

“Mung beans for one who needs mung beans, rice for one who needs rice, salt for one who needs salt, sugar for one who needs sugar, oil for one who needs oil, and ghee for one who needs ghee”—according to this statement, it is proper for one crossing such a wilderness to seek out provisions. But how should they be sought?
If some give them of their own accord once they have learned [of the need], that is good.
If no food is given, it should be sought from a place where one is invited by relatives, or through the practice of wandering for alms.
If it is not obtained in that way, it may be accepted even by requesting it from a place where one is not invited by non-relatives.
On a journey to be completed in a single day, one should seek enough for a single meal. On a long journey, one should seek enough to cross the wilderness.
That much should be sought. 67.
“Monks, whatever I have not prohibited by saying, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms with what is unallowable and obstructs what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
Whatever, monks, I have said, ‘This is not allowable’...”
If that which has not been prohibited conforms to what is allowable, excludes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.
Monks, if that which has not been permitted by me as "this is allowable" conforms to what is unallowable and excludes what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
Monks, if that which has not been permitted by me as "this is allowable"...

“If that conforms to what is allowable (*kappiya*) and excludes what is unallowable (*akappiya*), then that is permissible for you”—thus did the Blessed One speak these four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*) to the monks for the purpose of grasping the method.
Therein, the Elder Theras who compiled the Dhamma, having taken up the Sutta and scrutinized it, saw this:
“Except for the juice of grain-fruits,” [referring to] the seven juices of grain, “after the meal...”

These are prohibited, as it is said, "it is not allowable. The nine great fruits—namely, the palm, coconut, plantain, jackfruit, bottle gourd, pumpkin, cucumber, *tipusa*, and *eḷāluka*—as well as all other non-cereal vegetables, fall under the category of grain (*dhaññagatika*). Although these are not specifically prohibited, they conform to what is unallowable;
therefore, they are not allowable after the meal. Eight drinks have been permitted.
The remaining minor fruit drinks—such as those made from vetta, tintiṇika, mātuluṅga, kapittha, kosamba, karamanda, and so forth—belong to the same category as the eight allowable drinks.
Although these have not been specifically permitted, they conform to what is allowable; therefore, they are permissible.

For it is stated in the *Kurundi*: "Apart from the juice of grain-fruit which does not conform [to the rules], there is no other fruit drink that is impermissible; all such drinks are indeed 'for the duration of a watch' (yāmakālika)."
The Blessed One authorized six types of robes, saying: "Monks, I allow you six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and jute.
The Elders who compiled the Dhamma further authorized another six types that are compatible with those:
dukūla, pattuṇṇa, cīnapaṭṭa, somārapaṭṭa, those produced by supernormal power, and those given by deities.
In this context, *pattuṇṇa* refers to cloth produced by insects in the Pattuṇṇa country. Two types of *paṭa* are mentioned by way of their names alone.
Three types are suitable for silk (*koseyya*), *dukūla* for linen (*sāṇa*), and the other two for cotton (*kappāsika*), or they may be suitable for all of them.
After the Blessed One had rejected eleven kinds of bowls, he authorized two: the iron bowl and the clay bowl.
A copper bowl, an earthenware bowl, and a bronze or iron bowl are the corresponding types for those [three]. The Blessed One permitted three kinds of water-vessels (*tumba*):
a metal vessel, a wooden vessel, and a fruit-vessel. A water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a golden one, and a water-vessel made of a gourd are the corresponding types for those very same vessels.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: "These are the corresponding types for drinking cups and water-cups."
It has been stated. Two types of waistbands (*kāyabandhana*) were permitted: the *paṭṭikā* and the *sūkaranta*.
Waistbands made of cloth strips or rope are likewise suitable for those two. Three types of umbrellas were permitted: the white umbrella, the palm-leaf umbrella, and the leaf umbrella.
A single-leaf umbrella is likewise suitable for those three. Following this method, the Canon (*pāḷi*)...

Without relying solely on the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), a master of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) should also understand other matters that are in accordance with what is permissible and what is impermissible.

68. Furthermore, a person who is a master of the Vinaya obtains five benefits rooted in the study of the Vinaya, six benefits, seven benefits, eight benefits, nine benefits, ten benefits, and eleven benefits. What are the five benefits?
What does he obtain? His own protection of the aggregate of virtue and so forth. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five advantages for a person who is an expert in the Vinaya: his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected;
he is a refuge for those overcome by remorse; he speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha; [his adversaries...]
“He rebukes one who is rightly rebuked according to the Dhamma; he is practicing for the stability of the true Dhamma.
How is his own aggregate of virtue well-guarded and well-protected? Here, a certain bhikkhu, when committing an offense, commits it in six ways:
through lack of shame, through ignorance, through being overcome by remorse, or through the perception of what is unallowable as allowable.
Perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, or through forgetfulness. How does one incur it through lack of shame?
One who knows full well that something is unallowable yet crushes it and transgresses. And this has been said:
"He intentionally commits an offense; he conceals his offense."
“He goes upon a wrong path; such a person is called one devoid of shame.
How does one fall into [an offense] through ignorance? For a person who is ignorant is dull and deluded;

not knowing what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, he does what should not be done and fails in what should be done. Thus one falls through ignorance. How [does one fall] through being overcome by remorse?
Does he incur [an offense]? When remorse has arisen concerning what is permissible and what is impermissible, if one asks a master of the Vinaya and it is found to be permissible, it may be done;
if it is impermissible, it should not be done. Yet this person, crushing [the matter] with the thought "it is allowable," simply transgresses.
Thus, he incurs [an offense] through being overcome by remorse.
How does one incur an offense through the perception of what is allowable regarding what is unallowable?
One eats the flesh of a raw fish thinking it is "pig's meat"; one eats the flesh of a leopard thinking it is "deer meat"; one eats unallowable food thinking it is "allowable food";
one eats at the improper time with the perception that it is the proper time; one drinks an unallowable beverage thinking it is "allowable beverage. Thus, regarding what is unallowable...
One commits an offense through the perception that what is permissible is impermissible. How does one commit an offense through the perception that what is permissible is impermissible?
One eats pork thinking it is "bear meat"; one eats deer meat thinking it is "leopard meat"; one eats permissible food thinking it is "impermissible food";
one eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time; one drinks a permissible beverage thinking it is "an impermissible beverage."

Thus one incurs an offense through the perception of what is improper regarding what is proper. How does one incur an offense through forgetfulness? One incurs an offense through forgetfulness on account of sleeping together, being separated from one’s robe, [the rules for] medicine, and the transgression of the time limit for robes.
In this way, a certain monk incurs an offense in these six ways.
However, one who is a bearer of the Vinaya does not incur an offense in these six ways. How does one avoid incurring an offense through modesty?
For thus, even while guarding against the reproach of others—“See, sirs! This man, though knowing what is allowable and what is not, transgresses the formal rule”—he does not incur [the offense].

Being thus possessed of shame, he does not incur it; and even if he should inadvertently commit one, having confessed it as a fault leading to confession (*desanāgāminī*), and having emerged from it by means of that which leads to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*), he establishes himself in the state of purity. Then—
“He does not intentionally commit an offense; he does not conceal an offense;
and he does not go upon a wrong path—it is such a person who is called ‘one possessed of moral shame.
Thus, he is indeed established in this state of moral shame.
How does one not fall into error through knowledge? For he knows what is allowable and what is unallowable;
therefore, he performs only what is allowable and does not perform what is unallowable. Thus, one does not fall into error through knowledge.

How does one not fall into error through being free from remorse? When remorse arises concerning what is allowable or unallowable, one examines the basis [of the action], the matrix, the word-commentary, and the intermediate offense.
Having looked for what is non-offensive, if it is allowable, he does it; if it is unallowable, he does not do it. Thus, by being free from remorse, he does not fall into an offense.
How does he avoid falling into an offense through such things as perceiving what is unallowable as allowable? For he knows what is allowable and what is unallowable;
therefore, he does not perceive what is unallowable as allowable, nor does he perceive what is allowable as unallowable. His [understanding] is well-established.
When this exists, he resolves what should be resolved and designates what should be designated.
Thus, by these six modes, he does not commit an offense. Not committing an offense, he possesses unbroken virtue and pure virtue.
In this way, his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected.

How is he a refuge for those overcome by remorse? Monks who have arisen with remorse in other kingdoms or other provinces, hearing that "a master of the Vinaya dwells in such-and-such a monastery," come into his presence from afar and ask about their remorse.
He examines the basis of the action performed by them and [explains] the distinctions of offense and non-offense, heavy and light, and so forth.
Having observed [the case], he causes one who is fit for instruction to receive instruction; having caused one who is fit for ordination to be ordained, he establishes them in purity.
In this way, he is a refuge for those overcome by remorse.
"He speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha" means that fear arises for one who does not master the Vinaya when speaking in the midst of the Saṅgha.
He falls into timidity; that does not happen for one who holds the Vinaya. Why? Because he speaks having known:
"In speaking thus there is fault; in speaking thus there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "he thoroughly refutes adversaries with the Dhamma," here "adversaries" are of two kinds.

There are those who are enemies of oneself and those who are enemies of the Teaching. In this regard, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, along with Vaḍḍha the Licchavi, charged [the Venerable Sāriputta] with a groundless matter concerning an offense involving the ultimate defeat; these are called "enemies of oneself.

Furthermore, all others who are immoral and of evil character are also enemies of oneself. However, those with perverted views—such as the monk Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, the Vesālika, and the Vajjiputtaka—are enemies of the Teaching.
Those who hold views such as the denial of the Buddha’s teachings, ignorance, doubt, and the transcendence of doubt, as well as the Mahāsaṅghikas and others,
are called "enemies of the Dispensation" because they have embraced what is not the Buddha’s teaching while claiming it to be "the Buddha’s teaching.

He thoroughly refutes them all by means of the true Dhamma, with logical reasons and authoritative statements, so that they are well-subdued and unable to establish that which is contrary to the Dhamma.

Regarding the phrase "he is practicing for the preservation of the true Dhamma," here the true Dhamma is threefold, by way of the Dhamma as scripture (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*).
Among these, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*) is called the true Dhamma as scripture.
The thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), the fourteen rules of conduct in the *Khandhaka*, and the eighty-two major rules—this is called the true Dhamma as practice. The four paths...
And the four fruits—this is what is called the True Dhamma of realization (*adhigama-saddhamma*).

Regarding this, some elders say, based on the Sutta: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and laid down by me for you shall be your teacher after my passing," that "the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) is the root of the Dispensation. Some elders...
Having stated with this sutta, “Subhadda, if these monks were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants,” they said, “The practice is the root of the Dispensation;
as long as five monks who have entered upon the right practice exist, so long does the Dispensation endure.
However, the other elders [said]: “When the learning has disappeared, even for one who practices well...”
Having said, "There will be no realization of the Dhamma," they spoke thus:

"Even if five bhikkhus are guardians of the four pārājika rules, they shall ordain faithful sons of good family in the border regions, and having completed a quorum of ten with that group, they will perform the full ordination in the Middle Country; by this means, a Saṅgha of twenty members..."
Having fulfilled [the training] themselves and performed the act of clearing away obscurations for others as well, they will cause the Dispensation to reach growth and increase.
In this way, this bearer of the Vinaya is one who practices for the long endurance of the Triple Gem in its three aspects.
Thus, it should be understood that this bearer of the Vinaya first obtains these five benefits.

What six benefits does he obtain? He is one under whose authority there are the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), going forth (pabbajjā), and full ordination (upasampadā);
he gives dependence (nissaya) and causes a novice (sāmaṇera) to attend upon him. Furthermore, there are these:

the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the Uposatha on the fifteenth, the Uposatha for concord (sāmaggi-uposatha), the Uposatha in the Saṅgha, the Uposatha in a group (gaṇa), the Uposatha for an individual (puggala), the recitation of the Suttas (suttuddesa), and the declaration of purity (pārisuddhi).
The Uposatha of formal resolution consists of nine types of Uposatha; all of these depend upon those who hold the Vinaya.

Furthermore, there are nine types of Pavāraṇā: the fourteenth-day [Pavāraṇā], the fifteenth-day [Pavāraṇā], the Pavāraṇā by a complete assembly, the Pavāraṇā before the Saṅgha, the Pavāraṇā before a group, the Pavāraṇā before an individual, the threefold recitation Pavāraṇā, the twofold recitation Pavāraṇā, and the Pavāraṇā for those of the same year of seniority—all of these also depend upon those who hold the Vinaya.
In this way, they belong to him; he is their master.

Furthermore, regarding these four formal acts of the Saṅgha—the act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*), the act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), the act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and the act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—and also the going forth and full ordination of sons of good family by means of acting as a preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
And these [duties] must be performed; they too depend solely upon one who is a holder of the Vinaya. For no one else, even if they are a holder of two Piṭakas, is permitted to act in this way.
Only he gives formal dependence (*nissaya*) and provides a novice (*sāmaṇera*) with attendance; no one else is permitted to give formal dependence, nor to provide a novice with attendance.
Therefore it was said: "Monks, one person should not provide attendance for two novices."
Having rejected [the proposal] with the words, "Whoever should attend to them, there is an offense of wrong-doing," he then granted permission again:

"Monks, I allow a competent monk to attend to two novices; or as many as he is able to exhort and instruct, so many may he attend to. Thus, the attendance upon novices was permitted only for one who is competent.
However, one who desires to have a novice ordained may receive the going-forth (upajjhā) in the presence of a master of the Vinaya and is permitted to undertake the duties of service.
In this context, the granting of dependence (nissaya) and the attendance upon the novice constitute a single factor.
Thus, with one of these six benefits, there are six including the previous five; with two, seven; with three...

"Together with eight, together with four nine, together with five ten, and together with all these eleven"—thus it should be understood that a person who is a master of the Vinaya obtains five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven benefits.
Such is the great benefit; always skillfulness in the Vinaya.
"One who makes a formal request here should apply himself to it again and again.
Thus ends the discussion on miscellaneous rulings in the *Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha*.
This compendium of Vinaya exegesis independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*) is now completed. Concluding Remarks:
At the request of King Parakkamabāhu, I, having been thus commissioned...
In this delightful place, adorned with hundreds of palaces, filled with various groves of trees,
a dwelling for those who delight in meditation,
built by him alone out of a desire to establish the true Dhamma and to illuminate the Dispensation;
In this Jeta Grove, endowed with cool water, he composed this *Vinayasaṅgaha*,
the essence [of the Vinaya], for the benefit of practitioners.
Whatever merit has been accomplished by this work, and whatever other merit has been performed by me—
By this meritorious deed, in his second existence,
rejoicing in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and delighting in the virtues of moral conduct and behavior,
unattached to the five sensual pleasures, he attained the first fruit [of the path].
In his final existence, having seen the bull among sages, Maitreya— the supreme person in the world,
the protector who delights in the welfare of all beings—
and having heard the teaching of the True Dharma from that wise one, he...
"Having attained the supreme fruit, may I bring glory to the teaching of the Jina.
The *Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā* is completed.
